By enforcing favorable helix-capping propensities and amphiphilic periodicity at these locations, the caps bias the conformational ensemble toward states that preserve correct ER insertion (in yeast), improve soluble holoenzyme folding (in E. coli truncations), and enhance productive CPR docking on the proximal face. This structural stabilization increases the fraction of correctly folded, heme-loaded CYP that is productively coupled to NAD(P)H flux, thereby raising effective catalytic turnover and phenolics-to-flavonoids conversion without altering intrinsic active-site chemistry. Directed evolution constrained to cap modules and a minimal, electrostatically justified CPR-interface residue set will selectively amplify variants with improved folding“coupling synergy rather than uncoupled expression gains, overcoming a central translational bottleneck in microbial flavonoid biosynthesis.
Plan: Step 1: Structural definition of cap targets and topology constraints.
1.1 Target enzyme: select a well-characterized flavonoid hydroxylase (e.g., CYP75B1/F3'H or CYP93B) with low activity in yeast and E. coli. Generate AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold-Multimer models of CYP“CPR complexes, cross-referenced to solved plant CYP structures (e.g., CYP97A3, CYP76AH1) to map conserved topology.
1.2 N-cap site: engineer immediately downstream of the N-terminal signal-anchor/A-helix junction. In yeast, retain residues 1“25 (signal-anchor, type II ER orientation) and place cap at residues ~26“40 stabilizing the A-helix entrance. In E. coli, use a soluble ΔTM truncation (Δ1“25) and place the N-cap at the new N-terminus to nucleate A-helix formation and prevent aggregation.
1.3 C-cap site: engineer residues ~480“500 (numbering CYP-dependent), flanking the C-terminal end of the L-helix and adjacent to the conserved heme-binding loop (FGxGPR/CxG). Caps are designed to stabilize helix termination without perturbing the axial cysteine loop or heme ligation.

Step 2: Rational cap module design.
2.1 Use position-specific helix-capping propensities (N1“N6, C1“C6) to design 8 N-cap and 8 C-cap modules (6“12 aa each) with controlled polarity and hydrophobic periodicity. N-caps enriched in Asn/Gln/Ser/Thr at N1“N3 for hydrogen bonding; C-caps enriched in Gly/Asn/His to satisfy backbone unsatisfied H-bonds while avoiding steric clash with the heme loop.
2.2 Exclude charged residues predicted (by AF2-Multimer electrostatics) to interfere with CPR docking or ER membrane proximity.

Step 3: Minimal CPR-interface micro-library.
3.1 Based on docking models and literature hotspots, diversify only 5“6 proximal-face residues (e.g., basic residues on the B′“C loop and proximal K-helix surface known to contact CPR FMN domain). Each position limited to 2“3 amino acids (charge-conserving substitutions).
3.2 Resulting library size: 8 (N-cap) × 8 (C-cap) × ~64 interface variants ≈ 4,096 variants, fully coverable.

Step 4: Library construction and coverage.
4.1 Assemble factorial libraries by Golden Gate cloning with unique 12-bp DNA barcodes.
4.2 Transformation targets: ≥1 × 10^6 yeast transformants or ≥5 × 10^5 E. coli transformants to ensure >100× coverage.
4.3 Deep sequencing pre- and post-selection to quantify variant frequencies; use negative binomial models to call enriched hits.

Step 5: High-throughput folding/function proxy (host-appropriate).
5.1 Primary screen: activity-linked flavonoid biosensor (e.g., FdeR- or UGT-coupled transcriptional sensor) responding to hydroxylated flavonoid product, ensuring signal only arises from catalytically competent CYP.
5.2 Secondary folding calibration: subset validation by CO-difference spectroscopy (450 nm peak), heme staining, and targeted proteomics to correlate biosensor output with holoenzyme abundance.
5.3 Optional coupling reporter: split-CPR/P450 complementation assay where productive docking reconstitutes a fluorescent or luminescent signal, calibrated against NADPH consumption and LC-MS product formation.

Step 6: Decision tree and iteration.
6.1 Normalize product formation to CYP abundance to separate expression effects from coupling efficiency.
6.2 Quantify coupling efficiency (product/NADPH) and ROS/peroxide shunt markers.
6.3 Only after convergence on high-expression/high-coupling cap variants introduce limited second-shell active-site diversity to modulate regioselectivity.

Step 7: Validation and generalization.
7.1 Biophysical assays: DSF, protease sensitivity, membrane fractionation, SPR/BLI for CPR binding kinetics.
7.2 Transfer best-performing cap modules into 2“3 additional flavonoid/phenolics CYPs to test portability across the family.
Feasibility: This proposal directly addresses reviewer concerns by anchoring cap engineering to explicitly defined CYP structural elements (A-helix junction and C-terminal L-helix/heme-loop boundary) while respecting host-dependent topology constraints (ER signal-anchor in yeast; soluble truncation in E. coli). The folding/function proxy is not an abstract reporter but an activity-linked flavonoid biosensor calibrated against CO-difference spectroscopy and LC-MS, ensuring selection for catalytically competent holoenzyme rather than mere expression. Library size is explicitly bounded (~4,000 variants) with justified restriction of CPR-interface residues based on electrostatic docking models and known proximal-face hotspots, making full coverage statistically achievable. The decision tree—normalizing product to CYP abundance and explicitly measuring coupling efficiency—cleanly separates gains from folding versus electron-transfer coupling before any active-site diversification. Mechanistically, the approach is grounded in established helix-capping propensity rules and prior consensus-based stabilization of repeat proteins, now transferred to CYP terminal helices that gate membrane anchoring, reductase docking, and active-site access. By constraining evolution to this mechanistically privileged space, the strategy increases the fraction of functional variants, reduces epistatic noise, and offers a generalizable solution to a long-standing bottleneck in microbial deployment of plant P450s.

Hypothesis: Temperature-sensitive (ts) phenotypes of Drosophila Enhancer of zeste [E(z)] arise from failure of one of two mechanistically distinguishable modules under restrictive temperature: (A) destabilization of PRC2-core assembly and/or catalytic competence (E(z)“Su(z)12“Esc/EED interfaces that support H3K27 methyltransferase activity), or (B) destabilization of chromatin-recruitment coupling (interfaces that connect PRC2 occupancy at Polycomb response elements (PREs) to PRC1-associated factors including Polyhomeotic and Zeste). The prior observation that Zeste chromatin binding persists while other Polycomb proteins dissociate at non-permissive temperatures is most parsimoniously explained by a PRC2-centered defect that secondarily disrupts PRC1/Polyhomeotic occupancy rather than a direct E(z)“Zeste binding loss. Therefore, the proposal will first map and experimentally validate the temperature-liable E(z) interaction surface(s) using orthogonal physical and functional evidence, explicitly testing PRC2-core partners (Su(z)12, Esc/EED) as competing hypotheses. Only after identifying a causal interface will we perform phylogenetically informed, structure- and energetics-guided micro-engineering (ancestral/ortholog residue reversion plus minimal patch substitutions) designed to increase interface ΔG stability (negative ΔΔG) without altering expression kinetics or catalytic mechanism. We hypothesize that restricting edits to evolutionarily constrained contact patches (rather than domain swaps) will decouple thermal sensitivity from repression by restoring PRC2 occupancy and H3K27me3 deposition at PRE-controlled loci at restrictive temperature while preserving normal developmental timing and transcriptional programs at permissive temperature.
Plan: Step 0: System definition, alleles, and target loci panel (pre-registered).
0.1 Select a well-characterized ts E(z) allele (or recreate the causative amino-acid substitution(s) by CRISPR if necessary) in an otherwise isogenic D. melanogaster background; generate matched controls: WT E(z), catalytic-dead E(z) (SET-domain point mutant) and PRC2-core disruption control (known Su(z)12/Esc-binding mutant if available).
0.2 Predefine a panel of 8“12 canonical PRE-regulated targets spanning strong/weak Polycomb domains (e.g., BX-C/Hox PRE-associated loci, and additional validated PRE targets), plus 3“4 non-PRE negative-control loci. Pre-register primary endpoints: (i) PRC2 occupancy at PREs, (ii) H3K27me3 levels, (iii) target gene expression, (iv) developmental phenotype rescue.

Step 1: Mechanistic mapping of the ts failure—distinguish PRC2-core assembly/catalysis vs recruitment-coupling.
1.1 Time-resolved temperature-shift design: rear staged larvae at permissive temperature, then shift to restrictive temperature and sample at 0, 1, 4, 12, and 24 hours post-shift to separate immediate biochemical failure from downstream transcriptional feedback.
1.2 Quantify PRC2-core integrity and partner dependence under temperature shift.
- Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) of endogenous-tagged E(z) (3xFLAG or GFP knock-in) followed by targeted Westerns and quantitative mass spectrometry (TMT or DIA) for Su(z)12, Esc/EED, Nurf55, Caf1, and PRC1-associated components (Pc, Psc/Su(z)2, Polyhomeotic).
- Execute co-IP with truncation constructs in S2 cells (parallel system) to map interaction regions: N-terminus, SANT domains, CXC region, SET domain. Use temperature incubations (permissive vs restrictive) prior to lysis to capture temperature-dependent complex stability.
1.3 Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) to localize contact patches.
- Apply lysine-reactive crosslinker DSSO (MS-cleavable; ~10.1 Å spacer) on native nuclear extracts at both temperatures.
- Enrich E(z)-containing complexes via affinity pull-down, run LC“MS/MS, and identify differential crosslinks (present at permissive, lost at restrictive) to pinpoint interfaces that specifically fail in ts conditions.
- Prioritize crosslinks connecting E(z) to Su(z)12/Esc (core) versus links to PRC1-associated proteins.
1.4 Targeted alanine scanning / contact-patch mutagenesis to validate causality.
- From XL-MS and co-IP truncation data, define 2“3 candidate E(z) contact patches (8“20 residues each) and perform focused alanine scanning (or charge reversal) in S2 cells to test which patch recapitulates temperature-dependent loss of PRC2 assembly or chromatin association.
- Readouts: (i) partner pull-down efficiency (quantified), (ii) in vitro methyltransferase activity on recombinant nucleosomes (H3K27me1/2/3 by Western or MS), (iii) thermal shift/denaturation proxy for complex stability (nanoDSF on purified minimal complexes if feasible).
Decision gate #1 (go/no-go): Proceed to evolutionary engineering only if at least one E(z) patch shows temperature-dependent reduction in (a) PRC2-core association and/or (b) catalytic activity and this correlates with in vivo occupancy/mark loss (Step 2). If not, pivot to testing ts effects on E(z) global stability/abundance as primary mechanism.

Step 2: Replace “live-imaging-compatible ChIP-seq” with a concrete temperature-shift chromatin profiling pipeline.
2.1 CUT&Tag (primary) and CUT&RUN (orthogonal) profiling with time resolution.
- Perform CUT&Tag for: E(z) (tag antibody), Su(z)12, and H3K27me3 at defined timepoints post temperature shift.
- Use pA“Tn5 tethered transposase for CUT&Tag; include E. coli DNA spike-in or exogenous chromatin (e.g., D. virilis) for normalization across temperatures.
- Libraries: 2 biological replicates per condition; depth sufficient for confident PRE peak quantification.
2.2 Transcript output: targeted RT“qPCR panel + RNA-seq (subset).
- Quantify expression changes of predefined PRE targets by RT“qPCR across timepoints; perform RNA-seq at 0, 4, 24 h for global off-target assessment and to ensure rescue is not achieved via compensatory pathways.
2.3 Polytene chromosome immunostaining as spatial validation (secondary).
- Immunostain polytene chromosomes for Pc/Polyhomeotic/Zeste and E(z)/Su(z)12 at permissive vs restrictive temperature; use this as a localization sanity check rather than primary mechanism proof.

Step 3: Quantitative controls for protein abundance and intrinsic stability (distinguish interface stabilization from expression effects).
3.1 Thermal proteome profiling (TPP) / cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) in larvae or S2 cells.
- Measure temperature-dependent solubility/aggregation of E(z) (WT vs ts) and key partners; identify whether ts primarily shifts the melting/aggregation profile of E(z) globally or selectively affects complexed fraction.
3.2 Cycloheximide chase and proteasome dependence.
- Perform cycloheximide chase at permissive and restrictive temperatures to estimate E(z) half-life; include MG132 (where feasible in cell culture) to test proteasome-mediated degradation.
3.3 Quantify nuclear localization.
- Endogenous tag imaging (fixed tissue) or biochemical fractionation (cytosol/nucleus/chromatin) to ensure engineered variants do not rescue by altering localization rather than interface energetics.

Step 4: Phylogenetically informed, energetics-guided micro-engineering (minimal edits; no broad domain swaps).
4.1 Phylogenetic dataset and ancestral reconstruction constrained to validated interface.
- Build maximum-likelihood phylogenies for E(z) across ~15“20 Drosophila species; incorporate Asset 1 insights on rate heterogeneity to annotate conserved vs accelerated branches.
- Perform ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) specifically for residues within the validated contact patch(es) and immediate structural neighborhood (±10 residues).
4.2 Pre-registered engineering decision rule linking phylogeny to predicted ΔΔG.
- Candidate substitutions must satisfy: (i) present in ≥1 extant ortholog and/or inferred with high posterior probability in ASR at key nodes, (ii) not predicted to disrupt catalytic motifs (if SET/CXC vicinity), (iii) predicted to stabilize the experimentally validated interface with ΔΔG ≤ −0.5 kcal/mol (Rosetta interface ΔΔG or FoldX) and/or increase predicted local secondary structure propensity without increasing disorder.
- Prioritize 6“10 single mutants and 3“4 combinatorial “patch” mutants (2“4 substitutions) rather than saturation mutagenesis initially.
4.3 Computational benchmarking tied to experimental constraints.
- Do not rely solely on AlphaFold for complex inference; instead, model only the local interface using: (i) known PRC2 structural templates (where available) plus (ii) XL-MS distance restraints to filter/score models. Use AF2-multimer only as a hypothesis generator, not as decisive evidence.

Step 5: In vivo genome editing and functional validation.
5.1 CRISPR precise editing.
- Introduce prioritized substitutions into the endogenous E(z) locus in the ts background (or into WT with ts mutation present), preserving regulatory regions to avoid expression artifacts. Validate by sequencing and confirm protein levels by quantitative Western.
5.2 Functional endpoints (must demonstrate true decoupling of thermal sensitivity from repression).
- Primary: restoration of E(z)/Su(z)12 occupancy (CUT&Tag), restoration of H3K27me3 at PREs (CUT&Tag), and repression of PRE targets (RT“qPCR/RNA-seq) at restrictive temperature.
- Secondary: developmental rescue metrics (viability to adult, homeotic transformation scoring, fertility) under restrictive temperature. Include permissive-temperature phenotyping to exclude neomorphic effects.
5.3 Mechanistic confirmation.
- Repeat co-IP and (if feasible) XL-MS on the best-rescued engineered variant to verify that the same interface that failed in ts is physically stabilized.
Decision gate #2 (scale-up): Only if ≥1 engineered variant rescues occupancy + H3K27me3 + expression with minimal permissive-temperature perturbation will we expand to limited site-saturation mutagenesis within the validated patch to map the stability“function landscape.

Risk mitigation and alternatives.
- If ts phenotype is driven by global E(z) instability (TPP/CETSA indicates broad destabilization), pivot to engineering based on overall fold stabilization (surface charge optimization, helix-capping) but still constrained by phylogenetic plausibility and preserving catalytic activity.
- If recruitment failure is primarily PRE/PRC1-coupling rather than PRC2-core, extend mapping to PRC1-mediated chromatin retention factors and test whether restoring H3K27me3 alone suffices for Pc/Polyhomeotic re-binding under heat stress.
Feasibility: 1) Mechanistic plausibility is explicitly tested rather than assumed. The plan incorporates competing hypotheses flagged by reviewers: PRC2-core failure (E(z)“Su(z)12“Esc/EED) versus indirect PRC1/Zeste/Polyhomeotic effects. Co-IP with truncations, XL-MS, and focused alanine scanning provide orthogonal evidence to localize the causal temperature-liable interface before any evolutionary engineering.

2) Structural claims are benchmarked with experimental constraints. Instead of overreliance on AlphaFold for multi-protein/disordered assemblies, the proposal uses XL-MS distance restraints and interaction-loss signatures across temperatures to validate/triangulate contact patches. Computational ΔΔG is used as a decision tool only after interface mapping, and only within local patches.

3) Chromatin profiling is defined and standard. Time-resolved CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN replaces the ambiguous “live-imaging-compatible ChIP-seq,” with spike-in normalization, explicit targets (E(z), Su(z)12, H3K27me3), and prespecified sampling intervals post temperature shift. This directly measures occupancy and catalytic output.

4) Engineering minimizes pleiotropy by avoiding domain swaps and controlling expression. Endogenous-locus CRISPR edits preserve regulatory context, while TPP/CETSA, cycloheximide chase, and fractionation control for protein abundance/localization artifacts. This directly addresses the concern that “rescue” could reflect altered expression kinetics rather than interface stabilization.

5) Functional rescue is quantified at molecular and organismal levels. Rescue criteria include restoration of H3K27me3, PRC2 occupancy, PRE target repression, and developmental phenotypes. This ensures the engineered variants truly decouple temperature sensitivity from repression function rather than shifting the repression mechanism.

6) The evolutionary component is tightly constrained and testable. Using Asset 1’s rate heterogeneity logic, ASR is applied only to validated interfaces, and candidate substitutions are selected by a preregistered rule linking phylogenetic plausibility to predicted stabilizing ΔΔG. A small prioritized mutant set is tested before any saturation mutagenesis, reducing technical overreach while preserving the proposal’s conceptual innovation.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that an SH3-domain designer binding module can be converted into an ultra-stable, genetically encoded ELISA reagent by (i) preserving the native SH3 beta-barrel fold, while (ii) selectively constraining only the ligand-binding RT and/or n-Src loops using a cyclotide-inspired cystine-knot “exoloop” graft plus backbone cyclization. Mechanistically, the construct is designed so that the SH3 core secondary-structure framework (beta-strands and hydrophobic core) remains unchanged, while the engineered proline-rich“binding loops are rigidified by (a) a defined N“C backbone cyclization junction placed in a solvent-exposed terminal extension (not within the SH3 beta-barrel) and (b) two to three engineered disulfide bonds arranged in a cyclotide-like topology that mechanically limits loop conformational entropy without distorting the binding geometry. This architecture is expected to reduce the conformational ensemble of the binding loops (lower loop RMSD and reduced entropic penalty upon binding), increasing apparent affinity and, more importantly for diagnostics, increasing functional stability under heat/proteases/pH extremes. Maltose-binding protein (MBP) is used as an expression and immobilization handle (amylose affinity and orientation), while oxidative folding and cyclization are achieved via a specified periplasmic/in-vitro redox route that directly addresses disulfide and cyclization feasibility. Performance claims versus antibodies will be tested only under format-matched ELISA conditions (same antigen, valency, matrices), isolating the contributions of cyclization, disulfide constraint, and MBP immobilization with predefined go/no-go criteria.
Plan: Step 0 — Select target/assay context and define format-matched ELISA benchmark
0.1 Target: choose a clinically relevant proline-rich epitope presented as (a) a synthetic peptide with a terminal biotin and (b) the same sequence embedded in a carrier protein (e.g., BSA fusion) to mimic epitope context; define intended ELISA role (capture reagent on plate; detection via anti-tag HRP) and keep this role identical for antibodies and engineered binders.
0.2 Benchmark antibodies: select one monoclonal antibody that recognizes the same peptide/protein context (or generate a peptide-directed monoclonal if available) and run it in the same capture format (matched coating density and detection chemistry).
0.3 Matrices: predefine test diluents: PBS-T + 1% BSA; 10% human serum; 10% human plasma; and a “dirty matrix” (e.g., 1 mg/mL cell lysate protein) to quantify non-specific binding.

Step 1 — Replace “embed SH3 into cyclotide” with a precedented, fold-preserving architecture
1.1 Base scaffold: select a well-characterized SH3 domain with solved structure and known tolerance to loop engineering (e.g., Abl-SH3 or Src-SH3 family), and a proline-rich ligand-binding mode (PxxP).
1.2 Architecture: engineer an SH3 core flanked by short N- and C-terminal solvent-exposed tails (5“12 aa each) that serve exclusively as the N“C ligation/cyclization junction (“terminal loop”), leaving the SH3 beta-barrel sequence intact.
1.3 Cyclotide-inspired constraint: introduce a compact cystine-knot-like “exoloop” module appended to (or replacing a short segment within) the RT loop and/or n-Src loop, designed as a disulfide-rich mini-domain that is topologically connected to the SH3 loop region via two peptide linkers. The cysteine positions are chosen so disulfides bridge within the exoloop and between exoloop and loop-adjacent positions, constraining loop motion while avoiding strand-disrupting cysteine insertions in the SH3 beta-strands.
1.4 Disulfide plan: design 2“3 disulfides total:
  - DS1/DS2 form a cyclotide-like knot inside the exoloop (cysteine spacing consistent with known cyclotide motifs).
  - Optional DS3 is a “staple” between two positions flanking the RT loop (or RT-to-n-Src) to reduce loop flexibility; staple sites are selected based on Cβ“Cβ distance targets (4.5“6.5 Å for disulfide feasibility) in the SH3 structure.

Step 2 — Define explicit cyclization chemistry and oxidative folding route (risk-mitigated)
2.1 Primary cyclization strategy (genetic): intein-mediated expressed protein ligation (EPL) for backbone cyclization.
  - Construct: MBP“TEVsite“SH3(terminal-tail)“Intein“Chitin-binding domain (CBD), with an engineered N-terminal cysteine revealed after TEV cleavage (or a self-cleaving intein design that generates a C-terminal thioester).
  - Reaction: generate C-terminal thioester on SH3, then intramolecular ligation with N-terminal cysteine to yield N“C backbone-cyclized SH3-tail ring.
2.2 Secondary cyclization fallback (enzymatic): sortase A (LPXTG/oligoglycine) ligation between C-terminus and N-terminus on purified protein if EPL yields are low.
2.3 Oxidative folding route:
  - Expression: periplasmic expression of the SH3/exoloop construct (pelB leader) to promote disulfide formation; MBP can be periplasmic as a fusion or used as a cytosolic solubility tag followed by in vitro refolding.
  - In vitro refolding (if needed): denature/reduce (6 M guanidine-HCl + 5“10 mM DTT), then refold in redox buffer (e.g., 0.1 M Tris pH 8.0, 0.5 M arginine, 1“3 mM reduced glutathione (GSH), 0.1“0.3 mM oxidized glutathione (GSSG), 1“5 mM EDTA) at 4“16°C; optimize GSH:GSSG ratio and protein concentration to minimize aggregation.
2.4 Disulfide mapping: confirm connectivity by LC“MS/MS after protease digestion under non-reducing conditions (and compare to reduced control), plus intact mass shifts after alkylation.

Step 3 — Computational structural validation before wet-lab library builds
3.1 Model building: generate structural models of (i) native SH3, (ii) SH3 with engineered RT/n-Src loop sequences, (iii) SH3 with exoloop cystine-knot and optional staple disulfide, and (iv) cyclized vs linear termini.
3.2 Rosetta design/relax: constrain SH3 beta-strands and hydrophobic core; allow loop/exoloop and terminal-tail regions to move; score disulfide geometry and minimize strain.
3.3 MD simulations (explicit solvent): 100“300 ns for each design to quantify:
  - SH3 core stability (beta-barrel RMSD; preservation of key strand H-bonds)
  - Loop RMSF/RMSD (RT and n-Src) and predicted reduction in conformational heterogeneity
  - Binding-competent geometry relative to known SH3“PxxP peptide binding pose (dock peptide and monitor interface stability)
3.4 Computational go/no-go thresholds:
  - Core RMSD < 2.0 Å over final 50 ns window
  - No persistent exposure of hydrophobic core residues (aggregation proxy)
  - Disulfide strain within acceptable χ angles; no repeated disulfide rupture events in MD

Step 4 — Build-test sequence with explicit controls to isolate each contribution
4.1 Constructs (minimum panel):
  A. Linear SH3 binder (engineered loops; no extra cysteines; no cyclization)
  B. Cyclized-only SH3 (EPL/sortase cyclization; no added disulfides)
  C. Disulfide-stapled SH3 (engineered disulfide(s) constraining loops; linear backbone)
  D. Cyclized + cyclotide-inspired exoloop (full design)
  E. Cyclotide/exoloop module alone (no SH3) as negative control for binding and for non-specific adsorption
  F. MBP-fusions vs cleaved forms (for A“D) to test MBP effects on folding and on ELISA immobilization
4.2 Folding/assembly assays (must-pass before ELISA):
  - SEC-MALS to confirm monomeric state and rule out aggregation/oligomers
  - CD spectroscopy for beta-rich fold signature; thermal melts (Tm)
  - Limited proteolysis (trypsin/chymotrypsin) followed by MS to compare protease resistance and infer compactness
  - Optional: 1D/2D NMR (HSQC) on non-MBP cleaved versions for fold dispersion (prioritize top candidates)

Step 5 — Directed evolution and affinity maturation in a fold-safe way
5.1 Library design: restrict diversification to SH3 binding loops (RT and n-Src) and immediately adjacent solvent-exposed residues; do not mutate beta-strand core positions or cysteines forming the knot/staple.
5.2 Display: phage display or yeast surface display of the non-MBP form to select binders against immobilized target peptide and target-in-carrier protein; include negative selections against carrier and against unrelated proline-rich peptides.
5.3 Selection stringency: progress from low-stringency binding to off-rate selection; include harsh-condition selection rounds (e.g., brief 55“65°C exposure or protease pulse) to enrich stability.

Step 6 — Quantitative binding kinetics and stability profiling
6.1 Kinetics: SPR or BLI using identical antigen presentation across variants; report kon/koff/KD; include competition with soluble PxxP peptide to confirm binding mode.
6.2 Stability panels (predefined):
  - Temperature: 25°C, 37°C, 60°C (1 h), 80°C (10 min)
  - pH: 2.0, 4.0, 7.4, 10.0 (30“60 min, then neutralize)
  - Proteases: trypsin and proteinase K at defined units/mg for 30 min
Acceptance thresholds: retain ≥70% binding signal vs untreated control after each challenge for the lead construct; linear SH3 expected to fail at least one panel.

Step 7 — ELISA integration with immobilization risk controls
7.1 Oriented immobilization tests:
  - Amylose-coated plates with MBP-fusions (measure coating efficiency and leaching)
  - Parallel immobilization via anti-MBP antibody capture (orthogonal orientation method)
  - Parallel immobilization via direct adsorption of cleaved cyclized binder (no MBP) to assess MBP necessity
7.2 Maltose competition/leaching: evaluate signal with and without maltose (0“50 mM) in wash buffers to quantify MBP“amylose dependence and decide whether anti-MBP capture is the more robust orientation method under harsh conditions.
7.3 Non-specific binding: run no-antigen wells, irrelevant peptide wells, and high-matrix wells; quantify background and set acceptance criterion (e.g., signal-to-background ≥10 in PBS and ≥5 in 10% serum).

Step 8 — Format-matched benchmarking versus antibodies
8.1 Same assay role: engineered binder and monoclonal antibody both used as capture reagents; detection via a common detection system (e.g., anti-tag HRP for binder; anti-IgG HRP for antibody) with matched incubation/wash conditions.
8.2 Valency/avidity control: compare monovalent formats (engineered binder monomer; antibody Fab if available) and bivalent formats (full IgG; engineered binder dimerized via a defined linker) to avoid conflating avidity with intrinsic affinity.
8.3 Readouts: LoD, EC50, dynamic range, intra-/inter-assay CV, and post-stress signal retention across the harsh-condition panel in PBS and in serum/plasma.

Step 9 — Go/no-go decision points (risk mitigation)
9.1 Go/no-go #1 (post-expression/purification): if SEC-MALS shows >20% aggregates or misfolding (CD inconsistent), pivot to disulfide-stapled-only SH3 or cyclized-only SH3 without knot.
9.2 Go/no-go #2 (post-disulfide mapping): if incorrect/heterogeneous disulfides dominate, reduce cystine-knot complexity (2 disulfides only) or switch to periplasmic-only expression with DsbC co-expression.
9.3 Go/no-go #3 (ELISA immobilization): if amylose/MBP is unstable under harsh wash conditions, adopt anti-MBP capture or biotinylate a defined tag (AviTag) for streptavidin plates while keeping MBP only as expression aid.

Feasibility: Structural feasibility (addresses “nontrivial embedding”): The revised architecture explicitly preserves the SH3 beta-barrel and relocates backbone cyclization to terminal solvent-exposed tails, avoiding disruption of SH3 secondary structure. Cyclotide-like stabilization is implemented as an exoloop cystine-knot/staple system that constrains only targeted binding loops (RT/n-Src) rather than forcing the entire SH3 domain into a cyclotide fold. This is supported by a required computational validation stage (Rosetta + MD) with quantitative thresholds (core RMSD, loop RMSF, disulfide strain) before committing to library construction.

Expression and chemistry feasibility (addresses disulfides/cyclization in E. coli): The plan specifies an experimentally precedented cyclization route (intein-mediated EPL) with a defined fallback (sortase ligation). Oxidative folding is treated as a first-class risk with two routes: periplasmic expression (oxidizing environment) and in vitro refolding with explicit redox-buffer compositions, followed by disulfide connectivity mapping by LC“MS/MS.

Mechanistic rigor and contribution isolation: The build-test panel (linear SH3, cyclized-only, disulfide-stapled-only, full cyclotide-inspired, cyclotide-only, ±MBP) isolates which constraint(s) improve stability/affinity. Folding and monodispersity are verified by SEC-MALS, CD, limited proteolysis, and disulfide mapping, preventing false-positive ELISA improvements driven by aggregation or misfolding.

ELISA benchmarking validity (addresses format equivalence and immobilization artifacts): The ELISA is redesigned to be format-matched (same capture role, antigen presentation, and matrix panels). Immobilization risks specific to MBP/amylose (maltose competition, leaching, nonspecific adsorption) are explicitly tested with orthogonal capture methods (anti-MBP capture and/or AviTag“streptavidin). Harsh-condition panels and acceptance thresholds are predefined, ensuring that claims of superiority are tied to controlled stress tests rather than uncontrolled assay variability.

Alignment with concept chain: The proposal remains centered on protein engineering of SH3 designer binding modules (Asset 1), MBP as an expression/assay handle (Asset 1), and cyclotide/topological stabilization principles (Asset 2), but implements them in a structurally defensible, experimentally staged manner with explicit go/no-go criteria.

Hypothesis: Surgical-stress“like ROS elevations in the Drosophila lymph gland suppress prohemocyte maintenance by chemically oxidizing extracellular Wingless (Wg) at a small, quantifiable set of redox-labile residues that are functionally required for Wg retention/presentation (HSPG binding) and productive receptor engagement (DFz2-CRD binding). This oxidation collapses short-range Wg availability, reduces canonical Wg output in the medullary zone/PSC niche, and biases hematopoiesis toward an emergency differentiation program (lamellocyte skew; altered crystal cell outputs) analogous to stress hematopoiesis. 

Mechanistic rationale for the refined approach: reviewers’ central concern is false attribution of oxidation to the capture method and poor interpretability due to low-stoichiometry/labile oxidative PTMs on a lipidated/glycosylated Wnt. We therefore (i) decouple ‘PTM discovery’ from any peroxide-requiring proximity labeling by adding H2O2-free, in vivo, cell-impermeant oxidative-PTM trapping and rapid acid/anaerobic processing; (ii) require stringent pre-registered criteria to call a PTM ‘stress-induced’ (dose-response with stress, blockade by ROS quenchers, and persistence without enzymatic labeling); (iii) quantify PTM occupancy (not just identification) with isotope-coded standards so ROS→PTM→binding→signaling is quantitatively identifiable; and (iv) normalize each wg recoding allele for secretion/processing (extracellular abundance, lipidation/processing state, ER retention/Porcupine dependence, tissue distribution) prior to interpreting hematopoietic rescue, preventing biogenesis artifacts from masquerading as oxidation-resistance. Finally, we formally rank oxidative lesions across ligand vs HSPG scaffold vs receptor by combining targeted PTM-PRM on Wg/Dally/Dlp/DFz2 with reciprocal genetic ‘protection’ (oxidation-resistant recoding where structurally permissible) and epistasis tests that map which protected node restores Wg binding/signaling under stress.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration, stress calibration, and primary readouts (interpretability scaffolding)
0.1 Pre-register ‘stress-induced PTM’ criteria: A candidate oxidation site must (A) increase with stress intensity (injury±hypoxia/reoxygenation) across ≥3 doses; (B) be reduced by at least two mechanistically distinct ROS suppressors (e.g., NAC feeding + genetic catalase/SOD overexpression) without globally blocking immune differentiation; and (C) be detectable with the H2O2-free capture pipeline (Step 2B/2C) even when APEX/HRP labeling is omitted.
0.2 Define a surgical-stress ROS paradigm in larvae: sterile injury (standardized puncture site/needle gauge) combined with controlled transient hypoxia (e.g., 5% O2, defined duration) followed by reoxygenation. Acquire time-resolved lymph-gland ROS curves (0“180 min) using (i) chemical dyes (e.g., DHE for superoxide, H2DCFDA for general ROS, used only for kinetics) and (ii) genetically encoded sensors expressed broadly (e.g., roGFP2-Orp1 for H2O2; Grx1-roGFP2 for glutathione redox), with imaging parameters fixed (laser power, exposure) and ratiometric quantification.
0.3 Establish baseline hematopoietic metrics (same staging and gland segment): prohemocytes (dome+; medullary-zone fraction), PSC integrity (Antp+ cell number/volume), differentiation outputs (lamellocytes: msn/Atilla; crystal cells: PPO1/lozenge), and gland disruption indices.
0.4 Establish Wg pathway outputs: Armadillo stabilization (nuclear Arm), TCF/LEF reporter activity (standard Wg reporter), and extracellular Wg retention measured under non-permeabilizing immunostaining.

Step 1 — Orthogonal oxidative-PTM capture and artifact-control package (mandatory Directive #1)
1.1 H2O2-free extracellular sulfenic-acid trapping (primary orthogonal capture): Immediately after stress, incubate dissected lymph glands briefly (minutes) in ice-cold, oxygen-restricted buffer containing a cell-impermeant sulfenic acid trap (e.g., a membrane-impermeant dimedone-derivative with biotin handle). Rationale: captures transient Cys-SOH formed in vivo without adding peroxide; cell-impermeant design biases labeling to extracellular/luminally exposed proteins. 
1.2 Rapid acid quench + anaerobic processing (artifact suppression): Within seconds of collection, quench glands in cold acidified buffer (e.g., 0.1“0.5% formic acid compatible with downstream cleanup) to stop redox cycling; perform homogenization and immunoprecipitation in degassed buffers under inert gas (N2/Ar), include metal chelators (EDTA/DTPA) to limit Fenton chemistry, and include methionine oxidation suppressors during processing where compatible. 
1.3 Differential alkylation to preserve native thiol states: Immediately after acid quench neutralization, alkylate free thiols (e.g., iodoacetamide) under low oxygen; optionally apply a two-step alkylation workflow to distinguish reduced vs reversibly oxidized cysteines if needed.
1.4 Controlled ‘labeling artifact’ arm for APEX/HRP (secondary triangulation, not primary discovery): If extracellular APEX/HRP proximity labeling is used, run matched controls: (i) no-enzyme controls, (ii) no-biotin-phenol controls, (iii) stress vs no-stress with identical minimal H2O2 pulse, (iv) catalase present during pulse, and (v) pulse before stress (to gauge labeling-induced oxidation). Enzymatic labeling is used mainly to enrich the Wg microenvironment proteome, not to define oxidation chemistry.

Step 2 — Quantitative PTM mapping on Wg, scaffold, and receptor (Directives #3 and #4)
2.1 Endogenous tagging and enrichment: Use an endogenously tagged wg allele (small epitope tag validated for function) to immuno-enrich Wg from pooled lymph glands. In parallel, enrich Dally/Dlp and DFz2 (tagged or high-affinity antibodies) from the same biological conditions. 
2.2 Target PTM classes and detection modes:
- Methionine oxidation: quantify MetO occupancy with isotope-coded peptide standards (synthetic light/heavy pairs for each candidate peptide in reduced vs MetO forms) and PRM.
- Cysteine oxidation: quantify sulfenylated/overoxidized sites via the H2O2-free trapping (Step 1.1) plus PRM for modified peptides; include negative controls for probe specificity.
- Carbonylation (optional): detect via derivatization-based enrichment only if initial discovery indicates robust carbonylation.
2.3 PTM stoichiometry and dose-response: For each candidate site on Wg/Dally/Dlp/DFz2, compute occupancy (modified/(modified+unmodified)) across stress doses and timepoints. Define a priori a ‘functional-threshold’ analysis: identify sites whose occupancy crosses a threshold concurrent with measurable Wg binding loss (Step 3). 
2.4 Distinguishing ligand vs scaffold vs receptor as dominant lesion: Rank nodes using a composite score per protein: (i) PTM occupancy change with stress, (ii) sensitivity to ROS quenchers, (iii) temporal precedence relative to signaling loss, and (iv) correlation with binding deficits.

Step 3 — Binding and presentation consequences with quantitative linkage to PTM occupancy
3.1 DFz2-CRD capture assay (quantitative receptor binding): Produce recombinant DFz2-CRD (quality-controlled for disulfide integrity) immobilized on beads. Incubate with lymph gland“conditioned media collected post-stress (standardized gland number/time). Quantify captured Wg by immunoblot and, where possible, targeted MS (PRM) normalized to input Wg abundance.
3.2 HSPG-binding assay: In parallel, capture Wg on heparin/HSPG-mimetic matrices. Include competition with soluble heparin to validate specificity. 
3.3 Normalization to extracellular Wg abundance: For each sample, measure extracellular Wg abundance directly (non-permeabilizing staining quantified per gland volume; plus biochemical measurement of secreted Wg in conditioned media). Binding readouts are reported as ‘binding per extracellular Wg’ to separate biogenesis effects from binding chemistry.
3.4 Stoichiometry→binding model: Fit mixed-effects models linking site-specific occupancy (Step 2) to DFz2/HSPG binding loss (Step 3.1“3.2) to identify which PTMs explain the majority of functional variance.

Step 4 — CRISPR recoding with secretion/processing QC (Mandatory Directive #2)
4.1 Allelic series design: Generate endogenous wg edits for only high-confidence stress-induced sites (per Step 0.1“2.3). Prioritize Met→Leu (oxidation-resistant) for MetO sites; for cysteines, restrict to surface-exposed, non-disulfide cysteines based on Wnt/Wg structural homology and disulfide mapping, avoiding cysteines predicted essential for folding. Include oxidation-mimetic controls only when chemically defensible.
4.2 Biogenesis and secretion QC for every allele (pass/fail gate before hematopoiesis interpretation):
- ER retention/UPR: assess ER stress markers and Wg co-localization with ER markers in producing cells.
- Porcupine dependence and lipidation/processing state: test sensitivity to Porcupine inhibition/knockdown; assess Wg electrophoretic mobility and/or lipidation proxy assays as feasible; confirm that edited alleles still require normal Wg processing pathways.
- Extracellular abundance and distribution: quantify extracellular Wg levels (non-permeabilizing staining) and spatial distribution in lymph gland; compare to wild-type and a known Wg secretion-impaired control.
Only alleles meeting secretion/processing criteria proceed to Step 5 phenotyping.

Step 5 — Reciprocal protection/recoding of scaffold and receptor (Mandatory Directive #3)
5.1 Targeted PTM-PRM on Dally/Dlp and DFz2: Use the same stress series to quantify oxidation occupancy on Dally/Dlp/DFz2 extracellular peptides (Step 2). 
5.2 Genetic ‘protection’ tests:
- Scaffold: use alleles or engineered variants that increase effective HSPG presentation (e.g., increased sulfation capacity or stabilized Dally/Dlp expression) to test rescue of Wg retention/signaling under stress.
- Receptor: if DFz2 extracellular cysteines show stress-sensitive oxidation and are not disulfide-essential, generate conservative oxidation-resistant edits (minimal cysteine edits; prioritize Met edits on receptor first if present). Validate receptor surface expression and signaling competence under baseline conditions.
5.3 Formal ranking experiment: Under identical stress conditions, compare rescue efficacy across (i) oxidation-resistant wg, (ii) scaffold-protection, (iii) receptor-protection, and (iv) combinations. The dominant oxidative lesion is the node whose protection restores Wg binding/signaling and prohemocyte maintenance with the largest effect size at matched ROS levels.

Step 6 — Hematopoietic outcomes and immune-context validation (Assets 1“3 alignment)
6.1 Under surgical-stress ROS, quantify whether protected-node genotypes maintain prohemocytes (dome+), preserve PSC integrity (Antp+), and prevent stress-biased emergency differentiation (lamellocytes), while not abolishing appropriate immune responsiveness.
6.2 Immune challenge interaction: Perform wasp parasitization ± surgical-stress pretreatment. Test whether stress normally alters lineage choice (e.g., lamellocyte bias and/or altered Serrate/Notch-linked crystal cell outputs), and whether oxidation-resistant Wg (or scaffold/receptor protection) specifically uncouples ‘stress compounding’ from pathogen-driven differentiation.
6.3 Benchmark controls: Compare to global antioxidants and generic ROS inducers. Requirement: node-specific protection should preserve hematopoietic homeostasis without broadly suppressing immune competence, distinguishing targeted mechanism from systemic ROS dampening.

Step 7 — Minimal quantitative mechanism model (identifiable, not qualitative)
7.1 Build a hierarchical model: ROS dose/time → site-specific PTM occupancy (Wg/scaffold/receptor) → DFz2/HSPG binding capacity (normalized) → Wg transcriptional output → cell-fate metrics. 
7.2 Identifiability ensured by: (i) measured PTM stoichiometries with isotope-coded standards, (ii) independent binding assays, (iii) allele series that selectively modulates PTM susceptibility without changing baseline processing, and (iv) reciprocal protection at multiple nodes.
Feasibility: Addresses (i) H2O2/APEX confounding: Oxidation mapping is anchored in H2O2-free, cell-impermeant sulfenic-acid trapping plus rapid acid quench/anaerobic workflows; APEX/HRP is demoted to secondary enrichment with stringent matched controls. A PTM is only called ‘stress-induced’ if it increases with stress, is blocked by ROS quenchers, and persists without enzymatic labeling.

Addresses (ii) low-stoichiometry/labile PTMs on Wg: The plan explicitly includes (a) pooling strategy (many glands per condition), (b) rapid quench + oxygen-exclusion to minimize artifactual oxidation, (c) immediate thiol blocking, and (d) targeted PRM quantification using isotope-coded standards for both modified and unmodified peptides to measure occupancy (not presence/absence). This makes small, labile PTM signals interpretable and comparable across conditions.

Addresses (iii) ligand vs scaffold vs receptor ambiguity: Wg, Dally/Dlp, and DFz2 are all subjected to the same quantitative PTM-PRM pipeline and then to reciprocal genetic ‘protection/recoding’ tests. Dominance is inferred by effect size on binding (DFz2-CRD and heparin capture normalized to extracellular Wg) and signaling/fate outcomes at matched ROS, providing a formal ranking rather than assumption.

Addresses (iv) recoding may disrupt Wg biogenesis: Every wg allele passes a predefined secretion/processing QC gate (ER retention/UPR, Porcupine dependence, extracellular abundance/distribution). Hematopoietic rescue is interpreted only if baseline processing and extracellular levels are comparable, ensuring that observed protection reflects oxidation-resistance rather than altered folding/trafficking.

Overall feasibility: The proposal leverages strong prior biological grounding (Wg maintains prohemocytes/PSC; ROS triggers immune activation) while upgrading the redox-MS core with orthogonal, minimally perturbative capture and quantitative stoichiometry standards. This converts a high-risk qualitative redox claim into a controlled, multi-node, quantitatively testable mechanism that remains tightly aligned with the original ROS→Wg availability→hematopoietic fate chain.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a *structure-guided, affinity-coupled dual-stabilization architecture*—comprising (i) a calcium-rigidified, engineered class III chitinase functioning as a **specific lipase-binding interlayer** and MOF nucleation scaffold, and (ii) confinement of the resulting chitinase“lipase complex within a protein-compatible Co“Cys BioMOF—will yield quantitatively superior encapsulation efficiency, thermal robustness, and recyclability compared to single-enzyme or non-affinity co-encapsulation systems. Mechanistically, Ca2+ binding at pre-validated surface loops of the chitinase increases local backbone rigidity (ΔTm-driven stabilization without fold disruption), while engineered lipase-affinity patches enforce spatial colocalization, preventing nonspecific crowding. Subsequent MOF growth occurs preferentially around the chitinase scaffold via defined His/Cys coordination sites, generating a hierarchical composite in which lipase stability arises from *both* reduced conformational entropy (via chitinase binding) and controlled mesoporous confinement (via BioMOF), rather than from altered crystallization kinetics or passive co-entrapment.
Plan: Step 1: Structure-guided chitinase engineering.
- Template selection: Use a resolved class III chitinase structure with high homology to PSC (e.g., PDB ID: 1KFW or closest plant class III chitinase fold).
- Ca2+-binding design: Identify two solvent-exposed, non-catalytic loops (≥8 Å from active site, low sequence conservation) and introduce *minimal* Ca2+-binding motifs (DXH or EHX, not DXDXD) based on EF-hand“inspired geometries to reduce electrostatic destabilization. Computational screening will target Ca2+ KD in the 50“200 µM range.
- Affinity interface: Introduce a shallow hydrophobic/aromatic patch (e.g., W/F/Y-enriched, ~300“500 Å²) complementary to CALB surface regions distal to the active site (guided by docking), yielding micromolar chitinase“CALB affinity.
- MOF nucleation sites: Add 2“3 spatially clustered His/Cys residues on the *opposite face* of the lipase-binding interface to spatially decouple lipase binding from Co“Cys coordination.
- Validation criteria: SEC-MALS (monodispersity), CD spectra overlap ≥90% with WT, Ca2+-dependent ΔTm ≥ +5 °C by DSC, no >10% loss of intrinsic chitinase activity.

Step 2: Protein compatibility and Co“Cys BioMOF growth optimization.
- Establish protein-safe MOF conditions: pH 7.0“7.5, ≤25 °C, Co2+ ≤1 mM, cystine:Co ratio optimized to minimize free thiols; include ROS scavenger (e.g., 1 mM methionine) during growth.
- Compatibility assays prior to encapsulation: CALB activity after exposure to Co2+/Cys without MOF; thiol oxidation state via Ellman’s assay; cobalt leaching baseline via ICP-MS.

Step 3: Hierarchical encapsulation workflows and mechanistic control matrix.
- Primary system: Pre-form chitinase“Ca2+“CALB complex (verified by MST or ITC), initiate in-situ Co“Cys BioMOF growth.
- Controls (mandatory): (a) CALB@MOF ± Ca2+; (b) CALB + WT chitinase@MOF ± Ca2+; (c) CALB + engineered chitinase lacking His/Cys nucleation sites@MOF; (d) post-synthetic CALB loading into preformed MOF; (e) engineered chitinase“CALB without MOF.

Step 4: Localization, accessibility, and stabilization metrics.
- Co-localization: Dual fluorescent labeling + confocal microscopy; FRET efficiency as proximity readout.
- Pore accessibility: Protease protection assays; nitrogen sorption with size-exclusion probes.
- Functional kinetics: Determine Km and kcat for esterification to confirm active-site accessibility versus diffusion limitation.
- Stability metrics: T50 and half-life at 60 °C; activity retention after 10, 15, and 20 cycles.

Step 5: Quantitative go/no-go criteria (pre-registered).
- Encapsulation yield ≥85%; activity recovery ≥75%.
- ΔT50 (composite vs free CALB) ≥ +15 °C.
- ≥80% activity retained after 10 cycles and ≥65% after 20 cycles.
- Cobalt leaching ≤5% over full recycling study.
Feasibility: This refined workflow directly addresses reviewer concerns by converting a conceptual synergy into a falsifiable, structure-driven engineering strategy. Unlike arbitrary DXDXD insertions, Ca2+-binding motifs are placed using fold-aware constraints and validated biophysically, minimizing destabilization risk. The engineered chitinase is no longer a passive co-encapsulant but a defined affinity interlayer enforcing lipase colocalization, enabling true mechanistic synergy. Comprehensive control matrices disentangle Ca2+ effects, chitinase effects, MOF confinement, and encapsulation mode. Explicit protein-compatible Co“Cys conditions and metal/thiol monitoring mitigate cobalt-related risks. Finally, pre-registered quantitative performance thresholds transform the proposal into a deliverable engineering program grounded in precedents from BioMOF encapsulation (Asset 2), nanostructured lipase immobilization (Asset 1), and Ca2+-mediated chitinase stabilization (Asset 3), while advancing them through a rigorously testable hierarchical design.

Hypothesis: In primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), the disease-shifted steroid enzyme balance (↓SULT1E1, ↑STS) increases the local capacity of bile-duct epithelium to desulfate circulating/ductal DHEA-S into DHEA precisely at the inflamed ductular interface. Under bile-acid/ROS stress, a controlled pulse of intra-cholangiocyte DHEA can bias stress-response programs toward anti-apoptosis and redox buffering while dampening maladaptive cholangiocyte-to-portal paracrine outputs that drive portal inflammation and hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation (TGF-β/PDGF/CTGF/CCL2/IL-6 axis), thereby reducing fibrogenesis (Asset 1 mechanistic link) and preserving duct integrity (Asset 2 cytoprotection link). To overcome the key translational risks identified by reviewers—(i) STS ubiquity and (ii) aryl-sulfamate triggers behaving as irreversible inhibitors rather than clean substrates—we will engineer and quantitatively validate a bile-duct-enriched, STS-activated “substrate-not-inhibitor” prodrug system whose activation is governed by: (a) demonstrable catalytic turnover by purified STS (high kcat with low time-dependent inactivation), (b) a PK/PD model integrating measured STS activity distributions across human PBC ducts/hepatocytes/immune cells and nanoparticle exposure to predict on-target DHEA release vs systemic burden, and (c) explicit control of downstream steroid metabolism (DHEA→androstenedione/testosterone/estradiol), enabling causal attribution to ERα and/or AR in cholangiocytes (with aromatase/17β-HSD blockade to isolate direct receptor signaling from downstream sex-steroid conversion). We predict that a duct-targeted, STS-activated DHEA prodrug will achieve higher cholangiocyte-local receptor engagement under cholestatic oxidative stress with lower systemic androgenic/estrogenic exposure than free DHEA/DHEA-S, yielding net suppression of immune-mediated portal injury and HSC-driven collagen deposition in both cholestatic injury (BDL) and bona fide autoimmune cholangitis models.
Plan: Step 1 — Quantitative human mapping (activity, not just expression) to parameterize selectivity and PK/PD.
1.1 Spatial “STS activity distribution” atlas in human PBC.
- Samples: human PBC explants/biopsies stratified early vs late stage; non-PBC cholestatic controls where available.
- Readouts:
  (i) Multiplex IF + RNAscope: STS, SULT1E1, ERα, AR co-registered with KRT19/SOX9 (ductular reaction), COL1A1/ACTA2 (fibrosis), CD68/CD163 (macrophages), EPCAM.
  (ii) Quantitative enzyme activity: apply sulfatase activity-based probes (ABPs) optimized for STS (fluorophosphonate/arylsulfate-mimetic ABPs where appropriate) plus orthogonal biochemical activity from laser-capture microdissected ducts vs periportal hepatocytes vs immune infiltrates; report activity as pmol substrate converted/min/mg protein.
  (iii) Single-cell/spatial transcriptomics (targeted panel acceptable): confirm STS/SULT1E1 and steroid-metabolism nodes (HSD3B, HSD17B isoforms, CYP19A1/aromatase, SRD5A1/2) in cholangiocytes vs macrophages vs HSC.
- Output: probability distributions of STS activity per cell-type compartment (duct epithelium, hepatocyte, macrophage) to feed Step 2 PK/PD.

1.2 Microphysiological PBC platform with compartment control.
- Chip architecture: dual-channel microfluidic device with (a) apical “bile” channel lined by cholangiocyte organoid-derived epithelium under flow, and (b) basolateral “portal” channel containing Kupffer-like macrophages and primary human HSC embedded in ECM hydrogel (collagen I/Matrigel blend, stiffness tuned 1“5 kPa).
- Stressors: deliver GCDC to apical channel; deliver controlled ROS flux (e.g., menadione or H2O2 microdosing) with real-time ROS sensors; maintain bile-acid gradients (apical>>basolateral) to mimic cholestasis.
- Patient relevance: prioritize PBC patient-derived cholangiocytes when feasible; otherwise iPSC-cholangiocytes conditioned with PBC-like cytokines (IL-17A, IFN-γ, TNF-α) to approximate inflammatory cholangitis.

Step 2 — Prodrug chemistry redesign and a mandatory substrate-vs-inhibitor validation package.
2.1 Trigger strategy: explicitly de-risk aryl-sulfamate irreversible inhibition.
- Parallel trigger families (screened head-to-head):
  A) Sulfate ester self-immolative prodrug (preferred “substrate-first”): DHEA-O-SO3− linked via a para-hydroxybenzyl (PHB) self-immolative spacer that releases native DHEA after STS-catalyzed sulfate hydrolysis and 1,6-elimination; electronics tuned (para substituents) to reduce non-enzymatic hydrolysis at pH 7.4 while maintaining STS turnover.
  B) “Soft-sulfamate” analogs only if A fails: N-alkyl/aryl sulfamates engineered to minimize time-dependent STS inactivation (avoid classic aryl-sulfamate motifs known for suicide inhibition); include leaving-group tuning and sterics to favor turnover.
- Decision gate: advance only triggers meeting strict enzymology thresholds in 2.2.

2.2 Mandatory substrate-vs-inhibitor validation (purified enzyme + cellular genetics).
- Purified STS assays:
  (i) Steady-state kinetics: measure kcat, KM, kcat/KM for each candidate trigger using recombinant human STS (membrane prep or nanodisc-reconstituted STS); quantify product DHEA by LC“MS/MS.
  (ii) Time-dependent inhibition (TDI): preincubate STS with candidate at multiple concentrations and times; measure residual activity on a standard fluorescent STS substrate; fit kinact/KI. Hard criterion: minimal TDI (kinact/KI below predefined threshold relative to a known irreversible inhibitor control).
  (iii) Partition ratio (turnover vs inactivation): determine molecules of DHEA released per STS molecule before activity loss.
- Cellular genetic rescue:
  (i) STS knockout (CRISPR) and STS overexpression in human cholangiocytes; confirm that prodrug→DHEA conversion and phenotypes scale with STS abundance.
  (ii) Rescue experiment: reintroduce STS in KO background to restore activation.
  (iii) Off-target sulfatase panel: evaluate activation in ARSA/ARSB/other sulfatases (purified or cell lines) to ensure specificity is not broadly sulfatase-driven.

2.3 Bile-duct enrichment: nanoparticle parameters specified and measurable.
- Carrier: PEG-PLGA nanoparticles (50“90 nm target hydrodynamic diameter; PDI <0.2) with (i) near-neutral zeta potential (−5 to +5 mV) to reduce nonspecific uptake, (ii) prodrug loading quantified (wt% and release stability in plasma/bile simulant).
- Targeting ligands (dual mode, tested empirically):
  (i) Basolateral cholangiocyte targeting: anti-EpCAM scFv or anti-KRT19-binding peptide (screen for internalization).
  (ii) Ductal retention: bile-acid-mimetic surface moiety (e.g., cholate-conjugated PEG) to enhance biliary/ductal association under cholestasis.
- Uptake benchmarking: quantify nanoparticle uptake (flow cytometry + confocal) in cholangiocytes vs hepatocytes vs macrophages under inflammatory conditions; report uptake rate constants for PK/PD.

Step 3 — PK/PD modeling that combines STS activity distributions with exposure to predict therapeutic index.
3.1 Model structure.
- Multi-compartment model: plasma, liver sinusoid, hepatocyte, portal immune compartment, bile-duct epithelium (apical/basolateral), bile.
- Processes:
  (i) Nanoparticle transport/uptake (measured from biodistribution/uptake assays).
  (ii) Intracellular prodrug activation: Michaelis“Menten using measured STS kcat/KM and cell-type STS activity distributions from Step 1.
  (iii) DHEA diffusion/efflux and metabolism.
- Outputs: predicted local ductal DHEA AUC, systemic DHEA AUC, and proportion activated in off-target tissues.
- Decision gate: proceed to in vivo only if model predicts ≥X-fold (predefined) ductal-vs-systemic exposure advantage relative to free DHEA.

Step 4 — Mechanistic causality with explicit steroid-metabolism mapping and receptor disentangling.
4.1 Steroid metabolite fate mapping (mandatory).
- LC“MS/MS steroid panel in chip and in vivo tissues: DHEA-S, DHEA, androstenedione, testosterone, DHT, estrone, estradiol; quantify in cholangiocytes, media (apical vs basolateral), and liver compartments.
- Enzyme-expression coupling: correlate metabolite patterns with HSD3B/HSD17B/CYP19A1/SRD5A1/2 expression.

4.2 Receptor and metabolism dissection controls.
- Receptor dependence:
  (i) ERα and AR CRISPRi/siRNA in cholangiocytes.
  (ii) Pharmacology: ERα antagonist (e.g., MPP) and AR antagonist (e.g., enzalutamide) in-chip, with dose“response.
- Metabolic blockade to separate direct DHEA actions from downstream sex steroids:
  (i) Aromatase inhibitor (letrozole) to block DHEA→estrogens.
  (ii) 17β-HSD inhibitors (isoform-appropriate; select based on expressed HSD17B in cholangiocytes).
  (iii) 5α-reductase inhibitor (finasteride/dutasteride) to block DHT formation.
- Interpretability: compare phenotypes under (a) receptor block, (b) metabolic block, (c) both, to assign causal weight to ERα vs AR vs downstream estradiol/testosterone.

4.3 Phenotypic endpoints aligned to fibrosis causality.
- Cholangiocyte stress survival: Annexin V/caspase 3/7, mitochondrial ΔΨm, Nrf2 targets, DNA damage markers.
- Ductular reaction vs “protective proliferation”: quantify Ki67/EdU along with differentiation/repair markers; explicitly test whether prodrug reduces maladaptive proliferative/inflammatory programs under stress despite preserving viability.
- Paracrine outputs to portal niche: TGF-β, PDGF, CTGF, IL-6, CCL2, osteopontin; multiplex ELISA + transcript.
- HSC response: α-SMA, COL1A1, hydroxyproline/procollagen I, MMP/TIMP ratio; include HSC RNA-seq module for activation states.
- Mediation analysis: pre-specified causal model where treatment → (cholangiocyte paracrine reduction) → (HSC activation reduction) → (fibrosis reduction).

Step 5 — In vivo translation with required autoimmune cholangitis + cholestasis model pairing.
5.1 Models (mandatory pairing).
- Autoimmune cholangitis: commit to at least one bona fide PBC-like model (choose based on facility):
  (i) dnTGFβRII mouse (autoimmune cholangitis with portal inflammation) and/or
  (ii) NOD.c3c4 (autoimmune biliary disease features).
- Cholestasis/fibrosis comparator: bile duct ligation (BDL) to test bile-acid/ROS injury context independent of autoimmunity.

5.2 Dosing, biodistribution, and on-target activation.
- Biodistribution: fluorescence/PET-labeled nanoparticles; quantify ductal enrichment by imaging + tissue LC“MS/MS.
- On-target activation: measure prodrug and released DHEA/metabolites in microdissected bile ducts vs parenchyma; align with STS activity.
- Comparator arms: targeted prodrug vs free DHEA vs DHEA-S vs inactive prodrug (non-cleavable analog).

5.3 Efficacy and immune-fibrosis linkage.
- Histology: ductopenia/ductular reaction (CK19), portal inflammation scoring, Sirius Red morphometry, second-harmonic generation collagen architecture, α-SMA.
- Molecular: portal cytokine/chemokine signatures; HSC activation signatures; oxidative stress markers.
- Functional: liver stiffness (where feasible), serum ALP/ALT/bilirubin.

5.4 Safety/therapeutic index.
- Endocrine burden: systemic steroid panel; reproductive tissue gene panels (uterus/prostate equivalents), lipid/coagulation profile.
- Off-target immune modulation: macrophage polarization markers; ensure no generalized immunosuppression driving false-positive fibrosis reduction.

Step 6 — Rigor, preregistration, and go/no-go criteria.
6.1 Pre-registered primary endpoints: (i) ductal DHEA exposure advantage (duct/parenchyma and duct/systemic AUC), (ii) cholangiocyte apoptosis under GCDC+ROS, (iii) HSC activation index, (iv) fibrosis area fraction.
6.2 Power calculations and blinded quantification for histology and image analysis.
6.3 Go/no-go gates:
- Chemistry gate: must meet substrate-not-inhibitor enzymology thresholds (2.2).
- Selectivity gate: PK/PD predicts and in vivo confirms ductal enrichment and reduced systemic exposure vs free DHEA.
- Mechanism gate: phenotype must be attenuated by ERα/AR perturbation and remain interpretable after metabolic-block controls.
Feasibility: 1) Enzymology/selectivity de-risking (addresses reviewer point 1): Rather than assuming aryl-sulfamates behave as clean substrates, the plan explicitly implements a substrate-vs-inhibitor validation package: purified STS kcat/KM, time-dependent inhibition (kinact/KI), partition ratio (turnover before inactivation), and cellular genetics (STS KO/overexpression/rescue). A parallel trigger strategy prioritizes sulfate-ester self-immolative designs to avoid the known failure mode of irreversible STS inhibition by classic aryl-sulfamates. Advancement is gated by quantitative thresholds, preventing mechanistic confounding from STS inhibition.

2) Quantitative therapeutic index via PK/PD modeling (addresses reviewer point 1): Because STS is broadly expressed, “kinetic gating” is insufficient without quantitative exposure modeling. The proposal therefore measures STS activity distributions in human PBC ducts vs hepatocytes vs immune cells and combines these with nanoparticle uptake/biodistribution data in a multi-compartment PK/PD model to predict on-target DHEA release and systemic steroid burden. This explicitly tests whether bile-duct enrichment + activation kinetics can yield a meaningful duct/systemic AUC advantage.

3) Causality under pleiotropic steroid biology (addresses reviewer point 2): Asset 2 supports DHEA/DHEA-S cytoprotection under bile-acid/ROS stress with ER involvement and AR contribution, but DHEA’s metabolism could redirect effects. The plan therefore includes mandatory LC“MS/MS steroid metabolomics (DHEA→androstenedione/testosterone/DHT/estrone/estradiol) and uses aromatase, 17β-HSD, and 5α-reductase inhibitors to separate direct ERα/AR signaling from downstream sex-steroid conversion. Receptor perturbations (ERα/AR CRISPRi/antagonists) are combined with metabolic blockade to tightly constrain mechanism attribution.

4) Biological coherence with PBC fibrogenesis (Assets 1 and 2) while avoiding overreach: Asset 1 indicates fibrogenesis in PBC-like disease is linked to inflammatory bile duct injury/ROS and portal crosstalk rather than “pure” cholestasis alone. The revised plan therefore commits to testing in at least one autoimmune cholangitis model (dnTGFβRII and/or NOD.c3c4) alongside BDL, ensuring immune-mediated portal inflammation claims are directly evaluated in a PBC-relevant context. The microfluidic platform explicitly models apical (bile) vs basolateral (portal) compartments, enabling compartmentalized exposure and paracrine-to-HSC causality testing.

5) Translational practicality: Each risk is tied to measurable go/no-go criteria (enzymology thresholds, predicted/observed ductal AUC advantage, receptor/metabolism-dependent phenotypes). This structure increases the likelihood of generating interpretable outcomes even if some components underperform (e.g., trigger family A vs B), while preserving the original concept chain: PBC enzyme asymmetry → cholangiocyte stress survival + reduced maladaptive paracrine signaling → reduced HSC activation → reduced fibrosis.

Hypothesis: Engineering a genetically encoded diiron-bacterioferritin (Bfr) metallocage chimera in which an MMO/RNR-like diiron 4-helix-bundle is transplanted into the *native Bfr heme pocket* (via a designed helix“turn“helix insert plus second-shell hydrogen-bond network) will enable *kinetically gated O2 activation* whose oxidizing equivalent is delivered locally to a proximal, engineered Ser“His“Asp catalytic module to drive *classical acyl-enzyme esterase chemistry* while minimizing off-pathway ROS.

Chemically grounded coupling mechanism (falsifiable): The intended dominant manifold is not “diffuse oxidation” but a *redox-gated increase in His general-base strength* (via H-bond/electrostatic coupling to the diiron peroxo/oxo state) that accelerates: (1) His-mediated deprotonation of Ser-OH → Ser-O−, (2) nucleophilic attack on the ester carbonyl to form a covalent *acyl“Ser enzyme intermediate*, and (3) hydrolysis of the acyl“Ser by activated water to release carboxylate + regenerated Ser. The diiron site’s role is to create a *transient, state-dependent electrostatic field / proton relay reconfiguration* (diferrous → peroxo/diferric) that shifts the His pKa and orders a flexible catalytic loop (“order-on-oxidation switch”), thereby gating acylation to periods when O2 has been productively activated.

Predicted detectable species and discriminants:
- A covalent acyl“Ser intermediate detectable by rapid-quench followed by intact-protein MS and peptide LC“MS/MS (mass shift matching the acyl group), abolished by Ser→Ala and strongly reduced by His→Gln.
- Product oxygen source: incorporation of solvent-derived 18O from H2(18)O into the carboxylate product (expected for hydrolysis via acyl“enzyme), with *minimal* incorporation from 18O2 (distinguishing hydrolysis from oxidative cleavage/oxygenation).
- Kinetic signatures: a burst phase consistent with pre-steady-state acylation (stopped-flow/rapid-quench), and solvent isotope/KIE patterns (H2O/D2O effect on deacylation; minimal primary 18O2 KIE on product formation if O2 is gating rather than being inserted).
- Off-pathway oxidation readouts (protein sulfoxides, dityrosine, carbonylation; substrate radical products) must remain below pre-specified thresholds; otherwise the mechanism is rejected.

Why this overcomes reviewer-identified failure modes: (i) It commits to a *canonical esterase covalent intermediate* (acyl“Ser) with explicit MS/isotope tests, rather than an underspecified “Ser activation by Fe“O.” (ii) It treats the heme-pocket transplant as a constrained, negative-designed metal site with explicit criteria for rigidity, solvation control, and exclusion of alternate Fe nucleation sites. (iii) It redesigns directed evolution so survival cannot be achieved by loss-of-function: expression/metallation are normalized, and variants must first pass a minimum diiron O2-activation signature before esterase screens; alternatively, selection is coupled to prodrug activation rather than ROS reduction alone.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-commitment: staged program with go/no-go milestones
0.1 Milestone A (metal site reality check; GO/NO-GO): Demonstrate a bona fide diiron(II/III)-O2 intermediate *in the engineered heme pocket* with correct stoichiometry (≈2 Fe per pocket), spectroscopic signature, and controlled lifetime (stopped-flow UV“vis + Mössbauer/EPR on rapid-freeze-quench). If not achieved, halt Ser“His“Asp installation and iterate pocket geometry/negative design.
0.2 Milestone B (local oxidizing-equivalent containment; GO/NO-GO in parallel): In a simplified construct lacking the Ser triad, install a proximal redox-reporting residue pair (e.g., engineered Tyr/Trp reporter or redox-sensitive fluorophore-adjacent motif) to quantify local oxidation vs diffuse ROS (dityrosine/Trp oxidation mapping). Proceed to triad only if oxidation remains localized and low globally.

Step 1 — Scaffold choice and pocket mapping (explicit structural constraints)
1.1 Select 3“5 Bfr homologs with: (i) high soluble expression and stable cage assembly, (ii) high-resolution heme-pocket structures (or high-confidence AlphaFold + experimental validation), (iii) minimal competing ferroxidase/mineralization activity under assay conditions (screen for low nonspecific Fe(II) oxidation/mineral core growth).
1.2 Quantitatively map the heme pocket for: (i) cavity volume and solvent occupancy (MD + water mapping), (ii) O2 access pathways (CAVER/MD), (iii) side-chain plasticity. Define geometric acceptance windows for the transplant: target Fe“Fe distance 3.2“3.6 Å (peroxo-competent), carboxylate bridging topology (μ-1,3 or μ-η1:η1 patterns), and one/two His ligands positioned for facial diiron coordination.

Step 2 — Methodological adaptation: heme-pocket-to-diiron 4-helix microbundle transplant with negative design
2.1 Design an internal helix“turn“helix insert that, together with two pre-existing pocket helices, forms a constrained 4-helix microbundle. Architectural parameters:
- Bundle crossing angles and helix register chosen to minimize diiron-site drift (<0.8 Å RMSD in MD for first-shell ligands in the diferrous state).
- Introduce a steric ‘buttress’ (hydrophobic packing layer) behind ligand helices to reduce breathing motions that would favor ROS leak.
2.2 First-shell ligand set (explicit): build a diiron motif using 4 carboxylates + 1“2 histidines (E/D…E/D…H pattern) consistent with MMO/RNR families; enforce a single dominant bidentate/monodentate pattern by local packing (negative design to disfavor alternate rotamers).
2.3 Second-shell network to tune intermediate lifetime:
- Install defined H-bond donors/acceptors that stabilize peroxo vs oxo (e.g., one H-bond donor to terminal peroxo oxygen; one polar residue positioning a bound water as proton relay). Target an intermediate half-life window (e.g., 10“500 ms at 10“25 °C) suitable for gating without long-lived oxidants.
2.4 Water activity and alternate-site suppression (negative design requirements + validation plan):
- Reduce adventitious metal-binding patches by mutating surface Asp/Glu clusters near pocket entrances; add repulsive electrostatics around non-target cavities.
- Disable mineralization nucleation: mutate ferroxidase-channel residues and inner-surface acidic patches implicated in core growth while preserving cage assembly.
- Add a ‘metal selectivity filter’ at the pocket mouth (geometry + charge) to disfavor nonspecific Fe binding elsewhere.

Step 3 — Build the redox-gated Ser“His“Asp esterase module only after Milestone A
3.1 Catalytic module placement: position Ser on a short internal loop adjacent to the ester-binding channel; place His within H-bonding distance to Ser and within electrostatic-coupling distance to a diiron second-shell carboxylate (to shift His pKa upon diferric-peroxo/oxo formation). Asp/Glu placed to orient/activate His.
3.2 Order-on-oxidation switch (explicit, testable):
- Apo/diferrous state: loop partially disordered; His engaged in a salt bridge that suppresses basicity.
- Upon O2 activation (diferric-peroxo/oxo state): designed rearrangement breaks the suppressive salt bridge and forms a new H-bond network anchored to the oxidized diiron second shell, increasing His basicity and aligning the oxyanion hole.
3.3 Oxyanion hole: specify two backbone NHs plus a side-chain (Asn/Gln) positioned to stabilize the tetrahedral intermediate; validate by mutational knockdowns (Asn→Ala reduces kcat without changing O2 intermediate formation).

Step 4 — Assays that hard-wire falsifiable mechanism into selection and validation
4.1 Diiron intermediate assays (required for progression):
- Stopped-flow UV“vis kinetic traces consistent with peroxo/diferric formation and decay.
- Rapid-freeze-quench Mössbauer/EPR quantifying Fe(II)/Fe(III) populations and intermediate yield.
- O2 consumption stoichiometry vs Fe loading.
4.2 Acyl“enzyme detection (mandatory):
- Rapid-quench reactions with ester substrate followed by intact-protein MS for acyl adduct; confirm site by peptide LC“MS/MS.
- Time-resolved formation/decay of acyl“Ser to separate acylation vs deacylation rates.
4.3 Isotope tracing to distinguish hydrolysis vs oxidation:
- Run in H2(18)O: expect 18O incorporation into product carboxylate (hydrolytic deacylation).
- Run under 18O2 with unlabeled water: expect minimal 18O incorporation into product if O2 is gating rather than inserted.
- Solvent KIE (H2O/D2O) and optional 18O2 KIE: patterns must match hydrolytic chemistry; deviations trigger redesign.
4.4 Off-pathway oxidation quantification (mandatory negative validation):
- Proteomics for Met sulfoxide, Trp oxidation, Tyr dimerization, backbone carbonylation; set acceptance thresholds (e.g., <5% oxidized peptides under catalytic turnover conditions).
- Small-molecule side products by LC“MS to detect oxidative cleavage/oxygenation.
- ROS perturbation controls: catalase and SOD addition should not abolish esterase activity if coupling is intramolecularly gated; peroxide-clamp (exogenous H2O2) tests whether activity is due to free peroxide.

Step 5 — Directed evolution redesigned to avoid loss-of-function escape
5.1 Library design (focused, mechanistically partitioned):
- Set A: second-shell residues controlling peroxo/oxo lifetime and proton relay.
- Set B: loop/switch residues controlling oxidation-dependent ordering and His pKa.
- Set C: substrate channel residues controlling binding and exclusion of bulk water (to suppress uncoupled ROS chemistry).
5.2 Stage-1 gate (cannot be satisfied by inactivity): enforce expression and metallation normalization
- Express variants with a quantitative expression reporter (e.g., C-terminal fluorescent tag or standardized ELISA/Western quantitation) and discard low-expression variants.
- Enforce Fe loading criteria (ICP-MS on pooled lysates or plate-based colorimetric iron quantitation after purification) and discard under-metallated variants.
- Require a minimum O2-activation signature: plate-adapted O2-consumption kinetics or a diiron-state reporter signal must exceed a preset threshold before any survival/activity selection.
5.3 Stage-2 functional selection/screen with coupling metric:
- Primary screen: fluorogenic ester turnover.
- Coupling screen in parallel: quantify product/O2 and product/H2O2; prioritize variants maximizing product per O2 consumed and minimizing H2O2 leakage.
5.4 In vivo selection redesigned (two options; choose based on implementability):
Option 1 (preferred): prodrug-activation-linked survival—engineer a strain where growth depends on hydrolysis of an ester-masked essential nutrient/antibiotic-resistance precursor; this selects for productive esterase chemistry rather than merely low ROS.
Option 2 (if ROS filter retained): ROS-stress filter *with enforced activity gate*—apply oxidative-stress conditions but only after confirming expression/metallation and minimum diiron O2-activation; incorporate an orthogonal activity reporter so ‘safe but inactive’ cannot win.
5.5 Recombination: DNA shuffling among top performers within and across Sets A“C; re-screen under identical expression/metallation constraints.

Step 6 — Structural verification and metal-site specificity mapping
6.1 Metal-site specificity: Mössbauer/EPR titrations across Fe equivalents to map whether iron populates unintended sites; confirm dominant diiron population localized to engineered pocket.
6.2 Structures of key states: cryo-EM/X-ray of apo, diferrous-loaded, and O2-exposed forms where feasible; validate microbundle formation, ligand geometry, and catalytic loop ordering.

Step 7 — Biomedical/biotechnological proof-of-concept (only after mechanism validated)
7.1 Demonstrate selective ester prodrug activation under physiological-like buffers with ROS monitoring; include chelator and O2-depletion controls.
7.2 Cytocompatibility: mammalian cell oxidative-stress assays (e.g., H2O2 readouts, viability) alongside activity readouts; confirm that activity correlates with the diiron intermediate signature and acyl“Ser formation rather than generalized oxidation.
Feasibility: 1) Chemical plausibility is made falsifiable and measurable. The revised proposal no longer relies on an ambiguous “reversible covalent activation by Fe“O.” It commits to a canonical esterase pathway with a covalent acyl“Ser intermediate and specifies direct detection (rapid-quench + intact MS/peptide mapping), oxygen-source tracing (H2(18)O vs 18O2), and kinetic signatures (burst kinetics; solvent isotope effects). These tests will decisively distinguish hydrolysis via acyl“enzyme from oxidative cleavage or radical pathways.

2) Structural risks of the heme-pocket transplant are mitigated with explicit negative design plus validation.
