Hypothesis: Engineered, allosterically switchable PRC1 (“Opto-PRC1”) that couples a light-gated conformational clamp to RING1A/B E3 ligase positioning will enable causally separable control of (i) PRC1 chromatin-compaction/remodeling antagonism and (ii) H2AK119 ubiquitination, thereby producing tunable and reversible transcriptional repression with defined chromatin-structural trajectories. Mechanistically, forcing a controllable geometric proximity between RING1 (E2~Ub-loaded active site) and the H2A N-terminus on nucleosomes while independently modulating CBX/PHC-mediated chromatin bridging will allow us to disentangle and optimize two repression modes: steric inhibition of SWI/SNF-type remodeling (as suggested by PRC1/PCC effects on nucleosome organization) and enzymatic deposition of H2AK119ub that stabilizes Polycomb occupancy and propagates silencing. The methodological adaptation is a structural re-engineering of PRC1 subunit architecture: (a) insertion of an optogenetic dimerization module (iLID/SspB or CRY2/CIBN) between RING1 and a nucleosome-anchoring reader (CBX chromodomain or a minimal H3K27me3-binding module) to light-control RING1 residence time and orientation on chromatin; and (b) incorporation of a mechanically stiff, length-tunable helical linker (“molecular ruler”) plus a leucine-zipper clamp to bias the RING1“E2~Ub trajectory toward H2A Lys119, increasing catalytic efficiency only when the clamp is engaged. This guarantees superiority over constitutive recruitment because repression will be achieved at lower PRC1 abundance with fewer off-target chromatin interactions, and because the two mechanisms (compaction vs ubiquitination) can be orthogonally gated to determine which is necessary/sufficient for stable repression in mammalian cells.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a human cell model with Polycomb-dependent lineage programs (e.g., hESCs or AML cells with high PcG dependence) and generate a safe-harbor landing pad (AAVS1) for single-copy integration of Opto-PRC1 components under doxycycline control.
1.2 Establish dual reporters: (i) a PRC2-primed, H3K27me3-marked synthetic Polycomb response element upstream of a destabilized fluorescent gene; (ii) an endogenous locus readout (e.g., HOX cluster gene) tagged with MS2/PP7 nascent RNA imaging for real-time transcription.
1.3 Create RING1A/B-null or degron lines (auxin-inducible degron) to remove endogenous RING1 activity, ensuring repression arises from engineered complexes.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Build modular Opto-PRC1 variants:
- Variant A (Orientation-gated ubiquitination): RING1B fused to SspB; CBX7 (or CBX4) fused to iLID; between RING1B and SspB insert a rigid ER/K helical linker of defined length (e.g., 10, 20, 30 nm) and a conditional leucine-zipper clamp that engages only upon iLID/SspB binding, constraining the active-site approach to H2A.
- Variant B (Compaction-gated remodeling antagonism): PHC1/PHC2 SAM domain polymerization module fused to CRY2 for light-inducible oligomerization to enhance chromatin bridging independent of RING1 catalytic gating.
- Variant C (Orthogonal control): Combine A and B with distinct wavelengths (e.g., blue-light iLID; near-IR bacterial phytochrome BphP1/QPAS1) to independently toggle ubiquitination vs compaction.
2.2 Quantitatively map structure“function:
- Measure H2AK119ub kinetics at targeted loci using CUT&Tag time courses (minutes to hours) after light pulses; use catalytically dead RING1B (Cys-to-Ala in RING) as a control for compaction-only effects.
- Assay chromatin structure changes using Micro-C (nucleosome-level contacts), ATAC-seq (accessibility), and live-cell single-locus compaction via CRISPR-dCas9 fluorescent tagging.
- Challenge remodeling directly: recruit a defined SWI/SNF ATPase module (e.g., BRG1 tethered via dCas9) and quantify whether Opto-PRC1 compaction mode blocks remodeling without requiring H2AK119ub (inspired by PCC/PSC inhibition of hSWI/SNF).
2.3 Engineer catalytic efficiency and specificity:
- Perform focused mutagenesis on RING1B“BMI1/PCGF interface residues that tune E2 (UBCH5/UBCH6) engagement and test variants under the same light-gated geometry to identify combinations that maximize on-target H2AK119ub while minimizing global ubiquitination.
- Compare CBX paralogs (CBX2/4/6/7/8) as anchoring readers (reflecting distinct PRC1 compositions) to test how reader choice alters repression potency and off-target binding.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Causality decomposition: Use factorial designs (ubiquitination ON/OFF; compaction ON/OFF) and quantify transcriptional repression onset time, depth, and memory (persistence after light-off), separating immediate steric remodeling inhibition from longer-term epigenetic stabilization.
3.2 Proteomic validation: Use proximity labeling (TurboID fused to engineered subunits) during light ON vs OFF to confirm assembly states and to identify unintended interactors (e.g., 14-3-3 effects on CBX4-like behavior).
3.3 Off-target and safety profiling: Genome-wide CUT&Tag for H2AK119ub and CBX occupancy plus RNA-seq to quantify collateral repression; assess DNA damage and replication stress markers to ensure chromatin perturbation does not induce toxicity.
3.4 Translational test: In a cancer-relevant model (e.g., Polycomb-addicted lymphoma), evaluate whether transient Opto-PRC1-mediated silencing of a driver enhancer network induces differentiation/apoptosis more selectively than global PRC1 inhibition, using xenograft-compatible red-shifted gating modules for in vivo feasibility.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: PRC1 components (including RING1/dRING1) can directly inhibit chromatin remodeling and alter nucleosome configurations, and mammalian PRC1 exists as CBX-mutually exclusive assemblies with distinct repression potencies. RING1’s E3 ligase activity (H2AK119ub) and CBX chromodomain-mediated recognition of H3K27me3 provide natural, modular handles for engineered recruitment and mechanistic separation.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Optogenetic proximity control and rigid-linker “molecular ruler” strategies are established in protein engineering for controlling enzyme“substrate geometry; adapting them to PRC1 directly addresses a key limitation in epigenetic therapy/biology—current perturbations (knockouts or inhibitors) are global, slow, and confound enzymatic and structural roles. The proposed architecture converts PRC1 from a constitutive, multi-factorial regulator into a tunable bioengineered actuator suitable for causal biomedicine.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with standard CRISPRi (which recruits generic repressors) or pharmacologic PRC1 inhibition (global loss of function), Opto-PRC1 offers (i) orthogonal control of compaction vs ubiquitination, (ii) reversible, time-resolved perturbations to infer mechanism, (iii) enhanced on-target catalytic efficiency via enforced geometry reducing required expression levels, and (iv) the ability to select CBX paralog-specific complexes to match disease context and minimize off-target repression.

Hypothesis: A LOCKR fold-switching cage“latch architecture can be converted into a quantitatively gated, multi-turnover abzyme for activated ester hydrolysis by (i) designing a near-attack-conformation (NAC)“biased paratope rather than maximal transition-state-analog (TSA) affinity, (ii) enforcing switch-dependent dehydration and electric-field alignment within explicitly defined physical bounds, and (iii) optimizing backbone and sequence across OFF, ON“apo, and ON“substrate states using a multistate, backbone-first design pipeline. Mechanistically, ligand-induced latch docking completes a split catalytic triad (Ser“His“Asp) and simultaneously collapses a hydrophobic microcage that reduces local dielectric constant and aligns helix dipoles to generate an internal electric field of ~5“10 MV/cm along the scissile C=O bond. This field, combined with reduced water competition and precise NAC geometry, lowers ΔG‡ by ~1“2 kcal/mol relative to the OFF state. Critically, product release and turnover are preserved by designing weaker complementarity to the tetrahedral intermediate collapse/product state than to the NAC, thereby decoupling catalytic efficiency from excessively tight TSA binding.
Plan: Step 0: Kill-switch de-risking milestone (binding + switching only, no catalysis).
0.1 Engineer a LOCKR variant in which a TSA hapten for p-nitrophenyl acetate (PNPA) hydrolysis binds only in the ON state but with catalytic residues mutated to Ala.
0.2 Verify input-dependent switching and TSA binding via FRET (cage“latch distance), ITC (ΔGbind, ON vs OFF), and HDX-MS. Proceed only if ON/OFF binding ratio ≥50-fold and ΔGswitch ≤ “3 kcal/mol upon key addition.

Step 1: Reaction and kinetic targets.
1.1 Reaction class: activated ester hydrolysis (PNPA → p-nitrophenol + acetate) as a model for prodrug ester cleavage.
1.2 Substrate/TSA/product triad: PNPA (substrate), phosphonate monoester TSA (binds NAC geometry, not full tetrahedral intermediate), p-nitrophenol/acetate (product).
1.3 Quantitative targets: ON-state kcat/KM ≥ 10^3“10^4 M⁻¹ s⁻¹; OFF-state activity ≤1% of ON; product KD ≥10× weaker than substrate KD to ensure turnover.

Step 2: Structural hydration constraints and dehydration design.
2.1 Define ON-state hydration metrics: (i) no continuous solvent channel with probe radius >1.3 Å from bulk to catalytic Ser Oγ; (ii) ≤2 high-occupancy (>0.2) waters within 5 Å of the catalytic center as computed by GIST from 200 ns explicit-solvent MD; (iii) local dielectric constant ≤10 estimated from dipole fluctuation analysis.
2.2 OFF-state requirement: at least one continuous solvent pathway (>1.5 Å radius) to the catalytic center and ≥5 high-occupancy waters within 5 Å.
2.3 Implement an apolar gasket (Leu/Ile/Val/Phe) enclosing the pocket in ON, while allowing transient hydration in OFF via alternative latch register.

Step 3: Multistate backbone-first design protocol.
3.1 Backbone generation: SCUBA-inspired NN/statistical backbone sampling focused on latch helix docking groove and pocket volume, generating ~10^4 candidate backbones compatible with both docked (ON) and undocked (OFF) states.
3.2 Sequence design: Rosetta multistate design with three states (OFF“apo, ON“apo, ON“substrate/NAC). State weights: ON“substrate (0.5), ON“apo (0.3), OFF“apo (0.2). Hard constraints enforce violation of catalytic distances in OFF.
3.3 Acceptance thresholds: ΔGswitch ≤ “3 kcal/mol with key; RMSD between designed and MD-relaxed structures ≤2.0 Å; folding ΔΔG ≤2 kcal/mol in both states.

Step 4: Catalytic geometry and turnover engineering.
4.1 Place Ser nucleophile and oxyanion-hole NH donors on cage helices; His general base on latch helix; Asp positioned to stabilize His only in ON.
4.2 Encode ground-state strain/repulsion (e.g., steric clash with planar ester) and NAC complementarity to avoid over-stabilizing the TSA or product.

Step 5: Electrostatics quantification.
5.1 Introduce a nitrile probe adjacent to the oxyanion hole with known Stark tuning rate (~0.5“1 cm⁻¹ per MV/cm).
5.2 Pre-register target field change: ΔE ≥5 MV/cm between OFF and ON as measured by IR Stark spectroscopy.
5.3 Correlate field strength, hydration metrics, and kcat across a gasket-polarity mutant series to separate electrostatic effects from desolvation.

Step 6: Experimental validation.
6.1 Express and purify top designs; verify folding (CD), oligomeric state (SEC-MALS).
6.2 Measure switching (FRET, HDX-MS), hydration changes (MD-validated), and catalysis (steady-state kinetics).
6.3 Perform alanine scans and gasket mutations to test causal links between geometry, hydration, electric field, and rate.

Step 7: Cellular proof-of-concept.
7.1 Express switch extracellularly or on the cell surface; couple key to disease-relevant ligand.
7.2 Demonstrate input-gated prodrug ester activation in mammalian cells; benchmark against always-on designed enzyme.
Feasibility: This revised pipeline directly addresses reviewer-identified risks. Turnover is protected by NAC-biased rather than maximal TSA complementarity and by explicit product-release affinity targets, mitigating the classic abzyme trapping problem. Water exclusion is no longer assumed but enforced through hard, testable hydration metrics validated by explicit-solvent MD and dielectric analysis, ensuring compatibility with switching energetics. The multistate design protocol is grounded in a concrete SCUBA-inspired backbone generator coupled to Rosetta multistate sequence optimization with defined state weights and acceptance thresholds, reducing overfitting risk. Electrostatic claims are quantified a priori with explicit field targets and a nitrile Stark probe, enabling causal separation of electric-field effects from desolvation. Finally, the early kill-switch milestone (switching + TSA binding without catalysis) de-risks the central coupling logic before introducing chemical complexity. Together, these constraints convert the original concept into a falsifiable, quantitatively benchmarked engineering program that builds directly on established de novo scaffold electrostatics, backbone-first design, and LOCKR fold-switching principles.

Hypothesis: Endoglucanase thermostability can be increased by engineering a more dehydration-resistant and mechanically coupled hydrogen-bond network around the catalytic cleft, and this can be achieved more reliably than standard Rosetta-only or MD-only design by a methodological adaptation that (i) replaces generic stability scoring with an FTIR-calibrated secondary-structure/solvation constraint and (ii) uses Adaptive Biasing Force (ABF) to compute unfolding-initiating free-energy profiles for specific “weak modes” (β-strand peeling/loop opening) that are then directly penalized during ROSETTA sequence design. Mechanistically, thermostability improvement arises when mutations increase the free-energy barrier to the first irreversible unfolding events (local strand detachment and active-site loop opening) while preserving the catalytic geometry; the FTIR-calibrated constraint ensures that designed mutations maintain (or enhance) the experimentally observed helical/β content and hydration signatures under heat stress, preventing designs that score well in silico yet shift secondary structure in vitro.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a target endoglucanase scaffold (GH family appropriate for biomass conversion) with an available structure or AlphaFold model; define catalytic residues and substrate-binding cleft.
1.2 Build a sequence/structure comparative set via bioinformatics: mine amphibian (frog) skin microbiome metagenomes and amphibian-associated isolates for endoglucanase homologs; compute consensus motifs, coevolutionary couplings, and identify naturally enriched thermostability-associated features (salt-bridge patterns, proline distribution, aromatic clusters).
1.3 Express/purify a small panel: wild-type scaffold + 3“5 natural frog-associated homologs (or closest available homologs if direct frog isolates are limited). Record temperature-ramped FTIR (amide I/II) in H2O and D2O to quantify secondary-structure retention and hydration-shell changes (amide I peak deconvolution; H/D exchange kinetics).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 FTIR-to-constraint model (“Spectral Stability Prior”): fit a mapping from FTIR observables (fractional α/β content, unfolding onset temperature from amide I shifts, hydration sensitivity from H/D exchange rates) to structural descriptors (backbone H-bond counts, solvent-accessible backbone area, local packing/frustration indices) across the panel in 1.3. Convert this into residue-level soft constraints used in ROSETTA (e.g., penalize mutations predicted to increase solvent exposure of backbone in regions whose FTIR indicates heat-stable secondary structure; reward mutations increasing local H-bond cooperativity where FTIR shows early loss).
2.2 ABF “weak-mode barrier” computation: identify 2“3 dominant unfolding initiation coordinates using short high-temperature unbiased MD plus principal component/collective variable discovery (e.g., distance between β-strand pairs at the edge of the sheet, active-site loop opening angle, catalytic cleft mouth radius). For each coordinate, run ABF to obtain free-energy profiles (ΔG vs CV) for wild-type. Define target barrier increases (e.g., +2“4 kcal/mol) without altering catalytic geometry.
2.3 Rosetta design with ABF-informed objective (“Barrier-augmented Rosetta”): iterate design in localized regions implicated by ABF (sheet edges, loop hinges, helix caps). For each design batch:
- Use ROSETTA FastDesign with the Spectral Stability Prior (2.1) and functional constraints (active-site geometry and substrate docking constraints).
- Filter designs by rapid MD screening and re-run ABF on the same CVs to estimate barrier changes relative to wild-type.
- Select designs that increase barriers for at least two weak modes while keeping predicted binding/docking and catalytic residue geometry within preset RMSD tolerances.
2.4 Build a focused library for wet-lab: encode 20“60 top-ranked single and combinatorial mutations (including epistatic pairs suggested by coevolution and ABF sensitivity). Use site-directed mutagenesis and a small combinatorial library with degenerate codons at 3“6 positions.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Enzyme stability/thermostability assays: measure Tm (DSF/CD), half-life at process-relevant temperatures (e.g., 60“80°C depending on scaffold), and residual activity after heat challenge. Quantify kinetic parameters (kcat/KM) on CMC and/or defined cello-oligosaccharides to ensure no activity collapse.
3.2 FTIR validation under temperature ramps: confirm that improved variants show delayed amide I/II transitions, preserved secondary-structure signatures, and reduced hydration-shell destabilization (H/D exchange slower in protected regions). Compare against wild-type and against Rosetta-designed controls lacking the Spectral Stability Prior/ABF barrier objective.
3.3 Mechanism tests: map mutation effects onto structure; verify that stability gains correlate with ABF barrier increases and with FTIR-indicated secondary-structure retention. Use limited proteolysis or HDX-MS (optional) to corroborate reduced local unfolding at the ABF-identified weak modes.
3.4 Comparative benchmarking: head-to-head with (i) standard ROSETTA stability design (ΔΔG-only), (ii) consensus/consurf-guided mutagenesis, and (iii) directed evolution without mechanistic priors. Primary endpoint: thermostability at constant activity (e.g., ≥2“3× half-life increase at target temperature with ≤20% loss in kcat/KM).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 supports integrating bioinformatics, ROSETTA, and enhanced-sampling MD (including ABF) for stability engineering, but typical pipelines optimize static ΔΔG rather than barriers to unfolding initiation. Asset 2 demonstrates FTIR as a sensitive readout of thermally driven secondary-structure retention and hydration-linked stability mechanisms, motivating an FTIR-calibrated constraint rather than relying solely on in silico proxies.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Industrial biocatalysis needs enzymes that retain function at elevated temperatures; the adaptation directly targets the mechanistic bottleneck—early local unfolding events that precipitate global denaturation—while enforcing experimentally anchored secondary-structure behavior through FTIR-derived priors. Frog-associated biodiversity provides a realistic bioinformatics source of alternative stabilizing motifs shaped by amphibian microenvironments, feeding rational design.
3. Comparative Advantage: (i) ABF-derived barriers address kinetic stability (unfolding resistance) often missed by equilibrium scoring; (ii) FTIR-calibrated priors reduce false-positive designs that misfold or shift secondary structure despite favorable computed energies; (iii) focusing mutations on ABF-identified weak modes yields smaller, more efficient experimental libraries than unguided directed evolution, improving hit rate and preserving catalytic geometry.

Hypothesis: Engineering a structurally constrained, protease-resistant, allosterically coupled ω-transaminase from Comamonas testosteroni—using site-directed mutagenesis to install a designed “electrostatic clamp” at its dimer interface—will yield a biocatalyst whose catalytic competence is stabilized against trypsin-rich processing environments and whose flux in multistep biotransformation is increased by enforced productive oligomerization. Mechanism: (i) many fold-type I PLP-dependent transaminases rely on dimerization to correctly assemble the active-site architecture (PLP alignment, gate-loop positioning, and substrate-channel geometry); (ii) exposure to trypsin (e.g., during downstream processing, co-cultures, or protease-containing feedstocks) preferentially cleaves flexible, Lys/Arg-rich surface loops near subunit interfaces, shifting the conformational ensemble toward partially dissociated/loosely associated dimers with reduced kcat/KM; (iii) introducing a rationally designed network of complementary charges and short H-bonding motifs across the dimer interface (electrostatic clamp) increases the lifetime of the catalytically competent dimer while simultaneously removing/reshaping high-risk trypsin cleavage motifs on adjacent flexible loops. This adaptation is structurally novel because it replaces protease-gated activation concepts with an engineered, interface-level allosteric stabilization strategy that couples protein-protein interaction energetics directly to catalytic geometry and proteolytic robustness.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and structural risk mapping.
1) Select a well-characterized C. testosteroni ω-transaminase (ω-TA) used for chiral amine synthesis; generate a high-confidence structural model (crystal structure if available; otherwise AlphaFold2 with multimer mode) and identify the obligate dimer interface and adjacent flexible loops.
2) Perform in silico trypsin susceptibility mapping: predict solvent exposure and local disorder, then annotate Lys/Arg-containing motifs likely to be cleaved; experimentally verify baseline cleavage sites by limited proteolysis with trypsin followed by LC“MS/MS peptide mapping.
3) Quantify baseline protein-protein interaction strength (dimerization KD) and conformational stability (DSF/DSC), and establish baseline biotransformation performance in a representative multistep cascade (e.g., ketone → chiral amine via ω-TA with appropriate amine donor; optionally coupled to an upstream alcohol dehydrogenase step to supply the ketone).

Step 2: Methodological adaptation—interface electrostatic clamp + protease-risk reshaping via site-directed mutagenesis.
1) Design an “electrostatic clamp” across the native dimer interface: introduce paired charge networks (e.g., Asp/Glu↔Lys/Arg salt bridges) and short polar triads positioned to (a) increase inter-subunit residence time and (b) bias the interface toward the catalytically competent relative orientation. Candidate positions will be selected by Rosetta interface design with explicit constraints to preserve active-site geometry (PLP-binding residues and gate-loop contacts).
2) Concurrently redesign nearby flexible, trypsin-prone surface segments (not the active site) by conservative substitutions that remove exposed Lys/Arg at verified cleavage hotspots (e.g., Lys→Gln/Asn; Arg→Gln; or local helix-capping substitutions) while maintaining net surface properties needed for solubility. This is coupled to the clamp design to avoid destabilizing the interface.
3) Construct a focused mutant panel (single, combinatorial, and epistatic combinations) via site-directed mutagenesis; express and purify variants. Measure: dimerization KD (SEC-MALS and/or analytical ultracentrifugation), kinetics (kcat, KM for ketone and amine donor), PLP occupancy, and structural integrity (CD, DSF).
4) Test protease robustness explicitly: expose variants to physiologically relevant trypsin concentrations and time courses; quantify residual activity, cleavage patterns (LC“MS/MS), and dimer integrity post-challenge. The expected signature of success is preserved dimerization and unchanged active-site peptides despite extensive trypsin exposure.

Step 3: Rigorous validation in multistep biotransformation and mechanistic analysis.
1) Run the ω-TA within a defined multistep process where protease exposure is a realistic stressor (e.g., whole-cell lysate-based upstream step, protease-containing feedstock, or intentionally added trypsin challenge as a standardized “bioprocess proteolysis” condition). Compare WT vs best clamp variants for space“time yield, TTN, enantioselectivity, and operational half-life.
2) Mechanistic confirmation of allosteric coupling: perform hydrogen“deuterium exchange MS (HDX“MS) or limited proteolysis kinetics in the absence of trypsin to show reduced flexibility at interface-adjacent loops and stabilization of gate-loop conformations; optionally validate interface geometry via cryo-EM (if oligomeric) or X-ray crystallography for top variant.
3) Establish that improvements derive from engineered protein-protein interaction energetics rather than nonspecific stabilization by: (a) reversing key clamp charges (charge-swap controls) to abolish the effect; (b) testing performance across ionic strengths to demonstrate salt-bridge dependence; and (c) correlating dimer KD with catalytic metrics and protease resistance using a quantitative structure“function model.
4) Deliverables: a protease-robust ω-TA variant and a design rule-set linking PPI interface electrostatics → active-site geometry → multistep biotransformation performance under proteolytic stress.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: ω-transaminases are commonly obligate dimers where interface integrity impacts active-site assembly; electrostatic interface engineering is a proven protein design lever for tuning complex stability. Trypsin cleavage is strongly enriched at exposed Lys/Arg in flexible regions, and limited proteolysis coupled to MS is a mature workflow for pinpointing liabilities. 
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal directly links protein-protein interaction engineering (dimer-interface energetics) to enzyme performance as a microbial biocatalyst in biotransformation, addressing a process-relevant failure mode (proteolytic destabilization) without relying on protease-mediated activation schemes. Site-directed mutagenesis is the enabling technique for precise interface and cleavage-site remodeling. 
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to standard activity-focused mutagenesis or generic thermostabilization, the electrostatic clamp is a mechanistically targeted adaptation that simultaneously (a) enforces the catalytically competent oligomeric state and (b) reduces trypsin vulnerability at structurally critical regions. This yields higher sustained flux and reliability in multistep processes where proteases or proteolytic impurities otherwise erode enzyme lifetime and selectivity.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that *surface- and pore-mouth“restricted* microbial transglutaminase (mTG)-catalyzed isopeptide ligation can be engineered into a quantitatively tunable “mechanical clutch” between Candida rugosa lipase (CRL) and a water-stable, amine-presenting ZIF-8/calix-modified MOF, such that (i) defined attachment *valency* (2“4 Gln-donor motifs per enzyme) and (ii) defined *spacer compliance/length* (short alkyl vs PEGn amines on the MOF exterior) jointly stabilize productive catalytic microstates while preserving the lid’s interfacial activation dynamics. Mechanistically, we posit that multipoint anchoring on the MOF *external surface and pore entrances only* suppresses global unfolding, desorption, and non-productive reorientation under shear/solvent/temperature, while compliant spacers maintain the conformational entropy needed for lid opening/closing and substrate ingress. This yields a measurable design map linking (A) conjugation stoichiometry (bonds per enzyme), (B) tether compliance (force“extension/rupture distributions), and (C) lid-dynamics readouts (HDX-MS protection patterns) to functional outcomes (kcat, Km, E-value, reuse half-life).
Plan: Step 0 — Fix the immobilization geometry (surface/pore-mouth only) and material selection gates.
0.1 Geometry decision: Restrict CRL immobilization to MOF *external surface and pore mouths*; do not claim full pore encapsulation because mTG (~38 kDa) cannot access ZIF-8 micropores. The “nanoreactor” is therefore defined as an external catalytic shell with pore-mouth substrate preconcentration (calix) and surface-confined enzymes.
0.2 MOF size and morphology: Synthesize ZIF-8/calix particles in a size range enabling high external area (e.g., 50“200 nm) and high dispersion; confirm morphology by TEM/SEM and hydrodynamic size (DLS).
0.3 Water/buffer stability pre-screen (no enzyme yet): Incubate MOF in candidate mTG buffers (e.g., Tris or HEPES, low-phosphate, moderate ionic strength) across pH 6.0“8.0; exclude phosphate-rich buffers. Gate with PXRD (crystallinity retention), N2 sorption (surface area/porosity retention), ICP-OES (Zn leaching), and ligand release assays. Lock a single buffer/pH condition that preserves MOF structure and supports mTG activity.

Step 1 — Engineer true multipoint, controlled-valency CRL variants without perturbing lid/active site.
1.1 Tag architecture: Create a small panel of CRL constructs containing 2, 3, or 4 spatially separated Gln-donor motifs (e.g., short Q-rich mTG-recognition peptides) placed on solvent-exposed regions *distal from the lid and active-site vicinity*. Include a single-tag construct as a low-valency comparator.
1.2 Placement rationale: Use structural modeling + MD to (i) identify high-SASA loops opposite the lid face, (ii) avoid known interfacial activation surfaces, and (iii) maximize inter-tag spatial separation (to support multipoint anchoring rather than clustered single-point ligation).
1.3 Expression/quality control: Confirm folding and baseline activity (free enzyme) using standard ester hydrolysis assays; verify that lid dynamics are not grossly altered pre-immobilization via HDX-MS baseline maps (free WT vs engineered).

Step 2 — Build amine-presenting MOF surfaces with explicit spacer compliance as a design variable.
2.1 Surface-functional amines (acceptors): Introduce primary amines on ZIF-8/calix MOF *external surfaces* via (a) post-synthetic modification of surface-accessible linkers or (b) mixed-linker growth incorporating a low fraction of amine-bearing imidazole derivatives, with explicit checks that crystallinity/porosity is preserved.
2.2 Spacer series (compliance/length): Prepare at least three acceptor chemistries on otherwise matched MOFs:
  - Short/rigid: “(CH2)2“NH2
  - Medium: PEG4“NH2
  - Long/compliant: PEG12“NH2
Quantify amine density by colorimetric/fluorometric amine assays and XPS/N content; keep amine densities within a controlled window across variants.
2.3 Critical negative control surfaces:
  - “Amine-minus” MOF (no acceptor amines)
  - “Blocked-amine” MOF (amine-capped with an inert acylation reagent to retain similar surface chemistry but eliminate mTG acceptors)

Step 3 — mTG-mediated ligation constrained to the external surface: quantify geometry and stoichiometry.
3.1 Ligation reaction: Perform immobilization under the pre-selected MOF-stable, mTG-compatible buffer. Maintain conditions that minimize MOF degradation and nonspecific adsorption (ionic strength tuning; optional mild nonionic additives if compatible).
3.2 Control matrix (mandatory attribution controls):
  - CRL(Q-tag+) + amine+ MOF + mTG (test)
  - CRL(Q-tag+) + amine+ MOF “ mTG (adsorption control)
  - CRL(Q-tag“/WT) + amine+ MOF + mTG (enzyme control)
  - CRL(Q-tag+) + amine“ MOF + mTG (material control)
  - CRL(Q-tag+) + blocked-amine MOF + mTG (acceptor-block control)
3.3 Conjugation stoichiometry and valency readout:
  - SDS-PAGE densitometry of supernatant depletion + wash fractions (immobilization yield)
  - Intact MS (where feasible) and/or peptide mapping to confirm isopeptide formation
  - Quantify average number of covalent attachments per enzyme indirectly by combining (i) remaining free amines on the MOF post-ligation, (ii) enzyme loading, and (iii) MS mapping of modified Gln sites (report as “effective valency”).
3.4 Enzyme leaching assay: Challenge immobilized catalysts under catalytic buffers/solvents and quantify released protein (BCA/fluorescence) vs time; compare covalent vs adsorption controls.

Step 4 — Replace qualitative “elasticity” with measurable mechanical parameters (force spectroscopy) and link to catalysis.
4.1 Single-molecule/single-particle force readouts:
  - Use AFM-based single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) or single-particle pulling (as available) to measure tether rupture forces and force“extension profiles across spacer series and valency variants.
  - Report distributions (median rupture force, contour-length signatures for PEG linkers) as operational compliance metrics.
4.2 Nanoindentation (ensemble mechanical resilience): AFM nanoindentation of MOF particles pre/post functionalization and after buffer exposure to ensure material robustness is not confounded by structural collapse.

Step 5 — Pre-registered causal test of lid preservation: dynamics“function correlation across a 2D design matrix.
5.1 Design matrix: Systematically vary (A) valency (1 vs 2 vs 3“4 Gln motifs) and (B) spacer compliance (short vs PEG4 vs PEG12) to create a matrix of immobilized catalysts with quantified stoichiometry.
5.2 HDX-MS as the causal mechanistic readout:
  - Map deuterium uptake changes in lid-associated peptides and global scaffolding regions for each matrix condition.
  - Define a priori “lid preservation score” (e.g., minimal perturbation in lid peptides relative to free enzyme while showing increased protection in non-lid stabilizing regions).
5.3 Functional assays (matched conditions):
  - Determine kcat, Km, kcat/Km on model ester substrates.
  - Determine enantioselectivity (E value) using kinetic resolution of naproxen methyl ester (benchmark against CRL@ZIF-8 and CRL@Calix-ZIF-8 literature baselines).
  - Reusability: activity retention over ≥6 cycles; report half-life under thermal/alkaline stress.
5.4 Statistical linkage: Correlate (i) lid preservation score and (ii) mechanical compliance metrics with catalytic outputs. Hypothesis: A Rosetta-based protein design workflow that is structurally adapted to explicitly model coiled-coil registry shifts and helix-fraying penalties during binding will produce alpha-helical coiled-coil pairs with substantially higher partner specificity (reduced off-target hetero-association) than standard fixed-backbone or static-oligomer Rosetta design. Mechanistically, enforcing an explicit energetic separation between (i) the intended heptad registry and (ii) nearby alternative registries/oligomerization states, while simultaneously penalizing terminal fraying and buried unsatisfied polar groups, increases the free-energy gap (ΔΔGgap) between on-target and off-target bound ensembles; this gap—not just absolute stability—drives orthogonality in crowded cellular environments and improves functional performance for biomedical heterodimerization (e.g., split-protein therapeutics, targeted recruitment modules).
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1. Curate a benchmark set of natural and de novo coiled-coils with known oligomeric state and partner specificity (including known promiscuous pairs) and standardize constructs (length, terminal caps) to quantify off-target binding.
2. Define design targets: (a) obligate heterodimers (A/B) and (b) orthogonal sets (A1/B1, A2/B2, …) intended to function as interaction modules in mammalian cells.
3. Build a Rosetta modeling library of alternative bound states for each target: enumerate ±1, ±2 heptad registry shifts, alternative oligomeric states (dimer vs trimer/tetramer where plausible), and homodimeric alternatives (A/A, B/B). Generate ensembles with small backbone flexibility (backrub + helix-parameter sampling) rather than a single rigid backbone.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
4. Methodological Adaptation (multi-state registry/oligomer explicit design): Modify the standard RosettaDesign objective into a competitive multi-state optimization across an ensemble of bound states.
   - Positive state: intended A/B heterodimer at the intended registry.
   - Negative states: (i) registry-shifted A/B, (ii) A/A and B/B homodimers, (iii) alternative oligomers (e.g., trimeric bundle), and (iv) partially frayed terminal states.
   - Optimize a gap-based objective: minimize E(on-target) while maximizing min{E(negative states)} using a weighted “free-energy gap” score ΔΔGgap = E(on-target) − min(E(negative)).
5. Add a helix-fraying and end-capping term to the Rosetta score for coiled-coils: explicitly penalize exposed backbone H-bond donors/acceptors at helix termini in bound and unbound ensembles; implement terminal capping motifs (e.g., Asn/Asp at N-cap; Gly at C-cap when appropriate) as designable but constrained positions.
6. Enforce buried-polar satisfaction constraints at a/d core positions: if polar residues are placed in the hydrophobic core for specificity, require explicit intra-/inter-helical H-bonding geometry or salt-bridge networks; otherwise apply a strong penalty. This reduces “false-specific” designs that become promiscuous by accommodating water or alternative registries.
7. Rational coiled-coil heptad encoding: constrain a/d positions to hydrophobics with periodic exceptions for specificity; tune e/g electrostatics to create complementary charge patterns that are registry-sensitive (i.e., charge pairing only in the correct registry). Use Rosetta constraint files to limit design search to biophysically plausible coiled-coil grammar while still permitting innovation.
8. Design and downselect candidates by: (i) predicted ΔΔGgap across enumerated negative states, (ii) predicted melting temperature proxy (monomer and dimer stability), (iii) predicted assembly state (avoid higher-order collapse), and (iv) sequence complexity filters to reduce aggregation.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
9. Biophysical validation in vitro: synthesize peptides/proteins; quantify secondary structure (CD spectroscopy), thermal stability (CD melt/DSC), oligomeric state (SEC-MALS/AUC), and binding thermodynamics (ITC) for on-target and key off-target pairs.
10. Specificity matrix: perform a full cross-pairing assay for orthogonal sets using fluorescence anisotropy or FRET-based binding to measure Kd across all combinations; compute an “orthogonality index” = Kd(off-target)/Kd(on-target).
11. Mechanism checks: test registry-shift susceptibility by inserting single-residue indels or using designed ‘registry reporter’ mutations; verify that off-target states predicted by the ensemble are disfavored experimentally.
12. Biomedical demonstration: implement coiled-coil modules as heterodimerization tags to reconstitute a split therapeutic payload (e.g., split cytokine agonist or split transcriptional activator) in mammalian cells; quantify dose“response, off-target activation, and stability in serum.
13. Iteration loop: feed experimental negatives back into the multi-state ensemble (add newly observed off-target modes) and re-run design to further widen ΔΔGgap.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Coiled-coil specificity is known to be governed by heptad register, electrostatic complementarity (e/g positions), and core packing (a/d). Promiscuity often arises from alternative registries and oligomeric states that are close in energy; therefore, explicitly optimizing the energy gap across these competing states is a principled route to orthogonality. The provided literature assets support the maturation of de novo protein design toward computational frameworks (Rosetta) while retaining rational constraints, and highlight coiled-coils as a tractable motif built from alpha-helices.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Biomedical coiled-coil modules must work in complex cellular milieus where many off-target interactions exist and concentration varies. Designing for absolute stability alone is insufficient; widening the on-target/off-target free-energy gap is directly aligned with therapeutic safety (reducing unintended pathway activation) and robustness (consistent assembly under variable expression).
3. Comparative Advantage: Standard Rosetta coiled-coil design often assumes a single intended bound geometry; it can inadvertently create sequences compatible with alternative registries or higher-order bundles. The proposed adaptation (multi-state registry/oligomer explicit design + fraying and polar-satisfaction constraints) converts the design problem into a competitive specificity optimization, yielding designs expected to outperform conventional approaches in orthogonality matrices and in-cell functional selectivity, not merely in melting temperature.

Hypothesis: A charge-programmable Fe/ZIF-8@cellulose aerogel, engineered by (i) quantitatively controlled polyelectrolyte grafting to set the pH-dependent interfacial potential and (ii) Fe-site redox/coordination tuning to introduce fluoride-reactive Lewis-acid sites, will enable *binding-mode-selective* capture of (A) tetracycline predominantly via saturable, site-limited interactions (Fe-chelation + H-bonding/π“π at ZIF/cellulose domains) and (B) fluoride via a mechanistic transition from outer-sphere electrostatic accumulation to inner-sphere Fe“F complexation depending on Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio and pH. The key mechanistic advance over isotherm-only inference is that adsorption ‘regime switching’ will be demonstrated by direct signatures of (1) tetracycline functional-group coordination/hydrogen bonding without Fe“F formation, and (2) fluoride inner-sphere Fe“F coordination (EXAFS/XPS) with distinct thermodynamic fingerprints (ITC enthalpy/entropy) and kinetic/transport diagnostics that rule out mass-transfer artifacts. Rather than presuming Langmuir vs Freundlich as proof, the proposal predicts: (i) tetracycline adsorption will exhibit apparent site saturation when Fe-accessible chelation sites are limiting and zeta potential is tuned to minimize nonspecific electrostatic partitioning at the selected operating pH, and (ii) fluoride adsorption will exhibit greater site-energy heterogeneity when polyelectrolyte domains create distributed electrostatic microenvironments and when Fe“F complexation occurs across non-equivalent Fe sites created by Fe2+/Fe3+ tuning—validated by operando spectroscopy and calorimetry alongside rigorous controls and stability/leaching constraints required for biomedical water-treatment applicability.
Plan: Step 0 — Quantitative design targets and speciation map (pre-registered before synthesis)
0.1 Define operating windows and explicit targets:
- pH windows: 5.5“8.5 (antibiotic-relevant wastewater) and 6.0“7.5 (defluoridation near neutral; avoids extreme ZIF-8 instability).
- Ionic strength windows: 1“50 mM (NaCl background) with defined competition sets: Cl−/HCO3−/SO42−/PO43− (fluoride) and NOM/proteins (biomedical relevance).
- Zeta potential targets (measured as ζ(pH) curves):
  • “TC-mode”: near-neutral or mildly negative surface at pH 7.0 (ζ = −5 to −15 mV) to reduce purely electrostatic uptake and emphasize saturable Fe-chelation/H-bonding.
  • “F-mode”: net positive or charge-patchy surface at pH 6.5“7.0 (ζ = +10 to +25 mV) to preconcentrate F− near Fe sites.
- Grafting density targets (quantified): 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 mmol ionic groups per g aerogel (three discrete tiers), chosen to span the ζ targets while avoiding pore occlusion.
- Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio targets in Fe/ZIF-8 nodes: 80/20, 50/50, 20/80 (verified by Mössbauer/XPS), selected to test fluoride inner-sphere binding propensity vs stability.
0.2 Compute/compile speciation guidance:
- Tetracycline charge-state distribution vs pH (cationic/zwitterionic/anionic fractions) using literature pKa values; choose two diagnostic pH points (e.g., pH 6.0 and 8.0) where TC functional groups change protonation to stress-test mechanism.
- Fluoride competition/speciation: include bicarbonate/phosphate at realistic levels; explicitly track free F− by ion-selective electrode (ISE) and confirm with ion chromatography (IC) in selected conditions.

Step 1 — Material bioengineering with architectural controls
1.1 Base scaffold and MOF integration:
- Fabricate cellulose aerogels with defined porosity (target: macroporous network for flow; BET/porosimetry for micro/mesopore retention).
- In situ growth or impregnation of ZIF-8 nanocrystals followed by Fe incorporation (Fe-doping) while maintaining crystallinity; characterize via XRD, SEM/TEM, BET.
1.2 Fe-site coordination/redox tuning (mechanism-linked):
- Implement controlled Fe incorporation routes that bias Fe2+ vs Fe3+ (e.g., precursor choice + post-synthetic redox conditioning), then lock-in with mild treatments to prevent drift during adsorption.
- Verify Fe chemical state and coordination environment: Mössbauer (Fe2+/Fe3+ quant), XPS (Fe 2p shifts), and Fe K-edge XAS/EXAFS (first-shell coordination; baseline Fe“N/O distances).
1.3 Polyelectrolyte grafting with quantified density and spatial distribution:
- Graft zwitterionic sulfobetaine-containing copolymers with chitosan backbone (CS“SB) onto cellulose via covalent coupling (e.g., carbodiimide/epoxide strategy, selected for aqueous stability), generating charge-regulating domains.
- Quantify grafting density (elemental analysis/S, N content; polyelectrolyte mass gain; titration of accessible groups).
- Map ζ(pH) and point of zero charge (pHPZC) for each tier; reject formulations failing the ζ targets.
1.4 Transport-preserving architecture checks (prevents false “isotherm switching”):
- Measure permeability/flow-through pressure drop; assess pore accessibility with probe uptake (e.g., neutral dye) and BET changes. Down-select formulations that maintain ≥70% of baseline permeability and avoid severe pore blocking.

Step 2 — Mechanism-discriminating adsorption experiments (not model-fitting-driven)
2.1 Rigorous control matrix (mandatory):
- C1: ZIF-8@cellulose (no Fe, no grafting)
- C2: Fe/ZIF-8@cellulose (Fe, no grafting)
- C3: grafted cellulose aerogel (grafting, no MOF/Fe)
- C4: grafted ZIF-8@cellulose (grafting, no Fe)
- Test articles: grafted Fe/ZIF-8@cellulose at each Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio and grafting density tier.
2.2 Tetracycline binding mechanism verification:
- Operando ATR-FTIR/Raman during TC exposure: track shifts/intensity changes in TC amide/phenolic/enol/ketone bands indicative of chelation and H-bonding; compare with controls to isolate Fe-site contribution.
- XPS (N 1s/O 1s and Fe 2p) pre/post TC to detect coordination-induced shifts.
- ITC (isothermal titration calorimetry): quantify ΔH, ΔS, and stoichiometry (n) for TC binding across pH 6.0 and 8.0; electrostatic-dominated binding should show stronger salt dependence and smaller site-specific stoichiometry signatures than chelation-dominated binding.
- Salt-dependence test: measure TC uptake at 1, 10, 50 mM ionic strength; disproportionately reduced uptake indicates electrostatic partitioning, whereas preserved uptake supports specific coordination/H-bonding.
2.3 Fluoride binding mechanism verification:
- Fe K-edge XAS/EXAFS pre/post F exposure to directly detect Fe“F first-shell contributions (bond distance/coordination number changes) distinguishing inner-sphere complexation from outer-sphere accumulation.
- XPS F 1s and Fe 2p shifts + depth profiling (where appropriate) to confirm chemical association.
- Complementary solid-state NMR where feasible (e.g., 19F MAS NMR) to distinguish bound vs free fluoride environments (presence/shift/broadening relative to aqueous F−).
- ITC for fluoride: distinguish enthalpy-driven inner-sphere complexation vs entropy-driven electrostatic adsorption; repeat under competing anions (HCO3−/SO42−/PO43−) to quantify mechanism robustness.
2.4 Adsorption performance mapping with selectivity metrics:
- Conduct batch isotherms only after mechanism verification, across pre-defined concentration ranges relevant to contamination (TC: low mg/L to tens mg/L; F−: 1“20 mg/L typical plus stress up to higher).
- Fit Langmuir/Freundlich as *descriptors*, but interpret only alongside spectroscopy/ITC and transport modeling.

- Collect time-resolved uptake curves under well-mixed and flow-through conditions.
- Fit pseudo-second-order and intraparticle diffusion (Weber“Morris) models; identify rate-limiting steps.
- Vary particle/aerogel thickness and flow rate to test if “isotherm changes” correlate with diffusion limitations (a red flag).
3.2 Pore accessibility and fouling diagnostics:
- Quantify pore blocking by polyelectrolytes and by adsorbates (TC/NOM) via BET change, confocal mapping (if fluorescent TC analog available), and breakthrough curve shape analysis.

- Monitor ZIF integrity (XRD), surface area, and morphology after exposure at pH 5.5“8.5 with bicarbonate/phosphate.
- Define fail criteria: loss of crystallinity beyond a set threshold; severe surface area collapse; irreversible performance loss.
4.2 Metal leaching control (critical for biomedical framing):
- Quantify Zn and Fe leachates by ICP-MS under all operating conditions and regeneration steps; include time-dependent release.
- Define acceptance thresholds a priori (aligned to intended exposure route; at minimum, demonstrate substantial suppression vs ungrafted controls and provide risk rationale).
4.3 Biomedical relevance endpoints with explicit metrics:
- Endotoxin (LPS) removal: quantify via LAL assay; set a target threshold appropriate for treated water intended for biomedical/lab use (report EU/mL before/after).
- Cytocompatibility: define extract testing conditions and endpoints (e.g., viability assays on a relevant mammalian cell line) using leachate extracts; pass/fail criteria predetermined.
4.4 Regeneration with mild triggers and mechanism retention:
- Regenerate via controlled ionic strength/pH pulses (e.g., moderate salt for electrostatic release; mild pH shift within ZIF stability window).
- After each cycle: re-measure ζ(pH), Fe speciation (quick XPS spot-check), and key binding spectral signatures to prove mechanistic reversibility rather than mere capacity retention.

Step 5 — Integrated demonstration in realistic matrices
- Simulated pharmaceutical wastewater: TC + NOM + mixed anions; quantify removal, selectivity, and breakthrough in a column configuration.
- Defluoridation matrix: F− with bicarbonate/phosphate; quantify free fluoride reduction to guideline-relevant levels.
- Report performance with uncertainty and replicate counts; provide a decision matrix linking formulation parameters (ζ targets, graft density, Fe2+/Fe3+) to mechanism readouts (spectroscopy/ITC) and to application metrics (selectivity, stability, leaching).
Feasibility: Mechanistic grounding beyond isotherm preference: The plan pre-registers quantitative material targets (ζ(pH), graft density, Fe2+/Fe3+) and directly tests predicted binding motifs using operando ATR-FTIR/Raman (TC functional groups), Fe K-edge XAS/EXAFS + XPS/19F NMR (Fe“F inner-sphere evidence), and ITC to separate electrostatic partitioning from specific coordination via thermodynamic signatures and salt-dependence. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: hPSC-to-renal differentiation under defined morphogens can yield CITED1+ progenitor populations and renal cell types suitable for drug testing; PSC gene regulatory networks exhibit state transitions that are highly sensitive to timed transcription factor perturbations, and Cdx2 is a known driver of distinct fate attractors whose effects depend on signal context and duration.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation imports a control-systems principle (pulse-width modulation with feedback) into developmental bioengineering by converting a static TF perturbation into a precisely timed, quantitatively tunable input that reshapes chromatin and lineage competence. Using CRISPRa avoids permanent genome rewiring and enables reversible, titratable activation compatible with manufacturing and screening workflows.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to morphogen-only protocols, the Cdx2-pulse circuit is designed to (i) reduce stochastic entry into competing lineages by synchronizing early competence, (ii) expand and stabilize the CITED1+ progenitor reservoir (higher yield, lower variance), and (iii) improve downstream drug-screen signal-to-noise and cross-batch reproducibility, directly addressing a core limitation of PSC-derived renal models for high-throughput nephrotoxicity screening.

Hypothesis: PSC-RANTES produces unusually durable CCR5 down-modulation because it shifts post-endocytic fate at a defined sorting checkpoint: after canonical β-arrestin/AP-2/clathrin internalization, PSC-RANTES“phosphorylated CCR5 preferentially engages an endosome-to-TGN retrieval axis composed of the retromer core (VPS35“VPS26“VPS29) plus a restricted set of SNX adaptors (primary candidates: SNX27; secondary candidates: SNX1/2 with SNX5/6; and WASH/FAM21 as the actin-polymerization effector). This retrieval engagement diverts CCR5 away from Rab4/Rab11-mediated recycling and/or degradative routing, producing TGN sequestration that is functionally equivalent to long-lived desensitization (reduced surface receptor, impaired resensitization).

Mechanistic rationale addressing reviewer gaps: (i) retromer does not typically bind GPCRs directly—cargo selection is frequently mediated by SNX adaptors and sequence motifs (e.g., PDZ-binding for SNX27 cargos) and can be strongly modulated by receptor phosphorylation “barcodes” that control adaptor handoff; thus we pre-specify SNX nodes and explicitly test whether CCR5 uses an SNX27-like PDZ module or an SNX-BAR/WASH-dependent pathway. (ii) TGN sequestration will be distinguished from generic endosomal retention by orthogonal evidence: time-resolved colocalization with TGN markers and retrieval intermediates, functional dependence on VPS35/SNX/WASH, and demonstration of increased endosome→TGN flux (not merely slowed recycling). (iii) The engineered ‘sorting switch’ will be designed to be phosphorylation-gated without constitutive binding by separating (a) a GRK2/3-tuned phospho-acceptor cassette that is only modified under agonist-activated CCR5, from (b) a docking module whose affinity is masked until phosphorylation triggers a local conformational/charge change; additionally, a failsafe inducible-recruitment variant will be included to enforce conditionality if phospho-gating is leaky.

For the CXCR4 arm, we do not assume generic clathrin/AP-2 scarcity. Instead, we test a quantitative ‘shared-node competition’ model at the specific retrieval/sorting layer (retromer/SNX/WASH) and in parallel test alternative cross-desensitization mechanisms (GRK/β-arrestin redistribution, kinase sequestration, endosomal signaling cross-talk). We predict that heterologous CXCR4 desensitization—if present—will scale with measurable occupancy/saturation of shared sorting effectors (β-arrestin-2 and/or retromer/WASH) rather than bulk clathrin/AP-2, and that selective replenishment of the limiting node will rescue CXCR4 responsiveness.
Plan: Step 0 — Engineering acceptance gates (prevents misinterpretation of ‘handoff’):
0.1 Construct strategy: endogenous-locus CCR5 and CXCR4 CRISPR knock-in in Jurkat-derived CD4+ T cell“like cells (and HEK293 as imaging-optimized control) using minimal tags: (i) an extracellular 1× HA or ALFA epitope in the N-terminus for pulse-chase surface labeling (inserted after signal peptide to preserve trafficking), (ii) a small intracellular tag for proximity labeling (TurboID-mini or APEX2) fused to the C-terminus via a flexible (GGGGS)2 linker, and (iii) optional HaloTag on a subset of constructs only in HEK293 for single-particle tracking. All edits will be heterozygous first, then homozygous only if acceptance gates pass.
0.2 Acceptance gates for every CCR5 ‘switch’ variant (must pass all before trafficking interpretation):
  - Surface expression: flow cytometry with anti-HA/ALFA at 4°C; acceptance ≥70% of WT median fluorescence (endogenous WT knock-in control).
  - Ligand binding: fluorescent CCL5 and PSC-RANTES binding (or radioligand if available); acceptance: KD within 3× of WT and saturable binding.
  - G-protein coupling: acute Gi signaling (cAMP suppression assay) and Ca2+ flux; acceptance: Emax ≥70% of WT for CCL5 and PSC-RANTES; potency shift ≤5×.
  - β-arrestin recruitment: NanoBiT or BRET (CCR5“SmBiT / β-arrestin2“LgBiT or equivalent); acceptance: PSC-RANTES produces robust recruitment comparable to WT (≥70% AUC), and CCL5 recruitment is not artificially abolished.
  - Basal activity/leakiness: basal internalization and basal β-arrestin signal must be ≤1.5× WT.

Step 1 — Mechanistically discriminative trafficking map with explicit TGN-retrieval nodes:
1.1 Compartment markers (imaging + biochemical fractionation):
  - Internalization: clathrin light chain (CLTA) and AP2M1; early endosome: EEA1/Rab5; recycling: Rab4/Rab11; late endosome/lysosome: Rab7/LAMP1; TGN: TGN46 and Golgin-97; endosome-to-TGN retrieval intermediates: SNX6 (SNX-BAR), SNX27, VPS35, FAM21 (WASH complex).
1.2 Stimulation design: PSC-RANTES vs CCL5 matched by receptor occupancy (dose normalized to equal initial β-arrestin recruitment AUC to separate trafficking effects from different activation magnitudes). Time course: 0, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 90, 180 min; washout + recovery: 1, 2, 4, 8, 24 h.
1.3 Quantification: automated segmentation with per-receptor ‘fate fractions’ (surface, EE, recycling endosome, TGN, lysosome). Include a kinetic compartmental model with explicit endosome→TGN flux term (k_ETGN) distinct from recycling (k_ER) and degradation (k_ED). Model selection will compare: (A) increased k_ETGN, (B) decreased k_ER, (C) increased k_internalization only.
1.4 Orthogonal validation that signal is true TGN retrieval (not generic retention):
  - Brefeldin A (Golgi/TGN disruption) and temperature block (20°C) assays to perturb TGN trafficking; predict loss of PSC-RANTES-induced ‘TGN accumulation’ if it is genuine retrieval.
  - Endosome-to-TGN cargo control (e.g., CI-MPR) co-trafficking behavior to benchmark retrieval pathway integrity.

Step 2 — Pre-specified candidate TGN-sorting nodes and epistasis logic (mandatory directive #1):
2.1 Candidate node list (tested in a defined order):
  - Retromer core: VPS35, VPS26A/B, VPS29.
  - SNX adaptors:
    (Primary) SNX27 (PDZ-domain cargo adaptor often linked to recycling and retromer coupling; tested for CCR5 engagement via engineered PDZ-binding options and endogenous association).
    (Secondary) SNX1/2 with SNX5/6 (SNX-BAR tubulation module associated with retromer-mediated retrieval) and the WASH complex (FAM21) as effector.
  - Controls/alternates: GGA adaptors and AP-1 (TGN sorting), to ensure the phenotype is retrieval-specific rather than generic TGN retention.
2.2 Perturbation architecture:
  - Acute depletion: AID2 (auxin-inducible degron) or dTAG on VPS35 and SNX27 (fast, reversible) in HEK293; inducible CRISPRi (dCas9-KRAB) in Jurkat-like cells for longer assays.
  - Epistasis design: For each perturbation, measure (i) CCR5 internalization rate (k_int), (ii) k_ETGN (from model), (iii) TGN colocalization fraction at 40“180 min, (iv) surface recovery half-life post-washout.
  - Decision criteria:
    *If PSC-RANTES phenotype requires VPS35 and SNX6/WASH (but not SNX27):* supports SNX-BAR/WASH tubulation retrieval route.
    *If requires SNX27 and VPS35:* supports SNX27-retromer cargo adaptor mechanism.
    *If independent of retromer/SNX but sensitive to AP-1/GGA:* suggests alternative TGN sorting not retromer retrieval.
2.3 Interaction validation (co-IP + proximity labeling with time-window control):
  - Proximity labeling: CCR5-miniTurboID or CCR5-APEX2 biotinylation in short windows (e.g., 0“5, 5“15, 15“40, 40“90 min) after PSC-RANTES vs CCL5; streptavidin pulldown + targeted PRM mass spectrometry for VPS35, VPS26, SNX27, SNX6, FAM21, AP-1.
  - Co-IP: crosslinker-assisted co-IP (DSP) at matched timepoints to validate direct/complex association.
  - Quantitative readout: enrichment fold-change normalized to receptor abundance and internalization extent.

Step 3 — Engineering the phospho-gated ‘sorting switch’ with explicit chemical/architectural parameters (mandatory directive #3):
3.1 Switch designs (two-tier, with a failsafe):
  - Design A (phospho-exposed PDZ ligand): Insert a short C-terminal helix + PDZ-binding motif (Class I: -[S/T]-X-Φ, e.g., -STVL) preceded by a GRK2/3-favored phosphocluster (6“8 Ser/Thr within ~15 aa, enriched in acidic context to favor GRK2/3). Rationale: phosphorylation can electrostatically unmask the PDZ ligand by disrupting membrane-proximal basic residues and/or intramolecular packing, enabling SNX27 engagement only after activation.
  - Design B (phospho-primed 14-3-3 gate controlling adaptor recruitment): Embed a high-specificity 14-3-3 binding site (mode I RSXpSXP) adjacent to a masked docking peptide for a retromer/SNX-interacting module. Upon phosphorylation, 14-3-3 binding changes local conformation to expose the docking element. This reduces constitutive adaptor binding risk.
  - Failsafe Design C (inducible recruitment): CCR5 fused to FRB and an endosome/TGN adaptor module fused to FKBP; rapalog addition recruits the adaptor only when desired, providing a non-phospho-dependent contingency to prove causality between recruitment and TGN sequestration.
3.2 Library and build constraints:
  - Small, interpretable library: 6“10 barcode variants varying Ser/Thr spacing and local charge; 2 docking motif variants per design; total ≤20 constructs.
  - Expression control: single-copy landing pad in HEK293 for screening; then best 3 moved to CCR5 locus in Jurkat-like cells.
3.3 Mechanistic verification that the switch rewires sorting (not activation):
  - Re-run acceptance gates (Step 0).
  - Demonstrate preserved β-arrestin recruitment kinetics but altered post-endocytic associations (increased SNX/retromer proximity labeling after PSC-RANTES without increased initial internalization).

Step 4 — CXCR4 heterologous desensitization: quantitative capacity/competition and alternative hypotheses (mandatory directive #2):
4.1 Capacity/competition experiments with explicit saturation logic:
  - Dose-response matrix: PSC-RANTES concentration × exposure time to generate graded CCR5 internalization and graded retromer/SNX/WASH occupancy.
  - Measure limiting-node occupancy directly:
    * β-arrestin2 redistribution: live-cell imaging of β-arrestin2-mScarlet knock-in (or Halo) with CCR5; quantify fraction of β-arrestin in endosomal puncta.
    * Retromer/WASH occupancy: VPS35-GFP or FAM21-GFP knock-in in HEK293; quantify puncta intensity and colocalization with CCR5 endosomes.
  - CXCR4 functional assays: CXCL12-induced Ca2+ flux and receptor internalization after PSC-RANTES pretreatment.
  - Rescue-by-titration: re-express candidate limiting factors (β-arrestin2, VPS35, SNX27, FAM21) under doxycycline-tunable promoter across a defined range; criterion for competition model: CXCR4 responsiveness is restored in proportion to the replenished node and correlates with reduced occupancy.
4.2 Alternative hypotheses and discriminating readouts:
  - GRK sequestration: measure GRK2/3 membrane recruitment and availability (BRET-based GRK translocation sensor); test whether GRK overexpression rescues CXCR4.
  - β-arrestin redistribution (without clathrin limitation): compare effect of β-arrestin2 overexpression vs AP-2 overexpression; competition model predicts β-arrestin rescue > AP-2 rescue.
  - Endosomal signaling cross-talk: assay ERK phosphorylation and endosomal G protein signaling reporters; block with MEK inhibitor or endocytosis inhibitors to see if CXCR4 desensitization depends on downstream signaling rather than trafficking capacity.
  - CXCR4-specific ubiquitination program: quantify CXCR4 ubiquitination (IP-western) and test E3 ligase involvement (e.g., AIP4/ITCH literature pathway) to rule in/out independent regulation.

Step 5 — Causality, translational relevance, and success criteria:
5.1 Causality tests:
  - For top ‘TGN-locking’ switch: show prolonged surface down-modulation and impaired resensitization without changes in k_int; then abolish phenotype by acute VPS35/SNX/WASH depletion (epistasis).
  - For ‘fast-recycling’ switch: show accelerated surface recovery and preserved signaling.
5.2 Primary cell validation:
  - Introduce 1“2 best designs into primary CD4+ T cells and macrophages via CRISPR knock-in (RNP + AAV6 donor) with minimal tags.
  - Outcomes: duration of R5-tropic HIV-1 entry inhibition after PSC-RANTES washout; chemotaxis impairment duration (CCR5 ligands); reversibility (recovery of CCR5 surface and signaling).
5.3 Explicit success criteria (go/no-go):
  - Mechanism: PSC-RANTES increases k_ETGN (model) by ≥2× vs CCL5 and this increase is VPS35- and at least one SNX/WASH-dependent.
  - Engineering: at least one switch variant produces a programmable ≥3× change in CCR5 surface recovery half-life (vs WT) while passing acceptance gates.
  - CXCR4: if heterologous desensitization observed, it must (a) correlate with quantified occupancy of a specific limiting node and (b) be rescued by titrated replenishment of that node; otherwise, pivot to the best-supported alternative mechanism from 4.2.

Risk mitigation:
  - Tag/misfolding risk: minimal epitopes; heterozygous validation; immediate elimination if acceptance gates fail.
  - Phospho-conditional leakage: advance only variants with low basal internalization/association; deploy failsafe Design C to prove causality even if phospho-gating is imperfect.
  - Ambiguity of ‘TGN sequestration’: require triple evidence—TGN colocalization, retrieval-intermediate dependence (VPS35/SNX/WASH), and sensitivity to TGN trafficking perturbations.
Feasibility: 1) Why the mechanism is now sufficiently specified: The proposal pre-defines the exact retrieval machinery to test (VPS35/VPS26/VPS29; SNX27; SNX1/2“SNX5/6; WASH/FAM21) and lays out an epistasis framework that distinguishes true endosome→TGN retrieval from generic endosomal retention or slowed recycling. Time-window proximity labeling plus targeted MS and crosslinker co-IP provide orthogonal interaction evidence, while acute degrons/CRISPRi provide causal dependence.

2) Why phospho-gated engineering is interpretable and de-risked: Each switch variant is gated by explicit acceptance criteria (surface expression, ligand binding, Gi signaling, β-arrestin recruitment, low basal activity), ensuring that altered trafficking is not conflated with altered receptor activation or folding. The switch architectures include mechanistic safeguards against constitutive binding (phospho-unmasking or 14-3-3 gating) and a reversible inducible-dimerization failsafe that can enforce conditional recruitment to directly test sufficiency.

3) Why the CXCR4 arm is no longer a logical leap: Instead of assuming clathrin/AP-2 limitation, the plan quantitatively tests whether a specific shared node is limiting (β-arrestin2 and/or retromer/SNX/WASH) using occupancy metrics, saturation dose“response designs, and rescue-by-titration. In parallel, it enumerates and experimentally discriminates alternative explanations (GRK sequestration, β-arrestin redistribution, endosomal signaling cross-talk, CXCR4 ubiquitination control), preventing post hoc interpretation.

4) Practical feasibility: All methods are standard in modern receptor trafficking studies (CRISPR knock-in tagging, automated imaging with compartment markers, AID/dTAG depletion, TurboID/APEX2 proximity labeling, kinetic modeling). The design reduces scope risk by (i) screening constructs in a controlled landing-pad system, (ii) limiting library size, and (iii) defining explicit go/no-go criteria that prevent resource-intensive primary cell work until mechanism and engineering performance are demonstrated.

Hypothesis: Lineage-accelerated nonsynonymous substitutions in E(z) re-tune PRC2 catalytic output (H3K27me3 product profile and residence time) by altering an allosteric coupling pathway between the SET catalytic core and partner-binding regions, which in turn changes the threshold for PRC1 (Psc-containing) recruitment at PREs organized by Zeste/Ph, ultimately shifting homeotic gene repression stability. Methodological adaptation: we will engineer a DNA-barcoded, nucleosome-tethered “PRC recruitment rheostat” (a modular PRE mimic) that converts PRC2 catalysis into a quantitative, multiplex readout of PRC1 capture in vivo—overcoming the limitation that native chromatin context confounds causal attribution of E(z) amino-acid substitutions to PRC1 recruitment and homeotic silencing.
Plan: Step 1: Build a multiplexed PRE“nucleosome recruitment rheostat panel.
- Design a library of synthetic PRE cassettes containing: (i) Zeste motifs, (ii) Pho/Pho-like motifs (as the PcG DNA-anchoring control), and (iii) tunable spacing/valency to emulate PRE architecture; each cassette is paired with a unique 18“20 bp DNA barcode.
- Embed each cassette upstream of a minimal promoter driving a short-lived reporter (e.g., destabilized GFP) plus MS2 stem loops for nascent transcription imaging.
- Genomically integrate the cassette library as a single-copy landing-pad array at a neutral locus in Drosophila (or Drosophila-derived cell lines), ensuring identical chromosomal position effects across variants.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation—nucleosome-tethered PRC “capture” with catalytic-state sensing.
- Adapt split-enzyme proximity labeling into a chromatin-state“dependent capture system: fuse TurboID-half A to Psc (PRC1) and TurboID-half B to a chromatin reader that binds H3K27me3 (engineered CBX/HP1-like chromodomain with calibrated affinity). Reconstitution occurs only when PRC1 is within nanometers of H3K27me3-marked nucleosomes at the rheostat cassette.
- Engineer an E(z) variant panel derived from evolutionary rate hotspots (dN/dS-informed) but implemented as domain-swapped micro-alleles (short motif replacements rather than full-length allele swaps) to isolate mechanistic coupling: (i) ancestral-motif, (ii) derived-motif, (iii) catalytic-dead control, (iv) allosteric-pathway disruption mutants predicted from coevolutionary coupling analysis of PRC2 subunits.
- Readout: biotinylation is captured by streptavidin pulldown followed by barcode sequencing (BioID-Barcode-seq). This yields a quantitative “PRC1 capture index” per PRE cassette per E(z) variant.
- In parallel, quantify catalytic output by CUT&Tag at the barcoded array using spike-in normalization for H3K27me1/2/3, enabling product-profile shifts to be linked to PRC1 capture.
- Introduce controlled nuclear pH perturbations only as a stress test (not as the primary method): use genetically encoded pH clamps (v-ATPase modulators) to probe whether E(z) substitutions buffer PRC recruitment under physiological challenge.

Step 3: Rigorous validation, mechanism tests, and homeotic gene linkage.
- Mechanistic causality: (i) correlate PRC1 capture index with H3K27me3/2 ratios across PRE architectures; (ii) fit a kinetic threshold model where PRC1 capture depends on local H3K27me3 density and predicted E(z) residence time.
- Validate physical interfaces without imaging polytenes: perform crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) on PRC2 purified from each E(z) background to detect allosteric/interaction rearrangements; compare to functional PRC1 capture shifts.
- Functional consequence: using the same E(z) variants, measure derepression sensitivity of endogenous homeotic genes (Ubx, Abd-B) by precision nuclear run-on sequencing (PRO-seq) and H3K27me3 CUT&Tag at their PREs; test whether variants that lower PRC1 capture at rheostats also destabilize homeotic silencing.
- Controls: Pho/Phol depletion to confirm dependency on canonical PRE anchoring; Zeste motif ablation in rheostats to isolate Zeste-mediated organization; Psc catalytic/interaction mutants to confirm capture specificity.
- Statistical framework: hierarchical Bayesian model to partition variance attributable to (a) PRE architecture, (b) E(z) motif state, (c) interaction term (epistasis), with multiple-testing control over barcodes.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: PcG repression is mediated by PRC2-catalyzed H3K27 methylation and PRC1 (including Psc) recruitment; Drosophila studies show PcG proteins remain chromatin-associated while specific DNA-binding components (e.g., Pho/Phol) are critical for robust homeotic repression, and evolutionary analyses indicate accelerated nonsynonymous substitution in E(z) with signatures of positive selection. These support a model where E(z) substitutions can alter catalytic output and thereby PRC1 recruitment thresholds.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal bioengineers an epigenetic “sensor-actuator” assay that converts chromatin enzymology into a multiplexable quantitative readout, enabling mechanistic dissection of adaptive amino-acid changes in an epigenetic regulator—directly relevant to biomedical epigenetics where PRC2/PRC1 dysregulation drives developmental disorders and cancers.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike static chromatin staining or locus-by-locus assays, the recruitment rheostat provides (i) controlled PRE architecture, (ii) single-copy genomic context, and (iii) high-throughput, quantitative coupling of PRC2 catalytic state to PRC1 proximity via split proximity labeling and barcode sequencing. This structurally novel platform isolates causality between E(z) substitutions, H3K27 methylation product profiles, PRC1 (Psc) capture, and downstream homeotic gene repression—without relying on live polytene imaging or generic tagging workflows.

Hypothesis: A plasmon-gated, mixed-valence 2D CoFe-MOF nanosheet membrane (AuNR@CoFe-MOF//nanocellulose) will achieve light-switchable, low-activation-energy gas separation and simultaneous dye photodegradation/biomedical readout because (i) Au nanorod LSPR generates hot electrons that inject into Co/Fe nodes, transiently increasing Co/Fe mixed-valence density and electronic conductivity, (ii) this lowers the activation energy for charge-assisted adsorption/diffusion of quadrupolar gases (e.g., CO2) through 2D slit pores by strengthening reversible metal“gas interactions under bias/light, and (iii) the same hot-electron/valence-tuned surface accelerates electrocatalytic redox of azo dyes (model pollutants) and activates a tethered NIR dye as an optical reporter for membrane state in biomedically relevant aqueous media. Methodological adaptation: convert a conventional 2D MOF membrane into a dual-mode ‘plasmonic-electrochemical’ separation platform by (a) enforcing Co/Fe mixed valency via redox-active triazolate/catecholate co-linkers to create a contiguous charge-transport pathway, (b) confining Au nanorods at the nanosheet basal planes with sub-2 nm dielectric spacers to maximize hot-electron injection while preventing pore blockage, and (c) laminating the nanosheets on oxidized nanocellulose to create mechanically robust, hydrated nanochannels that preserve 2D slit selectivity in wet/biological conditions.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Design the 2D CoFe-MOF: select Co/Fe nodes with paddlewheel/oxo-bridged secondary building units compatible with 2D sheet growth; implement a mixed-linker strategy using (L1) 1,2,3-triazolate (for strong metal“N bonding and mixed-valence charge delocalization logic) and (L2) catecholate/quinone-type ditopic linker (for redox buffering and tunable M(II/III) ratios). Target nanosheet thickness 2“10 nm to minimize electron-transport distance from Au.
1.2 Synthesize CoFe-MOF nanosheets by modulated solvothermal/ultrasonic exfoliation; tune Co:Fe ratio (e.g., 1:1, 3:1, 1:3) to optimize redox density and open-metal-site population.
1.3 Prepare Au nanorods (LSPR matched to 808 nm for tissue-transparency) and functionalize with a short, pore-nonblocking dielectric spacer/anchor (e.g., 3-mercaptopropionic acid + ultrathin polydopamine or Al2O3 via 1“2 cycles of ALD) to set an injection-favorable Au“MOF separation (~0.5“2 nm).
1.4 Build a nanocellulose support: TEMPO-oxidized nanofibrillated cellulose (TOCNF) cast into a porous film; introduce carboxylate anchoring sites to promote oriented lamination of positively charged CoFe-MOF sheets.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Assemble AuNR@CoFe-MOF nanosheets: electrostatic/coordination anchoring of spacer-modified AuNRs onto basal planes (not edges) by exploiting catecholate/Fe affinity; quantify Au loading (ICP-MS) and ensure pore-access retention (N2/CO2 sorption, positron annihilation if available).
2.2 Fabricate laminated 2D membrane on TOCNF: vacuum-assisted filtration to align nanosheets and create sub-nanometer slit channels; crosslink lightly with multivalent ions (e.g., Ca2+) or covalent carbodiimide coupling between TOCNF-COO− and MOF-surface amines (if introduced) to maintain integrity under hydration.
2.3 Introduce a reporter dye for biomedical-relevant readout: covalently tether a NIR dye (e.g., cyanine derivative) to TOCNF or to pendant linker groups, positioned outside transport slits to avoid altering selectivity. The dye should be redox-/local-field-sensitive so that hot-electron events shift emission (ratiometric preferred).
2.4 Gas separation testing under operando plasmonic/electrochemical control:
- Measure single-gas and mixed-gas permeance/selectivity for CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4 (dry and humid) in a membrane module.
- Apply (a) dark, (b) 808 nm irradiation, (c) small bias across the membrane (if configured as an electroactive membrane) to map light/bias-gated transport.
- Extract apparent activation energies for permeation (Arrhenius from 273“343 K) in each mode to quantify barrier lowering.
2.5 Coupled dye conversion as a mechanistic proxy and application demo:
- In aqueous flow-through mode, test electrocatalytic/photocatalytic degradation of model dyes (e.g., methyl orange, rhodamine B) while simultaneously running gas separation (or sequentially).
- Correlate dye degradation kinetics with membrane conductivity changes under light (EIS) to link hot-electron injection to catalytic acceleration.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Confirm mixed valency and its modulation: XPS (Co 2p, Fe 2p), Mössbauer (Fe), XANES/EXAFS under dark vs irradiated conditions; quantify reversible Co(II/III) and Fe(II/III) shifts.
3.2 Prove hot-electron injection pathway: ultrafast transient absorption (Au bleach + MOF polaron signatures), surface photovoltage spectroscopy, and photocurrent action spectra matching AuNR LSPR; compare with nonplasmonic Au spheres and with AuNRs insulated by thick shells (control for photothermal effects).
3.3 Separate photothermal vs nonthermal contributions: identical membrane temperature control (IR camera + thermocouple feedback), use chopped illumination and intensity-dependent kinetics; demonstrate selectivity/permeance shifts that exceed purely temperature-driven expectations.
