3.4 Transport mechanism deconvolution: fit mixed-gas permeation to solution“diffusion + Langmuir adsorption; compare dark/light adsorption isotherms and heats of adsorption (microcalorimetry) to show hot-electron-enhanced reversible CO2 binding at open metal sites.
3.5 Stability/biocompatibility gates: leaching tests (ICP in saline), repeated cycling (100+ light on/off cycles), and cytotoxicity screening of leachates (standard cell viability) to support biomedical adjacency claims for sensing/filtration modules.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: (i) Au/CoFe-MOF nanosheets already demonstrate LSPR-driven hot-electron injection that lowers activation energy and boosts electrocatalytic currents (Asset 3). (ii) Mixed-valence Fe-triazolate frameworks show dramatically enhanced conductivity and measurable activation energies for charge transport tied to valence delocalization (Asset 2), providing a blueprint for engineering a lower-barrier electron/hole pathway in CoFe-MOFs. (iii) Nanocellulose“MOF composites are established as robust, functional platforms spanning gas separation, dye treatment, and biomedical contexts (Asset 1), supporting the membrane-support architecture and wetted operation.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation is molecularly rational: triazolate/catecholate co-linking is used to stabilize mixed valency and create charge-delocalized pathways in a 2D MOF; AuNR placement with controlled nanogap maximizes injection while preserving pore accessibility; nanocellulose lamination provides mechanically stable, hydrated slit channels—addressing the known limitation that many MOF membranes lose selectivity or crack under humidity/handling.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional MOF membranes, this system offers an external ‘knob’ (LSPR light and/or bias) to reversibly tune activation energy for permeation and adsorption selectivity, enabling on-demand CO2 capture/release without bulk heating. Compared with standalone plasmonic catalysts, confining the plasmonic junctions within an electronically percolating 2D mixed-valence MOF increases hot-electron utilization efficiency (shorter transport distance, more acceptor states), while the integrated dye conversion and NIR reporter provide operando validation and biomedical-adjacent sensing functionality in the same material platform.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that externally (surface-only) functionalized 2D zeolite nanosheets can be assembled into a desalination membrane whose interlayer slit size and electrostatics are simultaneously and quantitatively controlled by a hydrolytically robust coordination-crosslink network. Specifically, we will (i) confine chelating ligands to external silanol nests (avoiding internal micropore poisoning), (ii) set ligand surface density into a narrow target window that supports percolating interlayer crosslinks without excessive hydrodynamic drag, and (iii) use high-formation-constant, chloride/sulfate-tolerant metal“ligand pairs (prioritizing Zr(IV)“catecholate/salicylate and Ni(II)“bipyridine in sterically protected geometries) to form a quasi-2D coordination “spacer” lattice between adjacent nanosheets. The core transport mechanism is not single-file water transport (which is unlikely in disordered lamellae), but a falsifiable combination of: (a) size-regulated hydrated-ion exclusion set by the measured slit-size probability distribution function (PDF) and its low-tail cutoff, and (b) charge-regulated partitioning (Donnan exclusion) governed by pH- and salinity-dependent fixed charge density localized at coordination nodes and tethered functional groups. The refined claim is that high rejection is achieved when the slit-size PDF is centered near 0.8“1.2 nm with a narrow width (σ ≤ 0.15 nm) and when the membrane maintains a stable negative effective fixed charge density under RO conditions; high permeability is preserved by limiting grafted-ligand coverage to a regime that stabilizes spacing/charge while minimizing frictional penalties (quantified via activation energy and H2O/D2O isotope tests).
Plan: Step 1 — 2D zeolite selection, exfoliation feasibility, and external-surface baseline metrology.
1.1 Candidate frameworks and delamination approach: Use layered/2D-zeolite precursors where exfoliation is experimentally demonstrated or strongly indicated by low cut-density orientations (per graph-theory screening). Primary targets: layered MFI-derived precursors (e.g., MWW-family layered analogs if MFI proves intractable) and FER-related layered precursors; we will down-select after a 6-week feasibility sprint based on yield and defect metrics below.
1.2 Exfoliation protocol (top-down): Swell layered precursors with structure-directing surfactant (e.g., quaternary ammonium) followed by sonication-assisted delamination in alcohol/water mixtures; remove surfactant by mild extraction to preserve silanols.
1.3 Acceptance criteria (actionable): (i) Exfoliation yield ≥ 30 wt% nanosheets after centrifugation fractionation; (ii) thickness by AFM/TEM: median 1“3 unit cells with ≥70% of population <5 nm; (iii) lateral size distribution: D50 ≥ 200 nm (goal 0.2“2 µm) with polydispersity reported; (iv) defect density assessed by 29Si MAS NMR (Q3/Q4 ratio) and Raman/IR signatures—target Q3 fraction consistent with external silanols without collapse; (v) micropore integrity: N2/Ar sorption (and/or CO2 sorption) consistent with intact zeolite micropores.
1.4 External vs internal functionalization map (must-prove control): Perform probe-molecule exclusion tests using a bulky silylating agent (e.g., triisopropylsilyl chloride) and compare pore-volume loss vs small silanes; require ≤10% loss in intrinsic micropore uptake after intended functionalization (Step 2) to confirm external-only grafting.

Step 2 — Quantitative ligand grafting with surface-density targets and pore-blocking controls.
2.1 Ligand families and design rules: Use short, rigid, hydrolytically stable chelators with minimal conformational freedom to reduce spacing disorder: (A) catechol/salicylate-silanes (for Zr(IV) strong binding and hydrolysis resistance), (B) sterically shielded bipyridine/phenanthroline-silanes (for Ni(II) complexes less prone to chloride displacement), and (C) optional sulfonated variants to tune fixed negative charge without relying on metal hydrolysis.
2.2 Grafting chemistry: Silane coupling onto external Si“OH under anhydrous conditions (controlled water dosing) to minimize oligomerization. Use a two-step approach: (i) passivation of a fraction of silanols with a non-chelating short alkylsilane to control spacing of chelator sites; (ii) graft chelator-silane.
2.3 Quantitative targets and acceptance criteria:
- Ligand surface density (external) target window: 0.3“1.0 sites nm−2 (to be refined after initial drag vs stability tests). Reject batches outside 0.2“1.2 sites nm−2.
- Reporting in two units: mmol ligand g−1 (from TGA/elemental analysis) and sites nm−2 (from BET external surface area estimate + AFM size statistics).
- Functionalization confinement: micropore uptake loss ≤10% (Step 1.4) and dye/probe exclusion consistent with external grafting.
2.4 Metrology suite for graft quantification: (i) TGA + CHN, (ii) solid-state 13C/29Si NMR to confirm covalent attachment, (iii) FTIR (amide/catechol bands), (iv) XPS (N 1s, O 1s, Si 2p) to quantify surface composition.

Step 3 — Crosslinking strategy with controllable spacing: in situ co-assembly vs post-diffusion, and statistical interlayer-spacing verification.
3.1 Two crosslinking routes (both executed, down-select by uniformity):
Route A (in situ co-assembly): Disperse functionalized nanosheets in solvent containing pre-formed metal“ligand complexes (or metal precursor + ligand on sheet) at defined stoichiometry, then vacuum-assisted filtration to assemble while crosslinks form uniformly.
Route B (post-assembly diffusion): Assemble nanosheet film first, then introduce metal solution by controlled counter-diffusion (metal from one side, competing ligand/anion buffer from other) to reduce diffusion gradients.
3.2 Stoichiometry control (mandatory quantitative definition):
- Define metal:ligand feed ratios spanning 0.25:1 to 1.5:1; primary target at 0.5“1.0:1 depending on complex geometry.
- Maintain ionic strength and pH to suppress metal hydroxide precipitation (e.g., Zr(IV) handled in chelated precursor form; Ni(II) buffered at pH 6“8).
- Introduce competitive anion intentionally during optimization (Cl− and SO4^2− at 0.1“0.6 M) to pre-screen robustness.
3.3 Interlayer spacing target and realism: Replace the fixed “6“8 Å locked spacing” with a measured distribution target consistent with hydrated-ion exclusion and lamellar disorder:
- Target mean slit (interlayer gallery free width): 0.8“1.2 nm (tunable by ligand length and crosslink density).
- Target distribution width: σ ≤ 0.15 nm (from PDF/total scattering and GIWAXS line-shape modeling).
- Reject membranes with bimodal spacing or σ > 0.25 nm, as these imply percolating defects.
3.4 Spacing/disorder metrology (beyond GI-XRD):
- GIWAXS + total scattering/PDF analysis to extract spacing distribution (not just average d-spacing).
- Cross-sectional TEM/cryo-TEM with statistical analysis across ≥1000 layer spacings.
- Positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) or ellipsometric porosimetry (if available) to corroborate sub-nm free volume distribution.

Step 4 — Definitive coordination-environment verification and mapping of crosslink topology.
4.1 XAS (XANES/EXAFS):
- Collect at metal K-edge to distinguish metal“ligand (M“N/M“O) vs metal“chloride (M“Cl) coordination.
- Fit coordination numbers and bond distances; acceptance criterion: ≥70% of metal sites show intended ligand coordination signature under (i) DI water, (ii) 0.6 M NaCl, (iii) mixed-salt (NaCl + MgSO4) at RO-relevant pH.
4.2 XPS depth profiling: Confirm metal and ligand co-localization through film thickness and rule out surface-only metallation.
4.3 ICP-MS leaching and mass balance:
- Static soak and cross-flow leach under RO feed (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl, pH 6.5“8) for ≥7 days; quantify leached metal (µg m−2 day−1).
- Acceptance criterion: <1% total metal loss over 7 days; proceed to 30-day testing only if met.
4.4 Operando/near-operando spectroscopy during cycling:
- Flow-cell XAS or ATR-FTIR to monitor coordination changes during salinity and pH swings (pH 4“10) and during oxidant exposure (free chlorine protocol below).

Step 5 — Desalination testing with falsifiable transport diagnostics (replace “single-file” with measurable mechanisms).
5.1 Performance metrics under defined conditions:
- Nanofiltration (NF): 5“20 bar; Reverse osmosis (RO): 30“60 bar (as appropriate for film integrity).
- Report water permeance (LMH bar−1) and rejection for NaCl and MgSO4; include mixed-salt and real brine (e.g., seawater simulant).
5.2 Mechanism-resolving transport tests:
- Temperature-dependent permeance (10“50 °C) to extract activation energy (Ea). Compare Ea across graft densities to quantify added friction.
- Isotope test (H2O vs D2O) to probe transport mechanism changes; interpret relative permeance ratio as a constraint (not proof) on hydrogen-bond disruption.
- Streaming potential / membrane potential + ion conductance to separate surface-charge-governed transport from pure size sieving.
- Salt-permeability vs concentration (0.01“1.0 M) to test Donnan breakdown at high ionic strength.
5.3 Structure“property closure coupling:
- Use measured slit-size PDFs (Step 3.4) as direct inputs to MD/continuum models; do not assume uniform slit.
- Fit experimental permeance/rejection with models incorporating (i) slip length/viscosity penalty from grafting, (ii) fixed charge density from titration/zeta/streaming potential, and (iii) defect-path fraction inferred from spacing-distribution tails.

Step 6 — Stability and failure-mode testing (explicitly addressing reviewer concerns).
6.1 Competitive anion binding and coordination integrity:
- Challenge with Cl−, SO4^2−, HCO3− at seawater-relevant concentrations; evaluate XAS for M“Cl emergence and performance drift.
- For Ni(II) systems: include imidazole or sterically hindered chelators to reduce ligand exchange if needed.
6.2 Hydrolysis/demetallation and pH cycling:
- Cycle pH 4 ↔ 10 under flow; monitor metal leaching (ICP-MS), XPS composition, and rejection stability.
6.3 Redox and oxidant tolerance:
- Avoid Cu/Co as primary systems unless stabilized; prioritize redox-inert Zr(IV) and Ni(II).
- Free chlorine exposure protocol (e.g., 200“1000 ppm·h): monitor ligand integrity (ATR-FTIR/XPS) and performance.
6.4 Mechanical compaction/swelling:
- Pressure cycling 5 ↔ 60 bar for ≥100 cycles; monitor d-spacing distribution changes (GIWAXS/PDF), thickness, and permeance.
- Long-duration cross-flow (≥30 days) with periodic characterization checkpoints.

Step 7 — Down-selection logic and decision gates.
- Gate 1 (end Step 1): proceed only if nanosheet yield/thickness/lateral size criteria are met.
- Gate 2 (end Step 3): proceed only if spacing distribution meets mean 0.8“1.2 nm and σ ≤ 0.15 nm with no strong bimodality.
- Gate 3 (end Step 4/6): proceed only if XAS confirms dominant metal“ligand coordination under salt, and ICP-MS leaching <1% over 7 days.
- Final success criteria: stable NaCl rejection meeting target class (NF/RO appropriate) with <20% permeance decline over 30 days, and mechanistic consistency between measured slit PDFs + electrostatics metrics and transport modeling.

Deliverables (explicit): (i) ligand-density vs spacing-PDF maps, (ii) coordination speciation maps from XAS under realistic feeds, (iii) stability envelopes (pH, ionic strength, chlorine, pressure cycling), and (iv) validated transport model grounded in experimentally measured structural distributions.
Feasibility: 1) Addressing spacing-uniformity skepticism: The proposal replaces a single “locked 6“8 Å” claim with a measurable interlayer slit-size distribution target and acceptance thresholds (mean and σ), explicitly acknowledging lamellar disorder. Uniformity is tackled by (i) controlling ligand surface density (sites nm−2) via mixed-silane passivation + chelator grafting, and (ii) comparing in situ co-assembly versus post-assembly counter-diffusion to minimize metal-ion gradients. GIWAXS is augmented with total scattering/PDF and cross-sectional TEM statistics to quantify spacing heterogeneity rather than infer it.

2) Transport mechanism realism (avoiding overstated single-file claims): Rather than asserting single-file transport, we commit to falsifiable diagnostics (Ea, H2O/D2O isotope effect, streaming potential/ion conductance) that can confirm whether grafting increases friction and whether charge regulation contributes beyond sterics. The design uses short, rigid chelators and bounded graft densities to stabilize channels while limiting drag; any permeability loss becomes quantifiable and can be optimized against stability/rejection.

3) Stability under saline RO conditions: Reviewer-identified failure modes (anion competition, hydrolysis/demetallation, redox instability, pH weakening) are mitigated by: (i) prioritizing hydrolytically robust, high-formation-constant pairs (Zr(IV)“catecholate/salicylate; Ni(II)“protected bpy/phen), (ii) explicitly screening competitive Cl−/SO4^2− binding with XAS speciation under realistic salt feeds, and (iii) implementing ICP-MS leaching thresholds plus operando/near-operando spectroscopy during pH/salinity cycling. Cu/Co are demoted to secondary candidates unless stability criteria are met.

4) Decisive chemistry/structure verification: The revised plan directly verifies coordination topology and environment using EXAFS/XANES (metal“ligand vs metal“halide), XPS depth profiling (through-thickness distribution), and leaching mass balance. These methods close the gap left by GI-XRD/AFM alone and provide a direct test of whether “gating nodes” persist under operation.

5) Exfoliation feasibility is operationalized: The graph-theory orientation premise is converted into actionable experimental gates—yield, thickness, lateral-size distributions, defect density (29Si Q3/Q4), and micropore integrity via sorption. External-only functionalization is validated by pore-blocking controls and ≤10% micropore uptake loss, ensuring that performance changes can be attributed to interlayer engineering rather than internal pore poisoning.

Overall feasibility rests on leveraging well-established silane grafting chemistry on aluminosilicates, coordination complexes with documented aqueous robustness, and a metrology-driven optimization loop that explicitly quantifies and controls the parameters reviewers flagged as underdefined.

Hypothesis: A hydrolytically robust Zr6-node MOF (UiO-66 family) can be engineered to simultaneously (i) resist humidity-driven pore flooding during organophosphorus CWA-simulant capture and (ii) accelerate organophosphorus hydrolysis by a *spatially segregated, topology-retentive* dual modification that is validated by explicit transport/crystallographic acceptance criteria rather than assumed SCSC behavior. The central mechanistic claim is refined as follows: (1) an *aperture-localized perfluoroaryl “gate”* increases the free-energy penalty for capillary condensation and multi-body water clustering at windows by lowering local surface polarity and disrupting H-bond network nucleation *at the entry* (not by globally excluding water), thereby preserving DMMP partitioning into micropores under humid streams; and (2) *interior, node-proximal isolated Lewis-acid co-catalysts* (M2+ bound to deliberately designed chelating defect caps) cooperate with adjacent Zr“OH/Zr(IV) pairs to polarize P=O and stabilize the pentacoordinate TS for P“X/P“OR hydrolysis. The proposal explicitly addresses the reviewer’s ‘water excluded yet required’ concern by predicting and testing a *non-monotonic* relationship: gating should strongly suppress water uptake at high a_w (reducing pore-filling and clustering) while maintaining sufficient low-coverage water at node environments (measured by water isotherms + microcalorimetry + in situ spectroscopy) to sustain catalytic turnover. Synergy is expected only if (i) the gate measurably reduces effective window diffusivity/entry probability for water (and/or delays water condensation) more than for DMMP and (ii) interior M sites remain isolated, stable, and product-tolerant; both conditions will be operationally defined and experimentally validated with orthogonal quantitative metrics (diffusivity/size-exclusion series + microtomed F-mapping + co-adsorption/breakthrough + site-normalized kinetics).
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration of acceptance criteria, size regime, and quantitative site balance (addresses SCSC/topology and normalization critiques)
0.1 Crystal/particle regimes (two-track to de-risk crystallographic claims):
- Track A (single-crystal validation): grow UiO-66-(Br)x crystals ≥ 50“150 µm (modulated solvothermal; low nucleation density) specifically for SCXRD after each modification.
- Track B (application-relevant microcrystals): 200“800 nm particles for breakthrough/kinetics; structural retention assessed by PXRD + total scattering/PDF + line-broadening + N2/Ar porosity.
0.2 Topology/retention acceptance criteria (stepwise gate → chelator-cap → metalation):
- For Track A: SCXRD R1/GOF within acceptable increase (pre-registered), no loss of long-range order; unit-cell change < ~1“2% unless justified; no new phases.
- For Track B: (i) PXRD: no extra peaks; (ii) Rietveld: lattice parameter change bounded; (iii) total scattering/PDF: preservation of Zr6“O and Zr“Zr peak positions/intensities within tolerance; (iv) BET/micropore volume retained above thresholds per step (e.g., ≥80% after gating, ≥70% after full G+C) with clear mass-balance of added groups.
0.3 Quantitative defect and site-balance plan (pre-registered):
- Defect density: TGA (organic/inorganic ratio), digestion 1H NMR (linker/modulator/cap ratios), and chloride/formate/acetate quantification if modulators used.
- Functionalization level: digestion 1H/19F NMR (Br-to-aryl conversion; F content), ICP-OES for Pd trace, ICP-OES for M loading (Ni/Zn/etc.), and elemental analysis.
- Accessible Zr“OH quantification: probe titration (e.g., CD3CN adsorption + IR, or acid“base titration on digests as control) plus comparison to defect statistics.
- Accessible M sites: CO/pyridine/MeCN titration (IR), plus XAS-derived coordination number where feasible.

Step 1 — Scaffold and handle installation with controlled defect statistics (pristine vs handle control)
1.1 Baseline scaffold: UiO-66 (Zr6O4(OH)4(BDC)6) synthesized solvothermally with controlled modulator equivalents to target comparable defect densities across batches.
1.2 Reactive-handle variant: UiO-66-(Br)x using 2-bromoterephthalate at x = 0.05“0.10 mol fraction of total dicarboxylate (kept low to avoid mixed-linker property drift). Controls: P0 (UiO-66) and P1 (UiO-66-(Br)x) synthesized under identical size/defect targets.
1.3 Initial characterization (all batches): PXRD, SEM/TEM size distribution, N2 (77 K) + Ar (87 K) adsorption (BET, micropore volume, NLDFT pore/window distribution), and water vapor sorption (0“90% RH) baseline.

Step 2 — Operationally defined ‘aperture-selective’ perfluoroaryl gating with quantitative validation beyond surface spectroscopy
2.1 Reaction design: diffusion-limited Suzuki coupling executed to favor near-surface/window modification rather than uniform internal conversion.
- Substrate: activated UiO-66-(Br)x (solvent exchange to low-swelling solvent; rigorous activation).
- Coupling partner: bulky perfluoroaryl boronic ester (e.g., pentafluorophenyl-Bpin or 3,5-bis(CF3)-phenyl-Bpin) chosen to reduce intracrystalline diffusion and to maximize hydrophobicity per installed group.
- Conditions: low catalyst loading (ppm“0.1 mol% Pd vs Br), weak base compatible with Zr nodes (screen K3PO4 vs Cs2CO3 vs organic bases), 40“60 °C, short times, and stirred slurry with controlled solvent composition to minimize framework swelling. Time series (t = 5, 15, 30, 60, 180 min) to generate functionalization gradients.
- Termination: rapid quench, exhaustive washing (including chelator wash to remove Pd), re-activation.
2.2 Quantitative *Metric A* (transport/size-exclusion kinetics): extract effective window diffusivities pre/post gate.
- Measure uptake kinetics (gravimetric sorption or QCM for films; alternatively volumetric time-resolved sorption) for a homologous probe set spanning kinetic diameters/polarities: CO2, CH4, Xe (small), n-butane/i-butane (branched size sensitivity), and a larger aromatic (toluene or p-xylene) where safe/feasible.
- Fit uptake curves to intracrystalline diffusion models to extract Deff (or characteristic time constants) and identify whether gating preferentially slows larger/branched probes consistent with narrowed/modified apertures.
- Acceptance criterion for “aperture-selective” behavior: significant Deff reduction (and/or induction time) without proportional loss of total micropore volume (from Ar/N2) and with a stronger effect on larger probes than on small probes.
2.3 Quantitative *Metric B* (spatial gradient mapping via microtomed cross-sections):
- Embed crystals/particles in epoxy; ultramicrotome cross-sections.
- Map F distribution (and Br residual) across cross-sections by STEM-EELS(F) or nanoSIMS (F−) and/or SEM-EDS(F) where sensitivity permits.
- Use calibration standards: physically mixed known-F polymer or F-doped reference particles embedded and microtomed identically to calibrate signal vs areal density.
- Acceptance criterion: demonstrable F enrichment at outer 50“200 nm (or first few unit-cell depths for large crystals) with substantially lower F in the core compared to uniform-functionalization control (generated by long-time/high-swelling condition).
2.4 Supportive spectroscopy (non-decisive but corroborative): angle-resolved XPS (F 1s enrichment near surface), ToF-SIMS depth profiling, and digestion 19F NMR to quantify total installed gate.

Step 3 — Interior chelating defect-cap installation with controlled speciation (addresses “defect-only” uncertainty)
3.1 Strategy shift from “assumed defect-only SALE” to controlled defect-cap exchange with explicit quantitation.
- Starting material: UiO-66 or gated UiO-66 after Step 2 (two sequences tested: gate→cap and cap→gate; choose the one preserving gating gradients and porosity).
- Cap candidates (screened by stability/geometry): nicotinate (monodentate pyridyl), triazolate-containing benzoate, or bipyridyl-monocarboxylate if sterically feasible. Selection criterion: strong M2+ binding yet minimal disruption to Zr connectivity.
- Exchange conditions: low water activity (anhydrous alcohol/DMF mixtures), controlled equivalents, mild temperature, time series.
3.2 Quantitation of cap incorporation and defect redistribution:
- Digestion 1H NMR to quantify BDC:cap:modulator ratios.
- TGA to corroborate organic loading.
- Compare porosity (Ar/N2) and PDF signatures to ensure no defect-driven collapse.
- Acceptance criterion: cap incorporation occurs without introducing new crystalline phases and with bounded changes in micropore volume/window distribution.

Step 4 — Postsynthetic metalation (PSM) to generate isolated interior Lewis-acid sites and mitigate deactivation risks
4.1 Co-catalyst selection and rationale (screened set rather than single choice):
- Primary: Zn(II) (hard Lewis acid, phosphate affinity moderate), Ni(II) (stronger binding but higher phosphate inhibition risk), and a third option for deactivation resistance (e.g., Co(II) or Mg(II) depending on chelator).
- Metalation conditions: non-aqueous salts (M(OTf)2, M(NO3)2 in dry solvent), controlled equivalents to cap loading, low temperature, rigorous washing.
4.2 Speciation/isolation verification (explicitly addressing hydroxide/oxo/salt residues):
- ICP-OES (bulk loading) + XPS (surface check for residues) + XAS (EXAFS/XANES) to confirm chelator-bound coordination and rule out M(OH)x/oxide clusters.
- Probe titration (pyridine/MeCN) to estimate accessible M sites.
- Pd residue check post-gating (ICP-OES) to avoid confounding catalysis.
4.3 Product inhibition/deactivation tests (pre-registered):
- Expose catalysts to phosphate products (e.g., dimethyl phosphate / p-nitrophenyl phosphate hydrolysis products) at relevant activities; measure loss of rate and changes in IR/31P NMR signatures.
- Regeneration protocols: mild acid wash or chelator competition to remove bound phosphate, followed by re-metalation if needed; quantify retained crystallinity/porosity.

Step 5 — Water management mechanism: direct measurement of water uptake, energetics, and co-adsorption under controlled a_w (mandatory additions)
5.1 Water vapor sorption isotherms (0“90% RH) at multiple temperatures (e.g., 298 K and 313 K) for P0, P1, G, C, G+C.
- Extract Henry constant region, inflection/condensation behavior, hysteresis.
5.2 Isosteric heats / microcalorimetry:
- Water adsorption calorimetry to quantify differential enthalpy vs coverage; gating hypothesis predicts reduced high-coverage clustering enthalpy/entropy signatures relative to P0/C while retaining node-associated low-coverage binding.
5.3 DMMP/H2O co-adsorption:
- Binary vapor co-adsorption (gravimetric or breakthrough-based) at fixed a_w to measure competitive uptake and selectivity.
- Dynamic breakthrough with DMMP at 0/40/80% RH and controlled a_w; quantify working capacity, MTZ length, and humidity-induced loss.

Step 6 — Detoxification kinetics with rigorous normalization and mechanistic testing under humid conditions
6.1 Substrates:
- Adsorption/breakthrough: DMMP.
- Hydrolysis: paraoxon-ethyl or p-nitrophenyl phosphate derivatives (UV-vis for p-nitrophenolate) and 31P NMR mass balance; optional higher-fidelity simulant (DFP) only if policy-approved.
6.2 Reactor formats:
- Vapor-fed microreactor for humid-stream catalysis (controlled RH/a_w), and complementary liquid-phase assays with controlled water activity (salt solutions or cosolvent systems) to decouple transport from intrinsic kinetics.
6.3 Rate normalization (site-balance enforced):
- Report kobs per gram, per BET area, and critically per (accessible Zr“OH) and per (accessible M) using defect/site quantification from Step 0.3.
- Ensure same particle size regime across P0/G/C/G+C for intrinsic comparisons; where not possible, apply effectiveness factor analysis using measured Deff.
6.4 Mechanistic spectroscopy under humidity (mandatory):
- In situ DRIFTS: DMMP P=O stretch shifts as function of RH; compare C vs G+C to test predicted increased polarization without pore flooding.
- Solid-state 31P MAS NMR after DMMP dosing at controlled RH to identify bound intermediates/products and quantify phosphate accumulation.
- KIE (H2O/D2O) under controlled a_w to assess water activation; compare C vs G+C.
- Inhibitor poisoning: pyridine/MeCN to selectively bind M sites; quantify differential rate suppression.

Step 7 — Synergy quantification and decision gates
7.1 Explicit synergy indices (pre-registered) for (i) humid DMMP working capacity, (ii) intrinsic hydrolysis rate per active site, and (iii) stability after cycling.
- S = Perf(G+C) / [Perf(G)+Perf(C)−Perf(P0)] with confidence intervals from replicate datasets.
7.2 Go/no-go criteria:
- “Aperture-selective gate” is accepted only if both Metric A (size-dependent Deff shift) and Metric B (F gradient in cross-sections) are positive and micropore volume retention meets threshold.
- “Cooperative catalysis” is accepted only if site-normalized rates increase superadditively and mechanistic signatures (DRIFTS/NMR/KIE/inhibitors) align with dual-site activation.
7.3 Contingency paths:
- If gating is not sufficiently aperture-localized: shift to larger gating groups, lower swelling solvents, shorter times, or alternative covalent chemistry (e.g., SNAr on pre-installed phenols) while maintaining the same validation metrics.
- If metalation causes deactivation via phosphate binding: switch chelator denticity/geometry or metal identity; implement regeneration cycling as part of deliverables.

Deliverable: a quantitatively validated spatially segregated UiO-66-derived architecture (gate + isolated interior Lewis-acid co-catalyst) with demonstrated humid-stream DMMP capture retention, controlled water uptake energetics, and site-normalized hydrolysis acceleration beyond additive effects, backed by transport-gradient mapping and crystallographic/total-scattering acceptance criteria.
Feasibility: 1) Literature-anchored rationale and scope control: MOFs (including UiO-66) are established as tunable platforms for organophosphorus simulant capture and detoxification, with performance strongly impacted by humidity competition and functional group engineering (Asset 1). Mixed-functionality can generate genuine synergistic adsorption behavior when chemical heterogeneity is controlled (Asset 2), but this proposal explicitly avoids uncontrolled bulk mixed-linker solid solutions by (i) low-fraction Br handles for gating and (ii) quantified defect-cap chemistry with a site-balance. The solvothermal synthesis and postsynthetic modification/metalation logic is consistent with robust Zr-MOF platforms and PSM precedents (Asset 4), while explicitly acknowledging that multi-step transformations may introduce disorder; hence the stepwise SCXRD/PDF/Rietveld acceptance framework replaces any blanket SCSC claim.

2) Why aperture-localized gating is plausible and how it will be *proven*: The diffusion-limited coupling design is treated as a hypothesis that must satisfy two orthogonal quantitative criteria: (i) size-exclusion/uptake kinetics that reveal window-level transport changes without wholesale pore-volume loss, and (ii) cross-sectional F mapping (microtome + STEM-EELS/nanoSIMS) with calibrated standards to directly evidence radial functionalization gradients. This directly addresses the review board’s concern that surface spectroscopy alone is suggestive but not definitive.

3) Water mechanism made testable (not narrative): The refined hypothesis does not assume water is “excluded” categorically; instead it predicts selective suppression of high-coverage water clustering/condensation while preserving low-coverage node-associated water required for hydrolysis. This is experimentally interrogated by water vapor isotherms (0“90% RH), microcalorimetry-derived differential heats, and DMMP/H2O co-adsorption/breakthrough under controlled a_w—exactly the missing evidence highlighted by reviewers.

4) Defect-cap and metalation risks are controlled by quantitation, speciation checks, and deactivation/regeneration studies: Because defect-site exchange can redistribute defects and alter acidity/porosity, the plan includes digestion NMR + TGA + PDF/porosity tracking to decouple “new sites” from unintended framework changes. Metal site isolation/speciation is verified by ICP-OES + XAS and residue checks; phosphate product inhibition is explicitly tested and paired with regeneration protocols, mitigating the stated deactivation risk.

5) Mechanistic and computational coherence with decisive readouts: A concrete structural model (DFT cluster or periodic) will be used to rank co-catalyst/chelator combinations by predicted P=O binding energies and TS stabilization, then validated by in situ DRIFTS and solid-state 31P NMR under humid conditions. Together with KIE and inhibitor poisoning, this closes the mechanistic ambiguity gap and ties structure → energetics → kinetics under realistic humidity.

Overall feasibility is strengthened by (i) a pre-registered validation framework, (ii) orthogonal proof of aperture selectivity, (iii) direct water/co-adsorption measurements, and (iv) site-normalized kinetics with deactivation/regeneration, ensuring that any claimed synergy is experimentally defensible and not an artifact of defect redistribution or pore blockage.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a flexible, single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC“SC) transformable Zr-based MOF with *verified ≥2.0 nm accessible channels* can be engineered as a mechanically encoded, integrin-targeted biosensing/drug-interface by coupling (A) an externally displayed, MDC/codon-usage-optimized, non-gelling WPT2-3R-derived integrin ligand (purely for cell recognition) with (B) an internally confined, enzyme-free target-catalyzed hairpin assembly (TCHA) circuit whose apparent kinetics are modulated by mechanically induced changes in (i) effective pore diameter/neck size (ΔD in Å) and (ii) intrapore electrostatics (Δζ / Δionic strength / ΔDonnan potential). Mechanistically, SC“SC switching alters both steric accessibility (hybridization/branch migration requires a minimum effective free volume and reduced entropic penalty under confinement) and electrostatic screening (strand displacement rates depend on salt-dependent base-pairing kinetics and toehold binding), enabling a predictable, reversible fold-change in k_obs *beyond* what can be explained by target diffusion/partition alone. The refined design explicitly addresses feasibility concerns by (1) selecting/engineering a Zr-MOF family with demonstrated breathing/SC“SC behavior and ≥2 nm 1D channels, or (fallback) redesigning the nucleic-acid chemistry to operate in true micropores using shortened hairpins and/or PNA clamps; (2) predefining quantitative modulation targets (ΔD, Δζ, expected k_obs fold-change) and separating intrinsic kinetics from uptake limitations via independent partition/transport measurements; and (3) rigorously proving spatial orthogonality (protein-only outside; H1-only inside) with orthogonal chemistries plus quantitative localization/leakage metrics. The output is read chemically/optically (FRET/fluorogenic strand accumulation and/or DNA-gated drug sequestration/release), avoiding electrochemical composite artifacts while preserving a crystalline, mechanically switchable reaction environment.
Plan: Step 0 — Define quantitative go/no-go criteria (set before synthesis)
0.1 Pore-access criterion: MOF must show an *accessible* channel/neck diameter ≥2.0 nm for at least one SC“SC state (validated by adsorption/uptake of calibrated dyes or PEG standards, not only crystallographic voids). Go/no-go: uptake of a 2.0“2.5 nm hydrodynamic diameter probe (e.g., labeled dextran/PEG or rigid dye dimer) ≥20% of external-surface-only control.
0.2 Reversibility criterion: ≥10 mechanical switching cycles with crystallinity retained. Operational threshold: PXRD peak positions reversible with <0.2° 2θ hysteresis and integrated intensity retention ≥80% (plus microscopy confirming no gross cracking).
0.3 Kinetic modulation target: mechanically switched states must yield ≥3× fold-change in *intrinsic* TCHA k_obs at constant bulk composition, after correcting for target uptake/partition. If <1.5×, pivot to micropore-compatible oligo redesign (Step 1.4).
0.4 Clinical performance targets (miRNA-122 exemplar): LOD ≤10 fM in 50% human serum (or 10% if justified by antifouling constraints), time-to-signal ≤30 min, and specificity: ≥10× discrimination vs single-base mismatch.

Step 1 — Materials selection/design: flexible Zr-MOF with ≥2 nm channels + SC“SC evidence
1.1 Primary MOF track (mesochannel Zr-MOF): select a Zr-MOF architecture reported to combine (i) single-crystal growth, (ii) breathing/SC“SC-like transformations under guest/osmotic stimulus, and (iii) ≥2 nm 1D channels. Candidate families to prioritize in scouting: 
• Zr“porphyrin/mesoporous channel MOFs (e.g., PCN-type Zr6 frameworks with large 1D channels) where single crystals can be grown and post-synthetic linker/node functionalization is established.
• Zr frameworks with deliberately elongated/hinged dicarboxylate linkers that introduce shear/slip degrees of freedom and known pore-shape changes under guest exchange.
Deliverable: choose one platform with literature or preliminary confirmation of (a) accessible ≥2 nm channels and (b) reversible unit-cell/pore metric changes (Δa/Δb/Δc or aperture change) under a practical stimulus (osmotic pressure/guest).
1.2 SC“SC actuation mode: replace “uniaxial compression SCXRD” as the primary actuator/readout with *osmotic/guest-driven* SC“SC transitions (PEG, glycerol, salt, or solvent activity gradients) that are routinely implemented in capillaries/microfluidics and compatible with operando PXRD/optical kinetics. Uniaxial microcompression becomes a secondary confirmation tool (nanoindentation + optical reporter).
1.3 Mixed-linker chemical addressability: incorporate 5“10% of an orthogonally reactive linker while preserving pore accessibility:
• Internal address (DNA anchoring): include a minor fraction of Zr-binding “strong anchor” sites inside pores—e.g., pendant phosphate/phosphonate-containing linkers or defect-engineered Zr“OH/H2O sites tuned to bind phosphonate-modified oligos.
• External address (protein click): include a minor fraction of azide (or strained alkyne) terminated linkers enriched at the external surface via post-synthetic exchange (PSE) under diffusion-limited conditions (short time, larger reagent, low temperature), creating a surface-biased click layer.
Acceptance test: quantify azide enrichment near surface by reacting with a bulky fluorescent DBCO-dye and depth-profiling by confocal.
1.4 Fallback micropore track (if ≥2 nm access fails): redesign the amplification chemistry to fit 0.7“1.2 nm windows by using (i) shortened hairpins (minimal toeholds), (ii) LNA/PNA segments to reduce required length and enhance kinetics at low ionic strength, and/or (iii) a catalytic “toehold exchange” circuit with smaller footprint. Go/no-go decision after Step 2.2 pore-access tests.

Step 2 — Quantitative mechanochemical expectations (precompute → validate)
2.1 Define target mechanochemical perturbations grounded in strand-displacement salt dependence:
• Target ΔD(neck): 3“8 Å reversible change between states (enough to change confinement penalty for duplex formation/branch migration).
• Target Δζ or equivalent Δionic strength in pore: shift corresponding to ~20“50 mM effective monovalent salt (via Donnan partitioning in a charged pore), expected to change toehold binding and displacement kinetics by ~2“10× depending on design.
2.2 Precompute “intrinsic vs transport” contributions:
• Transport: measure effective diffusion/uptake of labeled miRNA mimic into MOF (D_eff, partition coefficient K_pore/bulk) in each mechanical state.
• Intrinsic kinetics: design a FRET hairpin pair where rate is limited by strand displacement after binding, and fit to a model incorporating measured K and D_eff to extract k_intrinsic.
Deliverable: predicted k_obs(state A)/k_obs(state B) and the portion attributable to transport vs intrinsic changes.

Step 3 — WPT2-3R re-engineering as external integrin ligand (not hydrogel)
3.1 Genetic construction: apply MDC-based codon-usage-balanced PCR assembly to produce a *non-gelling* WPT2-3R variant:
• Remove/shorten electrostatically crosslinking blocks responsible for triblock hydrogel formation.
• Insert a high-affinity integrin-binding motif (e.g., cyclic RGD-like presentation or WPT-derived motif as justified by literature) placed in a solvent-exposed loop.
• Add a single site-specific conjugation handle (C-terminal azide/alkyne via engineered residue or enzymatic tag), plus a protease-cleavable spacer to enable “protease-access” localization assays.
3.2 Expression/purification/QC: E. coli expression, purification by affinity + SEC; verify mass (intact LC“MS) and sequence fidelity (peptide mapping). Confirm non-gelling by rheology (G′~0 under formulation conditions used for MOF work).
3.3 Conjugation to MOF surface only: perform strain-promoted click (DBCO“azide) using size-exclusion constraints (protein too large to enter pores) *and* surface-biased azide distribution (Step 1.3). Quantify protein loading by BCA/UV and by amino-acid analysis after digestion.

Step 4 — TCHA circuit design compatible with confinement
4.1 Hairpin architecture: design H1/H2 with:
• Hairpin stem lengths tuned to remain metastable in serum (minimize leak), toeholds 5“7 nt (adjustable) to confer salt sensitivity.
• H1 includes a Zr-binding anchor (terminal phosphonate/catechol) chosen based on stability constants on Zr6 nodes; H2 remains free.
• FRET reporting: donor on H1, acceptor on H2 (or quencher) so that duplex accumulation yields a monotonic optical signal.
4.2 Confinement compatibility: choose oligo total lengths that physically fit ≥2 nm channels (primary track) while retaining catalytic turnover; if primary track fails pore-access, switch to Step 1.4 micropore circuit.

Step 5 — Proving orthogonality (external protein vs internal DNA) with quantitative localization + leakage metrics
5.1 Confocal/super-resolution mapping:
• External-only protein: label protein with fluorophore; perform z-stack imaging of single crystals. Protease-access assay: add protease that cannot enter pores (size-exclusion) and quantify loss of fluorescence to confirm surface exposure.
• Internal-only H1: use fluorophore-labeled H1 and a pore-inaccessible quencher added externally; lack of quenching implies internal localization.
5.2 Chemical compartment mapping:
• Digest-and-map: sequentially (i) mild surface etch to remove outer layer, (ii) full digestion; quantify P (from DNA) by ICP-OES/ICP-MS and quantify protein by amino acid analysis to derive surface vs core distributions.
5.3 Leakage and cross-contamination tests:
• H1 leakage: incubate functionalized crystals in buffer/serum, quantify released DNA over time by fluorescence/qPCR (as analytical readout, not amplification step).
• External adsorption control: incubate non-functionalized MOF with H1/H2 to quantify nonspecific adsorption; block with phosphate/citrate and compare.
Acceptance: ≥90% of protein signal removable by protease; ≥80% of H1 signal retained after protease; H1 leakage <5% over assay timeframe.

Step 6 — Operando mechanochemical switching + kinetic readout (practical instrumentation)
6.1 Actuation: implement osmotic/guest switching in a microfluidic chamber containing single crystals:
• Switch between low and high osmotic pressure solutions (PEG/glycerol) or between two solvent activities known to trigger SC“SC in the selected MOF.
• Monitor crystal integrity by optical microscopy; avoid uniaxial load as primary mode.
6.2 Structure readout under switching:
• Operando PXRD in capillary/microfluidic-compatible holders to track peak shifts (unit cell change) during switching.
• Complement with Raman/IR (linker breathing/guest signatures) and uptake assays (dye/solute adsorption) in each state to infer ΔD and internal environment changes.
6.3 Kinetic readout during switching:
• Real-time fluorescence microscopy (single-crystal) to record FRET/quenched signal vs time after target addition.
• Fit kinetics using the transport-corrected model from Step 2.2 to extract k_intrinsic for each state.

Step 7 — Pharmaceutical interface demonstration (chemical readout and DNA-gated cargo)
7.1 Cargo strategy: select a cationic fluorogenic intercalator or a clinically relevant small molecule whose retention increases with duplex DNA accumulation (electrostatic/π-stacking) or use a DNA-gated pore-blocking scheme.
7.2 Show mechanical gating: demonstrate that state A vs state B produces different duplex accumulation → different cargo retention/release profiles at equal target concentration.

Step 8 — Biological validation: integrin targeting + clinically relevant matrices
8.1 Integrin binding/uptake:
• Compare integrin-high vs integrin-low cell lines, plus competition with soluble RGD.
• Quantify association/internalization by flow cytometry/confocal; confirm that WPT2-3R variant changes adhesion without altering MOF switching (PXRD unchanged before/after protein conjugation).
8.2 miRNA-122 detection benchmarking:
• Matrices: 10“50% human serum and cell lysate.
• Metrics: LOD, dynamic range, time-to-signal, mismatch discrimination.
• Controls: (i) non-switchable rigid Zr-MOF analog (same chemistry, no breathing) and (ii) switched vs unswitched states at same bulk conditions to isolate mechanochemical effect.

Decision points (explicit pivots)
D1 (after Step 2.2): if ≥2 nm access not met → activate micropore circuit (Step 1.4).
D2 (after Step 6.3): if k_intrinsic modulation <1.5× after transport correction → redesign toehold length/salt sensitivity, increase intrapore charge modulation (linker functionalization), or shift to a more flexible MOF.
D3 (after Step 5): if orthogonality fails (protein blocks pores or DNA adsorbs externally) → introduce antifouling surface layer (PEGylation), reduce external defects, or change anchoring chemistry to enforce internal binding only.
Feasibility: Materials feasibility (addressing micropore/mesopore and SC“SC concerns): The revised plan removes reliance on NU-901/UiO-67 as default (typically microporous) and instead requires a Zr-MOF platform with *demonstrated* ≥2 nm accessible channels and reversible stimulus-induced structural change. It also includes a hard fallback: redesign of the nucleic-acid circuit (shortened hairpins/LNA/PNA) to operate within genuine micropores if ≥2 nm access cannot be validated experimentally. Operando SCXRD-under-uniaxial-load is de-emphasized in favor of practical switching/readouts (osmotic/guest switching + PXRD/Raman/uptake), with explicit crystallinity retention thresholds.

Mechanistic rigor (quantitative expectations + diffusion controls): The proposal now predefines the magnitudes of mechanochemical perturbation needed (ΔD in Å; Δζ/Δionic strength equivalents) and treats k_obs as a convolution of (i) target partition/transport and (ii) intrinsic strand-displacement kinetics. Independent measurement of intrapore uptake/partition (K_pore) and effective diffusion (D_eff) in each mechanical state enables extraction of k_intrinsic; only modulation of k_intrinsic constitutes evidence for mechanochemical control beyond diffusion/partition artifacts.

Orthogonality and failure-mode mitigation: Spatial segregation is no longer assumed. It is validated quantitatively via (i) depth-resolved fluorescence imaging, (ii) protease-accessibility (surface-exposed protein), (iii) pore-inaccessible quencher tests (internal DNA), and (iv) digestion/ICP mapping of phosphorus vs protein. Explicit leakage metrics and nonspecific adsorption controls are included, directly addressing protein corona/pore blocking and DNA adsorption to external Zr sites.

Operational realism: The instrumentation pathway is made executable by using microfluidic osmotic switching (compatible with optical kinetics) and operando PXRD/Raman rather than demanding simultaneous SCXRD under mechanical load. Acceptance criteria for reversibility and retained crystallinity are defined, enabling go/no-go decisions.

Clinical relevance: The analyte (miRNA-122) and matrices (human serum/cell lysate) are specified with explicit performance targets (LOD, time-to-signal, mismatch discrimination) and benchmarking against non-switchable MOF controls, ensuring the mechanically switched functionality is causally linked to improved analytical behavior rather than generic signal amplification.

Hypothesis: Creating hydroxyl-terminated node defect sites at Zr6 clusters in a prototypical proton-conductive MOF (UiO-66/NU-1000 family) will simultaneously (i) lower the proton-transfer activation barrier via a defect-anchored, percolating hydrogen-bond network (Grotthuss-dominant under controlled hydration) and (ii) increase electronic conductivity by introducing defect-derived mid-gap states and strengthened H-bond-assisted polaron/charge delocalization along node“linker junctions. The key methodological adaptation is a defect-chemistry-controlled ‘hydroxylation protocol’ that converts missing-linker/missing-cluster defects into uniformly OH-capped Brønsted sites (rather than mixed OH/H2O/anion terminations), coupled to a DFT-to-impedance workflow where DFT-computed proton migration barriers and defect-state densities are used as quantitative design targets for synthesis and post-synthetic exchange.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a robust Zr6-node MOF platform with well-studied defect chemistry and water stability: UiO-66 (BDC) for dense 3D connectivity and NU-1000 for accessible node pockets; prepare a small matrix of crystals/powders with systematically varied modulator content (formic/acetic acid) to tune missing-linker defect density.
1.2 Implement a controlled termination strategy to bias node defect sites toward hydroxyl groups: (a) post-synthetic washing to remove residual monocarboxylate modulators; (b) mild base hydrolysis (carefully buffered, e.g., dilute NH4OH/EtOH-H2O) to convert labile Zr“O2CR terminations into Zr“OH; (c) optional isotopic labeling (D2O exchange) to enable mechanistic spectroscopy.
1.3 Quantify defect density and termination identity: TGA/solution 1H NMR of digested samples for missing-linker metrics; DRIFTS/IR (O“H stretch signatures), XPS (O 1s components), and pair distribution function (PDF) or total scattering to confirm node-local disorder.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation (defect ‘hydroxylation’ as a design variable): rather than treating defects as random, use sequential, stoichiometrically constrained post-synthetic exchange (PSE) of charge-compensating species to enforce predominantly terminal “OH/μ2“OH at the Zr6 node. Execute a two-step PSE: (i) remove/replace bound monocarboxylates with weakly coordinating anions (e.g., nitrate) under solvothermal mild conditions; (ii) hydrolyze to “OH while maintaining crystallinity (optimize pH/time via in situ PXRD).
2.2 Build DFT models that explicitly encode experimentally measured defect populations: generate periodic supercells of UiO-66/NU-1000 containing missing-linker sites with different terminations (“OH, “OH2, residual “O2CR) and varying spatial distributions (isolated vs. clustered defects).
2.3 Compute mechanistic descriptors with DFT: (a) proton transfer pathways using NEB (nudged elastic band) along H-bond chains connecting hydroxylated nodes (barriers, ΔG‡); (b) hydration-dependent H-bond network statistics via ab initio MD (limited cells) or cluster-continuum approximations; (c) electronic structure changes (DOS, projected DOS, defect-state energies) and small-polaron hopping proxies (reorganization energy estimates on node“linker junctions).
2.4 Close the design loop: use DFT targets to refine synthesis—aim for a percolation threshold of OH sites (defect density and spatial correlation) that yields a continuous hydrogen-bond network without framework collapse; iterate hydroxylation conditions accordingly.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Measure proton conductivity (σH+) with AC impedance spectroscopy under controlled RH and temperature; extract activation energies from Arrhenius plots and correlate with DFT NEB barriers and AIMD-derived proton diffusion coefficients.
3.2 Deconvolute Grotthuss vs vehicular mechanisms using: (a) H/D isotope effect (D2O equilibration) on σ; (b) variable RH dependence; (c) solid-state 1H NMR (T1/T2, line-shape changes) to quantify proton mobility and site exchange.
3.3 Measure electronic conductivity separately (σe−) to test the ‘defect-state’ claim: perform DC polarization/Hebb-Wagner-type measurements (blocking electrodes) and temperature dependence; confirm defect-related mid-gap states via UV“vis diffuse reflectance and EPR (paramagnetic centers, trapped electrons).
3.4 Establish structure“property causality: multivariate regression/physics-informed modeling linking experimentally quantified OH density, defect distribution metrics (PDF), DFT descriptors (barriers, DOS features) to σH+ and σe−; validate on a hold-out set of independently synthesized batches.
3.5 Stress-test stability: cycling RH/temperature and mild acid exposure to ensure the hydroxylated defect terminations do not trigger node dissolution; monitor crystallinity (PXRD) and porosity (N2 sorption).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zr6-node MOFs (UiO-66/NU-1000) exhibit tunable node defect sites and well-defined node terminations; hydroxyl groups are known to seed hydrogen-bond networks that facilitate proton hopping, and DFT has proven effective in resolving node chemistry and bonding-site specificity at Zr6 clusters.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Defect engineering is already a central lever in Zr-MOF chemistry, but defect terminations are often chemically heterogeneous. The proposed adaptation converts ‘defect density’ into ‘defect identity control’ (OH-enforced terminations), enabling a mechanistically interpretable mapping between node chemistry, proton pathways, and conductivity—directly aligning with coordination-polymer design principles.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional strategies that add external acids/ionic guests, hydroxyl-terminated node defect sites create intrinsic, framework-anchored proton relays that are less prone to leaching and can be optimized via computable descriptors (NEB barriers, defect DOS). The integrated DFT-to-impedance loop reduces trial-and-error by making OH percolation and defect-state formation explicit design targets, enabling simultaneous tuning of proton conductivity and electrical conductivity within a single robust MOF scaffold.

Hypothesis: A porphyrin-sensitized, defect-engineered Hf12 MOF will outperform conventional porphyrinic MOFs for light-driven Escherichia coli inactivation by enforcing a contact-dependent Type I ROS sequence (O2•− → H2O2 → •OH-equivalents) localized at bacteria“MOF interfaces, while retaining low mammalian cytotoxicity due to nm-scale ROS range and heterogeneous confinement. Mechanistically, we explicitly avoid claiming intrinsic Hf(IV) redox cycling: instead, the porphyrin triplet/excited-state supplies electrons to O2 (via an interfacial PCET/electron-relay installed at undercoordinated Hf defect sites), generating O2•− and subsequently H2O2 in a mass-balanced, quantifiable pathway. The Hf12 node’s role is (i) to create a high-density, hydroxo/aqua, Lewis-acidic microenvironment that binds/activates O2•−/HO2•/H2O2 (including pKa shifting and inner-sphere stabilization), (ii) to template and immobilize the redox relay in an inner-sphere fashion (preventing diffusional loss and enabling rapid interfacial electron/PCET steps), and (iii) to enhance interfacial ROS damage by concentrating bacteria at the MOF surface through tunable surface charge/adhesion. The decisive claim is therefore ‘Hf-assisted, defect-registered Type I photochemistry’ rather than ‘Hf-Fenton’: •OH (or •OH-equivalent oxidizing radicals detected by orthogonal probes) arises from photoredox-generated peroxide intermediates activated/decomposed within the Lewis-acidic defect pocket, and must exhibit catalytic turnover with respect to the immobilized mediator (no net mediator consumption/leaching) and a strict correlation between (a) site-occupancy at defects, (b) O2•−/H2O2 accumulation rates, and (c) antibacterial kinetics under photon-flux-normalized irradiation (500 W xenon arc lamp).
Plan: Step 0 — System definition, normalization, and benchmarking
0.1 Lamp normalization: calibrate 500 W xenon arc lamp photon flux by chemical actinometry (ferrioxalate for UV“vis; Reinecke’s salt or Aberchrome as cross-check depending on spectral window). Report photon flux (einstein·s−1), irradiance (mW·cm−2), and spectral distribution at sample plane; use bandpass filters (e.g., 420±20 nm for porphyrin Soret excitation; 550±25 nm for Q-band; and long-pass >420 nm to suppress deep-UV artifacts). Enforce identical geometry/optical path for all MOFs and textiles.
0.2 Benchmark materials: reproduce/obtain PCN-224 on woven cotton fabric (PCN-224/WCF) as Asset-2 comparator under identical normalized light dose and oxygenation; include porphyrin-free Hf12 MOF and porphyrin-only controls.

Step 1 — MOF architecture: Hf12 framework + controlled missing-linker defects + porphyrin dilution
1.1 Base MOF selection: use an Hf12-oxo cluster MOF known to tolerate missing-linker chemistry and aqueous handling (e.g., an Hf-UiO-66/67-derived topology or an Hf12-based framework analogous to cationic Hf12 constructs), engineered as nanoscale crystallites (50“200 nm) for high external surface contact with bacteria.
1.2 Mixed-linker strategy: incorporate (i) a tetracarboxylate porphyrin linker (TCPP derivative) at controlled mol% (e.g., 2, 5, 10, 20% of total carboxylate equivalents) and (ii) an inert spacer dicarboxylate/benzenedicarboxylate (or biphenyl dicarboxylate) to dilute chromophore density and reduce self-quenching. Record porphyrin loading by digestion 1H NMR/UV“vis calibration.
1.3 Defect engineering: generate missing-linker defects using monotopic modulators (formic/acetic acid) with controlled modulator:Hf ratios (e.g., 10, 30, 60, 120 equiv) to create undercoordinated Hf sites capped by “OH/H2O. Quantify defect density by (i) TGA (mass loss modeling), (ii) digestion 1H NMR (modulator incorporation), and (iii) PDF analysis to validate local-node disorder.

Step 2 — “Spatial registration” of the redox relay at defect sites (inner-sphere binding proof)
2.1 Relay design: post-synthetically install a monocarboxylate-anchored redox relay that binds specifically at undercoordinated Hf sites: (A) catechol-carboxylate, (B) hydroxamate-carboxylate, and (C) redox-inert analogue control (e.g., methylated catechol or fluorinated phenylcarboxylate lacking redox activity but retaining binding geometry). Maintain low relay loading targets (e.g., 5“30% of defect sites) to avoid becoming the dominant chromophore.
2.2 Site occupancy quantification (mandatory):
  - Competitive ligand displacement: challenge bound relay with phosphate/citrate (known strong Hf binders) and quantify released relay by HPLC/UV to estimate binding strength and occupancy.
  - DRIFTS/ATR-IR: monitor carboxylate binding modes (Δνas“νs), catechol/hydroxamate signatures, and changes upon displacement.
  - Hf L3-edge EXAFS: detect changes in first-shell coordination (Hf“O distances/coordination number) consistent with relay binding vs hydroxyl/water capping; compare defective MOF ± relay and non-defective MOF ± relay.
  - Solid-state NMR where feasible (13C CPMAS on labeled relay) to confirm immobilization and exclude free relay.
2.3 Distance constraint (≤2 nm) substantiation: implement FRET/photoluminescence quenching distance constraints by incorporating a spectrally matched acceptor/donor pair (e.g., porphyrin emission quenched by relay absorption) and fit quenching vs loading to infer proximity; corroborate with transient absorption lifetimes consistent with static quenching at defect-bound relays.

Step 3 — Mass-balanced ROS sequence with orthogonal quantification (O2•− → H2O2 → •OH-equivalents)
3.1 O2•− quantification:
  - EPR spin trapping: DMPO/DEPMPO to distinguish •OH vs O2•− adducts (DEPMPO preferred for O2•− stability), with full spectral simulation/deconvolution.
  - Complementary colorimetric assays: XTT or cytochrome c reduction for O2•− (with SOD suppression control).
3.2 H2O2 quantification (mandatory):
  - Amplex Red/HRP assay calibrated in the same buffer, with adsorption/inner-filter controls (MOF present but dark; MOF removed prior to readout via centrifugation/filtration).
  - Titanium sulfate method as a second orthogonal assay less sensitive to some organic interferences.
  - Time-course mass balance: relate O2 consumption (Clark electrode or optode) to H2O2 accumulation and decay under illumination.
3.3 •OH / •OH-equivalent detection (hardened selectivity):
  - Primary: HPF (hydroxyphenyl fluorescein) and coumarin → 7-hydroxycoumarin assays (cross-check), with calibration and adsorption corrections.
  - Secondary: terephthalic acid assay retained but only after demonstrating negligible adsorption and correcting inner-filter effects (measure excitation/emission attenuation by MOF scattering; front-face fluorescence geometry if needed).
  - EPR: DMPO-•OH/DEPMPO-•OH assignment with scavenger validation.
3.4 1O2 quantification:
  - Replace DPBF as primary with SOSG (Singlet Oxygen Sensor Green), including adsorption controls (SOSG + MOF dark; SOSG + MOF light without O2) and verification that SOSG does not photo-oxidize on its own under the lamp.
  - DPBF used only as supporting data with radical-scavenger controls to demonstrate non-selectivity in the MOF matrix.
3.5 Scavenger and enzyme controls (mechanistic): NaN3 (1O2), isopropanol/mannitol (•OH), SOD (O2•−), catalase (H2O2). Require consistent suppression patterns across all ROS assays and antibacterial outcomes.

Step 4 — Decoupling “Hf Lewis acid assistance” from “relay redox locus” (mandatory comparative matrix)
4.1 Material matrix (minimum):
  - Defective Hf12-porphyrin MOF (no relay)
  - Defective Hf12-porphyrin MOF + redox relay
  - Defective Hf12-porphyrin MOF + redox-inert relay analogue (binding control)
  - Zr-analogue MOF matched in topology/porphyrin loading/defect density (± same relays)
  - Non-defective (low-defect) Hf12-porphyrin MOF ± relay (defect necessity)
4.2 Relay integrity and turnover:
  - Leaching: quantify relay in supernatant after irradiation/wash cycles by LC-MS/HPLC.
  - Photoproduct mapping: LC-MS of irradiated suspensions to identify oxidized relay species; criterion: antibacterial activity and ROS generation must persist without stoichiometric relay loss (turnover demonstrated by constant relay loading and sustained ROS rates over repeated cycles).
  - Node integrity: XPS (Hf 4f/O 1s), PXRD, and porphyrin UV“vis/DRS to confirm no catastrophic decomposition that could generate soluble radicals.

Step 5 — Interfacial contact engineering and quantification (bacteria“MOF colocalization)
5.1 Substrate fabrication: immobilize nMOFs onto (i) cotton (PCN-224/WCF comparator) and (ii) inert polymer fibers/films using covalent anchoring (e.g., silane coupling on polymer, or poly(dopamine) interlayer) to prevent particle detachment; quantify MOF mass loading (mg·cm−2) and wash resistance.
5.2 Surface charge tuning: adjust outer-surface chemistry to promote E. coli adhesion (e.g., mild cationic polymer overlayer at sub-monolayer coverage, or retain cationic framework character). Measure zeta potential in the same ionic strength buffer used for killing assays.
5.3 Contact quantification:
  - Adsorption isotherms: quantify bacterial binding to MOF-coated substrates (CFU depletion from solution vs time).
  - Microscopy colocalization: confocal live/dead staining overlaid with MOF fluorescence (porphyrin signal) to show killing localized where bacteria contact MOF; SEM to visualize membrane disruption at attachment points.
  - Flow-cell assay (optional but strong): quantify adhesion and killing under shear to mimic realistic textile conditions.

Step 6 — Antibacterial performance, kinetics, and selectivity
6.1 E. coli inactivation: use a defined strain (e.g., K-12 or ATCC 8099), standardized inoculum, buffer, oxygenation, and light dose. Report log reduction vs time and extract apparent rate constants. Include dark controls and ‘light-only’ substrate controls.
6.2 Benchmarking: compare directly to PCN-224/WCF under identical photon dose (not just time), using the same substrate area and bacterial loading.
6.3 Mammalian cytotoxicity/selectivity: MTT/CCK-8 on representative mammalian cells with ± illumination, hemolysis, and leachate controls. Require that supernatants (after removing substrate) show minimal toxicity to support heterogeneous, localized ROS action.

Step 7 — Mechanistic closure and falsification criteria (tightened)
7.1 Required causal chain (must all hold): (i) relay occupancy at Hf defects verified (EXAFS/DRIFTS/displacement), (ii) enhanced O2•− and H2O2 rates under light relative to no-relay and to redox-inert relay, (iii) •OH-equivalent probe signals suppressed by catalase and •OH scavengers, (iv) antibacterial kinetics track •OH-equivalent flux and bacterial contact metrics, not SOSG (1O2) alone.
7.2 Failure modes:
  - If Zr analogue behaves identically to Hf in ROS/kill despite matched occupancy and defects, Hf-specific Lewis-acid assistance is not supported.
  - If relay is consumed stoichiometrically (LC-MS shows progressive oxidation/leaching correlating with activity), the system is mediator-driven rather than catalytic/templated; redesign relay or lower loading.
  - If killing correlates primarily with SOSG and is NaN3-sensitive while catalase/•OH scavengers show minimal effect, the pathway is Type II dominated and the hypothesis is rejected.

Feasibility: 1) Mechanistic plausibility without invoking ‘Hf-Fenton’ redox cycling: The refined mechanism assigns electron delivery to O2 to the photoexcited porphyrin/relay ensemble (photoredox competent) while positioning Hf12 nodes as Lewis-acidic, hydroxo-rich, defect-localized activation pockets that bind/stabilize peroxide intermediates and accelerate interfacial PCET steps. This addresses the reviewer’s core concern that Hf(IV) is redox-inert in water: Hf is not required to undergo Hf(IV)/Hf(III) cycling for the ROS sequence to proceed.
2) Decisive attribution controls: The mandated Hf vs Zr analogue matrix, redox-inert relay analogue, defect vs non-defect comparisons, and relay integrity/leaching + LC-MS photoproduct tracking collectively decouple (i) metal-node Lewis acidity, (ii) defect registration/inner-sphere binding, and (iii) relay-driven stoichiometric radical formation. These controls directly respond to the confounding risk that the mediator itself could be the primary radical source.
3) Mass-balanced intermediate validation: Quantifying O2•− (EPR + XTT/cytochrome c), H2O2 (Amplex Red + titanium sulfate), and •OH-equivalents (HPF/coumarin + EPR) under photon-flux-normalized conditions converts the mechanistic claim into a testable kinetic network, rather than relying on single-probe inference. Enzyme/scavenger suppression patterns provide orthogonal verification.
4) Spatial registration and contact dependence are made measurable: Inner-sphere binding/occupancy is substantiated by EXAFS/DRIFTS/competitive displacement and distance constraints from photophysics (quenching/FRET-like analysis). Bacteria“MOF contact—essential for •OH efficacy—is engineered via surface charge tuning and quantified by zeta potential, adsorption isotherms, and microscopy colocalization of live/dead staining with MOF location.
5) Strong precedent for ROS enhancement in high-Z Hf systems and porphyrinic antibacterial MOFs: Asset 1 supports that Hf-based architectures in close-proximity multi-component constructs can amplify ROS outputs (including •OH signals) under irradiation, motivating the emphasis on sub-nm to nm interfacial registration. Asset 2 establishes that porphyrinic MOFs under a 500 W xenon lamp can inactivate E. coli with low mammalian cytotoxicity and provides a direct benchmark; our refinement aims to surpass Type II-limited performance by shifting to contact-localized Type I chemistry validated by mass-balanced intermediates and catalytic turnover criteria.

Hypothesis: A BTC-based Cu(II) MOF deliberately engineered to contain a controllable fraction of labile, coordinatively unsaturated Cu sites (dynamic metal centers) and then postsynthetically “gated” with reversible, competitive chelating pendants will outperform static analogues in drug loading capacity and uptake property. Mechanistically, the methodological adaptation is a two-stage defect-and-gate design: (i) introduce missing-linker defects in a Cu“BTC lattice to generate a tunable density of open Cu sites that can switch coordination number/geometry upon guest approach; (ii) install pore-facing, reversible O/N-donor chelators via postsynthetic modification so that the pendant groups transiently bind/unbind to Cu during adsorption, creating an adaptive host-guest interaction landscape. This dynamic coordination gating increases the adsorption enthalpy for polar/chelating drug motifs at low coverage (via open-metal-site binding) while preventing pore blocking and enabling high-capacity packing at high coverage (via reversible pendant displacement), thereby increasing both maximum loading and uptake kinetics without framework collapse.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Synthesize a baseline Cu“BTC framework (HKUST-1-type) under solvothermal conditions, then prepare a defect series by partial substitution of BTC with a monotopic modulator (e.g., benzoic acid or acetic acid) to generate controlled missing-linker defects while preserving topology.
1.2 Quantify defect/open-metal-site density using TGA (modulator content), acid digestion + 1H NMR (linker/modulator ratio), and ICP-OES (Cu content). Activate under vacuum with a standardized thermal protocol to generate Cu open sites.
1.3 Select two drug probes with distinct coordination propensities to map mechanism: (A) ibuprofen (carboxylate; moderate Cu affinity), (B) doxorubicin (multiple O/N donors; strong Cu affinity). Establish solubility/solvent systems compatible with framework stability.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Postsynthetic modification (PSM) “gate installation”: introduce pore-facing reversible chelators by grafting small, flexible N/O-donor pendants onto accessible carboxylate-adjacent positions using coordinate-covalent anchoring at Cu sites plus weak secondary interactions. Concretely:
- Perform controlled partial ligand exchange at defect sites using a pyridyl-carboxylate or hydroxamate-bearing monocarboxylate (e.g., 4-pyridinecarboxylic acid derivative or acetohydroxamic acid derivative tethered to a carboxylate), to create pendant chelators that can transiently occupy Cu.
- Tune grafting fraction (e.g., 10%, 30%, 50% of defect-capping sites) by stoichiometry and time.
2.2 Create a comparative matrix of materials:
- M0: pristine Cu“BTC (minimal defects, no PSM)
- M1: defect-engineered Cu“BTC (variable defect levels, no PSM)
- M2: defect + gated PSM series (variable defect levels, variable pendant fraction)
2.3 Establish dynamic-metal-center behavior:
- In situ DRIFTS/FTIR with CO or pyridine as probe to quantify open Cu sites and their reversibility after gating.
- Variable-temperature EPR and/or XAS (if available) to monitor coordination environment changes upon guest exposure (drug vapor or solution dosing).
2.4 Drug loading and uptake measurements:
- Equilibrate MOFs with drug solutions at controlled concentrations; determine loading by UV“vis/HPLC of supernatant depletion and by digestion-NMR where applicable.
- Measure uptake kinetics (time-dependent loading) and construct adsorption isotherms (loading vs concentration) to extract capacity and affinity.
- Conduct pH-triggered release studies (physiological vs acidic) to test whether dynamic coordination accelerates release via competitive protonation/ligand displacement.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Morphology/structural integrity: SEM to compare crystal habit and detect etching/collapse across defect/PSM series; PXRD to confirm topology retention; N2 sorption (BET/DFT pore size distribution) to separate “capacity from porosity” vs “capacity from binding”.
3.2 Mechanistic confirmation of adaptive host-guest interactions:
- Competitive binding tests: add a benign competitor (e.g., imidazole or acetate) during loading to see if capacity/kinetics shift as predicted for coordination-gated binding.
- Microcalorimetry or van ’t Hoff analysis (temperature-dependent isotherms) to deconvolute enthalpy changes; expectation: higher initial heats for M2 vs M0/M1 but less drastic pore-blocking at higher coverage.
- Solid-state NMR/FTIR signatures of drug coordination (carboxylate shifts for ibuprofen; anthracycline O/N interactions for doxorubicin) correlated with open-site density.
3.3 Performance metrics and decision criteria:
- Primary: maximum drug loading capacity (wt% and mmol/g) and uptake half-time.
- Secondary: framework stability after loading/release (PXRD, SEM), retention of porosity, and reproducibility across batches.
- Benchmark against mixed-ligand Cu-MOF literature values (BTC/IPA systems) under matched conditions to demonstrate superiority of the dynamic-gating mechanism rather than simple compositional tuning.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Cu“BTC frameworks are established drug carriers; open Cu sites are known to increase guest affinity, while postsynthetic modification is a validated route to tune pore chemistry and stability. The literature indicates that PSM can modulate uptake properties and that dynamic metal centers amplify host-guest interactions; defect engineering is a controllable way to tune unsaturated site density.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal uses rational coordination chemistry—missing-linker defects create coordinatively unsaturated Cu nodes (dynamic centers), while reversible chelating pendants introduce a designed competition for metal coordination. This is a MOF-native, molecularly programmable approach that directly links node chemistry, pore functionality, and adsorption thermodynamics.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with (i) pristine Cu“BTC (static binding landscape) and (ii) mixed-linker approaches (property shifts dominated by pore size/shape changes), the defect-and-gate adaptation targets the limiting tradeoff in drug MOFs: strong binding increases affinity but can cause pore blocking and slow kinetics. Dynamic coordination gating yields high initial affinity without permanently immobilizing the drug, enabling higher capacity at saturation and faster uptake/release control while maintaining crystallinity (validated by SEM/PXRD).

Hypothesis: A spatially graded, *fixed-charge* defect landscape in a water-stable Zr6-oxo MOF—engineered as an anionically terminated outer shell (Zr“O“SO3− capped missing-linker sites) over a minimally defective, electronically benign core—will generate a measurable shell-to-core electrostatic potential (built-in field) that biases photogenerated carrier separation toward the catalytic surface and accelerates interfacial proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET). When a confined visible absorber is grown *only within a phase-confinement loading window* in the near-surface channel network (initially iodoplumbate MTP; contingency iodobismuthate/Cs3Bi2I9-like clusters), the combined architecture will (i) improve electron delivery to surface HER sites via band bending/potential gradient, (ii) increase HER kinetics via defect-local Zr“OH/Zr“OH2+ Brønsted acidity and optimized H* adsorption at defect-capped nodes (analogy to defect-driven CB/d-band tuning in photocatalytic MOFs), and (iii) suppress deleterious mobile-ion contributions to hysteresis by physically confining the absorber to sub-critical domain sizes and chemically tethering it at defect-capped sites—*provided* a pre-validated aqueous compatibility gate is met (no significant Pb/I leaching or I−/I3− photoredox runaway under the exact illumination/pH/ionic strength). The junction claim is rendered non-metaphorical by (a) specifying the fixed-charge chemistry (controlled fraction of Zr“O“SO3− vs neutral Zr“OH caps) and (b) pre-registering a falsifiable criterion: a reproducible shell-to-core contact potential difference ≥50“100 mV with correlated depth-dependent band-edge shifts by UPS/XPS; if this criterion is not met, the mechanism will be downgraded to ‘defect-site kinetics only’ and field-driven claims removed.
Plan: Step 0 — System choice and quantitative design targets (set before synthesis)
0.1 MOF platform: select a Zr6-carboxylate with straight channels and known defect tolerance + aqueous stability. Primary: NU-1000 (Zr6 nodes, 1D mesoporous channels ~3 nm with microporous windows) to accommodate confined clusters while maintaining water stability; Alternative: UiO-67 derivative with enlarged apertures if NU-1000 chemistry proves incompatible with absorber precursors.
0.2 Defect-mode target: missing-linker defects only (node preserved). Acceptance bounds prior to absorber growth: (i) crystallinity retained (single-crystal or microcrystal PXRD peak broadening <15% vs parent), (ii) BET/Ar sorption pore volume loss <25%, (iii) no significant missing-cluster signatures in PDF/STEM (see Step 2).
0.3 Built-in field target: shell-to-core potential difference ≥50“100 mV across a 50“300 nm shell (measured on cross-sections), with matching depth-resolved band-edge/band-bending signatures.
0.4 Absorber phase-confinement target: absorber domain size (TEM/Scherrer) ≤ channel diameter and non-percolated (no continuous 3D MAPbI3-like domains). Define loading window as Pb (or Bi) wt% such that (i) PXRD lacks intense bulk perovskite reflections, (ii) STEM-EDX shows discontinuous domains confined to channels/shell region.

Step 1 — Grow low-defect starting crystals and pre-functionalize for controlled defect chemistry
1.1 Synthesize NU-1000 single crystals or large microcrystals via modulated solvothermal conditions (benzoic/formic acid modulators; low water activity), targeting low initial defect density (verified by digestion 1H NMR + TGA).
1.2 Introduce a minor fraction (5“15%) of linker functionality capable of later anchoring/capping chemistry without destabilizing Zr6 connectivity: (a) sulfonate-bearing dicarboxylate as *post-capable anion source* OR (b) pendant pyridyl groups to coordinate Pb/Bi without introducing strong acid in the same step.
