Step 1 — Materials synthesis with stability-by-design
1.1 ZIF-8 template synthesis (morphology standardization)
• Prepare ZIF-8 rhombic dodecahedra (300“600 nm) by controlling Zn2+:2-methylimidazole ratio and mixing rate; tighten dispersity by seed-mediated growth if needed.
• QC: SEM (size distribution, n≥200); PXRD (phase purity); zeta potential (for later deposition consistency).

1.2 Conductive MOF-derived carbon core (preserve polyhedral geometry)
• Infiltrate ZIF-8 with dopamine (or furfuryl alcohol) to create an in situ polymer network; polymerize under mild conditions.
• Carbonize under N2 (optimize 700/800/900 °C) to obtain N-doped porous hollow carbon polyhedra.
• QC: Raman (ID/IG); XPS (N species); conductivity (four-point probe on films); TEM for hollow structure.

1.3 Semiconductor shell with engineered interfaces (ZnS → CdS/ZnCdS)
• Deposit ZnS interlayer by SILAR (Zn2+/S2−) to passivate carbon surface states and provide a chemically uniform sulfide surface.
• Grow CdS or ZnCdS shell by controlled ion exchange/sulfurization to form a conformal photoactive layer.
• QC: HAADF-STEM/EDS line scans to confirm continuous shell and composition; UV“Vis (band edge); XPS (Cd/Zn/S chemical states).

1.4 Mandatory CdS photocorrosion protection: conformal ALD barrier
• Apply ALD TiO2 or Al2O3 on the sulfide shell (screen 1.5, 3.0, 5.0 nm). Rationale: sub-5 nm layers can suppress oxidative photocorrosion while still enabling electron tunneling and preserving PEC response.
• Select oxide based on (i) best stability (least photocurrent decay), (ii) lowest Cd leaching (ICP-MS), and (iii) retained photocurrent.
• Acceptance criteria: ≤10% photocurrent loss after 2 h chronoamperometry (see Step 3.1) and Cd in electrolyte below method LOQ (or below pre-set ppb threshold) for the selected condition.

Step 2 — ZIF-90 “growth mode” defined by chemistry + uniformity metrics (not assumed epitaxy)
2.1 Replace unsupported “epitaxy” with a demonstrated nucleation strategy
• Use oxide ALD surface (TiO2/Al2O3) as the chemically justified anchor: surface “OH groups coordinate Zn2+ and promote heterogeneous nucleation of ZIF-90.
• Optional priming: brief exposure to Zn2+ to create a Zn“OH enriched surface; avoid PEI/thiol primers unless needed, because they can introduce variability and light attenuation.

2.2 ZIF-90 ultrathin shell growth (5“15 nm) with statistical acceptance criteria
• Perform room-temperature ZIF-90 growth (Zn2+ + imidazole-2-carboxaldehyde) under dilute conditions and short times to confine thickness.
• QC/acceptance:
  - TEM thickness statistics over n≥50 particles: mean 10±1.5 nm, CV ≤15%.
  - PXRD/FTIR: ZIF-90 fingerprint retained.
  - Porosity/biogating proxy: uptake/permeability of a size/charge probe series through the shell (see Step 4): e.g., [Fe(CN)6]3−/4− (anionic, ~0.9 nm hydrated), Ru(NH3)6]3+ (cationic), and ferrocene methanol (neutral), before/after ZIF-90 growth; require that transport is not fully blocked pre-assay.

Step 3 — Define operating window and stability protocol (mandatory)
3.1 Operating window pre-registration
• Buffer: near-neutral PBS (pH 7.4) as default for protein stability; also test pH 6.5“8.0 to map corrosion risk.
• Illumination: calibrated LED (e.g., 420“450 nm for CdS response) at fixed intensity (e.g., 50“100 mW cm−2) with temperature control.
• Bias: screen 0 to +0.2 V vs Ag/AgCl (or minimal anodic bias needed) to minimize sulfide oxidation; select bias giving maximal SNR with acceptable stability.

3.2 Stability assays and leaching (pass/fail)
• Chronoamperometry under chopped light for 2 h in assay buffer with hole scavenger (ascorbate or TEOA) and without (worst case).
• Measure Cd2+ leaching by ICP-MS from the electrolyte after 2 h and 8 h operation.
• Compare four conditions: (i) no ALD, (ii) 1.5 nm ALD, (iii) 3.0 nm ALD, (iv) 5.0 nm ALD; select the thinnest layer that meets stability and leaching criteria while preserving ≥70% of initial photocurrent.

Step 4 — Quantify “biogating” as a falsifiable transport model
4.1 Define the gating model and measurable parameters
• Treat ZIF-90 shell as a porous diffusion/partition layer. Effective permeability P = (Deff · Kpartition)/L, where L is shell thickness.
• Hypothesis to test: binding/precipitation decreases Deff and/or Kpartition, increasing Rct and decreasing photocurrent. Quantify ΔDeff and ΔRct and correlate with ΔIph.

4.2 Measure size/charge selectivity and extract Deff
• Use EIS with redox probes of different size/charge (anionic/cationic/neutral as above) to extract Rct changes and infer charge exclusion.
• Use IMPS to derive kinetic parameters under illumination (charge transfer vs recombination contributions) before/after (i) antigen binding and (ii) CN precipitation.
• Acceptance: demonstrate ≥3× larger ΔRct (or Δktr) upon immunorecognition for ZIF-90-gated electrodes vs non-gated passivation controls (SiO2 or polymer of similar thickness).

4.3 Geometric/steric framing tied to pore size
• ZIF-90 micropores (~sub-nm aperture typical of ZIFs) should exclude large proteins (CEA, ~5“10 nm scale) from entering, enforcing surface-near binding and making gating sensitive to surface blockage/charge.
• Precipitate amplification: enzymatic CN precipitate forms at/near the MOF outer surface and pore mouths, reducing accessible pathways for mediator/scavenger diffusion; quantify by comparing permeability before/after HRP reaction.

Step 5 — Site-specific nanobody immobilization (mandatory) + direct measurement of orientation/coverage
5.1 Replace non-specific aldehyde coupling with orthogonal single-point attachment
• Engineer nanobody with a single N-terminal cysteine tag (or ybbR/AviTag for enzymatic labeling) to enforce one attachment site.
• Convert ZIF-90 aldehydes to a selective handle: (option A) reductive amination to introduce a linker terminating in maleimide (for Nb“Cys); (option B) introduce azide/alkyne handle via aldehyde chemistry, then click to Nb bearing the orthogonal partner.
• Avoid Protein G as the primary strategy; use it only as a comparator control to quantify heterogeneity effects.

5.2 Quantify receptor density Γ and active fraction factive
• QCM-D (or ellipsometry on planar analogs) to quantify mass uptake and viscoelastic layer properties during Nb immobilization.
• Fluorescent labeling of Nb (single dye per Nb via site-specific tag) to calibrate surface density (molecules cm−2) and spatial uniformity.
• Binding capacity per area: measure captured antigen vs Γ to estimate factive; acceptance: factive ≥0.5 and Γ RSD ≤5% across batches.

Step 6 — Electrode fabrication with reproducibility controls separated by source
6.1 Standardized deposition/mass loading
• Electrophoretic deposition (EPD) of particles onto TiO2/ITO with controlled time/field; verify areal mass by QCM (planar witness) or gravimetry.
• Acceptance: mass loading RSD ≤3% (n≥10).

6.2 Decouple RSD contributors (mandatory)
• For each batch: (i) measure mass loading, (ii) measure Γ and factive, (iii) measure baseline photocurrent and Rct. Use variance partitioning to attribute inter-electrode RSD to deposition vs biofunctionalization vs intrinsic photoelectrode drift.

Step 7 — Immunoassay formats aligned to analyte class and amplification asset
7.1 Protein biomarker (CEA) sandwich PEC
• Capture: site-specifically immobilized anti-CEA Nb on ZIF-90.
• Detection: HRP@MAF-7 (Asset 1 logic: high enzyme payload) conjugated to secondary Nb/antibody.
• Readout: HRP catalyzes CN precipitation; quantify photocurrent decrease and correlate with ΔRct/ΔDeff.

7.2 Small molecule toxin (AFB1) competitive PEC
• Immobilize hapten on ZIF-90-gated electrode; competition with HRP@MOF“Nb probe (Asset 1) to form precipitate when bound.

Step 8 — Controls that directly test each mechanistic claim
• Stability controls: CdS with/without ALD; compare photocurrent decay and ICP-MS leaching.
• Growth-mode controls: ZIF-90 on ALD-oxide vs on bare sulfide; compare thickness CV and permeability.
• Biogating controls: replace ZIF-90 with dense SiO2 (similar thickness) and with nonporous polymer; compare probe permeability and ΔRct upon binding.
• Orientation controls: site-specific Nb vs random aldehyde coupling vs Protein G; compare Γ, factive, and electrode-to-electrode RSD.
• Photoarchitecture controls: no carbon core; no type-II cascade (single semiconductor); quantify TRPL/IMPS differences and LOD.

Step 9 — Performance endpoints (pre-registered)
• LOD: 3σ/slope; require ≥10× improvement over non-gated PEC control.
• Inter-electrode RSD: ≤5% at low/mid/high concentrations (n≥10, ≥3 batches).
• Mechanistic confirmation: (i) improved lifetimes/IMPS metrics (type-II + carbon), (ii) quantified ΔDeff/ΔRct gating (ZIF-90 + precipitate), (iii) stability/leaching compliance (ALD + operating window).
Feasibility: 1) Stability/compatibility risk (CdS photocorrosion) is converted into a tested operating envelope plus a defined barrier design. Instead of relying on TiO2 as a general mitigation, the plan mandates an ALD TiO2/Al2O3 conformal layer (1.5“5.0 nm screen), hour-scale chronoamperometry under calibrated illumination, explicit bias/pH screening, and Cd2+ leaching quantification by ICP-MS. This makes the “photostable under assay conditions” claim falsifiable.

2) The ZIF-90 shell is no longer assumed “epitaxial”; it is specified as a chemically justified heterogeneous nucleation on hydroxylated ALD oxide. Uniformity is enforced by acceptance criteria (TEM statistics over n≥50, thickness CV ≤15%) and by functional porosity tests using a size/charge redox probe series. This directly addresses variability risk and links shell quality to gating performance.

3) The central transduction mechanism (biogating → Δkct) is elevated from qualitative plausibility to a quantitative transport/kinetics model. By extracting effective permeability (via Deff/Kpartition) and correlating it with photocurrent modulation using EIS and IMPS before/after binding and precipitation, the proposal establishes a measurable causal chain from MOF gate physics to analytical sensitivity.

4) Orientation and receptor standardization are made truly site-specific by engineering a single-point attachment on the nanobody (e.g., N-terminal cysteine or orthogonal enzymatic tag) and coupling through orthogonal chemistry rather than relying on statistically random aldehyde reactivity or Protein G. This, combined with MOF-derived morphology control (ZIF-8 templating) and standardized EPD mass loading, provides a concrete pathway to achieve ≤5% inter-electrode RSD across batches while maintaining the high-gain amplification logic demonstrated in MOF-encapsulated enzyme precipitation systems (Asset 1) and MOF-derived multi-shell photoactive architectures (Asset 2).

Hypothesis: A two-stage chemical-editing strategy—(i) statistically controlled NaOH defect/mesopore formation in an ethanol-rich medium followed by (ii) fluoride capping that is proven to be node-bound (terminal Zr“F/bridging Zr“F“Zr) rather than residual NaF—will yield a hierarchically porous Fe-porphyrin Zr-MOF whose peroxidase-like activity and alkaline durability improve simultaneously. Mechanistically, NaOH introduces a measurable density of missing-linker/terminal “OH(H2O) sites that increases transport and exposes a higher fraction of intact Fe“N4 porphyrins to substrates (effective site accessibility, not merely higher BET). Subsequent fluoride exchange replaces the most hydrolysis-prone terminal Zr“OH(H2O) with stronger Zr“F bonds, decreasing OH−-driven node dissolution and suppressing defect-propagation during pH 10“13 operation. Any apparent ‘redox tuning’ of the Fe(III)/Fe(II) couple will be treated as a testable (not assumed) secondary effect and will only be claimed if confirmed by node-independent, solution/operando spectroscopies and if rate enhancements persist after normalization to independently quantified active-site density. The core advance is a quantitatively validated decoupling: NaOH sets pore hierarchy and accessible-site fraction under explicit etch-stop criteria, while verified node fluorination locks in alkaline robustness without conflating physisorbed salt or amorphous fluoride phases with true Zr“F gating.
Plan: Step 0 — Platform selection, baseline standards, and acceptance thresholds
0.1 Primary scaffold: PCN-222(Fe) (Zr6-oxo nodes + Fe-porphyrin linkers). Contingency: MOF-545(Fe) or PCN-224(Fe) if PCN-222(Fe) shows unacceptable Fe demetalation under the mildest etch conditions.
0.2 Baseline synthesis: modulator route (benzoic acid or acetic acid) targeting reproducible crystallinity and particle size; record baseline PXRD, BET, UV“vis (Soret/Q bands), ICP (Fe, Zr), and porphyrin content via digestion.
0.3 Predefine success criteria (used later in DOE):
- Structural retention: PXRD similarity index ≥ 0.85 vs pristine (Rietveld/Le Bail or correlation metric) after editing and after pH 13 soak.
- Leaching limits: Zr loss ≤ 5% and Fe loss ≤ 3% (relative to initial loading) after 24 h soak at pH 13.
- Fluoride incorporation: F:Zr within a targeted window consistent with partial terminal-site exchange (initial target 0.3“2.0; final window refined by EXAFS/XPS speciation).
- Catalysis: ≥ 2× improvement in Vmax or TOF_site at pH 10“11 vs pristine while maintaining ≥ 70% activity at pH 13 (relative to its own pH 7 rate).

Step 1 — Activation and salt-removal protocols (controls that prevent misassignment)
1.1 Activation: solvent exchange to ethanol (3× over 24 h), then mild vacuum/heat (e.g., 80“120 °C; temperature chosen to avoid porphyrin degradation) to standardize starting porosity.
1.2 Salt-removal SOP (applied to all NaF-treated samples and “NaF-adsorption controls”): repeated ethanol/water washes (e.g., 10 cycles), conductivity monitoring of supernatant to baseline, and final dialysis (if particle size permits) or Soxhlet extraction in ethanol for ≥ 12 h. Collect all washings for ion chromatography (F−) to mass-balance residual soluble fluoride.

Step 2 — Factorial DOE for NaOH etch (hierarchical porosity) with etch-stop criteria
2.1 DOE variables (initial 2-level factorial + center points; expand to response-surface if needed):
- [NaOH] = 5, 20, 50 mM
- Water fraction in EtOH/H2O = 5%, 20%, 40% v/v
- Etch time = 5 min, 30 min, 2 h
- Temperature = 25 °C (fixed initially; add 40 °C only if kinetics too slow)
(27 runs with center-point replication; reduce using fractional factorial if material throughput is limited.)
2.2 Etch procedure: disperse activated MOF at fixed solid loading (e.g., 1“2 mg/mL) in EtOH/H2O; add NaOH as pre-diluted aliquots with timed sampling. Quench at each time point by rapid separation and immediate ethanol washing.
2.3 Etch-stop criteria (measured as time-course; stop/flag conditions are quantitative):
- Leaching kinetics: ICP-OES/ICP-MS on supernatants for Zr and Fe at each time point; terminate etch condition if incremental Zr loss exceeds 1% per 10 min (or if Fe appears above background).
- Porphyrin integrity: UV“vis diffuse reflectance (or solution after digestion) tracking Soret band position/intensity; if Soret intensity drops > 10% (normalized to Zr), flag as porphyrin loss/demetalation.
- Missing-linker density: digest aliquots (acid digestion that fully dissolves framework) and quantify linker by 1H NMR vs Zr by ICP to estimate missing-linker fraction (linker:Zr deviation from pristine).
- Crystallinity: quick PXRD screen; discard conditions showing major peak loss/broadening beyond threshold.
2.4 Output of Step 2: a ranked subset (e.g., 3“5) of “safe etched states” spanning low/medium/high mesoporosity while meeting leaching + porphyrin integrity thresholds.

Step 3 — Fluoride capping DOE with node-resolved validation (distinguish Zr“F from NaF adsorption/amorphous phases)
3.1 Fluorination variables (applied to the selected etched states and pristine):
- [NaF] = 1, 10, 50, 100 mM
- Solvent = EtOH/H2O with minimal water required for F− mobility (e.g., 95/5 and 80/20)
- Time = 0.5 h, 4 h, 24 h
Maintain constant ionic strength controls where possible (e.g., NaCl at matched [Na+]) to identify non-specific electrolyte effects.
3.2 Speciation and quantification of fluoride incorporation (mandatory causal-link test #1):
- Bulk F:Zr ratio: digest MOF; quantify F− by ion chromatography and Zr by ICP-OES → report molar F:Zr with error bars.
- Quantitative XPS with depth profiling (gentle Ar cluster sputter if available): deconvolute F 1s and Zr 3d regions; compare surface vs subsurface F distribution.
- Zr K-edge EXAFS (preferred): fit Zr“F scattering path vs Zr“O; distinguish terminal Zr“F from bulk amorphous ZrF_x by coordination number/bond length and disorder parameters. If EXAFS access is limited, use combined quantitative XPS + 19F solid-state NMR (with reference compounds) and demonstrate persistence of F signal after aggressive salt-removal SOP.
- Salt adsorption controls: (i) pristine MOF exposed to NaF without etch; (ii) etched MOF exposed to NaCl; (iii) physical mixing of MOF with NaF followed by identical washing; all must show substantially lower retained F and/or different XPS/NMR signatures than true fluorinated samples.
3.3 Rule-out amorphous surface Zr“F phases: TEM/EDS mapping for F distribution; compare to PXRD amorphization signatures; ensure no new broad features consistent with amorphous ZrF_x dominate. If detected, adjust fluorination solvent (lower water), reduce NaF concentration/time, or introduce competitive ligands (acetate) to avoid precipitation.

Step 4 — Active-site density and integrity: move beyond BET as proxy (mandatory causal-link test #2 and #4)
4.1 Quantify intact Fe-porphyrin site density (Fe“N4 integrity):
- Fe and Zr by ICP (bulk).
- Porphyrin linker quantification by digestion + 1H NMR (linker per Zr) and compare to Fe content (Fe per linker). Deviations indicate demetalation or linker loss.
- Fe environment: Mössbauer (if available) and/or Fe K-edge XAS to verify Fe remains porphyrinic (vs μ-oxo Fe clusters or leached Fe redeposition). At minimum, compare UV“vis Q-band pattern + EPR signatures across treatments.
4.2 Define “accessible active-site fraction” independent of BET:
- Probe-molecule binding calibrated to porphyrin content where feasible: NO or CO binding (IR/UV“vis difference spectroscopy) to porphyrin Fe sites under controlled conditions, giving a measurable fraction of Fe capable of axial ligation.
- If gas binding is not feasible, use a competitive axial ligand titration (e.g., imidazole/pyrazine) with spectroscopic readout (Soret shift) to quantify accessible Fe sites.
4.3 Report catalytic metrics normalized three ways: per gram, per total Fe, and per accessible Fe site (TOF_site). Claims about “BET → accessibility → activity” are only accepted if TOF_site increases or remains constant while accessible-site fraction increases; a BET-only increase without preserved Fe“N4 integrity will be interpreted as non-productive porosity.

Step 5 — Peroxidase-like activity and ROS mechanism with artifact-free redox attribution (mandatory causal-link test #3)
5.1 Standard kinetics: TMB/ABTS + H2O2 over pH 7“13; extract Km, Vmax; measure initial rates in regimes avoiding mass-transfer limitation.
5.2 ROS assignment: EPR spin trapping (•OH/•OOH) + scavengers (isopropanol, SOD mimics, etc.) to differentiate radical vs heterolytic pathways.
5.3 Decouple electrochemical film artifacts:
- Run CV/DPV on identical films with matched mass loading and thickness; include EIS to quantify film resistance and separate conductivity changes from redox shifts.
- Node-independent Fe redox probing: (i) mediated redox titration in suspension with a series of soluble mediators spanning potentials; (ii) operando Fe K-edge XANES under H2O2 to observe Fe valence changes directly during catalysis. Only if these methods show systematic shifts correlating with verified Zr“F speciation will “F− tunes Fe redox microenvironment” be claimed.
- Control for electrolyte/adsorption effects: repeat kinetics with constant ionic strength and with fluoride-free sodium salts; assess H2O2 adsorption isotherms/uptake if needed.

Step 6 — Alkaline durability demonstration tied to node fluorination
6.1 Soak tests: pH 10, 12, 13 (NaOH) for 6 h, 24 h, 7 days in water and in EtOH/H2O matrices; quantify:
- PXRD retention, BET retention, pore size distribution evolution.
- Zr/Fe leaching (ICP) time-course.
- Persistence of node-bound F (digest + IC; XPS after soak).
6.2 Demonstrate causality: correlate stability improvements with node-bound F fraction (F:Zr and EXAFS/XPS speciation), not merely with total F added.

Step 7 — Application-relevant cascade demonstration (ethanol context preserved)
7.1 Cascade: alcohol oxidase (or alternative oxidase) generates H2O2 from ethanol; MOF nanozyme performs chromogenic readout at alkaline pH. Compare pristine vs etched vs etched+fluorinated under identical ethanol content and pH.
7.2 Show robustness: sustained response after repeated cycles and after alkaline pre-aging; quantify signal drift vs leaching and vs retained accessible-site fraction.

Deliverables and decision gates
- Gate A (after Step 2): identify etched conditions meeting stop criteria.
- Gate B (after Step 3): confirm node-bound fluoride via F:Zr + speciation (EXAFS or quantitative depth-profile XPS + NMR) with salt-removal mass balance.
- Gate C (after Step 4“6): accept or reject each causal link using predefined acceptance rules (below).

Acceptance rules (explicit falsification)
- If retained F is removed by salt-removal SOP and/or lacks node-bound signatures (EXAFS/XPS/NMR), “fluoride gating” is rejected; any stability/activity changes will be attributed to ionic strength or surface salt effects.
- If etching increases BET but decreases intact porphyrin density or accessible-site fraction, “BET→accessibility” is rejected for that condition; etch severity is reduced.
- If Fe redox shifts appear only in films (not in mediated titration/operando XANES) and track EIS resistance, “F− tunes Fe redox” is rejected as an artifact; mechanistic emphasis returns to transport + node stabilization.
Feasibility: The proposal is feasible because each contested causal link is converted into a quantitative, discriminating measurement with built-in controls. (1) Node fluorination is not inferred from a single spectroscopy: bulk F:Zr (digestion + ion chromatography/ICP) plus node-level speciation (Zr K-edge EXAFS or, at minimum, quantitative depth-profile XPS reinforced by 19F ssNMR) and rigorous salt-removal mass balance directly address the reviewer’s concern about residual NaF adsorption or amorphous fluoride phases. (2) NaOH etching risk is managed by an explicit factorial DOE with real-time stop criteria based on Zr/Fe leaching kinetics (ICP), porphyrin integrity (Soret band metrics), crystallinity (PXRD), and missing-linker quantification (digestion 1H NMR vs Zr). This converts ‘minutes“hours’ into statistically defensible windows tied to measurable damage thresholds. (3) The activity claim is protected against BET overinterpretation by independently quantifying intact porphyrin/Fe“N4 density and an accessible-site fraction (axial ligand/probe binding), then reporting TOF normalized per accessible Fe site. (4) Redox and ‘microenvironment’ effects are treated as conditional outcomes: electrochemical observations are cross-validated by solution-phase mediated redox titration and/or operando Fe XANES under H2O2 to eliminate film/conductivity artifacts. Together, these additions maintain the original concept chain (NaOH→hierarchical pores; NaF→base tolerance; porosity/accessibility→activity) while making each arrow testable and falsifiable with node- and site-resolved quantification.

Hypothesis: A covalently interface-locked ZSM-5@LIFM-28 core“shell composite, in which (i) a quantified, externally accessible trialkoxysilyl“(CH2)n“CO2− graft layer provides high-density, spatially uniform Zr-nucleation sites and (ii) the LIFM-28 shell is “gate-programmed” by PVSI to open at a CO2 partial pressure matched to real PSA/TSA swing windows, will deliver higher *humid* cyclic CO2 working capacity and capacity retention at 333“373 K than either parent or non-covalent mixtures. Mechanistically, the performance gain is not assumed from generic ‘pre-concentration’ but from two testable effects: (1) **Interfacial confinement + mechanical boundary condition**: nanoscale, zeolite-tethered LIFM-28 domains reduce the amplitude of breathing, suppress defect-mediated collapse, and limit crystallite coarsening under hot CO2/H2O, preserving the reversible open/closed transition over many cycles; (2) **PVSI-controlled cooperative gating under realistic pCO2**: spacer length/polarity tunes (a) the free-energy difference between closed/open states and (b) CO2 binding enthalpy in the installed pocket, shifting the adsorption step into a defined target pCO2 window (go/no-go defined below). Any additional synergy from ZSM-5 (heat tolerance, diffusion stiffness, and optional Al/extra-framework cation tuning) is treated as an experimentally verified transport/thermodynamics benefit rather than an assumed CO2 ‘pre-concentrator’; we will directly test sequential filling and transport resistance by transient breakthrough and spatially resolved spectroscopies/tracers.
Plan: Step 0 — Define the operating envelope and quantitative adsorption targets (mandatory).
0.1 Target separations and gas matrices:
• Post-combustion capture (PSA/TSA-relevant): 10“15 vol% CO2 in N2, 3“12 vol% H2O, 3“8 vol% O2, balance N2; optional 50“200 ppm SO2/NO2 for robustness screening.
• Temperature/pressure windows: 333“373 K; adsorption at 1.0 bar total with pCO2 = 0.10“0.15 bar; desorption by (A) TSA: 373“423 K at 1 bar (dry N2 purge) and/or (B) VSA: 0.05“0.20 bar total.
0.2 Gate-position/working-capacity criteria (go/no-go):
• Gate-opening (inflection) pCO2* at 333“353 K must lie within 0.05“0.20 bar for post-combustion capture; for any higher-pressure application (e.g., natural gas sweetening), a secondary target set is pCO2* = 0.5“2 bar at 298“323 K.
• Humid working capacity: ΔqCO2(humid, 10% H2O) ≥ 1.5 mmol g−1 over the chosen swing (adsorption to desorption conditions), and ≥30% improvement vs (i) LIFM-28 analogue without anchoring and (ii) ZSM-5 core alone.
• Cyclic retention: ≥90% of initial Δq after 200 cycles (screen) and ≥85% after 1000 cycles (qualification) under wet CO2.

Step 1 — Engineer ZSM-5 cores with controlled external silanol density and (optional) CO2-affinity tuning.
1.1 Synthesize/obtain ZSM-5 with two compositional regimes:
• High-silica ZSM-5 (Si/Al ~ 100“200) for minimal intrinsic CO2 adsorption (acts primarily as thermally stable scaffold/heat sink).
• Moderately acidic ZSM-5 (Si/Al ~ 30“60) and/or ion-exchanged ZSM-5 (Na+, K+, or Mg2+) to optionally enhance CO2 quadrupole interactions; this becomes a variable only after baseline gating is demonstrated.
1.2 External surface silanol/accessibility control:
• Mild desilication (e.g., dilute NaOH) and/or controlled steaming to increase external silanol density without destroying MFI crystallinity.
• Remove extra-framework debris by acid wash if needed.
1.3 Characterization (external vs internal):
• XRD for crystallinity; Ar/N2 physisorption for micro/mesopore; SEM for particle morphology.
• External silanol quantification: DRIFTS (isolated vs H-bonded Si“OH), quantitative 29Si MAS NMR (Q3/Q4 ratio), and H2O adsorption at low p/p0 as an accessibility proxy.
• Acidity (only as secondary descriptor): pyridine-FTIR (external vs internal acid sites via steric bases) complemented by NH3-TPD.

Step 2 — Mandatory interface verification package with acceptance criteria (hard gate before MOF growth scale-up).
2.1 Surface grafting chemistry (anchor layer):
• Use (EtO)3Si“(CH2)n“CO2H with n = 2, 3, 6 as a controllable spacer to tune tether flexibility and carboxylate presentation.
• Conduct silanization under rigorously dried conditions (water-controlled to avoid multilayer polymerization): anhydrous toluene or ethanol, 60“90 °C, controlled silane loading.
• Post-graft conditioning: thorough Soxhlet extraction to remove physisorbed silane.
2.2 Quantify grafting density and chemical state (acceptance criteria):
• TGA mass loss assigned to organosilane: target 0.5“2.0 mmol silane g−1 ZSM-5 (tunable); accept if reproducibility ±10% across batches.
• XPS: increase in C 1s and carboxylate O 1s components; Si 2p chemical shift consistent with siloxane formation; accept if surface C/Si ratio matches TGA-derived coverage within ±20%.
• Quantitative 13C CP/MAS (carboxylate signal) and 29Si MAS (T-sites/T2/T3 signals if resolvable): accept if covalent graft signature present and stable after solvent extraction.
2.3 Prove external accessibility/ordering:
• Probe esterification/back-titration of “CO2H (e.g., base titration in non-aqueous medium) to quantify accessible acid sites; accept if ≥60% of total grafted “CO2H are accessible.

Step 3 — Interface-locked LIFM-28 growth with explicit controls to exclude solution-grown contamination.
3.1 Heterogeneous nucleation protocol:
• Disperse grafted ZSM-5 in LIFM-28 precursor solution under conditions biased toward surface nucleation (dilute linker concentration, controlled supersaturation, addition order where ZSM-5 is present before Zr source).
• Use modulator control (e.g., monotopic acids) to slow homogeneous nucleation; tune time/temperature to favor conformal shells and nanoscale MOF domains.
3.2 Control matrix (mandatory):
• (i) ungrafted ZSM-5 subjected to identical MOF growth;
• (ii) grafted ZSM-5 with methyl-terminated silane (no “CO2H) to test specificity;
• (iii) pure LIFM-28 (solution-grown) to establish size/phase references.
3.3 Shell continuity/thickness distribution (acceptance criteria):
• FIB-SEM cross-sections + SEM imaging for shell thickness statistics (≥50 particles): accept if ≥80% particles show a continuous shell with thickness 50“300 nm (or defined target range) and no large bare patches.
• STEM-EDS tomography or at minimum STEM-EDS mapping: Zr signal must spatially colocalize as a shell around Si-rich cores; accept if Zr/Si radial profiles are consistent with core“shell architecture across multiple particles.
• PXRD: presence of both MFI and LIFM-28 reflections without significant amorphization.
3.4 Mass balance to rule out free MOF crystallites (acceptance criteria):
• Size-fractionation: differential centrifugation/sieving to isolate the core“shell particle fraction; analyze supernatant for free MOF.
• Digestion ICP-OES/MS: quantify Zr in (a) isolated core“shell fraction and (b) supernatant/fines. Accept if ≥90% of total Zr is associated with the core“shell fraction.
• Optional corroboration: digestion 1H NMR for linker/spacer accounting vs Zr content.

Step 4 — PVSI ‘breathing gating’ programming with a spacer set designed to hit the target pCO2* window.
4.1 Spacer library design rule (explicit objective):
• Short nonpolar (baseline minimal CO2 affinity shift; primarily steric gating), short polar (adds binding enthalpy), long polar (amplifies free-volume change and polar pocket density).
• Include at least one water-tolerant polar motif (e.g., amide/urea-like, fluorinated polar, or sterically shielded heteroatoms) and one hydrophobic motif to reduce H2O co-adsorption; avoid hydrolysis-prone groups if stability screening fails.
4.2 PVSI execution on anchored shells:
• Perform PVSI installation/uninstallation under reported kinetically reversible conditions, but explicitly validate that diffusion into tethered nanodomains is not rate-limiting (time-to-equilibrium test with in situ IR or gravimetry).
• Acceptance: reversible PVSI (≥80% of installed spacer removable and reinstallable over 3 cycles without crystallinity loss).
4.3 Gate-position screening (go/no-go):
• Record CO2 isotherms at 333/353/373 K (dry first) and extract pCO2* (inflection) and hysteresis width.
• Down-select spacers that place pCO2* within 0.05“0.20 bar at 333“353 K and maintain hysteresis compatible with cycling (no progressive trapping).

Step 5 — Mechanism tests upgraded from narrative to direct evidence (transport + sequential filling).
5.1 Transient breakthrough (primary evidence for synergy):
• Shape materials into comparable pellets/monolith fragments with identical binders and similar pressure drop.
• Measure breakthrough for dry and humid feeds at 333“373 K: 10“15% CO2 in N2 with controlled RH.
• Extract dynamic capacity, mass-transfer zone length, and apparent mass-transfer coefficients; compare anchored vs physical mixtures vs parents.
5.2 Spatially resolved uptake / sequential filling:
• In situ DRIFTS under stepwise pCO2 with and without H2O to distinguish adsorption environments (zeolite vs MOF signals; CO2 bands and framework vibrations).
• Isotopic tracing: 13CO2/12CO2 switching during uptake to quantify intracrystalline exchange kinetics; if feasible, pair with micro-IR mapping on single particles or packed beds.
• Treat ‘pre-concentration then gating’ as confirmed only if time-resolved spectroscopy shows early uptake signatures attributable to ZSM-5 followed by delayed MOF-gated uptake at the programmed pCO2*.
5.3 In situ structure“adsorption coupling (breathing verification):
• VP-PXRD under dry CO2 and wet CO2 (controlled water activity) to correlate unit-cell transitions with uptake steps.
• Microcalorimetry (dry vs humid) to deconvolute strong-site adsorption from phase-transition enthalpy; acceptance: preserved, reproducible gating enthalpy profile over repeated cycles.

Step 6 — Humid/steam stability and competitive adsorption as a primary qualification (mandatory).
6.1 Co-adsorption and cycling protocol:
• Run mixed-gas co-adsorption (CO2/N2/H2O) by dynamic vapor sorption or controlled-humidity volumetrics.
• Cycling: 200-cycle screen at 353 K adsorption (10% CO2, 10% H2O) / 403 K regeneration (dry N2), then 1000-cycle test for best candidates.
• Include periodic exposures to O2 (5%) and ppm-level SO2/NO2 in short stress tests.
6.2 In situ tracking under wet duty:
• PXRD after defined cycle blocks (0/50/200/1000); DRIFTS to monitor hydrolysis/chemical changes.
• Post-mortem: SEM/FIB-SEM for shell integrity, ICP for Zr leaching (if any), and N2 physisorption for porosity retention.
• Acceptance: ≥85“90% capacity retention targets (as defined in Step 0.2) and preserved core“shell morphology.

Step 7 — Data analysis, modeling, and benchmarking tied to the target window.
7.1 Fit models that explicitly accommodate gating:
• Use dual-site Langmuir (or Toth) for background + a cooperative/gating term (sigmoidal) to extract pCO2*, step height, and hysteresis metrics.
7.2 Report performance in application-relevant metrics:
• Working capacity (humid and dry), regeneration energy proxy (integrated heat of adsorption + sensible heat estimate), and productivity from breakthrough.
7.3 Benchmark comparators:
• ZSM-5 variants, bare LIFM-28, PVSI-modified LIFM-28, physical mixtures, non-covalent composites, and anchored-no-PVSI shells; test under identical humid protocols.

Milestone logic (stop/go):
M1 Interface readiness: passes graft density + accessibility + shell continuity + Zr mass-balance criteria → proceed to PVSI library.
M2 Gate positioning: identifies ≥1 spacer set meeting pCO2* criterion at 333“353 K → proceed to humid cycling.
M3 Humid durability: meets ≥200-cycle retention criterion under wet CO2 → proceed to 1000-cycle qualification and shaped-body breakthrough optimization.
Feasibility: 1) Interface feasibility is converted from assumption to a quantified acceptance-gated package. The proposal explicitly measures (a) silane graft density (TGA + XPS + quantitative ssNMR), (b) accessibility of “CO2H anchors (back-titration/DRIFTS), (c) core“shell continuity and thickness statistics (FIB-SEM + STEM-EDS/tomography), and (d) a Zr mass balance tied to the zeolite fraction (size-fractionation + digestion ICP) to rule out free MOF crystallites. These are standard, high-confidence methods for heterogeneous nucleation claims.
2) The operating window is explicitly defined (pCO2, T, H2O/O2/acid gases), and PVSI is no longer an open-ended ‘library’: spacers are screened against a quantitative gate-opening target pCO2* that matches PSA/TSA swing conditions. Go/no-go criteria on pCO2*, humid Δq, and cycle retention prevent over-interpretation.
3) Elevated-temperature humid stability is treated as a primary duty cycle, not optional. The plan includes wet CO2 structural tracking (in situ VP-PXRD/DRIFTS), co-adsorption measurements, and stress tests with O2/SOx/NOx. The anchoring rationale is mechanistically linked to constrained breathing and suppressed coarsening; success is evaluated by morphology retention (FIB-SEM), crystallinity, and capacity retention.
4) The ‘cooperative adsorption’ mechanism is reframed as testable transport/sequence phenomena rather than presumed thermodynamics. Transient breakthrough on shaped bodies provides application-relevant evidence; time-resolved spectroscopy and isotopic switching provide direct proof (or falsification) of sequential filling and quantify mass-transfer resistances. If sequential filling is not observed, the proposal still yields an empirical performance comparison with clear attribution to anchoring and gate programming.
5) The approach is strongly grounded in prior art: LIFM-28 tolerates PVSI with tunable breathing and maintained integrity (Assets 1“2), while zeolite scaffolds can preserve thermal stability and improve adsorption selectivity in MOF“zeolite hybrids (Asset 3). This proposal adds the missing engineering rigor (interface quantification, humid duty cycling, and target-window gate programming) required for credible elevated-temperature cyclic CO2 capture claims.

Hypothesis: A MOF-templated, pore-size-distribution-controlled interlayer that is solvent-swollen by 3% DIO during coating will impose a higher fraction of face-on oriented donor/acceptor crystallites and simultaneously suppress interfacial trap-assisted recombination. Mechanistically, (i) DIO transiently plasticizes the active-layer precursors, allowing crystallites to reorient while the interlayer’s nanoconfinement selectively stabilizes face-on nuclei via surface-energy minimization and directional pi“pi registry at MOF pore mouths; (ii) a redox-buffered MOF node chemistry (e.g., Ni(II)/Ni(III) accessible within the operating potential window) electrostatically screens interfacial charge accumulation, lowering non-radiative recombination. This dual control increases open-circuit voltage by reducing the quasi-Fermi level splitting losses, thereby lowering photon energy loss without sacrificing charge extraction.
Plan: Step 1: System setup—design and synthesize an ultrathin, conductive MOF-derived coordination polymer interlayer with programmable pore size distribution.
1.1 Select a 2D/lamellar MOF platform that can be processed as an oriented thin film (e.g., Ni3(HITP)2-like coordination network or a SURMOF analogue) and introduce a mixed-linker strategy to tune pore size distribution (PSD): combine a primary planar linker (HITP or related hexaaminotriphenylene) with a low-fraction sterically biased co-linker (e.g., fluorinated catecholate/aminocatecholate analogue) to create a bimodal PSD (dominant 1“2 nm pores with a controlled tail to 3“5 nm).
1.2 Fabricate interlayers (5“30 nm) on ITO/PEDOT:PSS or ZnO using layer-by-layer growth (SURMOF) or interfacial polymerization; quantify PSD by gas sorption on thicker analogues + ellipsometric porosimetry on films, and verify crystallographic texture (GIWAXS).
1.3 Choose a representative OPV active layer (polymer donor:nonfullerene acceptor or donor:PC71BM blend) and prepare inks with and without 3% DIO.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation—DIO-assisted nanoconfinement annealing (DANA) using the MOF PSD as a “morphology phase-space filter.”
2.1 Coat active-layer ink onto the MOF interlayer while maintaining a controlled solvent/DIO vapor environment; implement a two-stage drying protocol: (A) short dwell in DIO-rich atmosphere to keep the blend above its local glass transition, enabling reorientation; (B) rapid DIO extraction by switching to a poor-solvent vapor or mild vacuum to freeze in the oriented morphology.
2.2 Systematically vary PSD (via co-linker fraction) and DIO dwell time to map how confinement length scales couple to crystallite orientation; target the regime where pore mouths act as preferential nucleation/templating sites but do not induce excessive phase separation.
2.3 Integrate redox-buffer functionality: incorporate a small fraction of redox-active nodes (e.g., Ni sites with accessible Ni(II)/Ni(III) or Cu(I)/Cu(II) couples) or tethered quinone/catechol groups to the framework interior to act as a reversible interfacial charge reservoir, tuned so the redox potential sits near the interfacial quasi-Fermi levels.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analysis—link PSD → orientation → electrochemical energetics → Voc → photon energy loss.
3.1 Face-on orientation: quantify using GIWAXS (pi“pi stacking out-of-plane intensity ratios, Herman’s orientation factor) and correlate with PSD metrics (mode pore size, dispersity, tail fraction).
3.2 Electrochemical energetics: use cyclic voltammetry on donor, acceptor, and donor/acceptor films deposited on inert electrodes, then repeat with MOF interlayer underneath to detect interfacial dipole shifts and redox-buffer signatures (peak positions, capacitive currents, apparent doping/charging onset).
3.3 Recombination diagnostics: measure light-intensity dependence of Voc, transient photovoltage/photocurrent, and impedance spectroscopy to quantify ideality factor changes consistent with reduced trap-assisted recombination.
3.4 Photon energy loss: determine optical gap (Eopt from absorption onset) and compute Eloss = Eopt − qVoc; deconvolute radiative vs non-radiative losses using electroluminescence EQE and FTPS-EQE.
3.5 Controls: (i) non-porous coordination polymer interlayer of similar work function; (ii) MOF with similar chemistry but shifted PSD; (iii) devices without DIO; (iv) DIO with inert nanoporous oxide to separate chemical vs confinement effects.
3.6 Success criterion: demonstrate a statistically significant Voc increase (≥50“100 mV) accompanied by reduced non-radiative loss and increased face-on fraction, with PSD-dependent trends that match a confinement/templating model rather than simple surface-energy changes.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Nanoconfinement is known to bias polymer crystallization pathways and orientation; solvent additives such as DIO are established morphology modulators in OPVs, and Voc is tightly coupled to non-radiative recombination and energetic disorder. Electrochemical node/linker functionalities in coordination networks can provide reversible charge buffering and interfacial dipole control.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The core innovation is a MOF/coordination-network interlayer whose pore size distribution is a rationally designed structural parameter (set by mixed-linker chemistry) and is actively engaged during film formation via a DIO-swollen, single-process “confinement anneal.” This leverages MOF-specific strengths—programmable porosity, redox-tunable nodes, and oriented thin-film growth—rather than using MOFs as passive fillers.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional additive-only morphology control, the PSD-programmed MOF interlayer provides a deterministic length-scale selector that narrows morphology variance and directly targets face-on orientation. Compared with non-porous interlayers, the redox-buffered porous network reduces interfacial charge accumulation and trap-assisted recombination, improving Voc and reducing photon energy loss without relying solely on deeper HOMO/LUMO tuning of the organic semiconductors.

Hypothesis: A Zn(II)“BDC framework adopting the cristobalite topology can exhibit *intrinsic, reproducible photoactivity* when missing-linker defects are not merely introduced but *thermodynamically biased toward a correlated vacancy sublattice* during crystallization. We hypothesize that under DMF/formate coordination competition, one symmetry-inequivalent BDC coordination mode in the cristobalite net becomes preferentially labile due to (i) differential Zn“O(carboxylate) bond dissociation energies under strongly coordinating amide solvents, (ii) local charge compensation by Zn“OH⁻/Zn“formate caps stabilized through hydrogen bonding with DMF, and (iii) reduced elastic strain when vacancies propagate along a specific <111>-type direction of the diamondoid net. Periodic or short-range“correlated vacancy ordering is thus favored over random dilution because it minimizes lattice strain and electrostatic frustration while maximizing favorable Zn“DMF/formate interactions at crystallographically equivalent nodes. These ordered, under-coordinated Zn(II) sites generate persistent defect-associated excited states best described as ligand-to-node charge-separated states (BDC π* → Zn“OH/DMF“perturbed node), rather than classical LMCT in a redox-active sense. Reduced symmetry and altered ligand fields at these nodes stabilize long-lived charge-separated excitations, suppressing non-radiative decay pathways dominant in defect-free Zn“BDC. The rigid cristobalite connectivity enforces uniform Zn···Zn distances and defect“defect coupling, enabling coherent charge transport and measurable visible-light photoresponses without heterometal doping or post-synthetic modification.
Plan: Step 1: Predictive modeling of defect ordering.
1.1. Perform periodic DFT and cluster calculations on an ideal cristobalite Zn“BDC net to evaluate relative energies of linker removal at symmetry-distinct BDC sites, explicitly including DMF and formate as terminal ligands.
1.2. Map vacancy“vacancy interaction energies along different crystallographic directions to identify whether correlated ordering (e.g., 2×2×2 supercell) lowers elastic/electrostatic penalties versus random vacancies.
1.3. Compute electronic excited states (TD-DFT/ΔSCF) of defect-free vs defect-capped Zn nodes to generate spectral fingerprints (expected absorption onsets, transient features) for later experimental assignment.

Step 2: Defect-biased crystallization with structural readout.
2.1. Synthesize cristobalite Zn“BDC under solvothermal conditions in DMF using Zn(NO3)2·6H2O, systematically varying DMF:BDC ratios (10“40 equiv) and formic acid modulators (0“5 equiv) identified from modeling to stabilize the predicted vacancy sublattice.
2.2. Grow microcrystalline but electron-diffraction-suitable samples; prioritize kinetic regimes (slow cooling, low supersaturation) predicted to allow vacancy correlation.
2.3. Structural verification: (i) high-resolution synchrotron PXRD to detect superlattice reflections or peak splitting indicative of vacancy ordering; (ii) 3D electron diffraction/RED to resolve local symmetry breaking; (iii) total-scattering/PDF modeling comparing ordered-vacancy vs random-vacancy models; (iv) diffuse scattering analysis to quantify short-range correlation lengths if long-range order is incomplete.

Step 3: Quantification and stability of defect caps.
3.1. Establish cap identity and persistence using in situ variable-temperature/vacuum IR spectroscopy, tracking the coordinated DMF C=O stretch versus temperature.
3.2. Employ 15N-labeled DMF and solid-state 15N/13C NMR to confirm node-bound DMF and distinguish it from pore DMF.
3.3. Conduct post-activation digestion NMR and TGA“MS to quantify residual DMF/formate/OH content, defining an activation window that preserves node-bound caps.

Step 4: Electronic-origin validation of photoactivity.
4.1. Optical characterization: diffuse-reflectance UV“vis correlated directly with photocurrent action spectra to confirm that defect-induced absorption drives charge generation.
4.2. Transient absorption spectroscopy to identify long-lived charge-separated states matching computed defect-node excited states; compare with defect-free and randomly defective controls.
4.3. EPR spectroscopy with spin traps under illumination to detect trapped electrons/holes at defect nodes, excluding purely ligand-centered π“π* excitations.
4.4. Cap-removal controls: rigorously exchange/remove DMF (e.g., acetonitrile treatment) to demonstrate loss or shift of visible absorption and photoresponse, establishing causality.

Step 5: Functional benchmarking.
5.1. Measure photocurrents, impedance spectra, and model reactions (e.g., aerobic alcohol oxidation) across a series with quantified vacancy correlation lengths.
5.2. Correlate performance with degree of defect ordering (not just density), testing the central hypothesis that correlated defects outperform random ones.
Feasibility: 1. Thermodynamic/Kinetic Plausibility: Coordination modulation is known to bias carboxylate lability; by explicitly identifying symmetry-inequivalent BDC sites and modeling vacancy“vacancy interactions, this proposal replaces assertion with prediction. Even partial or short-range ordering is sufficient and experimentally accessible.
2. Structural Rigor: The combined use of synchrotron PXRD, 3D electron diffraction, and total scattering directly addresses the reviewer concern that conventional PDF/NMR cannot prove ordering. The plan explicitly distinguishes ordered vs random vacancy models.
3. Electronic Assignment: By pairing action spectra, transient absorption matched to computed states, EPR under illumination, and cap-removal controls, the origin of visible absorption is unambiguously assigned to defect-node states rather than ligand excimers or impurities.
4. Chemical Robustness: Quantitative, labeled-spectroscopy verification of DMF/formate caps ensures that the proposed chromophore is a persistent structural motif, not a processing artifact.
5. Comparative Advantage: Relative to heterometal doping or POM incorporation, this approach maintains compositional simplicity while achieving tunable photoactivity through symmetry-informed defect engineering grounded in thermodynamics and validated by multi-scale structural probes.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that *deterministic, symmetry-enforced intrapore “soft-contact clamps”* can be achieved—and translated into strongly suppressed or sign-inverted anisotropic thermal expansion—by **decoupling (i) framework construction from (ii) clamp locking** using a two-node architecture with orthogonal binding pockets. Specifically, we will construct a permanently porous pillared-layer MOF in which (A) the 2D sheet is formed by carboxylates bound to a **square-planar M(II) node (no axial sites available; e.g., Ni(II)/Pd(II) in square-planar environments)**, while (B) a *separate, symmetry-fixed clamp-locking site* is provided by **a secondary metal (M′) embedded in the pillar or as a dedicated post-synthetic docking site** that binds the **imidazolyl N** of 4-(1H-2-methylimidazol-1-yl)benzoate (MImBz−) with high site selectivity. This eliminates the reviewer-flagged conflict where paddlewheel axial sites would be simultaneously demanded by solvent/modulator, the pillar, and the imidazolyl N.

Mechanistically, we posit that ordered opposing-wall placement of MImBz− generates a temperature-dependent free-energy landscape for interwall separation (w):
- At low T, the clamp region sits near a shallow minimum governed by **dispersion + quadrupolar π/heteroaromatic interactions** between facing methylimidazolyl“aryl surfaces (vdW-dominant regime in ~5“8 Å pores).
- At higher T, increased librational amplitude and steric excluded-volume between opposed methylimidazolyl rings causes an **entropic/anharmonic upshift in ∂G/∂w**, effectively stiffening (or over-stiffening) the low-frequency transverse modes that normally expand the pore (soft-mode suppression). This produces **α⊥ → 0 or α⊥ < 0** (perpendicular to the channel axis) while preserving permanent porosity.

Crucially, the proposal now defines measurable thermodynamic requirements for the claimed crossover: we require a computed and experimentally consistent **ΔG(w,T)** such that (i) the curvature κ(T)=∂²G/∂w² increases with T over 200“400 K in the clamp-active direction and (ii) the location of the free-energy minimum shifts to smaller w with T (dw*/dT < 0) to enable negative expansion. By design, the clamp couples to the specific lattice degree of freedom governing channel width, not to generic framework breathing. The approach further anticipates disorder risks by embedding an enforceable orientation element (secondary metal docking geometry or steric buttress) rather than relying on crystallization kinetics.
Plan: Step 0 — Architecture selection (explicit de-risking of coordination/orientational disorder)
0.1 Two-node, orthogonal-site design: Select a pillared-layer topology where **sheet formation uses nodes without accessible axial sites** (eliminates solvent/pillar competition) and **clamp locking uses a distinct, saturable site**.
- Sheet node (M): square-planar-preferred M(II) (target: Ni(II) with strong ligand-field stabilization in square-planar carboxylate environments; backup: Pd(II) if needed for strict square-planarity). Design goal: each sheet metal has no labile axial sites.
- Clamp-locking site (M′): a dedicated metal-binding pocket that selectively coordinates imidazolyl N (examples: tetrahedral Zn(II) in a pillaring unit; or octahedral Co(II)/Zn(II) in a preorganized chelating pillar). This site is *not* required for sheet connectivity.
0.2 Symmetry-enforced opposing-wall pairing: Choose a channel geometry in which two equivalent rows of MImBz− must face across the pore by space-group constraints (e.g., mirror/inversion relating opposite walls). Design criterion: the asymmetric unit contains one MImBz− orientation; the opposite wall is generated by symmetry, enforcing pairwise registry.
0.3 Contingency “steric buttress”: Predefine a backup variant of MImBz− bearing a small ortho substituent (e.g., F or Me on the benzoate ring) positioned to bias a single rotamer, increasing the energetic penalty for orientational disorder without blocking porosity.

Step 1 — Construct the ordered clamp framework (coordination explicitness)
1.1 Ligand implementation: Use MImBz− as a heterotopic linker where:
- Carboxylate binds only to the sheet node M (no axial competition).
- Imidazolyl N binds only to M′ at a dedicated docking site (pillaring unit or post-synthetic docking site).
1.2 Pillar strategy (decoupled from clamp locking): Employ a *separate* rigid pillar to define channel width (L) in the vdW window (target interwall aromatic“aromatic centroid distance 5.5“7.5 Å at 300 K).
- Pillar choice: linear ditopic linker (e.g., 4,4′-bipyridine or an isoreticular analogue) that connects sheets through nodes designed to avoid axial site competition with imidazolyl.
- Channel targeting: select pillar length such that the clamp contact patch area per unit cell is maximized while maintaining accessible free volume (success metric in Step 3).
1.3 Clamp-locking implementation options (choose primary + backup):
Option A (primary): Pillar contains a preorganized chelating pocket that binds M′ and presents a fixed coordination vector toward the pore interior; imidazolyl N docks to M′ during assembly.
Option B (backup): Post-synthetic metalation (PSM) of a preinstalled chelating site (on pillar or side-arm) with Zn(II)/Co(II), then imidazolyl docking to M′ under controlled conditions.
Deliverable: a framework where the *pillar connectivity* and *clamp orientation* are orthogonal constraints, preventing mixed axial environments.

Step 2 — Disorder quantification and ordering validation (explicit methods, not implied)
2.1 Single-crystal XRD (if available): refine occupancies and anisotropic displacement parameters for methylimidazolyl orientation; require single orientation in the asymmetric unit.
2.2 Total scattering/PDF + diffuse scattering: quantify short-range vs long-range orientational order; look for signatures of correlated disorder vs random orientation.
2.3 Solid-state NMR (mandatory per critique):
- 13C/15N CPMAS to resolve distinct imidazolyl environments; multiple resonances/line broadening indicates disorder.
- If feasible, 15N labeling at imidazolyl N to sensitively quantify coordination fraction to M′.
2.4 Axial-site occupancy is no longer a relevant failure mode for the sheet node (by design); instead quantify **M′ docking fraction** (target ≥90% at 300 K by refinement/NMR).
Contingency trigger: if docking fraction <90% or diffuse scattering indicates major orientational disorder, activate steric-buttress ligand variant and/or shift to Option B (PSM) to force completion.

Step 3 — Quantitative success metrics and go/no-go criteria (thermomechanical + structural)
3.1 Structural clamp metrics (must pass before deep thermo testing):
- Opposing-wall contact distance (d): aromatic/heteroaromatic plane-to-plane or centroid distance across pore: **d(300 K)=5.5“7.5 Å**.
- Angular registry (θ): relative orientation of facing rings within **±15°** of the designed face-to-face/slipped-stack geometry.
- Temperature derivative: require **dd/dT ≤ 0** over 200“400 K in the clamp-active direction (a structural prerequisite for negative α⊥).
Go/no-go: if d is outside window or dd/dT > 0 strongly, redesign pillar length (L) or adjust M′ coordination geometry.
3.2 Thermal expansion acceptance criteria (anisotropic, explicit):
Measure lattice parameters by variable-temperature synchrotron PXRD (100“400 K) and extract anisotropic coefficients.
- Target for “suppressed expansion”: **α⊥ ≤ +5 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹** (channel-width direction).
- Target for “negative expansion”: **α⊥ ≤ −5 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹** sustained over at least a 100 K interval.
- Requirement: porosity retained (see 3.4).
3.3 Thermodynamic crossover proof (free-energy requirement):
Obtain/validate ΔG(w,T) for wall separation coordinate w.
- Required profile: κ(T)=∂²G/∂w² increases with T (stiffening), and the minimum w*(T) shifts to smaller w with increasing T over the interval where α⊥ becomes small/negative.
Experimental proxy: temperature-dependent Raman/IR shifts of clamp-associated librational modes must blue-shift (increasing effective stiffness) with increasing T in the same range.
3.4 Permanent porosity criteria (explicit):
- N2 sorption at 77 K: retain ≥80% of initial BET area after 10 thermal cycles (100↔400 K).
- In situ PXRD during activation: no phase change; unit cell volume change upon desolvation ≤3% unless reversible.

Step 4 — Mechanistic stress tests with guests (vdW competition vs reinforcement)
4.1 In situ VT-PXRD under controlled loadings of CH4, CO2, H2 to interrogate clamp-guest competition.
- Acceptance logic: if guests occupy clamp region, expect reduced clamp effect (α⊥ becomes more positive); if guests adsorb elsewhere or reinforce wall registry, α⊥ remains suppressed/negative.
4.2 Neutron/X-ray diffraction (as feasible) to locate adsorption sites; prioritize conditions where pore-wall interactions dominate (cf. aromatic-linker binding sites).

Step 5 — Computation reduced to a staged hierarchy with observables and checkpoints
Stage I (fast screening; go/no-go for synthesis targets):
5.1 Build structural models varying pillar length and M′ geometry; use force-field or ML potential with explicit dispersion to compute (i) equilibrium d, (ii) clamp contact energy, (iii) elastic response along w. Observable link: predicted d and stiffness correlate to PXRD-derived geometry and elastic trends.
Stage II (anharmonic classical MD; mechanism-to-observable mapping):
5.2 Run NPT MD across 100“400 K to predict anisotropic thermal expansion and identify dominant low-frequency modes coupling to w. Observable link: compare α(T) tensor to VT-PXRD.
Stage III (selective DFT validation; limited scope):
5.3 Perform periodic DFT-D4 only on (a) the best candidate and (b) one control to validate clamp interaction geometry and energy decomposition at 0 K and constrained w.
Stage IV (PIMD only for a narrowly defined question):
5.4 Apply PIMD on a reduced supercell focusing on methylimidazolyl librations below ~150 K to quantify nuclear quantum effects on clamp-associated heat capacity/mode softening. Observable link: low-T heat capacity trend and Raman mode behavior.

Step 6 — Controls (causality isolation)
6.1 Chemical control: isoreticular framework replacing MImBz− with benzoate lacking imidazolyl/methylimidazolyl surface (removes clamp vdW patch).
6.2 Geometric control: identical composition but M′ docking site absent or blocked (imidazolyl cannot lock), probing disorder vs ordered clamp.
6.3 Guest control: measure α⊥ under a guest known to strongly bind aromatic walls vs a weakly interacting gas to distinguish generic adsorption stress from clamp-specific competition.
Feasibility: Addresses (i) ordering/axial disorder risk: The revised design removes the core failure mode of paddlewheel axial-site competition by using a sheet node without labile axial sites and moving imidazolyl locking to a *separate, saturable docking site* (M′). Opposing-wall pairing is enforced by crystallographic symmetry (one orientation per asymmetric unit) rather than by crystallization kinetics. Disorder is not assumed away: it is *quantified* via diffuse scattering/PDF and solid-state NMR, with explicit pass/fail thresholds (≥90% docking; single dominant orientation).

Addresses (ii) quantitative thermodynamic basis for “sign-inverted” expansion: The proposal now defines explicit targets for anisotropic thermal expansion (α⊥ thresholds), explicit structural metrics (d, θ, dd/dT), and a required free-energy signature ΔG(w,T) demonstrating the intended temperature crossover (stiffening and w* shift). These are directly measurable via VT-PXRD and vibrational spectroscopy and directly computable via staged simulation.

Addresses (iii) internal coordination ambiguity: Pillaring and clamp-locking no longer compete for the same coordination site. The pillar defines channel width; M′ defines clamp orientation; the sheet node does not provide axial binding. This eliminates mixed axial environments and reduces the likelihood of partial occupancy and solvent capping dominating the structure.

Addresses (iv) computational feasibility and causality: Computation is reduced to a model hierarchy with go/no-go checkpoints and explicit observable links. Force-field/ML screening selects geometries; anharmonic MD predicts α(T) and mode coupling; DFT-D4 is reserved for validation on a minimal set; PIMD is constrained to low-T quantum effects on librations (a precise question aligned with known needs for quantum/anharmonic treatments in guest-loaded frameworks). This staging improves feasibility while strengthening causal attribution to the designed vdW clamp.

Alignment with the thermal expansion → vdW interactions → functionalized pore walls → permanent porosity chain: The clamp is explicitly an intrapore vdW contact patch between functionalized pore walls placed in the pore-size regime where wall interactions dominate adsorption. Permanent porosity is protected by activation protocols and cycle-tested sorption metrics, while guest-loading experiments explicitly test whether vdW interactions at the pore wall are the mechanistic lever for the thermal response.

Hypothesis: A cuboctahedral metal-organic polyhedron (MOP) nanoball constructed by reticular chemistry from BDC-NH2-functionalized linkers and biocompatible Zr6/Hf6 oxo-cluster vertices, and then “topologically crosslinked” into a MOP-of-MOP nanoshell by a reducible disulfide bis-anhydride/diacid bridge, will show superior intracellular drug release and biocompatibility versus conventional NMOFs because (i) the cuboctahedral shell imposes a uniform, diffusion-limited gate (geometric tortuosity + fixed window size) that suppresses premature leakage, while (ii) the disulfide crosslinks undergo rapid GSH-triggered cleavage inside cells, producing a deterministic connectivity drop that disassembles the nanoball into renal-clearable fragments and opens transport pathways for burst/programmable release. Methodological adaptation: replace standard “bulk framework + polymer coating” MOF drug carriers with a symmetry-defined cuboctahedral MOP nanoball whose surface amines (from BDC-NH2) are post-synthetically converted into a stoichiometrically controlled, GSH-cleavable covalent crosslink network that couples polyhedral topology to intracellular redox chemistry.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a cuboctahedral MOP design with 12 metal vertices and 24 linkers (cuboctahedral connectivity) using Zr6 (or mixed Zr/Hf) oxo-clusters for hydrolytic robustness; incorporate BDC-NH2 as the primary linker (and optionally dilute with BDC to tune amine density).
1.2 Reticular synthesis of discrete nanoballs: optimize solvothermal conditions to favor MOP formation over extended MOF growth by using modulators (e.g., monocarboxylic acids) and controlling concentration/stoichiometry; isolate monodisperse particles (50“200 nm) via antisolvent precipitation and size-selective centrifugation.
1.3 Establish cargo loading protocol with a model anthracycline (DOX) and one hydrophobic dye/drug surrogate to decouple electrostatic vs hydrophobic contributions; quantify loading by HPLC/UV-vis and TGA.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Topological crosslinking (core adaptation): perform post-synthetic modification on BDC-NH2 sites with a bifunctional disulfide-containing acylating linker (e.g., 3,3′-dithiodipropionic anhydride or activated diacid) to form surface/near-surface amide bridges between adjacent amines across MOP edges/windows.
2.2 Control crosslink density by feed ratio and time to generate a defined series (low/medium/high crosslinking). Verify extent by quantitative 1H NMR after digestion, XPS (N 1s shifts), and fluorescamine assay for residual amines.
2.3 Optional supramolecular gating layer (secondary adaptation for leakage suppression): cap remaining amines with a competitive, pH-sensitive macrocycle/host motif (pillararene or cyclodextrin derivative) using reversible interactions; compare to purely covalent crosslinks to isolate the role of topology vs host“guest gating.
2.4 Build a mechanistic release model: treat the nanoball as a shell with windows whose effective diffusivity depends on (a) crosslink connectivity and (b) cargo“framework interactions (electrostatic with “NH3+ at acidic pH, hydrogen bonding). Parameterize with time-resolved release data.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural confirmation: single-crystal or microED for MOP identity if feasible; otherwise SAXS/PDF for polyhedral signature; confirm cuboctahedral morphology by cryo-TEM and STEM tomography; DLS for hydrodynamic size; zeta potential vs pH.
3.2 Stability/leakage tests: quantify cargo leakage in PBS + serum (10% FBS) at pH 7.4 over 48 h; compare against (i) non-crosslinked cuboctahedral MOP, (ii) extended UMCM-1-NH2-type NMOF, and (iii) polymer-coated MOF control.
3.3 Triggered intracellular-mimic release: perform release in buffered solutions with 2“10 mM GSH (intracellular) vs 2“20 µM GSH (extracellular), at pH 7.4 and pH 5.5. Fit kinetics to connectivity-loss model; confirm disulfide cleavage by Ellman’s assay and LC-MS of released linker fragments.
3.4 Cell studies: assess biocompatibility (MTT/CellTiter-Glo, hemolysis, ROS) in at least two lines (e.g., cancer + healthy). Quantify uptake (flow cytometry/confocal) and intracellular release (FRET cargo pair or DOX nuclear localization). Use buthionine sulfoximine (GSH depletion) as a mechanistic control to prove GSH-causality.
3.5 Degradation/clearance proxy: incubate in lysosomal-mimic media; track fragment size evolution by SEC/SAXS and quantify Zr release by ICP-MS; evaluate protein corona changes by SDS-PAGE/proteomics as a predictor of in vivo behavior.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Discrete polyhedral MOP/nanoball and cuboctahedron motifs are established supermolecular building blocks in reticular chemistry, and large-pore polyhedral MOFs have demonstrated accessibility to bulky guests. Separately, disulfide chemistry is a validated intracellular trigger due to high cytosolic GSH, enabling reductive cleavage and controlled release. BDC-NH2 provides high-density, addressable amines for quantitative post-synthetic modification.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal uses MOF/MOP principles (node-and-spacer geometry, polyhedral SBUs) but adapts them into a topology-programmed nanoshell where connectivity is the “switchable variable.” This is a chemically precise alternative to empirical polymer coatings: the crosslink is installed via amide formation on BDC-NH2, directly integrating coordination-assembled geometry with covalent, stimulus-labile bonds.
3. Comparative Advantage: Versus conventional NMOFs, the cuboctahedral nanoball offers (i) monodisperse, symmetry-defined windows that reduce batch-to-batch variability in release, (ii) minimized premature leakage through crosslink-controlled diffusivity, and (iii) faster intracellular unloading via GSH-driven connectivity collapse rather than slow bulk framework dissolution. Versus purely supramolecular gates, disulfide crosslinks provide a quantifiable chemical trigger with clear mechanistic controls (GSH depletion/rescue). Using Zr6/Hf6 oxo nodes preserves extracellular stability while still permitting triggered disassembly through the covalent crosslink pathway, improving the biocompatibility“efficacy balance.

Hypothesis: A mechanically reinforced, humidity-resilient proton-conducting derivative of MIL-101(Cr) can be realized if (and only if) sulfonic-acid tethers are (i) truly node-bound at defined Cr(III) node terminations (terminal “OH/“H2O on the Cr3O cluster rather than ambiguous physisorption) and (ii) achieve a quantifiable, non-random population of window-adjacent “bridge-capable” conformations that create persistent, confined hydrogen-bond networks spanning inter-cage apertures. Mechanistically, node-anchored, window-proximal tethers act as dual-function structural elements: (1) mechanical reinforcement arises from suppressing cage/window compliance (local hinge-like motions around the super-tetrahedron) via an internal ‘tether-spring’ network whose effect should scale with a measurable bridging-fraction proxy rather than total sulfur loading alone; (2) proton conduction arises when “SO3H groups template percolating water-mediated pathways with Grotthuss-dominated hopping, evidenced by low apparent activation energy, a measurable H/D isotope effect, and a quantitative correlation between water dynamics (QENS/NMR timescales) and conductivity. This refined hypothesis directly addresses reviewer concerns by pre-registering: (a) a geometric/energetic feasibility gate for true inter-cage bridging based on MIL-101 window metrics plus tether conformational sampling, (b) an orthogonally verified Cr“O“(tether) binding mode at substitution-inert Cr(III) nodes, and (c) a causal test that modulus/yield increases track intrinsic framework-level reinforcement (microcrystal pillars) rather than pellet densification or defect evolution.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registered structural targets and definitions (before synthesis)
0.1 Define the structural ‘bridge’ objective in MIL-101(Cr) using crystallographic metrics. Use reported MIL-101(Cr) cage architecture (two cage types connected through pentagonal/hexagonal windows) and extract window diameters and node-to-window geometric descriptors from the CIF. Operational definition: a tether is “bridge-capable” if its terminal S atom (or sulfonate O centroid) can reside within a predefined window-adjacent shell while remaining node-bound, with an end-to-end reach that can place the “SO3H within hydrogen-bonding distance (≤3.2 Å O···O) of a water cluster that is simultaneously within the adjacent cage’s window-adjacent shell. This avoids over-claiming literal covalent crosslinks while keeping the mechanistic requirement (inter-cage proton-relay continuity).
0.2 Pre-register measurable bridging proxies:
  • PDF/total scattering: appearance/shift/intensity change of S···S and S···Cr pair correlations in the 3“10 Å range relative to a non-acid tether control at matched loading; target observables are (i) an S···Cr peak consistent with node binding and (ii) an S···S distance distribution consistent with window-proximal clustering/bridging rather than random pore dispersion.
  • Solid-state NMR distance restraints: 13C/19F/31P labeling options (see Step 2) to enable REDOR/TRAPDOR-type distance constraints between tether endgroups and framework/linker nuclei; or 1H“1H spin diffusion changes consistent with tether-end proximity across windows under controlled hydration.
  • Water sorption + calorimetry: an additional bridging-consistent signature is a discrete increase in isosteric heat (Qst) at low coverage plus a plateau in σ(RH) at high RH for samples predicted to exceed the percolation threshold in hydrogen-bond connectivity.

Step 1 — Node-state control and de-risked Cr(III) grafting chemistry
1.1 Synthesize MIL-101(Cr) with controlled defect populations using a modulated hydrothermal route, but explicitly target a node termination state that is ligand-exchange-accessible: Cr3O clusters bearing terminal “OH/“H2O. Avoid assumptions of facile substitution at “open metal sites”; instead, generate and quantify terminal aquo/hydroxo sites.
  • Activation protocol: stepwise solvent exchange to remove strongly coordinating guests, followed by controlled thermal/vacuum activation that preserves terminal “OH/“H2O rather than creating unstable under-coordinated Cr sites.
1.2 Baseline node speciation and defect quantification (pre-grafting):
  • IR: identify terminal “OH and bound H2O signatures.
  • TGA + elemental analysis: quantify residual anions/solvent.
  • CO/NO probe-IR only as supportive evidence (recognizing kinetic limitations at Cr(III)); interpret cautiously.
  • PXRD + total scattering/PDF: establish baseline local Cr“O and Cr···Cr distances to detect later node restructuring.
1.3 Choose headgroups with a kinetic/thermodynamic rationale compatible with substitution-inert Cr(III) nodes:
  • Primary headgroup: phosphonate (“PO3H2) or hydroxamate (“CONHO“) variants in addition to carboxylate. Rationale: multidentate, higher-affinity binding to hard Cr(III) centers and ability to bind via terminal “OH/“H2O displacement without requiring full node rearrangement.
  • Include a carboxylate-only tether as a comparator but not the sole route.
1.4 Grafting conditions designed for Cr(III) exchange without hydrolysis/defect evolution:
  • Use anhydrous, non-aqueous solvents (e.g., dry acetonitrile/DMF depending on stability) with controlled temperature (e.g., 40“80 °C) and time-course sampling.
  • Use stoichiometric control to target fractional occupancy (e.g., 5“60% of terminal sites), determined by uptake kinetics.
  • Implement a kinetic study: measure tether uptake vs time and temperature; fit to a simple kinetic model to demonstrate whether exchange is diffusion-limited or reaction-limited.
1.5 Orthogonal verification of binding mode (mandatory):
  • Cr K-edge EXAFS/XANES: detect changes in Cr first-shell coordination (Cr“O distances, coordination number) consistent with tether binding to terminal positions rather than framework dissolution/reprecipitation.
  • S K-edge XANES/EXAFS (or P K-edge for phosphonate): confirm sulfonate oxidation state and local environment; identify whether sulfonic acid is intact after processing.
  • Combine with digest-NMR/ICP for loading and mass balance.

Step 2 — Tether library engineered around the window-spanning feasibility gate
2.1 Build a tether library where (a) end-to-end length and flexibility are systematically varied and (b) at least one member is conformationally biased toward window adjacency.
  • Length series: (CH2)n“SO3H with n chosen from geometric analysis (Step 0) to bracket the predicted window-adjacent bridging regime; include short (n~3“4), medium (n~6“8), and longer (n~10“12) variants.
  • Flexibility/solvation series: include an oligo(ethylene glycol) spacer (e.g., “(CH2CH2O)m“) to promote structured hydration while keeping size compatible with pore apertures.
  • Headgroup series: carboxylate vs phosphonate vs hydroxamate for the same spacer length to test binding robustness at Cr(III).
  • Controls: (i) non-acid terminal group (“CH3) at matched length/headgroup to decouple pore filling/mechanics from proton chemistry; (ii) free sulfonic acid impregnation control at matched sulfur content to demonstrate immobilization advantage.
2.2 Include at least one spectroscopically “trackable” tether to enable distance proxies:
  • Option A: incorporate 19F near the sulfonate terminus (without changing acidity drastically) to enable 19F-based ssNMR proximity experiments.
  • Option B: 13C labeling at specific tether positions for 13C{1H} REDOR-type constraints.
2.3 Post-synthetic tether installation and deprotection pathway designed to avoid node hydrolysis:
  • Prefer direct installation of sulfonic acid (“SO3H) rather than harsh deprotection; if protection is required, use mild ion-exchange steps and verify with XANES that the framework remains intact.

Step 3 — Quantifying “bridging fraction” and ruling out alternative explanations
3.1 Geometry + conformational sampling workflow (executed early; informs which tethers proceed):
  • Use the MIL-101(Cr) structure to generate a node-anchored tether model.
  • Perform classical conformational sampling (MD or Monte Carlo) of single and multiple tethers at relevant loadings (e.g., 10%, 30%, 50% site occupancy), explicitly including steric constraints from windows.
  • Output: distribution of terminal S positions relative to window planes; compute a “bridge-capable fraction” f_bridge defined by the pre-registered criteria in Step 0.
  • Energetics: estimate free-energy preference for window-adjacent vs cage-interior conformations (umbrella sampling or restrained MD) for representative tethers.
3.2 Experimental bridging proxies:
  • Total scattering/PDF: collect for dry and hydrated states; fit with models that include sulfur scatterers to extract S···Cr and S···S distance distributions. Compare against simulated distributions from Step 3.1.
  • ssNMR (if labeled tether used): acquire distance-sensitive experiments under controlled hydration to detect increased cross-window proximity relative to non-acid controls.
  • Water sorption isotherms (H2O and D2O): measure uptake and hysteresis; fit to identify threshold-like uptake consistent with formation of confined water networks.
3.3 Defect/porosity evolution controls (mandatory to refute “densification/annealing” explanations):
  • PXRD for long-range crystallinity pre/post grafting.
  • PDF for local node integrity and detection of node restructuring.
  • N2 sorption (BET, pore size distribution) plus CO2 sorption (micropore sensitivity) to verify retention of window accessibility.
  • H2O sorption to quantify hydrophilicity change and relate directly to proton transport behavior.

Step 4 — Mechanics: decouple intrinsic framework reinforcement from pellet artifacts
4.1 Make single-particle mechanics central:
  • Prepare microcrystals suitable for microcompression; fabricate FIB-milled pillars from single crystals or individual crystallites mounted to minimize interparticle contacts.
  • Target statistical robustness: n≥15“30 pillars per condition (baseline MIL-101, non-acid tether, acid tether at multiple loadings/lengths) to resolve variability.
4.2 Measure:
  • Elastic modulus and yield/incipient plasticity from microcompression stress“strain.
