  • Failure mode mapping by SEM/TEM of deformed pillars.
4.3 Use pellets only as a secondary, application-relevant metric and explicitly control for compaction:
  • Standardize pressing pressure, dwell time, and pellet density; report porosity loss.
  • No binders unless unavoidable; if used, quantify and keep constant.
4.4 Mechanistic attribution test:
  • Test whether modulus/yield correlates with f_bridge (from Step 3) more strongly than with total sulfur loading or pellet density.
  • Compare acid vs non-acid tethers at matched loading: if reinforcement is truly from tether-spring connectivity/window stiffening, both should increase modulus similarly; any additional changes due to water uptake/acid chemistry should be separable.

Step 5 — Proton transport: falsifiable criteria for Grotthuss vs vehicular contribution
5.1 EIS measurements under rigorously controlled hydration:
  • Measure σ(RH,T) from 20“95% RH and 25“90 °C; ensure equilibration time is sufficient and report it.
  • Extract Ea from Arrhenius plots at fixed RH.
5.2 Isotope effect as a required discriminator:
  • Repeat σ measurements under D2O humidification (same RH protocol) and compute σH/σD; a significant isotope effect supports Grotthuss contributions.
5.3 Quantitative linkage between water dynamics and conductivity:
  • QENS (or 2H/1H solid-state NMR relaxometry/diffusometry, depending on access) to extract correlation times and mobility of confined water near “SO3H.
  • Correlate: (i) QENS/NMR-derived timescales vs σ, and (ii) timescales vs Ea across the density×length matrix.
  • Falsifiable expectation: samples with higher f_bridge should show (a) higher σ at a given water uptake, (b) lower Ea, and (c) reduced conductivity loss after dry“rehydrate cycling.
5.4 Desorption sensitivity / cycling test:
  • Vacuum-dry to a defined endpoint (mass stability), then rehumidify; track σ recovery. Immobilized tethers should yield higher reversibility than free-acid impregnated controls at matched sulfur content.
5.5 Optional mechanochemical coupling test (kept but clarified):
  • Perform EIS under controlled uniaxial compressive stress on a standardized pellet fixture; interpret only after intrinsic pillar data establish framework-level reinforcement.

Step 6 — Modeling narrowed to an executable, validated workflow
6.1 Stage 1 (predictive, low risk): classical MD with explicit water + tethered acids.
  • Force field: use a MOF-validated framework force field (e.g., MOF-FF/UFF4MOF class) plus compatible parameters for sulfonic acids; validate key structural observables against PXRD/PDF and water uptake.
  • Outputs: hydration structure, H-bond network graph metrics (connectivity, percolation probability across windows), residence times of water near “SO3H.
6.2 Calibration to experiment (mandatory before reactive transport):
  • Fit/validate MD-derived water residence/correlation times against QENS/NMR for 1“2 representative samples (low vs high f_bridge).
  • Validate spatial S-distribution against PDF/ssNMR distance proxies.
6.3 Stage 2 (only on validated subdomains): reactive/proton hopping modeling.
  • Build representative subdomains (window-adjacent region with two cages + tether configurations) selected from MD ensembles.
  • Apply a reduced proton transport model (e.g., empirical valence bond on a small cluster or a parametrized hopping model on an H-bond graph) to estimate relative trends, not absolute σ.
  • Success criterion: correctly predict ordering of σ and isotope effect across a small subset; expand only if predictive.

Milestones / go-no-go criteria
M1 (Feasibility of binding): EXAFS-confirmed node binding without loss of MIL-101 local structure (PXRD+PDF) at ≥10% loading.
M2 (Bridging plausibility): measurable PDF/NMR proxy consistent with non-random window-adjacent S distributions and an f_bridge > threshold predicted by sampling.
M3 (Mechanics causality): micro-pillar modulus/yield increases that correlate with f_bridge (and persist when pellet artifacts are excluded).
M4 (Transport mechanism): significant isotope effect + quantitative correlation of σ and Ea with hydration dynamics; superior dry“rehydrate recovery vs free-acid control.
Feasibility: Cr(III) grafting risk is addressed by (i) explicitly targeting terminal “OH/“H2O node terminations rather than assuming facile “open site” substitution, (ii) expanding headgroups beyond carboxylate to stronger, multidentate hard-base binders (phosphonate/hydroxamate) suited to substitution-inert Cr(III), (iii) using non-aqueous, temperature-controlled ligand-exchange conditions with time-resolved uptake kinetics, and (iv) requiring Cr K-edge EXAFS as an orthogonal binding-mode proof (supplemented by S/P K-edge where relevant). Bridging feasibility is no longer assumed: it is gated by a pre-registered geometric model built from MIL-101 pore-window metrics and conformational sampling that yields an explicit f_bridge, then experimentally constrained using PDF/total scattering and (where enabled) ssNMR distance restraints. Mechanical reinforcement attribution is deconvoluted from pellet densification by making microcrystal/FIB-pillar compression the primary mechanical readout with adequate statistics, and by tracking defect/porosity evolution (PXRD+PDF+gas sorption+water sorption) pre/post functionalization to rule out annealing/densification as dominant drivers. Proton-transport mechanism assignment is tightened using mandatory water uptake isotherms, H2O/D2O isotope effect, and a quantitative correlation between water dynamics (QENS/NMR timescales) and σ/Ea to distinguish Grotthuss-dominated hopping from vehicular transport. Finally, modeling scope is narrowed to an executable pipeline: classical MD + graph-theoretic H-bond connectivity metrics calibrated against QENS/NMR and scattering-derived spatial constraints, with reactive proton transport modeling restricted to validated representative subdomains for trend prediction. This integrated, falsifiable design directly couples guest-dependent elasticity (via tether density/length and bridge-capability) to proton conductivity (via anchored acid density and percolating water-wire networks) while remaining realistic about MIL-101(Cr) node chemistry and the statistical nature of tether configurations.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that **programmed, node-confined conversion** of 4-connected indium carboxylate nodes (CPM-9-type) into **crystallographically registered In“O(In(OH)3→In2O3) nanodomains** inside a Ni2+-paddlewheel MOF host will create a **high-density, short-path internal heterojunction** that enforces directional photocarrier separation and lowers the apparent photoelectrochemical kinetic barrier. This will manifest as (i) a lower interfacial charge-transfer resistance under illumination (Rct,light) and higher exchange current density (j0) and therefore (ii) a reduced Tafel slope relative to controls where In2O3 is randomly dispersed or physically mixed. The key mechanistic refinement is that the conversion is performed **chemically and at low temperature**, avoiding oxidative combustion of linkers and preserving the Ni-carboxylate backbone, while the junction type (type-II vs Z-scheme-like) is **quantitatively decided** from measured band alignment (UPS/Kelvin probe/Mott“Schottky) and validated by operando spectroscopies. By confining In“O nucleation to pre-defined CPM-9 node positions, the interface area per volume is maximized and the carrier travel distance to the junction is minimized, suppressing recombination (Asset 2/3 logic) and enabling kinetics comparable to optimized Ni-derived catalysts (Asset 1 logic), without conflating effects from bulk conductivity or mass transport.
Plan: Step 1 — Reticular design and de-risked synthesis of a dual-node framework (avoid phase separation).
1.1. Build a ‘compartmentalized’ mixed-SBU framework by **sequential SBU installation** rather than one-pot mixed-metal assembly: (a) crystallize a CPM-9-type In-carboxylate framework (4-connected In nodes) using a rigid dicarboxylate (primary candidate: 2,6-naphthalenedicarboxylate, NDC) under conditions known to stabilize In-carboxylates; (b) introduce Ni2+ paddlewheel nodes by **post-synthetic node insertion / transmetalation at defined carboxylate sites** (or by growing a Ni-paddlewheel MOF shell on In-MOF crystals to form a core“shell single-crystal composite). The decision between ‘true mixed-node single phase’ and ‘epitaxial core“shell’ will be made by early diffraction screening; both preserve the central concept: **CPM-9 node registry + intimate Ni/In proximity**.
1.2. Thermodynamic/kinetic controls to suppress phase separation: fixed ligand set (single dicarboxylate), controlled modulator ratio (monocarboxylate modulators), slow diffusion layering (microfluidic or liquid“liquid diffusion), and stoichiometry that biases In-node formation first (In3+ higher oxophilicity) followed by Ni2+ incorporation.
1.3. Structural acceptance criteria before conversion: single-crystal integrity by optical microscopy; crystallinity by PXRD; metal distributions by ICP-OES and SEM/STEM-EDS mapping; confirm Ni paddlewheel formation by IR (carboxylate Δν), XAS (Ni K-edge), and magnetic/UV“vis signatures.

Step 2 — Mandatory low-temperature, chemically selective indium-node conversion (no O2 calcination; topology-retentive target).
2.1. ‘Protect-the-Ni-paddlewheel’ pretreatment: exchange synthesis solvents with anhydrous alcohol (EtOH/iPrOH) and then non-coordinating solvent (toluene) to reduce hydrolytic stress; optionally introduce a mild hydrophobic pore additive (e.g., alkyl ammonium) if hydrolysis sensitivity is observed.
2.2. **Node-selective hydrolysis/oxidation of In-carboxylate to In“OH (In(OH)3) at ≤60“80 °C**: expose crystals/films to controlled water activity (H2O/EtOH mixtures) containing a weak base buffer (e.g., acetate) and/or urea (slow OH− release) to drive In“O formation while minimizing Ni-carboxylate cleavage. Rationale: In3+ nodes hydrolyze preferentially (hard acid), enabling selective conversion under conditions too mild to decompose Ni paddlewheels.
2.3. Convert In(OH)3 → In2O3 by **mild dehydration (150“220 °C)** under inert gas (N2/Ar) or vacuum (no O2), with temperature ramp rates ≤1“2 °C·min−1 to limit framework stress. Target: ultrasmall In2O3 domains confined to former In-node positions.
2.4. Keep conductivity enhancement orthogonal (per directive):
   • Primary route: incorporate conductivity without pyrolysis by (i) using a π-conjugated linker fraction (e.g., NDC plus a small fraction of an electron-rich dicarboxylate) and/or (ii) adding a thin conformal conductive overlayer post-conversion (PEDOT:PSS or ultrathin carbon via low-temperature glucose dehydration) that does not require O2.
   • Secondary, optional route (only after structural retention is proven): inert-atmosphere pyrolysis of a **separately prepared, sacrificial replicate** (not the topology-retentive sample) to benchmark the best-possible conductivity.

Step 3 — ‘Topology-retentive/epitaxial’ validation package (before/after conversion, with explicit pass“fail metrics).
3.1. Diffraction: SCXRD on representative crystals pre- and post-conversion where feasible; otherwise synchrotron PXRD with Rietveld refinement plus PDF (pair distribution function) analysis to quantify retention of long-range order vs local In“O formation.
3.2. Microscopy: HRTEM/HRSTEM to image embedded In2O3; SAED to determine whether In2O3 reflections share fixed orientation relationships with the host (topotactic/epitaxial criterion: reproducible orientation relation across multiple particles/crystals). If beam sensitivity limits exist, use cryo-TEM or low-dose protocols.
3.3. Spatial chemistry: STEM-EDS/EELS line scans and maps to show In“O confined at former node positions; nano-XPS or TOF-SIMS depth profiling (for films) to prove non-random distribution.
3.4. Chemical state: In 3d XPS (In3+ oxide), O 1s deconvolution (M“O vs OH), Ni 2p to confirm Ni node retention; In K-edge XANES/EXAFS to track In“O coordination evolution.

Step 4 — Band alignment and junction-type decision (quantitative, not asserted).
4.1. Measure work function and valence positions by UPS; measure surface potential shifts by Kelvin probe; obtain semiconductor type and flat-band potentials by Mott“Schottky (dark and illuminated).
4.2. Construct band diagrams for: (i) Ni-MOF host (or Ni-MOF-derived conductive phase if used), (ii) In2O3 nanodomains, and (iii) the heterostructure. Decide whether interfacial energetics correspond to type-II or Z-scheme-like behavior.
4.3. Validate carrier pathways: time-resolved PL / transient absorption (Asset 2/3 logic) plus surface photovoltage spectroscopy; correlate lifetime changes with interfacial area and In2O3 loading.

Step 5 — Kinetic model linking interface to Tafel slope; rigorous electrochemical controls.
5.1. Photoelectrochemical testing on identical-area electrodes with controlled catalyst loading and film thickness; measure LSV under chopped light, Tafel plots in kinetically controlled region, and EIS under illumination to extract Rct,light and capacitances.
5.2. Use a mechanistic framework: j = j0·exp(αFη/RT) (low overpotential) and relate the apparent Tafel slope b to α and to interfacial kinetics by correlating b with Rct,light (from EIS) and j0 (from extrapolation and/or impedance-derived exchange current). Report and correct for uncompensated resistance (iR) and verify linearity regions.
5.3. Controls required by reviewers:
   (C1) Ni-MOF host without In conversion;
   (C2) In-MOF converted to In2O3 without Ni component;
   (C3) physical mixture of Ni-MOF + commercial In2O3 matched in In content;
   (C4) non-topotactic composite made by depositing In2O3 nanoparticles onto Ni-MOF externally;
   (C5) same total In loading but deliberately ‘de-programmed’ distribution (e.g., ion exchange then precipitation).
5.4. Photocatalytic benchmarks: HER and CO2 reduction (as in original), but report quantum efficiency/turnover metrics; use isotope or scavenger tests to confirm charge utilization pathways; for CO2, in situ FTIR to track intermediates (parallel to Asset 5).
5.5. Stability: operando/after-test PXRD + XPS to distinguish true catalysis from surface reconstruction; leaching tests (ICP of electrolyte) for In and Ni.
Feasibility: Addresses (i) thermal/O2 incompatibility: The proposal eliminates oxidative calcination in O2 and replaces it with **selective In-node hydrolysis (≤80 °C) followed by mild dehydration (150“220 °C)** under inert/vacuum, conditions far more compatible with Ni2+ paddlewheel carboxylate frameworks. Conductivity enhancement is explicitly decoupled and, by default, achieved without pyrolysis; any inert pyrolysis is relegated to a non-topology-retentive benchmark sample.

Addresses (ii) SCSC/topology-retentive credibility: ‘SCSC-like’ is treated as a testable claim with a **defined validation suite**: SCXRD where possible; otherwise synchrotron PXRD + Rietveld + PDF, plus HRTEM/SAED orientation-relationship evidence, and nanoscale chemical mapping (STEM-EDS/EELS, nano-XPS/TOF-SIMS). Success criteria are explicit: retention of host diffraction features + confined In“O domains + reproducible orientation relation.

Addresses (iii) mechanistic grounding and Tafel interpretation: Band alignment is measured (UPS/Kelvin probe/Mott“Schottky) to determine junction type (type-II vs Z-scheme-like), while kinetics are separated from artifacts using iR compensation, thickness/loading controls, and **EIS-under-illumination** to link Rct,light and j0 to the observed Tafel slope. This directly tests whether programmed interfaces improve charge-transfer kinetics rather than merely increasing conductivity or surface area.

Addresses (iv) reticular compatibility risk: Rather than assuming one-pot co-assembly of Ni paddlewheels with CPM-9 In nodes, the synthesis is de-risked via **sequential assembly (In framework first, then Ni insertion or epitaxial Ni growth)**, with go/no-go structural criteria and early-phase diffraction/compositional mapping. This preserves the original concept chain (CPM-9 indium node → confined In2O3; Ni-based scaffold → favorable kinetics) while using a synthesis logic more consistent with known mixed-SBU constraints.

Literature anchoring: The approach leverages (a) MOF-derived Ni-based catalysts where local N/C environments tune kinetics (Asset 1), (b) hollow/heterostructured MOF systems where carrier recombination is suppressed by architecture (Asset 2) and efficient e“h separation correlates with activity (Asset 3), (c) CPM-9/4-connected In-node design principles (Asset 4), and (d) In2O3 heterojunction-driven charge transfer validated by KPFM/DFT and in situ spectroscopy paradigms (Asset 5), but replaces the non-viable O2/calcination step with a chemically selective, topology-aware conversion pathway demanded by the reviewers.

Hypothesis: Crystal-size“dependent immobilization selectivity in hL/ZIF-8 can be made mechanistically interpretable—and predictably tunable—only if (i) the *location* of enzyme (external surface vs intracrystalline) is quantitatively partitioned and (ii) the “orientation-biasing chemistry” is implemented as a *surface-localized, spatially heterogeneous* modification whose distribution is demonstrated independently of ideal Miller-index assumptions. We hypothesize that narrowing ZIF-8 crystals to 30“150 nm increases the fractional contribution of external-surface immobilization (shorter diffusion length, higher external area per mass) and therefore amplifies any orientation bias imposed by sparse surface anchoring sites. Orientation bias will be generated by low-conversion post-synthetic ligand exchange (PSLE) that yields *surface-enriched microdomains* (patches) of functional imidazolates; these microdomains reduce lysozyme’s rotational entropy at the interface and enrich a subset of docking geometries that place the catalytic cleft accessible (“active-site-out”) while maintaining sufficient substrate approach. Critically, to overcome the reviewer-identified weakness of claiming facet-selective exchange, the refined hypothesis does not require strict {110}/{100} exclusivity. Instead, it predicts that *wherever* PSLE concentrates (facet, edge, defect-rich region), selectivity gains will scale with: (a) the *measured spatial heterogeneity* of exchanged-linker density on the outer 1“3 nm of the crystal, and (b) the *measured surface-accessible fraction* of enzyme. A causal orientation mechanism is supported if: (1) patch heterogeneity correlates with EPR-derived orientation order parameters; (2) selectivity changes persist after correcting for transport via an effectiveness-factor/Thiele-modulus kinetic model; and (3) the effect is reproduced with a non-thiol polar PSLE control (matched exchange %) and attenuated/abolished when patch interactions are chemically blocked. This reframing directly addresses surface reconstruction/defect confounds: patch localization is treated as an experimentally measured variable (and potentially defect-driven), and Zn“S coordination is isolated from generic polarity/charge effects via matched non-coordinating controls.
Plan: Step 1 — ZIF-8 libraries with controlled size and quantified defect density
1.1 Size regimes: Prepare ZIF-8 in (i) 30“60 nm, (ii) 80“120 nm, and (iii) 300“600 nm regimes. Use identical Zn:2-methylimidazole stoichiometry and total solids; vary only nucleation/growth kinetics using (a) base (NH4OH) dose and addition rate, (b) mixing intensity (stopped-flow for ≤120 nm; conventional solvothermal for ≥300 nm), and (c) ligand concentration while holding ionic strength constant. Quench at matched conversion (monitored by supernatant Zn by ICP-OES).
1.2 Normalize activation history: identical solvent exchange sequence (MeOH → CHCl3 or MeOH → acetone, pre-defined number of exchanges, identical temperatures) and vacuum activation protocol. Record residual solvent via TGA/FTIR to ensure comparability.
1.3 Defect metrics (explicitly to decouple size from defects): quantify missing-linker/under-coordination proxies by (a) solution 1H NMR of digested MOF (linker:Zn ratio), (b) modulator incorporation if used, and (c) CO2 adsorption at 273 K (defect-sensitive uptake) alongside N2-BET.

Step 2 — PSLE chemistry redesigned to *prove* surface localization and test facet vs defect correlation
2.1 Two functional PSLE linkers + one strict non-coordinating control (matched exchange %):
  • L1 (thiol): 2-mercaptoimidazole (2-SH-Im) to test soft-base/Zn interactions.
  • L2 (polar, weakly coordinating): 2-hydroxyimidazole (2-OH-Im) or 2-methoxyimidazole (2-OMe-Im) as a polar control expected to alter H-bonding/polarity with minimal Zn“S-like coordination.
  • L3 (charge/polarity control, minimal Zn binding): 2-methylimidazole-4,5-d2 (isotopically labeled) or an imidazole bearing a short PEG-like substituent with steric hindrance to Zn coordination (chosen based on stability screening); purpose is to match surface polarity/sterics without introducing strong new coordination.
2.2 PSLE conditions engineered to bias *outer-surface* exchange (not bulk): perform PSLE on activated crystals in anhydrous alcohol (MeOH or iPrOH) with controlled water activity (≤0.5% v/v H2O), dilute linker (0.5“5 mM), short times (5“60 min), room temperature, and immediate quench by rapid centrifugation and washing. The target is 0.5, 1, 3, and 5 mol% exchanged linker (relative to total linker), verified by digest-1H NMR (or LC-MS if needed). Avoid aqueous PSLE to suppress deep diffusion and framework dissolution.
2.3 Mandatory proof of localization and heterogeneity (patchiness) on the external shell:
  • Angle-resolved XPS (ARXPS): quantify S (or O) enrichment vs take-off angle to estimate functional-group depth profile; fit to layered model to estimate modified-shell thickness (goal: outer ~1“3 nm enriched).
  • ToF-SIMS depth profiling (cluster ion sputter): map S−/O− fragment intensity vs depth; verify steep decay within first few nm. Include an internal standard sample with intentionally “uniform” high exchange (e.g., 20“30% PSLE under longer time) to calibrate depth-profiling response.
  • Correlative (S)TEM on indexed crystals: for ≥300 nm crystals, acquire HRTEM/SAED to assign major facets; perform STEM-EDS/EELS mapping for S (thiol) or O (polar) signal across specific facet planes vs edges/corners. For ≤120 nm crystals where facet indexing is harder, use ensemble methods (ARXPS + ToF-SIMS) plus shape statistics.
  • Selective facet/edge blocking experiment (to test whether exchange tracks defects/edges rather than ideal facets): pre-passivate external Zn sites with a reversible, bulky base (e.g., 1-methylimidazole) or a polymeric steric blocker (PVP) prior to PSLE; quantify reduction in PSLE uptake and compare effect across size regimes. If exchange is edge/defect-driven, blocking will disproportionately suppress PSLE in smaller, higher-curvature particles.
  • Defect-correlation test: regress measured PSLE uptake rate/extent (initial slope from time series) against defect proxies (digest-NMR linker:Zn deviation, CO2 uptake, zeta potential trends). This explicitly tests the reviewer’s concern that exchange correlates more with defect density than facet identity.
2.4 Stability and Zn“S perturbation checks (for thiol-specific confounds): measure Zn leaching (ICP-OES of supernatant), framework integrity (PXRD), and local coordination changes (Zn K-edge XAS if available; otherwise XPS Zn 2p shifts + FTIR/Raman signatures). Compare L1 vs L2 at identical exchange % to isolate Zn“S effects.

Step 3 — Enzyme immobilization with orthogonal quantification of surface vs intracrystalline populations
3.1 Two immobilization routes (as before) but with explicit population partitioning:
  (A) Post-synthetic adsorption (surface-dominant): immobilize at pH 6.0“7.0 (hL net positive) in buffered low-ionic-strength medium; control loading by enzyme:MOF ratio and time.
  (B) Biomimetic mineralization/encapsulation (encapsulation-dominant): grow ZIF-8 around hL under standardized precursor addition; wash rigorously to remove surface-bound protein.
3.2 Mandatory orthogonal “location” assays (quantitative):
  • Protease-accessibility assay: treat composites with a non-specific protease too large to enter ZIF-8 (e.g., trypsin or proteinase K; select based on hydrodynamic size and ZIF-8 aperture constraints). Quantify remaining intact hL (SDS-PAGE densitometry and activity) to infer protected (intracrystalline) fraction. Include controls showing protease cannot penetrate empty ZIF-8 (fluorescently labeled protease binding assay).
  • Impermeant fluorescence quenching: label hL with an external fluorophore; apply an aqueous, membrane-impermeant quencher (e.g., iodide/tryptophan quenching variant or a sulfonated dye quencher). Quenching efficiency reports surface-exposed fraction. Calibrate with fully surface-bound standards.
  • Spatial mapping on larger crystals (≥300 nm): confocal fluorescence z-stacks (or super-resolution if available) to visualize shell vs core distribution; correlate with protease/quenching outputs.
3.3 Match total loading across conditions: quantify total hL by mass balance (Bradford/UV) and verify with elemental N content (CHN) where possible; report both total loading and surface-accessible fraction for every sample.

Step 4 — Orientation measurement and linkage to selectivity with a predefined kinetic framework
4.1 Orientation readout (SDSL-EPR) upgraded for interpretability: prepare 3“4 single-cysteine hL variants at positions: (i) near active-site rim, (ii) opposite face, (iii) lateral face, (iv) flexible loop region. Use cw-EPR line-shape for mobility + DEER (where feasible) to constrain orientation distributions. Analyze with restricted-rotation models to extract: order parameters, fraction of immobilized vs mobile subpopulations, and an “active-site exposure index” derived from the set of labels.
4.2 Catalytic substrate panel with validated ZIF-8 partitioning/permeability differences (pre-screened):
  • Substrate S1: small chromogenic/fluorogenic peptidoglycan mimic (low MW) known to access pores or at least rapidly reach surface sites.
  • Substrate S2: larger/charged oligosaccharide or polymeric peptidoglycan fragment (higher hydrodynamic radius) expected to be transport-limited and more sensitive to surface accessibility.
  • Validation step: independently measure substrate uptake/partitioning into ZIF-8 (time-resolved depletion in supernatant +, if possible, PFG-NMR for small substrate; for large substrate, fluorescence uptake kinetics). Only retain substrate pairs that show a clear, quantifiable difference in effective diffusivity/partitioning.
4.3 Predefined kinetic model to decouple intrinsic catalysis from transport:
  • Fit initial-rate data to an effectiveness-factor model: v_obs = η(ϕ)·v_intrinsic, with ϕ (Thiele modulus) computed from particle size, measured/estimated D_eff (from uptake), and intrinsic kinetic parameters. Implement separate η for (i) surface-accessible population and (ii) intracrystalline population using the location fractions from Step 3.
  • Report selectivity as ratios of intrinsic specificity constants (kcat/KM) corrected for η, plus the raw observed selectivity to show the magnitude of transport distortion.
4.4 Experimental matrix designed to avoid parameter coupling and test causality:
  • Factorial design across size (3), PSLE linker (L1 thiol, L2 polar, L3 control, plus 0% PSLE), and exchange density (0.5“5%).
  • Within each condition, run both immobilization routes (A, B), and measure: (i) patch localization metrics (ARXPS/ToF-SIMS), (ii) defect metrics, (iii) surface-accessible enzyme fraction, (iv) EPR orientation metrics, (v) substrate uptake/D_eff, (vi) kinetics/selectivity.

Step 5 — Explicit controls demanded by the review
5.1 Non-thiol PSLE controls at matched exchange %: L2/L3 as above, to isolate Zn“S coordination effects from generic changes in surface polarity/charge.
5.2 Patch erasure/neutralization controls:
  • For thiol samples: cap “SH with a small, non-chelating electrophile (e.g., iodoacetamide) after PSLE to remove thiol-specific interactions while keeping the exchanged linker in place; confirm by XPS S 2p shift and ToF-SIMS fragments.
  • “Uniform exchange” control: intentionally drive near-uniform exchange (higher linker concentration/longer time) at the same net % exchange where possible (or a higher % benchmark), to demonstrate that spatial heterogeneity—not merely composition—drives orientation/selectivity.
5.3 Enzyme-property controls: include a charge-modified hL (or chemically acetylated lysines) to disrupt electrostatic docking; observe whether orientation order/selectivity collapses specifically in patchy PSLE samples.

Step 6 — Deliverables and decision criteria (go/no-go)
6.1 Facet/patch claim is accepted only if: (i) ARXPS+ToF-SIMS support a surface-enriched shell and (ii) heterogeneity is demonstrated by correlative mapping (STEM-EDS/EELS on ≥300 nm crystals) or by a statistically significant anisotropy/edge-enrichment signature relative to uniform-exchange controls.
6.2 Orientation→selectivity causality is accepted only if: (i) EPR-derived order parameters predict selectivity trends after η-correction, and (ii) non-thiol controls separate Zn“S-specific effects from polarity/charge effects.
6.3 Determinism language is constrained: results will be presented as probabilistic enrichment of productive orientations (population shifts), not absolute single-orientation locking.
Feasibility: 1) Addressing the central technical risk (facet-selective PSLE): The revised plan treats “facet selectivity” as a testable variable rather than an assumption. By combining ARXPS (depth sensitivity), ToF-SIMS depth profiling (nm-scale localization), and correlative TEM/STEM mapping on indexable large crystals, the proposal can *prove surface localization* and directly evaluate whether enrichment tracks facets vs edges/defects. The explicit defect-correlation regression and facet/edge blocking experiments operationalize the reviewer’s concern that exchange may be defect-driven in 30“150 nm particles.

2) Preventing misattribution of selectivity (surface vs intracrystalline enzyme): The protease-accessibility assay plus impermeant-quenching provides an orthogonal, quantitative partition of enzyme location that does not rely on indirect sorption metrics. This prevents conflating improved selectivity with a mere shift from encapsulated to surface-bound populations as size varies.

3) Transport“intrinsic catalysis separation: A predefined effectiveness-factor/Thiele-modulus framework, parameterized by independently measured uptake-derived D_eff and by experimentally determined location fractions, enables selectivity to be compared on an intrinsic basis across particle sizes and immobilization routes. This directly counters the risk that diffusion/partitioning dominates the apparent selectivity.

4) Isolating Zn“S coordination confounds: Matched-% exchange using non-thiol polar imidazolates (and an additional minimal-coordination control) ensures that any unique effects of thiols (Zn“S coordination, altered micro-pH, node perturbation) can be separated from generic changes in hydrophilicity/charge. Thiol capping (iodoacetamide) adds a within-sample chemical “off switch” for thiol-specific interactions.

5) Empirical rationale grounded in prior observations: Prior MOF work indicates that crystal size can improve selectivity even when surface area decreases, consistent with size-mediated changes in external-surface contribution and transport length scales. Separately, SDSL-EPR has already resolved lysozyme orientation in hL/ZIF-8 composites, establishing feasibility of orientation quantification. The revised proposal integrates these two assets but adds the missing rigor demanded by reviewers: spatially resolved surface chemistry verification, quantitative enzyme-location partitioning, and a kinetic model that explicitly corrects for transport.

6) Realistic claims and statistical power: The revised hypothesis replaces “deterministically lock facets” with measurable, statistically testable enrichment of orientations driven by measured patch heterogeneity and surface-accessible fractions. The factorial design and uniform-exchange controls ensure the mechanism can be supported (or falsified) without over-interpreting coupled parameters.

Hypothesis: A single Zr6-based, mixed-linker MOF platform can be engineered to deliver three *mechanistically distinct* and therefore defensible selectivity modes—(1) equilibrium multigas selectivity predicted by IAST in rigid, accessible pores; (2) aqueous heavy-metal capture governed by speciation-coupled inner-sphere complexation at thiol sites; and (3) stimuli-responsive dye/drug uptake“release governed by transport gating/kinetics—provided that each regime is modeled and validated with the appropriate framework and with explicit go/no-go metrics. Mechanistically, we hypothesize that: (i) CO2/N2/CH4 separation will be dominated by quadrupole“field interactions and confinement in a water-tolerant Zr6 MOF with controlled missing-linker defects that generate polar adsorption sites while maintaining pore rigidity; under these conditions, multicomponent adsorption will be quantitatively captured by IAST using uncertainty-propagated fits to single-component isotherms (DSL/Langmuir-Freundlich), including controlled humidity as a competitive adsorbate. (ii) In water, soft heavy-metal selectivity (Hg2+ ≫ Pb2+ > Cd2+ ≫ Ca2+/Mg2+) will arise from thiol/thiolate inner-sphere binding (Hg“S) on pendant “SH groups, with uptake limited by metal speciation (chloride/hydroxide complexes), thiol pKa/oxidation state (“SH/“S−/“S“S“), and Zr-node hydrolytic stability; therefore, predictive capability requires surface-complexation/speciation modeling rather than IAST. (iii) For dyes/drugs, azobenzene units will not be claimed to change equilibrium adsorption thermodynamics directly; instead, measurable differences will arise from light/pH-modulated *transport accessibility* (effective pore-limiting diameter and diffusion coefficient), so a gated-access kinetic model (non-equilibrium diffusion“reaction) will be used to link switching extent to uptake/release rates and deliverable dose. This refined structure overcomes the reviewer’s concern about conceptual overreach by restricting IAST to its validated domain (multigas physisorption in rigid pores) while using mechanistically appropriate, experimentally constrained models for aqueous ion capture and gated molecular delivery, all mapped onto a single, tunable MOF architecture (linker ratio, defect density, thiol oxidation state, azobenzene loading) with clear quantitative success criteria.
Plan: Step 1 — Platform selection, linker identities, and topology/pore targets (design freeze before synthesis).
1.1 Base framework choice: Use a UiO-type Zr6O4(OH)4 node platform to maximize hydrolytic stability (Zr“carboxylate bonds), targeting an fcu topology for synthetic robustness and scalable defect control.
1.2 Mixed-linker set (explicit candidates; final selection by solubility/compatibility screening):
  • L1 (thiol linker): 2,5-dimercaptoterephthalic acid (DMTPA) *or* 2-mercapto-terephthalic acid (MTPA) as a pendant thiol/carboxylate heterofunctional dicarboxylate for soft-metal binding.
  • L2 (inert pore-shaping linker): terephthalic acid (BDC) as a diluent to tune thiol-site density and preserve crystallinity.
  • L3 (azobenzene linker): azobenzene-4,4′-dicarboxylic acid (AzoBDC) to introduce photoswitchable moieties within the pore wall (not assumed to create large, flexible “mesocages”; instead targeted to modulate pore-limiting diameter/transport).
1.3 Structural descriptor targets:
  • Pore limiting diameter (PLD) target: 5“9 Å for strong CO2 confinement while allowing N2/CH4 access; PLD to be extracted from Ar(87 K) or N2(77 K) sorption + pore size analysis.
  • Defect (missing-linker) density target: 0“10% of linker sites to introduce polar sites while maintaining water stability; quantified by TGA/solution NMR of digested samples and complemented by positron annihilation or adsorption-based defect proxies.

Step 2 — Synthesis with engineering resolution (linker ratio, modulator, thiol protection/oxidation control).
2.1 Solvothermal synthesis matrix (DoE): Prepare a compositional library UiO-66-(BDC)x(MTPA/DMTPA)y(AzoBDC)z with x+y+z=1.
  • Initial molar grids: (y=0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20), (z=0, 0.05, 0.10), balance BDC.
  • Modulator control (defects): acetic acid or formic acid (0“100 equiv vs. Zr) to tune missing-linker defects; water content in DMF controlled (0“5 vol%).
2.2 Thiol integrity plan:
  • Handle thiol linkers under inert atmosphere when feasible; include antioxidant (e.g., trace BHT) during linker storage.
  • Quantify thiol vs disulfide: Raman (S“S band), XPS S 2p (thiol/disulfide/thiolate), and Ellman’s assay after digestion to determine accessible “SH.
  • If thiol oxidation is unavoidable during synthesis, implement post-synthetic reduction (mild, framework-compatible reductant) and re-quantify “SH; set acceptance criterion (≥70% thiol in “SH/“S− form).
2.3 Node protection/water stability:
  • Avoid high defect levels in thiol-rich compositions; set preliminary ceiling defect density at which PXRD crystallinity and water stability remain acceptable (defined in Step 4).
  • Post-synthetic solvent exchange (MeOH) + activation under controlled temperature to avoid thiol oxidation and collapse.

Step 3 — Structural and chemical descriptor mapping (inputs → descriptors → performance).
3.1 Quantify descriptors for each library member:
  • Linker incorporation: digested 1H NMR/LC-MS for BDC:MTPA/AzoBDC ratios.
  • Defect density/open site proxies: TGA, acid uptake titration, CO adsorption IR (for Lewis acidity), and water sorption hysteresis.
  • Porosity: N2 (77 K) and CO2 (273 K) isotherms; PLD and surface area.
  • Switching extent: in situ UV“Vis diffuse reflectance or solid-state NMR to quantify trans/cis fraction under irradiation; define “switching amplitude” as Δ(trans→cis) under application-relevant irradiation in hydrated and dry states.

Step 4 — Regime A (valid IAST domain): CO2/N2/CH4 multigas separation under dry and controlled humidity.
4.1 Single-component isotherms: CO2, N2, CH4 at 273/298/313 K up to 1 bar (and optionally to 10 bar if equipment permits). Fit isotherms using dual-site Langmuir (DSL) and Langmuir“Freundlich; select model by AIC/BIC and residual analysis.
4.2 Uncertainty propagation: Use bootstrap resampling of isotherm fits to generate confidence intervals on IAST-predicted selectivities and working capacities.
4.3 Humidity as competitive adsorbate:
  • Measure H2O vapor isotherms (298 K) and repeat CO2 isotherms at fixed relative humidity (e.g., 20% and 50% RH) using a humidified gas stream or pre-equilibration.
  • Treat H2O explicitly as a competing component where equilibrium is reached; report CO2/N2 selectivity retention under RH.
4.4 Mixture validation beyond IAST:
  • Breakthrough experiments for CO2/N2 (15/85) and CO2/CH4 (e.g., 10/90) at 298 K; include dry and 20% RH conditions.
  • Go/no-go metrics (Regime A):
    “ IAST CO2/N2 selectivity ≥ 30 at 298 K, 1 bar for 15/85 feed (benchmarking Asset 1 logic), with ≥70% selectivity retained at 20% RH.
    “ Dynamic CO2 working capacity ≥ 1.5 mmol g−1 between adsorption (0.15 bar CO2) and desorption (0.01 bar) at 298 K.
    “ ≥50 cycles with <10% loss in breakthrough capacity.

Step 5 — Regime B (aqueous heavy metals): speciation-coupled surface complexation + stability/leaching tests.
5.1 Water stability and leaching gate before adsorption claims:
  • Immerse MOF in DI water and synthetic wastewater (pH 5“8, 10 mM ionic strength) for 1, 7, 30 days; monitor PXRD, BET retention, Zr leaching (ICP-MS), and linker loss (TOC/LC-MS).
  • Go/no-go stability: Zr leaching < 1% of total Zr over 7 days; PXRD crystallinity retained; thiol content loss < 20%.
5.2 Speciation-aware adsorption design:
  • Target ions: Hg2+, Pb2+, Cd2+ as soft/borderline; competitors Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+; anions Cl−/SO42−/HCO3−.
  • Conduct batch isotherms and kinetics at controlled pH (5.5, 7.0, 8.0) and ionic strengths (1“100 mM NaCl). Include NOM proxy (humic acid) to assess fouling.
  • Model metal speciation in solution (e.g., hydroxo/chloro complexes) and fit uptake to a surface complexation model where binding sites are quantified from thiol assays (site density) and pH-dependent thiol deprotonation is included.
5.3 Mechanistic validation:
  • XPS S 2p shifts (S“Hg), Hg LIII-edge EXAFS where available to confirm inner-sphere Hg“S coordination; compare to Pb/Cd to quantify selectivity origin.
  • Regeneration: thiol-compatible elution (e.g., thiourea or mild chelator) vs pH swing; track thiol oxidation after cycles.
  • Go/no-go metrics (Regime B):
    “ Distribution coefficient Kd(Hg) ≥ 10^5 mL g−1 at pH 7, 10 mM NaCl, with Ca/Mg present (1“5 mM).
    “ Selectivity factor Hg/Ca ≥ 10^3 under the above conditions.
    “ Capacity ≥ 200 mg Hg g−1 (or justified by site density) with ≥80% capacity retained after 5 adsorption/desorption cycles.

Step 6 — Regime C (dye/drug): transport gating and non-equilibrium uptake/release (not IAST).
6.1 Guest selection and conditions:
  • Dye: methylene blue (cationic) and methyl orange (anionic) to decouple electrostatics from size.
  • Drug: doxorubicin as a canonical cationic, π-stacking-capable payload.
  • Media: buffered aqueous solutions (pH 5.5 and 7.4) with physiologically relevant ionic strength.
6.2 Demonstrate that azobenzene switching changes *transport*:
  • Quantify uptake/release kinetics under dark vs irradiation (365“450 nm as appropriate), and at pH values that modulate framework/guest charge.
  • Fit to a gated diffusion model (effective diffusivity D_eff and/or permeability P as a function of switching state) rather than equilibrium-only models.
  • Measure pore accessibility changes by time-resolved uptake (stopped-flow UV“Vis) and, where possible, pulsed-field gradient NMR (guest diffusion) or QCM on thin films.
6.3 Go/no-go metrics (Regime C):
  • Demonstrate ≥3× change in apparent uptake rate constant (k_app) or D_eff between switched states at constant concentration.
  • Demonstrate reversible modulation over ≥10 light on/off cycles with <15% drift in kinetic response.
  • Maintain framework crystallinity and <1% Zr leaching in the delivery buffer over 72 h.

Step 7 — Integration logic (single platform, separate validation frameworks).
7.1 Use the same material library to identify compositions that satisfy Regime A metrics first (IAST-valid gas separation), then filter by Regime B stability/leaching gates, then test Regime C gating.
7.2 Explicitly avoid “orthogonal selectivity” claims unless the same composition passes the quantitative metrics in all three regimes; otherwise report a Pareto front (gas vs water stability vs gating amplitude) and identify best-in-class compositions for each application.

Step 8 — Risk controls and contingencies.
8.1 If azobenzene switching amplitude is too small in rigid UiO pores: move AzoBDC to a lower fraction (≤5%) and use it as a surface/defect-adjacent gate (more free volume), or fabricate a thin-film/particle-shell architecture where switching modulates entrance rather than internal cavities.
8.2 If thiol causes instability or excessive defectivity: reduce y, use BDC dilution, or switch to thioether (less oxidation-prone) while accepting lower Hg affinity; alternatively, confine thiols to post-synthetically modified defect sites to decouple them from the primary lattice.
8.3 If humidity collapses CO2 selectivity: decrease defect density (fewer strong H2O sites) and/or add hydrophobic linker fraction (e.g., methylated BDC) while tracking CO2 capacity/selectivity trade-offs.
Feasibility: 1) IAST scope is narrowed to where it is defensible and testable: multicomponent physisorption of CO2/N2/CH4 in rigid pores at equilibrium. This directly leverages the precedent that open/polar sites in robust MOFs yield high CO2 selectivity and that IAST can predict mixture behavior from high-quality single-component isotherms (Asset 1). By adding explicit isotherm models (DSL/Langmuir-Freundlich), model selection criteria, and uncertainty propagation, the proposal converts IAST from a rhetorical “unifier” into a quantified, falsifiable design-and-validation loop.

2) Heavy-metal capture is treated with correct controlling chemistry: aqueous uptake depends on speciation, hydration, thiol pKa/oxidation, and node stability—factors not parameterized by IAST. The revised plan therefore uses speciation-coupled surface complexation modeling, competitive-ion matrices, and direct coordination probes (XPS/EXAFS), aligning with established mechanisms for MOF-based toxic ion removal where defects/functional groups control selectivity and kinetics (Asset 2). The inclusion of stringent hydrolytic stability and leaching gates prevents over-interpretation of adsorption data from partially degraded solids.

3) Dye/drug behavior is recast as gated transport (kinetics), not equilibrium selectivity: photoswitching and pH-triggered gating inherently introduce accessibility limits and time dependence that violate IAST assumptions. The plan explicitly measures switching extent and demonstrates functional gating by quantifying changes in uptake/release kinetics (≥3×), thereby meeting the reviewer requirement to show transport modulation “not just spectroscopy.” The use of composite/thin-film contingencies is consistent with established MOF-composite strategies for functional deployment and stability (Asset 3).

4) Engineering-resolution mapping connects synthesis knobs to structure to performance: linker ratios, modulator-controlled defects, thiol oxidation state, and azobenzene fraction are treated as independent variables; measurable descriptors (site density, defect density, PLD, switching amplitude, leaching) serve as intermediates; and each application has quantitative go/no-go metrics under defined operating conditions (RH, partial pressures, pH, ionic strength, competitors). This directly addresses the critique about missing topology/pore targets, unclear open-site generation without sacrificing water stability, and lack of success criteria.

5) The proposal remains coherent with the original concept chain (dual-function mixed-linker Zr6 MOF; thiol sites; azobenzene switching; competitive adsorption modeling) while preventing conceptual overreach by using the right physical chemistry model for each regime and by requiring experimental validation that matches each model’s assumptions.

Hypothesis: Constructing a topology-programmable, multichromophore MOF in which quantum dots are not used as external donors but are instead replaced by an isoreticular ‘antenna-linker dilution series’ (high-absorption donor linkers) covalently co-assembled with a sparse array of long-lived lanthanide acceptor nodes in a single-phase framework will increase overall photoluminescence quantum efficiency and enable lifetime-encoded chemical sensing. The methodological adaptation is to implement a MOF-level, distance-defined Förster/Dexter energy-transport network by (i) statistically diluting donor chromophores with electronically inert spacers to suppress excitonic self-quenching and triplet“triplet annihilation, and (ii) positioning Ln(III) acceptors at predetermined coordination sites (metalloligand nodes) so that donor“acceptor distances fall within an engineered FRET window. Mechanistically, dilution increases donor radiative yield (reduces k_nr by suppressing excimer formation and exciton“exciton annihilation), while the fixed periodicity of acceptor sites enforces efficient, directional donor→Ln transfer (k_ET competing favorably with k_nr) and yields a long-lived emission channel whose lifetime and transfer rise-time are perturbed by analyte binding through changes in local refractive index, competitive coordination, and vibrational quenching—providing a time-resolved sensing axis that is intrinsically decoupled from intensity fluctuations.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Framework selection (structurally novel vs rejected approach): Use a RETicular chemistry platform that natively supports mixed-linker co-assembly and robust porosity without core“shell stratification, e.g., an isoreticular Zr6 or Hf6 cluster MOF (UiO-68-type) with large pore apertures to accommodate analytes; avoid porphyrinic PCN-224/MOF-545 and avoid any QD attachment.
1.2 Donor chromophore library: Synthesize a donor linker series with matched geometry but tunable oscillator strength and excited-state energy, e.g., 4,4′-biphenyldicarboxylate (spacer, S), 4,4′-stilbenedicarboxylate (D1), and 4,4′-bis(phenylethynyl)-biphenyl-2,2′-dicarboxylate (D2) as high-absorption antenna linkers. Ensure identical connectivity to enable true isoreticular mixed-linker MOFs.
1.3 Lanthanide acceptor site design (metalloligand node adaptation): Prepare a ditopic carboxylate linker bearing an internal chelating pocket (e.g., DPA- or DO3A-derived pendant chelator) that can pre-bind Eu(III) or Tb(III) (forming a neutral metalloligand, LnL) while still presenting two carboxylates for framework formation. This creates periodic Ln acceptor sites as part of the linker population rather than postsynthetic exchange.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Mixed-linker ‘dilution series’ synthesis: Solvothermally synthesize a family of single-phase mixed-linker MOFs: Zr6(S)_{1−x−y}(D1/D2)_x(LnL)_y with x = 0.01“0.30 and y = 0.001“0.05. Keep total linker stoichiometry constant; vary x to tune absorption/light harvesting and vary y to tune donor“acceptor spacing and acceptor density.
2.2 Defect control as a mechanistic lever: Implement modulated synthesis (e.g., benzoic acid or formic acid modulators) to tune missing-linker defects; quantify defect density and correlate with nonradiative decay. The adaptation is to treat defect density as an explicit design variable to minimize trap-assisted quenching while preserving analyte diffusion.
2.3 Spectral overlap programming: Choose D1/D2 such that donor emission overlaps Ln absorption (antenna effect) and minimize back-transfer by ensuring Ln emission is substantially red-shifted. Optionally incorporate a second acceptor (e.g., Tb plus Eu) to create dual lifetime channels and internal calibration for ratiometric/time-gated readout.
2.4 Sensing interface engineering without pore blocking: Introduce a low fraction (≤2%) of open metal sites or weakly basic functional groups (e.g., “NH2 on a co-linker) to promote selective adsorption of analytes (amines, nitroaromatics, VOCs) while keeping chromophore dilution intact. No external coating is used; sensing occurs within pores.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural verification: PXRD (phase purity across x,y series), N2 sorption (surface area/porosity retention), SEM/TEM (morphology), ICP-MS (Ln content), solid-state NMR/DRIFTS (linker ratios), and thermogravimetric analysis (defect/modulator content).
3.2 Photophysics and energy-transfer dynamics (time-resolved emission study):
- Measure absolute PLQY (integrating sphere) for each x,y composition under matched absorbed-photon conditions.
- Perform TCSPC/laser flash photolysis to obtain donor lifetimes (τ_D) and Ln rise/decay kinetics; extract k_ET from donor lifetime shortening and Ln rise times (confirm true transfer via acceptor rise component, not static quenching).
- Differentiate mechanisms: (i) FRET-dominated transfer (distance-dependent, spectral overlap-driven) vs (ii) Dexter/triplet-mediated transfer (sensitive to orbital overlap and oxygen).
3.3 Mechanism tests for dilution benefit: Demonstrate suppression of self-quenching by showing (a) increased τ_D and PLQY as x decreases at constant absorbance, (b) reduced excimer signatures in emission spectra, and (c) diminished power-dependent annihilation in time-resolved traces.
3.4 Chemical sensing assays (lifetime-encoded):
- Target analytes: amines (vibrational quenchers/coordination), nitroaromatics (electron acceptors), and polar VOCs (dielectric perturbation).
- Record analyte-dependent changes in (i) τ_D, (ii) Ln lifetime (τ_Ln), and (iii) Ln rise-time (energy-transfer rate proxy). Fit to competitive adsorption/coordination models and modified Stern“Volmer relationships that separate static adsorption from dynamic quenching.
- Implement time-gated detection using Ln emission to suppress scattering and background fluorescence; quantify LOD, selectivity, and reversibility (adsorption/desorption cycling).
3.5 Controls: (i) MOF with only S (no donors, no LnL), (ii) donors without LnL (tests dilution/quenching only), (iii) LnL without donors (tests direct excitation), (iv) same x,y but higher defect density (tests trap-assisted quenching), and (v) oxygen vs deoxygenated conditions (triplet involvement).
3.6 Stability/robustness: Evaluate photostability under continuous irradiation, chemical stability under humid air, and retention of crystallinity/porosity post-sensing cycles.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 2 validates that time-resolved emission can quantify high (>80%) energy transfer efficiencies in MOF-based light-harvesting architectures and that engineered donor→acceptor coupling can substantially enhance photon harvesting. The proposed system uses the same measurable observables (donor lifetime shortening, acceptor rise times, PLQY) but replaces QD→MOF interfacial transfer with an intraframework, distance-defined donor→Ln network to eliminate interface-state quenching.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): MOFs uniquely enable (i) crystallographically constrained donor“acceptor distances, (ii) mixed-linker statistical control (synthetic tunability), and (iii) permanent porosity for analyte access. Embedding metalloligand Ln acceptors as part of the linker population is a coordination-chemistry-native strategy that keeps acceptor sites periodic and avoids postsynthetic gradients or surface-only architectures.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to QD-coated or stratified relay approaches, this single-phase mixed-linker/metalloligand MOF (a) removes the dominant interfacial quenching pathway, (b) uses dilution to raise intrinsic donor PLQY while maintaining high absorption cross-section, (c) yields long-lived Ln emission enabling time-gated sensing with improved robustness against scattering/intensity drift, and (d) preserves pore accessibility because no external nanocrystal layer or pore-blocking coating is required.

Hypothesis: Embedding L-proline as a chiral, monodentate/bidentate secondary coordinating modulator inside a tetraphenylethylene (TPE)-based single-walled metal-organic nanotube will enforce weak, yet directionally biased pi-stacking among TPE panels, producing a synergistic effect between (i) stabilized single-walled tube formation (defect-suppressed, uniform channels) and (ii) increased local concentration/activation of epoxide and CO2 at Ni open sites via proline’s H-bonding and Lewis base functionality. This dual stabilization + microenvironment tuning will raise intrinsic turnover frequency (TOF per accessible Ni site) while enabling hierarchical assembly (bundles/flowers) that improves mass transport without collapsing the single-walled tube topology. Methodological adaptation: replace conventional monotopic modulators (e.g., acetate/benzoate) with L-proline (and N-protected derivatives) as a stereochemically programmed modulator/guest that simultaneously (a) coordinates transiently to Ni during solvothermal growth to bias tube topology and (b) remains in the channel as a removable/partially retained co-catalytic lining to tune substrate diffusion and transition-state stabilization.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a Ni-based TPE-derived multitopic ligand system that is known to form single-walled nanotubes (benchmark against Ni“TCPE-type chemistry) and define two synthetic baselines: (A) no modulator and (B) standard monotopic modulator (acetate or benzoate) to reproduce tube vs non-tube outcomes.
1.2 Prepare a modulator library: L-proline, D-proline (stereochemical control), N-Boc-L-proline (reduced metal binding; preserves H-bond donor/acceptor pattern differently), and proline methyl ester (suppresses carboxylate coordination). These enable separating coordination effects from purely supramolecular effects.
1.3 Define a catalytic probe reaction identical to Asset 1 (CO2 cycloaddition to epoxides) with standardized epoxide set (epichlorohydrin + one bulky epoxide) to diagnose diffusion vs intrinsic-site effects.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Proline-programmed solvothermal assembly: conduct solvothermal syntheses where proline is introduced as (i) a coordination modulator (0“50 mol% vs metal), and (ii) a post-synthetic channel guest via solvent exchange to decouple growth effects from microenvironment effects.
2.2 Topology steering via weak pi-stacking control: tune solvent polarity (DMF/MeCN/EtOH ratios) and ionic strength to favor offset TPE pi-stacking. Hypothesis-driven control variable: proline enforces a specific offset/rotation between TPE panels through stereochemically biased H-bonding to linker substituents, yielding uniform tube circumference and suppressing inter-tube fusion.
2.3 Hierarchical structuring without pyrolysis: induce controlled nanotube bundling into flower-like superstructures (analogy to Asset 2’s hierarchical benefit but kept as coordination polymer) by slow antisolvent vapor diffusion (e.g., Et2O into DMF) in the presence of low equivalents of proline zwitterions as inter-tube “soft glue” (electrostatic + H-bond) while maintaining weak pi-stacking between adjacent tubes. Implement a two-stage protocol: (Stage I) grow discrete single-walled nanotubes; (Stage II) assemble hierarchically via antisolvent and proline-mediated bridging.
2.4 Active-site accessibility engineering: partially remove proline by thermal/vacuum activation to create a mixed lining state (fraction retained) and quantify retained proline via elemental analysis and ssNMR; target an optimum where proline enhances CO2/epoxide preorganization but does not block Ni sites.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structure confirmation: use single-crystal XRD when possible; otherwise combine PXRD/Rietveld refinement with PDF analysis to confirm single-walled tube metrics (outer/inner diameters) and to distinguish from alternative topologies (e.g., thicker-walled or interpenetrated structures). Use TEM/cryo-TEM for direct tube diameter and wall count; AFM for bundle thickness.
3.2 Mechanism of weak pi-stacking modulation: quantify TPE stacking geometry using solid-state UV“vis/fluorescence (aggregation-induced emission changes), variable-temperature PXRD (stacking sensitivity), and ssNMR (chemical shift anisotropy changes). Compare L- vs D-proline to prove stereochemically biased packing. Complement with periodic DFT/MD to compute stacking energies and proline-mediated H-bond networks.
3.3 Catalytic metrics with site normalization: measure TOF normalized to accessible Ni sites using CO chemisorption or in situ IR probe binding (and/or acid titration where appropriate). Perform kinetic isotope/competition tests (small vs bulky epoxide) to separate diffusion limitation from intrinsic activation.
3.4 Synergy quantification: establish a factorial design with variables (tube topology: yes/no), (proline present: yes/no; retained fraction), (hierarchical assembly: discrete/bundled). Synergistic effect is validated if TOF increase exceeds the additive contributions of (i) topology-only improvement and (ii) proline-only microenvironment effects. Use Thiele modulus/Weisz“Prater analysis to verify reduced internal diffusion resistance in hierarchical samples.
3.5 Stability and recyclability: perform 20-cycle tests (as in Asset 1) and leaching analysis (ICP-MS). Track single-walled integrity post-catalysis by PXRD/TEM and monitor single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) or quasi-SCSC behavior during activation/guest exchange by in situ PXRD.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 demonstrates that single-walled metal-organic nanotube channel architecture and site distribution can deliver very high TON/TOF for CO2“epoxide cycloaddition, implying that further control of channel microenvironment and defect density is a direct lever on TOF. L-proline is a well-characterized chiral, bifunctional molecule (carboxylate + secondary amine) capable of transient metal coordination, H-bonding, and zwitterionic electrostatics—features that can bias supramolecular packing and stabilize specific assemblies.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Coordination modulation is an established MOF method to control crystal growth and topology, but the adaptation here is using an amino acid modulator to simultaneously (a) program weak pi-stacking among aromatic panels (TPE) and (b) act as a removable/partially retained channel lining that provides cooperative activation (Lewis base/H-bond) near Ni Lewis acidic sites. This is a molecule-level, rationally designed intervention rather than a generic additive.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with standard monotopic modulators, proline introduces stereochemically defined, multipoint interactions that can reduce polydispersity and suppress tube-wall thickening/fusion, yielding more uniform single-walled nanotubes with higher accessible site density. Compared with simply making hierarchical structures (Asset 2), the proposal preserves the intact coordination polymer (no pyrolysis), enabling true site-defined catalysis while still leveraging hierarchical assembly to reduce transport limitations—thereby improving intrinsic TOF and apparent rates simultaneously, with mechanistic separability via L/D and protected-derivative controls.

Hypothesis: Embedding X60(TFSI)2 as a confined ion-pair dopant inside the mesochannels of metallated PCN-224 will generate a verifiable mixed electronic/ionic conductor only if (a) the X60/X60•+ redox couple is thermodynamically capable of oxidizing the porphyrin π-manifold in the MOF (rather than being quenched at the Fe/Co center or at the Zr6 node), and (b) TFSI− exhibits measurable anion mobility under a controlled, explicitly defined level of solvent/electrolyte uptake without dopant leaching or pore collapse. Mechanistically, we posit a two-network transport model: (1) Electronic network: partial outer-sphere electron transfer from PCN-224(M)-porphyrin to X60(TFSI)2 produces a population of porphyrin π-radical cations (Por•+) that can hop between proximate porphyrins (through-space/through-bond via the rigid TCPP arrangement), while X60 remains as a counter-cationic redox buffer that stabilizes Por•+ and suppresses back-electron transfer. The intended charge-compensation locus is the porphyrin π-system (Por → Por•+), not the axial metal center; Fe(III) and Co(III) are used only after pre-validating that their redox states do not serve as dominant electron sinks (go/no-go: Por•+ yield per dopant ≥ 0.2 by spin quantification). (2) Ionic network: confined TFSI− anions provide local electroneutrality and enable ionic polarization/charge screening, but only when a small, quantified amount of sorbed solvent/electrolyte raises the effective dielectric constant and reduces ion-pair binding energy. We therefore hypothesize an optimum ‘wet-but-not-swollen’ state (defined by gravimetric sorption and in situ lattice parameter tracking) where anion mobility increases (measurable ionic transference number) while mesoporosity retention and dopant immobilization remain high. Under these validated transport conditions, oxidation catalysis rates will increase because (i) higher steady-state Por•+ (or metal“oxo equivalent) density lowers the charge-transfer resistance and (ii) faster anion rearrangement reduces local charge buildup at catalytic sites, improving Faradaic efficiency. We will test this in one stability-validated catalytic window: electrocatalytic oxygen evolution (OER) in near-neutral buffered electrolyte where porphyrinic frameworks and Zr6 nodes are substantially more stable than in strongly alkaline media, allowing operando correlation of carrier density (EPR/UV“vis“NIR/XAS), transport (Hebb“Wagner/EIS), and activity without confounding demetallation/oxidative linker destruction.
Plan: Step 0 (Front-loaded pre-validation): Redox alignment + explicit spectroscopic predictions (mandatory).
0.1 Build a redox-level alignment table (all potentials reported vs Fc/Fc+ and converted to NHE where needed):
  - Measure oxidation potentials of (i) H2TCPP linker, (ii) PCN-224 (free-base), and (iii) PCN-224(M) (M = Fe, Co) as thin films on FTO/GC using non-aqueous electrolyte (e.g., 0.1 M TBAPF6 in MeCN) by CV/DPV. Extract E1/2(Por/Por•+) and (if present) metal-centered couples.
  - Measure X60/X60•+ (and/or X60•+/X60•2+ if accessible) under identical conditions (same solvent/electrolyte, same reference) to avoid systematic offsets.
  - Define a doping driving force ΔE = Eox(Por/Por•+) − Ered(X60/X60•+) and set a quantitative criterion for viable p-doping: ΔE ≥ +0.10“0.20 V.
0.2 Define charge-compensation locus and expected signatures (pre-registered predictions):
  - If porphyrin-centered doping occurs: UV“vis“NIR should show attenuated Soret band plus emergent NIR polaron/Por•+ absorption; EPR should show an organic radical signal (g ~ 2.002“2.004) with intensity scaling with dopant loading; for Fe/Co variants, deconvolute metal signals using frequency/temperature dependence.
  - If metal-centered trapping dominates: expect changes in XPS/XAS at Fe/Co edges and weaker/absent Por•+ NIR features; treat this as a failure mode.
0.3 Quantify radical yield per dopant (go/no-go metric):
  - Perform spin counting by quantitative EPR (calibrated standard) on a loading series (0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50 X60 per porphyrin). Require ≥0.2 spins per X60 at the optimum loading window to proceed to catalysis.

Step 1: Host framework construction with stability and redox control.
1.1 Synthesize PCN-224 with high crystallinity; activate via solvent exchange (DMF → acetone/MeOH) and vacuum activation. Confirm structure by PXRD and porosity by N2 sorption.
1.2 Post-synthetic metallation (two-track to manage redox traps):
  - Track A (primary): Co(II) insertion followed by controlled oxidation to Co(III) only after doping validation; Co offers cleaner porphyrin-centered spectroscopy relative to Fe in many cases.
  - Track B (secondary): Fe insertion for comparison; employ Mössbauer/XAS to monitor Fe valence/spin-state and identify electron-trapping.
1.3 Establish a degradation/demetallation diagnostic baseline (before doping): soak PCN-224(M) in the intended buffered electrolyte for 24“72 h; check PXRD, UV“vis diffuse reflectance, ICP of supernatant, and porosity.

Step 2: Architected X60(TFSI)2 confinement with explicit anti-leaching design criteria.
2.1 Infiltration solvent design (dielectric + swelling control):
  - Use a binary solvent system that dissolves X60(TFSI)2 yet minimizes framework swelling: chlorobenzene:acetonitrile (v/v tuned via preliminary swelling screening). Target minimal PXRD peak shift (<0.2% d-spacing change) during solvent exposure.
2.2 Doping protocol (incipient wetness with loading ceiling):
  - Load X60(TFSI)2 at 0.02“0.20 equivalents per porphyrin as the primary window; avoid >0.20 unless porosity and diffusion metrics remain acceptable.
  - Anneal 60“80 °C under mild vacuum to remove free solvent while retaining confined ion pairs.
2.3 Two spatial architectures (to separate transport vs blocking):
  - Uniform loading: slow diffusion infiltration (hours) followed by solvent removal.
  - Shell-enriched gradient: short infiltration (minutes) + rapid solvent stripping; intended to create an electronically conductive shell while preserving internal pore volume.
2.4 Confinement verification and quantitative failure checks:
  - N2 sorption: go/no-go BET/mesopore retention ≥70% of undoped PCN-224(M).
  - TGA + elemental analysis to quantify X60/TFSI content.
  - Solid-state NMR (19F) and XPS (F 1s/S 2p) to confirm TFSI presence.
  - TOF-SIMS depth profiling to validate spatial distribution and post-test migration.

Step 3 (Mandatory): Separate and quantify ionic vs electronic transport, tied to controlled uptake.
3.1 Define “operating uptake states” by sorption isotherms:
  - Measure gravimetric uptake of (i) water vapor and (ii) buffered electrolyte vapor/aerosol surrogate if feasible; define three states: dry (≤0.5 wt%), intermediate (1“5 wt%), and wet (5“15 wt%).
  - Monitor structural response with in situ PXRD during uptake to flag swelling thresholds.
3.2 Electronic conductivity (σe) under each uptake state:
  - Four-probe on pressed pellets and thin films (to avoid grain-boundary artifacts). Target: ≥10× increase vs undoped PCN-224(M) at intermediate uptake.
3.3 Ionic conductivity and transference (σion, tion) using blocking-electrode methods:
  - AC impedance with ion-blocking electrodes (e.g., Au) to extract σion; complement with DC polarization / Hebb“Wagner (ion-blocking/electron-blocking configurations) to obtain tion and te.
  - Correlate σion with uptake and with dopant loading; confirm that σion rises at intermediate uptake without concurrent dopant loss (ICP of soak solutions; F/S quantification in electrolyte).
3.4 Leaching/migration stress test (explicit failure mode control):
  - Soak doped samples in the buffered electrolyte at open circuit and under bias; quantify leached X60/TFSI and metal by LC/UV (X60), ion chromatography (TFSI−), and ICP-MS (Fe/Co/Zr). Go/no-go: ≤5% dopant loss and ≤1% metal loss over 24 h.

Step 4: Single, stability-validated catalytic test-bed + operando correlation (mandatory).
4.1 Primary reaction: OER in near-neutral buffer (e.g., borate or phosphate, pH ~7“9) using immobilized MOF films on conductive substrates.
  - Rationale: avoids harsh alkaline conditions that accelerate porphyrin oxidation/demetallation; enables clearer linkage between carrier density and catalytic current.
4.2 Film architecture and mass-transport control:
  - Prepare reproducible MOF films (doctor blade/electrophoretic deposition) with identical mass loading; confirm electrochemically active surface area proxies and film thickness.
4.3 Operando/near-operando mechanistic readouts synchronized to rate:
  - Operando UV“vis“NIR (reflectance mode) during potential steps to track Por•+ population vs applied bias.
  - Operando EPR (if feasible) or quasi-operando freeze-quench EPR to quantify radical density under turnover.
  - XAS (Co/Fe K-edge) pre/post and at selected potentials to confirm whether the metal center changes valence (and whether this correlates with activity).
  - EIS under catalytic potentials to extract charge-transfer resistance (Rct); require that Rct decreases in proportion to σe and Por•+ density.
4.4 Performance metrics and attribution logic:
  - Compare: undoped PCN-224(M), doped PCN-224(M) uniform, doped gradient, physical mixture with free X60(TFSI)2, and polypyrrole-in-PCN-224 benchmark.
  - Report: onset potential (defined current), Tafel slope, Faradaic efficiency (O2 quantification), stability (chronoamperometry), and turnover frequency normalized per metalloporphyrin.
  - Attribution criterion: activity enhancement must track (i) increased σe and/or Por•+ density and (ii) decreased Rct, while leaching remains below thresholds; otherwise classify as surface/hydrophobicity effect and pivot.

Go/No-Go Criteria (explicit):
G1 Porosity retention after doping: ≥70% BET and preserved mesopore signature.
G2 Electronic conductivity gain: ≥1 order of magnitude at intermediate uptake state.
G3 Mixed conduction proof: tion between 0.05“0.5 under intermediate uptake (non-zero ionic contribution) with stable σe.
G4 Chemical stability: ≤5% X60/TFSI loss and ≤1% Fe/Co loss after 24 h soak + ≤5% loss after electrolysis.
G5 Mechanistic correlation: operando spectroscopy shows Por•+ (or defined carrier) density correlates with current and Rct across loading series.

Contingency pivots (pre-defined):
- If ΔE is insufficient for porphyrin oxidation or Por•+ yield is low: switch to a more oxidizing confined dopant (same confinement strategy) or reduce metallation redox traps by using free-base PCN-224 for transport validation first.
- If σion is negligible without excessive uptake/swelling: operate under controlled humidity/solvent co-adsorption to reach intermediate uptake, or redesign to introduce localized polar sites (minimal linker functionalization) while maintaining hydrophobicity.
- If Fe/Co act as dominant traps: prioritize metal-free or Co-only systems and re-introduce metal catalysis only after transport is validated.
Feasibility: This revision directly addresses the reviewers’ two main uncertainties by making the mixed-conduction mechanism conditional on quantifiable thermodynamics and transport metrics prior to catalysis.

1) Electronic transport feasibility (thermodynamic and locus-validated): The plan explicitly measures, on the same reference scale and in the same medium, (i) Por/Por•+ oxidation potentials in the MOF film and (ii) the X60 redox couple, producing a redox alignment table that determines whether p-doping is thermodynamically allowed (ΔE threshold). The charge-compensation locus is explicitly defined as porphyrin-centered; competing metal-centered redox trapping is treated as a measurable failure mode using EPR spin counting, UV“vis“NIR polaron bands, and Fe/Co XAS/XPS. The required dopant-to-radical yield (≥0.2) and ≥10× σe improvement provide pre-catalysis evidence of a percolative electronic network rather than localized, quenched charge.

2) Ionic transport feasibility (anion mobility under controlled uptake, not hand-waving): Rather than assuming TFSI− mobility in a low-dielectric mesochannel, the proposal defines discrete uptake states via sorption and tests ionic transference directly with blocking-electrode EIS and Hebb“Wagner polarization. This design explicitly anticipates that some solvent/electrolyte uptake is necessary to reduce ion-pair binding, while simultaneously guarding against swelling and leaching with in situ PXRD thresholds and strict dopant/metal loss limits. The result is a falsifiable claim: measurable tion in an intermediate uptake window without structural compromise.

3) Sharpened catalytic test-bed and stability window: The proposal narrows to a single primary reaction—OER in near-neutral buffered electrolyte—to reduce confounding degradation pathways associated with strongly alkaline OER. A dedicated diagnostic plan (ICP leaching, PXRD/porosity retention, metal-edge XAS) is integrated to distinguish true mixed-conduction-driven rate enhancement from dopant migration, surface deposition, or hydrophobicity-only effects.

4) Mechanism-to-performance causality: By synchronizing operando (or quasi-operando) carrier-density readouts (EPR/UV“vis“NIR) with EIS-derived Rct and catalytic current across a dopant loading series and architecture variants (uniform vs gradient), the proposal can attribute improved activity to increased charge-carrier density and reduced charge-transfer resistance, or else reject the mechanism. This is reinforced by direct comparisons to physical mixtures and polymer-filled PCN-224, aligning with literature that polymer infiltration boosts conductivity but risks pore blocking—here tested against explicit porosity and diffusion preservation criteria.

Hypothesis: Humidity-induced water pore filling in flexible/open-metal-site MOFs can be converted from a performance liability into a controllable “hydric gate” for gas separation and storage if the framework is methodologically adapted to include (i) spatially diluted water-nucleation sites and (ii) hydrophobic constrictions that delay percolating H-bond networks. Specifically, we hypothesize that engineering a mixed-node NU-1500-type topology with partial capping of Cr3+ open sites (to suppress early chain formation) plus perfluoro-aryl ‘pore-lining’ at the channel“pore junction will shift the water adsorption step to higher RH, prevent continuous water wires that cause pore filling, and preserve dry-gas uptake/selectivity under humid feeds. Mechanistically, dilution/capping reduces the density of strong primary adsorption enthalpy sites that seed 1D water chains; hydrophobic constrictions raise the free-energy barrier for hydrogen-bond network propagation into larger pores, thereby preventing capillary-like filling. In situ diffuse-reflectance IR (DRIFTS) with isotopic H2O/D2O will directly resolve the transition from metal-bound OH to chain-like water to liquid-like pore filling, enabling a quantitative structure“hydration“separation relationship.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select NU-1500-Cr as the mechanistic baseline (known RH-dependent sequence: metal-site saturation → chain growth → hexagonal pore filling) and define target gas pairs relevant to humid separations/storage (CO2/N2, CO2/CH4; optional H2/CO2) at 298“323 K.
1.2 Design two adapted variants (same topology, different water-network propensity):
  A) Site-diluted/capped NU-1500: post-synthetic partial capping of Cr3+ open sites with weakly coordinating, sterically small ligands (e.g., formate/acetate or neutral pyridine-N-oxide) to reduce water nucleation density without collapsing porosity.
  B) Junction-hydrophobized NU-1500: covalent linker modification introducing perfluoro-aryl substituents positioned at channel“pore junctions (synthetic linker swap or post-synthetic electrophilic aromatic substitution where compatible) to create hydrophobic constrictions.
1.3 Prepare controls: pristine NU-1500-Cr; a fully capped analogue (upper bound for water suppression); and a hydrophilic analogue (e.g., hydroxylated linker) to validate directionality.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Synthesis/functionalization:
  - Grow NU-1500-Cr (or closely isoreticular analogue) under solvothermal conditions; activate via solvent exchange and supercritical CO2 or carefully programmed thermal vacuum activation.
  - Implement controlled partial capping: expose activated MOF to dilute solutions/vapors of capping agents under anhydrous conditions; tune extent by time/activity; quantify via ICP/OES (metal), 1H/19F NMR of digested samples, and IR marker bands.
  - Implement hydrophobic constrictions: incorporate fluorinated linker (isoreticular design to preserve pore size distribution) or perform post-synthetic modification to install “C6F5/“CF3 groups oriented into the pore.
2.2 Humidity-programmed sorption + spectroscopy coupling (methodological adaptation):
  - Build a humidity-stepped gas dosing manifold coupled to in situ DRIFTS and a microbalance (gravimetric vapor sorption). Execute RH ramps (0“90% RH) at fixed T with simultaneous IR acquisition.
  - Use H2O/D2O isotopic substitution to separate framework OH/OD, metal-bound water, and H-bonded network signatures; deconvolute ν(OH)/ν(OD) envelopes to track chain formation vs liquid-like filling.
  - Add co-adsorption experiments: at each RH plateau, dose CO2 (and CH4/N2) while maintaining RH; record competitive uptake (dual-component gravimetry or volumetry) and IR bands (e.g., ν3(CO2), carbonate/bicarbonate signatures if formed).
2.3 Mechanistic modelling tightly coupled to experiments:
