(C) Cage + window: two cavities connected by a narrow aperture (mimics FAU/CHA cage coupling). Place adsorbate in one cage; show that long-range contributions from atoms around the neighboring cage must be included even if regions are ‘inaccessible’ to the methane center.
3.3 Outcome and implementation decision:
• The production TTRSD uses ρj(r) without pore masking.
• Accessibility is handled by (i) standard overlap rejection in GCMC and (ii) the real-space repulsion; no long-range exclusion mask is used.
• If any geometry suggests the need for an adsorbate-position“dependent operator (e.g., line-of-sight screening), implement it as a *separate*, explicitly justified correction and quantify its effect; default assumption: dispersion is not line-of-sight blocked in condensed matter and should not be masked by accessible volume.

Step 4 — Induction model with short-range damping and validation vs periodic DFT
4.1 Electric field evaluation:
E(R) computed from periodic electrostatics (Ewald/PPPM) using the same charge/multipole model as in the simulation.
4.2 Regularized induction:
Uind(R)=−1/2 αCH4 |Eeff(R)|2
where Eeff uses Thole-style damping between methane polarizability center and each charged site i:
Eeff(R)=∑i fi(R) Ei(R)
fi(R)=1−exp(−a (R/ρi)^3)
with ρi=(αCH4 αi)1/6 and a a dimensionless damping parameter (initial a=2.6; sensitivity range 2.0“3.5).
• For frameworks without explicit polarizable sites (αi), treat αi as an effective parameter tied to atom type (e.g., O2−, metal cation) from literature polarizabilities; report values and perform sensitivity analysis.

• For MOF-74 and MIL-101(Cr), augment point-charge description with site-centered quadrupoles or distributed multipoles (from DFT) if field anisotropy materially affects Uind.

• Rigid frameworks primary; optional framework flexibility for MOF-74/UiO-66 node breathing sensitivity.
• Moves: insert/delete/translate/rotate (if AA methane); Widom insertion for Henry and infinite-dilution Qst.
5.2 Cutoff sweep and methods compared:

(i) naive truncation (shifted LJ)
(ii) conventional homogeneous tail correction
(iii) TTRSD (dispersion only)
(iv) TTRSD + damped induction

For small benchmark cells (one zeolite, one MOF), compute adsorption energies and Widom KH using very large real-space cutoff (rmax 40“50 Å with image sums) as reference.

A) Methane model: TraPPE-UA vs AA-OPLS
B) Charges: literature vs DFT-derived (REPEAT/DDEC) for MOFs; alternative Al/Si charge models for zeolites
C) Mixing rules: Lorentz“Berthelot vs Kong
D) Defect model (UiO-66): defect-free vs two defect densities + cap chemistry variants
E) Induction: off vs on (Thole-damped)
F) Tail method: truncation vs homogeneous tail vs TTRSD

• MOF pair: UiO-66 pristine vs defective (quantified), or MOF-74 activated.

9.1 If TTRSD improves cutoff invariance in both neutral silicalite-1 and strongly Lewis-acidic MOF-74, but only adding damped induction repairs Qst(0) and low-pressure uptake for MOF-74, this supports mechanistic separability (dispersion vs induction).
9.2 If a masked-density variant (M(r)ρj(r)) systematically underestimates ΔUdisp near walls in the slit/cylinder tests and degrades agreement with brute-force references, it is rejected (documented negative control).

This avoids the reviewer-flagged conceptual error of multiplying framework density by a pore-accessibility mask. The masking strategy is addressed by (i) a formal statement of the correct integral and (ii) mandatory controlled numerical proofs in slit/cylinder/cage geometries showing that pore masking biases the tail, thereby justifying the unmasked density formulation.
2) Explicit Wrc(k) and numerical control: Rather than asserting a closed-form kernel, Ŵrc(k) is constructed by a controlled 1D quadrature of the spherical-Bessel transform for the specified damped+smooth-truncated kernel, with explicit treatment of the k=0 term and quantified grid/aliasing errors. 3) Energy continuity and GCMC correctness: The smooth truncation χtail and Tang“Toennies damping ensure no discontinuity at rc in the attractive part; the repulsive part remains shifted at rc. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a ZIF-8“derived, hierarchically porous carbon framework fabricated via spatially confined chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and dual-metal (Co/Cd) heteroatom doping will exhibit a significantly lowered onset potential and enhanced electrocatalytic performance for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). The core mechanism is that (i) Cd2+ incorporation into the ZIF-8 lattice acts as a sacrificial, weakly coordinating pore-expanding modulator during carbonization, generating an optimal pore architecture, while (ii) Co“Nx moieties formed in situ during CVD-driven carbon deposition serve as the dominant ORR active sites. The methodological adaptation lies in decoupling pore optimization and active-site generation by using Cd as a transient structural dopant and Co as a persistent electronic dopant, synchronized through a CVD-assisted carbon growth process that preserves framework-derived order.
Plan: Step 1: Rational precursor design and system setup.
Synthesize bimetallic ZIF-8 analogues Zn1−x−yCoxCdy(MeIm)2 (x = 0.05“0.15, y = 0.02“0.08) via controlled solvothermal assembly, exploiting the larger ionic radius and weaker M“N bond strength of Cd2+ to pre-program lattice strain and pore expandability while maintaining sodalite topology.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation “ spatially confined CVD with concurrent framework conversion.
Subject the bimetallic ZIF crystals to low-pressure CVD using acetonitrile or pyridine vapor as a combined carbon and nitrogen source at 700“850 °C. Unlike conventional pyrolysis, the continuous gas-phase supply enables gradual carbon deposition along internal ZIF channels, suppressing pore collapse. During this process, Cd species preferentially volatilize or aggregate into removable CdO/Cd nanoparticles, generating mesoporous defects, while Co is stabilized as atomically dispersed Co“Nx sites anchored in the carbon matrix.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and mechanistic analysis.
Characterize pore architecture (BET, NLDFT, SAXS), metal speciation (XAS, aberration-corrected STEM), and nitrogen configurations (XPS). Evaluate ORR electrocatalytic performance in alkaline media, focusing on onset potential, half-wave potential, and durability. Correlate onset potential shifts with Co“Nx density and micro/mesopore connectivity. Use selective acid leaching controls to confirm the sacrificial role of Cd and operando Raman/electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to probe charge-transfer kinetics.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Prior MOF-derived carbons demonstrate that Co“Nx sites govern ORR activity, while CVD has been shown to preserve ordered porosity and enable heteroatom incorporation. Cd“imidazolate bonds are weaker than Zn“ or Co“imidazolate bonds, rationalizing its role as a pore-modulating, sacrificial dopant.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): This approach leverages coordination chemistry principles (differential metal“ligand stability, lattice strain) and adapts CVD from simple coating to an internal pore-shaping and doping tool, fully aligned with MOF-to-functional-carbon transformation strategies.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with single-metal ZIF-8 or purely pyrolyzed systems, this dual-metal, CVD-assisted route enables independent tuning of optimal pore structure and electronic active sites, yielding lower onset potentials, improved mass transport, and superior electrocatalytic stability without relying on noble metals.

Hypothesis: A single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC“SC) post-synthetic cation/metal exchange performed selectively through the A-site channels of perovskite-like formate MOFs will enable installation of a dilute, site-isolated lanthanide center (e.g., Dy3+/Tb3+) into a mixed-metal MOF lattice while preserving the rhombohedral paraelectric phase; the resulting rigid, trigonal distortion field around the lanthanide (imposed by the rhombohedral framework and H-bond network) will enforce strong axial crystal-field anisotropy and suppress transverse terms, producing single-molecule magnet behavior with an open magnetic hysteresis loop at higher temperatures than in the non-exchanged parent. Mechanistically, the exchange-created Ln“O(formate) coordination polyhedron becomes symmetry-locked by the paraelectric order-disorder landscape of the A-site cation sublattice; this reduces low-frequency phonon coupling and quantum tunneling of magnetization (QTM), thereby increasing the effective barrier (Ueff) and coercivity.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Synthesize single crystals of the perovskite-like formate framework [(CH3)2NH2]M(HCOO)3 (M = Mg2+ or Zn2+ as diamagnetic host; and/or a controlled fraction of Mn2+ for exchange-coupled variants) targeting the known rhombohedral paraelectric phase at 160“185 K, ensuring large crystals suitable for SCXRD.
1.2 Establish baseline phase behavior: variable-temperature single-crystal XRD (VT-SCXRD) and dielectric spectroscopy to confirm the rhombohedral paraelectric window; DSC/specific heat to map order“disorder transitions; Raman/THz to quantify low-frequency lattice modes relevant to spin“phonon coupling.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation: "channel-gated, symmetry-preserving SC“SC post-synthetic exchange".
- Replace the conventional bulk metal exchange (often amorphizing or phase-mixing) with a diffusion-limited, stepwise exchange conducted inside the paraelectric rhombohedral window, where the A-site cation dynamics increase transient free volume for ion transport while maintaining long-range crystallinity.
- Execute sequential exchanges:
  (i) A-site cation exchange: partially substitute DMA+ with a bulkier, more H-bond-directing cation (e.g., guanidinium, Gua+) in controlled fractions to tune H-bond topology without triggering the monoclinic antiferroelectric phase; quantify exchange via 1H solid-state NMR and elemental analysis.
  (ii) B-site metal exchange (dilute Ln installation): expose crystals to anhydrous, weakly coordinating lanthanide salts (Dy(OTf)3, Tb(OTf)3) in polar aprotic solvents (MeCN/DMF mixtures) with added formic acid buffer to maintain formate coordination; use slow concentration gradients (microfluidic or vapor-diffusion) to avoid cracking and preserve SC“SC integrity.
- Create mixed-metal MOFs with controlled compositions: [(A-site mixture)](M1(1−x)Lnx)(HCOO)3 where M1 = Mg/Zn (diamagnetic) or Mn (magnetic), x = 0.5“5% for single-ion SMM regime and higher x for interaction studies.
2.2 Structural verification of the intended anisotropy field.
- Perform SCXRD before/after exchange to confirm retention of rhombohedral symmetry and to resolve Ln occupancy and local coordination metrics (Ln“O distances, trigonal distortions).
- Use XAS/EXAFS at the Ln edge to quantify local geometry and disorder; PDF analysis to detect any nanoscale phase segregation.
2.3 Magnetic and ferroic characterization tied to mechanism.
- AC susceptibility (frequency/field dependence) to extract relaxation times and Ueff; identify QTM suppression via field-dependent relaxation.
- Micro-SQUID or PPMS hysteresis loop measurements vs temperature/sweep rate to determine coercivity and blocking temperature; compare to (i) parent MOF, (ii) Ln-doped by direct solvothermal synthesis (control), and (iii) exchanged samples outside paraelectric window (negative control).
- Correlate magnetism with lattice dynamics: VT-Raman/THz and inelastic neutron scattering (if available) to connect altered phonon density to relaxation rates.
- Track dielectric anomalies after exchange to confirm persistence/tuning of the paraelectric-to-antiferroelectric transition; evaluate magnetodielectric coupling in mixed-metal (Mn/Ln) variants.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Causality tests for the proposed mechanism.
- Symmetry locking test: deliberately drive samples into the monoclinic phase (cooling or A-site composition shift) and re-measure relaxation/hysteresis; the hypothesis predicts increased QTM and reduced hysteresis openness when symmetry lowering introduces transverse crystal-field components and/or stronger spin“phonon coupling.
- Phonon-coupling test: isotopic substitution (D-formate or deuterated A-site cations) to shift vibrational modes; quantify predicted changes in relaxation pathways (Raman/Orbach contributions).
3.2 Quantitative modeling.
- Ab initio CASSCF/SINGLE_ANISO calculations on Ln local environments extracted from SCXRD/EXAFS to compute crystal-field parameters, g-tensors, and transverse anisotropy; compare computed QTM gaps with experimental field-sweep hysteresis.
- Spin“lattice relaxation modeling using measured phonon spectra to fit Orbach/Raman/direct processes.
3.3 Success criteria.
- Demonstrated SC“SC exchange with preserved rhombohedral paraelectric phase and controlled Ln incorporation (x) without phase separation.
- Observation of SMM signatures (AC peaks, slow relaxation) and a reproducible magnetic hysteresis loop with enhanced coercivity/blocking temperature relative to solvothermal-doped and non-paraelectric-exchanged controls.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Perovskite-like formate MOFs exhibit a rhombohedral paraelectric phase governed by A-site cation order“disorder and show dielectric anomalies across phase transitions (Asset 3). MOFs can act as rigid matrices that constrain coordination geometry; lanthanide centers exhibit SMM behavior when axial crystal fields are enforced and magnetization dynamics are constrained (Asset 4). Post-synthetic modification/exchange is a validated route to tune MOF composition and properties, with stability depending on robust coordination environments (Asset 1).
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Conventional post-synthetic metal exchange in MOFs often compromises crystallinity or yields heterogeneous distributions. The proposed adaptation explicitly uses the rhombohedral paraelectric window as a "transport-enabled yet symmetry-preserving" regime to gate diffusion while maintaining SC“SC integrity, enabling precise, crystallographically verifiable installation of dilute Ln sites in a mixed-metal framework.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to direct solvothermal Ln incorporation (which frequently gives uncontrolled coordination environments and higher defect densities), channel-gated SC“SC exchange targets site-isolated Ln centers with a symmetry-locked coordination field, reducing disorder-driven transverse anisotropy and phonon-mediated relaxation—both key factors that typically collapse hysteresis in Ln-SMMs. Mixed-metal variants (Mn/Ln) additionally allow engineered exchange fields without sacrificing the Ln single-ion regime, offering a tunable route to widen hysteresis loops while maintaining MOF porosity and ferroic phase control.

Hypothesis: Pre-organizing oligoguanosine strands into a defined G-quadruplex topology and using them as removable, bidentate “crystal-directing co-linkers” for Cu(II) paddlewheel MOFs will increase crystallinity and simultaneously raise elastic modulus and thermal stability by enforcing oriented attachment and higher node connectivity during growth. Methodological adaptation: replace conventional monotopic modulators with a topology-locked, ditopic oligoguanosine-based ligand (GQ-diPy) that presents two terminal pyridyl donors at a fixed separation only in the folded quadruplex state; after crystallization, the G-quadruplex co-linker is selectively extracted (ion/solvent triggered unfolding), leaving behind a healed, more crystalline Cu-carboxylate framework with reduced intergrowth/stacking faults. Mechanism: the G-quadruplex acts as a transient geometrical constraint that biases Cu2 paddlewheel-to-paddlewheel registration (suppresses rotational disorder) and promotes long-range periodicity; this reduces microstrain and defect density (higher crystallinity), increases effective crosslink density (higher elastic modulus), and delays thermally induced framework collapse (higher thermal stability).
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a Cu(II) paddlewheel MOF family whose crystallinity/mechanics are sensitive to growth defects and stacking faults: (i) 2D-layered HKUST-1-analogues with axial sites accessible during growth (Cu2(BTC) or mixed-linker BTC/isophthalate), and (ii) a pillared-layer Cu-carboxylate MOF (e.g., Cu2(benzenedicarboxylate)2(bpy) where axial ligation/pillaring controls registry).
1.2 Design and synthesize a topology-responsive, ditopic axial ligand: GQ-diPy. Construct a short oligoguanosine (e.g., dG8“dG12) bearing two terminal pyridyl groups via click-linked alkynylpyridine handles at both ends. The key design constraint is that only the folded quadruplex brings the two pyridyl donors into a defined, near-collinear separation compatible with bridging Cu paddlewheel axial sites; unfolded strands remain flexible and predominantly monodentate/chelating-incompetent.
1.3 Establish quadruplex folding/topology under MOF-relevant solvent/ionic conditions using CD spectroscopy and melting curves: K+ (strong folding), Na+ (intermediate), Li+/TBA+ (unfolded). Confirm persistence in DMF/EtOH/H2O mixtures used for Cu-MOF synthesis.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Growth protocol A (quadruplex-directed crystallization): Perform solvothermal or diffusion growth of the target Cu-MOF in the presence of pre-folded GQ-diPy (pre-incubated with K+). Use sub-stoichiometric GQ-diPy relative to Cu (e.g., 0.5“10 mol% vs Cu) to avoid permanent incorporation as a dominant linker. Rationale: act as transient axial bridge aligning paddlewheels/layers during nucleation and early growth.
2.2 Growth protocol B (topology control): Repeat with Na+ (partially folded) and with Li+/TBA+ (unfolded) keeping total ionic strength matched. This isolates the effect of quadruplex topology rather than salt effects.
2.3 Growth protocol C (small-molecule axial ligand control): Replace GQ-diPy with a conventional ditopic axial ligand (e.g., 4,4′-bipyridine) at the same mol% to test whether the advantage stems from the quadruplex-defined multiscale scaffold rather than generic pillaring.
2.4 Post-growth “extract-and-heal” step (core adaptation): Exchange crystals in a competitive axial-ligand solution that unfolds/disengages GQ-diPy without dissolving the MOF (e.g., LiClO4 in EtOH/H2O or low-K+ buffer + dilute pyridine). The aim is to remove transient GQ-diPy while preserving the now-registered framework; then re-activate by solvent exchange and evacuation. Track leaching by UV/Vis or fluorescence-tagged trace GQ-diPy.
2.5 Parameter map: vary (i) GQ-diPy loading, (ii) K+ activity, (iii) growth rate (temperature, modulator acid if used minimally), and (iv) diffusion vs solvothermal crystallization. Target the regime where GQ-diPy improves order but does not become a permanent structural component.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Crystallinity and defect/microstrain: PXRD (FWHM, Williamson“Hall microstrain), variable-temperature PXRD to monitor order retention, total scattering/PDF to quantify short-range order vs stacking disorder (especially for layered systems), and single-crystal XRD when possible to directly observe reduced disorder.
3.2 Confirm transient axial coordination and subsequent removal: (i) EPR/XAS at Cu to detect axial ligand field changes during growth vs after extraction, (ii) FTIR/Raman signatures of pyridyl coordination, (iii) elemental analysis/ICP and ssNMR (13C/15N if labeled) to quantify residual GQ-diPy.
3.3 Mechanical properties: AFM nanoindentation on individual crystals and/or nanoDMA on pressed pellets with controlled density to obtain elastic modulus distributions. Correlate modulus with microstrain/defect metrics from PXRD/PDF.
3.4 Thermal stability: TGA/DSC for decomposition onset; in situ VT-PXRD for collapse temperature; compare activated samples after identical solvent exchange histories. Hypothesis-predicted outcome: higher collapse temperature and slower loss of long-range order for quadruplex-directed samples.
3.5 Mechanistic falsification experiments:
(i) Topology dependence: K+ > Na+ > Li+/TBA+ trend in crystallinity, lower microstrain, higher modulus.
(ii) Sequence control: replace oligoguanosine with length-matched oligo(dA) bearing identical pyridyl terminations (no quadruplex). Predict loss of enhancement.
(iii) Geometry control: replace GQ-diPy with a flexible PEG-diPy of similar length. Predict weaker or no improvement if geometric preorganization is essential.
(iv) Timing control: add pre-folded GQ-diPy only after nucleation (late addition). Predict reduced benefit if the main role is nucleation/oriented attachment.
3.6 Application-relevant readouts (optional): methane/CO2 uptake hysteresis and cycling after thermal shock to test whether improved crystallinity/defect reduction translates into more reproducible adsorption and better cycling stability.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: (i) Cu(II) paddlewheel MOFs possess open axial sites during growth and are known to exhibit stacking faults and intergrowth that broaden PXRD peaks and reduce modulus; axial ligation/pillaring strongly influences layer registry and mechanical response. (ii) Oligoguanosine G-quadruplexes provide a well-defined, ion-stabilized topology with high thermal robustness and can be end-functionalized (e.g., via click chemistry) to present donor groups with constrained geometry. (iii) Crystallinity correlates with reduced microstrain/defects, which in turn increases elastic modulus and delays thermally driven amorphization/collapse in coordination networks.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal operates within coordination polymer self-assembly by exploiting Cu paddlewheel axial coordination as a kinetic/structural handle. The G-quadruplex topology is used not as a modulator analog but as a transient, geometry-encoded co-linker that enforces registry during nucleation/growth and is later removed to restore porosity—directly connecting quadruplex topology → self-assembly pathway control → crystallinity → elastic modulus/thermal stability.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional monotopic modulators, the approach provides a topology-defined, long-range geometric constraint rather than simple acid-base competition; compared with small ditopic ligands (bpy), the quadruplex offers a larger, information-rich scaffold that can suppress rotational/stacking disorder over multiple nodes and can be switched off by ion-triggered unfolding for removability. This yields a structurally novel, falsifiable route to simultaneously improve crystallinity and mechanics without permanently blocking pores.

- Functional handles: incorporate a controlled fraction (1“5%) of aldehyde- or carboxyl-terminated monomers (or post-synthetic modification) to tune wettability and reduce nonspecific serum adsorption.
1.2 Co-MOF-on-COF ultrathin shell with redox-hopping support:
- Grow Co-MOF shell by layer-by-layer (LBL) room-temperature growth to control thickness precisely: target 5, 10, 20 nm shells (not 50 nm by default). Stop when continuous coverage is achieved (AFM step height + SEM continuity).
- MOF chemistry: Co(II) nodes + rigid aromatic dicarboxylate ligand (e.g., 2,6-naphthalenedicarboxylate) to promote π-stacking/packing and improve electronic coupling; activate to expose Co OMS (solvent exchange + mild thermal/vacuum activation compatible with film).
- Built-in redox mediator option (explicit): co-introduce a small fraction (0.5“2 mol%) of redox-active linker (catechol/quinone-like or ferrocene-dicarboxylate analogue) during LBL cycles to enable defined redox-hopping across the ultrathin MOF shell; verify incorporation by XPS/ToF-SIMS.
1.3 Mixed-valence tuning with an explicit electrochemical model:
- Create controlled Co(II)/Co(III) ratio via potentiostatic conditioning in benign electrolyte (e.g., phosphate-buffered saline without halides that strongly complex Co) using fixed potentials and times; quantify Co valence by XPS/XANES.
- Replace the single Randles assumption with a porous-electrode / transmission line model (TLM) fit: extract film resistance (Rf), distributed charge-transfer (Rct,dist), and CPE dispersion (α) to explicitly test whether the observed ‘steepness’ arises from transport limitations vs interfacial blocking.
- Thickness dependence: measure EIS vs shell thickness (5/10/20 nm) to confirm that Rf scales with thickness while the nonlinear Rct jump correlates with crosslinking metrics (Step 3), not merely with thickness.

Step 2 — DNA anchoring redesigned to preserve accessibility and reduce fouling (addresses Critique #3).
2.1 Anti-fouling and controlled probe spacing:
- Introduce a short mixed monolayer strategy at the Co-MOF surface: co-immobilize initiator strands with a diluent (PEGylated or zwitterionic short oligo/thiol surrogate) to control probe density and reduce serum adsorption.
- Use a single primary anchoring mode to avoid overconstraint: prefer Co“imidazole coordination at OMS with a spacer (e.g., hexaethylene glycol or polyT) to lift the initiator away from the surface; keep π“π/COF interactions secondary (non-covalent) rather than a required attachment.
- Quantify surface density and accessibility by: (i) fluorescently labeled initiator calibration; (ii) SPR association kinetics; (iii) nuclease/strand-displacement accessibility assay.
2.2 Competitive coordination/fouling stress tests (built-in controls):
- Challenge with histidine/imidazole (1“10 mM) and EDTA (0.1“1 mM) under controlled conditions to determine how much of the signal depends on Co“DNA coordination vs mere adsorption.
- Serum fouling panel: 10% and 50% serum exposure, with and without BSA/casein blocking; track baseline drift in Rf and CPE to separate fouling capacitance effects from true Rct changes.

Step 3 — Y-CHA circuit engineered for coordination crosslinking and independently quantifiable threshold (addresses Critique #2).
3.1 Y-CHA design with crosslinkable arms (chemically explicit):
- H1/H2 sequences selected for miR-133a triggering with target recycling; design for minimal off-target to close miRNA family members using mismatch discrimination in toehold region.
- Y-product arms:
  (A) Imidazole-bearing domain: multiple imidazole-modified nucleotides (e.g., imidazole-dU) spaced to enable multidentate binding to Co OMS.
  (B) Phosphorothioate (PS) tract: 6“10 consecutive PS linkages positioned to chelate Co and bridge nearby nodes; use a defined PS count to enable XPS quantification of S.
  (C) Optional inert arm for sterics: polyT/PEG segment to increase excluded volume and enhance pore constriction without adding charge-binding ambiguity.
- Negative controls: identical Y-CHA lacking imidazole/PS features (no crosslinking), and a linear hybridization probe with equivalent net charge.
3.2 Operational definition of percolation threshold (quantitative criterion):
- Define the threshold as the surface state where the second derivative of log(Rct) vs X becomes positive and maximal (inflection to superlinear regime), where X is an independent coverage/crosslink metric (mass uptake or elemental ratio), not miRNA concentration.
- Independent observables for X:
  (i) QCM-D on Au: Δf/ΔD to obtain areal mass uptake and viscoelasticity during Y-CHA growth.
  (ii) SPR on Au: resonance shift to confirm binding kinetics and surface coverage trends.
  (iii) AFM: thickness increase (Δh) and roughness changes mapping the emergence of a connected layer.
  (iv) XPS elemental quantitation: P (DNA backbone) and S (PS tracts) normalized to Co to estimate crosslink density per area; track S/P ratio to verify PS incorporation independent of total DNA.
- Correlate the onset of nonlinearity in EIS with the above metrics to claim a true ‘connectivity transition’ rather than a smooth surface-coverage increase.

Step 4 — Mechanistic deconvolution package mandated by reviewers (explicit separation A/B/C).
4.1 Multi-mediator EIS to separate electrostatics from pore-gating:
- Perform EIS in:
  (i) Anionic outer-sphere: [Fe(CN)6]3−/4− (electrostatic repulsion expected to be strong).
  (ii) Cationic outer-sphere: [Ru(NH3)6]3+/2+ (electrostatic attraction expected).
- Compare ΔRct signatures: pore-gating should increase Rct in both mediators (direction-independent), while pure electrostatics should show opposite or strongly asymmetric behavior.
4.2 Mediator-free interfacial redox to isolate electron-transfer physics:
- Introduce a surface-tethered ferrocene (Fc) reporter (either Fc-initiator strand or Fc-diluent strand) such that the Fc is proximal to the electrode and reports local electron transfer independent of diffusion through pores.
- Measure Fc EIS/voltammetry before/after Y-CHA: if Fc kinetics remain stable while solution-mediator Rct jumps, the dominant mechanism is pore-access gating rather than a global loss of electronic conductivity.
4.3 Film resistance and distributed kinetics (avoid overfitting Randles):
- Use TLM/porous electrode model fits to extract Rf and distributed Rct; validate Rf independently via conductive AFM (nanoscale) and/or four-point probe on larger-area films where feasible.
- Thickness series (5/10/20 nm) under identical Y-CHA conditions to confirm that superlinearity appears at a similar coverage metric X, not simply at a particular thickness.

Step 5 — EIS readout protocol and analytical claims.
5.1 EIS acquisition and fitting:
- Frequency range and perturbation amplitude fixed; report fit quality metrics and parameter confidence intervals.
- Primary outputs: distributed Rct (or pore-associated charge-transfer resistance), Rf, and low-frequency phase angle; treat changes in CPE (α) as diagnostics for fouling/heterogeneity.
5.2 Performance evaluation:
- Determine LOD/LOQ in buffer and serum; dynamic range; mismatch selectivity against miR-21/miR-499 and single-base mismatches; regeneration using mild strand displacement and re-activation of Co OMS (validated by XPS).

Step 6 — LC“MS/MS orthogonal verification with explicit stoichiometry (addresses Critique #4).
6.1 Stoichiometric MS design (preferred):
- Place a single cleavable isotopic reporter on the surface initiator strand (not on Y-CHA products). Design the sensing so that target binding triggers one-time initiator processing (e.g., target-assisted cleavage/strand displacement releasing exactly one reporter per captured target) while Y-CHA amplification proceeds without generating additional reporters.
- After EIS, cleave/release the reporter quantitatively (photocleavage or chemical cleavage) and quantify by LC“MS/MS with an isotopically labeled internal standard.
- Validate stoichiometry in a calibration series by comparing MS reporter counts to independently quantified target inputs under conditions where amplification is active vs suppressed.
6.2 If stoichiometry cannot be guaranteed (fallback):
- Reframe LC“MS/MS as qualitative/confirmatory (presence/identity) and semi-quantitative (trend) rather than absolute ‘captured equivalents’; explicitly report amplification factor uncertainty.

Step 7 — Decision gates and risk mitigation.
7.1 If Rf dominates (high film resistance):
- Reduce MOF thickness, increase redox-linker fraction, or switch to a more conductive MOF chemistry while retaining Co OMS at the outer surface (core-shell concept preserved).
7.2 If electrostatics dominate (anionic vs cationic mediator diverge strongly):
- Increase ionic strength, introduce charge-neutral spacers, and rely on mediator-free Fc reporting plus pore-access metrics.
7.3 If serum fouling overwhelms signals:
- Add zwitterionic/PEG passivation, optimize probe spacing, and include pre-filtration or microfluidic washing; verify with QCM-D dissipation and XPS N/C ratios.

Deliverables (explicit evidence chain):
- Proof of transport pathway: Rf vs thickness (TLM + c-AFM/four-point) and stable Fc kinetics.
- Proof of pore-gating vs electrostatics: consistent Rct increase in both anionic and cationic mediators + Fc control.
- Proof of percolation-like transition: correlated nonlinear Rct onset with QCM-D/SPR/AFM/XPS-derived coverage/crosslink density threshold.
- Proof of MS linkage: validated reporter stoichiometry or explicit qualitative framing.
Feasibility: 1) Electron-transport feasibility (resolves ‘insulating COF + MOF shell’ concern): The revised architecture constrains the Co-MOF shell to ≤20 nm and optionally embeds a small fraction of redox-active linkers to support redox-hopping transport. Mixed-valence Co(II)/Co(III) is no longer asserted as a vague ‘steepness’ enhancer; it is quantified (XPS/XANES) and modeled with a porous-electrode/TLM framework that separates film resistance from interfacial charge transfer. This directly addresses mediator choice and CPE dispersion confounders.

2) Mechanistic proof of superlinearity (resolves percolation ambiguity): The percolation threshold is operationally defined using independent coverage/crosslink metrics (QCM-D/SPR mass uptake, AFM morphology, and XPS P/S-to-Co ratios). Nonlinearity is claimed only when the Rct inflection coincides with a threshold in these independent observables and persists across mediator charge sign.

3) Discrimination of pore-gating vs electrostatic repulsion (mandatory directive): EIS will be performed in both anionic [Fe(CN)6]3−/4− and cationic [Ru(NH3)6]3+/2+ mediators plus a mediator-free surface-tethered ferrocene reporter. This three-pronged approach isolates (A) electron-transfer changes, (B) pore/ionic access constraints, and (C) electrostatic effects, preventing misinterpretation of increased Rct as purely Donnan exclusion of anions.

4) Probe accessibility and fouling risk control (addresses Co-OMS coordination concerns): The anchoring strategy is simplified to a primary Co“imidazole coordination with a spacer and explicit probe-density dilution plus anti-fouling passivation. Competitive coordination (imidazole/histidine/EDTA) and serum exposure tests are built in as go/no-go gates to ensure that the platform is not dominated by nonspecific adsorption or unstable coordination chemistry.

5) LC“MS/MS orthogonal confirmation made quantitative (or explicitly not): The reporter is moved to the initiator strand so that one cleavable tag corresponds to one captured target event, independent of Y-CHA amplification. This makes MS a true calibrant for captured miR-133a equivalents; if stoichiometry cannot be validated, MS is explicitly downgraded to qualitative/semi-quantitative verification, preventing overclaiming.

Collectively, these revisions preserve the original concept chain (Co-MOF/COF heterointerface + Y-CHA + coordination crosslinking/pore gating + EIS + MS verification) while adding the quantitative mechanistic package needed to withstand alternative explanations.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a *high-density, cooperative* array of photoisomerizable azo units incorporated as *in-line struts* (not pendant substituents) within a water-stable cationic Ni(II) MOF will produce a quantifiable, reversible photomechanical response (pore-aperture gating) that modulates (i) anion diffusion barriers and (ii) ion-exchange binding energetics in water. Specifically, we will engineer an azo-bridged imidazolyl linker such that each unit cell contains ≥2“4 azo switches aligned with the principal channel axis, enabling collective cis“trans strain to overcome solvation-damped flexibility. A quantitative photomechanical model (DFT/MM → flexible-force-field MD → GCMC) will predict the light-state-dependent change in key geometric descriptors—linker end-to-end distance (ΔL), dihedral/hinge angles (Δθ), and minimum pore limiting diameter (ΔDlim)—and will translate these into an expected shift in anion self-diffusivity (Dself) and free energy of adsorption/ion exchange (ΔGbind) for one primary anion class.

To avoid size/charge ambiguity, the primary target will be arsenate (As(V)) in buffered water (pH 6.8“8.5), where speciation is well-defined (dominant HAsO4^2−/H2AsO4− depending on pH) and size is compatible with sub-nanometer gating. We posit that the *expanded (trans-dominant)* state increases ΔDlim and decreases diffusion activation barriers (ΔG‡diff), enabling faster approach to exchange sites, while the *contracted (cis-enriched)* state increases local cationic field strength (higher charge density per accessible volume) and strengthens inner-sphere/outer-sphere electrostatic stabilization, increasing selectivity against monovalent competitors (Cl−, NO3−). We further hypothesize that operando optical readout is best implemented as *localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR)* using (a) a MOF thin film grown on a nanostructured Au sensor substrate (preferred) or (b) embedded AuNPs with dark-field scattering, where resonance shifts can be quantitatively calibrated to refractive-index/mass loading and decoupled from dye-like absorbance/photothermal artifacts. The integrated platform will thus provide (1) light-gated ion exchange, (2) mechanistic linkage between photoisomerization → aperture/field change → transport/binding, and (3) real-time LSPR monitoring of uptake kinetics and switching stability under aqueous conditions.
Plan: Step 0 — Down-selection of the *switch architecture* (to ensure cooperative photomechanics):
0.1 Design two linker candidates derived from Tris(4-(1H-imidazol-1-yl)phenyl)amine (TIPA) logic but modified so the azo group is *structurally load-bearing*: (A) an azo-bridged bis(imidazolyl-phenyl) strut (Im“Ph“N=N“Ph“Im) that directly connects metal nodes; (B) a mixed-linker strategy combining TIPA (rigid, cation-stabilizing) with an azo-bridged imidazolyl strut (actuator). Target an actuator fraction of 33“67% of linkers to reach ≥2“4 azo units per unit cell (switch density criterion).
0.2 Pre-screen linkers by DFT (gas phase + implicit solvent) to quantify cis/trans geometries: end-to-end distance ΔL, dihedral preferences, and isomerization barrier (E‡iso). Accept only designs with predicted ΔL ≥ 3“5 Å or hinge-angle change Δθ ≥ 15“25° upon trans→cis, sufficient to plausibly alter Dlim by ≥1“2 Å in a flexible framework.

Step 1 — Framework selection and *water-stable cationic topology* development:
1.1 Metal node: prioritize Ni(II) (water stability precedent from cationic iMOF-like systems) with octahedral coordination; evaluate Co(II) as backup only if Ni topology is inaccessible.
1.2 Counteranion for exchange: synthesize the as-made framework with SO4^2− or NO3− as the initial pore anion. Choose SO4^2− for stronger retention during synthesis/crystallization, then convert to NO3− (more labile) by gentle soaking to enable reproducible arsenate exchange.
1.3 Channel target: design for 1D channels with Dlim(trans) ~ 6“9 Å and Dlim(cis) reduced by ~1“2 Å (or equivalent window contraction). This size regime is intentionally matched to arsenate/hydrogen-arsenate (small oxoanions) while still allowing measurable gating.
1.4 Crystallinity protocol: (i) optimize modulator (e.g., low equivalents of imidazole/acid modulator) and slow-diffusion conditions to obtain 50“200 µm single crystals for SCXRD attempts; (ii) separately prepare nanocrystalline batches for thin films and LSPR devices (to decouple device fabrication from SCXRD requirements).

Step 2 — Quantitative photomechanical model that directly links to diffusion and binding:
2.1 Build periodic structural models for trans-rich and cis-enriched states:
- Use DFT/MM or periodic DFT on linker fragments + force-field parameterization (including azo torsions and Ni“imidazole coordination).
- Generate two limiting structural ensembles: “expanded/trans” and “contracted/cis-enriched” with varying cis fractions (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%).
2.2 Flexible-framework MD in explicit water + background electrolyte (NaCl, Na2SO4) to quantify:
- Pore limiting diameter distribution Dlim(t)
- Accessible volume and ion-accessible free volume
- Mechanical modulus/soft modes and the extent of solvation damping.
2.3 GCMC or alchemical free-energy methods to compute:
- ΔGbind for H2AsO4− and HAsO4^2− at relevant pH states (see Step 3)
- Competitive binding/exchange selectivity vs Cl−, NO3−, SO4^2−
- Diffusion barriers (umbrella sampling or metadynamics) through windows for arsenate.
2.4 Define quantitative go/no-go metrics prior to full device integration:
- Predicted ΔDlim ≥ 1.0 Å between light states OR predicted ≥3× change in Dself(As(V)) OR ≥5 kJ mol−1 change in ΔGbind/ΔGexchange between states.

Step 3 — Single-anion-class focus: As(V) uptake with full aqueous speciation and competition matrices:
3.1 Primary target: arsenate in buffered aqueous media.
- pH windows: 6.8, 7.5, 8.5 (buffered; ionic strength controlled).
- Speciation handling: treat H2AsO4−/HAsO4^2− fractions using known pKa values; report uptake as total As.
3.2 Competition matrices (realism controls):
- Background electrolytes: 1“10 mM Cl− and 0.5“5 mM SO4^2−; include bicarbonate in one condition to mimic natural waters.
3.3 Isotherms and kinetics:
- Measure equilibrium capacity (mg g−1) and fit to Langmuir/Freundlich; target capacity benchmark ~85 mg g−1 as an upper reference (from cationic MOF literature) but explicitly interpret outcomes in terms of charge density and accessible exchange sites.
- Kinetics: pseudo-second-order and intraparticle diffusion modeling; extract effective diffusivity and compare light states.
3.4 Mechanistic proof of ion exchange vs adsorption:
- Quantify released counteranion (NO3− or SO4^2−) in solution (ion chromatography) concurrently with As uptake (ICP-MS), requiring near-stoichiometric exchange where applicable.
- XPS/EDX mapping for As localization; ATR-FTIR/Raman for arsenate vibrational signatures inside pores.

Step 4 — Photochemistry + in situ structural verification without single-point dependence on SCXRD:
4.1 Azo state quantification:
- Solid-state UV“vis and Raman/IR markers for cis/trans; photostationary state determination under specific wavelengths (e.g., 365 nm for cis enrichment; 450“520 nm for back-isomerization), with intensity and temperature logged.
4.2 In situ diffraction:
- Begin with dry-state switching (in capillary) using lab PXRD, then move to buffered water capillary PXRD.
- Use synchrotron PXRD for time-resolved tracking of peak shifts/broadening during irradiation and arsenate exchange.
4.3 Mechanical/shape-memory descriptors:
- Track reversible unit-cell parameter changes and peak-position hysteresis upon alternating irradiation (shape-memory criterion).
- Confirm retained porosity changes with in situ gas sorption where applicable (dry) and indirect aqueous porosimetry proxies (uptake kinetics + MD comparison).

Step 5 — LSPR operando transduction (explicit buildable geometry + calibration):
5.1 Primary LSPR architecture (preferred): MOF thin film on nanostructured Au sensor.
- Fabricate Au nanodisks/nanorods (e-beam or colloidal lithography) on glass; characterize baseline LSPR.
- Grow an oriented MOF thin film (SURMOF-like liquid-phase epitaxy or seeded solvothermal) to thickness 50“200 nm to remain within the evanescent near-field sensing depth.
5.2 Secondary architecture (backup): embedded AuNPs (5“10 nm) introduced *after* demonstrating switching in the pristine MOF.
- Use gentle infiltration with ligand-capped AuNPs (e.g., citrate/PEG) to minimize framework damage; cap loading to avoid percolation/scattering losses.
5.3 Optical measurement mode:
- Use dark-field scattering or transmission extinction spectroscopy for LSPR peak tracking (λmax shifts).
- Operando cell: flow cell with controlled pH/ionic strength; integrate LED irradiation for switching.
5.4 Calibration and artifact controls:
- Calibrate Δλ vs refractive index using standard solutions (e.g., glycerol-water) and correlate with QCM-D mass uptake on matched chips.
- Explicit controls to decouple absorbance/photothermal effects: (i) identical MOF film without Au nanostructures (UV“vis baseline); (ii) Au nanostructure without MOF (photothermal baseline); (iii) dark control (no irradiation).
- For any colored species, avoid spectral overlap by choosing LSPR λmax away from absorption bands; for As(V) this is intrinsically favorable (non-absorbing), enabling clean LSPR readout.

Step 6 — Stability, cycling, and realistic performance validation:
6.1 Water stability tests: PXRD retention, Ni leaching (ICP), and porosity proxy before/after 7“30 days soaking across pH 6.5“8.5.
6.2 Cycling: ≥20 light-switch cycles under buffered water with intermittent As(V) exchange/regeneration (e.g., NO3− wash), tracking:
- Capacity retention
- LSPR response amplitude retention
- Structural retention (PXRD)
6.3 Benchmarking: compare to non-photoactive parent cationic MOF (no azo strut) and to a low-switch-density analogue (pendant azo only) to directly test the reviewer-flagged “insufficient cooperative strain” risk.
Feasibility: Photomechanics rigor (addressing critique i): The design explicitly avoids a single pendant azo substituent and instead uses *load-bearing azo struts* and/or mixed-linker actuator fractions to reach a defined switch density (≥2“4 azo per unit cell). Quantitative modeling (DFT/MM → explicit-water MD → GCMC/free-energy) will predict ΔL/Δθ and an experimentally testable ΔDlim (target ≥1 Å) and will directly output diffusion and binding metrics (Dself, ΔGbind, ΔG‡diff). This converts the concept chain into falsifiable, quantitative go/no-go criteria.

SC“SC feasibility and realistic structure strategy (addressing critique ii): The plan does not rely solely on single-crystal tracking under harsh conditions. It uses (1) staged validation: dry-state switching → buffered-water switching → ion exchange → optional nanoparticle integration; (2) explicit crystal-size/defect management (separate single-crystal vs thin-film/nanocrystal batches); and (3) complementary in situ methods (synchrotron PXRD, IR/Raman azo-state tracking, QCM-D mass uptake) to demonstrate reversible structural response even if SCXRD becomes impractical after exchange or device fabrication.

Ion-exchange specificity (addressing critique iii): The proposal selects one primary anion class—As(V)—with explicit pH/speciation control and competitive-ion matrices (Cl−/SO4^2−/HCO3−). Uptake will be mechanistically distinguished as true exchange by simultaneously measuring counteranion release (ion chromatography) and As uptake (ICP-MS), supported by spectroscopic signatures and mapping. The ~85 mg g−1 benchmark is treated as a literature reference for comparable cationic MOFs, not as an unqualified claim for bulky dye anions.

Operando optical readout corrected to LSPR with buildable geometry (addressing critique iv): The proposal replaces ambiguous “SPR” with explicit LSPR architectures. A thin MOF film on nanostructured Au ensures strong near-field coupling within a defined sensing depth and enables robust, chip-based operando readout in a flow cell. Calibration converts Δλ to refractive index/mass loading (cross-validated by QCM-D), and the As(V) target eliminates dye-absorbance deconvolution problems. Photothermal and irradiation artifacts are handled via matched controls and spectral planning.

Overall coherence and advantage: The refined approach maintains the original concept chain—photoisomerization → framework-level shape-memory/gating → modulated ion exchange → operando plasmonic readout—while adding quantitative mechanical/thermodynamic predictions, a single chemically coherent anion target, and an experimentally realistic operando LSPR device pathway.

Hypothesis: Sub-angstrom control of MOF pore apertures can be achieved by a mechanically interlocked “molecular ratchet” linker strategy: co-assembling an adipic-acid-derived dicarboxylate (adipate) that provides compliant reach with an acetylene dicarboxylate (ADC) that provides linear, high-force-constant directionality, then converting only the adipate struts into conformationally frozen rotaxane-like components via in-pore, template-directed macrocyclization around the adipate chain (mechanically interlocked crosslinking). Mechanistically, the mechanical bond suppresses low-frequency linker libration and window ‘jitter’ without increasing node connectivity or relying on defect chemistry; ADC simultaneously defines a stiff, linear edge at the pore-limiting window. The combined effect narrows the instantaneous distribution of pore-limiting diameters into the sub-angstrom regime, yielding (i) higher and sharper hydrogen sorption enthalpy at low loading via stabilized adsorption pockets and reduced dynamic averaging, and (ii) higher membrane separation selectivity for size-proximate gases (e.g., C2H2/CO2, H2/CO2) by eliminating pressure-induced gate-opening and thermal breathing while preserving permeance through a non-collapsing, rigidified aperture.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Topology selection to enable interlocked chemistry: choose a MOF family with (a) accessible 1D channels ≥6“10 Å to host macrocyclization, (b) chemically robust nodes for post-synthetic organic reactions, and (c) carboxylate linkers so adipic acid and ADC are native. Primary target: a Zr(IV)-carboxylate framework with large 1D channels (e.g., a mesoporous Zr6-based topology rather than UiO-66) that tolerates mixed dicarboxylates; secondary target: an Al(III) or Ti(IV) carboxylate MOF known for film processability.
1.2 Mixed-linker design (new, non-defect-based): incorporate three organic components during solvothermal synthesis: (i) ADC as a rigid “window edge” linker, (ii) adipate bearing an internal, click-reactive handle (e.g., an azide- or alkyne-functionalized adipate analog placed at the 2/3-position to project into the channel), and (iii) a small fraction (≤5“10%) of a non-interfering diluent dicarboxylate to tune channel diameter to match the macrocycle size window.
1.3 Membrane-ready crystal engineering: prepare (a) oriented thin films by seeded, layer-by-layer growth on alumina supports (carboxylate-terminated surface to anchor Zr nodes), and (b) matched powders for sorption and calorimetry. Ensure identical synthesis history for powder vs film to avoid morphology-driven artifacts.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation—mechanically interlocked linker rigidification (MILR):
2.1.1 Template loading: diffuse a preorganized, linear ‘threading template’ guest into the channels that transiently binds carboxylate-rich walls (e.g., a diammonium or pyridinium dication) to position the adipate handle in a defined orientation near the channel centerline.
2.1.2 In-pore macrocyclization to form the mechanical bond: introduce two complementary macrocycle precursors that react only when co-localized around the adipate handle (examples: (a) CuAAC “clip” macrocyclization around an alkyne/azide handle on the adipate; or (b) imine-based dynamic covalent ring closure followed by reduction to lock). Reaction conditions are chosen to be node-inert (no carboxylate exchange): anhydrous solvent, mild base if needed, and temperatures below framework degradation. The macrocycle forms around the adipate segment, creating a rotaxane-like mechanically interlocked element anchored by the MOF lattice.
2.1.3 De-templating and activation: remove the threading template and unreacted precursors via solvent exchange, then activate under vacuum. The macrocycle remains mechanically trapped around the adipate ‘axle,’ restricting its conformational space and thereby rigidifying the pore window environment.
2.2 Sub-angstrom aperture metrology by crystallography-informed dynamics:
2.2.1 Single-crystal X-ray crystallography where possible on MILR-treated crystals to directly locate macrocycle occupancy, constrain linker conformations, and quantify anisotropic displacement parameters (ADPs) for window-defining atoms. If single crystals are not available, use synchrotron PXRD with Rietveld refinement + maximum entropy electron density to resolve the macrocycle distribution.
2.2.2 Variable-temperature X-ray diffraction (VT-SCXRD/VT-PXRD): quantify thermal expansion and breathing amplitudes; MILR samples should show reduced lattice parameter change and reduced ADP growth vs non-interlocked controls.
2.2.3 In situ gas-loading diffraction under H2 and C2H2/CO2 mixtures to test whether adsorption induces window opening in controls but not in MILR materials; refine guest positions to identify stabilized H2 binding pockets.
2.3 Hydrogen sorption: measure H2 isotherms at 77/87 K and (where instrument allows) 160“298 K; obtain Qst by virial fitting and corroborate with microcalorimetry at low coverage. Compare MILR vs non-interlocked mixed-linker analogs at matched pore volume.
2.4 Membrane separation: fabricate MILR thin films and evaluate single-gas permeance and mixed-gas selectivity for H2/CO2, H2/CH4, and especially C2H2/CO2. Conduct pressure-dependent tests to detect suppression of gating (selectivity stability with feed pressure).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Matched-pair causality: prepare three isoreticular materials with the same node/topology and similar ADC:adipate ratio: (A) no handle (cannot interlock), (B) handle but no macrocyclization reagents (process control), (C) MILR-interlocked. This isolates the mechanical bond effect from simple functionalization.
3.2 Quantify ‘sub-angstrom control’ as a distribution, not a single value: compute pore-limiting diameter distributions from crystallographic ensembles (ADPs/thermal ellipsoids) and complement with positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) or high-resolution gas adsorption kernel analyses to capture angstrom-level distribution narrowing.
3.3 Mechanistic linkage between rigidity and performance: correlate (i) reduction in VT-XRD breathing amplitude and ADP-derived window fluctuations with (ii) reduced adsorption-induced hysteresis, (iii) increased low-pressure H2 uptake/Qst, and (iv) enhanced mixed-gas selectivity without catastrophic permeance loss.
3.4 Stability and reversibility: cycle sorption and membrane tests over humidity and temperature to confirm the interlocked architecture resists hydrolysis and does not relax over time. Use solid-state NMR/IR to confirm macrocycle integrity post-cycling.
3.5 Benchmarking: compare MILR materials against literature rigid ZMOF-like systems for Qst and uptake, and against state-of-the-art MOF membranes for C2H2/CO2 selectivity, emphasizing selectivity stability under pressure swings as the key differentiator.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Rigid TBUs and directional ligands are known to increase structural stiffness and improve hydrogen sorption energetics by stabilizing adsorption pockets; crystallography has resolved guest-induced structural changes and correlates framework rigidity with sorption behavior. Mechanically interlocked molecules (rotaxanes) are established to suppress conformational freedom without requiring stronger covalent bonds; translating this to ‘mechanically locked linkers’ provides a physics-grounded path to narrowing dynamic aperture distributions.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The approach remains within coordination polymer/MOF design rules (carboxylate nodes; mixed dicarboxylate linkers from adipic acid and acetylene dicarboxylate) but introduces a structurally novel, pore-internal post-synthetic organic transformation that changes linker mechanics rather than node connectivity or defect density. X-ray crystallography and VT-XRD directly report the intended rigidity change via ADPs and breathing metrics, enabling mechanism-driven iteration.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike conventional mixed-linker tuning (often limited by dynamic disorder) or defect/chelation ‘locking’ (which can reduce porosity or introduce heterogeneity), MILR creates a mechanical constraint that selectively damps the motions responsible for sub-angstrom aperture fluctuations while preserving open channels. This should deliver simultaneously higher low-loading H2 Qst/uptake and more pressure-stable membrane selectivity for near-size gas pairs (notably C2H2/CO2), addressing the key limitation that flexible frameworks lose sieving precision under operating conditions.

Hypothesis: Installing isotopically addressable terminal OH groups (O“H/O“D) at catalytically relevant nodes in a cds-net-derived MOF (constructed from Zr6-oxo nodes and a CdS-net-topology organic linker set) will create a node-local proton/hydrogen-bond electric field that measurably red-shifts and intensity-modulates nearby linker C“H stretch modes via vibrational Stark coupling. A methodological adaptation is proposed: instead of conventional node functionalization (random “OH/“OR distributions), we will enforce a “site-isolated, topology-locked” terminal OH pattern by (i) defect-programmed synthesis to generate a fixed fraction of missing-linker vacancies and (ii) post-synthetic, stoichiometric hydroxylation/deuteration that targets only the open metal sites at these vacancies. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations will explicitly include anharmonic vibrational treatment and local-field analysis to predict C“H stretch shifts as a quantitative reporter of node microenvironment and connectivity in the cds net. Mechanistically, the terminal OH dipole and hydrogen-bonding network at the node perturbs the electron density of adjacent aromatic C“H bonds through through-space electrostatics and through-bond polarization (node“carboxylate“aryl), producing reproducible, topology-dependent IR fingerprints that can be used to map node states and validate cds-net connectivity.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a cds-net MOF platform (cds topology) using Zr6 nodes (UiO/NU-like inorganic building unit) and a linker set known to realize cds connectivity; design linkers with at least one spectroscopically isolated aryl C“H (e.g., mono-deuterated ring positions on a subset of linkers) to simplify assignment.
1.2 Synthesize crystals under modulated conditions (monocarboxylic acid modulators) to program a controlled missing-linker defect density that yields coordinatively unsaturated sites (CUS) on Zr6 nodes without framework collapse.
1.3 Post-synthetically convert CUS to terminal OH with rigorously stoichiometric water dosing; then perform parallel O“D labeling using D2O under identical conditions to generate paired samples differing only by terminal OH isotopologue.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Structural/topological verification: single-crystal or high-resolution powder XRD with topology refinement (node/net/vertex-symbol analysis) to confirm cds net and quantify defect fraction; corroborate with pair distribution function (PDF) if disorder is significant.
2.2 Node-state spectroscopy: collect variable-temperature IR spectra focusing on (i) O“H/O“D stretches and bends (node identity) and (ii) linker C“H stretch region. Use difference spectroscopy (OH vs OD; hydrated vs dehydrated) to isolate node-induced perturbations on C“H modes.
2.3 DFT calculation workflow (adapted):
  - Build periodic models of the cds-net MOF with explicit missing-linker defects and site-isolated terminal OH; generate matched OH and OD models.
  - Use periodic DFT (e.g., PBE-D3 or SCAN+rVV10) for geometry optimization; then compute vibrational spectra with (a) finite-displacement phonons for the framework and (b) localized-mode, anharmonic treatment (VSCF/VCI or 1D/2D potential scans) for O“H/O“D and the coupled C“H stretches.
  - Quantify local electric fields at specific C“H bonds and compute vibrational Stark tuning rates; correlate predicted Δν(C“H) with node OH orientation, H-bonding motif, and node connectivity.
2.4 Mechanistic perturbation tests: systematically vary (i) OH surface density (by controlled dehydroxylation/rehydroxylation), (ii) H-bond acceptor strength at the node (MeOH/EtOH dosing to form methoxy/ethoxy as in known Zr6-node chemistry), and (iii) topology-preserving linker substitutions that alter node“aryl through-bond polarization. Track how each perturbation changes C“H stretch shifts relative to DFT predictions.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Validate that observed C“H shifts originate from node terminal OH fields (not bulk adsorption) by: (i) OH/OD isotope pairing, (ii) reversible dehydration cycles, (iii) comparing defect-poor vs defect-rich samples, and (iv) spatially selective quenchers (e.g., weak bases that bind CUS).
3.2 Cross-validate node assignments by complementary probes: solid-state 1H/2H NMR (OH/OD populations), thermogravimetric analysis with MS (water/methanol uptake), and CO-IR as a CUS reporter if accessible.
3.3 Establish a quantitative “node-state readout”: a regression between measured Δν(C“H) and DFT-computed local field/H-bond metrics; demonstrate topology dependence by comparing the cds net to a closely related non-cds topology analogue built from the same Zr6 node chemistry.
3.4 Deliverables: (i) a validated spectral descriptor linking terminal OH configuration at a node to C“H stretch shifts, (ii) a DFT-calibrated map of node microenvironments in cds-net MOFs, and (iii) design rules for tuning node fields via controlled hydroxylation/methoxylation without changing net connectivity.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Prior MOF studies show terminal OH groups on Zr6 nodes can be interconverted with alkoxy species and fingerprinted by IR with DFT support; defect-engineered nodes exhibit distinct binding and electronic behavior that DFT can mechanistically rationalize. Vibrational Stark effects and hydrogen-bond-induced frequency shifts are well-established physical mechanisms that can translate node dipoles/H-bond motifs into measurable vibrational changes.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation directly leverages node chemistry (terminal OH at Zr6 nodes) and net/topology control (cds net) to solve a MOF-specific limitation: ambiguity in node state/distribution under realistic conditions. By enforcing site-isolated, topology-locked hydroxylation at programmed defects, the framework becomes a controllable platform where node microenvironments can be read out through linker C“H stretch reporters.
3. Comparative Advantage: Conventional IR assignments focus on O“H bands that are often broad, overlapping, and sensitive to physisorbed guests. Using coupled C“H stretch shifts as an indirect but sharper reporter—validated by OH/OD pairing and anharmonic DFT—adds specificity and quantification. Embedding this strategy in a cds net further provides a topology-defined constraint, enabling structure“property correlations that are harder to achieve in less topologically resolved or more disordered MOFs.

Hypothesis: Embedding a boron-Lewis-acid photogating layer within the sub-nanometer channels of a graphene-nanosheet-supported ZIF-90 (GNS“ZIF-90) will introduce a light-tunable, pH-amplified energy barrier for ionic species, thereby enabling (i) rectification-ratio switching via controllable space-charge asymmetry and (ii) enhanced photocatalysis via field-assisted charge separation and selective mass-transfer of redox-relevant ions. Mechanistically, tethered triarylborane/BODIPY-borane moieties installed as post-synthetic, orientation-biased channel linings will (a) reversibly bind OH−/Cl−/H2O to modulate local Donnan potential and dehydration penalty (energy barrier) for ion entry, and (b) under illumination, undergo excited-state charge transfer to the ZIF-90/graphene interface to generate a built-in photovoltage that further reshapes the ionic potential landscape (photogating). This methodological adaptation converts GNS“ZIF-90 from a purely electrostatic rectifier into a dual-mode (chemical + optical) mass-transfer regulator that couples ionic transport rectification directly to photocatalytic kinetics.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Synthesize baseline ZIF-90 on glass nanopipette tips with graphene nanosheet (GNS) integration using the reported in situ growth route to reproduce sub-nanometer channel rectification at high ionic strength (1 M KCl) and alkaline pH.
1.2 Prepare boron-based channel-lining precursors: (i) amino-terminated triarylborane (TAB“NH2) and (ii) aldehyde-reactive BODIPY“borane (BDP“NHNH2 or BDP“ONH2) variants designed to preserve strong Lewis acidity at boron while providing a conjugated photoactive unit.
1.3 Computational pre-screening (periodic DFT + implicit/explicit electrolyte micro-solvation) to estimate: (a) binding energies of OH−/Cl−/H2O to boron sites, (b) ion dehydration penalties in pristine vs boron-lined ZIF-90 apertures, and (c) potential-of-mean-force (PMF) profiles for K+/Cl− transport through representative apertures.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Post-synthetic channel functionalization (PSM) of ZIF-90 aldehydes: perform Schiff-base (imine) formation between ZIF-90 “CHO and TAB“NH2 or BDP-functional nucleophiles under anhydrous conditions, followed by mild reductive amination (NaBH(OAc)3) to lock the linkage and improve hydrolytic stability.
2.2 Orientation-bias engineering: create an axial gradient of boron functionalization along the nanopipette-grown MOF by diffusion-limited PSM (ligand introduced from one side only). This intentionally breaks symmetry to maximize rectification via an asymmetric fixed-charge/Lewis-acid distribution.
2.3 Photogating integration: for BDP-bearing boron motifs, co-anchor a small fraction of redox mediator sites (e.g., viologen-like pyridinium tether) to favor excited-state electron transfer into graphene (GNS) while keeping boron sites available for anion binding.
2.4 Structural/chemical confirmation: (i) confocal Raman/FTIR mapping along the tip to verify the functionalization gradient (C=N / C“N bands; B“C signatures), (ii) XPS (B 1s, N 1s, O 1s) to quantify boron incorporation and imine reduction, (iii) GIWAXS/PXRD to confirm framework retention, (iv) N2 sorption/CO2 sorption and PALS or positron annihilation to verify maintained sub-nanometer porosity with controlled narrowing.
2.5 Ionic mass-transfer/rectification assays: perform I“V measurements in symmetric electrolytes (1 M KCl) from pH 7“12.5 with and without illumination (wavelength matched to BODIPY absorption). Quantify rectification ratio, limiting current, and hysteresis. Use ion-specific replacements (KCl vs NaCl vs KNO3) to decouple cation/anion contributions.
2.6 Energy-barrier extraction: fit I“V and concentration-dependent conductance using Poisson“Nernst“Planck (PNP) with steric effects and a spatially varying fixed-charge term; validate with PMF from MD umbrella sampling in model apertures. Report ΔG‡(ion entry) changes vs pH and light.
2.7 Photocatalysis coupling tests (mechanism-driven): choose a reaction where ionic access controls rate (e.g., photocatalytic Cr(VI) reduction or oxidative degradation with ROS generation) using the same GNS“ZIF-90 membrane as both transport diode and photocatalyst support. Measure (i) apparent quantum yield, (ii) ROS signatures (EPR spin trapping), and (iii) reaction rate under forward vs reverse bias and under dark vs light, correlating with rectification-controlled ion flux.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Controls: pristine GNS“ZIF-90; ZIF-90 functionalized with non-boron aromatic amines (same sterics, no Lewis acidity); homogeneous boron functionalization (no gradient); graphene-free ZIF-90 nanopipettes.
3.2 Causality tests for Lewis-acid mechanism: add competitive Lewis bases (fluoride at trace levels or pyridine) to quench boron binding and observe collapse of pH/light tunability in rectification and extracted ΔG‡.
3.3 Photogating specificity: compare illumination at on-resonance vs off-resonance wavelengths; transient photovoltage/photocurrent at the GNS interface; time-resolved PL quenching of BODIPY to confirm charge transfer.
3.4 Stability: repeated I“V cycling and photocatalysis cycles; post-mortem XPS/FTIR to confirm retention of boron motifs and reduced hydrolysis; leaching tests (ICP-MS for Zn; boron quantification).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: GNS“ZIF-90 already demonstrates exceptionally high rectification (>500) at 1 M KCl under alkaline conditions, implying that small changes in channel charge and ion“wall interactions strongly modulate the transport energy barrier. Boron-based metal“organic motifs (triarylboranes/BODIPY-boranes) provide strong, tunable Lewis acidity and photophysics suitable for light-harvesting and excited-state charge transfer.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): ZIF-90 uniquely offers aldehyde handles for covalent post-synthetic modification, enabling precise installation of boron-containing ligands without reconstructing the framework. Creating a functionalization gradient is a MOF-specific architectural adaptation that directly engineers asymmetric channel chemistry—the key requirement for rectification and for coupling to photocatalysis via interfacial fields.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with pristine GNS“ZIF-90, boron-lined channels introduce an additional, chemically addressable energy-barrier term (Lewis-acid anion/H-bond complexation + dehydration modulation) and an optically addressable term (photogating-induced potential reshaping). Compared with conventional photocatalytic MOFs, the proposal adds a measurable transport metric (rectification ratio) that predicts catalytic rate via controlled mass transfer, enabling a mechanistically grounded design rule: maximize reaction by synchronizing forward-biased ion delivery with illumination-driven charge separation.

Hypothesis: Pre-installing a thymine-derived, Zn(II)-addressable “gate ligand” (Thy-L) in KBM-1 can enable sequence-selective ssDNA capture and pH-triggered release only if (and because) Thy-L exchange occurs at a chemically defined, labile Zn coordination environment that is proximal to accessible adenine Watson“Crick (WC) faces, rather than through nonspecific adsorption or framework-linker substitution. We hypothesize that KBM-1 contains a subpopulation of (i) terminal aqua/hydroxo ligands on Zn sites and/or (ii) defect/undercoordinated Zn sites that are sufficiently labile in water to support reversible binding of a monocarboxylate (Thy-1-alkylcarboxylate), while the native multidentate framework linkers remain kinetically inert under the same conditions. In this model, Thy-L binds as a weak, monodentate Zn“O2CR ligand (or outer-sphere ion-paired adduct) positioned to sterically and H-bond-competitively occlude nearby Ade WC edges; A-rich ssDNA then displaces Thy-L through multivalent A“T pairing amplified by confinement and local effective molarity (multiple Ade faces per pore segment engaging multiple adenines along a single ssDNA), producing cooperative uptake only when a geometric multivalency criterion is met (Ade-face linear density and spacing commensurate with ssDNA base spacing and persistence length under the chosen ionic strength). Acidic pH reverses capture primarily by protonating adenine (reducing WC pairing) and diminishing net electrostatic attraction, while framework integrity is maintained if Zn leaching and linker protonolysis remain below pre-defined thresholds. Thus, the ‘toehold-like’ behavior is not assumed a priori; it is predicted to emerge only after (1) mapping the true Thy-L binding site/lability at Zn by EXAFS/XANES and competition experiments, and (2) empirically quantifying A“T pairing energetics under the exact buffer/salt conditions and translating those energetics into a pore-confinement multivalency criterion that is then directly stress-tested by a DNA library designed around spacing/valency, not merely A-tract length.
Plan: Step 0 — Lock down KBM-1 coordination environment and identify the exchangeable site (mandatory before displacement claims).
0.1 Reproduce KBM-1 with strict aqueous stability benchmarking: synthesize per Ade/Zn2+/unnatural amino acid protocol; verify phase purity (PXRD), porosity (N2 sorption), morphology (SEM). Establish baseline aqueous robustness by soaking in the exact buffers planned (see below) for 24“72 h and measuring: (i) PXRD retention, (ii) Zn leaching by ICP-MS, (iii) linker/ligand loss by solution 1H NMR/LC (digest or supernatant as appropriate), and (iv) water vapor sorption hysteresis as an early capillary-condensation damage indicator.
0.2 Define working buffer space (for all subsequent steps): select two ionic strengths to explicitly bracket base-pair screening: (A) 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM NaCl, pH 7.4; (B) 10 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.4. Maintain Mg2+-free conditions initially to avoid strengthening nonspecific DNA adsorption and altering Zn chemistry.
0.3 Spectroscopic node mapping (Zn K-edge XANES/EXAFS): collect Zn K-edge spectra for (i) activated KBM-1, (ii) water-equilibrated KBM-1 in buffer A and B, and (iii) after exposure to small competitive ligands (acetate, imidazole, phosphate; see 0.4). Fit EXAFS with models spanning Zn“N/O coordination numbers and Zn“O distances to detect terminal aqua vs carboxylate binding and to quantify any ligand exchange at Zn without bulk phase change. Pre-commit to acceptance: no significant change in Zn“Zn (if present) or long-range scattering consistent with node reconstruction, and <10% change in average Zn first-shell CN upon benign competitors.
0.4 Systematic competition experiments to map affinity/lability of the putative exchange site:
- Incubate KBM-1 in buffer A with graded concentrations (0.1“50 mM) of sodium acetate, imidazole, and sodium phosphate (or NaH2PO4/Na2HPO4 at pH 7.4), each for defined times (0.5, 2, 8, 24 h).
- Readouts: solution Zn by ICP-MS; PXRD; and quantification of competitor uptake/depletion where feasible.
- Decision rule: if phosphate causes rapid Zn leaching/structural loss, it becomes a ‘dissolution positive control’ to distinguish destructive processes from designed exchange; acetate/imidazole define a “safe” competitive window. This maps whether monocarboxylates can bind reversibly without displacing framework linkers.

Step 1 — Design and validate Thy-L chemistry and negative controls (recognition vs coordination decoupling).
1.1 Gate ligand set (all synthesized/purchased with full characterization by 1H/13C NMR, HRMS, pKa estimation/measurement):
- Thy-L(weak Zn-binding): thymine-1-acetate and thymine-1-propionate (monocarboxylate; chain length tunes approach and hydrophobicity).
- Coordination-preserving, base-pair-broken decisive negative control: N3-methylthymine-1-acetate (blocks WC H-bonding at N3 but retains carboxylate for Zn binding) and/or 2,4-difluorothymine-1-acetate (attenuates H-bonding while maintaining shape).
- Non-coordinating thymine control: thymine-1-methyl (preserves recognition but removes Zn“O2CR handle).
- Optional orthogonal base control: uracil-1-acetate (weaker methyl effect; tests recognition energetics differences).
1.2 LC-MS method development for Thy-L quantification in DNA-containing matrices (addresses mass-balance critique):
- Use LC-MS (ESI− preferred for carboxylates) with isotopically labeled internal standard (e.g., 13C2-acetate analog of Thy-L or deuterated Thy-L) spiked into every sample at collection.
- Validate separation from nucleobases, oligonucleotides, HEPES, and salts; include matrix-matched calibration curves in buffer A/B with and without representative ssDNA.
- Quantify adsorption-to-plastic/glass artifacts: run Thy-L solutions with and without DNA in empty vessels; correct recovery by mass balance.

Step 2 — Post-synthetic installation (PSI) with explicit site model tests.
2.1 PSI protocol (buffer-controlled): activate KBM-1 (mild vacuum/temperature consistent with KBM-1 stability), then equilibrate in buffer A or B. Add Thy-L at 0.1“5 mM (below any threshold identified in 0.4 that perturbs the framework). Stir gently at constant solid:liquid ratio.
2.2 Quantify Thy-L uptake kinetics and capacity by LC-MS with internal standard. Perform timepoints (5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 360 min; 24 h). Fit to adsorption/exchange models.
2.3 Differentiate true coordination from nonspecific adsorption:
- Repeat PSI in the presence of competing acetate (e.g., 1“10 mM) and imidazole (1“10 mM). A coordination-driven installation should be suppressed competitively; nonspecific adsorption should be less sensitive.
- Measure Zn K-edge XANES/EXAFS of Thy-L@KBM-1 to detect Zn“O(carboxylate) signature changes relative to water-equilibrated KBM-1. Complement with FTIR (Δνasym“Δνsym carboxylate as qualitative binding-mode indicator) as secondary evidence.
- Acceptance criterion for proceeding: Thy-L loading is reproducible, competitor-sensitive (acetate reduces loading in a dose-dependent manner), and EXAFS indicates added Zn“O(carboxylate) contribution without PXRD degradation and with Zn leaching below threshold (defined in Step 4).

Step 3 — Quantify A“T pairing energetics under exact conditions and translate into a geometric multivalency criterion.
3.1 Solution-phase pairing benchmark (no MOF): measure A“T interaction strength under buffer A and B using at least two orthogonal methods:
- UV melting (Tm) of short complementary oligos (e.g., dA10 with dT10; and mismatched controls) to extract ΔG° at 25 °C.
- ITC for short oligo association (if signal permits at low ionic strength) or alternative: MST (microscale thermophoresis) with labeled strand.
3.2 Confinement proxy (if direct in-pore pairing is hard): use KBM-1 analog experiments where Ade WC faces are present but mobility is restricted:
- Measure ssDNA binding isotherms to ungated KBM-1 vs Thy-L@KBM-1 in buffer A/B; use the difference to infer effective penalty/benefit consistent with A“T pairing.
3.3 Define and test a multivalency/geometry criterion:
- From KBM-1 crystal structure (literature SCXRD), compute/estimate: (i) density of accessible Ade WC faces per nm of channel length and (ii) typical spacing between faces along the pore wall. Translate into a predicted “matching condition” where an ssDNA segment of length L can engage n faces simultaneously given base spacing (~0.34 nm per nucleotide in extended form) and electrostatic persistence length (salt-dependent).
- Prediction: cooperative displacement should emerge only when the number of simultaneously engageable A bases (n_eff) exceeds a threshold (e.g., n_eff ≥ 3“5), and should weaken at 150 mM NaCl (buffer B) relative to buffer A.

Step 4 — Displacement experiments with mass-balance, stoichiometric benchmarks, and dissolution controls.
4.1 DNA library designed to test geometry (not just A-tract length):
- Keep total length constant (e.g., 30 nt) while varying distribution of adenines: (i) terminal A-block (A10 + mixed remainder), (ii) periodically spaced A’s (A every 3 bases), (iii) clustered internal A-block, (iv) A-poor control with same length/charge.
- Include T-rich and random controls.
4.2 Coupled kinetics with full mass balance:
- For each DNA, run displacement at fixed DNA:MOF ratios under buffer A and B.
- Measure simultaneously: (i) Thy-L released to solution by LC-MS (internal standard), (ii) DNA depletion/uptake by fluorescence (labeled DNA) with calibration and quench controls, and (iii) solution Zn by ICP-MS at matched timepoints.
- Define stoichiometric benchmarks and acceptance windows: report mol Thy-L released per mol nucleotide adsorbed (or per mol DNA).
