Comparative Advantage: Classical adsorption-stress models treat the host as electronically inert, so they miss stress anomalies and stability/working-capacity optima arising from redox/IVCT changes during uptake. The coupled electro-chemo-mechanical model predicts when adsorption will localize or delocalize charge (changing t and λ), thereby altering modulus and stress, enabling a priori selection of oxidation level/counterion/guest pairs that maximize storage performance while preventing structural fatigue—capabilities not accessible to purely mechanical or purely electronic descriptions alone.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a redox-active, intrinsically hydroxylated 2D magnetic MOF with exchangeable interlayer protons will exhibit superior Rhodamine B capture and degradation due to a cooperative mechanism combining (i) permanent porosity within 2D sheets, (ii) Brønsted-acidic μ2“OH bridges acting as fixed ion-exchange sites, and (iii) long-range magnetic ordering from mixed Fe/Co nodes that enables facile magnetic separation and accelerates Fenton-type redox cycling. The core methodological adaptation is the bottom-up self-assembly of a layered MOF using a pre-hydroxylated, sulfonate-free catechol“dicarboxylate linker that enforces dense “OH functionality without post-synthetic modification, while mixed-valent Fe/Co paddlewheel clusters simultaneously provide Brønsted acidity, magnetism, and catalytic redox activity. This design circumvents pore blockage and chemical instability associated with grafting strategies and creates a chemically programmed ion-exchange microenvironment within the galleries that preferentially concentrates cationic dyes such as Rhodamine B.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Design and synthesize a rigid, pre-hydroxylated ditopic linker: 2,3-dihydroxyterephthalic acid (DHTPA), where ortho-catechol “OH groups are locked into the aromatic backbone to ensure high hydroxyl density and metal-chelation capability.
1.2 Select mixed-metal nodes capable of magnetic coupling and redox cycling: Fe(II/III)“Co(II) paddlewheel or trinuclear clusters, targeting a Fe:Co ratio that balances ferrimagnetism and framework stability.
1.3 Employ solvothermal conditions that favor 2D sheet formation (high modulator concentration, e.g., benzoic acid) to generate layered MOF nanosheets with accessible interlayer galleries.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Bottom-up formation of intrinsic Brønsted acid sites (methodological adaptation): during self-assembly, allow partial protonation of μ2“OH bridges and catechol “OH groups by controlling pH and metal oxidation state. These protons function as immobile Brønsted acid/ion-exchange sites without introducing bulky sulfonates.
2.2 Engineering porosity and ion-exchange pathways: induce turbostratic stacking of 2D sheets via solvent exchange (DMF → water/ethanol) to create mesoporous interlayer gaps while preserving intrinsic microporosity within sheets. The galleries host exchangeable H+ counterions, enabling Donnan-type uptake of cationic Rhodamine B.
2.3 Magnetic functionality without composites: exploit superexchange interactions between Fe“O“Co chains within the 2D sheets to generate intrinsic ferrimagnetism, eliminating the need for Fe3O4 cores or external shells.
2.4 Catalytic activation pathway: under Fenton or electro-Fenton conditions, Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycling at the nodes generates •OH radicals. Proximity of Brønsted acid sites protonates Rhodamine B, lowering its oxidation potential and promoting ring-opening degradation within the confined galleries.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural and chemical characterization: PXRD (layered structure, turbostratic disorder), AFM/TEM (sheet thickness), N2 sorption (micro/mesoporosity), FTIR and solid-state 13C NMR (catechol “OH), XPS and Mössbauer (Fe oxidation states), ICP-OES (Fe/Co ratio).
3.2 Brønsted acidity and ion-exchange quantification: NH3-TPD and n-butylamine titration for acid site density; H+/Na+ exchange experiments to quantify cation-exchange capacity.
3.3 Magnetic measurements: VSM to confirm ferrimagnetism and magnetic retrievability under aqueous conditions.
3.4 Rhodamine B studies: adsorption isotherms and kinetics across pH and ionic strength; in situ fluorescence quenching to monitor confinement; degradation tests under Fenton/electro-Fenton conditions with LC“MS identification of intermediates.
3.5 Stability and recyclability: repeated adsorption/degradation cycles with magnetic separation; leaching tests and post-cycle PXRD/BET analysis; benchmarking against H-UiO-66 and MIL-88A(Fe).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Pre-hydroxylated aromatic linkers are known to enforce high hydrophilicity and strong hydrogen-bond networks, while mixed Fe/Co nodes provide both magnetic coupling and redox activity. Layered MOFs with turbostratic disorder have demonstrated enhanced mass transport and ion exchange compared to rigid 3D analogues.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal leverages rational linker design and controlled self-assembly—core MOF principles—rather than post-synthetic grafting. Intrinsic Brønsted acidity and magnetism are encoded at the coordination level, aligning with coordination polymer chemistry and avoiding instability from external composites.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to sulfonated or composite MOFs, this system maintains high porosity and chemical robustness while delivering fixed acid sites, ion-exchange capability, and magnetism in a single crystalline phase. The 2D architecture shortens diffusion paths, enhances Rhodamine B preconcentration, and accelerates catalytic degradation, offering superior performance under realistic water-treatment conditions.

Hypothesis: A MOF-templated, peptide-imprinted double-hollow heterostructure—In2S3 hollow nanorods (HNRs) bearing a conformal, ultrathin In/Fe“MIL-101(BDC)-analog shell that is kinetically “arrested” during sulfidation into a nanometric Fe/In“Sx“(oxy)carboxylate“C interlayer—will deliver (i) photocurrent amplification from decoupled optical and electronic gain mechanisms (multi-light scattering in the hollow architecture + improved charge separation/transport from a type-II or quasi“type-II interfacial band gradient) and (ii) biosensing specificity enforced by an epitope-imprinted cavity whose binding-face presentation is *experimentally verified post-immobilization*, not assumed from solution NOE alone.

Mechanistic rationale addressing reviewer concerns:
1) Conformal MOF coating is enabled by a defined surface-priming nucleation strategy that converts the chemically “inert/defect-rich” In2S3 surface into a high density of carboxylate/phosphonate anchoring sites, thereby controlling heterogeneous nucleation, shell continuity, and thickness at the 5“20 nm scale.
2) Partial MOF-to-sulfide conversion is treated as a parameterized kinetic map (temperature, time, sulfur activity) with in situ/time-resolved phase/chemistry readouts. The interlayer’s carbon is hypothesized to originate from *BDC linker carbonization/graphitization under sulfidation* and to act as (a) a percolating electronic bridge and (b) a defect-stabilizer that suppresses macroscopic FeSx segregation by trapping Fe in mixed Fe“S“C/O coordination environments. The conversion is purposely stopped before complete collapse to dense sulfides, preserving mesoporosity and residual coordination handles (carboxylate/Fe sites) for recognition chemistry.
3) NOE defines the epitope’s solution contact map, but surface presentation is ensured through a *single-point, site-specific anchoring* design plus direct experimental verification (surface-sensitive/FRET/STD-NMR on immobilized peptide). Imprinting is performed under conditions that minimize peptide refolding and polymer shrinkage, and cavity fidelity is validated against scrambled-sequence and immobilization-geometry controls.

Together, these refinements make coating continuity, interlayer composition/porosity, and epitope face exposure measurable “control knobs,” enabling deconvolution of scattering vs junction vs recognition contributions to PEC performance.
Plan: Step 0 — Define controls and normalization (pre-registered):
0.1 Build a full control matrix to deconvolute effects:
- Geometry controls: solid In2S3 rods (no void) with matched external dimensions; hollow In2S3 with collapsed void (post-anneal) to decouple scattering.
- Shell controls: (i) no shell, (ii) non-MOF-derived FeSx deposition (CBD or SILAR) with matched Fe loading, (iii) pure In“MIL-101 shell (no Fe), (iv) pure Fe“MIL-101 shell (no In) where possible.
- Recognition controls: non-imprinted polymer (NIP), scrambled epitope imprint, and altered anchoring geometry (multi-point vs single-point).
0.2 Normalization plan (mandatory for each PEC dataset):
- Fix catalyst mass loading on FTO (µg cm−2) by quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) during deposition or by gravimetric difference with replicate electrodes.
- Determine electroactive surface area (ECSA) by double-layer capacitance (Cdl) in non-faradaic window and report photocurrent normalized to ECSA.
- Measure optical absorption (integrating sphere UV“Vis DRS on films) and report incident-photon-to-current efficiency (IPCE) and absorbed-photon-to-current efficiency (APCE) to separate absorption/scattering from charge-separation.
- Report film roughness/thickness (profilometry/AFM) and keep within ±10% across comparisons.

Step 1 — In2S3 hollow nanorods with tunable cavity for scattering:
1.1 Synthesize In2S3 HNRs via hard-template route (AAO or polymer rods):
- Target outer diameter 150“300 nm; inner diameter 60“200 nm; shell thickness 10“30 nm.
- Acceptance criteria: TEM statistics on ≥200 rods: shell thickness CV ≤ 15%; void fraction 0.30“0.70; >90% rods hollow (no fully solid rods).
1.2 Quantify scattering potential:
- Integrating-sphere DRS on powder and on deposited films; extract scattering coefficient via Kubelka“Munk and fit with Monte Carlo photon transport using measured film thickness.

Step 2 — Surface priming for conformal MIL-101-like growth on sulfide (explicit nucleation protocol):
2.1 Clean/activate In2S3 surface without oxidation:
- Mild plasma (Ar, low power, short duration) or UV“ozone minimized; confirm In(III)/S(−II) states by XPS (no excessive sulfate).
2.2 Install an anchoring interfacial primer (choose one as primary, one as backup):
Primary (phosphonate primer; high affinity to In sites):
- Treat HNRs with 2-carboxyethylphosphonic acid (CEPA) or 11-phosphonoundecanoic acid (PUA) in ethanol/water (pH 4“5) to form In“O“P bonds; terminal “COOH presents carboxylate nucleation sites.
Backup (polydopamine“carboxylate co-primer):
- Deposit ultra-thin PDA (2“5 nm) followed by succinic anhydride ring-opening to enrich “COOH; preserves adhesion and increases nucleation density.
2.3 Verify priming density and uniformity:
- XPS: P 2p (phosphonate) and O 1s increase; attenuated In 3d consistent with sub-2 nm overlayer.
- ζ-potential shift to more negative at neutral pH.
- Acceptance: primer present on ≥95% particles (XPS survey across batches) and no aggregation (DLS, TEM).

Step 3 — Conformal bimetallic MIL-101(BDC)-analog shell growth with thickness control:
3.1 Use a “seeded, modulated” growth to force heterogeneous nucleation:
- Pre-seeding: expose primed HNRs to dilute Fe3+/In3+ solution (e.g., FeCl3 + In(NO3)3, total 1“5 mM) to form surface-bound metal“carboxylate/phosphonate complexes.
- Growth solution: BDC (terephthalic acid) + Fe3+/In3+ in DMF/EtOH/H2O with monocarboxylate modulator (acetic acid) to suppress homogeneous nucleation.
- Metal ratio series: Fe:In = 0.2:0.8, 0.5:0.5, 0.8:0.2 (molar in feed) to tune band alignment/Fe site density.
3.2 Thickness tuning knobs:
- Total metal concentration (e.g., 5“50 mM), modulator:BDC ratio (e.g., 10“50), temperature (80“120 °C), time (0.5“6 h).
- Apply a “stop-growth” wash with excess modulator to cap surfaces and limit secondary growth.
3.3 Quantitative acceptance criteria for conformality:
- TEM/STEM: shell continuity ≥ 90% of rod surface length with no pinholes >5 nm; thickness 5“20 nm with σ ≤ 3 nm across ≥50 rods.
- Porosity retention: N2 sorption (powder) shows measurable micro/mesoporosity; BET not necessarily MIL-101-level, but must exceed primed HNR baseline by ≥50%.
- Phase/structure confirmation: XRD/FTIR consistent with MIL-101-like coordination (carboxylate bands) while recognizing nanoshell broadening.

Step 4 — Controlled partial sulfidation: conversion map + operando/time-resolved characterization:
4.1 Define sulfidation parameter space (“conversion map”):
- Sulfur sources: thioacetamide (solution, 80“120 °C) and/or H2S/Ar (gas, 150“350 °C) as orthogonal methods.
- Variables: T (80“350 °C), time (5“240 min), sulfur activity (TAA concentration or H2S partial pressure), ramp rate.
- Goal window: convert outer MOF coordination network into mixed Fe/In“Sx while retaining (i) residual carboxylate/oxycarboxylate signatures and (ii) an sp2/sp3 carbon fraction from linker carbonization.
4.2 Carbon origin/role hypothesis and tests:
- Hypothesis: BDC linker partially carbonizes under sulfidation (especially in gas-phase at ≥200 °C), forming a thin amorphous/graphenic carbon that electronically couples Fe/In sulfide domains and suppresses FeSx crystallite coarsening.
- Tests: Raman (D/G bands), XPS C 1s (sp2/sp3), and elemental analysis; correlate carbon content with conductivity (four-point probe on films) and with FeSx domain size (STEM).
4.3 Time-resolved/operando readouts to avoid phase ambiguity:
- Time-resolved XRD during conversion (where feasible) to detect emergence of FeSx/In2S3 reflections.
- Raman mapping to track linker→carbon evolution and sulfide vibrational modes.
- XPS depth profiling (gentle Ar cluster) to map Fe/In/S/C vs depth and confirm interlayer rather than segregated outer FeSx crust.
- STEM-EDS/EELS mapping at nanometer resolution to quantify co-localization (Fe and S) and whether Fe concentrates at outer surface or is interdispersed.
4.4 Acceptance criteria for “partial conversion, porous, handle-rich interlayer”:
- No macroscopic FeSx crystallites >10“15 nm (STEM);
- Residual O/C signatures consistent with remaining carboxylate/oxycarboxylate at ≥10“20% of initial carboxylate signal (FTIR/XPS) to preserve coupling handles;
- Mesoporosity retained (hysteresis/uptake) and shell not densified into impermeable layer (electrochemical probe diffusion test with Fe(CN)6 3−/4−).

Step 5 — PEC electrode assembly and mechanism deconvolution:
5.1 Deposition onto FTO:
- Electrophoretic deposition (EPD) in low-water alcohol with iodine or Mg(NO3)2 charging agent; target uniform films of controlled thickness (e.g., 1“3 µm).
- Mild anneal under inert (e.g., 150“250 °C) only if needed for contact; verify hollows preserved by TEM on scraped film.
5.2 PEC testing:
- Chopped illumination, wavelength-resolved IPCE/APCE; mediator screening (ascorbate vs O2) selected to match band positions and avoid sulfide photocorrosion.
- Mechanism suite with controls: TRPL quenching, transient photocurrent, EIS, Mott“Schottky, UPS/XPS for band edges.
- Explicit deconvolution: compare (hollow vs solid) at constant composition to isolate scattering contribution; compare (MOF-derived interlayer vs non-MOF FeSx) at constant Fe loading to isolate junction/interlayer chemistry.

Step 6 — NOE-guided epitope design AND verified surface presentation (closing the “NOE-to-surface” gap):
6.1 Epitope selection/design:
- Choose CA15-3 (MUC1) epitope (10“20 aa) from solvent-exposed repeat region; incorporate a designed aromatic/cationic pair (Trp/Phe with Lys/Arg) to enable a C“H···π/cation“π signature.
- Prepare mutants disrupting the NOE contact: Lys→Nle and/or Trp→Cha (as per literature logic) while keeping overall hydrophobicity comparable.
6.2 Solution conformation validation:
- 2D NOESY/ROESY to define key intrapeptide distances for aromatic“Lys proximity and any β-turn propensity.
6.3 Site-specific single-point immobilization to preserve face presentation:
- Engineer a unique anchor handle at peptide terminus (e.g., N-terminal cysteine or azido-lysine) separated by a short spacer (PEG2“PEG6) to minimize surface-induced refolding.
- Surface coupling options:
  (i) Maleimide-functionalized carboxylate handle on interlayer (EDC/NHS to introduce maleimide-amine linker) for Cys anchoring;
  (ii) Click chemistry (surface alkyne/azide) if residual carboxylates are abundant.
- Avoid multipoint adsorption by passivating residual Fe sites with weak ligands (e.g., acetate) prior to peptide coupling, then selectively re-open sites post-coupling if needed.
6.4 Direct verification that the NOE-defined face is exposed after immobilization:
- FRET geometry test: label peptide with donor near aromatic and acceptor near anchor; compare FRET efficiency in solution vs immobilized; loss indicates surface-flattening.
- Surface-sensitive spectroscopy: PM-IRRAS or SFG to assess orientation changes (amide I/II and aromatic modes).
- Binding-site accessibility: antibody/lectin probing specific to the epitope segment as an orthogonal check.
- Optional high-rigor: STD-NMR on immobilized peptide with soluble “cavity monomer” or target protein fragment to confirm the same contact face participates.

Step 7 — Imprinting with cavity fidelity controls:
7.1 Form thin imprint layer with controlled shrinkage:
- Use a metal“ligand crosslinked imprint (PICN-like) or a low-shrinkage sol“gel/coordination polymer; keep thickness 5“30 nm (ellipsometry/TEM).
- Polymerization under buffered aqueous conditions approximating NMR conditions to reduce conformation drift.
7.2 Template removal:
- Competitive elution (high ionic strength + mild chelator) designed not to strip interlayer Fe excessively; confirm by ICP-MS of eluate.
7.3 Fidelity/negative controls:
- NIP on same substrate;
- Imprint using scrambled epitope;
- Imprint using mutant epitope (Lys→Nle / Trp→Cha);
- Immobilization geometry variants (single-point vs intentionally multipoint) to show specificity collapses when orientation is not controlled.

Step 8 — Biosensing validation in complex media:
8.1 Analytical figures of merit:
- Calibration in buffer and 10“50% serum; report LOD, linear range, slope, RSD (intra/inter-assay), and 2+ week storage stability.
8.2 Selectivity panel:
- Closely related glycoproteins and abundant serum proteins (albumin, IgG, transferrin); compute cross-reactivity factors and apparent Kd via SPR/QCM-D.
8.3 Structure“function maps:
- Hollow geometry (void fraction, shell thickness) vs scattering coefficient vs APCE.
- Conversion degree (XPS depth + Raman D/G + XRD) vs EIS Rct, band edges, and photocurrent.
- Imprint thickness vs mass transport (probe diffusion) vs specificity factor.
Feasibility: 1) Conformal MIL-101-like shell feasibility is converted into measurable process control: phosphonate/carboxylate surface priming creates deterministic nucleation sites on In2S3, while modulated solvothermal growth (acetic-acid modulation + pre-seeding) is a well-established route to suppress homogeneous MOF nucleation and enforce thin, continuous coatings. Quantitative acceptance criteria (shell continuity %, thickness σ, porosity gain) prevent “hand-wavy” conformity claims.

2) Partial conversion feasibility is addressed via a kinetic conversion map tied to multi-modal compositional/phase mapping (time-resolved XRD/Raman, XPS depth profiling, STEM-EELS/EDS). Rather than asserting an Fe/In“Sx“C interlayer exists, the proposal defines what counts as success (no large FeSx segregation; retained O/C handles; retained permeability) and how carbon is generated (BDC carbonization) and validated (Raman/XPS/EA). The interlayer is intentionally formed under kinetically limited conditions to avoid full collapse to dense sulfides and to retain porosity/handles.

3) The NOE-to-surface orientation gap is closed by design and verification: NOE is used to choose an epitope with a defined contact map, but face presentation is enforced by single-point, site-specific immobilization with spacers and is experimentally checked post-attachment (FRET/orientation-sensitive IR/SFG and/or STD-NMR). Imprint fidelity is proven with scrambled/mutant epitopes and immobilization-geometry variants, directly testing the reviewer’s concern that surface-induced folding or polymer shrinkage can scramble the contact map.

4) Mechanistic claims are deconvoluted with strict normalization and matched controls: APCE/IPCE separates absorption/scattering from charge separation; ECSA normalization and constant loading isolate intrinsic activity; solid vs hollow and MOF-derived vs non-MOF shells isolate scattering vs junction chemistry. This makes type-II/quasi-type-II alignment and scattering gains testable rather than inferred.

5) Empirical precedent supports the core concept chain: double-hollow heterostructures are known to enhance PEC via multi-light scattering and reduced recombination (Asset 1 logic), while aromatic/cationic contacts provide specificity that can be interrogated by NOE and mutant-cycle-like disruptions (Asset 2 logic). The revised plan adds the missing materials-chemistry and surface-biophysics rigor needed to reliably implement and validate those principles in a MOF-templated PEC biosensor.

Hypothesis: A ZIF67@ZIF8 core“shell can be converted into a visible-light-responsive, micropore-confined photocatalyst for selective C“C coupling of methanol-derived C1 intermediates to ethanol **only if** (a) the Ni chemical endpoint is explicitly constrained to a *defect-docked, imidazolate/N-donor coordinated Ni(II) single-site* within an intact ZIF8 shell (not “O-vacancies” in the ZIF lattice), (b) the shell is engineered to support *measurable* interfacial electronic communication with the Co-rich core via a deliberately introduced short-range electronic bridge, and (c) ethanol formation is validated by strict atom/redox balance closure with identified coproducts and electron sinks.

**Defined Ni-site/defect model (replaces ‘O-vacancy’):** Ni is installed post-synthetically into the ZIF8 shell as isolated Ni(II) bound to 2-methylimidazolate (mIm−) and nitrate-derived inner-sphere ligands at pre-existing or induced shell defects. The intended coordination is **Ni(II)(mIm)3“4(ONO2)0“1(H2O/ROH)0“1**, i.e., a mixed N/O donor environment where nitrate is a *labile spectator/charge-balancing ligand* rather than a lattice oxygen source. Upon mild activation (≤250 °C, inert), nitrate is **removed/converted** to volatile NOx (tracked by TGA-MS) leaving **coordinatively unsaturated Ni“Nx sites (Ni(II)“N3/4)** and/or **Ni“OH/Ni“OMe** after exposure to methanol—these are the chemically explicit, testable “defects”. No claim is made of true lattice O-vacancies, and no Ni“N4 ‘M“N“C’ motif is claimed unless partial carbonization is intentionally invoked as a separate, gated branch.

**Mechanistic rationale for ethanol plausibility (with redox/atom balance):** Under visible light, photoexcitation in the Co-containing core (or core“shell interfacial states) generates separated charges that are funneled to the shell Ni site, enabling a *two-step C1→C2 coupling sequence* that competes with over-oxidation because methanol is enriched inside micropores (Type I regime) and oxygen is excluded/limited.

Two operating regimes are explicitly proposed and will be distinguished by product closure:

(1) **Inert (no external oxidant) “acceptorless” coupling with H2 as coproduct (primary target):**
Overall target stoichiometry (carbon/oxygen balanced):
**2 CH3OH → C2H5OH + H2O + H2**
This is redox-neutral overall but requires photocatalytic charge separation to enable dehydrogenation/coupling steps at low temperature. The proposed elementary accounting is:
- Two sequential PCET-enabled dehydrogenations: CH3OH → HCHO + 2H+ + 2e− (occurs twice)
- C“C formation via confined coupling/hydrogenation cascade: HCHO + CH3OH → C2 oxygenate (e.g., HOCH2CH2OH or CH3CHO) followed by reduction/hydrogenation to ethanol.
- Electrons/protons are balanced by **H2 evolution** on Ni/Co interfacial sites: 2H+ + 2e− → H2.
**Pass/fail prediction:** If ethanol is truly formed under inert conditions, measurable H2 must be co-produced with a molar relationship consistent with closure (within experimental error after accounting for minor side products).

(2) **Trace O2 (controlled ppm“0.5%) “oxidant-assisted” coupling with H2O2/H2O as sinks (secondary regime):**
O2 functions as terminal electron acceptor to pull electrons away, suppressing recombination, but must not drive total oxidation.
Representative balanced variant (one admissible closure model):
**2 CH3OH + 1/2 O2 → C2H5OH + H2O**
Here, O2 accepts the net 2e−/2H+ equivalents that otherwise appear as H2. Alternative sink: H2O2 formation (to be measured), e.g., O2 + 2H+ + 2e− → H2O2.
**Pass/fail prediction:** In trace O2 runs, H2 yield should decrease; H2O2 (or increased H2O) must appear to satisfy electron balance, and COx must remain low if selectivity claim holds.

**Charge-transfer across shell—explicit constraint:** Meaningful Co(core)→Ni(shell) electronic communication is not assumed for 20“100 nm shells. Instead, the shell thickness is constrained to **≤5“15 nm** (primary design window) and/or an electronic bridge is introduced by **mixed-linker or redox-mediator doping** in the shell that creates through-bond/through-state hopping sites (quantitatively verified by thickness-dependent kinetics and action spectra). Thus, the revised hypothesis claims *distance-limited interfacial ET* rather than generic ‘junction’ behavior.

**Why the refined approach overcomes reviewer-identified limitations:** (i) the Ni endpoint is chemically explicit and verifiable (Ni“N/O defect-docked single site; no lattice O-vacancy claim), (ii) the activation window is chosen to preserve ZIF8 while enabling nitrate removal and Ni coordination unsaturation (≤250 °C, with PXRD/sorption gating), (iii) ethanol plausibility is enforced by strict atom/redox closure with explicit coproduct predictions (H2 under inert; H2O2/H2O under trace O2), and (iv) interfacial ET is engineered and quantified via shell-thickness limits and deliberate bridge states rather than assumed through an intact thick shell.
Plan: Step 0 — Hard gating decision tree (mandatory): choose one of two Ni endpoints and lock conditions accordingly.
0A. **Endpoint A (primary): defect-docked Ni(II)“Nx/NO3 in intact ZIF8** with activation ≤250 °C, preserved crystallinity/microporosity.
0B. **Endpoint B (secondary, separate aim): Ni“Nx in partially carbonized shell (M“N“C-like)** requiring ≥500“700 °C and accepting loss of ZIF crystallinity. Endpoint B is optional and will only be pursued if Endpoint A fails ethanol selectivity/closure.

Step 1 — Core“shell synthesis with shell thickness in ET-relevant regime.
1.1 Synthesize ZIF67 cores in methanol (Co2+ + 2-methylimidazole) targeting 100“300 nm cores (monodisperse) to ensure resolvable core“shell gradients.
1.2 Overgrow ZIF8 shell in methanol to **5, 10, 15, 30 nm** thickness series (not 20“100 nm as default). Control via Zn2+ feed rate, mIm/Zn ratio, and growth time.
1.3 Characterize: STEM-EDS line scan (Co core/Zn shell), PXRD (ZIF67+ZIF8), N2 sorption (77 K) targeting Type I isotherm with preserved micropore volume after shelling.

Step 2 — Ni installation as defect-docked single sites (chemically specified).
2.1 **Solvent and hydrolysis control:** Perform Ni loading under rigorously anhydrous alcohol (absolute ethanol or methanol) with ≤0.05% H2O; N2 glovebox if needed. Maintain pH-neutral conditions (no added base) to suppress Ni(OH)2 precipitation.
2.2 **Defect-docking protocol (low driving force):** Suspend ZIF67@ZIF8 in EtOH/MeOH (1:1) containing Ni(NO3)2·6H2O at 1“10 mM, plus a controlled mIm co-feed (Ni:mIm = 1:4 to 1:8) to rapidly re-ligate transient Zn“N bond cleavage and prevent shell etching.
2.3 **Limit Ni to isolated sites:** Target Ni loading 0.1“1.0 wt% initially; iterate only after site proof. Short contact times (0.5“6 h), low temperature (20“40 °C).
2.4 **Post-treatment wash sequence (removes extraframework Ni nitrate):** alcohol washing → weakly coordinating wash (acetonitrile) → final alcohol wash. Collect wash liquors for ICP to quantify removable Ni.

Step 3 — Activation that is consistent with intact ZIF8 and explicit nitrate fate.
3.1 **Thermal window:** 180“250 °C under flowing N2 (or Ar), 1“4 h. This is chosen to drive partial nitrate dissociation/NOx evolution without ZIF8 decomposition/carbonization.
3.2 **Nitrate fate verification (no “O-vacancy” language):** TGA-MS/TPD-MS to quantify NO, NO2, N2O evolution; XPS N 1s/O 1s before/after to track nitrate removal and formation of Ni“OH/Ni“OMe after methanol exposure.
3.3 **Framework integrity gating:** PXRD peak retention + N2 sorption micropore volume retention ≥80% relative to parent ZIF67@ZIF8; failure triggers re-optimization or Endpoint B branch.

Step 4 — Engineering and verifying interfacial electronic communication (quantitative).
4.1 **Thickness-dependent kinetics:** Run identical photocatalysis on thickness series (5“30 nm). A monotonic decay of activity with thickness consistent with short-range ET supports interfacial communication; no dependence indicates shell-isolated chemistry.
4.2 **Electronic bridge (implemented if thickness dependence is weak):** Introduce a mixed-linker shell fraction (e.g., low % amino-functionalized imidazole derivative) to create mid-gap/hopping states while preserving ZIF topology; alternatively, incorporate a tethered redox mediator (e.g., viologen-like cation) confined in shell pores by ion-pairing. Selection is validated by DRS/Tauc shifts and increased transient photocurrent.
4.3 **Action spectra requirement:** Measure wavelength-dependent AQY and compare to absorption; matching trends are required to claim true photodriven chemistry.

Step 5 — Photocatalysis with strict atom/redox balance closure (pass/fail criteria).
5.1 Reactor: sealed batch photoreactor (quartz), temperature-controlled with internal thermocouple; parallel dark controls at matched temperature profile.
5.2 Feeds:
- Inert regime: methanol (neat or MeOH/H2O defined ratios), N2 purge; quantify dissolved gases.
- Trace O2 regime: controlled O2 addition (ppm“0.5%) using mass-flow mixing; verify by GC.
5.3 Analytics (mandatory closure):
- Liquid: GC-FID/GC-MS + 1H NMR (internal standard) for ethanol, formaldehyde (derivatize if needed), methyl formate, dimethyl ether, ethylene glycol, acetaldehyde.
- Gas: GC-TCD for H2, CO, CO2; GC for O2 consumption; quantify H2O2 in liquid (titration or colorimetric).
5.4 **Closure metrics:**
- Carbon balance ≥95% and O/H closure within defined tolerance.
- In inert regime: ethanol formation must correlate with H2 formation per proposed stoichiometry; otherwise ethanol claim is rejected or reinterpreted.

Step 6 — Decisive active-site proof and confounder controls (mandatory additions).
6.1 **Acid wash test (extraframework Ni removal):** mild acid in alcohol (e.g., acetic acid in EtOH) to strip exposed/weakly bound Ni without collapsing ZIF; re-test activity. Large activity loss implies extraframework Ni dominance.
6.2 **Chelator/poison tests:** introduce thiol/chelating agents (e.g., mercaptoethanol or EDTA in controlled minimal water) to selectively poison accessible Ni; compare to unpoisoned. Coupled with porosity data to infer whether Ni is internal vs external.
6.3 **Operando/quasi-operando XAS (Ni K-edge):** confirm absence of Ni“Ni scattering under working conditions and track Ni(II)↔Ni(I) signatures under illumination.
6.4 **EPR/spin trapping + in situ DRIFTS:** detect methoxy/*CH2OH, carbon-centered radicals, and C2 oxygenate intermediates.
6.5 **Photothermal exclusion:** dark thermal controls precisely matching the illuminated catalyst temperature (PID-controlled heating); additionally vary light intensity at constant temperature to demonstrate photochemical rate dependence.

Step 7 — Benchmarking and decision points.
7.1 Compare to: ZIF8, ZIF67, Ni/ZIF8 (no core), physical mixture (no junction), and NiO/ZnO/NC derived materials.
7.2 Normalize by Ni moles, photon flux, and illuminated area; report TOF (per accessible Ni from chemisorption/probe reaction) and selectivity at matched conversion.
7.3 If Endpoint A cannot meet closure/selectivity, proceed to Endpoint B (partial carbonization) as a clearly separated fallback with revised claims (no ‘intact ZIF8’ requirement).
Feasibility: 1) Chemical consistency of the defect model (addresses critique #1/#2): ZIF8 contains no lattice oxygen; the revised plan therefore treats nitrate exclusively as a removable/transformable ligand to Ni (inner-sphere NO3−) and an NOx precursor under mild activation. The structural endpoint is explicitly **defect-docked Ni(II) coordinated to imidazolate N donors with variable residual O-donor ligation** (Ni“NxOy), verifiable by XAS/XPS/DRIFTS and by the absence of Ni“Ni EXAFS. The activation window (≤250 °C) is chosen to preserve ZIF8 crystallinity/microporosity and is gated by PXRD+sorption retention thresholds.

2) Ethanol plausibility is made testable by redox/atom-balance closure (addresses critique #3): Two explicit regimes are defined with predicted coproducts and electron sinks. Under inert conditions, ethanol formation requires H2 co-production consistent with **2 CH3OH → C2H5OH + H2O + H2**; under trace O2, oxygen must appear in H2O/H2O2 with controlled O2 consumption. Carbon/hydrogen/oxygen closure is elevated to a pass/fail criterion rather than an interpretive afterthought, reducing the plausibility barrier to an experimentally decidable question.

3) Charge transfer is no longer assumed across thick shells (addresses critique #4): The shell thickness is constrained to 5“15 nm (primary), and charge/energy transfer is validated quantitatively by thickness-dependent kinetics plus action spectra (AQY vs wavelength). If communication is weak, an explicit electronic bridge (mixed-linker or confined mediator) is introduced and verified by optoelectronic metrics (TRPL, transient photocurrent, EIS) and by restoration/enhancement of thickness dependence.

4) Confounders are directly controlled (addresses critique #5): Hydrolysis/precipitation is suppressed by low-water alcoholic media and low Ni concentration with mIm re-ligation; extraframework Ni is tested by acid washing and chelator/poison experiments; operando EXAFS excludes hidden Ni“Ni aggregation during turnover; and photothermal artifacts are ruled out by matched-temperature dark controls and intensity/temperature decoupling.

5) Alignment with literature assets: The proposal retains the original concept chain—ZIF67@ZIF8 architecture prepared in methanol/ethanol (Asset 2), micropore-limited Type I adsorption as the confinement lever (Asset 3), and heterometal synergy/visible-light charge separation in mixed-metal MOF motifs (Asset 1)—but replaces chemically vague claims with explicit coordination chemistry and decisive validation gates.

Hypothesis: Grafting a fluorinated leaning pillararene (FLP) as a conformationally fixed, perfluoro-rich “molecular gate” at the pore mouths of an ultrarobust, defect-engineered Zr(IV) MOF will accelerate hydrogen adsorption/desorption kinetics while improving H2/impurity selectivity under practical pelletized conditions. Methodological adaptation: instead of using FLP as a MOF linker or as a periodic pore-lining unit, we will (i) create a UiO-66-type Zr6 framework with a deliberately high density of missing-linker defects that present accessible Zr“OH/H2O sites at external crystal surfaces and grain boundaries, then (ii) post-synthetically anchor an FLP-phosphonate (or FLP-catecholate) “cap” selectively at these Zr sites to form a sub-nanometer, fluorinated entrance collar (gating layer) without occupying internal micropore volume. Mechanism: (a) Zr“O“P (or Zr“O“catecholate) anchoring gives hydrolytic/mechanical robustness and prevents FLP leaching during cycling; (b) the fluorinated FLP cavity at the entrance creates a low-barrier, high-frequency collision zone that reduces the surface-entry resistance for H2 (dominant kinetic bottleneck in densified beds), thereby increasing the apparent mass-transfer coefficient; (c) larger or more strongly polarizable/quadruple gases (CO2, CH4, N2) experience a higher steric/energetic penalty through the gated collar, producing kinetic selectivity even when equilibrium selectivity is modest; (d) by keeping FLP mostly at pore mouths (not as an internal lining), we preserve internal adsorption sites and deliverable capacity while still controlling transport.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select robust host: prepare UiO-66 or UiO-66-NH2 nanocrystals (50“200 nm) to maximize external surface area and shorten diffusion pathlengths; incorporate controlled missing-linker defects using monotopic modulators (formic/acetic) and water dosing. Quantify defect density by 1H NMR of digested MOF, TGA (cluster-to-linker ratio), and pair distribution function (PDF) analysis.
1.2 Design FLP anchoring chemistry (new from rejected draft): synthesize an FLP derivative bearing 1“2 phosphonic acid groups (preferred for Zr binding) tethered via a short, rigid spacer (e.g., “C6H4“CH2“P(O)(OH)2) positioned to maintain the leaning cavity while minimizing flexibility. Prepare a non-fluorinated pillararene phosphonate analog and a simple perfluoroaryl phosphonate as controls.
1.3 Establish a processing-relevant baseline: fabricate pellets/monoliths of the pristine MOF using a pressure-only compaction route (no hot-press growth) and measure pore retention and baseline H2 kinetics in pellet form to define the mass-transfer bottleneck.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Surface/defect-selective FLP grafting (entrance-gating): activate defective UiO crystals to expose Zr“OH sites; then perform post-synthetic metalation-like grafting by reacting with FLP-phosphonic acid in anhydrous polar solvent (e.g., DMF/EtOH) under mild heating. Use stoichiometry and time to confine grafting primarily to external surfaces and defect-rich grain boundaries (validated by depth-sensitive spectroscopy).
2.2 Conformational fixation of the gate: after anchoring, perform a “cap tightening” step by introducing a small Zr(IV) source (e.g., Zr(OiPr)4) at low loading to form secondary Zr“O“P cross-bridges between adjacent phosphonates on the outer surface only, increasing robustness of the grafted layer without nucleating a new MOF phase.
2.3 Build a hierarchical transport architecture: assemble the grafted nanocrystals into a mechanically robust, mesoporous monolith via a sacrificial, removable binder (e.g., polymer that decomposes cleanly) to create interparticle mesopores that feed the gated micropore mouths; ensure the gating layer remains accessible at intercrystal contacts (critical for pellet kinetics).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural/chemical proof of selective surface gating: use XPS (P 2p, F 1s) and angle-resolved XPS to confirm surface-enriched FLP; solid-state 31P MAS NMR to identify Zr“O“P bonding motifs; SEM-EDS mapping for F localization; N2 sorption (77 K) and Ar sorption (87 K) to confirm minimal loss of micropore volume relative to internal-functionalization controls.
3.2 Robustness under cycling and contaminants: humidity/steam exposure (e.g., 80% RH, 60“80 °C), mechanical abrasion, and repeated pelletization tests; monitor PXRD, N2 uptake retention, and leach resistance (ICP of washings for P/F-containing species). Perform 50“100 H2 adsorption/desorption cycles in pellet form.
3.3 Adsorption kinetics and transport mechanism separation: measure time-resolved H2 uptake using constant-volume/variable-pressure or gravimetric step-response at 77 K and 298 K across multiple step sizes. Fit to dual-resistance models (surface barrier + intracrystalline diffusion) and compare apparent mass-transfer coefficients before/after gating. Use PFG-NMR (where feasible) or microcalorimetry-coupled uptake to distinguish entry barrier reduction vs changes in intrinsic diffusion.
3.4 Selectivity in realistic mixtures: mixed-gas breakthrough (H2/CO2, H2/CH4, H2/N2) at relevant pressures and temperatures; quantify kinetic selectivity from breakthrough front separation and compare to IAST from single-component isotherms to demonstrate transport-controlled discrimination. Evaluate performance after pellet aging and humidity exposure.
3.5 Mechanistic binding/energetics mapping: D2 dosing neutron diffraction (or in situ synchrotron PXRD) on representative samples to confirm that FLP does not create dominant internal binding sites; instead, use variable-temperature isotherms and zero-length column (ZLC) experiments to show the principal effect is on entrance resistance. Complement with DFT calculations on Zr“phosphonate-bound FLP fragments to estimate H2 vs CO2/CH4 free-energy barriers through the fluorinated collar.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zr(IV) carboxylate MOFs (UiO family) provide exceptional hydrolytic/mechanical robustness via strong Zr“O bonding, and phosphonate“Zr coordination is even more hydrolysis-resistant, enabling durable post-synthetic surface anchoring. Adsorption kinetics in shaped adsorbents are frequently limited by surface-entry and interparticle transport; engineering pore-mouth chemistry is a direct lever to accelerate apparent kinetics without sacrificing internal capacity. Fluorinated macrocycles are known to create selective, fast host“guest pathways via size/interaction tuning.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): This proposal translates the fast, selective adsorption behavior of FLP into a coordination-polymer platform not by embedding it as a linker (rejected approach), but by using coordination chemistry (Zr“O“P or Zr“O“catecholate) to immobilize FLP as a pore-mouth gate on a robust MOF. The adaptation is a chemically addressable, defect-targeted post-synthetic modification plus surface cross-bridging—an MOF-native strategy grounded in node/defect chemistry.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to (i) internal pore functionalization (which reduces capacity and can slow diffusion) and (ii) using porous molecular solids alone (poor shaping robustness), pore-mouth FLP gating preserves MOF storage capacity, improves pellet-scale mass transfer (key for deliverable hydrogen storage), and introduces kinetic selectivity against larger/strongly interacting gases. The defect-targeted anchoring and secondary Zr cross-bridging specifically address long-term robustness and anti-leaching under cycling.

Hypothesis: A potassium-hydroxide-assisted vapor-diffusion synthesis that pre-deprotonates a bithiopheneimide-derived dicarboxylate (BTI-(CO2H)2) and enforces slow, spatially separated delivery of Cu2+ will generate a microstructure-controlled Cu“BTI MOF with reduced interpenetration and a higher fraction of open Cu sites after activation, thereby increasing accessible microporosity and BET surface area as quantified by N2 adsorption/desorption. Mechanistically, KOH shifts the ligand speciation to carboxylate-rich, highly soluble BTI-(CO2−)2, accelerating metal“ligand nucleation only at the diffusion front while suppressing bulk precipitation; concurrently, the BTI core promotes π“π stacking that biases 2D sheet growth into uniform crystallite thickness. This combination yields a narrower crystal size distribution, fewer grain-boundary defects, and more stable pore apertures upon solvent removal, which collectively improves N2 uptake and hysteresis behavior compared to solvothermal or non-base-mediated diffusion routes.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Design and prepare ligand: synthesize BTI-(CO2H)2 (bithiopheneimide core bearing two carboxylic acids at terminal positions to enforce ditopic connectivity). Confirm structure/purity by 1H/13C NMR, HRMS, and elemental analysis.
1.2 Map solubility/speciation window: measure BTI-(CO2H)2 solubility in DMF/EtOH/H2O mixtures with incremental KOH (0“2.0 equiv) by quantitative 1H NMR (internal standard) and pH tracking; identify conditions giving complete dissolution without ligand degradation (monitor by HPLC/LC-MS).
1.3 Select Cu2+ source and counterion: compare Cu(NO3)2·3H2O vs Cu(OAc)2·H2O for diffusion behavior (anion effects on nucleation) using small-scale screening.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation—two-reservoir, base-gated vapor diffusion: in a sealed diffusion jar, place (A) an inner vial containing BTI-(CO2H)2 in DMF/EtOH with precisely metered KOH (target 1.0“1.5 equiv to reach BTI-(CO2−)2 while avoiding excess OH− that forms Cu(OH)2) and (B) a second inner vial containing Cu2+ salt solution in DMF with a small amount of water (to tune Cu2+ mobility). Use an outer reservoir containing a volatile antisolvent (e.g., Et2O or iPr2O) whose vapor slowly diffuses into both inner vials.
2.2 Spatially separated Cu2+ delivery: connect vial (A) and vial (B) through a narrow PTFE capillary/bridge (or place them adjacent with a controlled headspace path) so that Cu2+ reaches the ligand solution primarily via vapor-mediated concentration changes and limited liquid-phase diffusion, enforcing a moving reaction front and minimizing instantaneous bulk nucleation.
2.3 Microstructure programming by KOH gradient: exploit that KOH is nonvolatile; as antisolvent vapor enters vial (A), local supersaturation increases while carboxylate speciation remains fixed, yielding fewer nuclei but faster anisotropic growth. Systematically vary KOH (0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 equiv) and antisolvent choice to tune nucleation density/crystal thickness.
2.4 Isolation and solvent-exchange: collect crystals, wash with DMF then exchange to MeOH (3“5 days, twice daily) to remove residual K+ and nitrate/acetate. Optionally use mild acidified MeOH (trace acetic acid) briefly to remove K-carboxylate ion pairs without protonating the framework excessively.
2.5 Activation with open-metal-site preservation: activate under dynamic vacuum with stepwise heating (e.g., 60 °C then 120 °C) while monitoring mass loss (TGA) and crystallinity (in situ PXRD) to prevent collapse; compare to supercritical CO2 drying as an alternative for fragile microstructures.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Phase/structure: PXRD (Rietveld refinement if possible) to confirm a single MOF phase; single-crystal XRD on selected crystals to resolve topology, interpenetration degree, and Cu coordination environment.
3.2 Microstructure quantification: SEM for particle size/thickness; AFM for crystal lamella thickness (if 2D sheets form); FIB-SEM cross-sections to quantify internal grain boundaries; EDS mapping to confirm uniform Cu/S/O distribution and absence of K+ in the bulk.
3.3 Chemical state/defects: XPS and EPR to verify Cu2+ vs partial reduction; FTIR to confirm carboxylate binding mode; ICP-OES for residual K and Cu:ligand ratio; digestion 1H NMR to quantify missing-linker defects.
3.4 Porosity metrics: N2 adsorption/desorption at 77 K for BET area, pore size distribution (QSDFT), micropore volume, and hysteresis classification; compare isotherms across KOH levels to correlate microstructure/defects with transport limitations.
3.5 Mechanistic tests: (i) time-resolved sampling during diffusion (aliquots/PXRD/UV-Vis of supernatant) to map nucleation kinetics; (ii) control syntheses: no KOH, direct solvothermal, and one-pot diffusion without spatial Cu2+ separation; (iii) evaluate whether KOH primarily acts via solubility/speciation (supported by solubility curves and absence of K in product) rather than templating.
3.6 Performance-relevant stability: variable-temperature PXRD and humidity exposure; post-activation PXRD + N2 isotherms to quantify pore retention.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Vapor diffusion is empirically proven to yield high-crystallinity porous frameworks and is compatible with porosity evaluation by N2 adsorption/desorption. Base-mediated deprotonation is a well-established lever for increasing ligand solubility and controlling coordination kinetics; however, uncontrolled OH− typically causes Cu(OH)2 precipitation—our base-gated, diffusion-front approach explicitly mitigates this by limiting instantaneous Cu2+“OH− contact.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation integrates (i) solubility/speciation control (KOH → BTI carboxylate) with (ii) microstructure programming via diffusion-limited growth, aligning with MOF crystal engineering where nucleation density and growth anisotropy govern defect density, intergrowth, and accessible porosity. The BTI π-system is deliberately leveraged to bias anisotropic packing and stabilize pore walls through π“π interactions, rather than relying on arbitrary linker selection.
3. Comparative Advantage: Relative to solvothermal synthesis, the spatially separated, KOH-assisted vapor diffusion should (a) reduce amorphous byproducts and particle polydispersity, (b) suppress defect types that block pores (grain-boundary occlusion) while enabling controlled missing-linker density that can increase open Cu sites, and (c) improve activation outcomes (less pore collapse) leading to higher BET area and more ideal microporous N2 isotherms. The design offers a tunable, mechanistically grounded handle (KOH equivalents + diffusion geometry) to reproducibly optimize microstructure-porosity relationships.

Hypothesis: A MOFomics-guided, isoreticular dual-network MOF—comprised of (i) a hydrolytically robust, high-surface-area host with 1D channels and (ii) a geometrically confined, intrachannel-only mixed-valence Cu“(quinone/catecholate)“Cu sublattice—will deliver chemiresistive sensors that simultaneously maximize analyte uptake (host-controlled) and electrical signal transduction (sublattice-controlled). The key mechanistic advance over conventional ‘conductive MOF vs porous MOF’ tradeoffs is enforced spatial separation of function: adsorption occurs predominantly on the preserved host pore surface, while charge transport occurs on a topologically constrained 1D hopping backbone whose conductivity is governed by (a) percolation/continuity of Cu“L“Cu segments and (b) a tunable thermally activated hopping barrier (Ea) linked to ligand-to-metal charge transfer energetics and effective band gap. By pre-designing docking-site topology so that only intrachannel bidentate closure is sterically and geometrically allowed (and interchannel bridging is forbidden), the in-pore sublattice is confined, periodic, and resistant to pore-blocking precipitation. The targeted ‘operational band-gap window’ (0.8“2.5 eV) is justified not as an abstract semiconductor range, but because it corresponds—via a quantified hopping/percolation model incorporating mixed-valence ratio, segment correlation length, film/contact resistance, and humidity-dependent ionic leakage—to room-temperature σfilm that is high enough to overcome contact-limited noise yet low enough to preserve high chemiresistive modulation upon analyte-induced redox/coordination perturbations.
Plan: Step 0 — Hard design constraints (pre-synthesis) to guarantee confinement/continuity
0.1 Intrachannel-only docking geometry (exclude interchannel bridging): Select a 1D-channel host topology where (i) channels are separated by pore-wall thickness > 7 Å (through-framework distance between adjacent channel voids), and (ii) docking pockets are oriented strictly into the channel with a steric ‘backstop’ to prevent outward coordination. Implement with mixed-linker substitution where the minority docking linker bears a chelator (e.g., bipyridyl, hydroxamate, salicylaldimine-like O,N set) attached through a rigid spacer that fixes its bite vector toward the channel centerline.
0.2 Geometric acceptance rule (computational, before synthesis): For each candidate host, compute from the crystal structure:
- Intrachannel docking-to-docking distance (d_in) along the channel axis and its distribution.
- Minimum interchannel docking-pocket approach distance (d_out) through the framework.
Require: d_out − d_in ≥ 4 Å AND docking bite vectors deviate < 15° from the channel radial direction (ensures that a bidentate quinone/catecholate bridge can only close within the same channel). Reject hosts failing this.
0.3 Bridging ligand length matching: Choose quinone/catecholate derivatives with terminal coordination distances that match d_in within ±5% to suppress chain termination and off-axis coordination. Prepare a small ligand library (3“5 ligands) spanning electron-withdrawing/donating substituents (e.g., F/Cl/CF3 vs Me/OMe) while keeping the backbone length constant.

Step 1 — MOFomics dataset: descriptor provenance, size, and uncertainty strategy
1.1 Data assembly (minimum viable dataset sizes):
- Host scaffold dataset: ≥200 structures (experimental + hypothetical isoreticular variants) with measured or GCMC-predicted BET/pore volume/PSD and qualitative stability labels (water/acid/base tolerance) supplemented by computed bond valence/metal“ligand strength proxies.
- Electronic/transport dataset (label scarcity acknowledged): ≥50 frameworks/variants with experimentally measured band gap (DRS), σ(T), and/or activation energy; for mixed-valence Cu motifs include ≥20 entries with XAS/EPR-confirmed valence ratios.
1.2 Descriptor provenance (explicit):
- Measured: BET, PXRD stability, DRS band gap, σ(T), Ea, ICP-MS leaching.
- Computed: GCMC uptake/accessible surface after docking (geometric pore blocking model), DFT(+U) band edges/DOS for a *calibrated subset*, and polaron hopping barriers from cluster Marcus analysis (see Step 3).
1.3 DFT(+U) calibration protocol (to control U/spin/defects sensitivity):
- Calibrate U on Cu using a training subset where XPS/XAS valence ratios and optical gaps are measured; choose U that minimizes error in (i) band gap and (ii) Cu 2p core-level shifts/charge localization trends.
- Sample multiple charge/spin orderings for mixed valence (at least 3 orderings per structure) and propagate the spread as label uncertainty.
1.4 Model + acquisition: Use an uncertainty-calibrated surrogate (Gaussian process or GNN with conformal prediction) and a multi-objective acquisition function that penalizes high-uncertainty electronic labels unless they are within the ‘decision boundary’ for go/no-go. Maintain an external test set (≥20% of data, time-split if possible).
1.5 Candidate downselect (6“10 total): stratify by docking density (e.g., 2%, 5%, 10% docking-linker fraction) and by ligand substituent set (EWG/EDG) while holding host constant for mechanistic comparability.

Step 2 — Synthesis with engineered docking-site topology and controlled intrapore metallation
2.1 Host synthesis (robust high-area 1D channels):
- Primary host family: Ti-oxo carboxylate (MUV-10-like) for hydrolytic robustness and tunable band structure; secondary control family: Zr6-oxo carboxylate with analogous channel dimensions.
- Mixed-linker implementation: majority trimesate-type linker for rigidity + minority docking linker (2“10 mol%) bearing fixed inward chelator. Verify linker incorporation by digestion NMR and quantitative LC-MS of digests.
2.2 Crystallinity-preserving activation (SC“SC where possible): staged solvent exchange (DMF→EtOH→acetone) followed by supercritical CO2 drying; accept as ‘activated’ only if BET retention ≥80% of undocked host reference and PXRD matches within defined Rwp threshold.
2.3 Intrapore “pore-wall chelation docking” with precipitation suppression:
- Sequence: (i) pre-coordinate redox ligand to docking pockets at low concentration under diffusion-limited conditions; (ii) rinse to remove free ligand; (iii) introduce Cu precursor under conditions favoring pocket-first binding (use weakly coordinating anions, e.g., triflate) and low supersaturation.
- Confinement control: keep total Cu loading below the calculated monolayer capacity of docking sites (target 0.9“1.1 equiv per pocket) to avoid nucleation of bulk Cu“quinone phases.
- Redox control: establish mixed valence using either electrochemical poising (working electrode film) or buffered chemical redox pairs; target Cu(I)/Cu(II) or Cu(I)/Cu(III) ratios in a controlled series (e.g., 20/80, 50/50, 80/20).
2.4 Anti-crosslinking steric safeguard: include a ‘pocket cap’ design element—bulky substituent on the docking linker positioned behind the chelator—to block outward coordination. This is a design criterion in Step 0 and verified by SCXRD (if available) or Rietveld-refined PXRD + DFT geometry optimization.

Step 3 — Falsifiable engineering test plan for continuity and confinement (mandatory acceptance criteria)
3.1 Structural confinement tests (pass/fail):
(A) SCXRD / high-resolution PXRD (where SCXRD unavailable):
- Pass if electron density / refined occupancy for Cu is localized at docking pockets with no additional Cu sites in the pore center or interchannel region.
(B) XAS (EXAFS/XANES) with quantitative fitting:
- Fit Cu first-shell coordination: require ≥85% of Cu assigned to the intended pocket coordination environment (Cu“O/N distances consistent with design ±0.05 Å), and ≤15% ‘off-target’ fraction (Cu“O-only or Cu“Cu metallic-like contributions).
(C) PDF (pair distribution function) for 1D correlation length:
- Define the Cu“Cu (or Cu“ligand“Cu) axial repeat signature. Require a minimum correlation length Lcorr ≥ 4 repeats (i.e., ≥ ~4×d_in) to claim ‘continuous sublattice’ rather than isolated dimers/trimers.
- Fail if PDF indicates significant Cu“Cu distances corresponding to interchannel bridging or bulk Cu“quinone phases.
3.2 Pore preservation tests (pass/fail):
- BET retention after docking: ≥60% of host BET AND pore size distribution retains the primary channel mode (no disappearance of the 1D channel peak).
- Reject if hysteresis/PSD indicates pore blockage beyond a pre-set pore volume loss threshold (e.g., >40%).
3.3 Precipitation/external phase exclusion:
- SEM/TEM + EDS mapping: Cu signal must be spatially uniform without external nanoparticles.
- Leaching check during washing: Cu in supernatant quantified by ICP-MS must fall below threshold after final rinse (define threshold, e.g., <1% of total Cu per wash step).

Step 4 — Quantitative transport/percolation model tied to measurable targets (mandatory)
4.1 Model form (inputs → σfilm prediction):
- Treat the Cu“L“Cu chain as a 1D hopping network with site occupation probability p (fraction of docking pockets successfully metallated and bridged) and segment length distribution determined from Lcorr.
- Effective conductivity along channels: σchain(T) = σ0 · p · exp(−Ea/kT), where Ea is obtained from Marcus hopping: Ea ≈ (λ/4)·(1 + ΔG°/λ)^2; λ (reorganization) and ΔG° (driving force) are estimated from cluster calculations and experimentally constrained by optical/XPS redox energetics.
- Percolation/continuity criterion: require p above a critical value for finite-length channels; operationally enforce via Lcorr criterion in Step 3.
4.2 Incorporate film/contact resistance and humidity explicitly:
- Use a series resistance model: Rmeas = Rcontact + (L/A)/σfilm.
- Establish target σfilm range so that Rcontact does not dominate (e.g., require Rfilm ≤ 0.3·Rcontact in baseline to ensure measurable modulation; determine Rcontact empirically from transmission line method on blank electrodes).
- Humidity term: include parallel ionic leakage conductance Gion(RH) extracted from impedance spectroscopy; require σelectronic to exceed humidity-induced ionic contribution under operating RH (e.g., 20“60% RH) by a defined factor (≥5×) to maintain chemiresistive specificity.
4.3 Justify the 0.8“2.5 eV ‘band-gap window’ via targets:
- For room-temperature operation, aim for Ea ≈ 0.05“0.25 eV to obtain σfilm in ~10^−6 to 10^−3 S·cm^−1 (measurable on microelectrode films without being fully metallic). Use the calibrated relationship between optical gap / charge-transfer energy and Ea (from Step 4.1 + Step 3.2 data) rather than assuming a direct band-gap-to-σ mapping.
- Predetermine go/no-go conductivity: if σfilm(298 K) < 10^−8 S·cm^−1 (contact-limited/noise dominated) OR >10^−2 S·cm^−1 (response compression), deprioritize that candidate for sensing arrays.
4.4 Experimental extraction:
- Temperature-dependent two-/four-probe σ(T) on oriented films; fit ln(σT^n) vs 1/T to distinguish hopping vs band-like transport.
- Impedance spectroscopy vs RH to separate electronic/ionic components.

Step 5 — Redox/humidity stability protocol and decision tree (mandatory)
5.1 Cycling protocol (quantified):
- Redox cycling: 100 cycles between defined potentials (or chemical redox states) corresponding to Cu valence ratio swings (e.g., 20/80 ↔ 80/20), monitoring PXRD, XAS, and σ after 1, 10, 50, 100 cycles.
- Humidity aging: 7-day exposure at 50% RH and 25 °C + 24 h challenge at 80% RH; optionally include acidic/basic vapor pulses relevant to analytes.
5.2 Leaching and structural retention metrics:
- ICP-MS on condensate/extracts: cumulative Cu loss must be ≤5% after full protocol.
- BET retention after cycling/aging: ≥70% of post-docking BET.
- PXRD similarity: predefined threshold (e.g., peak positions retained; Rietveld residual change within set bounds).
5.3 Go/no-go decision tree:
- Go to sensor array scaling only if ALL are met: (i) confinement/continuity acceptance (Step 3.1), (ii) σfilm in target window and humidity specificity (Step 4), (iii) stability retention (Step 5.2).
- If continuity fails but porosity/stability passes: increase docking density or improve ligand length matching.
- If precipitation/off-target Cu fraction fails: reduce Cu activity (precursor/anion), lower loading, or strengthen pocket selectivity.
- If humidity causes ionic domination: introduce hydrophobic pore-surface modulation (minimal, to preserve uptake) or operate with RH compensation algorithm; only proceed if electronic/ionic separation is restored.

Step 6 — Sensor fabrication, mechanistic validation, and closed-loop MOFomics update
6.1 Film fabrication: oriented films on interdigitated electrodes via seeded growth or electrophoretic deposition of nanocrystals followed by mild necking; quantify Rcontact via TLM.
6.2 Sensing tests: analytes (NH3, H2S, NO2, VOCs) under controlled RH; report sensitivity, response/recovery times, drift over cycling.
6.3 Mechanistic causality: combine QCM uptake, in situ DRIFTS (adsorption site identification), in situ XAS/EPR/XPS (valence ratio shift), and in situ conductivity to verify that analyte adsorption perturbs Cu/ligand redox equilibrium and hence hopping rate.
6.4 Controls: host-only, sublattice-only analog (dense conductive CP with low area), and dual-network to demonstrate decoupling.
6.5 Feedback: update the surrogate model with measured labels and uncertainties; refine docking periodicity rules and ligand substituent selection for specific analyte classes.
Feasibility: 1) Chemical/structural feasibility is de-risked by ‘geometry-first’ confinement: docking-site topology is pre-screened so only intrachannel bidentate closure is allowed (steric backstop + inward bite vectors + d_out − d_in margin). This directly addresses the reviewer’s concern about interchannel crosslinking.
2) Off-target Cu“quinone precipitation and pore blockage are controlled by (i) pocket-first binding sequence, (ii) strict Cu loading capped to docking capacity, and (iii) explicit rejection criteria based on EXAFS off-target fraction (≤15%), PDF signatures, and microscopy. The proposal no longer assumes success; it defines what constitutes failure and how it will be detected early.
3) Continuity of the 1D sublattice is made falsifiable via a minimum Cu“Cu correlation length (Lcorr ≥ 4 repeats) from PDF plus SCXRD/PXRD site localization and XAS quantification—meeting the mandated engineering test plan.
4) The band-gap target is mechanistically justified through a quantitative transport framework: σfilm is predicted/fit as a function of docking occupation p, mixed-valence ratio, and hopping barrier Ea (Marcus), then translated into measurable Rmeas including contact resistance and humidity-induced ionic leakage. This converts the 0.8“2.5 eV ‘window’ into an operational requirement tied to σfilm and sensor SNR rather than a generic semiconducting range.
5) Stability concerns (redox cycling + humidity) are addressed with a defined protocol (cycle counts, RH levels) and hard metrics (ICP-MS Cu loss ≤5%; BET and PXRD retention thresholds) plus a go/no-go decision tree before scaling.
6) MOFomics predictive risk is bounded by explicit descriptor provenance, minimum dataset sizes, DFT(+U) calibration to experimental references, propagation of spin/charge-ordering uncertainty, and external test-set validation with uncertainty-calibrated acquisition to avoid overclaiming. This ensures that computation informs design without being treated as infallible.
Grounding in prior art from the provided assets: (i) electrically conductive coordination polymers and their sensor relevance motivate chemiresistive targets and the need for controlled doping/porous electrodes; (ii) mixed-valence Cu MOFs with non-innocent benzoquinoid ligands demonstrate feasible semiconducting transport pathways; (iii) robust Ti-oxo frameworks show high surface area and band-gap tunability via heterometal doping; (iv) MOFomics/high-throughput screening is established for adsorption and structure“property mapping and is extended here with disciplined uncertainty handling.

Hypothesis: In HKUST-1, external pressure does not directly “amplify” gas polarizability; instead, pressure increases loading and drives a coordination/packing transition in which O2 (and other quadrupolar/paramagnetic guests) increasingly populate the coordinatively unsaturated Cu(II) paddlewheel sites and their first-shell vicinity. This changes (i) site occupancy statistics, (ii) guest orientation distributions, and (iii) the local electric field magnitude and anisotropy experienced by both guest and node. We hypothesize that these loading-dependent local fields induce non-negligible polarization energy (induction + charge“quadrupole) at open Cu sites that is systematically underestimated by non-polarizable force fields, and that this polarization manifests as predictable, loading-dependent vibrational frequency shifts. Specifically, we predict two pressure-resolved adsorption regimes in HKUST-1: (Regime A) low loading where adsorption is dominated by pore-filling with weak field gradients and small induced dipoles; (Regime B) higher loading where Cu-site occupancy increases and local fields at/near Cu generate larger induced dipoles and altered Cu“O(carboxylate)/Cu“Cu force constants and guest intramolecular modes. By combining a fully specified induced-dipole (Thole-damped) polarizable GCMC protocol with a quantitative Raman linkage—mapping simulated local field/polarization energy and site populations to computed vibrational frequency shifts on representative loaded fragments—we will mechanistically separate electronic induction signatures from confounders (framework strain/compression, residual hydration/site blocking, and pressure-induced structural changes). A physically realistic comparison to zeolite NaX will be made by explicitly including Na+ cation sites and framework/guest polarizability, and by focusing on comparable observables (guest-mode Raman/IR shifts and adsorption thermodynamics) rather than non-analogous framework modes.
Plan: Step 0 — Materials control and activation state definition (HKUST-1 vs NaX)
0.1 HKUST-1 synthesis/activation: Synthesize phase-pure HKUST-1; activate under dynamic vacuum with a temperature program (e.g., 120“180 °C) to target a controlled fraction of open Cu sites. Prepare three controlled states: (i) fully activated (max open sites), (ii) partially hydrated (controlled H2O dose), (iii) site-blocked control (e.g., low-dose NH3 or pyridine as a strong ligand at Cu) to suppress open-site adsorption.
0.2 Verify open-site fraction and residual water: (a) CO-probe IR (Cu(I)/Cu(II)“CO band intensity as site metric), (b) TGA/DSC for residual solvent/water, (c) XANES/EXAFS at Cu K-edge to confirm coordination number changes upon activation/hydration, (d) PXRD to confirm phase purity.
0.3 NaX preparation: Ion-exchange NaX to a defined Na+ population (avoid mixed cations); dehydrate under controlled conditions. Quantify water content by TGA and confirm cation distribution consistency (as feasible) by composition analysis and literature-informed site occupancy (SI/SII positions).

Step 1 — Polarizable force field choice and full polarizable GCMC specification (mandatory: one formalism)
1.1 Polarization formalism: Use an induced point-dipole model with Thole damping (not Drude) to avoid adding explicit Drude particles in GCMC moves. Assign polarizabilities to: (i) Cu centers (anisotropic tensor, αCu, reflecting open-site directionality), (ii) key node atoms (carboxylate O, selected Cu-adjacent O/C atoms) with smaller isotropic α, and (iii) guest molecules (O2, N2, H2) with literature polarizability tensors (and quadrupole moments where appropriate). Organic linker atoms otherwise retain fixed partial charges.
1.2 Total energy per configuration:
Utotal = UvdW + Uperm-elec + Upol + U3body(optional)
where
- UvdW: Lennard-Jones 12-6 with Lorentz“Berthelot mixing (or refit near Cu if needed).
- Uperm-elec: Coulomb interactions among permanent charges and guest multipoles (include at least quadrupoles for N2/O2 if using explicit multipole model; otherwise represent via charged sites consistent with validated models).
- Upol = 1/2 μ^T α^{-1} μ − μ · Eloc, summed over polarizable sites, with μ induced dipoles and Eloc the local electric field from permanent charges/multipoles and other induced dipoles.
- Thole damping: Apply Thole screening to dipole“dipole interactions and field contributions using an exponential Thole function with damping parameter a (to be fit; initial a ≈ 0.3“0.4 typical) to prevent polarization catastrophe near open Cu.
1.3 Self-consistent induced dipole solution per MC move:
- For each trial insertion/deletion/translation/rotation, solve induced dipoles by iterative SCF (e.g., successive over-relaxation or conjugate gradient).
- Convergence: max| Δμ | < 1×10−5 Debye or relative change in Upol < 1×10−7 per polarizable site; cap iterations (e.g., 200) with fallback to rejected move if not converged.
- Use predictor: initialize induced dipoles from previous accepted configuration to accelerate convergence.
1.4 Long-range electrostatics:
- Periodic boundary conditions with Ewald summation for permanent charges/multipoles.
- For induced dipoles: use Ewald for dipole“dipole interactions (polarization Ewald) with Thole damping applied in real space; reciprocal-space handled consistently (or use a PME-like implementation if available in chosen code).
- Validate convergence with respect to Ewald parameters (real-space cutoff, κ, reciprocal vectors).
1.5 Ensemble and sampling:
- Perform polarizable GCMC for O2 (primary), and N2/H2 as mechanistic comparators, across 1“50 bar and multiple temperatures (e.g., 298 K and one higher/lower T).
- Compute: excess uptake, absolute uptake, site-resolved occupancy (Cu-site vs pore), isosteric heats Qst via fluctuation formula and via Clausius“Clapeyron across temperatures.
- Output mechanistic descriptors vs loading: (i) Cu-site occupancy fraction, (ii) induced dipole magnitude distributions on Cu and guests, (iii) local electric field distributions at Cu (vector magnitude and axial component along Cu open-site direction), (iv) polarization energy partition (Cu vs guest vs node).

Step 2 — Parameterization and tiered validation set (beyond isotherms)
2.1 Ab initio training set (cluster + periodic checks):
- Cluster models: Cu2(O2CR)4 with truncated benzoate/acetate ligands and an axial open site; generate geometries with O2/N2/H2 at multiple distances/orientations (including side-on/end-on for O2) and with/without co-adsorbates to mimic higher loading.
- Compute DFT binding energies, energy decomposition proxies (e.g., induction via SAPT on reduced models where feasible), and electric field/induced dipole response; extract anisotropic polarizability tensor at Cu site (or effective tensor fit) consistent with observed coordination environment.
- Periodic benchmark: a small set of periodic DFT single-point adsorption energies and charge response (e.g., Bader/CM5) at representative loadings to verify transferability.
2.2 Force field fitting targets:
- Match DFT binding energies at Cu site (low coverage) within ~1“2 kJ/mol.
- Match distance/orientation dependence of adsorption near Cu (potential energy surface).
- Match induced dipole magnitude trends and field response (effective polarizability) from DFT.
2.3 Experimental validation tiers:
Tier 1 (thermodynamics): high-pressure isotherms up to ≥30 bar (HKUST-1 benchmarked to known performance; connect to Asset 1 methodology) and Qst vs loading.
Tier 2 (site populations/structures): where feasible, use in situ PXRD or neutron diffraction (or literature data) to validate Cu-site vs pore filling populations; alternatively, use in situ XAS under gas pressure to track coordination changes at Cu.
Tier 3 (spectroscopy): Raman/IR guest-mode shifts and framework-mode shifts vs pressure/loading, with controls for hydration and site blocking.

Step 3 — Explicit pressure-to-loading-to-field mechanism and framework strain control
3.1 Pressure affects loading/packing: Convert pressure to chemical potential in GCMC; compute adsorption isotherms and occupancy transitions; identify pressures at which Cu-site occupancy sharply increases.
3.2 Framework mechanics/strain handling:
- Primary approach: justify rigid lattice for baseline by citing HKUST-1 structural robustness under cycling/high pressure (Asset 1) and confirm by in situ PXRD cell-parameter tracking under pressure.
- Add a correction/uncertainty analysis: incorporate an effective compressibility model by repeating GCMC on two to three lattices with cell parameters adjusted according to measured (or literature) compressibility; quantify impact on (i) uptake, (ii) Cu-site occupancy, (iii) predicted Raman shifts.
- Distinguish strain vs induction: if Raman shifts correlate with measured cell contraction rather than simulated local-field metrics, attribute accordingly; use blocked-site and hydrated controls to decouple.

Step 4 — Quantitative Raman linkage (mandatory mapping, not qualitative)
4.1 Define Raman observables:
- HKUST-1 framework modes sensitive to node environment: Cu“Cu stretch and Cu“O(carboxylate) vibrations (track both frequency and linewidth).
- Guest modes: O“O stretch (for O2) and N“N stretch (for N2) where detectable; if Raman weak, supplement with IR for guest modes.
4.2 Compute vibrational frequency shifts from representative loaded configurations:
- From polarizable GCMC, select statistically representative snapshots at multiple loadings (e.g., low, mid, high) and with defined Cu-site occupancy counts.
- Build embedded fragments: Cu2 paddlewheel + first coordination shell + nearest linker atoms, with external point charges/dipoles taken from the GCMC snapshot (electrostatic embedding including induced dipoles) to reproduce local field.
- Perform DFT vibrational frequency calculations on these fragments to obtain Δν for Cu“Cu, Cu“O, and guest intramolecular modes as a function of (i) Cu-site occupancy, (ii) computed local field component along the adsorption axis, and (iii) polarization energy Upol.
4.3 Establish a predictive correlation:
- Fit a regression/physics-informed model such as Δν = A·Eloc,ax + B·Upol(Cu) + C·nCu-guest + D·ΔV/V (strain term) to explicitly separate induction vs strain contributions.
- Use this to generate predicted Raman shift vs pressure curves by mapping pressure→loading (GCMC)→(Eloc, Upol, occupancy)→Δν.
4.4 Experimental Raman under pressure:
- Conduct in situ high-pressure Raman with controlled temperature; record spectra during adsorption/desorption to check reversibility and hysteresis.
- Compare measured Δν(P) and linewidth changes to predicted Δν(P) and to occupancy transitions; apply blocked-site and hydrated controls to verify that signatures vanish/shift as predicted when Cu sites are unavailable.

Step 5 — Realistic NaX comparison (mandatory: physically correct polarization + comparable observables)
5.1 NaX polarizable model:
- Include explicit Na+ cations at crystallographic sites with fixed +1 charge; represent framework (aluminosilicate) with fixed charges consistent with known NaX force fields.
- Add induced dipoles on oxygen atoms (and/or Si/Al if needed) with Thole damping; optionally include guest polarizability as above.
- Do not claim “delocalized polarization” without explicit induced-dipole sites; polarization is local on framework O atoms and interacts with strong static fields from Na+.
5.2 Comparable spectroscopic observables:
- Focus on guest vibrational shifts (O2/N2) in NaX rather than framework modes that are not symmetry-analogous to HKUST-1 node modes.
- Supplement with IR if Raman sensitivity is low in NaX; track how guest-mode shifts correlate with Na+ site occupancy and local fields predicted by GCMC.
5.3 Water/cation confounders:
- Maintain matched dehydration protocols and quantify residual water; perform a controlled “wet” NaX condition to show the effect of water on cation sites and guest-mode shifts.

Step 6 — Deliverables, robustness, and decision points
6.1 Deliverables:
- A validated polarizable GCMC workflow for HKUST-1 and NaX with full energy decomposition and occupancy statistics.
- Pressure-resolved mechanistic map: pressure→loading→Cu-site occupancy→local field/polarization energy→Raman/IR shifts.
- Clear discrimination criteria: (i) disappearance of induction-driven Raman signatures upon Cu-site blocking/hydration, (ii) distinct guest-mode shift“loading correlations in HKUST-1 vs NaX.
6.2 Robustness tests:
- Sensitivity to Thole parameter a, Cu polarizability tensor anisotropy, and partial charge set.
- Replicate simulations with alternative initial cation configurations in NaX to bound variability.
- Cycling experiments (adsorption/desorption) and post-cycling PXRD/XAS to ensure no irreversible structural change is misassigned to polarization effects.
Feasibility: Mechanistic specificity (pressure→loading→field): The revised premise removes the incorrect implication that pressure directly increases polarizability. Pressure increases chemical potential, raising loading and Cu-site occupancy; this changes local electric fields and induced dipoles, which we will compute explicitly (field and Upol distributions) and connect to spectroscopy via embedded fragment vibrational calculations. This directly addresses the reviewer request for a quantitative chain from loading-dependent fields/coordination to vibrational shifts while separating strain terms.

Algorithmic completeness of polarizable GCMC: The proposal now specifies a single polarization formalism (Thole-damped induced dipoles), explicit energy terms, SCF convergence criteria per MC move, polarization-catastrophe prevention (Thole damping), and long-range electrostatics (Ewald for charges and dipoles). These are standard, implementable components in modern polarizable simulation frameworks and are sufficient to evaluate transferability across loadings.
