Addresses (iv) mixed-linker crystallization/defects confounding: Linker incorporation and defect/modulator content are quantified by digestion 1H NMR (linker ratios + modulator), elemental analysis/ICP (cation and metal content), and sorption/stability checks. Performance is normalized to measured site density (aqueous titration), not inferred from surface area.
Addresses (v) open-site quantification mismatch: Gas-phase probe IR is replaced by aqueous-relevant site titration and (where feasible) ITC, giving a direct measure of accessible Lewis-acid sites under conditions comparable to tea. This strengthens attribution of kinetics/selectivity to the designed mechanism.
Overall, the proposal remains coherent with the original concept chain (charge-patterned pores + Al“F chemisorption), but de-risks operational realism by adding (a) explicit antifouling architecture, (b) quantitative competition mapping, and (c) a predictive electrostatics/specific-binding framework that can falsify or validate when cationic pockets improve fluoride selectivity in high-ionic-strength tea.

Hypothesis: A Zr6-oxo cluster MOF synthesized under hydrothermal/solvothermal conditions from ZrCl4 can be methodologically adapted into a covalently addressable, ratiometric signal-transduction platform by (i) embedding a low-density, spatially separated population of maleimide handles via mixed-linker incorporation and (ii) post-synthetically coupling Cy5 through a Sulfo-SMCC-derived thiol“maleimide conjugation scheme. The mechanistic superiority arises from (a) Zr“carboxylate bond robustness (UiO-type connectivity) preserving pore topology during aqueous bioconjugation, (b) enforced dye isolation within rigid cages minimizing Cy5 homo-FRET/self-quenching, and (c) stimulus-driven modulation of Cy5’s radiative vs nonradiative pathways through controlled proximity to Zr6 nodes and/or co-installed quenchers, converting molecular recognition events (e.g., target-triggered displacement or cleavage of a gatekeeper) into amplified fluorescence changes that constitute a transduced signal.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and MOF design.
1.1 Select a Zr6-node framework with high aqueous stability (UiO-66 or UiO-67 topology) and design a mixed-linker set: (A) terephthalic acid (or bpdc for UiO-67) for structural integrity; (B) a low-mole-fraction functional linker bearing a protected thiol or amine for later conversion into a maleimide-reactive handle (e.g., 2-aminoterephthalic acid or a thioacetate-functionalized dicarboxylate).
1.2 Define target handle density (e.g., 0.5“5 mol% functional linker) to keep average Cy5“Cy5 distances above the Förster radius and suppress self-quenching.

Step 2: Adapted methodology—hydrothermal/solvothermal ZrCl4 synthesis + orthogonal covalent dye wiring.
2.1 Synthesize the mixed-linker Zr-MOF using ZrCl4 under solvothermal/hydrothermal conditions (DMF/H2O with acid modulator such as HCl or acetic acid) to control defect density and preserve crystallinity; tune water fraction and modulator to minimize missing-linker defects that would create uncontrolled adsorption sites for dyes.
2.2 Post-synthetic handle installation (two routes, choose based on linker):
- Route A (amine-to-maleimide): Convert “NH2 linkers to surface/pore maleimides by acylation with a heterobifunctional NHS“maleimide reagent (or install a bismaleimide spacer) under mild conditions; verify by solid-state NMR/FTIR (maleimide C=O), and quantify by digestion NMR.
- Route B (protected thiol): Deprotect thioacetate to free “SH, then couple to a maleimide-bearing spacer anchored to the framework (or directly exploit thiol“maleimide using a maleimide-functionalized linker installed during synthesis).
2.3 Cy5 wiring via Sulfo-SMCC logic: Prepare a thiolated Cy5 (commercial Cy5“SH or generate by reducing Cy5“S“S“Cy5 analogs) and couple to MOF maleimide sites (thiol“maleimide Michael addition). If Cy5 is available as an amine derivative, use Sulfo-SMCC in solution to form Cy5“SMCC“maleimide/thiol intermediates, then couple to the complementary handle on the MOF (ensuring the sulfonated SMCC improves aqueous compatibility and limits nonspecific hydrophobic adsorption).
2.4 Build the signal-transduction element: Install a stimulus-responsive “gatekeeper” that modulates Cy5 emission. Two mechanistic implementations:
- DNA/aptamer displacement gate (Asset-1-compatible): Anchor a short thiolated DNA/aptamer strand to remaining maleimide sites; hybridize a complementary quencher-labeled strand positioned to quench Cy5 by FRET. Target binding triggers strand displacement, increasing Cy5 fluorescence.
- Cleavable linker gate: Introduce a disulfide- or enzyme-cleavable spacer between MOF and a proximal quencher; activation separates quencher from Cy5, producing turn-on signal.
2.5 Prepare controls: (i) MOF without Cy5, (ii) Cy5 physically adsorbed (no covalent linkage), (iii) MOF with high dye loading (intentional self-quenching), (iv) MOF with handles but no gatekeeper.

Step 3: Validation—structural integrity, covalent specificity, and mechanistic proof of transduction.
3.1 Confirm MOF crystallinity/porosity pre- and post-functionalization: PXRD, N2 sorption, TGA; assess aqueous stability in buffer (pH 6“8) and ionic strength.
3.2 Verify covalent conjugation and quantify loading/spacing: digestion 1H NMR (linker ratios), UV“vis (Cy5 loading), XPS (S/N signatures), confocal fluorescence mapping to check homogeneous distribution.
3.3 Mechanistic fluorescence assays: measure quantum yield and lifetime (TCSPC) to distinguish dequenching vs dye release; evaluate FRET efficiency where quenchers are used. Compare covalent vs physisorbed Cy5 to demonstrate reduced leaching and improved signal stability.
3.4 Signal-transduction performance: generate dose“response curves for the chosen trigger (target DNA, enzyme, reductant), determine LOD, dynamic range, and selectivity (mismatched sequences/competitive analytes). Demonstrate amplification by showing that small trigger concentrations yield large fluorescence changes due to gating/displacement rather than stoichiometric dye release.
3.5 Stress tests: repeated switching cycles (if reversible gate), storage stability, and operation in complex media (serum-mimic) to validate practicality.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zr6-node MOFs derived from ZrCl4 are among the most hydrolytically stable MOFs due to high-valent Zr“O bonds; mixed-linker strategies are established for introducing functional groups while retaining UiO topology. Fluorophore-loaded/gated MOFs have demonstrated amplified fluorescence readouts via displacement-controlled release/activation, supporting the transduction concept.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The key adaptation is not merely loading Cy5, but engineering a covalent, spatially diluted attachment architecture within a hydrothermally robust Zr-MOF so that aqueous bioconjugation chemistry (Sulfo-SMCC/thiol“maleimide) becomes compatible with rigid reticular scaffolds. Mixed-linker installation provides addressable sites without collapsing porosity, enabling mechanistic control over dye spacing and quenching interactions.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to noncovalent dye adsorption, the proposed covalent wiring minimizes dye leaching, improves reproducibility, and enables lifetime-based mechanistic discrimination. Compared to random high-loading fluorophore incorporation, controlled handle density suppresses Cy5 self-quenching and creates a larger effective signal swing upon gating. The Zr-MOF’s stability under hydrothermal-derived synthesis and aqueous assay conditions provides durability for repeated signal-transduction cycles.

Hypothesis: A structurally precise, aqueous-stable derivative of the Ca“btc framework can be converted into an ultralow-detection-limit electrochemical immunosensor by engineering (i) a single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC“SC) solvent-exchange/locking transformation that replaces labile DMF/H2O ligation with multidentate polyol anchoring and (ii) a micropore-volume-matched, hydrogen-bonded sucrose network that acts as a dielectric/solvation gate for hydrogen-spillover-generated H-atom flux, thereby transducing immunorecognition into a high-gain redox-current change. Mechanistically, sucrose (polyol) coordinates and hydrogen-bonds to Ca(II) nodes/carboxylates to create a confined proton-relay/solvation shell that increases the residence time and effective activity of spillover H species at the electrode“MOF interface; this sharply modulates charge-transfer resistance and faradaic amplification at a tethered redox mediator layer, yielding a lower detection limit than conventional MOF films limited by insulating behavior and slow ion transport.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 SC“SC framework locking (new methodological adaptation): synthesize single crystals/nanocrystals of [Ca3(btc)2(DMF)2(H2O)2]·3H2O, then perform stepwise SC“SC solvent exchange DMF→EtOH→H2O, followed by in-framework “polyol locking” using a Ca-binding multidentate polyol (sucrose or sucrose-derived polyol fragment) under mild conditions to partially replace terminal H2O ligands and bridge adjacent Ca sites without amorphization. Confirm SC“SC retention by single-crystal XRD (crystals) or total scattering/PDF + PXRD (nanocrystals).
1.2 Micropore-volume programming: generate a controlled series of locked Ca“btc samples with systematically varied micropore volume by adjusting the degree of polyol locking (short exposure/low activity → lightly locked; longer/higher activity → more locked). Quantify micropore volume and pore size distribution via CO2 sorption (273 K) and water sorption (303 K), and correlate with crystal water content/TGA.
1.3 Hydrogen-bond landscape mapping: characterize sucrose/polyol binding motifs and H-bond networks using FTIR (νOH/νC=O shifts), solid-state 13C NMR (polyol environments), and microcalorimetry (sucrose sorption enthalpy). Establish a quantitative descriptor: “H-bond relay density” from combined water uptake at low P/P0 and sorption enthalpy.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Electrode architecture (distinct from rejected draft): build a spillover-enabled transducer by depositing Pt/active-carbon nano-islands onto a conductive substrate (e.g., gold or glassy carbon) to generate dissociated hydrogen under mild electrochemical bias; overlay with a thin, binder-free layer of polyol-locked Ca“btc nanocrystals using electrophoretic assembly followed by a brief humid anneal to form interparticle necks through Ca“carboxylate recoordination (no polymer scaffold).
2.2 Hydrogen-spillover coupling to micropores: tune Pt/AC island density and MOF thickness (e.g., 100“500 nm) so that H spillover diffusion length matches the micropore network. Verify spillover incorporation by comparing H2 uptake proxies (ambient-pressure H2 adsorption or electrochemical hydrogen uptake signatures) across the micropore-volume series.
2.3 Immunosensor chemistry: functionalize the outer MOF surface with a minimal, site-specific linker layer (e.g., phosphonate-terminated PEG short chain) that binds Ca(II) nodes yet preserves pores; conjugate capture antibodies to terminal groups. Use a sandwich format where the detection antibody carries a redox mediator enzyme tag (e.g., HRP) or a redox nanoparticle label positioned within 10“30 nm of the MOF surface.
2.4 Sucrose-enabled gating (core mechanism): operate the assay in a sucrose-containing electrolyte so sucrose partitions into the locked micropores and maintains the designed hydrogen-bonded solvation shell. Upon immunocomplex formation, the labeled redox element locally consumes/produces electroactive species; the spillover H flux and sucrose H-bond relay co-modulate interfacial proton/electron-coupled transport through the MOF, producing an amplified change in DPV current and/or EIS charge-transfer resistance.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Mechanistic proof of the hydrogen-spillover/H-bond gate: (i) compare signals under H2 vs Ar atmosphere and with/without Pt/AC islands; (ii) isotope test using D2 (kinetic isotope effect on signal amplification); (iii) sucrose-dependence test using equiosmolar non-H-bond-matched controls (e.g., sorbitol, glucose) to separate polyol coordination strength vs mere viscosity/osmolarity.
3.2 Structure“property regression: relate detection limit and sensitivity to (a) micropore volume, (b) water/sucrose sorption enthalpy, (c) spillover efficiency metric (electrochemical H uptake or H2 adsorption proxy), and (d) film thickness/porosity from cross-sectional SEM.
3.3 Analytical performance: determine LOD (S/N=3), LOQ, linear range, selectivity against common interferents, batch-to-batch reproducibility, and operational stability in aqueous media. Benchmark against a standard MOF film (e.g., UiO-66-NH2 without spillover islands) and against unlocked Ca“btc (no polyol locking).
3.4 Failure-mode controls: verify framework integrity post-assay via PXRD/PDF; monitor Ca leaching by ICP-MS; ensure that polyol locking suppresses dissolution under working electrolyte conditions.
3.5 Optional cross-property validation: measure hydrogen uptake (ambient/cryogenic) before and after polyol locking and after sensor operation to confirm that the active state corresponds to a preserved, accessible micropore network rather than pore collapse or fouling.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: (i) Ca“carboxylate coordination environments are labile enough to allow SC“SC ligand/solvent exchange yet can be stabilized by multidentate O-donor binding; (ii) hydrogen bonding and hydrophilic sites are known to govern sorption/transport in microporous MOFs and correlate with micropore volume; (iii) hydrogen spillover is an established route to increase hydrogen uptake in MOFs and provides a chemically addressable flux of reactive H species that can modulate interfacial electrochemistry.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): This proposal converts a specific Ca“btc material into a new function by a molecularly defined SC“SC “polyol locking” transformation that simultaneously controls micropore volume and installs a persistent hydrogen-bond relay network (sucrose-derived). The sensing mechanism is not a generic MOF coating effect; it is a designed coupling between (a) spillover H transport through micropores and (b) polyol-stabilized solvation/proton-relay microenvironments at Ca nodes.
3. Comparative Advantage: Relative to conventional MOF-based immunosensors that are limited by insulating films or purely pH-triggered release schemes, the spillover-coupled, polyol-locked Ca“btc introduces an additional amplification axis (H-atom flux) while improving aqueous robustness through coordination locking. Micropore-volume matching provides a rational knob to maximize flux-to-current transduction, enabling lower detection limits with fewer labels and reduced background drift.

Hypothesis: A hierarchically porous HKUST-1 (Cu3(BTC)2) derivative can be reproducibly converted into a dual-function gas-storage/CT-imaging platform if—and only if—(i) mesoporosity is introduced by CTAB micelle co-assembly (target 5“20 nm) while (ii) Keggin phosphotungstate is rendered chemically compatible with Cu(II) paddlewheel formation and is forced to partition into the microporous wall domain via controlled ion-pair preorganization and acid-management. Mechanistically, unmodified H3PW12O40 is a strong Brønsted acid that can (a) lower local pH, (b) compete for Cu(II) coordination/hydrolysis equilibria, and (c) drive defect-rich or amorphous POM-rich segregates that mimic ‘loading’ but destroy microporosity and reproducibility. We therefore hypothesize that partially neutralized HPW salts (Na/Cs-exchanged) pre-ion-paired with a Cu(II)-chelating quaternized pyridinium-carboxylate additive will (1) suppress acid-driven framework defects by keeping the synthesis pH in a narrow window compatible with paddlewheel formation, and (2) kinetically trap intact Keggin anions inside the evolving microporous lattice (wall-confined) before CTAB micelles fully organize the mesophase. The resulting architecture—microporous walls containing immobilized W-rich HPW (high X-ray attenuation; strong polarizable adsorption field increasing low-pressure CO2 affinity) separated by ordered mesopores (short diffusion pathlengths; reduced intracrystalline mass-transfer resistance)—will outperform (a) CTAB-only meso-HKUST-1 (fast transport but no heavy-atom CT contrast and weaker CO2 fields) and (b) post-impregnated HPW@HKUST-1 (CT contrast but external/mesopore deposition, leaching, pore blockage, and slow/desorption-limited working capacity). The refined strategy explicitly overcomes reviewer-identified failure modes by: (i) decoupling POM acidity from crystallization through salt exchange/buffering and mapping pH/ionic strength to crystallinity/defect density, and (ii) proving wall-localization through quantitative partitioning assays and full W mass balance rather than qualitative mapping alone.
Plan: Step 0 — Define quantitative go/no-go metrics (pre-registered)
0.1 Acceptance thresholds for ‘successful wall-lined hierarchical HPW@HKUST-1’:
- Micropore volume retention: ≥70% of pristine HKUST-1 (from CO2 273 K + t-plot/DR; corroborated by Ar 87 K where feasible).
- Crystallinity/phase purity: HKUST-1 PXRD match with ≥90% relative peak intensity vs pristine after template removal; no extra broad hump indicative of amorphous POM/surfactant.
- W retention and leaching: <1.0% of total W leached into PBS (pH 7.4) and 10% serum simulant over 72 h at 37 °C; Cu leaching below predefined safety screen threshold (see Step 7).
- HPW partitioning index (defined in Step 5): ≥70% of W assigned to micropore-access-limited (wall) fraction; ≤30% in mesopore/external fraction.
- Gas performance: deliverable CO2 working capacity (298 K) in 1.0 bar → 0.15 bar window ≥20% higher than pristine HKUST-1 at matched pellet density OR same deliverable capacity with ≥2× faster uptake half-time.
- Kinetics: uptake half-time (t50) for CO2 at 298 K reduced by ≥2× vs HPW-impregnated HKUST-1 and ≤1.2× of CTAB-only hierarchical HKUST-1.
- CT: ≥2× HU per unit mass vs iodine benchmark at equal metal loading (W vs I comparison at matched mg mL−1 heavy element) and colloidal stability sufficient for phantom reproducibility (DLS PDI <0.2 after 24 h in PBS).

Step 1 — Acid-management and compatibility map (mandatory pH/ionic strength control)
1.1 Prepare three HPW forms to explicitly manage acidity and ionic strength:
- H-HPW: H3PW12O40 (baseline; expected to be disruptive).
- Na-HPW: Na3PW12O40 (fully neutralized counterions; minimized Brønsted acidity).
- CsxH(3−x)PW12O40 (x = 1“2): partially exchanged Cs salts to reduce acidity while increasing hydrophobicity/size for retention (Cs+ often increases POM retention in porous hosts).
1.2 Establish synthesis-buffering strategy compatible with HKUST-1:
- Operate within an empirically mapped pH window where Cu-BTC crystallizes without hydrolysis/defect surge (target initial pH ~2.2“3.2 for BTC deprotonation balance; exact window to be mapped).
- Use non-coordinating buffer/acid-base control that does not strongly bind Cu(II) (avoid phosphate/imidazole). Implement: acetate-formate mixed system (low coordination strength relative to BTC) at millimolar levels or controlled addition of triethylamine in microdoses, while tracking free Cu2+ by UV-vis/EPR proxy.
1.3 Quantitatively map pH and ionic strength vs defect/crystallinity:
- Design-of-experiments factors (expanded): (a) CTAB/Cu ratio (below CMC, near CMC, above CMC), (b) HPW salt identity (H/Na/Cs), (c) HPW loading target (5, 15, 30 wt%), (d) pyridinium additive/Cu ratio, (e) initial pH setpoint, (f) ionic strength step timing (see Step 3).
- For each run, log pH(t) during first 60 min and at end; record conductivity as ionic strength proxy.
- Defect proxies: BET vs micropore volume discrepancy; thermogravimetry for missing-linker estimates; water stability cycling loss.

Step 2 — Pre-ion-pair engineering (prevent amorphous POM-rich domains)
2.1 Synthesize/select the quaternized pyridinium-carboxylate additive with two functions: (i) strong electrostatic ion-pairing with HPW (charge matching), (ii) transient Cu(II) anchoring via carboxylate while minimizing permanent framework substitution.
- Example: N-(3-carboxypropyl)-4,4′-bipyridinium dibromide (as proposed) plus a second variant with steric bulk to reduce framework incorporation (e.g., benzyl-substituted viologen-carboxylate).
2.2 Pre-form HPW“additive ion pairs before MOF nucleation:
- Mix HPW salt + additive in EtOH/H2O (same solvent system as synthesis) at defined stoichiometry (target: charge-neutral ion pair; verify by zeta potential shift toward ~0 and by diffusion-ordered NMR where possible).
- Confirm intact Keggin prior to synthesis by FTIR (P“O, W“O bands) and 31P NMR in solution.
2.3 Anti-segregation criterion (pre-synthesis):
- DLS on HPW“additive solutions to ensure no large aggregates (>200 nm) prior to adding Cu/BTC; if present, tune solvent ratio and ionic strength.

Step 3 — Dual-templated crystallization with staged ionic strength (explicit locus control)
3.1 Nucleation-first sequence to trap HPW in walls:
- Stage A (micropore capture): Combine Cu(NO3)2·3H2O + pre-ion-paired HPW“additive at low ionic strength; then introduce H3BTC to initiate Cu“BTC nucleation while HPW“additive complexes are present and mobile.
- Stage B (mesophase stabilization): After a controlled delay (e.g., 10“30 min; DoE factor), add CTAB solution to exceed or approach CMC and promote ordered mesostructure around growing crystals.
3.2 Ionic strength ramp to prevent HPW migration to mesopores:
- After initial nucleation, increase ionic strength modestly (e.g., by NaNO3 at controlled mM concentration) to stabilize CTAB micelles without salting-out HPW into separate phases.
3.3 Solvothermal conditions explicitly bounded:
- 85“110 °C for 12“24 h (as drafted), but include a low-temperature option (e.g., 60“75 °C longer time) to reduce defect formation if H-HPW is problematic; all conditions evaluated against pH compatibility map (Step 1).

Step 4 — Template removal with retention safeguards (no calcination)
4.1 Remove CTAB by iterative solvent extraction:
- EtOH/NH4NO3 (or EtOH/NaNO3) at 60 °C, multiple cycles until bromide and surfactant signatures vanish (ion chromatography for Br−; FTIR for CTAB).
4.2 Define a ‘no-HPW-loss’ washing protocol:
- Collect every supernatant and wash; quantify W and Cu by ICP-MS to generate a full mass balance (Step 5.4). Stop washing when W in wash is below LOD and cumulative W loss remains within the leaching criterion.

Step 5 — Hard HPW partitioning assays (micro vs meso vs external), plus full mass balance
5.1 Stepwise pore-blocking/probe-access titration (quantitative partitioning index):
- Use size-selective probe sorbates to discriminate location:
  (i) CO2 at 273 K (accesses micropores; high sensitivity to micropore volume and fields),
  (ii) Ar at 87 K or N2 at 77 K (textural micro/meso),
  (iii) bulky vapor probe (e.g., 2,2,4-trimethylpentane or p-xylene depending on accessibility) that cannot enter micropores but can fill mesopores/external surface.
- Compare uptake changes before/after selective blocking of micropores by a reversible, small axial ligand at open Cu sites (e.g., NH3 or pyridine at controlled low coverage) to see whether W-correlated adsorption field changes track micropore-accessible domains.
5.2 Ar/CO2 sorption + t-plot/DR analysis (hard micropore retention):
- Quantify true micropore volume and micropore surface area; set acceptance threshold ≥70% pristine.
- Use CO2 273 K DR analysis to detect field-strength changes consistent with wall-confined POM rather than mesopore deposition (which minimally affects DR micropore characteristic energy).
5.3 Microtomed cross-sections with statistical STEM-EDS line profiling:
- Embed crystals, microtome to expose internal cross-sections.
- Acquire multiple radial line scans per particle (n≥30) and compute W intensity distribution vs radius.
- Define “wall-confined” signature: near-uniform internal W distribution with no edge-enriched spike; compare to impregnated control expected to be edge/mesopore enriched.
5.4 W mass-balance closure (mandatory):
- Quantify W in: initial synthesis liquor, post-synthesis mother liquor, each wash/extraction, and final solid digest.
- Require ≥95% mass-balance closure and report partitioning fractions with uncertainty.

Step 6 — Structural proof of hierarchical periodicity (beyond ‘presence’)
6.1 SAXS for mesopore periodicity and spacing; define criterion: presence of reproducible SAXS maxima corresponding to 5“20 nm repeat distances across batches.
6.2 Electron tomography (selected best samples) to quantify mesopore connectivity and wall thickness distribution; report statistical descriptors rather than representative images only.
6.3 HPW integrity in situ:
- Solid-state 31P MAS NMR (single dominant Keggin signal; absence of broad decomposition peaks).
- W L-edge XAS for oxidation state/coordination fingerprints; compare to HPW standards and to decomposed tungsten oxide reference.

Step 7 — Gas storage: bound the enthalpy/working-capacity trade-off and kinetics
7.1 Define test window and deliverable metric:
- CO2 isotherms at 273/298 K; deliverable capacity in 1.0→0.15 bar at 298 K (post-combustion relevant), and optionally 5→1 bar for other use-cases.
7.2 Qst and desorption penalty control:
- Compute Qst via Clausius“Clapeyron at multiple loadings. Predefine an upper bound to avoid ‘too-strong’ binding that kills working capacity (e.g., if Qst at low loading exceeds a set limit relative to pristine and coincides with reduced deliverable capacity, sample fails gas-storage criterion even if uptake at 1 bar is higher).
7.3 Kinetics and diffusion:
- Transient uptake (gravimetric/volumetric) fitted to appropriate diffusion models (spheres/plates); report effective diffusivities.
- PFG-NMR or QENS on top candidates to mechanistically separate transport improvement (mesopores) from adsorption-field changes (HPW).

Step 8 — Biomedical/CT translation rigor: particle size, dispersion, and minimal risk screen
8.1 Particle size control protocol:
- Tune crystallization/modulators to obtain sub-micron particles (target D50: 100“300 nm for dispersion; or explicitly justify micron-scale if only phantom demonstration is claimed).
- Measure PSD by DLS (dispersed) and SEM (dry); acceptance: PDI <0.2 after dispersion optimization.
8.2 Colloidal stabilization:
- Evaluate simple, non-destructive coatings compatible with porosity (e.g., PEGylation via surface adsorption or thin polydopamine at minimal thickness) and verify no catastrophic pore loss (still meeting ≥70% micropore volume retention).
8.3 CT phantom + stability under biorelevant media:
- Measure HU vs W concentration in agarose or hydrogel phantoms; include timepoints after 24“72 h incubation in PBS/serum simulant at 37 °C.
8.4 Minimal cytocompatibility/leach-tox risk screen (go/no-go, not full bio study):
- Quantify Cu and W leaching into cell culture media (protein-containing) by ICP-MS.
- Perform a viability screen (e.g., MTT/Alamar Blue) on at least one relevant cell line at practical concentration range; criterion: no acute toxicity beyond control threshold at imaging-relevant doses, or else reposition claim to ex vivo/phantom-only with explicit limitation.

Step 9 — Integrated structure“function model and optimization
9.1 Construct a multivariate model linking: mesopore volume/periodicity metrics (SAXS + sorption), micropore volume retention (CO2/DR), W partitioning index (Step 5), and W content to outcomes: (i) t50 and Deff, (ii) deliverable CO2 capacity, (iii) HU per mg W and per mg material.
9.2 Identify Pareto-optimal formulations that satisfy all acceptance thresholds; finalize one ‘gas-optimized’ and one ‘CT-optimized’ variant if a single optimum is not feasible.

Controls (run throughout)
- Pristine HKUST-1.
- CTAB-only hierarchical HKUST-1 (no HPW).
- HPW@HKUST-1 by post-synthetic impregnation (no CTAB), prepared at matched W loading.
- ‘Acid control’: synthesis with equivalent acid (e.g., HNO3) to match pH drop without POM, to decouple acidity-induced defects from POM-specific effects.
Feasibility: 1) Chemical compatibility is made testable and controllable: HPW acidity is the principal risk for Cu-paddlewheel disruption and defect/amorphous domain formation. By explicitly comparing H-HPW vs Na/Cs-exchanged HPW under logged pH(t) and conductivity, the proposal converts a plausibility argument into a compatibility map with direct observables (PXRD crystallinity, micropore retention, defect proxies). The pre-ion-pair step reduces POM ‘free anion’ behavior, lowering the probability of phase-separated POM-rich deposits.

2) Wall-localization is elevated from qualitative to quantitative: the combined partitioning package (size-selective probe sorption + Ar/CO2 microanalysis + microtomed statistical STEM-EDS line profiles) explicitly differentiates micropore-wall confinement from mesopore/external deposition. The full W mass-balance (initial → liquor → washes → solid) enforces closure and reproducibility, addressing the reviewer’s concern that mapping/spectroscopy alone cannot establish periodic, wall-confined positioning.

3) Performance claims are bounded by acceptance criteria and trade-off logic: the proposal now defines ‘non-catastrophic pore-volume loss’ (≥70% micropore volume retention), leaching thresholds (<1% W/72 h), kinetic targets (≥2× faster t50 vs impregnated), and a deliverable-capacity window at 298 K. Qst is treated as a constrained variable (beneficial only until it penalizes deliverability/desorption), preventing over-interpretation of higher enthalpy as automatically better storage.

4) The CT/biomedical endpoint is no longer phantom-only: particle size distribution, dispersion stability, and a minimal leach-tox risk screen (Cu/W release + basic viability assay) are incorporated as go/no-go gates. This aligns the imaging claim with biorelevant constraints while keeping scope appropriate (screening-level, not full in vivo).

5) Strong precedent and coherent mechanism chain remain intact: the approach leverages the demonstrated dual-templating concept in HKUST-1 derivatives (CTAB + HPW) while upgrading it with acid-neutralized POM chemistry and quantitative localization assays. The expected function coupling—hierarchical mesopores improving mass transport kinetics and wall-confined W-rich POM providing both adsorption-field enhancement and CT attenuation—remains the same core concept, but now is supported by a falsifiable, reviewer-proof experimental logic.

Hypothesis: A ZIF-90 coating can be engineered into a spatially segregated, dual-function architecture—(i) an outer, diffusion-limited hydrophobic “gatekeeping” shell that measurably suppresses H2O/Cl− ingress and underfilm delamination, and (ii) an internal, covalently immobilized, enantiopure imidodiphosphoric-acid (IDP) Brønsted-acid microenvironment that remains pore-accessible for asymmetric N,N-acetalization—provided that (a) ZIF-90 is operated within explicitly defined aqueous stability windows and (b) the depth distribution of post-synthetic modifications obeys a quantitatively validated reaction“diffusion functionalization model.

Mechanistic rationale (falsifiable): (1) Corrosion protection arises when the hydrophobic shell lowers effective water activity at pore mouths and increases ionic transport resistance, producing an order-of-magnitude retention in low-frequency impedance (|Z|0.01Hz) over immersion time relative to ungated ZIF-90. This is not claimed as “porosity elimination” but as a switch from continuous, water-wet percolation to intermittent/retarded wetting at the external microns, shifting the dominant EIS element from diffusion/Warburg to barrier capacitance with reduced water uptake. (2) Enantioselective catalysis persists because the IDP sites are placed predominantly beyond the shell thickness (depth-segregated) and remain accessible to organic substrates with kinetic diameters below the ZIF-90 aperture constraint, while water (and hydrated Cl−) transport is preferentially inhibited at the shell. The chiral outcome is predicted to scale with confinement: a measurable increase in ee (and/or inversion of selectivity relative to solution) that collapses when pores are blocked, when IDP is immobilized on a nonporous support, or when an enlarged-pore analogue removes confinement. (3) The entire concept is gated by MOF structural integrity: ZIF-90 crystallinity/porosity retention and Zn2+ release rates under chloride at defined pH are treated as go/no-go endpoints; failure triggers pivot to stabilization strategies (crosslinking density, shell thickness, polymer grading) rather than assuming chemical robustness.

Thus, the central claim is not merely that ‘hydrophobic gating + internal chiral acidity’ can coexist, but that spatial segregation can be quantitatively demonstrated and used to predict (and optimize) two coupled performance metrics—chloride-media barrier retention and site-normalized enantioselective turnover—within experimentally defined ZIF-90 stability boundaries.
Plan: Step 0 — Define ZIF-90 stability windows and go/no-go endpoints (mandatory risk control).
0.1 Prepare powder and film analogues of baseline ZIF-90 (same linker/metal ratio, same modulator history as coating synthesis) to decouple intrinsic framework stability from adhesion/coating defects.
0.2 Stability matrix: immerse powders and films in (i) 3.5 wt% NaCl, (ii) pH 3 chloride (HCl/NaCl), (iii) pH 10 chloride (NaOH/NaCl), and (iv) deionized water as control, at 25 °C and 60 °C (accelerated). Timepoints: 1 h, 6 h, 24 h, 7 d, 28 d.
0.3 In situ structural endpoints (go/no-go):
  - In situ GI-XRD on films during immersion (time-resolved loss of characteristic ZIF-90 reflections; define failure as >30% drop in integrated intensity of main peaks within 24 h in any target medium).
  - In situ ATR-FTIR (monitor imidazolate ring modes + “CHO band evolution; define failure as emergence of broad Zn“OH/H2O features concomitant with linker loss).
  - Zn2+ release rate by ICP-MS of immersion media (define acceptable window as ≤1% of total Zn leached per day during first 72 h at 25 °C; adjust threshold as coating thickness is known).
  - Porosity/uptake retention on powder analogues (Kr/N2 uptake; define failure as >40% loss of uptake after 7 d in target medium).
0.4 If any medium fails go/no-go: implement stabilization levers before proceeding to dual-function testing: (a) increase external hydrophobe shell density/thickness (Section 2.2), (b) introduce graded polymer infiltration (Section 2.4) to suppress continuous wetting, and/or (c) shift corrosion testing emphasis to media where stability is demonstrated while reporting the boundary explicitly.

Step 1 — Coating architecture and baseline characterization.
1.1 Substrates: mild steel and AA2024 coupons (polished to defined roughness, e.g., Ra < 50 nm), then hydroxylated oxide formation via O2 plasma (controlled dose) or mild alkaline activation; record oxide chemistry by XPS (O 1s components) to standardize nucleation.
1.2 Primer compatibility screening (addresses reviewer concerns).
  - Candidate primers: (i) phosphonate-only (alkyl bisphosphonate), (ii) catechol-only (dopamine), (iii) catechol-phosphonate hybrid.
  - Electrochemical stability screen of primer-only films on metal in NaCl via OCP drift + EIS; oxidation sensitivity via cyclic voltammetry (catechol/quinone couple) and XPS after immersion.
  - Growth compatibility: test whether each primer perturbs ZIF-90 nucleation (GI-XRD texture, SEM continuity). Downselect primer that (a) survives immersion without severe redox degradation and (b) does not inhibit ZIF-90 crystallization.
1.3 Baseline ZIF-90 film growth: seeded or interfacial solvothermal growth targeting continuous 1“10 µm films with controlled thickness (profilometry/cross-sectional SEM). Characterize:
  - GI-XRD (texture, crystallinity), SEM/AFM (coverage/roughness), FIB-SEM cross-sections (defects, through-thickness continuity).
  - Quantify “CHO density and accessibility: DRIFTS/ATR-FTIR (“CHO stretch), solid-state 13C NMR on powder analogue, and derivatization titration using a small aminooxy dye probe (UV-vis or fluorescence quantification) to estimate accessible aldehydes.

Step 2 — Quantitative reaction“diffusion model for depth-functionalization + experimental validation (mandatory).
2.1 Model definition (falsifiable): treat aldehyde functionalization as pseudo-first-order in aldehyde with a reagent concentration field C(x,t) penetrating from the external surface into the film.
  - Governing equation: ∂C/∂t = D_eff ∂^2C/∂x^2 − k_app C (where k_app lumps intrinsic oxime/imine formation kinetics under given water activity/solvent; x is depth).
  - Predict functionalization fraction f(x,t) via ∂f/∂t = k_app C (1−f), with boundary condition C(0,t)=C0 (external reagent activity) and no-flux at metal interface.
  - Extract a dimensionless segregation number: Φ = (k_app L^2 / D_eff) where L is film thickness. Target regime for surface-biased gating: Φ >> 1 for bulky hydrophobe reagents (fast consumption near surface relative to diffusion).
2.2 Experimental parameterization:
  - Determine D_eff for representative reagents using uptake kinetics on powder analogues (gravimetric sorption or QCM on thin films) and/or time-dependent XPS signal evolution on thin films.
  - Determine k_app via solution-phase model reaction of imidazole-2-carboxaldehyde with each reagent under matching solvent/water content, then adjust for confinement using early-time film data.
2.3 Depth-profile validation (critical discriminant):
  - Perform time-series functionalization with isotope-labeled or fluorinated reagents to enable ToF-SIMS depth profiling (e.g., CF3-tagged aminooxy/alkylhydrazide for gating; 19F as tracer).
  - Acquire ToF-SIMS profiles after controlled reaction times; fit f(x,t) to model to back-calculate D_eff and k_app and predict shell thickness δ(t) defined as depth where f reaches 0.8 of surface value.
  - Acceptance criterion for “true spatial segregation”: demonstrate δ_gating ≤ 10“20% of total thickness while internal region retains ≥70% of accessible pore volume (from uptake) and ≥50% of internal “CHO available for IDP installation.

Step 3 — Install internal chiral Brønsted-acid sites with quantified loading and wet stability.
3.1 IDP tether design (chemical specificity): synthesize enantiopure IDP bearing (i) aminooxy tether for oxime linkage (IDP“(CH2)n“ONH2) and/or (ii) primary amine tether for reductive amination (IDP“(CH2)n“NH2). Choose n to balance sterics and pore access (screen n=2,4,6).
3.2 Linkage selection by hydrolytic robustness (explicit test):
  - Route A (preferred): oxime formation (“CHO + “ONH2) under low-water, mildly acidic catalysis (avoid framework attack), yielding hydrolytically robust C=N“O linkage.
  - Route B: imine then NaBH3CN reduction to secondary amine (evaluate whether reducing conditions perturb ZIF-90).
3.3 Loading control and verification:
  - Quantify IDP loading by elemental analysis/XPS (P 2p) and digestion + ICP-OES for P/Zn ratio on powder analogues.
  - Confirm linkage by FTIR (oxime/imine bands), solid-state 31P NMR (IDP environment), and XPS N 1s deconvolution.
  - Demonstrate immobilization: leaching tests under catalytic solvent and under NaCl immersion; quantify IDP in solution by LC-MS and P by ICP; pass criterion: <5% IDP loss over 24 h under each relevant condition.
3.4 Wet chloride survivability of IDP-functionalized films: repeat Step 0 immersion endpoints specifically tracking (i) P 2p retention profiles (angle-resolved XPS), (ii) persistence of chiral sites (31P NMR on retrieved powders), and (iii) maintained catalytic activity after exposure (see Step 6).

Step 4 — Hydrophobic pore-mouth gating engineered as a thin shell (spatially segregated, model-guided).
4.1 Gating reagents (size-controlled): bulky long-chain aminooxy or hydrazide reagents (C12“C18) and/or branched groups to maximize Φ and minimize deep penetration.
4.2 Implement diffusion-limited conditions:
  - Use solvent systems that reduce internal wetting (e.g., low-polarity/limited-swelling solvent compatible with ZIF-90) and short reaction times predicted by model to reach target δ_gating.
  - Apply sequential functionalization: (i) internal IDP installation first (with small/medium reagent and longer time), then (ii) gating second with bulky reagent and short time to avoid internal capping.
4.3 Verification:
  - ToF-SIMS depth profiles (hydrophobe tag), angle-resolved XPS (C enrichment gradient), contact angle mapping.
  - Transport proxy: water vapor uptake (DVS) and electrolyte uptake (capacitance from EIS) before/after gating. Target: significant reduction in water uptake with minimal loss of organic-probe uptake relevant to catalysis (Step 6).

Step 5 — Interfacial adhesion strategy with electrochemical compatibility checks.
5.1 Primer downselection outcome from Step 1.2 is enforced: reject catechol-containing primers if oxidation leads to loss of adhesion or increased galvanic activity.
5.2 Demonstrate primer does not perturb Zn nodes or accelerate Zn dissolution:
  - Compare Zn2+ release (ICP-MS) of primed vs unprimed ZIF-90 films under NaCl.
  - XPS at interface (if accessible via sputter depth profiling) for Zn“O“P signatures without excessive Zn depletion.
5.3 Adhesion and underfilm delamination tests:
  - Scratch adhesion (critical load), pull-off adhesion (ASTM), and wet adhesion after immersion.
  - Delamination kinetics by EIS fitting (two-time-constant models) and scanning Kelvin probe (if available) to track underfilm corrosion front.

Step 6 — Catalysis: substrate panel matched to ZIF-90 size constraints + confinement controls (mandatory).
6.1 Aperture/cage matching (explicit):
  - Determine accessible pore/aperture constraint experimentally using uptake of a calibrated probe set (e.g., aromatics/amines of increasing kinetic diameter) on powder analogues; fit a cutoff diameter.
  - Select N,N-acetalization substrates with kinetic diameters below cutoff (Panel S, “fits”) and above cutoff (Panel L, “excluded”).
6.2 Reaction selection: choose an established IDP-Brønsted-acid-mediated asymmetric N,N-acetalization (or closely related iminium/acetal-type transformation) that is water-sensitive, so hydrophobic gating provides a mechanistic lever; run under controlled low-water conditions with deliberate water spikes to quantify gating benefit.
6.3 Controls to prove confinement-driven ee:
  - (i) Dual-functional ZIF-90 (IDP internal + hydrophobe shell).
  - (ii) IDP on nonporous silica/alumina with similar P loading (tests whether ee arises without confinement).
  - (iii) Pore-blocked ZIF-90-IDP (complete capping with small reagent) to show activity/ee collapse with blocked access.
  - (iv) Enlarged-pore analogue (if accessible) or defect-enlarged ZIF via modulator route to reduce confinement; prediction: reduced ee if confinement dominates.
6.4 Metrics and normalization:
  - Quantify conversion, ee (chiral HPLC/GC), and site-normalized TOF (normalize to accessible P sites quantified by titration of acid sites and/or P content multiplied by accessibility factor from probe uptake).
  - Hot filtration and leaching tests: monitor Zn and P in filtrate (ICP-MS) and IDP by LC-MS; show catalysis is truly heterogeneous.
6.5 Mass transport vs catalysis disentanglement:
  - Measure substrate uptake kinetics into functionalized powders (time-resolved uptake) to correlate diffusion timescales with observed rates.
  - Demonstrate that gating decreases water uptake more strongly than organic substrate uptake for Panel S, explaining maintained catalysis with improved water tolerance.

Step 7 — Corrosion performance with mechanistic discriminants tied to the model.
7.1 Test matrix across media (NaCl neutral, pH 3, pH 10) but only within stability windows established in Step 0; explicitly report any excluded regimes.
7.2 Electrochemical endpoints:
  - Time-resolved EIS (|Z|0.01Hz, coating capacitance, pore resistance) up to 28 d; potentiodynamic polarization (icorr, Ecorr).
  - Localized mapping (SVET/SECM) at defects to quantify whether gating+primer suppress localized anode formation.
7.3 Direct transport/permeability tests:
  - Cl− permeability via diffusion cell + ion chromatography.
  - Water uptake via DVS and electrochemical capacitance; correlate to ToF-SIMS-derived shell thickness and model-predicted effective D_eff.
7.4 Post-exposure structural retention:
  - GI-XRD/ATR-FTIR after immersion, Zn2+ release totals, and ToF-SIMS profiles to see whether shell and IDP gradients persist or homogenize.

Step 8 — Design-space mapping and Pareto optimization (explicit tradeoff deconvolution).
8.1 Independent variables: IDP loading (P/Zn), shell thickness δ_gating, and primer type.
8.2 Responses: (i) |Z|0.01Hz retention at day 7/28, (ii) Cl− permeability, (iii) ee and site-normalized TOF for Panel S substrates, (iv) structural integrity (GI-XRD retention; Zn2+ release).
8.3 Outcome: identify Pareto-optimal region where δ_gating reduces water/Cl− ingress without pushing organic substrate diffusion below the catalytic timescale; validate with model predictions and depth profiles.

Milestones (go/no-go summary):
M1 (Stability): ZIF-90 retains ≥70% GI-XRD intensity and ≤1% Zn/day release in the target NaCl medium at 25 °C; otherwise pivot stabilization before proceeding.
M2 (Segregation): ToF-SIMS/XPS demonstrate δ_gating confined to outer ≤20% thickness and internal porosity retention ≥70%.
M3 (Catalysis): Dual-functional material delivers ee significantly above nonporous-IDP control and shows size-exclusion behavior (Panel L inactive/low ee) with negligible leaching.
M4 (Coupled performance): Compared to baseline ZIF-90, dual-functional coatings show sustained impedance improvement (≥10× |Z|0.01Hz at defined timepoint) while preserving ≥50% of catalytic TOF for Panel S substrates.
Feasibility: 1) De-risking ZIF-90 chemical stability (addresses critique i): The revised plan treats hydrolysis/ion exchange/defect evolution as a primary risk with explicit stability windows, accelerated endpoints, and quantitative go/no-go thresholds (in situ GI-XRD, in situ ATR-FTIR, Zn2+ release kinetics, and porosity retention). This prevents proceeding on assumptions and creates a clear pivot strategy (shell densification, graded polymer infiltration, or media boundary definition) if ZIF-90 fails under certain pH/chloride conditions.

2) Spatial segregation is no longer asserted; it is modeled and measured (addresses critique ii): A reaction“diffusion framework with measurable parameters (D_eff, k_app, Φ) is introduced to predict when bulky hydrophobe reagents will be consumed near the surface before penetrating deeply. The model is validated directly against ToF-SIMS depth profiles (with 19F/label tracers) to quantify shell thickness δ_gating and demonstrate internal aldehyde/porosity retention. This is falsifiable: if profiles homogenize or δ_gating grows too thick, the design fails and conditions/reagents are reformulated.

3) Catalysis claim is constrained by pore-size logic and proven by confinement controls (addresses critique iii): The catalysis plan explicitly matches a substrate panel to experimentally determined size cutoffs (uptake-based kinetic diameter screening), then uses mandatory controls (nonporous IDP support, pore-blocked ZIF-90, and enlarged-pore/less confined analogues) to test whether ee is confinement-driven rather than an intrinsic property of immobilized IDP. Site-normalized TOF/ee comparisons and leaching tests convert “high ee” into a mechanistically attributable, reproducible claim.

4) Primer compatibility and electrochemical side effects are explicitly screened: The primer is no longer assumed benign; it is downselected by growth compatibility, redox stability, and absence of accelerated Zn dissolution or galvanic effects. Adhesion and delamination are quantified (wet adhesion + EIS delamination modeling), and the interfacial chemistry is verified.

5) Coupled-function coexistence becomes a testable design space: By mapping IDP loading versus δ_gating (and primer type) against both corrosion and catalysis metrics, the proposal replaces a qualitative “dual function” promise with a Pareto optimization that can demonstrate the intended synergy or reveal unavoidable tradeoffs.

Overall, the revised proposal remains faithful to the original concept chain (ZIF-90 aldehyde chemistry enabling covalent chiral-acid immobilization plus surface-biased hydrophobization for corrosion media), but converts the key vulnerabilities—framework stability, gradient formation, and confinement/transport limits—into quantitative, experimentally verifiable discriminants that determine success or trigger defined pivots.

Hypothesis: Air-stable, high-affinity CO2 capture at 400 ppm can be achieved by a nanoscale HHTP-based MOF whose nucleation pathway is deliberately shifted from near-spinodal, defect-rich aggregation to classical, seed-dominated nucleation through a solvent-programmed suppression of π“π stacking among HHTP-derived linkers. The methodological adaptation is a two-stage ‘stacking-gated’ synthesis: (i) pre-complex HHTP as a transient boronate-ester/protected catecholate in an aromatic co-solvent that weakens face-to-face stacking and reduces supersaturation, then (ii) trigger rapid coordination polymerization onto CD-MOF seeds under ultrasonication to enforce single-event nucleation and size focusing. Mechanistically, solvent weakening of aromatic stacking increases the nucleation barrier (reducing spinodal decomposition and defect density), while seed surfaces provide heterogeneous nucleation sites that lower the barrier selectively and confine growth, yielding nanoscale crystals with maximized accessible metal sites and cooperative CO2-binding domains that remain kinetically accessible under dry and humid air.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select an HHTP-derived linker set: HHTP (catecholate) and a ‘stacking attenuated’ analogue (e.g., 2,3,6,7,10,11-hexamethoxytriphenylene as a protected precursor, deprotected in situ) to tune π“π interaction strength.
1.2 Select metals and node chemistry targeting strong CO2 affinity at low partial pressure: (A) Mg2+/Ni2+ catecholate 2D sheets (HHTP-MOF family) and (B) mixed-metal Mg/Al catecholate nodes to increase hydrolytic robustness.
1.3 Prepare CD-MOF seeds (e.g., K+-cyclodextrin MOF) with controlled size (200“500 nm) using sonication/seed-mediated crystallization; characterize by PXRD/DLS/SEM to establish seed crystallinity and dispersibility.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 ‘Stacking-gated’ pre-organization: dissolve HHTP (or protected HHTP) in a solvent pair chosen to weaken aromatic stacking (mesitylene/dioxane baseline; expand to anisole/dioxane and chlorobenzene/THF) and add a reversible protecting/complexing agent (e.g., pinacol-boronic acid or borate source) to form transient boronate esters that reduce immediate metal-catecholate crosslinking and lower effective supersaturation.
2.2 Seeded heterogeneous nucleation: disperse CD-MOF seeds into the pre-organization mixture; introduce metal salt solution slowly (syringe pump) at fixed ionic strength to minimize homogeneous nucleation.
2.3 Sonication-triggered nucleation pulse: apply pulsed ultrasonication (e.g., 1“5 min on/off cycles) to generate a short nucleation burst preferentially on seed surfaces; immediately switch to mild stirring aging to favor diffusion-limited growth without secondary nucleation.
2.4 Deprotection/locking step (if protected HHTP used): introduce a controlled deprotection trigger (mild base or transesterification conditions) after the nucleation pulse so coordination polymerization occurs primarily on existing nuclei, not in bulk.
2.5 Solvent-exchange and activation: exchange to low-surface-tension solvents (MeOH → acetone) and activate under mild vacuum with humidity conditioning (0“40% RH) to stabilize the open sites without collapse.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Nucleation mechanism diagnosis: time-resolved turbidity/DLS + aliquot PXRD to distinguish spinodal-like continuous growth vs discrete nucleation; quantify induction time changes with solvent composition and seed loading.
3.2 Defect/stacking assessment: total scattering/PDF and Raman/UV“vis to quantify π“π stacking changes; compare domain size and disorder (Williamson“Hall analysis) across solvent programs.
3.3 Particle metrics: SEM/TEM for size distribution; BET/porosimetry for accessible porosity; quantify external surface area contributions relevant to air capture kinetics.
3.4 CO2 capture performance at relevant conditions: low-pressure CO2 isotherms down to 0.4 mbar at 25 °C; dynamic breakthrough with 400 ppm CO2 in air (dry and 40“60% RH), reporting working capacity, selectivity over N2/O2, and kinetics.
3.5 Cycling and stability: 100“500 adsorption/desorption cycles with low-grade regeneration (60“90 °C, vacuum or dry purge); track crystallinity (PXRD), capacity retention, and metal/linker leaching.
3.6 Comparative controls: (i) no-seed, no-sonication (expected defect-rich); (ii) seed-only; (iii) sonication-only; (iv) solvent program without transient complexation; benchmark against an amine-appended MOF standard (e.g., mmen-Mg2(dobpdc)) under identical air-capture protocols.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: HHTP-containing layered frameworks are prone to strong aromatic stacking, which can drive non-classical assembly and defect formation; solvent modulation of stacking has been shown to shift assembly regimes away from spinodal decomposition toward discrete nucleation and improved crystallinity. Seed-mediated, sonication-assisted CD-MOF syntheses demonstrate controllable nucleation bursts and particle size focusing, providing an experimentally validated handle on nanoscale MOF formation kinetics.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation translates COF nucleation control concepts (stacking-strength modulation via solvent choice) into coordination polymer/MOF synthesis where π“π stacking of planar linkers competes with metal“ligand network formation. Introducing CD-MOF seeds creates heterogeneous nucleation sites that decouple ‘nucleation’ from ‘growth’, enabling rational control over crystal size and defect density—key determinants for low-partial-pressure CO2 kinetics.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional solvothermal synthesis (broad size distributions, high defect densities, slower air-capture kinetics), stacking-gated seeded nucleation is expected to (i) suppress homogeneous nucleation and aggregation, (ii) yield nanoscale particles with higher accessible site density and faster mass transfer, and (iii) improve humidity tolerance by reducing stacking-induced faults that act as hydrolysis entry points. Relative to purely amine-grafted systems, the proposed material aims to combine strong low-pressure uptake with faster adsorption/desorption kinetics and size-engineered contact efficiency under direct air capture flow conditions.

Hypothesis: A staged “competitive coordination modulation → crystallographically guided oriented attachment → chemically plausible defect-generation” strategy can produce ZIF-71 mesocrystals with predictable transport acceleration without invoking chemically implausible carboxylate-for-imidazolate substitution. Mechanistically, (1) DABCO (or a closely matched tertiary diamine control) transiently lowers free Zn2+ activity via measurable Zn“DABCO complexation in the pre-nucleation window, delaying imidazolate-driven growth and enabling a high nuclei density (nano-regime) under linker-rich conditions; (2) the same transient capping alters the relative growth rates of crystallographic faces by preferential binding to undercoordinated surface Zn sites, creating a facet-dependent surface charge/termination pattern that can be mapped by zeta potential and selective probe adsorption, thereby rendering oriented attachment (OA) a testable, non-accidental outcome; (3) stable defectivity is introduced in ZIF-71 by routes known to be chemically accessible in Zn“imidazolate frameworks—(i) controlled linker-deficient synthesis (Zn-rich, ligand-poor) to embed missing-linker/missing-node defects during growth and (ii) calibrated, subcritical acid/base etching and/or halide/neutral-ligand competitive coordination that creates vacancies and mesoporous pathways while preserving the ZIF-71 topology—rather than by post-assembly carboxylate exchange. The resulting hierarchical architecture couples (a) mesocrystal order (low-angle grain boundary density and coherent crystallographic alignment) with (b) a tunable population of coordinatively unsaturated Zn sites and defect-derived mesoporosity, yielding faster guest uptake/release and improved bioavailability proxies (dispersion stability in protein media and accelerated payload release) versus non-modulated ZIF-71. The same rule set—quantified ligand competition, proton-coupled linker deprotonation control, and falsifiable OA metrics—translates to MIL-53(Al)-NH2 using established monocarboxylate modulation, while DABCO·2HCl is treated explicitly as a buffered ionic/acidic additive whose role is validated via time-resolved pH profiles and Al speciation (27Al NMR/ESI-MS), with pre-registered diagnostics to prevent phase diversion (MIL-68/MOF-235-like impurities) and to exclude DABCO framework incorporation.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration of chemical windows, pass/fail criteria, and controls (addresses reviewer falsifiability).
0.1. Define solvent systems and water content explicitly:
- ZIF-71: (A) MeOH, (B) MeOH/H2O 95:5, and (C) EtOH as robustness checks; record water content by Karl Fischer (target ±0.05 wt%).
- MIL-53(Al)-NH2: DMF/H2O (typically 9:1 v/v) with controlled added acid.
0.2. Predefine “structural pass/fail” for ZIF-71 defect generation:
PASS requires all of: (i) PXRD matches ZIF-71 reference with no new crystalline impurity peaks and ≤10% loss of integrated peak area vs baseline after normalization; (ii) total scattering/PDF retains first-shell Zn“N and Zn“N“C correlations with <10% broadening vs baseline (local order preserved); (iii) 13C/15N solid-state NMR (if linker labeled or sensitivity sufficient) shows intact imidazolate environment without new dominant carboxylate/amide resonances; (iv) N2/CO2 sorption shows reproducible increase in mesopore contribution (e.g., hysteresis + NLDFT/QSDFT shift) without collapse in micropore signature.
FAIL triggers route change: if amorphization or topology loss is detected (PXRD/PDF), revert to purely in-growth linker-deficiency and abandon etch step.
0.3. Predefine “mesocrystal OA success” metric threshold:
- SAED: azimuthal spread of primary reflections across multiple regions ≤15° (target ≤10°);
- Texture/line broadening: synchrotron PXRD shows anisotropic broadening consistent with coherent domains and a March“Dollase texture parameter indicating preferred orientation beyond random aggregate controls (quantify vs control set);
- TEM: visible subunit boundaries with shared orientation (HRTEM lattice continuity across interfaces).
0.4. Control matrix (minimum set) for OA falsification:
C1 no DABCO (baseline nano-ZIF-71); C2 DABCO constant dose (no pulsing); C3 ionic strength ramp only (no DABCO); C4 polymer-only (DHBC or PEO-b-PMAA only); C5 DABCO + polymer (if polymer becomes essential, quantify its minimum effective concentration).

Step 1 — Quantitative ligand competition/speciation map for Zn2+“DABCO vs Zn2+“imidazolate (addresses reviewer point ii).
1.1. Measure Zn“DABCO association in the exact solvent window used for ZIF-71 nucleation:
- Prepare Zn2+ solutions (e.g., Zn(NO3)2 or ZnCl2 consistent with synthesis) at 1“20 mM in MeOH (and MeOH/H2O 95:5).
- Titrate DABCO (0“10 equiv vs Zn) and record:
  a) 1H NMR chemical shift changes (DABCO) and diffusion (DOSY if possible) to infer complexation;
  b) ITC (if feasible) for K and ΔH (use MeOH-compatible setup) or, alternatively, UV“vis with a competitive chromophore proxy ligand (e.g., pyridine derivative) to extract conditional stability constants.
- Fit to 1:1 and 1:2 Zn:DABCO binding models to obtain conditional β values.
1.2. Measure imidazolate competition under nucleation-relevant basicity:
- Generate linker base form in situ (e.g., using triethylamine) and titrate linker into Zn“DABCO solutions while monitoring:
  a) 1H NMR (disappearance/shift of linker resonances),
  b) time-resolved turbidity (onset of nucleation),
  c) stopped-flow DLS for early particle formation.
- Construct an operational “dominance map” plotting turbidity onset time and particle size vs [DABCO]/[Zn] and [linker]/[Zn] at fixed base equivalents.
1.3. Convert data into design rules and pulsing schedule:
- Define a target free-Zn activity suppression factor (e.g., 5“20× reduction) required to arrest growth at 20“80 nm.
- Set initial dosing where >50% Zn is DABCO-bound (from conditional β), then pulse additional DABCO to maintain this bound fraction during the first 1“5 minutes (nucleation/growth crossover) based on observed consumption/precipitation kinetics.

Step 2 — ZIF-71 nanocrystal formation with transient DABCO capping (mechanistically constrained size control).
2.1. Baseline ZIF-71 synthesis:
- Establish reproducible ZIF-71 nanocrystal synthesis (no DABCO) with documented size distribution (TEM, DLS), phase purity (PXRD), and yield.
2.2. DABCO-modulated nucleation (nano-regime):
- Use the speciation map to select 3 conditions (low/med/high Zn suppression) targeting mean sizes 20, 50, 80 nm.
- Keep linker:Zn high (e.g., ≥8:1 as starting point) while adjusting base to maintain consistent linker deprotonation kinetics.
- Collect aliquots at sub-minute resolution for time-resolved SAXS/PXRD (or lab SAXS if synchrotron not available) to extract growth rate constants.
2.3. Validate DABCO is transient and not incorporated:
- Post-synthesis exhaustive solvent exchange (MeOH → EtOH → water) and verify DABCO removal by:
  a) solution 1H NMR of washings,
  b) elemental analysis (N content vs expected),
  c) ATR-IR for DABCO signatures,
  d) XPS N 1s deconvolution (imidazolate N vs tertiary amine N).

Step 3 — Oriented attachment (OA) into ZIF-71 mesocrystals with explicit facet/charge rationale (addresses reviewer point iii).
3.1. Map facet-dependent surface termination/charge in nano-ZIF-71:
- Measure zeta potential as a function of pH/ionic strength for (i) no-DABCO particles and (ii) DABCO-pulsed particles.
- Use selective adsorption probes to infer facet chemistry (e.g., small anions/cations, or fluorescent probes with known charge) and correlate adsorption with morphology (SEM/TEM).
3.2. OA assembly protocol with falsifiable knobs:
- Start from purified nanocrystal sols at fixed solids concentration.
- Apply ionic strength ramp with a non-coordinating electrolyte (e.g., NaNO3) in a controlled microfluidic or syringe-pump addition mode to reach a defined Debye length window (predefine 3 final ionic strengths).
- In parallel, apply DABCO pulses timed to maintain partial surface coverage during the alignment window (timing derived from Step 1 kinetics).
- Optional polymer as a quantified variable, not a hidden reagent: if DHBC/PEO-b-PMAA is used, predefine a concentration series (e.g., 0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1 wt%) and require demonstration that OA metrics improve monotonically.
3.3. OA validation:
- SEM/TEM for hierarchical structure; SAED/HRTEM for shared orientation; synchrotron PXRD texture/anisotropic broadening; compare against controls C1“C5.

Step 4 — ZIF-71 defect chemistry: replace carboxylate ‘defect-writing’ with chemically plausible routes (addresses reviewer point i and mandatory directive 1).
4.1. Route A: In-growth linker-deficient defect introduction (primary, topology-preserving).
- Systematically lower linker:Zn ratio while keeping DABCO-based Zn suppression constant to decouple size from defectivity.
- Target a monotonic defect series (low/med/high) defined by digestion analysis + TGA/EA mass balance (missing linker equivalents per Zn).
- Confirm topology retention by PXRD + PDF (pass/fail criteria in 0.2).
4.2. Route B: Calibrated subcritical etching to open mesopores without phase loss (secondary, conditional on pass criteria).
- Apply mild acid vapor or solution etch compatible with Zn“imidazolate stability (pre-screen short exposures and low acid activity; strictly time-limited).
- Alternatively, use controlled base/solvent-assisted etch known to preferentially dissolve high-energy sites (e.g., grain boundaries) while preserving crystalline cores.
- After each etch, immediately quench and solvent-exchange; verify crystallinity and local order (PXRD/PDF).
4.3. Route C: Competitive neutral/halide ligation during growth (optional, hypothesis-driven).
- Introduce low equivalents of halide (Cl−/Br−) or neutral ligands with known Zn affinity (carefully chosen to avoid topology change) during nucleation to bias missing-node formation.
- Validate by XPS/EA (halide content), PDF, and porosimetry; fail-fast if new phases appear.
4.4. Defect quantification toolkit (pre-registered):
- PALS for vacancy/mesopore signatures;
- Total scattering/PDF for local disorder;
- TGA + elemental analysis for stoichiometry;
- XPS for surface composition and Zn unsaturation indicators;
- Gas sorption with NLDFT/QSDFT pore size distributions.

Step 5 — Translate rigorously to MIL-53(Al)-NH2 with explicit phase control and DABCO·2HCl role validation (addresses reviewer point iv).
5.1. Pre-nucleation Al speciation and pH-time profiling:
- Prepare precursor solutions (Al3+ + NH2-BDC + acetic acid ± DABCO·2HCl) and measure:
  a) pH vs time (room temp → heating ramp),
  b) 27Al NMR of pre-nucleation solutions (identify hydrolyzed/complexed Al species),
  c) ESI-MS (where feasible) to detect Al“carboxylate species distributions.
- Hypothesis test: DABCO·2HCl primarily shifts ionic strength and provides a controllable proton reservoir; it should not generate persistent Al“N complexes. Operational criterion: no new 27Al signatures consistent with stable Al“amine complexes; no DABCO incorporation detected by digestion 1H NMR.
5.2. Phase-control diagnostics during synthesis (pre-registered):
- In situ PXRD (where feasible) or time-resolved ex situ PXRD across heating to confirm MIL-53 formation trajectory.
- Define exclusion criteria for competing phases: presence of diagnostic peaks for MIL-68/MOF-235-like phases triggers condition elimination.
5.3. Modulation and defect control:
- Use acetic acid (and amine-compatible monocarboxylates) as the primary coordination modulator; vary equivalents to generate low/med/high defect series.
- Use DABCO·2HCl as an adjustable additive with a bounded range (predefine 0“2 equiv vs Al) based on speciation results.
- Quantify modulator incorporation and defects by digestion 1H NMR, TGA, ATR-IR (carboxylate termination), and variable-temperature PXRD to ensure breathing is retained.
5.4. Mesocrystal formation pathway:
- Two-step temperature program (low-T nucleation then higher-T growth) under controlled modulator speciation.
- Induce OA by solvent polarity shift (DMF → DMF/H2O → EtOH) with controlled ionic strength; apply the same OA metrics (SAED spread threshold, texture analysis) adapted to MIL-53 crystallography.

Step 6 — Bioavailability-relevant performance tests with normalization and mechanism linkage.
6.1. Payload selection and loading:
- Use one fluorescent model payload (e.g., rhodamine B) with standardized loading protocol; quantify loading by UV“vis/fluorimetry mass balance.
6.2. Release/transport kinetics:
- Measure release at pH 7.4 and 5.5 in PBS ± serum albumin; fit to diffusion/dual-porosity models; extract effective diffusivity and compare across defect series and OA metrics.
6.3. Colloidal stability and corona:
- DLS/zeta in PBS + albumin; protein corona profiling by SDS-PAGE (LC-MS optional) and correlate with surface chemistry (XPS) and defect level.
6.4. Mechanistic correlation:
- Multivariate correlation linking (i) OA orientation metric, (ii) defect metric (PALS/PDF/sorption), and (iii) transport/release parameters to test the central claim that OA + stable defectivity jointly accelerate kinetics.

Deliverables and decision gates (ensures predictability claims are earned):
- Gate G1: Speciation map yields a validated DABCO dosing regime (conditional β and turbidity/DLS onset shifts).
- Gate G2: OA metrics pass threshold versus controls.
- Gate G3: Defect routes A/B/C produce monotonic defect series while meeting topology-preservation pass criteria.
- Gate G4: Transport/release improvements correlate with defect+OA metrics rather than merely reduced size or amorphization.
Feasibility: 1) ZIF-71 defect chemistry is made chemically plausible by eliminating the unsupported premise of carboxylate substitution into a Zn“imidazolate lattice under mild conditions. Instead, defectivity is introduced via (A) linker-deficient growth (a direct, thermodynamically/kinetically consistent route to missing-linker/missing-node populations during framework formation) and (B) calibrated, subcritical etching/competitive coordination only under strict pass/fail crystallinity criteria. This directly addresses the reviewer’s concern that carboxylates would merely terminate surfaces or amorphize the ZIF rather than create stable, topology-preserving defects.
2) DABCO’s role is converted from qualitative to quantitative by requiring an experimentally measured Zn“DABCO conditional stability and a competition/speciation map against imidazolate in the exact solvent/base window used for nucleation. The pulsed-addition schedule is no longer heuristic; it is parameterized to maintain a target bound-Zn fraction during the nucleation/growth crossover, aligning with the literature principle that particle size is controlled by local metal-ion activity and metal“ligand competition (nano-MOF growth termination logic).
3) Mesocrystal assembly is made falsifiable and mechanistically constrained: OA is tied to measurable surface charge/termination changes (zeta potential and probe adsorption), explicit control sets are defined (no pulses, no ionic strength ramp, polymer-only), and a quantitative orientation threshold (SAED azimuthal spread and PXRD texture) is pre-registered. This prevents the polymer from becoming an unacknowledged critical reagent and distinguishes true mesocrystals from random aggregates.
4) MIL-53(Al)-NH2 translation is strengthened by treating DABCO·2HCl as a testable pH/ionic additive rather than an assumed ‘kinetic buffer’. Buffered pH-time profiles plus 27Al NMR/ESI-MS of pre-nucleation solutions are used to verify its effect on Al hydrolysis/speciation and to rule out unintended coordination pathways. In situ PXRD and digestion NMR are pre-registered to exclude competing phases and to quantify modulator incorporation, ensuring phase purity and breathing retention across a defined defect series.
5) The analytical plan is already strong; here it is explicitly coupled to decision gates that prevent over-interpretation (topology preservation criteria, OA metric thresholds, monotonic defect series requirement). This structure supports the proposal’s predictability claim with measurable constraints rather than aspirational control.

Hypothesis: A flame-resistant, humidity-tolerant, catalytically active MOF can be made deterministic (rather than asserted) by coupling (i) a carboxylate-reticulated, hydrolytically robust node chemistry with (ii) a pendant phosphorus chemistry that is *operationally proven* to remain largely non-coordinating after deprotection, and (iii) a quantitatively metered intrapore P“OH condensation that forms a confined polyphosphate nanophase while preserving crystallinity and transport. Mechanistically, the proposal hinges on two separable, testable modules:

Module A (Non-coordinating P“OH under MOF-relevant conditions): Pendant phosphinate/phosphonate groups are installed on a ditopic aromatic dicarboxylate such that carboxylates enforce reticulation and P groups project into pore space. After selective deprotection to P“OH, the pendant groups are designed to remain predominantly pore-facing (hydrogen-bonded and solvated) rather than node-binding. This is made chemically plausible by (1) steric/electronic shielding at phosphorus (bulky phosphinate substituents; optional α-aryl substitution adjacent to P to reduce oxyanion basicity), and (2) selecting a node/SBU family with demonstrably lower oxyanion “hard” binding competition than Mg/Al mixed SBUs if binding cannot be suppressed (go/no-go switch to Zr(IV) oxo/hydroxo SBUs with kinetically inert carboxylate bonding, or to Al(III)“oxo chains where oxyanion access is sterically constrained). The *reason* this overcomes reviewer risk (ii) is that we do not assume non-coordination; we quantify Mg/Al (or alternative node) affinity for pendant P“O(H)/P“O− using model-cluster competition experiments and in-MOF diagnostics, and only proceed to locking conditions when P“node coordination is below a defined threshold.

Module B (Gating-to-locking as a metered, nanoconfined condensation): Upon mild thermal treatment, a controlled fraction of pendent P“OH groups undergo dehydration/condensation to Q1/Q2 polyphosphate-like species confined to pore surfaces (a “glassy” nanophase) that (a) passivates defect-prone hydrolysis/acid sites and suppresses volatile fuel release during heating (condensed-phase flame retardancy), and (b) increases pore polarity and acid-gas binding under humidity through persistent P“O and P=O dipoles and H-bond networks. The key mechanistic refinement is that the extent of condensation is treated as a controllable state variable (Q0→Q1→Q2 distribution) governed by water activity and thermal ramp/hold, not as an assumed 10“30% target. By mapping quantitative 31P ssNMR speciation against crystallinity retention, pore metrics, and diffusion coefficients, we define a deterministic “locking window” where phosphate formation occurs without collapse or transport loss. This directly addresses reviewer risks (i), (iii), and (iv) by bounding the transformation with explicit strain/crystallinity/transport criteria.

Catalysis/pollutant conversion is integrated as a low-percentage Fe-porphyrin tetracarboxylate co-linker *only after* the material-risk modules are validated, and is protected by (1) spatial isolation (≤1“3 mol% to minimize defect-driven amorphization), and (2) diagnosing/mitigating demetalation/leaching under SO2/NOx + humidity via effluent ICP and Fe speciation (Mössbauer/XAS where available). The resulting material couples functional groups → gas separation/storage under humidity (CO2/SO2/NOx) → flame resistance (condensed-phase phosphate/char formation) → catalysis/pollutant conversion, with each link supported by quantified go/no-go constraints rather than assumed compatibility.
Plan: Phase 0: Architecture selection and de-risking logic (Month 0“3)
0.1 Node/SBU down-select with explicit fallback: Start with Mg(II)/Al(III)-carboxylate only if it meets thermal and competition thresholds (below). In parallel, synthesize a benchmark Zr(IV)-oxo carboxylate analogue (UiO-type or NU-type topology) as the pre-defined contingency platform because Zr“carboxylate bonds are kinetically inert at 220“320 °C and tolerate acidic functionalities better. Decision gate: if Mg/Al system fails either (A) P“node non-coordination threshold or (B) crystallinity/transport retention at locking, switch to Zr platform while keeping identical linker logic.

Phase 1: Linker and control lattice set (Month 1“8)
1.1 Linker set (primary and variants):
- L-P(steric): aromatic dicarboxylate bearing a pendant phosphinate (e.g., aryl“P(=O)(OR)(tBu) or diaryl phosphinate) designed for steric shielding and reduced tendency to chelate nodes after deprotection.
- L-P(less shielded): pendant dialkyl phosphonate as a “worst-case” coordination propensity comparator.
- L-H (non-P parent): isoreticular dicarboxylate without P (e.g., terephthalate analogue).
- L-P(protected): the permanently protected ester version of L-P(steric) (non-condensable control).
- Optional: L-P(electronic) variant with electron-withdrawing aryl substituent near P to reduce basicity.
1.2 Hard control lattices (mandatory set):
C1: non-P analogue MOF (L-H only).
C2: P-ester/protected analogue MOF (L-P(protected) only).
C3: P-only/no-Fe MOF (L-P only).
C4: Fe-only/no-P MOF (L-H + 1“3 mol% Fe-porphyrin co-linker).
C5: P+Fe MOF (L-P + 1“3 mol% Fe-porphyrin co-linker).
1.3 Crystallization constraints for SCSC feasibility: Grow single crystals (target ≥50“150 µm) under diffusion/slow-cooling conditions; in parallel produce microcrystalline powders for Rietveld/PDF. Record defect proxies (thermogravimetric linker/node ratios; modulator incorporation if used) to set allowable defect fraction.

Phase 2: Mandatory de-risking study A — P“OH coordination/competition quantification (Month 4“10)
2.1 Model-cluster competition (quantifies assumption #1):
- Prepare soluble Mg(II) and Al(III) carboxylate clusters or appropriate salts with carboxylate ligands that mimic node environment.
- Titrate deprotected L-P (P“OH) versus L-H into metal solutions under MOF-relevant solvent/water activities.
- Readouts:
  (i) Solution/solid-state 31P NMR: coordination-induced shifts/broadening; quantify bound vs free fraction.
  (ii) IR: P=O and P“O bands; monitor appearance of metal“O(P) signatures.
  (iii) Metal uptake/leaching: ICP-OES of supernatant after contact with L-P (P“OH), giving conditional stability constants/extent of complexation.
- Go/no-go criterion A1 (non-coordination threshold): Under conditions matching planned deprotection/locking (same solvent, ionic strength, and water activity), ≤10% of P sites show node-binding signatures (combined NMR/IR/ICP mass balance). If >10%, implement redesign:
  Redesign option A: increase steric bulk (phosphinate > phosphonate; bulky OR/aryl substituents).
  Redesign option B: enforce larger P“node separation (longer spacer/ortho substitution that blocks approach).
  Redesign option C: switch node to Zr(IV)-oxo platform with sterically constrained, kinetically inert SBUs.
2.2 In-MOF verification of P“node binding (post-deprotection):
- Perform deprotection on C3 (P-only/no-Fe) under mild conditions.
- Readouts:
  (i) 31P ssNMR: appearance of strongly shifted/broadened resonances consistent with immobilized metal phosphonates/phosphinates.
  (ii) VT-PXRD/Rietveld: detect topology change or new phase formation.
  (iii) Metal environment probes: 27Al ssNMR (if Al present) or XPS to detect new M“O(P) environments.
- Go/no-go criterion A2: No new crystalline phase by PXRD; unit-cell parameters change smoothly without symmetry breaking; absence of a dominant bound-P resonance.

Phase 3: Mandatory de-risking study B — Deterministic locking window (Month 8“18)
3.1 Define controlled extent-of-condensation “knob” (quantifies assumption #2):
- Perform locking as a designed experiment varying:
  (i) water activity aw (dry inert; controlled humid inert; trace water dosing),
  (ii) heating ramp (0.5“5 °C/min),
  (iii) hold temperature/time (200“320 °C; 0.5“8 h),
  (iv) optional mild acid catalysis/scavengers (only if non-coordination is proven; otherwise excluded).
3.2 Quantify phosphate speciation (extent-of-reaction):
