  - Correlate these defect metrics with triplet lifetimes (transient absorption) and ΦΔ (1270 nm 1O2 phosphorescence) to determine whether defect reduction increases or decreases effective Type II yield and under what humidity/protein conditions.
5.3 Validate epitaxial secondary growth vs homogeneous nucleation:
  - In situ monitoring: (i) time-resolved turbidity and/or DLS on mother liquor during growth to detect onset of homogeneous nucleation, (ii) mass-gain kinetics on fabric (gravimetric uptake vs time) comparing seeded vs unseeded WCF.
  - Cross-sectional TEM: look for coherent intergrowth/continuous crystalline overlayer rather than discrete, weakly attached crystallites; confirm by lattice/fringe continuity where possible.
5.4 Local O2 partitioning/transport (decouple MOF microenvironment from textile boundary layers):
  - O2 sorption on isolated MOF scraped/detached from fabric (or parallel powder synthesized under identical chemistry) under dry and controlled humidity to quantify fluorination-dependent O2 uptake.
  - Pore-tethered O2 probe approach: incorporate or post-load an oxygen-quenchable phosphorescent probe that resides within pores (or tethered to internal sites) so measured O2 quenching reflects pore-local O2 rather than external boundary layers; perform humidity-dependent Stern“Volmer analysis.
  - Humidity-dependent diffusion proxy: compare O2-response time constants of the pore probe across shells (0“30% F; gradient vs homogeneous) to quantify effective O2 permeability in the MOF microenvironment.
5.5 Wetting and bacteria-contact tradeoffs (ensure hydrophobicity does not reduce interfacial aPDI):
  - Contact angle (static/dynamic) on coated WCF; water uptake/swelling metrics.
  - Protein adsorption assays (e.g., BSA adsorption) to evaluate formation of quenching biofilms at the surface.
  - Bacterial adhesion quantification (S. aureus attachment under dark conditions) to ensure the fluorinated outer shell does not repel bacteria to the extent that ROS delivery becomes diffusion-limited.

Step 6 — Photophysics and Type II confirmation (tight linkage to structure/defects/O2)
6.1 Singlet oxygen quantification: primary metric is time-resolved 1O2 phosphorescence at 1270 nm to obtain ΦΔ and lifetime; secondary chemical probes (DPBF/ABDA) used only as supporting kinetics.
6.2 Triplet-state kinetics: transient absorption to measure porphyrin T1 lifetime; perform under controlled humidity and in protein-containing media to mimic biological quenching conditions.
6.3 ROS pathway discrimination: EPR TEMP→TEMPO for 1O2; scavenger set (NaN3 for 1O2; catalase/SOD for H2O2/O2•−) to exclude Type I dominance, explicitly checking whether any heavy-atom tuning increases Type I signals.

Step 7 — Antibacterial aPDI against Staphylococcus aureus and durability
7.1 Standardized aPDI assays (ATCC-6538): spectrally matched irradiation to porphyrin absorption (report irradiance and dose in J/cm2); log-reduction vs time; dose“response fitting. Include dark, light-only, and MOF-free fabric controls.
7.2 Interface evidence: live/dead staining and SEM of bacteria on fibers; correlate kill rate with ΦΔ × (pore-local O2 metric) × (adhesion/contact metric).
7.3 Reuse testing: repeated illumination + washing cycles (detergent/saline); track PXRD crystallinity, Zr/porphyrin leaching (ICP-OES/UV“vis of wash), and retained ΦΔ and kill rate.

Step 8 — Structure“function integration and decision criteria
8.1 Multivariate model: predict kill rate using measured triplet lifetime, ΦΔ(1270 nm), pore-local O2 parameter (probe quenching / sorption), defect density (digestion NMR/TGA/PDF), shell thickness/continuity, and bacterial adhesion. Identify (i) optimal fluorinated fraction and (ii) optimal defect window.
8.2 Go/no-go triggers: if fluorination reduces adhesion/wetting enough to reduce aPDI despite higher ΦΔ, pivot to gradient shells with fluorination restricted to an intermediate layer (retain hydrophilic outermost surface) or reduce F fraction while keeping defect/adhesion gains.
Feasibility: 1) Mechanistic claims are made testable and non-overreaching: Fluorination is not assumed to help by ‘hydrophobicity’ alone; it must (a) be spatially verified within the shell (ToF-SIMS/depth XPS + STEM F-maps + 19F/13C ssNMR) and (b) measurably increase pore-local O2 metrics (O2 sorption and pore-tethered probe quenching) under relevant humidity/protein conditions. This directly addresses reviewer concern that fluorinated linkers could be dispersed, patchy, or not proximal to photoactive domains.
2) Defects are treated as a tunable parameter with competing effects, not a monotonic ‘healing improves ΦΔ’ assumption. Quantitative missing-linker/capping-ligand metrics (digestion 1H NMR, TGA) plus PDF/microstrain analysis create a rigorous defect descriptor set. Correlating these to triplet lifetimes and 1270 nm ΦΔ under controlled humidity explicitly tests whether defects primarily act as quenchers, O2-transport enhancers, or both—thereby converting a reviewer-flagged uncertainty into a discovery axis with a defined optimum.
3) Mixed-linker epitaxial secondary growth is explicitly de-risked. The plan includes in situ nucleation monitoring (turbidity/DLS), seeded vs unseeded mass-gain kinetics, and cross-sectional TEM evidence for intergrowth to distinguish true secondary growth from homogeneous nucleation/independent crystallite deposition. The radial-gradient strategy (pure PCN-224 inner layer followed by fluorinated outer growth) further reduces microstrain/segregation risk by maintaining lattice match at the seed interface while still creating an F-enriched region relevant to O2 partitioning.
4) O2 measurements are localized to the MOF microenvironment rather than conflated with textile boundary layers. By combining (i) O2 sorption on isolated MOF produced under matched conditions and (ii) pore-resident O2-quenchable probe readouts with humidity dependence, the fluorination effect on pore-local O2 is isolated from macroscopic fabric effects.
5) Interfacial function is safeguarded by explicit wetting and contact assays. Contact angle, protein adsorption, and bacterial adhesion measurements ensure that hydration-repelling design does not reduce bacteria“MOF proximity or create an interfacial diffusion barrier that negates higher ΦΔ. This directly closes the reviewer-identified risk that hydrophobicity could impair ROS delivery.
6) The overall concept chain remains intact and strengthened: secondary-growth (architectural locking + defect/strain control) → validated mixed-linker shell microenvironment → Type II photosensitization enhancement (triplet lifetime + pore-local O2) → higher singlet oxygen flux at the bacteria“textile interface → improved S. aureus aPDI and reusability.

Hypothesis: A Zr6-based MOF constructed from a mixed-linker node-architecture—where 2,5-disulfhydrylbenzene-1,4-dicarboxylate (DSBDC) provides redox/thiol-rich microenvironments while a phosphonic-acid SALI layer partially caps Zr6 node “OH/H2O sites—will exhibit (i) superior water stability and (ii) lower apparent activation energy for proton/charge transport under humid conditions. The core mechanism is a cooperative, two-level stabilization/transport design: (1) phosphonate anchoring (strong Zr“O“P bonding) reduces capillary-condensation-driven pore collapse by decreasing hydrophilic defect density and controlling water uptake hysteresis at the node; (2) DSBDC introduces a hydrogen-bondable, polarizable thiol/disulfide sub-network that organizes confined water into continuous H-bond chains, enabling low-barrier Grotthuss-type proton hopping (and/or mixed-valent hopping if redox states are engaged), thereby reducing activation energy. Methodological adaptation: replace conventional post-synthetic ligand exchange/defect engineering with a kinetically gated, sequential SALI strategy performed in DMF that intentionally exploits DMF’s coordination dynamics to transiently open Zr6 coordination sites, enabling spatially biased phosphonate installation (node capping) without eroding framework crystallinity—yielding a metastability-controlled, MOF-5-analogue-like ‘dynamic coordination’ regime but translated to robust Zr6 nodes.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1. Synthesize microcrystalline Zr6 MOF scaffold (NU-1000-like topology or UiO-type with accessible Zr6“OH/H2O sites) using a mixed-linker feed: (A) terephthalate (BDC) to preserve high-connectivity scaffold formation and (B) DSBDC as a minority functional linker (e.g., 5“30 mol% of total dicarboxylate) to embed thiol/disulfide functionality while maintaining crystallinity.
1.2. Control DSBDC redox state: prepare two batches—(i) reduced dithiol form (protected/deprotected as needed to avoid disulfide scrambling during solvothermal synthesis) and (ii) oxidized disulfide-rich form—so transport/stability can be correlated with thiol chemistry.
1.3. Solvent history standardization: exchange as-synthesized solids into anhydrous DMF to establish a reproducible coordination environment at Zr6 nodes prior to functionalization.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1. Kinetically gated sequential SALI in DMF (adaptation):
- Use DMF as a transiently coordinating medium to modulate Zr6 node lability (via reversible DMF binding) and thereby control access to node “OH/H2O sites.
- Introduce a mono-/di-phosphonic acid (e.g., phenylphosphonic acid or perfluoroalkyl phosphonic acid for hydrophobization) under strictly metered equivalents relative to node “OH count, at moderate temperature (e.g., 60“90 °C) to favor Zr“O“P formation while minimizing linker displacement.
- Implement a two-pulse dosing protocol: Pulse 1 installs a sub-monolayer (partial capping) to reduce hydrophilic defect density; Pulse 2 installs a second fraction only if water sorption hysteresis remains high. Between pulses, wash in DMF to remove weakly adsorbed phosphonic acid.
2.2. Create a metastability window (MOF-5 analogue concept translated): intentionally retain a controlled amount of DMF coordinated at nodes after SALI (do not fully activate), generating a metastable but processable state where node coordination remains dynamic. Then perform programmed activation (vacuum + temperature ramp) to lock the phosphonate-capped node structure without capillary-stress collapse.
2.3. Comparative controls:
- Control A: parent Zr6 MOF (no DSBDC, no phosphonate).
- Control B: DSBDC-incorporated only (no phosphonate).
- Control C: phosphonate SALI only (no DSBDC).
- Control D: carboxylate SALI (benzoate) vs phosphonate SALI to isolate Zr“O“P bonding effects.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1. Structural/chemical verification:
- PXRD for crystallinity retention pre/post SALI and after humidity cycling.
- Pair distribution function (PDF) and/or total scattering to detect local node changes (Zr“O“P formation).
- Solid-state NMR (31P for phosphonate binding; 13C for linker environment; 1H to probe “OH populations).
- XPS/ICP to quantify P loading and S content; thiol/disulfide state via XPS S 2p and Raman.
3.2. Water stability and capillary condensation mechanism tests:
- Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) with multiple adsorption/desorption cycles at controlled RH; quantify hysteresis area and uptake kinetics.
- Post-cycling PXRD + N2 sorption to measure pore retention.
- In situ IR (OH stretch region) during water dosing to observe node hydration changes with/without phosphonate capping.
3.3. Activation energy determination (transport):
- Proton conductivity by AC impedance under controlled RH (e.g., 60“98% RH) and temperature range (e.g., 20“80 °C). Extract activation energies from Arrhenius plots.
- Optional: electronic/ionic decoupling via H/D isotope effect (H2O vs D2O) to confirm Grotthuss contribution.
3.4. Mechanistic falsification/confirmation:
- Correlate P-loading with reduced hysteresis (capillary-stress mitigation) and with conductivity vs RH.
- Compare reduced vs oxidized DSBDC states: if thiol-rich variants produce lower Ea and larger isotope effect, this supports water-mediated proton wire formation enhanced by thiol H-bonding/polarizability.
- Evaluate whether phosphonate capping preserves or improves conductivity by preventing catastrophic pore collapse while maintaining sufficient internal water ordering.
3.5. Success criteria:
- >90% PXRD crystallinity retained after ≥10 DVS water cycles at high RH.
- Significant reduction in water sorption hysteresis relative to uncapped controls.
- Activation energy for proton transport approaching the low-Ea regime (target: ≤0.25 eV under high RH) with clear isotope effect supporting Grotthuss transport.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zr6-node MOFs are established as among the most water-stable MOFs; however, capillary condensation can still induce pore collapse. Node functionalization (SALI) is empirically known to reduce hysteresis and improve cyclic water stability by modulating pore environment and node chemistry (Asset 1). Separately, phosphonate-based MOFs with free phosphonic acid groups can sustain humid environments and exhibit low activation energies for proton conduction via structured water networks (Asset 2), motivating phosphonate chemistry as both a stability and transport lever.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal transfers the concept of solvent-enabled dynamic coordination (highlighted in DMF-containing MOF-5 environments enabling metastable transformations; Asset 4) into a Zr6-node context as a deliberate kinetic gate for SALI. DMF is used not merely as a solvent but as a transient ligand that tunes node lability, enabling controlled installation of strongly binding phosphonates (Zr“O“P) without framework damage—an explicit methodological adaptation that targets the known limitation of uncontrolled functionalization leading to pore blockage or degradation.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to (i) unfunctionalized Zr6 MOFs, the phosphonate-capped nodes should show reduced capillary-stress susceptibility and improved long-term water cycling. Compared to (ii) purely phosphonate-based frameworks, retaining a Zr6 carboxylate scaffold preserves high connectivity and robustness while DSBDC introduces additional H-bond/soft-donor microenvironments to lower transport barriers. Compared to (iii) simple benzoate SALI, phosphonate SALI provides stronger, more hydrolysis-resistant anchoring at Zr nodes, and the sequential, DMF-gated protocol enables fine control over capping density to avoid over-hydrophobization or pore occlusion. Overall, the design couples water-stability engineering (node capping) with mechanistically motivated low-Ea transport pathways (thiol-structured water wires), rather than treating stability and conductivity as separate optimization problems.

Hypothesis: A proton-activity“programmable Janus tandem-photocatalyst can be realized as a bilayer MOF-on-MOF flow-through membrane in which (i) an upstream, permanently cationic dye-gating/bleaching layer concentrates anionic azo dyes and hosts an ultrathin HxMoO3 plasmonic laminate whose free-carrier density (and thus LSPR-assisted ROS yield) is governed by *local* proton activity at the oxide/MOF interface, while (ii) a downstream Au@Zr-oxo MOF nanoreactor selectively oxidizes aromatic alcohols with minimal dye exposure. This architecture overcomes the reviewers’ risks by: (1) enforcing *quantified* transport decoupling (≥99% azo-dye rejection at defined permeance) via a pinhole-free, interfacially sealed bilayer validated by tracer permeation and through-plane conductivity mapping; (2) replacing bulk-pH assumptions with an explicit Donnan-buffer-transport model and *independent* in situ interfacial pH proxies to establish a uniquely invertible calibration from LSPR/photoconductance → local aH+ under the same ionic strength and dye loading; (3) using a falsifiable energetic/kinetic discriminant matrix (action spectra, intensity/temperature dependence, transient absorption/photothermal readouts, and scavenger controls) to distinguish plasmonic hot-carrier/field effects from photothermal heating, semiconductor-like charge transfer, and dye-sensitized artifacts; and (4) demonstrating robustness in realistic water matrices with explicit thresholds for fouling, Mo/Au leaching, and retention of reversible Hx modulation over ≥100 proton-activity cycles. Mechanistically, local aH+ sets x in HxMoO3, shifting EF and carrier density to tune LSPR amplitude/position and interfacial band bending; these jointly modulate the rate and identity of ROS (•O2− vs •OH) generated at/near the oxide surface and therefore the dye bleaching kinetics and the membrane’s self-referencing response factor, while Layer A’s fixed charge and controlled defect/pinhole density prevent dye transport to Layer B, preserving Au catalytic selectivity for benzyl alcohol oxidation.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registered go/no-go criteria (hard acceptance thresholds)
G0.1 Bilayer integrity/gating: methyl orange (MO, ~327 Da, −1) and Congo red (CR, ~697 Da, −2) rejection R ≥ 99.0% at water permeance ≥ 1.0 L m−2 h−1 bar−1 (LMH/bar) in 10 mM Na2SO4, pH 7, 25 °C; and R ≥ 97.0% in 1“10 mM NaHCO3 + 5 mg/L humic acid.
G0.2 Pinhole ceiling: ionic tracer (Cl−/Na+) through-plane conductivity indicates defect-area fraction fdefect ≤ 10−5 (operationally: through-plane conductance ≤ 2× that of a thickness-matched defect-free reference film); fluorescent neutral tracer permeation (rhodamine B base or fluorescein neutral form) shows ≤ 1% breakthrough over 2 h.
G0.3 Local aH+ calibration: under fixed ionic strength (I = 10, 50 mM) and defined dye loading (0, 10, 50 mg/L MO), the mapping {LSPR peak position λp, LSPR extinction magnitude, photoconductance ΔGph} → local pH at the oxide/MOF interface yields R2 ≥ 0.95 and hysteresis ≤ 0.2 pH units over 10 cycles.
G0.4 Mechanism discriminants: action spectrum of bleaching matches LSPR absorption profile (not dye absorption) within ±10 nm; apparent activation energy for rate constant kbleach < 15 kJ/mol (rules out purely thermal); and scavenger/EPR signatures satisfy predefined ROS dominance criteria (see Step 3.3).
G0.5 Stability: Mo leaching ≤ 50 ppb (ICP-MS) after 100 h continuous flow and ≤ 5% loss in LSPR amplitude modulation after ≥100 pH cycles (pH 2 ↔ 9); Au leaching ≤ 10 ppb; Zr leaching ≤ 100 ppb.

Step 1 — Materials selection with epitaxy/compatibility constraints
1.1 Choose lattice-compatible Zr-MOF pair to minimize interfacial mismatch: Layer B = UiO-66-NH2 (or UiO-67 if larger pores needed for Au precursor ingress), Layer A = UiO-66-derived mixed-linker film (BDC/BDAc or BDC-NH2) followed by post-synthetic quaternization to install permanent cationic groups while retaining the *same inorganic Zr6O4(OH)4 node topology* to enable quasi-epitaxial intergrowth rather than true heterotopological epitaxy.
1.2 Define Layer A fixed-charge density target: ≥ 0.5 mmol cationic sites per g film (quantified by elemental analysis/XPS N 1s deconvolution and dye titration), ensuring Donnan exclusion of anionic dyes and controlled local proton partitioning.

Step 2 — Fabrication of a pinhole-minimized Janus bilayer with interfacial sealing
2.1 Support and primer layer: anodic alumina (AAO) or porous alumina/ceramic with pore size 50“200 nm; apply carboxylate-terminated SAM or polydopamine primer (≤ 5 nm) to improve nucleation density.
2.2 Grow Layer B (support-facing) UiO-66-NH2 thin film (target thickness 200“400 nm):
- Seeded solvothermal growth with modulator control (acetic acid/formic acid) to tune defect density; target missing-linker defect concentration 5“15% (from TGA/1H NMR of digested film) to create Zr“OH anchoring sites without collapsing crystallinity.
- Go/no-go: GIXRD indicates preferred orientation (e.g., (111) enhancement) and continuous coverage (no substrate peaks in grazing incidence mapping across area).
2.3 Confine Au nanoparticles exclusively in Layer B (target 1“3 nm, 0.3“1.0 wt%):
- Infiltrate HAuCl4 (ethanol) under vacuum-assisted impregnation; rinse; reduce by CO (25“60 °C) or mild H2 (80“120 °C) to avoid external Au nucleation.
- Verify spatial confinement: HAADF-STEM/EDX line scans across cross-section show Au only in Layer B (Au signal in Layer A < 5% of Layer B integrated intensity). XPS surface Au < detection limit.
2.4 Grow Layer A (feed-facing) cationic UiO-66-derived film (target thickness 100“250 nm) atop Layer B via secondary growth:
- Use same Zr precursor chemistry to promote node continuity; mixed-linker growth to incorporate reactive handles (e.g., BDC-NH2).
- Post-synthetic quaternization to permanent cationic sites (e.g., grafting imidazolium/trimethylammonium via alkylation or amidation + quaternization).
2.5 Interfacial sealing strategy (activated only if G0.1/G0.2 fail):
- Apply an ultrathin “microporosity-preserving seal” at the Layer A/Layer B interface: vapor-phase infiltration (VPI) of alumina (1“3 cycles) or sol“gel silica (≤ 2 nm equivalent) targeted to grain boundaries; acceptance requires <10% loss of micropore volume (ellipsometric porosimetry) and ≥10× reduction in ionic conductance anisotropy.

Step 3 — HxMoO3 nanosheet lamination and definition of local proton activity
3.1 Laminate ultrathin MoO3·xH2O nanosheets onto Layer A with controlled thickness (3“10 nm equivalent):
- Electrostatic assembly driven by Layer A cationic surface; no polyelectrolyte unless needed (if used, ≤ 1 nm PEI/PSS bilayer, verified by QCM-D).
- Confirm retained porosity: ellipsometric porosimetry and Kr adsorption on scraped films; acceptance: ≥70% of Layer A microporosity retained.
3.2 Convert to proton-intercalated HxMoO3 under controlled buffers and quantify x:
- Use buffered solutions (pH 2“9) at fixed ionic strength (I = 10, 50, 100 mM) to reach steady x; quantify Mo5+/Mo6+ by XPS/operando XANES (if available) and correlate with NIR LSPR extinction (UV“Vis“NIR).
3.3 Explicit local-aH+ model (Donnan + buffer + transport) and independent local pH proxy:
- Model: solve coupled Nernst“Planck“Poisson (or electroneutral Donnan approximation) for a cationic microporous film with fixed charge Xf, including buffer species (e.g., phosphate/acetate/carbonate) and salt; outputs: local [H+]int, Donnan potential ΔψD, and partitioning of dye anions.
- Independent measurement: anchor a ratiometric pH fluorophore (e.g., SNARF-derivative) covalently to Layer A linkers at low loading (<1% of linkers) to report local pH within the MOF near the MoO3 interface; validate with confocal microscopy under flow. Alternative/backup: SECM pH microelectrode mapping at the membrane surface under illumination.
- Calibration protocol: for each (I, dye loading), acquire {λp, ExtLSPR, ΔGph} vs fluorophore-reported local pH; require G0.3.

Step 4 — Transport gating characterization with quantitative leakage diagnostics
4.1 Dye rejection/breakthrough:
- Measure rejection for MO and CR at 1“3 bar transmembrane pressure; define flux J and rejection R; target G0.1.
4.2 Multi-tracer pinhole assay:
- Use a panel: (i) anionic fluorescein, (ii) cationic rhodamine 6G, (iii) neutral dye (coumarin), and (iv) 3“10 kDa fluorescent dextrans; quantify selectivity and identify pinhole signatures (simultaneous passage of all tracers indicates defects).
4.3 Through-plane ionic conductivity mapping:
- Perform scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) or micro-4-point mapping across the membrane to spatially resolve high-conductance spots; acceptance: no hotspots exceeding mean + 3σ, consistent with fdefect ≤ 10−5.

Step 5 — Mechanistic discriminant matrix for ROS generation and charge-transfer directionality
5.1 Action spectrum:
- Measure apparent quantum yield (AQY) of dye bleaching vs wavelength (bandpass filters) and compare to (i) MoO3 LSPR absorption, (ii) MOF absorption, (iii) dye absorption. Validation: AQY tracks LSPR, not dye.
5.2 Intensity dependence:
- Determine rate vs photon flux: hot-carrier/photochemical pathways show near-linear at low flux; thermal shows superlinear with temperature rise. Fit k ∝ I^n (n ~ 1 expected for single-photon ROS generation).
5.3 Temperature control / photothermal exclusion:
- Use IR thermography and embedded microthermocouple; run isothermal controls matching any observed ΔT in dark; require G0.4 (Ea and isothermal mismatch).
5.4 ROS identity and location:
- Operando EPR (DMPO for •OH/•O2−, TEMP for 1O2), plus probe assays (terephthalic acid for •OH, NBT for •O2−) under identical conditions.
- Predefined discriminants: 
  (D1) If superoxide is dominant: strong DMPO-OOH signal, NBT reduction correlates with bleaching, SOD suppresses kbleach ≥ 70% while tert-butanol suppresses ≤ 30%.
  (D2) If hydroxyl is dominant: terephthalic fluorescence correlates with bleaching, tert-butanol suppresses ≥ 70%, SOD suppresses ≤ 30%.
5.5 Hot-carrier vs defect-mediated semiconductor-like transfer:
- Transient absorption (TA) or time-resolved photoconductance on MoO3-laminated Layer A: look for sub-ps“ps carrier signatures and their dependence on x (carrier density).
- Photocurrent polarity and Mott“Schottky/Kelvin probe: test band bending direction vs protonation state; require consistency with electron transfer to O2 at the interface.
5.6 Dye-sensitization artifact exclusion:
- Repeat bleaching with (i) colorless anionic pollutant analogs, (ii) dyes with different absorption maxima, and (iii) dark adsorption controls.
- Critical test: excite at wavelengths where dye absorbs but LSPR does not; bleaching should not accelerate significantly if not dye-sensitized.

Step 6 — Tandem operation in flow with orthogonal catalysis
6.1 Device: feed contacts Layer A first; permeate contacts Layer B. Visible illumination 420“700 nm with calibrated photon flux; dissolved O2 monitored (optode).
6.2 Layer A function (dye bleaching + self-referenced sensing):
- Establish kbleach and response factors RFopt = (−dAdye/dt)/C and RFelect = Jph/C under standardized flux; apply pH renormalization using calibrated local pH from {λp, ΔGph}.
6.3 Layer B function (benzyl alcohol oxidation):
- Quantify conversion/selectivity to benzaldehyde; test effect of any dye leakage by deliberate spiking; acceptance: ≤10% loss in activity at dye concentrations corresponding to ≤1% breakthrough.

Step 7 — Realistic water matrices, fouling, regeneration, and durability thresholds
7.1 Matrix challenges: humic acid (2“10 mg/L), carbonate (1“10 mM), chloride (1“100 mM), mixed ions (Ca2+/Mg2+ at 0.5“2 mM), variable O2 (air-saturated vs O2-depleted).
7.2 Fouling metrics and regeneration:
- Track flux decline, rejection loss, and LSPR modulation amplitude. Regeneration protocol: mild alkaline wash (pH 9“10) + low-ionic-strength rinse; optional short H2O2 pulse if organic fouling persists (verify no loss of cationic functionality).
- Acceptance: after 5 fouling/regeneration cycles, retain ≥90% of initial rejection and ≥80% of initial kbleach.
7.3 Stability/retention:
- 100 h continuous operation + ≥100 pH cycles; apply G0.5 leaching thresholds; confirm crystallinity (GIXRD), chemical state (XPS), and preserved Au confinement (post-mortem TEM).
Feasibility: Heteroepitaxial compatibility and pinholes: The revised plan avoids claiming strict epitaxy between different topologies; instead it uses node/topology-matched UiO-66-derived films on both sides (Layer A and B), enabling coherent intergrowth via secondary growth while controlling mismatch through thickness limits (≤250 nm for Layer A) and defect management. Quantitative, spatially resolved leakage diagnostics (multi-tracer breakthrough + SECCM/through-plane conductance mapping) and a pre-defined interfacial sealing contingency (sub-2“3 nm VPI/sol“gel targeted to grain boundaries with <10% porosity loss) directly address the risk that pinholes defeat dye-gating.

Local proton activity under fixed charge: Cationic MOFs create Donnan potentials that can decouple bulk pH from interfacial aH+. The proposal now includes (i) a coupled electrostatic/transport model incorporating fixed charge, buffer equilibria, and ionic strength and (ii) independent measurement of local pH via an anchored ratiometric fluorophore (or SECM), performed under the same ionic strength and dye loading used for catalysis. This creates a falsifiable calibration that tests whether {LSPR, photoconductance} uniquely reports local aH+ (with explicit R2 and hysteresis criteria), thereby making the self-referencing response-factor claim experimentally accountable.

Mechanistic clarity for plasmonic ROS generation: The LSPR-tunable HxMoO3 concept is grounded in degenerately doped MoOx literature showing carrier-density-dependent NIR/visible plasmon resonance and enhanced visible absorption. The revised workplan adds an energetic/kinetic discriminant matrix (action spectra, intensity scaling, isothermal controls, TA/photothermal readouts) plus pre-registered scavenger/EPR outcome criteria to distinguish hot-carrier/field-assisted O2 activation from photothermal heating, defect-mediated semiconductor charge transfer, and dye-sensitization (a known confound for azo dyes). This makes the ROS pathway assignment (•O2− vs •OH) and directionality testable and rejectable.

Transport/performance tradeoffs and real-water robustness: The membrane is treated as a selective reactor with explicit targets for rejection and permeance, measured by flux-based rejection and breakthrough curves, and interpreted with transport modeling (Donnan partitioning + diffusion/convective flow). Realistic matrices (humics, carbonate, hardness ions, chloride, variable O2) are built into the validation with explicit regeneration protocols and stability/leaching thresholds, ensuring the claimed functionality persists beyond ideal laboratory water.

Overall, the revised proposal transforms the prior asserted assumptions (epitaxy quality, local pH control, ROS identity, and dye gating) into quantitative go/no-go criteria with independent measurements, contingency sealing chemistry, and mechanistic discriminants—while preserving the original concept chain: cationic dye capture + proton-tunable HxMoO3 plasmonic bleaching upstream, and Au@Zr-MOF aromatic alcohol oxidation downstream.

Hypothesis: Embedding a water-stable, defect-engineered Zn“imidazolate MOF as a continuous “proton highway phase” inside a polymer mixed-matrix membrane, then executing a post-casting, covalent imidazolium tethering reaction exclusively within the MOF pore system, will yield higher and more durable proton conductivity than conventional imidazole-doped MMMs. Methodological adaptation: instead of coordinating or physisorbing imidazole, we will (i) install pore-confined electrophilic handles on Zn“N linkers (via mixed-linker ZIF synthesis containing aldehyde- or chloromethyl-functionalized imidazoles), and (ii) perform a solvent-free, vapor-phase quaternization (Menshutkin-type) to convert infiltrated imidazole into covalently tethered imidazolium groups lining the accessible porosity. Mechanism: (a) the Zn“N coordination network provides rigid, connected micropores that template a percolating hydrogen-bonded water network at moderate RH; (b) tethered imidazolium sites create high local proton activity and strong hydration shells that stabilize continuous water wires and suppress imidazole leaching; (c) proton transport proceeds predominantly by Grotthuss hopping through coupled (H2O)n“H3O+ and imidazolium-associated water chains, with reduced interfacial resistance because the MOF phase itself becomes an internally ion-functionalized, water-structured conductor rather than a passive filler.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a Zn“imidazolate MOF platform with proven hydrolytic stability and accessible porosity: ZIF-8-derived topology as baseline, then move to more hydrophilic analogs by mixed-linker substitution.
1.2 Synthesize a mixed-linker ZIF where a controlled fraction (5“30 mol%) of linkers carry an electrophile for post-synthetic quaternization:
- Option A: 2-(chloromethyl)imidazole (CMim) + 2-methylimidazole (mIm) to form Zn(mIm)2-x(CMim)x.
- Option B: imidazole-4-carbaldehyde (Im-CHO) + mIm to form Zn(mIm)2-x(Im-CHO)x, followed by aldehyde-to-leaving-group conversion (e.g., chlorination) if needed.
Target: retain crystallinity and pore accessibility while introducing a uniform internal density of reactive sites.
1.3 Create defects (missing-linker) in a controlled manner to increase water uptake without collapse (e.g., modulated synthesis with monodentate imidazole/amine modulators); quantify defect density by TGA/elemental analysis and positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS).
1.4 Select polymer matrix emphasizing mechanical integrity and low intrinsic water swelling to isolate filler-driven conduction (e.g., PVDF-HFP or polysulfone as mechanically robust host). Prepare a secondary set with a mildly acidic polymer (low-IEC SPEEK) to test interfacial coupling while avoiding dominance by polymer conduction.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Form a percolated MOF microphase within MMM (structural novelty vs dispersed particles):
- Use shear-induced alignment + phase-inversion casting to bias MOF particles into a connected network (target near percolation threshold, typically 15“30 vol% depending on aspect ratio).
- Alternatively, grow a thin, continuous MOF “skeletal network” in situ on a sacrificial nanofiber template (electrospun polymer fibers), then embed the MOF network into the final polymer and remove the template if compatible (yielding an interpenetrating MOF/polymer architecture).
2.2 Preserve accessible porosity during embedding by using a pore-filling, removable neutral guest that does not coordinate Zn (e.g., cyclohexane or perfluorinated small molecules depending on MOF affinity), removed after casting by mild vacuum; verify no polymer intrusion by gas sorption and PALS.
2.3 Pore-confined, vapor-phase imidazolium tethering (core methodological adaptation):
- Load imidazole (Im) into the activated MMM by controlled vapor sorption (mass uptake target set by functional-site stoichiometry).
- Perform solvent-free quaternization inside pores: heat the membrane under Im vapor (or Im + mild base scavenger if required) to drive Menshutkin reaction between Im and “CH2Cl groups on CMim linkers, yielding tethered “CH2“Im+Cl− sites lining the pore walls.
- Optional anion exchange post-step to tune water structure and proton mobility (Cl− → HSO4− or H2PO4−) by exposing the membrane to vapor/solution of the corresponding acid, then drying to remove excess acid while retaining counterions in pores.
2.4 Condition the hydrogen-bonded water network: hydrate under precisely controlled RH steps (e.g., 30→60→90% RH at fixed T) to fill micropores and establish connected water wires around imidazolium sites; lock into operating state by equilibration at target RH.
2.5 Build mechanistic control series:
(A) polymer only; (B) MMM with nonfunctional ZIF (no electrophile) + no Im; (C) MMM with electrophile-ZIF but no Im treatment; (D) MMM with electrophile-ZIF + Im loading but no quaternization (low-T exposure only); (E) full quaternized (tethered imidazolium) MMM; (F) full quaternized MMM after anion exchange (HSO4− / H2PO4−). Keep filler fraction and processing identical.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Verify Zn“N framework integrity and accessible porosity after membrane processing and after quaternization:
- PXRD for crystallinity retention; N2/CO2 sorption on extracted filler and on microtomed MMM pieces; PALS for free-volume connectivity.
3.2 Confirm covalent tethering and quantify functional density (distinguish from coordination/physisorption):
- Solid-state 13C/15N NMR (use 15N-imidazole for unambiguous detection of quaternized N), FTIR/Raman for imidazolium signatures, XPS (N 1s chemical shifts; Cl 2p), and chloromethyl consumption (elemental analysis/ion chromatography of released Cl− during exchange).
- Chemical stability/leaching: exhaustive water soaking and accelerated humidity aging; quantify any released imidazole by HPLC/LC-MS (expect near-zero for tethered samples).
3.3 Map the hydrogen-bonded water network in pores:
- Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) to obtain RH-dependent uptake and hysteresis; variable-temperature IR of OH stretch to infer H-bond strength distribution; DSC to separate confined vs bulk-like water; if available, quasi-elastic neutron scattering (QENS) for confined water mobility.
3.4 Proton conductivity and mechanism under relevant conditions:
- Through-plane and in-plane EIS from 20“120 °C and 20“95% RH; fit Arrhenius/VTF to extract activation energies.
- Isotope effect: repeat EIS under D2O humidity to quantify Grotthuss contribution (expect significant drop if hopping dominates).
- Transference number and electrode polarization analysis to confirm proton-dominant conduction.
3.5 Microstructure/percolation and interfacial resistance:
- FIB-SEM tomography or nano-CT to confirm connected MOF microphase; SAXS/WAXS to monitor dispersion.
- Spatially resolved conductivity (humid-state conductive AFM or scanning microwave impedance microscopy) to verify conduction localized along MOF network and across polymer“MOF interfaces.
3.6 Success criteria:
- Conductivity: ≥10× improvement over polymer-only and ≥3× over non-tethered Im-loaded MMM at 60“80 °C, 50“95% RH.
- Mechanism: activation energy ≤0.30 eV at high RH with strong H/D isotope effect, consistent with Grotthuss hopping through structured water.
- Durability: <1% loss of tethered Im content after leaching/aging; stable conductivity over ≥300 h at 80 °C/80% RH.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Imidazole enhances proton transport when immobilized/organized; literature shows large conductivity gains from imidazole inclusion in porous solids under anhydrous conditions, while hydrogen-bonded water networks enable low-barrier Grotthuss transport under humid conditions. Imidazolium groups are known to strongly hydrate and can nucleate continuous water wires in confined pores, increasing proton hopping rates. Zn“imidazolate frameworks provide robust Zn“N coordination backbones with tunable linker functionality and stable microporosity.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): MOF chemistry uniquely enables mixed-linker synthesis and pore-confined covalent functionalization without destroying the coordination network. Converting neutral imidazole into tethered imidazolium inside the MOF transforms accessible porosity into a chemically programmed proton-transport channel. This addresses MMM limitations (additive leaching, interfacial resistance, and uncontrolled water structuring) via molecular-level design rather than composition-only optimization.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to free-imidazole MMMs, covalent tethering eliminates volatility/leaching and prevents polymer plasticization. Compared to MOF-filled MMMs without internal ion functionalization, the imidazolium-lined pores actively template hydrogen-bonded water networks and increase local proton activity, lowering activation energy. Compared to approaches relying on reversible coordination, the permanently grafted sites provide reproducible, humidity-tolerant conduction while maintaining Zn“N framework stability and accessible porosity.

Hypothesis: A pore-partitioned, redox-stratified MIL-88(NH2) heterometal MOF nanozyme—engineered by (i) introducing TPY as a rigid internal pore-partition ligand to stabilize MIL-88 breathing under serum/ROS conditions and (ii) spatially segregating CeO2 nanodomains at the crystal periphery while embedding Fe/Co-TPY catalytic nodes in the interior—will enforce a directional ROS-mediated cascade (maltase/GOx-generated H2O2/ROS -> MOF-confined peroxidase-like oxidation of TMB) that yields higher colorimetric fidelity and serum tolerance for maltose quantification than conventional co-dispersed CeO2@MOF or unpartitioned Fe/Co-MIL-88(NH2). Mechanistically, TPY partitioning increases local coordination saturation and suppresses linker/cluster hydrolysis, while the core“shell redox gradient minimizes radical quenching by serum antioxidants (ascorbate/urates) by generating •OH/Fe(IV)=O equivalents within confined pores and consuming ROS rapidly at the MOF interior surface where TMB is preconcentrated via π“π/hydrogen-bond interactions with aminoterephthalate and TPY.
Plan: Step 1: System setup (materials + assay architecture).
1.1 Synthesize Fe/Co-TPY-MIL-88(NH2) with controlled TPY loading (e.g., 0, 5, 10, 20 mol% vs aminoterephthalate) to tune partition density; characterize by PXRD (phase), N2 sorption (pore evolution), FTIR/XPS (TPY coordination), ICP-MS (Fe/Co ratio), and in situ PXRD in PBS/serum-mimic to quantify breathing/stability.
1.2 Create a redox-stratified composite: grow a thin CeO2 nanolayer selectively on external MOF surface via seeded deposition (Ce(III) precursor adsorption followed by mild oxidation/precipitation) to form CeO2@Fe/Co-TPY-MIL-88(NH2) core“shell; confirm spatial segregation by STEM-EDS line scans and depth-profile XPS.
1.3 Assemble a maltose cascade: immobilize maltase (α-glucosidase) upstream and glucose oxidase (GOx) co-localized or downstream (paper microfluidic or well-plate) to convert maltose -> glucose -> H2O2; position the MOF nanozyme zone downstream to oxidize TMB.

Step 2: Implement the methodological adaptation (directional cascade + confinement control).
2.1 Engineer directional transport: in a 3D μPAD, design sequential zones (enzyme zone -> diffusion delay -> MOF/TMB zone) and compare against a co-mixed single-zone format to test whether spatial separation plus MOF confinement reduces serum quenching.
2.2 Tune partition/redox gradient parameters: screen TPY loading and CeO2 shell thickness to maximize (i) peroxidase-like kinetics (TMB + H2O2) and (ii) cascade efficiency (maltose -> TMBox). Extract Michaelis“Menten parameters (Km, Vmax) for TMB and H2O2; determine ROS identity using scavengers (tert-butanol for •OH, p-benzoquinone for O2•−) and EPR spin trapping (DMPO) to link performance to confined radical generation.
2.3 Quantify TMB preconcentration and anti-interference: measure TMB adsorption isotherms on TPY-partitioned vs non-partitioned MOF; evaluate signal retention in the presence of physiological interferents (ascorbate, urate, cysteine, bilirubin) to demonstrate that rapid intrapore ROS turnover outcompetes solution-phase quenching.

Step 3: Validation and analytical framework (serum analysis + benchmarking).
3.1 Analytical performance in buffer and serum: build calibration curves for maltose (e.g., 10 µM“5 mM) in PBS and 10“50% (v/v) human serum; compute LOD/LOQ, linear range, and time-to-read.
3.2 Specificity controls: test glucose, sucrose, fructose; include enzyme-free and heat-inactivated enzyme controls; confirm that maltose response requires maltase+GOx and is not driven by endogenous serum H2O2 by catalase spiking.
3.3 Comparative benchmarking: compare to (i) CeO2@NH2-MIL-88B(Fe) co-dispersed composite, (ii) Fe/Co-MIL-88(NH2) without TPY, (iii) HRP-based TMB assay. Use identical μPAD geometry and readout (RGB or absorbance at 652 nm) and report relative error vs HPLC for spiked and real serum samples.
3.4 Mechanistic structure“function proof: correlate stability metrics (PXRD retention, leached metal by ICP, activity after incubation in serum) with cascade output; validate that pore partitioning suppresses framework degradation and maintains catalytic turnover under repeated ROS exposure (cycling tests).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 demonstrates CeO2@MOF synergistic mimic activity enabling sugar cascades with TMB readout; Asset 2 shows TPY pore partitioning stabilizes Fe/Co-MIL-88(NH2) and enhances peroxidase-like catalysis in bioassays. Combining these establishes a grounded route to both higher catalytic output and higher biological-matrix robustness.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal uses rational MOF-level architectural control (pore partitioning + heterometal nodes + core“shell redox stratification) to address a domain-specific limitation: MIL-88 instability/breathing and radical quenching in serum that degrade cascade fidelity. TPY acts as an internal coordination strut and pore modulator; CeO2 is positioned as a surface ROS modulator to shape ROS flux into the MOF.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike co-mixed nanozyme/enzyme systems where ROS are generated and quenched in bulk solution, the redox-stratified, partitioned MOF forces ROS generation/consumption into confined catalytic volumes, preconcentrates TMB, and resists serum-induced deactivation/leaching. This should deliver (i) lower LOD in serum, (ii) improved color uniformity and reduced background, and (iii) higher operational stability than CeO2@NH2-MIL-88B(Fe) and unpartitioned Fe/Co-MIL-88(NH2).

Hypothesis: By implementing a continuously variable mixed-linker strategy inside the CPM-26-Co (BCT zeotype) architecture—specifically, co-assembling BTC with a sterically matched, more rigid/less decarboxylation-prone trigonal linker at controlled ratios while preserving the 4-2-1 metal-hook motif—we can decouple pore size/surface area tuning from topology loss and thereby raise thermal stability at a given (or higher) BET surface area. Mechanistically, the rigid co-linker increases the energetic penalty for hook cleavage and carboxylate decarboxylation at elevated temperature, while the mixed-linker distribution introduces controlled elastic strain that suppresses cooperative bond-rupture pathways; simultaneously, maintaining BCT connectivity prevents the surface-cage ‘opening’ modes that typically reduce apparent surface area upon activation. The methodological adaptation is a topology-preserving “CVMOF-on-a-zeotype” approach: instead of isoreticular expansion (discrete) or additive-controlled surface changes, we impose continuous linker-ratio control within a fixed zeotype CPM-26-Co framework to tune surface area and stabilize the thermal response without phase transformation.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select co-linker candidates that are trigonal and size/angle-compatible with BTC to preserve BCT net formation while altering rigidity/rotational freedom: examples include 1,3,5-tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene (TCPB) (rigid, extended) and 1,3,5-triazine-2,4,6-tricarboxylic acid (TTCA) (electron-poor core, reduced propensity for decarboxylation), alongside BTC as the baseline.
1.2 Define a linker-ratio library (BTC:co-linker = 1:0, 0.9:0.1, 0.75:0.25, 0.5:0.5, 0.25:0.75) and keep metal sources constant to target CPM-26-Co-like node chemistry (Co-based, with optional secondary metal in the ‘hook’ position to mirror the dual-metal capture feature).
1.3 Pre-screen linker solubility/acid“base speciation by in situ 1H NMR of synthesis solutions (deuterated analog solvents) to ensure comparable deprotonation kinetics across ratios; adjust modulator identity/dose accordingly (formic acid vs acetic acid) to normalize nucleation rates.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Topology-preserving mixed-linker synthesis (adaptation): run solvothermal reactions under CPM-26-Co-forming conditions, but introduce a staged dosing protocol for linkers: (i) form a BTC-rich pre-nucleus to lock in BCT connectivity; (ii) slowly dose the rigid co-linker during crystal growth to favor statistical incorporation rather than separate nucleation. This is a deliberate adaptation to prevent phase separation typical of mixed-linker attempts in zeotype MOFs.
2.2 Enforce “hook integrity” via coordination environment control: add a competing monodentate ligand (e.g., low equivalents of pyridine-N-oxide) only during growth to bias the third carboxylate ‘hook’ into the desired immobilization geometry, then remove it by post-synthetic solvent exchange. This functional modification targets the covalent metal-hook interactions reported for CPM-26-Co while enabling mixed-linker incorporation.
2.3 Activation and thermal-stress protocol designed to diagnose surface vs bulk failure: (i) solvent exchange to low-surface-tension solvent (MeOH then acetone); (ii) supercritical CO2 drying or very slow vacuum ramping; (iii) stepwise thermal holds (100, 150, 200, 250, 300 °C) under dynamic vacuum to map onset of surface-cage opening and bulk collapse separately.
2.4 Optional heterometal ‘hook’ stabilization: prepare a second series where the immobilized cluster metal (hook-captured species) is varied (e.g., Co-only vs Co/Fe or Co/Ni in the captured site) to test whether stronger M“O bonds in the hook region synergize with rigid co-linkers to increase thermal stability without sacrificing topology.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Confirm mixed-linker homogeneity (avoid phase separation): digest-NMR quantification of linker ratios in the final solid; spatial mapping by confocal fluorescence quenching (using a trace fluorescent analog of one linker) to verify uniform distribution across single crystals; PXRD pattern fitting/Rietveld refinement to confirm BCT topology retention and continuous lattice-parameter shifts with ratio.
3.2 Quantify porosity and surface area: N2 sorption (77 K) to obtain BET and pore-size distributions; compare to parent CPM-26-Co and evaluate continuous tunability vs discrete jumps. Track any hysteresis indicative of surface-cage alteration.
3.3 Thermal stability metrics tied to mechanism: TGA coupled to MS/FTIR to identify decarboxylation/ligand loss; variable-temperature PXRD to determine the temperature of topology loss; in situ IR/Raman to monitor carboxylate coordination modes and “hook” bond persistence; low-dose HRTEM on crystal edges pre/post heating to directly observe surface-cage completeness/opening analogous to MIL-101 surface phenomena.
3.4 Structure“property modeling: build a quantitative map linking linker ratio → lattice metric/elastic strain proxy (from SCXRD/PXRD) → surface area (BET) → thermal stability onset (VT-PXRD, TGA) to test the proposed suppression of cooperative bond rupture and surface-cage opening. Use simple elastic-network/phonon proxy calculations (DFT or force-field) on representative mixed-linker supercells to correlate increased rigidity with higher decomposition barriers.
3.5 Performance-relevant stress tests: repeat activation/thermal cycling (e.g., 5 cycles to 250 °C) and measure retained BET and PXRD crystallinity; benchmark against unmixed CPM-26-Co and a high-surface-area mixed-linker control that does not preserve BCT topology.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Mixed-linker “continuously variable” strategies have already demonstrated smooth, ratio-controlled tuning of BET surface area and lattice dimensions without phase separation when linker distribution is controlled (Asset 1). Separately, thermal treatment can selectively alter surface structure while leaving bulk intact, and additive/synthetic history governs whether surface cages open or phase transformations occur (Asset 2). CPM-26-Co specifically demonstrates topology-directed immobilization via a 4-2-1 strategy and covalent metal-hook interactions, providing a clear structural handle to preserve connectivity while modifying ligand composition (Asset 3).
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation explicitly keeps CPM-26-Co’s BCT zeotype topology and metal-hook motif as the invariant scaffold while importing CVMOF-style continuous linker-ratio control as the variable. The staged dosing and hook-environment bias are MOF-native synthetic controls aimed at a known limitation: mixed-linker systems often phase-separate or shift topology; zeotype frameworks can be particularly sensitive. The thermal protocol is designed to separate surface degradation from bulk collapse, directly integrating insights from surface-cage completeness studies.
3. Comparative Advantage: Relative to single-linker CPM-26-Co, the mixed-linker CPM-26-Co series should offer (i) continuously tunable surface area at fixed topology (rather than discrete isoreticular analogs), (ii) higher thermal stability at comparable surface area by increasing linker rigidity and stabilizing hook bonds, and (iii) reduced surface-cage opening/porosity loss upon activation through suppression of cooperative failure pathways. Compared to additive-only approaches, linker-ratio tuning provides a persistent, built-in molecular control knob rather than a synthesis-history-dependent surface effect.

Hypothesis: Bu“MnCr can be converted into an ambient-condition, regenerable co-adsorbent for hydrophobic plasticizers and moderately polar pesticides by mechanically stabilizing its layered galleries with *chemically explicit, carboxyl-preserving interlayer straps* that (a) covalently bridge adjacent organic-ammonium layers to suppress humidity-driven breathing/collapse while maintaining open slit-access under 30“65% RH, and (b) introduce *unconsumed pendant “CO2H/“CO2− sites* to sustain a persistent H-bond/ion“dipole network for pesticide anchoring. The refined strap architecture is a bifunctional aromatic ‘pillar’ comprising: (i) a rigid π-rich aromatic core (dispersion/π capture plane for phthalates), (ii) two terminal coupling groups that react selectively with interlayer nucleophiles (diol/diamine handles) to form stable amide/urethane/carbonate linkages under controlled water activity, and (iii) at least one additional pendant carboxyl group intentionally left unreacted (trimellitic/pyromellitic-derived motifs or protected/deprotected carboxyl strategies) to preserve polar binding sites post-installation. Mechanistically, the straps impose a fixed interlayer registry and reduce the free-energy penalty of guest intercalation under ambient humidity by preventing gallery collapse and by stabilizing a confined water population; simultaneously, the aromatic strap faces create a low-polarity adsorption plane that concentrates plasticizers, while pendant “CO2H/“CO2− plus structured interlayer water cooperatively bind pesticide heteroatoms (e.g., triazine N, phosphoryl/sulfide motifs) through H-bonding and ion“dipole interactions. TGA is retained as a central tool but is repositioned from ‘DTG feature assignment’ to a *calibrated desorption/decomposition framework*: evolved-gas signatures will be validated against standards and intact-guest evolution will be independently quantified (TGA“GC/MS and stepwise isothermal desorption with analytical recovery), enabling defensible confinement-strength distributions and regeneration windows that avoid strap/framework damage.
Plan: Step 1 — Baseline material, stability envelope, and pollutant panel
1.1 Synthesize phase-pure layered Bu“MnCr ({Bu3NH}[MnCr(ox)3]·nH2O or the closest reported Bu“MnCr analogue) and confirm: (i) low-angle PXRD interlayer reflections, (ii) composition by ICP-OES (Mn/Cr) + CHN, (iii) interlayer water by DVS (30“90% RH) and TGA (under N2). Establish baseline ‘humidity-breathing’ by variable-RH PXRD (30/50/65/80% RH) to quantify Δd-spacing and reversibility.
1.2 Define adsorbate set spanning hydrophobicity/polarity and distinct MS fragments: plasticizers (DBP, DEHP), pesticides (atrazine, chlorpyrifos), optional polarity controls (2,4-D acid and 2,4-D ester). Prepare aqueous matrices at pH 6“8, ionic strength 1“10 mM, ±5“10 mg/L humic acid; concentrations μg“mg/L.

Step 2 — Chemically defensible strap architecture that preserves pendant acids
2.1 Install *interlayer nucleophile handles* by co-templated growth (not cation exchange) using a minor fraction (5“20 mol%) of functional ammonium templators that are (a) gallery-compatible and (b) provide high-yield coupling in confined media:
- Option A (diol handle): HO“(CH2)3“NH2+R2 (secondary/tertiary ammonium), providing terminal “OH.
- Option B (diamine handle): H2N“(CH2)3“NH3+R2 (one free “NH2 plus one protonated “NH3+), providing a faster acylation site than “OH.
Quantify incorporation by solid-state 13C CPMAS NMR (handle carbons), FTIR (O“H/N“H), and elemental analysis (N/C change vs parent).

2.2 Strap-linker selection explicitly preserving polar sites (reviewer directive)
Design strap molecules where only two positions are coupling-competent and ≥1 carboxyl remains pendant/unreacted after bridging:
- Primary strap motif: 1,2,4-benzenetricarboxylic (trimellitic) platform converted to *di-activated + one free acid*.
  • Route 2.2a (protected acid strategy): Start from trimellitic anhydride; selectively open/derive a mono-protected carboxyl (e.g., tert-butyl ester) leaving two carboxyls activatable. Convert the two to acid chlorides (SOCl2/oxalyl chloride) or activated esters (NHS/EDC) for coupling; after grafting, deprotect to regenerate “CO2H.
  • Route 2.2b (intrinsically mono-acid pendant): Use a pre-made di-functional coupling reagent bearing a pendant carboxyl (e.g., bis(NHS-ester) of trimellitic acid with one acid left free).
- Secondary strap motif (higher density of pendant acids): pyromellitic core where two opposite positions are used for bridging and remaining two remain as acids (via orthogonal protection/activation).
Explicit functional-group map for each strap type will be included in the synthetic plan (before/after coupling), documenting which “CO2H are consumed and which are preserved.

2.3 Diffusion- and selectivity-controlled post-synthetic strap installation (de-risking water/acylation)
2.3.1 Pre-conditioning to control water activity (aw): equilibrate crystals at defined RH (e.g., 30% RH) then solvent-exchange with dry acetonitrile or dry ethyl acetate to reduce free water while retaining structural water required for lattice integrity (verified by mass balance and DVS).
2.3.2 Compare two functionalization modes side-by-side:
- Vapor-phase (preferred for diffusion and low aw): expose crystals to strap reagent vapor (or sublimable activated ester) with catalytic base scavenger in a separated reservoir, minimizing hydrolysis.
- Low-water solution route: dry aprotic solvent with controlled ppm-water (Karl Fischer monitored); add base (2,6-lutidine) and catalytic DMAP for “OH coupling, or mild base for “NH2 coupling.
2.3.3 Use coupling chemistries that are less water-sensitive than acid chlorides when needed:
- For “NH2 handles: activated esters (NHS-esters) to form amides cleanly at low aw.
- For “OH handles: carbonate/urethane formation using di-activated carbonates/isocyanates bearing pendant acid (protected), avoiding direct acid chloride hydrolysis.
2.3.4 Control strap density by stoichiometry relative to quantified handle content (from CHN/NMR). Target low/med/high strap densities (e.g., 10/30/60% of handles reacted), anticipating that sparse bridging can already lock mechanics.

2.4 Removal of residuals and re-generation of pendant acids
Extensive washing (dry solvent) and vacuum activation at mild temperature below any strap cleavage threshold (set by model-compound TGA). If protection was used, deprotect under conditions compatible with Bu“MnCr (e.g., mild acidolysis for tert-butyl esters with minimal water exposure, or catalytic methods in organic media), then re-equilibrate at 30“65% RH.

Step 3 — Decisive structural proof of *covalent interlayer bridging* and functionalization depth
3.1 Structural proof beyond low-angle PXRD (mandatory)
3.1.1 Total scattering/PDF: Collect synchrotron total scattering for parent, handle-bearing, and strapped materials. Fit/compare real-space correlations expected for aromatic strap C“C distances and new interlayer correlations (e.g., handle“strap“handle vectors). A true bridge should introduce reproducible new pair correlations absent in (i) parent and (ii) physically intercalated aromatic controls.
3.1.2 Advanced SSNMR connectivity/distance constraints:
- Prepare 15N-labeled amine handle (for Option B) in a subset.
- Use 13C{15N} REDOR (or related dipolar recoupling) to measure distances between strap carbonyl/aromatic 13C signals and 15N sites. Interlayer bridging predicts consistent short-range 13C“15N proximities not achievable by surface-only adsorption.
- 1H“13C HETCOR to detect spatial proximity between aromatic strap carbons and interlayer water/protons.
3.1.3 Depth profiling to rule out surface-only grafting:
- ToF-SIMS depth profiling (strap-specific fragments, e.g., aromatic + carboxyl fragments) across particle cross-section.
- Complement with microtomed cross-sections + confocal Raman mapping (aromatic band intensity vs depth) and/or XPS depth profiling (gentle sputter) tracking O=C“O components.
Go/no-go for ‘true interlayer’ modification: strap signature must be present through ≥70% of particle thickness (normalized), and REDOR/PDF must support covalent proximity rather than mere intercalation.

3.2 Controls critical for interpretation
- Physical intercalation control: expose parent Bu“MnCr to nonreactive aromatic acids (no coupling group) under identical conditions to quantify mere adsorption/intercalation signatures.
- Intralayer tethering control: handle-bearing material treated with mono-functional acylating agent to form ‘dangling’ groups without bridging; compare mechanics and spectroscopy.

Step 4 — Adsorption performance with humidity-mechanics coupling
4.1 Ambient-condition uptake: kinetics and isotherms for single solutes and mixtures at 30“65% RH-equilibrated solids. Quantify by GC“MS (DBP/DEHP/chlorpyrifos) and LC“MS (atrazine/2,4-D). Report capacity, distribution coefficient (Kd), and selectivity factors in mixed matrices.
4.2 In situ variable-RH PXRD during adsorption to confirm: strapped materials show minimal Δd-spacing across RH and during loading (mechanical lock), whereas parent/control exhibits measurable breathing/collapse.
4.3 Verify pendant acid availability post-strap: titration of accessible acid sites (e.g., vapor-phase base uptake, or potentiometric titration on dispersions where framework is stable), FTIR of “CO2H/“CO2−, and XPS carboxyl speciation.

Step 5 — Mechanism dissection of dual binding physics
5.1 Separate contributions:
- Plasticizers: dependence on aromatic strap identity (tere-/naphthalene-based) and slit size; expect enhanced uptake correlated with aromatic content and constant spacing.
- Pesticides: dependence on pendant acid density and RH; expect maximum uptake at intermediate RH where structured water + “CO2H cooperate.
5.2 Competitive sorption under controlled RH and ionic strength to test ‘stabilized interlayer water’ hypothesis (asset-1 logic extended): compare uptake as a function of pre-equilibrated water content (from DVS) and measure whether strapped materials maintain uptake where parent collapses or excludes.
5.3 Spectroscopic evidence of binding:
- FTIR shifts: atrazine ring modes; chlorpyrifos P“O/P=S region; carboxylate changes upon guest binding.
- SSNMR (where feasible): observe guest-induced perturbations; 1H signatures for H-bonded water.

Step 6 — TGA-centered confinement quantification, calibrated and orthogonal (mandatory)
6.1 Build evolved-gas libraries and separate desorption from decomposition
- Run TGA“MS/FTIR on pure pollutants and on pollutants physically mixed with inert matrix to establish fragmentation vs intact volatilization signatures.
- Add TGA“GC/MS (or interface to trap evolved organics followed by GC/MS) to confirm whether intact DBP/DEHP/chlorpyrifos evolves at specific temperature windows.
- Implement stepwise isothermal desorption (e.g., hold at 40/60/80/100/120 °C under N2) and quantify desorbed intact guests by solvent trapping + GC/LC, generating direct desorption curves independent of DTG peak overlap.
6.2 Apply kinetic analysis only to validated ‘desorption-only’ regions
- Use modulated TGA (MTGA) or multi-rate TGA with isoconversional methods (Friedman/OFW) only on regions proven (by TGA“GC/MS + isothermal trapping) to correspond to intact guest release rather than decomposition.
6.3 Define regeneration windows
- Select regeneration temperature/time where (i) ≥95% guest is recovered/desorbed intact, (ii) strap bands (FTIR/NMR) remain unchanged, and (iii) interlayer spacing/mechanics remain constant (PXRD/DVS).

Step 7 — Environmental robustness, mitigation criteria, and contingency
7.1 Define acceptance thresholds (go/no-go)
- Humidity-mechanical stability: Δd-spacing ≤2% between 30“80% RH over 3 cycles; DVS hysteresis reduced vs parent.
- Adsorption performance targets (initial): Kd ≥10^3“10^4 L/kg for DBP/DEHP and ≥10^3 L/kg for atrazine in mixed matrices; selectivity vs humics maintained within 50% of clean-water performance.
- Leaching thresholds: Mn and Cr each <10 µg/L under pH 6“8 after 24 h contact (or aligned to local regulatory/WHO limits as applicable); TOC leachables from straps below method detection after washing.
7.2 Stress tests
- pH window mapping (pH 5“9), oxidant sensitivity (e.g., residual chlorine), and ionic strength. Track structural retention (PXRD), performance, and leaching (ICP“MS).
7.3 Contingency route if covalent bridging is nonuniform (mandatory)
If ToF-SIMS depth profiling/REDOR indicates surface-only grafting or insufficient penetration:
- Pivot to *noncovalent aromatic pillaring* using dicarboxylate salt-bridges: introduce aromatic dicarboxylates as dianions that ion-pair with interlayer ammonium (Bu3NH+) and/or mixed ammonium handles, creating reversible ‘ionic straps’ that still lock spacing. Validate via variable-RH PXRD (mechanical stabilization) and leaching/robustness tests. This preserves pendant carboxylates inherently and reduces synthetic water-sensitivity.

Deliverables
(i) Strap library with explicit pendant-acid density; (ii) decisive proof of interlayer covalent bridges (PDF + REDOR + depth profiling); (iii) calibrated desorption/decomposition model (TGA“GC/MS + isothermal trapping) with regeneration windows; (iv) adsorption/selectivity maps vs RH and strap parameters; (v) robustness/leaching acceptance report + contingency outcome if needed.
Feasibility: Addresses Reviewer Risk (i): chemistry selectivity/kinetics in hydrated, ion-rich galleries
- The strap architecture is redesigned so that *polar binding sites are not sacrificed*: pendant “CO2H/“CO2− groups remain after coupling via trimellitic/pyromellitic-derived motifs and/or protection/deprotection. Coupling is shifted toward less hydrolysis-prone activated esters (for “NH2 handles) and carbonate/urethane strategies (for “OH handles), with explicit water-activity control (RH pre-equilibration + dry solvent exchange + Karl Fischer monitoring). Vapor-phase functionalization is directly compared to low-water solution routes to maximize penetration and minimize acylation by adventitious water.

Addresses Reviewer Risk (ii): proving true interlayer bridging vs intercalation
- The plan adds *decisive structural proof*: total scattering/PDF to detect new real-space correlations; 15N-enabled SSNMR distance constraints (13C“15N REDOR) to demonstrate covalent proximity; and ToF-SIMS/confocal Raman/XPS depth profiling to confirm modification throughout particles and rule out surface-only grafting. Controls (nonreactive aromatic intercalation; mono-functional dangling graft) isolate mere adsorption effects.

Addresses Reviewer Risk (iii): TGA mechanistic fragility for complex organics
- The TGA approach is upgraded into a calibrated framework: evolved-gas assignments are benchmarked using pure standards and validated by TGA“GC/MS (intact parent detection) plus stepwise isothermal desorption with analytical recovery. Kinetic/isoconversional analysis is restricted to verified desorption-only regimes, explicitly separating desorption from decomposition/oxidation.

Addresses Reviewer Risk (iv): availability/orientation of carboxyl groups after coupling
- Functional-group accounting is built into the strap design: at least one carboxyl per strap is preserved (or regenerated by deprotection), and its accessibility is verified experimentally (carboxyl speciation by FTIR/XPS; acid-site titration/uptake tests). Thus, the pesticide-binding hypothesis remains chemically coherent post-reaction.

Addresses Reviewer Risk (v): environmental robustness and leaching
- The proposal defines explicit go/no-go acceptance criteria for humidity stability, adsorption/selectivity, and Mn/Cr leaching, and includes stress testing across pH/oxidant/ionic strength. A contingency pathway (ionic/noncovalent aromatic pillaring via dicarboxylate salt bridges) is pre-specified if covalent straps are nonuniform, preserving the central concept (mechanically stabilized π-rich slit + pendant acids) while reducing synthetic risk.

Anchor to provided assets
- Asset 1 supports the central role of interlayer water/hydrophilicity under ambient RH and the diagnostic value of TGA for retained volatiles; the revised plan uses this while enforcing structural locking.
- Asset 2 validates the lamellar-spacing control concept and the use of diffraction/TGA to quantify organic content and stability.
- Asset 3 supports dual-interaction adsorption (hydrophobic/π plus H-bonding) for plasticizers/pesticides; the revised architecture explicitly encodes these interactions with preserved pendant acids.

Hypothesis: Bu-FeCr layered oxalate MOFs can be converted into a water-stable, ambient-condition water adsorbent by installing a crystallographically testable “coordination-latched interlayer” motif that is distinct from (and experimentally separable from) simple intralayer strengthening or dissolution“reprecipitation. The latch will be created by partial substitution of oxalate with a mono-phosphonate/mono-carboxylate heterolinker (phosphonoacetate-type, abbreviated PA2−) that binds one metal center through a bidentate O“P“O chelate and a second metal center through a bidentate carboxylate/oxalate-like chelate. The key, falsifiable structural claim is that PA2− can adopt an out-of-plane bridging conformation in which the phosphonate binds a labile Fe(III) site on one layer while the carboxylate binds a facing Fe(III) site on the adjacent layer (Fe“O“P(O)“O···(interlayer gap)···O“C(O)“O“Fe), creating a discrete interlayer ‘pillar’ that increases the effective interlayer shear modulus and suppresses humidity-driven registry loss/delamination.

Mechanistic rationale (addressing reviewer points): (i) Cr(III) kinetic inertness is treated as a feature: latch formation is designed to occur predominantly at Fe(III) sites (fast ligand exchange) while Cr(III) remains as a topology-preserving anchor, preventing wholesale reconstruction. This creates a built-in kinetic constraint against dissolution“reprecipitation and provides a handle for attributing effects specifically to Fe-centered latching. (ii) The interlayer latch hypothesis yields two diagnostic signatures that are not expected for mere intralayer strengthening: (a) an RH-dependent but reversible change in interlayer (00l) spacing and stacking coherence length with reduced broadening under cycling, and (b) a substitution-dependent emergence/shift of low-angle (00l) reflections consistent with a reduced layer“layer repeat distance distribution (narrower microstrain) rather than only in-plane peak shifts. (iii) Increased hydrophilicity from phosphonate introduction is explicitly decoupled from mechanical stabilization by normalizing adsorption to independently measured accessible pore volume and by comparing isosteric heats and hysteresis at matched water loading; true latching predicts reduced hysteresis/cycling decay at comparable heats (thermodynamics) and comparable pore volume (capacity). (iv) ETEM is used only after a non-beam, structure-resolved latch decision is made; beam-driven artifacts are controlled through dose budgets, RH calibration at the specimen, mandatory no-beam trajectories, and post-mortem speciation/leaching checks.

Falsifiable outcomes: If PA2− incorporation results only in intralayer chelation strengthening (non-latched), then spatial P mapping will show uniform P but (00l) coherence will not improve and PXRD signatures will match an in-plane distorted model; if changes arise from dissolution“reprecipitation/phase segregation, then P will be heterogeneous (core“shell or separate phosphonate-rich domains), isotope tracers will show exchange/mass transport, and PDF will require multiple local environments inconsistent with the parent lattice. Only true latching should simultaneously produce: (1) uniform P distribution, (2) a latch-consistent PDF component (Fe“O“P and Fe···Fe interlayer distances), (3) a distinct low-angle (00l) signature/microstrain narrowing, and (4) improved RH cycling stability at matched adsorption thermodynamics.
Plan: Step 0 — Define the parent lattice, locate plausible latchable sites, and generate testable structural models (mandatory structure-resolved latch model).
0.1 Parent structure acquisition and indexing: Synthesize Bu-FeCr {NR3(CH2COOH)}[FeCr(ox)3]·nH2O (Bu = tributylammonium-derived cation as in Asset 2 family) and collect high-resolution PXRD (synchrotron if available) plus Rietveld/Le Bail fits to extract unit cell and specifically the interlayer repeat (c parameter or analogous stacking vector). Confirm layered nature and identify (00l) reflections.
0.2 Identify out-of-plane coordination availability: Use PDF (high-energy X-ray total scattering) and EXAFS at Fe K-edge/Cr K-edge to determine whether Fe sites exhibit any labile coordination (aqua/terminal oxalate oxygen environment) relative to Cr. The latch design proceeds only if Fe shows greater disorder/longer M“O distribution consistent with lability.
0.3 Explicit latch motif + simulated PXRD signature: Build two atomistic candidate models:
  Model L (latched): PA2− bridges adjacent layers with phosphonate bound to Fe(III) in layer n and carboxylate bound to Fe(III) in layer n+1, yielding a discrete interlayer Fe···Fe distance constraint and reduced stacking microstrain. Predict (i) modest contraction or tighter distribution of interlayer spacing (Δd00l), (ii) sharpening of (00l) peaks upon RH cycling compared to parent, and (iii) a new weak superstructure feature at low angle if latch periodicity is partially ordered.
  Model S (strengthened-only): PA2− binds intralayer (both donors chelate metals within same layer) or acts as a terminal chelator, increasing local rigidity but not creating interlayer constraints; predicted signature: primarily in-plane peak shifts/broadening changes with no systematic (00l) coherence improvement.
Simulate PXRD for both using Debye scattering (finite-crystal platelets) to include stacking disorder; define discriminating metrics: FWHM(00l), Williamson“Hall microstrain along stacking direction, and Δq for first (00l) peak.

Step 1 — Heterolinker selection and chemical constraints tuned to Fe(III) vs Cr(III).
1.1 Heterolinker choice (architectural parameterization): Use phosphonoacetic acid (H3PO3CH2CO2H) or closely related rigid mono-phosphonate/mono-carboxylate ligands that can present (a) bidentate phosphonate O“P“O to Fe(III) and (b) bidentate carboxylate to Fe(III). Select 1“2 derivatives with minimal extra rotatable bonds to reduce conformational entropy penalty for interlayer bridging.
1.2 Speciation window and kinetics plan (Fe vs Cr): Perform pH-dependent speciation calculations (Fe(III) and Cr(III) with oxalate and PA2−) and validate by UV“vis titration for Fe(III) complexation and by time-dependent measurements for Cr(III) (expected slow). Lock synthesis and post-synthetic steps into a window where Fe(III) exchange occurs but Cr(III) exchange is negligible:
  • Target pH 2.5“4.0 (suppress Fe(OH)3, keep phosphonate partially deprotonated for binding).
  • Control water activity (aw) using water/ethanol mixtures (e.g., 30“70% EtOH) to slow dissolution of oxalate framework while permitting local ligand exchange at Fe.
  • Time constraints: Fe exchange minutes“hours; Cr exchange days“weeks—use this to ensure ‘re-clamping’ does not rely on Cr.

Step 2 — Mixed-linker synthesis with controls for phase segregation and gradients.
2.1 Composition series with tight substitution targets: Prepare 0, 2.5, 5, 10, 15, 20 mol% PA2− relative to total linker equivalents (keep below amorphization threshold). Use modulated solvothermal conditions with acetate/formate modulator; explicitly maintain constant ionic strength and metal:linker ratio to prevent uncontrolled nucleation.
2.2 Anti-segregation protocol: Employ slow-diffusion or temperature-ramped solvothermal synthesis (e.g., 80→120 °C ramp) to promote equilibrium incorporation rather than kinetic core“shell growth.
2.3 Primary decision gate (bulk crystallography): Accept only batches whose PXRD retains the parent layered pattern with continuous, monotonic peak shifts and without extra crystalline phosphonate phases. Any extra reflections trigger segregation pathway (Decision Tree branch C).

Step 3 — Post-synthetic ‘Fe-selective reclamping’ with isotope tracing to exclude dissolution“reprecipitation.
3.1 Reclamping chemistry (explicit constraints): Treat mixed-linker crystals in Fe(III) salt solution (e.g., Fe(ClO4)3) in water/ethanol (aw reduced), buffered pH 3.0“3.5, at 25“40 °C, for 0.5, 2, 8, 24 h. Maintain low total metal concentration to minimize reprecipitation; quantify dissolved species continuously.
3.2 Isotope-labelled tracer experiments (mass-transport discriminator):
  • Linker tracer: use 13C-labelled phosphonoacetate (13CH2) or 18O-labelled phosphonate to track incorporation without requiring bulk recrystallization. Monitor incorporation by solid-state NMR (13C) and ToF-SIMS (18O/13C maps).
  • Metal tracer: perform reclamping with 57Fe-enriched Fe(III) and detect whether new Fe enters the lattice (57Fe Mössbauer / ICP mass balance). True ‘reclamping’ should show minimal net metal uptake (local coordination completion) versus dissolution“reprecipitation which would show significant metal exchange and composition drift.
3.3 Solution mass balance: Collect supernatants over time and quantify Fe/Cr leaching (ICP-OES) and linker release (LC-MS). A latch formation pathway must satisfy: leaching rate ≪ incorporation rate; otherwise classify as branch C.

Step 4 — Spatially resolved composition/coordination mapping (mandatory heterogeneity controls).
4.1 STEM-EDS/EELS mapping: Map P, Fe, Cr across individual platelets (cross-sectional lamellae via FIB if needed). Quantify P/Fe ratio as a function of radius and thickness; acceptance criterion for ‘uniform incorporation’: no systematic core“shell gradient exceeding, e.g., ±10“15% relative variation across thickness.
4.2 ToF-SIMS depth profiling: Quantify phosphonate fragments (POx−) and organic fragments (CH2CO2−) vs sputter time to detect surface-enriched phosphonate layers or buried domains.
4.3 Nano-FTIR (or IR s-SNOM) for coordination state mapping: Spatially map P“O stretching frequencies; chelated phosphonate should show characteristic shifts relative to free phosphonic acid. Compare edges vs basal planes to see whether latches preferentially form at interlayer interfaces.

Step 5 — PDF/EXAFS model discrimination (latch vs strengthened-only local structure).
5.1 Total scattering/PDF fitting: Fit PDFs against a two-model library (Model L vs Model S) focusing on:
  • Fe“O“P distance signatures,
  • Fe···Fe distances consistent with interlayer bridging constraint,
  • Changes in distribution width along stacking direction.
Require that Model L improves fit quality specifically in r-ranges sensitive to interlayer correlations, not just local Fe“O.
5.2 Fe/Cr-edge EXAFS: Look for increased Fe coordination number/changed scatterer identity consistent with phosphonate binding at Fe; Cr EXAFS should remain essentially unchanged if latch formation is Fe-selective.

Step 6 — Water sorption: decouple mechanical stabilization from altered sorption energetics.
