- Set B (click contingency): para-alkenyl (e.g., styrenyl) DPEB or para-azide/alkyne DPEB.
2.2 Confirm handle incorporation and preservation of NUS-1a structure: digestion 1H NMR (handle %), PXRD, Ar(87 K) sorption.

Step 3 — Intrapore bracing reaction with bounded, diffusion-controlled protocol + external-surface passivation
3.0 External-surface passivation (to suppress external polymerization/pore-mouth clogging): cap external reactive handles prior to coupling by brief exposure to a bulky, mono-functional “quench” reagent that cannot enter pores (size-exclusion chosen based on PSD; e.g., a bulky arylboronic acid or thiol with size > pore window), then wash thoroughly. Validate passivation by ToF-SIMS depth profiling (surface-enriched signal only).

3.1 Primary route (intrapore Suzuki“Miyaura bracing; only if stability gates are met)
- Crosslinker: geometry-selected di-boronate or di-halo aryl (from Step 0: short/medium/long around d*).
- Catalyst system: Pd(dppf)Cl2 (or Pd(PPh3)4) at ≤0.5“1 mol% relative to reactive sites.
- Base/solvent: weak inorganic base (K2CO3 or Cs2CO3) with rigorously limited water activity; use EtOH/toluene with controlled micro-water (≤1“2 vol%) to enable base solubility but minimize Zn-carboxylate hydrolysis.
- Temperature/time: 50“70 °C, 2“12 h; run time-series aliquots to stop in the target conversion window.
- Reaction format: packed-bed flow-through or gentle agitation with crystal-size control to promote uniform diffusion; track conversion vs time.
- Post-reaction cleanup: iterative solvent exchange (EtOH/MeOH), chelator wash (EDTA in alcohol), then activation. Verify Pd removal by ICP-MS.

3.2 Contingency route (MOF-compatible click chemistry; pre-planned, not “if time permits”)
Option B1: Thiol“ene intrapore bracing
- Use DPEB-styrenyl handles + a dithiol crosslinker of geometry-selected length.
- Initiation: photoinitiated (365“405 nm) or thermal radical initiator at low loading under oxygen-controlled conditions.
- Advantages: no strong base/water; typically high-yield; mild to Zn4O-carboxylate.
Option B2: CuAAC intrapore bracing
- Use azide/alkyne handles + difunctional alkyne/azide linker.
- Cu(I) source: CuBr + ligand (TBTA) at low loading; rigorous chelation wash post-reaction; monitor Cu by ICP-MS.

Step 4 — Decisive chemical proof of *intrapore covalent bracing* and spatial uniformity (mandatory)
4.1 Digest-and-analyze coupled fragments:
- Fully digest MOF (acidic digestion appropriate to Zn-carboxylate) and analyze by LC“MS and 1H/13C NMR to detect crosslinked linker“linker or linker“crosslinker adducts (mass shifts diagnostic of specific coupling). Quantify adduct fraction to determine true crosslink conversion.
4.2 Isotopic labeling for unambiguous assignment:
- Use 13C-labeled crosslinker (or 2H-labeled) and confirm incorporation by solid-state 13C CP/MAS NMR (appearance of labeled resonances) and ToF-SIMS mapping (labeled fragment distribution).
4.3 Spatial uniformity across crystallites:
- Perform confocal Raman/fluorescence mapping (if handle has distinct tag) and/or ToF-SIMS depth profiling on microtomed crystals to verify intrapore distribution (core vs shell). Pair with size-selected crystal batches to quantify diffusion limitations.
4.4 Rule out “pore fouling/graphitization-like byproducts”:
- Compare digestion LC“MS/NMR signatures with those from deliberate external polymerization control (Step 5 controls) to ensure the observed products correspond to discrete covalent braces rather than oligomeric tar.

Step 5 — Orthogonal controls explicitly demanded by reviewers (pre-registered)
C1 Catalyst/thermal-history control: expose pristine NUS-1a (no handles) to identical catalyst/base/solvent/time; assess PXRD, BET, PL/QY to quantify catalyst-induced changes.
C2 Inert-aryl control: use a mono-functional aryl analogue (cannot crosslink) under identical conditions to test adsorption/PL changes from mere guest uptake or physisorbed aromatic species.
C3 External-only coupling control: pre-block pore entrances with a reversible bulky guest, then run coupling; if crosslinking signatures appear only at the surface (ToF-SIMS), it validates the diffusion selectivity assumptions.
C4 Surface-passivation control: run coupling with and without external passivation; compare BET/PSD and depth profiles to quantify external polymerization contribution.

Step 6 — Quantify PSD tightening, accessibility, and CHCl3 binding energetics (structure“adsorption linkage)
6.1 PSD/accessibility: Ar 87 K + NLDFT/QSDFT (differential PSD), PALS for sub-nm free-volume change, and vapor uptake kinetics (time constants) for CHCl3/DCM/toluene.
6.2 CHCl3 binding strength/residence proxies:
- CHCl3 vapor isotherms at multiple temperatures (e.g., 298/308/318 K) to extract isosteric heats (Clausius“Clapeyron).
- In situ DRIFTS and/or solid-state NMR with CDCl3 to identify binding environments and distinguish specific confinement vs nonspecific condensation.

Step 7 — Photophysics with causality separation (rigidification vs pore redistribution vs guest-assisted RIM)
7.1 Intrinsic rigidification (no guest): compare QY and lifetime of activated samples under inert atmosphere; compute kr and knr (QY + TCSPC).
7.2 Guest-assisted rigidification: measure in situ PL/QY vs CHCl3 partial pressure; fit a two-regime model (low-loading “binding-site” regime vs high-loading “pore-filling” regime) to separate occupancy-dependent effects.
7.3 Decouple uptake from RIM: introduce a size-mismatched non-emissive guest that occupies volume but does not enhance emission (or use an analyte with similar uptake but different turn-on) to test whether QY tracks uptake alone.
7.4 Temperature-dependent PL (guest-free and guest-loaded) to verify suppression of vibrationally assisted nonradiative decay after bracing (reduced knr(T) slope).

Step 8 — Competitive selectivity, humidity tolerance, and quantitative sensing metrics (pre-registered)
8.1 Competitive vapor mixtures (mandatory): perform dynamic breakthrough-style vapor exposure and/or gravimetric mixture sorption with CHCl3 competing against DCM, CCl4, and toluene (and optionally acetone) at controlled partial pressures. Collect simultaneous PL response.
8.2 Humidity studies: run CHCl3 sensing at defined RH (0%, 30%, 60%) to test water interference and framework robustness; measure any QY drift and PXRD after cycling.
8.3 Sensing metric definitions (pre-registered):
- LOD: 3σ/slope using replicate blank noise (n≥10) and linear region of calibration curve (define exposure time and equilibration criterion).
- Response time: t90 (time to reach 90% of steady-state PL intensity) under a defined flow rate and film thickness/crystal mass.
- Reversibility: ≥20 adsorption/desorption cycles with maintained PXRD + BET retention ≥70% and PL baseline drift ≤10%.

Decision gates and success criteria (go/no-go)
G1 (post-crosslink): PXRD maintained + BET ≥70% + definitive digest-MS evidence of covalent adducts.
G2 (mechanism): QY increase must be explained primarily by decreased knr (not only increased uptake), and must correlate with PSD narrowing metrics (NLDFT/PALS) and/or increased CHCl3 isosteric heat.
G3 (selectivity): mixture experiments must show statistically significant preferential CHCl3 PL turn-on vs DCM/CCl4/toluene at equal partial pressures; humidity tolerance demonstrated at ≥30% RH.

Deliverable library
- Pristine NUS-1a
- Handle-only mixed-linker NUS-1a (no crosslink)
- Crosslinked series (low/medium/high conversion within target window)
- Full set of controls (C1“C4)
- Contingency-click crosslinked analogues (if primary route fails gates)
Feasibility: Chemoselectivity and framework integrity: The main feasibility risk (Pd/Cu coupling damaging Zn4O-carboxylate or causing uncontrolled polymerization) is addressed by (i) a geometry-constrained crosslinker choice derived from the actual NUS-1a pore geometry (reducing off-path coupling), (ii) a low-handle, low-conversion regime explicitly defined to preserve accessible porosity, (iii) diffusion-bounded protocols with crystal-size control and time-series stopping, and (iv) external-surface passivation to suppress surface-initiated oligomerization that would masquerade as “intrapore bracing.” Any catalyst/solvent/thermal effects are quantified via mandatory catalyst-exposure controls (C1).

Decisive proof of covalent intrapore bracing: Rather than relying on non-specific FTIR/Raman changes, the plan requires (a) digestion followed by LC“MS and NMR identification/quantification of the exact coupled adducts, and (b) isotopic labeling (13C/2H) with solid-state NMR and ToF-SIMS mapping to verify incorporation and spatial distribution (core vs shell), directly addressing reviewer concerns about distinguishing true bracing from pore fouling.

Causality separation: The hypothesis explicitly distinguishes intrinsic rigidification, PSD redistribution, and guest-assisted RIM, and the execution plan separates them experimentally by guest-free photophysics (intrinsic effect), PSD/uptake measurements (pore effect), and controlled loading/temperature dependence plus decoupling controls (guest-assisted effect vs mere uptake). Extracting kr/knr from QY+TCSPC provides the required mechanistic discriminator.

Selectivity claims made testable: Competitive mixture experiments (CHCl3 vs DCM/CCl4/toluene) and humidity-defined protocols are built into the core plan with pre-registered LOD and response-time definitions, preventing over-attribution to PSD changes alone.

Contingency chemistry: If Suzuki/Ullmann compromises crystallinity or porosity, the proposal contains a pre-engineered click-chemistry branch (thiol“ene or CuAAC) using built-in handles designed at the mixed-linker stage, enabling intrapore bracing under milder, MOF-compatible conditions that avoid strong base/high water activity. This maintains the central concept chain (intrapore covalent bracing → RIM/PSD control → enhanced CHCl3 turn-on QY) while reducing synthetic risk.

Hypothesis: A mechanically coherent donor“acceptor (D“A) MOF heterostructure with demonstrable crystallographic registry and engineered excited‑state energetics will yield long‑lived, spatially separated charge carriers that increase photocatalytic H2 evolution rates; a surface-confined Sonogashira-grown microporous organic network (MON) skin will suppress DMF/H2O competitive adsorption and hydrolytic attack at labile nodes without blocking mass transport. Feasibility is locked down by (i) selecting a *known, crystallographically solved* thiazine“tri(pyridyl) MOF (NKU‑111 family; an anionic thiazine“pyridyl framework that forms single crystals and supports PAH host“guest D“A photophysics) using realistic N-donor-compatible metal nodes (late-transition M(II) nodes typical for pyridyl ligation), and treating Zr/Ti clusters as a parallel, optional robustness benchmark rather than the core path; (ii) quantifying epitaxial registry by predefining lattice mismatch tolerances (target |f| ≤ 2.5% along at least one in-plane direction; ≤ 3.5% maximum with strain relaxation confirmed), mapping facet indices and interfacial strain fields, and correlating measured defect densities to charge-transfer (CT) kinetics; (iii) explicitly engineering D“A energetics so that PAH photooxidation and thiazine-framework reduction are thermodynamically allowed and kinetically competitive with recombination, using CV/DPV, optical gaps, and transient spectroscopy to select PAHs meeting predefined go/no-go thresholds (ΔG_CT < 0 and τ_CS ≥ 10× τ_unloaded); and (iv) enforcing truly surface-confined Sonogashira coupling by prelocalizing aryl-halide/alkyne handles *only at the outermost crystal layers*, using bulky polymer-supported Pd (and Cu-free conditions where possible) to prevent pore ingress, and rigorously excluding Pd/Cu as false HER catalysts via ICP-MS mass balances and blank HER controls. For in situ liquid uptake/stability correlations, diamagnetic-friendly QCM-D (MOF thin films) and microfluidic gravimetry/ellipsometric porosimetry replace magnetic sustentation unless a paramagnetic-node analogue is proven, by controls, to be uptake- and photophysics-neutral.
Plan: Step 0 — Risk-reduction “lockdown” experiments (Month 0“3)
0.1 Framework identity and crystallographic solvability (mandatory): reproduce a literature thiazine“tri(pyridyl) MOF that is crystallographically solved and forms mm“µm single crystals suitable for epitaxy (NKU‑111-type host“guest D“A framework as primary candidate; obtain/verify CIF; confirm phase purity by SCXRD/PXRD). Success criterion: single-crystal quality sufficient for facet indexing and growth studies; reproducible crystal habit.
0.2 Baseline hydrolytic/solvent sensitivity mapping: quantify structural retention after 24“168 h in DMF and DMF/H2O (0“20 vol% H2O) by PXRD + N2 sorption (or Ar at 87 K) + solution-phase linker leaching (UV“Vis/HPLC) to set the stability target for MON mitigation.

Step 1 — Quantitative epitaxy plan: facet selection, mismatch prediction, and defect metrics
1.1 Facet indexing and lattice mismatch prediction (pre-growth):
- Index dominant facets of the seed crystals by single-crystal morphology + goniometry + SCXRD-derived Wulff construction.
- Choose homoepitaxy first (same framework shell on seed) to minimize mismatch; heteroepitaxy only if a closely related isoreticular analogue exists.
- Calculate in-plane mismatch f = (a_shell − a_seed)/a_seed (and b) for candidate facet planes; predefine acceptance: |f| ≤ 2.5% (preferred) or 2.5“3.5% with measured strain relaxation and low misfit dislocation density.
1.2 Epitaxial growth protocol (diffusion-limited, defect-minimizing):
- Use stepwise growth cycles (multiple short growth pulses rather than one long growth) at low supersaturation.
- Use competitive modulators (e.g., benzoic acid or analogous modulators compatible with the node chemistry) to slow nucleation and preserve single-crystal-to-single-crystal integrity; vary modulator/metal/linker ratios to tune facet exposure and shell thickness (target shells: 20“200 nm for optical CT studies; 200“800 nm for catalysis).
1.3 Interfacial defect and strain quantification (must be quantitative):
- Cross-sectional HR-TEM + geometric phase analysis (GPA) to map local strain fields across the interface (nm-scale strain gradients; identify misfit dislocations).
- Synchrotron microdiffraction / scanning XRD across single crystals or films to quantify mosaicity/orientation spread (target FWHM ≤ 0.2“0.5° for epitaxial regions).
- Define defect density metric: dislocations per µm interface length + orientation spread; these become independent variables in the CT“defect correlation.

Step 2 — Engineer donor“acceptor energetics and define PAH go/no-go criteria
2.1 Energetics measurement stack (before PAH selection is “final”):
- Measure framework redox potentials by solid-state electrochemistry (CV/DPV on drop-cast films; electrolyte compatible with framework stability) and/or spectroelectrochemistry to locate the thiazine-based acceptor reduction.
- Measure PAH oxidation potentials (CV in aprotic solvent; match to DMF conditions where possible) and optical gaps (UV“Vis absorption/fluorescence).
- Compute/estimate excited-state redox potentials (Rehm“Weller; E*(D+/D*) and E*(A/A−*)) from E0“0.
2.2 PAH selection rules (pre-registered go/no-go):
- Thermodynamics: ΔG_CT ≈ −e[ Eox(PAH/PAH•+) − Ered(MOF/MOF•−) ] − E00 < −0.1 eV (go) in DMF; reject if ΔG_CT ≥ 0.
- Kinetics: transient absorption (TA) evidence of charge-separated state with lifetime τ_CS ≥ 1 µs (initial target) and ≥10× longer than PAH excited-state lifetime in the absence of MOF.
- Loading/geometry: guest uptake that preserves porosity (≤30% pore volume loss) and avoids aggregation (no excimer-dominated emission unless intentionally used).
2.3 Host“guest loading control:
- Load PAHs by vapor-phase or solution infusion under conditions that preserve crystallinity; quantify by digestion NMR + TGA + single-crystal diffraction/PL mapping when possible.
- Spatial distribution check: confocal fluorescence mapping across crystals; ensure homogeneous donor distribution for interpretability.

Step 3 — Photophysics-to-epitaxy correlation (the mechanism test)
3.1 Charge-transfer observables tied to interface quality:
- Time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) to extract quenching rates vs shell thickness and defect density.
- Transient absorption to quantify CT formation rate k_CS and recombination rate k_CR; correlate k_CR with measured defect densities (TEM-GPA/microdiffraction).
- EPR (light-induced) to detect PAH radical cations and framework-centered reduced species; quantify signal intensity vs defect density.
3.2 Interface thickness series (required):
- Prepare a thickness library (e.g., 20, 50, 100, 200, 500 nm shells) and a defect-density library (by tuning mismatch/modulator) to obtain a 2D map: {mismatch/defects, thickness} → {k_CS, τ_CS}.

Step 4 — Surface-confined Sonogashira MON skin with anti-artifact safeguards
4.1 Surface-handle localization (mandatory for “surface-only” claim):
- Introduce reactive handles only in the outer growth layers using a “last-layer” mixed-linker pulse: final epitaxial growth cycle uses a small fraction (e.g., 1“5 mol%) of an aryl-halide“functionalized pyridyl linker analogue (or an alkyne analogue) that is kinetically incorporated preferentially at the growth front.
- Verify handle depth profile by XPS angle-resolved measurements and ToF-SIMS depth profiling; acceptance: ≥80% of handle signal within outer 10“30 nm equivalent sputter depth.
4.2 Sonogashira conditions designed for exclusion:
- Use polymer-supported Pd catalyst (e.g., Pd on crosslinked polystyrene beads; bead size 50“200 µm) to prevent entry into MOF pores and intercrystal voids; use Cu-free Sonogashira (or Cu scavengers) to avoid Cu deposition and side reactions.
- Use bulky, rigid monomers that cannot enter the MOF apertures (monomer kinetic diameter intentionally above pore-limiting diameter), so coupling occurs only at the external surface.
- Thickness control: monomer equivalents/time series to target 5“50 nm MON (thin enough to limit diffusion penalty, thick enough for solvent barrier). Monitor thickness by ellipsometry on film analogues and cross-sectional TEM on crystals.
4.3 Metal contamination and false HER controls (required):
- Quantify Pd/Cu before/after extensive washing by ICP-MS (bulk digestion) and by XPS (surface); define acceptance: Pd < 50 ppm (or a project-justified threshold) for photocatalysis claims.
- HER blank tests: (i) MON-coated but no intentional co-catalyst; (ii) Pd-spiked control at measured ppm level; (iii) hot-filtration/leaching tests; (iv) Hg(0) poisoning test where applicable (to differentiate nanoparticulate Pd/Pt artifacts).

Step 5 — Photocatalytic H2 evolution with engineered co-catalyst placement
5.1 Co-catalyst strategy (avoid conflation with Pd residues):
- Use a non-Pd HER co-catalyst for primary claims (e.g., Ni2P, CoPx, or photodeposited Pt from rigorously purified precursors with independent quantification).
- Place co-catalyst preferentially on acceptor domain by photodeposition under conditions where electrons localize to acceptor (validated by EPR/TA); verify spatial distribution by STEM-EDX/EELS mapping.
5.2 Benchmarking matrix (factorial design):
- Compare: (a) no PAH vs PAH-loaded; (b) non-epitaxial physical mixture vs epitaxial core“shell; (c) uncoated vs MON-coated; (d) DMF vs DMF/H2O mixtures.
- Metrics: H2 rate (µmol g−1 h−1), apparent quantum yield, stability over ≥5“10 cycles, and correlation to solvent uptake kinetics.

Step 6 — In situ uptake/stability metrology for diamagnetic systems (replace magnetic sustentation)
6.1 QCM-D on oriented MOF films:
- Grow oriented films (same chemistry as crystals) on QCM sensors; measure Δf/ΔD during DMF and DMF/H2O exposure, illumination, and catalysis-like cycling.
- Extract uptake kinetics and viscoelastic changes; correlate with MON thickness and degradation signatures.
6.2 Ellipsometric porosimetry or microfluidic gravimetry:
- Use solvent-vapor and liquid-flow protocols to quantify solvent ingress/egress and pore accessibility after MON coating.
6.3 If (and only if) a paramagnetic variant is introduced:
- Validate “photophysics-neutrality” by showing identical (within error) uptake isotherms and TRPL/TA kinetics between paramagnetic-tagged and parent materials before using magnetic sustentation; otherwise do not use it for causal correlations.

Go/No-go gates (explicit):
G1 (framework): SCXRD-solved phase + reproducible facet indexing + survives DMF (≥24 h) without phase collapse.
G2 (epitaxy): registry demonstrated with |f| ≤ 2.5% (or strain-relaxed ≤ 3.5%) and orientation spread within target; defect density quantifiable.
G3 (energetics): ΔG_CT < −0.1 eV and TA/EPR shows charge-separated state τ_CS ≥ 1 µs.
G4 (MON): surface-confined handles verified; Pd/Cu below threshold; MON retains ≥50“70% of baseline pore accessibility to probe molecules while reducing water uptake/ingress rate.
G5 (catalysis): H2 enhancement attributable to D“A design (not Pd artifacts), with stability improvement correlated to reduced solvent uptake kinetics.
Feasibility: Framework/topology feasibility (addresses node critique): Rather than presuming a rare Zr(IV)/Ti(IV) N-donor cluster MOF, the core plan anchors on an experimentally precedented thiazine“tri(pyridyl) host“guest MOF (NKU‑111 family, Asset 2) that demonstrably forms donor“acceptor crystals with PAH guests and morphology control via epitaxial growth conditions. Zr/Ti robustness is relegated to a parallel benchmark track only if an N-donor-compatible Zr/Ti system is identified; it is not a dependency for epitaxy/photophysics.

Quantitative epitaxy and defect“kinetics linkage (addresses mismatch/defect critique): The revised plan predefines acceptable lattice mismatch (preferred ≤2.5%) and uses HR‑TEM strain mapping (GPA) plus synchrotron microdiffraction to turn “epitaxy quality” into measurable variables (strain fields, dislocation density, mosaic spread). These metrics are explicitly tied to CT parameters (k_CS, k_CR, τ_CS) obtained from TA/TRPL/EPR, enabling a falsifiable model: increasing defect density should increase k_CR and reduce τ_CS.

Energetics engineering (addresses asserted directionality critique): PAH identity is no longer chosen only by size matching; it is selected by measured redox potentials and optical energies to satisfy ΔG_CT and lifetime thresholds. CV/DPV + spectroelectrochemistry + TA provide a closed loop that verifies thermodynamic permission and kinetic competence of PAH→thiazine CT under illumination before proceeding to catalysis.

Surface-confined Sonogashira MON (addresses pore contamination + internal coupling critique): Handle localization is engineered through a final growth “surface pulse” (outer-layer mixed-linker incorporation) and verified by XPS/ToF‑SIMS depth profiling. Polymer-supported Pd (large beads) and Cu-free coupling conditions operationalize “size-excluded catalyst” in a physically defensible manner, while bulky monomers exceeding pore apertures prevent internal polymerization. ICP‑MS/XPS quantify residues, and HER blank/poisoning controls explicitly rule out Pd-derived false activity.

In situ uptake metrology (addresses magnetic sustentation critique): Because the primary N-donor MOF is expected to be diamagnetic, the plan replaces magnetic sustentation with QCM‑D and ellipsometric porosimetry/microfluidic gravimetry—standard, high-sensitivity liquid uptake tools compatible with thin films/crystals. A paramagnetic modification is optional only with a stringent neutrality validation; otherwise it is excluded to avoid confounding stability/photophysics.

Overall coherence with original concept chain: The scientific chain is preserved—(i) epitaxial registry to reduce interfacial traps and enforce orbital alignment, (ii) PAH guests as antennas/donors, (iii) Sonogashira MON skin to suppress solvent competition/hydrolysis—while each link is now testable with explicit materials choices, quantitative tolerances, anti-artifact safeguards, and go/no-go gates, substantially reducing build risk before stacking complexity.

Hypothesis: Methane storage performance in flexible Co(bdp)-type frameworks is governed not only by the static strength of edge-to-face aromatic interactions but by their dynamic adaptability under gas loading. We hypothesize that introducing a *rotationally frustrated ortho-difluorinated bdp ligand* in Co(o-F2-bdp), deliberately designed to undergo adsorption-coupled phenylene libration, will create a reversible, entropy-driven modulation of edge-to-face contacts during CH4 uptake. This dynamic interaction mode will lower the free-energy barrier for framework expansion while preserving a stabilized collapsed phase at low pressure, yielding a smoother, multi-site methane adsorption profile with enhanced deliverable capacity. The key methodological adaptation is the rational redesign of the bdp linker to function as a conformationally responsive element—transforming edge-to-face interactions from static stabilizers into gas-responsive, entropy-buffered hinges.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Design and synthesize a modified o-F2-bdp ligand incorporating a sterically biased ortho-F substitution pattern that enforces shallow torsional potentials of the phenylene rings (validated by DFT torsional scans).
1.2 Assemble Co(o-F2-bdp*) frameworks via solvothermal synthesis, targeting phase-pure flexible Co(bdp)-type topology; prepare Co(D4-bdp) and unmodified Co(bdp) as static-interaction controls.
1.3 Fully activate materials and establish baseline structural states using variable-temperature PXRD and N2 adsorption.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Adsorption-coupled dynamics probing: perform in situ CH4 adsorption (273“298 K) combined with synchrotron PXRD to track continuous changes in linker orientation and unit-cell parameters rather than discrete phase jumps.
2.2 Solid-state dynamic characterization: employ variable-temperature solid-state 19F NMR (for o-F2-bdp*) and 2H NMR (for Co(D4-bdp)) to directly measure phenyl ring libration amplitudes as a function of CH4 loading.
2.3 Energetic deconvolution: conduct adsorption microcalorimetry to separate enthalpic stabilization from entropic gains associated with linker motion, fitting results to a lattice“gas model incorporating conformational entropy terms.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Mechanistic validation: correlate onset of increased linker dynamics (NMR) with inflection points in CH4 isotherms and gradual PXRD shifts, confirming entropy-mediated gating rather than cooperative phase transition.
3.2 Performance metrics: evaluate methane deliverable capacity (65→5 bar, 298 K), hysteresis width, and cycling stability (≥300 cycles) and benchmark against Co(D4-bdp) and static Co(o-F2-bdp).
3.3 Falsification tests: (i) lock linker rotation via post-synthetic metalation at fluorine-adjacent positions and demonstrate loss of smooth adsorption; (ii) compare with para-difluorinated analogs lacking rotational frustration to isolate the ortho-driven dynamic effect.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Prior studies show that fluorination destabilizes the collapsed phase by weakening edge-to-face interactions, while deuteration preserves static dispersion forces. Extending this, physical organic chemistry establishes that ortho-fluoro substitution introduces low-barrier phenyl libration and significant conformational entropy. Coupling this dynamic behavior to adsorption provides a new thermodynamic lever beyond static interaction energy.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Flexible MOFs typically rely on cooperative, enthalpy-dominated phase transitions that cause sharp steps and hysteresis. Introducing conformationally responsive linkers is a chemically precise adaptation that remains within coordination polymer design principles while addressing a core limitation of gas storage materials.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike uniform functionalization or spatial patterning, this approach creates a single-phase material with intrinsically smooth, pressure-adaptive adsorption, reducing hysteresis without sacrificing uptake. The concept of entropy-buffered edge-to-face interactions is generalizable to other aromatic-linker MOFs, offering a new design paradigm for practical methane storage.

Hypothesis: A compositionally random mixed-linker Zn“imidazolate ZIF with node-proximal, atomically dispersed Cu(II/I) sites will enable *predictable* visible-light photocatalysis because (i) linker-electronics mixing shifts the ionization potential (IP) and electron affinity (EA) to straddle water/pollutant redox potentials at defined pH with a target optical gap of 1.9“2.5 eV, while (ii) isolated Cu sites introduce ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) and redox-trapping states that extend charge-separated lifetimes without creating CuOx clusters or homogeneous Cu pathways. The central mechanistic claim is falsifiable: if (a) the mixed-linker distribution is proven random at the nanometer scale with quantified defect density, (b) IP/EA-derived band edges (not Mott“Schottky alone) are within pre-registered windows vs NHE (pH 0 and 7) with bounded uncertainty, and (c) Cu remains predominantly single-site and non-leaching under illumination, then wavelength-dependent AQY/action spectra and photon-normalized kinetics will track the tuned band structure rather than oxide-skin activity or simple absorption increases. A deliberately ultrathin, discontinuous hydrophilic oxide overlayer (TiO2 or NiOOH; ≤1“3 nm, <~10“15% surface coverage by TEM/XPS) is used only as a kinetic interfacial promoter; selective excitation and absorption-normalized AQY will determine whether catalysis originates from the MOF electronic structure (mixed-linker/Cu) versus the oxide skin.
Plan: Stage 0 — Pre-registration of quantitative targets, uncertainty bounds, and go/no-go metrics
0.1 Band-edge targets (defined at 25 °C): convert measured IP/EA to E(VB/CB) vs NHE using vacuum-to-NHE offset (4.44 eV). Pre-register acceptance windows including uncertainty.
• At pH 0: CBM (EA-derived) ≤ 0.0 V vs NHE by ≥0.10 V margin (target: −0.2 to −0.6 V); VBM (IP-derived) ≥ +1.23 V by ≥0.10 V margin (target: +1.4 to +2.0 V). Optical gap 1.9“2.5 eV.
• At pH 7: apply Nernst shift (~−0.059 V·pH−1 for relevant proton-coupled couples): require CBM ≤ −0.41 V (≥0.10 V margin) and VBM ≥ +0.82 V (≥0.10 V margin).
0.2 Photophysics go/no-go: (i) transient absorption (TA) or TRPL indicates ≥5× lifetime increase upon Cu incorporation (same composition) and (ii) measurable trapped-electron signature (EPR) attributable to Cu(I) formation under illumination.
0.3 Stability go/no-go for advancing to overall splitting: after 20 h irradiation in the intended electrolyte: (i) PXRD retains key reflections with <20% loss in integrated intensity; (ii) BET surface area retains ≥70%; (iii) linker loss (solution NMR/LC) ≤5% and metal leaching (ICP-MS) ≤1% of total.
0.4 Performance benchmarks (photon-normalized): sacrificial HER: AQY(420 nm) ≥ 0.5% and TON (per Cu site) ≥ 50 over 20 h; sacrificial OER: AQY(420 nm) ≥ 0.1% with confirmed O2; pollutant mineralization: TOC removal ≥ 50% (not just decoloration) with demonstrated heterogeneous control (see Stage 3).

Stage 1 — Computational downselection anchored to measurable observables (IP/EA, not only band gaps)
1.1 Build a composition library in sodalite (SOD) ZIF topology with Zn nodes and 2“3 imidazolate linkers spanning Hammett parameters (electron donating/withdrawing), e.g., 2-methylimidazolate, 2-aminoimidazolate, 2-nitroimidazolate (and optionally 2-chloroimidazolate if synthetic compatibility holds).
1.2 Generate special quasi-random structures (SQS) for each composition (e.g., 25/75, 50/50, 75/25) to model true randomness; compute (i) IP/EA via slab/vacuum alignment or ΔSCF where feasible, (ii) optical gap (hybrid functional if tractable; otherwise calibrated GGA+U with correction to a reference ZIF measured by UPS/DRS), and (iii) density of states to flag defect-sensitive mid-gap states.
1.3 Model Cu single-site incorporation scenarios: (a) node-proximal substitution/coordination motifs consistent with ZIF chemistry (Cu bound to N sites, charge-compensated), (b) evaluate formation energies vs CuOx clustering propensity; compute LMCT transition signatures (TD-DFT on cluster models) to predict new absorption bands and EPR-relevant Cu(II)/Cu(I) fingerprints.
1.4 Downselect 2“3 lead compositions meeting pre-registered IP/EA windows with predicted minimal mid-gap defect states.

Stage 2 — Synthesis with explicit architectures that enable reliable band-edge measurement and nanoscale mixing verification
2.1 Mixed-linker ZIF synthesis: perform room-temperature or mild solvothermal co-crystallization with controlled linker feed ratios and identical total linker concentration; include modulator control (e.g., base concentration) to minimize defect variability across compositions. Prepare (i) powders for catalysis and (ii) oriented thin films for UPS.
2.2 Thin-film protocol for electronic measurements (replaces reliance on Mott“Schottky): grow ZIF films on conductive substrates with defined work function and minimal roughness (Au/ITO/FTO), using seeded growth to target thickness 50“200 nm (thick enough for UPS signal, thin enough to avoid charging). Verify uniformity by AFM/ellipsometry. Use low-energy electron flood gun if needed to mitigate charging; cross-check with Kelvin probe (work function) where possible.
2.3 Cu incorporation: prioritize routes that favor atomically dispersed Cu and suppress CuOx nucleation.
• Route A (preferred): post-synthetic cation exchange at low concentration (≤1“5 mol% relative to Zn sites), followed by gentle activation (≤150“200 °C under inert) to fix coordination without framework collapse.
• Route B (control): intentionally form CuOx clusters by higher loading or oxidative anneal to create a “cluster-positive” comparator.
2.4 Oxide overlayer (only after establishing MOF-only activity): employ confined hydrolysis/ALD-like limited-growth to generate discontinuous 1“3 nm TiO2 or NiOOH islands. Hard constraints: (i) XPS attenuation and TEM confirm <~10“15% surface coverage; (ii) N2 sorption shows ≤15% loss in pore volume; (iii) DRS shows no dominant new absorption from the oxide in the visible.

Stage 3 — Proving mixed-linker randomness and quantifying defects (mandatory attribution layer)
3.1 Composition and randomness:
• Digestive solution NMR: quantify linker ratios.
• Solid-state 13C/15N CP/MAS NMR: detect multiple local environments; compare to simulated/expected distributions for random mixing; extract evidence of clustering (peak splitting/broadening patterns beyond random expectation).
• Total scattering/PDF: quantify short-range order; fit Zn“N and linker“linker correlations; detect segregated domains or secondary phases.
• (S)TEM mapping: STEM-EDS/EELS (where feasible for N/C/O distributions and Cu) to check nanoscale homogeneity; use low-dose cryo/low-voltage strategies to mitigate beam damage.
3.2 Defect quantification and correlation to sub-gap absorption:
• Quantify missing-linker/unsaturated sites via TGA + elemental analysis + acid titration/IR of probe molecules; correlate with Urbach tail/sub-gap absorption (DRS) and with TA recombination kinetics.
• Establish a defect-performance map: if sub-gap absorption correlates with higher defect density rather than designed composition, that composition is deprioritized.

Stage 4 — Band-edge determination with bounded uncertainty (UPS/IP + optical gap + electrochemical validation)
4.1 UPS: measure secondary electron cutoff (work function) and valence onset (VBM relative to EF) on the defined films; compute ionization potential IP = WF + (EF−VBM). Report uncertainty from repeated samples (n≥3) and charging checks.
4.2 Optical gap: determine Eg,opt from diffuse reflectance (Kubelka“Munk/Tauc consistent method across samples) and cross-check with photothermal deflection spectroscopy if available to resolve Urbach tails.
4.3 Electron affinity and CBM estimate: EA = IP − Eg,opt; convert to E(CB) vs NHE using 4.44 eV offset; propagate uncertainties (ΔIP, ΔEg) and pre-register acceptable ΔE (e.g., ±0.15“0.20 eV).
4.4 Secondary validation (not primary): use redox mediators (outer-sphere couples) in photoelectrochemical measurements on the same films to bracket band positions; treat Mott“Schottky only as qualitative due to porosity/low conductivity.

Stage 5 — Cu speciation and leaching controls to exclude homogeneous/cluster-driven pathways
5.1 Ex situ speciation: XAS (XANES/EXAFS) to confirm Cu“N coordination and exclude Cu“O“Cu signatures; quantify average coordination number; XPS for surface oxidation state.
5.2 Operando/near-operando (if feasible): XAS under illumination in aqueous electrolyte to track Cu(II)↔Cu(I) cycling and detect emergence of CuOx.
5.3 Leaching/time-course: ICP-MS of aliquots during photocatalysis (0, 0.5, 2, 5, 20 h). Define pass criterion: ≤1% Cu loss over 20 h.
5.4 Hot filtration and reusability:
• Remove solid mid-reaction, continue illumination of filtrate; require negligible continued activity.
• Recycle catalyst ≥5 runs with stable rates and unchanged XAS signature.
5.5 Chelator suppression (heterogeneous vs homogeneous): add bathocuproine or EDTA in both light/dark; interpret carefully:
• If activity persists while leached Cu is complexed (and ICP shows no Cu), supports heterogeneous pathway.
• Run “homogeneous positive control”: add Cu2+ salt at measured leached-Cu concentration to a Cu-free ZIF and to a no-solid system to quantify any photo-Fenton-like contribution.
5.6 Cluster-positive comparator: test intentionally CuOx-clustered material; if it shows different action spectrum/ROS profile and stronger chelator sensitivity, supports that the single-site material operates differently.

Stage 6 — Photophysics and action spectra to attribute performance to band tuning (mandatory)
6.1 TRPL/TA: quantify carrier lifetimes and trapping dynamics across (i) single-linker, (ii) mixed-linker, (iii) mixed-linker+Cu, (iv) mixed-linker+oxide skin, maintaining equal absorbance at excitation wavelength.
6.2 EPR spin trapping (DMPO or equivalent): quantify •OH/•O2− generation rates; compare across variants; relate to band-edge alignment (oxidation strength) and Cu trapping.
6.3 Action spectra & wavelength-dependent AQY:
• Measure AQY(λ) at multiple wavelengths (e.g., 365/405/420/450/500 nm) with calibrated photon flux.
• Perform absorption normalization and apparent quantum yield calculations; require that AQY onset/shape tracks the MOF optical edge and shifts systematically with linker composition.
• Selective excitation tests: choose wavelengths where oxide absorbs minimally but MOF absorbs (and vice versa) to deconvolute contributions.

Stage 7 — Catalysis workflow with staged decision tree (half-reactions → overall splitting only if criteria met)
7.1 Sacrificial HER screen (visible light): standardized reactor geometry, photon flux, stirring, catalyst loading, and degassing; measure H2 by GC; report rates normalized by absorbed photons and by mass; determine TON per Cu.
7.2 Sacrificial OER screen: quantify O2 (GC) and confirm stoichiometry; use hole scavenger only in HER stage; for OER stage use electron acceptor as needed but pre-register the transition to unbiased conditions only after stability/photophysics gates are met.
7.3 Overall water splitting attempt (only if Stage 0.3 & 0.2 pass):
• Couple optimized HER/OER surfaces (NiOOH favored for OER; minimal loading) and verify 2:1 H2:O2 with isotopic labeling (H2O/D2O) to confirm source.
• Report STH (even if low) with full photon balance; if STH < pre-set minimal threshold (e.g., 0.01“0.05%) or stoichiometry deviates persistently, stop and revert to mechanistic refinement rather than performance claims.
7.4 Pollutant degradation with heterogeneous attribution:
• Model pollutants: dye + phenol-class; track concentration (HPLC/UV“Vis), intermediates (LC“MS), and mineralization (TOC).
• Run dark controls, no-catalyst controls, oxide-only controls, Cu-leachate homogeneous controls.
• Identify dominant ROS via scavengers and EPR; require that mineralization correlates with ROS generation and with action spectra rather than with dissolved Cu.

Stage 8 — Benchmarking and reporting discipline
8.1 Benchmarks: single-linker ZIF analogs, Cu-free mixed-linker ZIF, Ti-MOF benchmark (e.g., MIL-125-type), and commercial TiO2 under identical photon flux.
8.2 Report photon-normalized metrics (AQY, absorbed-photon rate) and full uncertainty; avoid “outperform” unless statistically significant vs benchmarks and attribution gates are satisfied.
Feasibility: 1) Band-edge alignment feasibility without unreliable Mott“Schottky: The plan centers on UPS-derived ionization potentials on well-defined ZIF thin films (50“200 nm on Au/ITO/FTO with charging mitigation) plus optical gaps to obtain EA/CB positions vs NHE with propagated uncertainty (target ±0.15“0.20 eV). Redox-mediator bracketing provides secondary validation. This directly addresses the known unreliability of Mott“Schottky for porous/insulating ZIFs.
2) Mixed-linker randomness and defect rigor: Statistical mixing is not assumed; it is *proven* by convergent evidence (digest NMR for global ratios; solid-state 13C/15N NMR for local environments; total scattering/PDF for short-range order; STEM-EDS/EELS for nanoscale homogeneity) and paired with quantitative defect metrics that are explicitly correlated with Urbach tails/sub-gap absorption and recombination lifetimes.
3) Cu single-site vs cluster/homogeneous exclusion: The proposal implements a stringent speciation/leaching attribution stack: ex situ and (if possible) operando XAS, time-resolved ICP-MS, hot-filtration, chelator suppression in light/dark, and homogeneous Cu spike controls at the measured leached concentration. An intentionally cluster-rich comparator provides a mechanistic contrast. These controls are designed to falsify the claim if activity arises from CuOx clusters or dissolved Cu rather than MOF-embedded single sites.
4) Attribution to band tuning rather than absorption/oxide dominance: Wavelength-dependent AQY/action spectra with absorption normalization and selective excitation are mandatory decision points. The oxide overlayer is constrained to an ultrathin, discontinuous morphology with explicit porosity/coverage caps and is introduced only after establishing MOF-only trends; thus, any apparent gains can be deconvoluted.
5) Credible staging toward overall water splitting: A go/no-go decision tree with hard thresholds (stability, lifetime enhancement, AQY and TON targets, and ≥20 h integrity constraints) prevents over-claiming and focuses effort on conditions where ZIF stability and charge transport are adequate before attempting overall splitting. This makes the endpoint ambitious but logically gated and reviewer-aligned.

Hypothesis: A diastereomerically gated, homochiral Cu2 paddlewheel MOF derived from the CPM-332 platform can be converted into an enantioselective “reactive adsorbent” for simultaneous (i) oxygen-specific binding at open Cu sites and (ii) chromatographic resolution of chiral carboxylate drugs (naproxen) by a deliberate methodological adaptation: post-synthetic, stereocontrolled installation of chiral benzylic alcohol (1-phenyl-1-propanol) at the axial sites of Cu2 paddlewheels to create a second, switchable chiral field. Mechanistically, the adapted material enforces diastereoisomerism at the node level (two distinct, long-lived Cu2 environments) that (a) differentially stabilizes O2 adduct geometries (end-on vs side-on/superoxo-like binding propensity) and (b) creates diastereomeric host“guest ion-pairing/CH“π pockets for (R)- vs (S)-naproxen near the Cu-carboxylate node, amplifying ΔΔG of adsorption and enabling resolution under mild flow conditions. Oxygen acts as an allosteric modulator: reversible O2 coordination changes the Cu“O(axial) bond strength and local electrostatics, toggling selectivity and enabling in situ regeneration and mechanistic readout.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1. Synthesize CPM-332 diastereomeric analogs (e.g., CPM-332-RR and CPM-332-RS or closest accessible CPM-33x isoreticular congeners) using isocamphoric-acid-derived linkers to ensure homochirality and known diastereoisomerism.
1.2. Activate materials to generate open Cu sites (solvent exchange to MeOH/acetone, then gentle vacuum/heat while preserving crystallinity). Confirm open-metal-site formation by IR of coordinated solvent removal and N2 sorption.
1.3. Prepare enantiopure 1-phenyl-1-propanol (R and S) and racemic naproxen; prepare naproxen as neutral acid and as sodium salt to probe ion-pairing contributions.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1. Methodological adaptation—stereocontrolled axial-site “chiral capping” to induce node-level diastereoisomerism:
  2.1.1. Perform post-synthetic modification (PSM) by dosing activated Cu-paddlewheel MOF with controlled vapor-phase or supercritical CO2-assisted infusion of (R)-1-phenyl-1-propanol or (S)-1-phenyl-1-propanol at substoichiometric to near-stoichiometric coverage relative to Cu sites.
  2.1.2. Lock in two distinct Cu2 environments by partial capping (target 30“70% occupancy) to create a statistical but kinetically persistent distribution of Cu2 sites (uncapped/open vs capped/benzylic-alcohol-bound), generating diastereomeric site pairs within a single homochiral lattice.
  2.1.3. Use single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC“SC) or high-resolution PXRD refinement to verify retention of topology and to quantify axial ligand occupancy; corroborate with Cu K-edge XAS (EXAFS) for Cu“O(axial) distance changes.
2.2. Oxygen binding and allosteric gating characterization:
  2.2.1. Measure O2 adsorption isotherms (77“298 K) and compare to N2/Ar to isolate specific O2 interactions. Use in situ EPR to detect Cu(II)/Cu(I) signatures indicative of superoxo/peroxo character; use in situ DRIFTS to detect O“O vibrational features if present.
  2.2.2. Map how O2 binding differs between capped and uncapped sites via operando XAS under controlled O2 partial pressures; quantify site-specific binding energies by combining isotherms with van’t Hoff analysis and DFT cluster models of Cu2 paddlewheels with/without axial 1-phenyl-1-propanol.
2.3. Enantioselective naproxen uptake and resolution:
  2.3.1. Conduct batch adsorption from racemic naproxen solutions (nonpolar and polar solvents; control water content) on (i) parent CPM-332, (ii) homochiral CPM-332, (iii) homochiral + (R)-1-phenyl-1-propanol-capped, (iv) homochiral + (S)-capped.
  2.3.2. Quantify enantiomeric excess (ee) in supernatant and in desorbed fraction using chiral HPLC; fit adsorption data to dual-site Langmuir models reflecting capped vs uncapped Cu sites.
  2.3.3. Test O2 as a switch: repeat adsorption under N2 vs O2 atmospheres to determine whether O2 coordination modulates naproxen selectivity/capacity (allosteric control). Evaluate cycling stability (≥20 adsorption/desorption cycles) using mild vacuum and O2/N2 purge.
2.4. Mechanistic validation by spatial and energetic mapping:
  2.4.1. Use microcalorimetry (or isosteric heat from isotherms) for (R)- and (S)-naproxen adsorption to extract ΔΔH and correlate with ee.
  2.4.2. Perform solid-state NMR (13C labeled naproxen if needed) and Raman/IR to identify binding motifs (carboxylate coordination vs hydrogen bonding to axial alcohol).
  2.4.3. DFT/periodic calculations: model diastereomeric pockets formed by homochiral framework + axial chiral alcohol; compute binding free energy differences for (R)/(S)-naproxen with and without O2 bound at adjacent Cu sites.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1. Structural integrity: PXRD before/after activation, PSM, O2 exposure, and naproxen cycling; SEM for morphology; BET for porosity retention.
3.2. Site quantification: TGA and 1H NMR of digested MOF to quantify alcohol loading; XPS/XAS for Cu oxidation state changes under O2.
3.3. Resolution performance metrics: enantioselectivity factor (α), uptake capacity, productivity (mg naproxen per g MOF per hour) in a packed-bed column; breakthrough curves for racemate under N2 vs O2.
3.4. Controls: achiral analog (if accessible), fully capped (≈100%) vs partially capped samples, and alcohol-free parent; nonbinding guest controls (e.g., ibuprofen) to benchmark specificity.
3.5. Resolution (analytical) improvement: couple chiral HPLC outcomes with high-resolution solid-state characterization; if needed, incorporate synchrotron PXRD to resolve subtle diastereomeric site ordering (linking “resolution” as measurement capability to structure“function readout).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: CPM-332-type homochiral frameworks derived from isocamphorate chemistry have demonstrated diastereoisomerism in isostructural MOFs and strong chiral recognition (Asset 2). Cu2 paddlewheel nodes are well-established to host open metal sites that bind small gases, including O2, with measurable site-specific energetics (Asset 3). Axial ligand binding at Cu paddlewheels is chemically tractable and can modulate redox/electronic structure, providing a plausible allosteric handle for O2 and guest binding.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Rather than changing linkers/metal nodes randomly, the adaptation targets a known functional bottleneck: chiral recognition in MOFs is often limited by weak, distributed chiral fields. By installing a second chiral element at the node (axial site) using 1-phenyl-1-propanol, the design concentrates chirality at the primary adsorption/reactivity locus (Cu2 paddlewheel), intentionally creating diastereomeric node environments within a single homochiral lattice. This is a direct supramolecular/coordination-chemistry adaptation of axial-site engineering to chiral separations.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with (i) parent CPM-332 (chirality only from linker), the adapted material should show higher ΔΔG for naproxen enantio-discrimination because binding occurs at/near a diastereomerically structured Cu2 pocket with added CH“π and H-bond donors. Compared with (ii) fully capped nodes, partial capping preserves open sites for O2 binding and introduces dual-site cooperativity, enabling switchable selectivity and easier regeneration. Compared with (iii) traditional chiral stationary phases, the MOF offers tunable open-metal-site chemistry, porosity-controlled mass transport, and an operando mechanistic probe (O2-induced spectral/adsorption changes) that links structure to performance.

Hypothesis: Embedding a grain-boundary (GB)-confined, electronically percolative 2D conductive MOF (2D c-MOF) network—formed in-crystallization and restricted to GBs/voids at sub‑1 vol%—will increase sustained operational power density and delivered energy yield in mixed-cation mixed-halide perovskite solar cells by (A) suppressing GB-limited trap-assisted recombination via a lateral charge-percolation scaffold and defect-state “electronic short-circuiting” at the nanoscale, (B) kinetically intercepting the dominant ROS actually present under defined O2/H2O partial pressures through fast proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) at redox-addressable nodes/linkers that outcompetes halide/organic-cation oxidation, and (C) reducing field-driven ion migration/hysteresis through a narrowly dosed Na+ GB occupancy strategy that neutralizes halide-vacancy-rich GB sites without introducing Na-driven band bending, halide segregation, or secondary phases.

Mechanistic elevation and causality commitments (addressing reviewer critiques):
1) Spin/AFM coupling is treated as a testable modifier—not an assumed advantage. We hypothesize that if antiferromagnetic (AFM) exchange in the GB c‑MOF reduces spin-mixed recombination at defect-rich GBs (via spin-dependent charge transfer/recombination), this will manifest as measurable magneto-optoelectronic signatures (magneto-photocurrent, field-dependent PL/EL, spin-dependent recombination rates). If these signatures are absent, performance gains will be attributed solely to conductivity/chemistry, and the AFM claim is rejected.
2) ROS specificity is established experimentally under controlled atmospheres and by kinetics modeling. The functional claim is not “OH-only”; rather: the GB c‑MOF provides a redox/PCET sink whose efficacy is mapped against superoxide (O2•−), singlet oxygen (1O2), and hydroxyl radical (•OH) under oxygen-free vs oxygen-containing operation. The decisive criterion is whether MOF-mediated ROS interception rate constants at GBs exceed the competing iodide oxidation/organic-cation fragmentation pathways under those same conditions.
3) Na+ acts as a GB defect-chemistry modulator only within a predefined narrow window (10“300 ppm relative to Pb; expanded only if acceptance criteria are met). Na+ is introduced using a low-coordination, low-nucleophilicity counterion strategy with explicit counterion-only controls to decouple Na+ effects from TFSI−/BF4− processing artifacts. Na incorporation is accepted only if band-edge shifts and leakage/shunting remain within strict bounds and no halide segregation is induced.
4) The engineering risk (continuous GB percolation without shunts) is de-risked before long stability tests via explicit go/no-go thresholds: (i) conductive-AFM evidence of GB-localized conduction, (ii) lateral conductivity increase without loss of shunt resistance statistics across >30 devices, and (iii) microscopy-confirmed GB coverage fraction within a target window that avoids planar overgrowth.

Overall, the refined hypothesis is: performance and stability improvements arise from a quantifiable combination of (i) GB-localized electronic percolation, (ii) atmosphere-dependent ROS interception kinetics (not assumed OH primacy), and (iii) narrowly constrained Na+ defect buffering; any additional AFM/spin-correlation benefit must be demonstrated by discriminating magneto-optoelectronic experiments against matched paramagnetic/nonmagnetic analogues.
Plan: Step 0 — Materials set and device baseline (lock-down for comparability)
0.1 Baseline perovskite absorber: FA0.8Cs0.2Pb(I1−xBrx)3 with x tuned to Eg = 1.55“1.65 eV (same ink composition and thermal history across all groups). Target film thickness: 450“600 nm; target grain size: 300“800 nm.
0.2 Two device stacks to decouple transport-layer chemistry:
  • n“i“p: ITO/SnO2/perovskite/spiro-OMeTAD/Au
  • p“i“n: ITO/NiOx/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag
0.3 Define baseline acceptance: PCE within ±0.7% absolute across batches; Rs and Rsh distributions stable; hysteresis index <0.08 after protocol stabilization.

Step 1 — GB-confined “in-crystallization MOF weaving” with explicit confinement parameters
1.1 Precursor timing window (in situ GIWAXS gate): cast perovskite to reach partial crystallization where perovskite (100)/(110) peaks emerge but prior to full grain coalescence (empirically defined; typically 10“60 s after antisolvent or during vacuum-assist).
1.2 MOF precursor delivery designed for GB wicking (exclude dense grains):
  • Use ultradilute polar alcohol (IPA/EtOH) or anisole/alcohol mixture with controlled water content <200 ppm.
  • Total metal-ligand concentration: 0.05“0.5 mM (screened) to prevent planar overgrowth.
  • Delivery: (a) vapor exposure (preferred for confinement) OR (b) brief 2“5 s spray/meniscus-contact followed by immediate spin-off.
1.3 MOF chemistries (three-way discriminating set; all engineered to be process-compatible and to nucleate at undercoordinated Pb/I GB sites):
  Group M1 (AFM-coupled conductive 2D c‑MOF): Ni“TTC-like (Asset 2 motif) adapted with catecholate/phenolate-rich linker enabling PCET; target conductivity ≥10−3 S·cm−1 in thin film.
  Group M2 (paramagnetic/nonmagnetic but similarly conductive 2D c‑MOF): Cu“HHTP-like (Asset 1 motif) or a diamagnetic analogue (e.g., closed-shell metal if feasible) tuned to similar sheet resistance (within 3× of M1) to isolate spin/AFM effects.
  Group M3 (insulating MOF control): isoreticular framework with similar functional groups/anchoring but low conductivity (≤10−7 S·cm−1) to isolate “chemical passivation only” vs “conductive percolation”.
  (All MOFs incorporate a GB-anchoring motif: tethered ammonium/pyridinium substituent at low density (e.g., 5“15% linker functionalization) to bias nucleation at halide-vacancy-rich GBs; maintain overall 2D stacking.)
1.4 Trigger chemistry (perovskite-compatible, confinement-preserving):
  • Ligand deprotonation using ppm-level triethylamine vapor (TEA) or buffered alcohol base for 10“60 s.
  • Temperature ≤80 °C; total exposure ≤3 min.
  • Rinse: 1“2 s pure solvent rinse to remove any non-confined residues.
1.5 Target structural metrics (must be met before proceeding):
  • GB ribbon thickness equivalent: 1“3 nm along GB walls (no continuous planar overlayer detectable by AFM step height mapping across terraces).
  • Coverage fraction along GBs: 40“80% of GB length in plan-view (below 40%: non-percolative; above 80%: shunt risk).
  • Total MOF volume fraction: 0.1“0.8 vol% (estimated by uptake + elemental quantification).

Step 2 — Na+ strategy with narrow dosing window and counterion controls (decouple chemistry)
2.1 Dosing range (predefined): 10, 30, 100, 300 ppm Na relative to Pb (stop at 300 ppm unless all acceptance criteria pass; only then explore 500“1000 ppm).
2.2 Introduction routes (factorial design):
  • Route A: Na+ in perovskite precursor via NaPF6 or NaClO4 (preferred to reduce strongly coordinating anion effects); keep total added anion constant across controls.
  • Route B: Na+ in MOF bath (same ppm range referenced to estimated perovskite mass uptake) to test preferential partitioning into GB/MOF microenvironment.
2.3 Mandatory controls:
  • Counterion-only: add TFSI−/BF4−/PF6− source without Na+ (e.g., tetrabutylammonium salts) at matched molarity to isolate anion/process effects.
  • K+ analogue at matched ppm (optional but recommended) to probe specificity of Na+ vs generic alkali occupancy.
2.4 Na acceptance criteria (must pass):
  • Band-edge shifts: ΔWork function (KPFM/UPS) ≤ 50 meV vs Na-free at same MOF condition.
  • No measurable increase in p/n-type bulk doping (Mott“Schottky/capacitance profiling consistent within 20%).
  • No new crystalline Na-containing phases (GIWAXS detection limit) and no Na-rich clusters in STEM-EDX.
  • No increase in halide segregation under illumination (operando PL peak-splitting < baseline + 10%).

Step 3 — Percolation and shunt-risk de-risking (go/no-go before long ISOS)
3.1 Conductive-AFM (c-AFM) maps on perovskite top surface and cross-sections:
  • Metric: GB-to-grain conduction contrast (I_GB/I_grain) and continuity of conductive pathways along GBs.
  • Go/no-go: median I_GB increases ≥10× over control, while grain interior remains unchanged (avoid bulk shunting).
3.2 Lateral conductivity vs loading (four-probe / TLM on dedicated test structures):
  • Go/no-go: ≥3× increase in lateral sheet conductance at ≤0.8 vol% MOF, without >20% drop in vertical device Rsh.
3.3 Device statistics (minimum n=30 per condition):
  • Go/no-go: shunt resistance Rsh distribution not degraded (median Rsh decrease ≤15%); leakage at −0.1 V in dark increases ≤2×.

Step 4 — AFM/spin-correlation claim: discriminating magneto-optoelectronic tests (mandatory)
4.1 Sample set: M1 (AFM), M2 (paramagnetic/nonmagnetic but conductive-matched), M3 (insulating) all GB-confined with matched coverage (±10%) and similar conductivity where required.
4.2 Measurements:
  • Magneto-photocurrent (MPC) and magneto-electroluminescence (MEL): field sweep (0“300 mT) at fixed bias/illumination.
  • Field-dependent PL (FDPL): quantify PL intensity/lifetime change vs B-field.
  • Temperature dependence (80“320 K) to probe spin-dependent recombination signatures.
4.3 Interpretation criteria:
  • If M1 shows statistically significant MPC/MEL/FDPL signatures distinct from M2 at matched conductivity and chemistry, attribute an additional spin-correlation role.
  • If M1≈M2 within error, remove AFM as causal and treat conductivity/PCET as the mechanism.

Step 5 — ROS specificity and kinetics dominance (separate OH, O2•−, 1O2; quantify rate competition)
5.1 Controlled atmosphere matrix during illumination + bias:
  • Dry N2 (O2 < 1 ppm, H2O < 1 ppm)
  • N2 + controlled O2 (0.1%, 1%, 21%) at <5 ppm H2O
  • N2 + controlled H2O (50“5000 ppm) at O2 < 1 ppm
  • Air with defined RH (10%, 50%)
5.2 ROS mapping (film-only and full stacks):
  • •OH: in situ spin-trapping EPR (DMPO“OH) with calibrated adduct kinetics.
  • O2•−: EPR with appropriate spin trap (e.g., DMPO“OOH signatures) and/or optical probe validated for perovskites.
  • 1O2: near-IR phosphorescence at 1270 nm and/or selective chemical trap (e.g., SOSG) with controls for probe photobleaching.
  • Include transport-layer-dependent tests (SnO2 vs NiOx vs C60) to identify interfacial ROS sources.
5.3 Kinetics modeling requirement:
  • Build a competitive reaction model at GBs: ROS generation terms (dependent on O2/H2O, bias, TL), competing sinks (perovskite iodide oxidation; organic-cation oxidation; MOF PCET sink).
  • Extract effective pseudo-first-order rate constants for ROS decay with and without MOF using time-resolved probe/EPR data.
  • Go/no-go: k_MOF,sink (effective) must exceed k_perovskite,damage by ≥5× under at least one realistic operating condition (e.g., 21% O2, RH 10“50%, 1 sun, MPP bias) to claim chemical protection.
5.4 Chemical corroboration (operando/post-mortem):
  • Operando XPS: suppression of I0/I+ species growth; O 1s evolution; Pb state shifts.
  • LC-MS/GC-MS of extracted organics: reduced signatures of organic-cation fragmentation products.

Step 6 — Recombination/transport and ion migration (separate contributions quantitatively)
6.1 Recombination:
  • TRPL + confocal PL mapping to extract GB vs grain lifetime distributions.
  • Intensity-dependent Voc and ideality factor; target: reduction in ideality factor toward 1 (trap-assisted reduced).
  • Transient photovoltage/photocurrent and impedance: separate recombination resistance and transport resistance.
6.2 Ion migration/hysteresis:
  • Temperature-dependent impedance to extract ionic activation energy.
  • Transient ion-drift (bias-step) and hysteresis index under stabilized protocol.
  • Go/no-go for Na benefit: Na-dosed must reduce hysteresis index by ≥30% vs Na-free at same MOF, without band-edge shift >50 meV.

Step 7 — Operational power density and delivered energy yield (only after go/no-go pass)
7.1 ISOS protocols:
  • ISOS-L3 (light, MPP) and ISOS-O2 (outdoor/ambient variant) as applicable.

Feasibility: 1) Why the 2D c‑MOF concept is feasible in perovskite GBs (and how we bound the risk)
• Conductive 2D MOFs with measurable conductivity and redox activity are established (Asset 2), supporting the premise that a sub‑vol% framework can provide lateral electronic percolation if it is spatially concentrated at GBs (where it matters most). The proposal does not assume “more MOF is better”; it sets a constrained volume fraction (0.1“0.8 vol%) and demands conductive-AFM evidence of GB-localized conduction.
• The core engineering risk—unintended shunting/planar overgrowth—is explicitly managed by kinetic exclusion (vapor/ultradilute delivery), short triggering, and quantitative go/no-go leakage/Rsh statistics across >30 devices before stability testing.

2) AFM exchange coupling: converted from assertion into a falsifiable, discriminating experiment set
• Asset 2 motivates AFM-coupled 2D c‑MOFs as robust electronic frameworks, but that does not automatically translate to PSCs. Therefore, the revised plan compares GB-confined MOFs that are (M1) AFM-coupled, (M2) paramagnetic/nonmagnetic but conductivity-matched, and (M3) insulating. Magneto-photocurrent, magneto-EL, and field-dependent PL explicitly test whether spin correlations measurably alter recombination/charge transfer. If no spin-dependent signatures appear, AFM is removed as a causal mechanism, preventing mechanistic overreach.

3) ROS mechanism credibility: radical specificity and rate competition are treated as the central proof
• Asset 1 demonstrates that conductive MOFs can participate in ROS-related electro/photochemistry, including hydroxyl radical pathways, but PSC degradation often involves O2•− and 1O2 depending on oxygen/water and interfaces. The revised proposal therefore (i) maps •OH, O2•−, and 1O2 under controlled O2/H2O partial pressures and (ii) requires kinetics modeling showing the MOF-mediated sink outcompetes perovskite damage kinetics at GBs. Oxygen-free experiments separate intrinsic photo-chemistry from ambient-driven pathways, directly addressing reviewer concern.

4) Na+ buffering: feasibility bounded by narrow dosing, counterion controls, and explicit acceptance criteria
• The proposal narrows Na+ to 10“300 ppm (initially), avoiding the unbounded 0.1% regime that risks secondary phases and unintended doping. Counterion-only controls isolate anion/crystallization effects from Na+. Na location/chemical state is verified (ToF-SIMS + XPS depth profiling + 23Na NMR where feasible). Acceptance criteria on band-edge shifts (≤50 meV), leakage, and halide segregation prevent “apparent stability” that is actually a doped/segregated artifact.

5) Why this should improve power density and energy yield (and how we will prove it)
• Power density gains are expected only if GB recombination is reduced without adding series resistance or shunts; hence the mandatory percolation/leakage gates plus TRPL/ideality/impedance decomposition.
• Energy-yield gains require suppressing the dominant operating degradation channel under the relevant atmosphere; hence the ROS mapping matrix and requirement that MOF sink kinetics dominate at least one realistic condition (air/RH/MPP). Delivered energy (time-integrated Wh·m−2) is used as the operational analogue of “energy density”, aligning with the proposal’s original framing while remaining PSC-appropriate.

In sum, each contested causal link (AFM/spin benefit, ROS identity, Na+ role, percolation vs shunt tradeoff) is converted into a controlled, quantitative, go/no-go-structured validation plan that can either substantiate the higher-level claims or force mechanistic down-selection without compromising the central GB-confined conductive-MOF concept.

Hypothesis: Embedding a negatively curved (Schwarz P-type) bicontinuous interlayer that hosts axially regulated M“N single-atom sites (e.g., Ni“N4“X, X = Cl/COO−) at the perovskite/ETL interface will simultaneously (i) suppress perovskite interfacial degradation and ion-driven hysteresis and (ii) maintain high Voc/FF by reducing interfacial recombination. Mechanistically, negative Gaussian curvature increases accessible interfacial area and creates continuous, low-tortuosity transport pathways for electrons while distributing local electric fields, thereby reducing hot-spot driven halide segregation. Axial coordination environment regulation (X = Cl vs COO−) tunes the single-atom site’s Lewis acidity/basicity and dipole moment to anchor/neutralize undercoordinated Pb“I species (defect passivation) and to immobilize mobile iodide via reversible coordination, increasing long-term operational stability. The same M“N sites are designed to stabilize a surface-bound carboxylate (COO−) motif that acts as a ‘buffer ligand’ to lower interfacial charge-transfer overpotential (i.e., reduce energetic/kinetic losses for electron extraction), improving fill factor without introducing ionic dopants.

Hypothesis: Embedding a coordination-programmed single-atom redox buffer directly inside a 2D/3D perovskite heterojunction (rather than as a separate carbonaceous interlayer) will simultaneously increase Voc and long-term operational stability by (i) converting under-coordinated surface Pb“I motifs into a neutral, low-trap coordination environment via chelation/halogen-bridging at the 2D/3D interface and (ii) enforcing a four-electron oxygen reduction pathway on isolated M“N4“X centers that rapidly consumes adventitious O2 without generating peroxide/superoxide intermediates that trigger iodide oxidation. Methodological adaptation: we will replace the rejected ‘SAC@N“C interlayer’ architecture with a solvent-compatible, microwave-synthesized SAC“salt that mechanochemically pre-assembles into a bulky-ammonium spacer ink; during a brief post-deposition conversion, the spacer self-organizes into an ultrathin Dion“Jacobson/Ruddlesden“Popper-like 2D cap where isolated metal atoms become axially coordinated (M“N4“X) and immobilized within the organic“inorganic lattice. This yields a built-in redox/coordination buffer that is electronically benign for extraction, chemically passivating, and operando oxygen-scavenging. Faraday’s law will be used to quantitatively relate charge passed through the redox buffer under illumination to the moles of O2 reduced (n≈4), providing a predictive ceiling for oxygen-driven degradation rates.

1.1 Baseline PSC stack (kept constant across all comparisons): glass/ITO/NiOx (or MeO-2PACz)/3D perovskite/C60 (or SnO2)/BCP/Cu (choose inverted or regular, but keep one architecture). Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Microwave synthesis (core adaptation #1: fast, coordination-preserving SAC salt production):
- Synthesize a metallomacrocycle single-atom complex as a microwave-assisted ionic salt: [M(macrocycle)(X)]^+ paired with a bulky organic counterion compatible with perovskite solvents (e.g., fluorinated sulfonylimide) to ensure solubility in low-polarity alcohols/esters.

2.2 Mechanochemical synthesis (core adaptation #2: solvent-minimized co-crystal ‘2D-spacer ink’):

- Objective: form a co-crystalline powder where the SAC salt is molecularly dispersed within the spacer matrix (no carbon, no pyrolysis). Confirm via PXRD (new co-crystal reflections), solid-state NMR/FTIR (ion-pairing), and HAADF-STEM on drop-cast films (no nanoparticles).
2.3 Formation of a built-in SAC-doped 2D/3D interface (structurally novel placement):
- After forming the 3D perovskite film, spin-coat a very dilute solution of the mechanochemically prepared co-crystal in a perovskite-benign solvent (e.g., IPA/EtOAc blends). Mild thermal treatment (≤100 °C) drives self-assembly into an ultrathin 2D cap (1“3 layers typical) at the surface.
- The SAC complex is designed to dock into the 2D lattice via ammonium/halide positioning while retaining M“N4“X coordination; it acts as (i) a chelating passivant for Pb-rich surface sites through halogen-bridging and (ii) a redox-active oxygen scavenger.

2.4 Coordination-environment control series:
- Axial ligand series: X = none / Cl / Br.
- Metal identity: Fe vs Co (oxygen binding energetics differ).

3.3 Demonstrate four-electron oxygen reduction pathway without peroxide intermediates (mechanism proof):

Deliverables/Go“No-Go criteria:

Hypothesis: Embedding a Schwarz P“type bicontinuous interfacial layer (20“50 nm curvature length scale) between the perovskite and SnO2 can generate a measurable, geometry-driven modulation of interfacial electrostatics (surface potential/work-function landscape) that improves electron-selective contact behavior only when (a) the curvature length is comparable to the interfacial screening length (Debye length) of the perovskite/ETL contact region, and (b) the interlayer chemistry is tuned to avoid midgap states and parasitic redox. Mechanistically, negative Gaussian curvature increases the interfacial area-normal electric-field components and redistributes charge accumulation at the perovskite/ETL boundary, producing a spatially averaged contact dipole and reduced local barrier for electron transfer into SnO2, thereby lowering interfacial recombination velocity (S) and increasing QFLS-derived Voc.
