Films are formed and programmed on robust electrodes/CTLs (ITO/FTO/SnO2/NiOx), then integrated by subsequent deposition steps. This avoids uncontrolled electrochemistry on C60 and avoids perturbing spiro-OMeTAD dopants, improving attribution.

Addresses critique (iv): Co“Nx single-site formation and persistence are treated as a hard deliverable with operando Co K-edge XAS/EXAFS (plus STEM-EELS/XPS/EPR). Utilization ratio is only interpreted as meaningful if EXAFS shows negligible Co“Co scattering and stable Co“N coordination during bias/humidity cycling; otherwise the design iterates on linker/monomer chemistry to enforce site isolation (mirroring the utilization-ratio logic of Asset 1).

Addresses critique (v): A quantitative energetics plan is built in: UPS/Kelvin probe (work function/dipole) + device QFLS/Voc + impedance/TPV/TPC disentangle dipole-driven band alignment from trap passivation and from parasitic conductivity changes. This directly tests the band-bending claim rather than asserting it.

Literature grounding (assets → PSC adaptation): Asset 2 supports that Co-MOF-derived cobalt species can exhibit low OER overpotential when the active environment is controlled; we translate this to humidity/ppm-water-controlled formation of water-oxidation intermediates at buried interfaces. Asset 3 supports that cobalt hydroxide-like motifs coupled to N-doped carbonic frameworks reduce overpotential and improve robustness; we leverage the N-doped conjugated framework to improve charge transfer and stabilize Co redox cycling at ultrathin thickness. Asset 1 motivates the central engineering knob—maximizing utilization ratio of M“N sites through architecture/site isolation—to increase effective redox buffering per area in a thin interlayer.

Overall feasibility increases because the only electrochemical steps occur on chemically robust substrates under anhydrous conditions, while the mechanistic claim is testable via a pre-defined potential/humidity selectivity window validated with operando XAS and controlled-humidity micro-PEC before full PSC demonstrations.

Hypothesis: Embedding a carboxylic acid-based Co-MOF as an ultrathin, bicontinuous interfacial scaffold with Schwarz P (negative Gaussian curvature) at the perovskite/HTL interface will simultaneously (i) lower interfacial charge-transfer overpotential for hole extraction and (ii) suppress interfacial degradation by immobilizing iodide and coordinating under-coordinated Pb2+. The specific methodological adaptation is to convert a conventional flat MOF interlayer into a conformal Schwarz P-architected MOF film whose curved, bicontinuous channels are infiltrated with a crosslinkable ionic polymer (Nafion-like sulfonate ionomer in trace loading) to (a) tune Co-node coordination toward transient Co“OHx/Co“O motifs that act as fast redox mediators for interfacial hole transfer and (b) create steric/ionic gating that reduces halide back-diffusion and metal-ion migration. Mechanistically, negative curvature increases accessible coordination site density and optimizes intermediate adsorption/charge localization (analogous to curvature-enhanced electrocatalysis), while carboxylate-Pb binding passivates trap states; together these reduce non-radiative recombination (higher Voc) and interfacial energetic losses (lower overpotential) under operational bias.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1. Select a high-Voc baseline perovskite stack (e.g., p“i“n: ITO/NiOx/FA0.83Cs0.17Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3/C60/BCP/Ag or n“i“p: FTO/SnO2/perovskite/spiro-OMeTAD/Au) and define the target interface to engineer (perovskite/HTL for n“i“p or perovskite/NiOx for p“i“n).
2. Prepare a carboxylic-acid linker set enabling robust Co-MOF growth at low temperature (e.g., trimesic acid/BTC, terephthalic acid/BDC derivatives) and incorporate a small fraction (1“5 mol%) of multifunctional linkers bearing latent crosslink sites (e.g., vinyl, epoxide) to lock morphology after formation.
3. Establish a curvature template route compatible with PSC processing: polymer cubosomes or block-copolymer bicontinuous templates that yield a Schwarz P-like network at 20“80 nm length scale, stable in perovskite-compatible solvents.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
1. Schwarz P templating on perovskite: Spin-coat a thin bicontinuous polymer cubosome layer (10“30 nm effective thickness) directly on the perovskite surface under dry inert conditions; anneal mildly (<80“100 °C) to set the cubic phase without damaging the perovskite.
2. Interfacial MOF conversion (adaptation): Grow a Co-carboxylate MOF conformally within/on the cubosome channels via a vapor-assisted or low-polarity solvent-assisted coordination process (to avoid perovskite dissolution). This converts the initially polymeric Schwarz P morphology into a mechanically supported, continuous Co-MOF framework with negative Gaussian curvature and high accessible site density.
3. Trace ionomer infiltration for controlled Co“OHx formation: Introduce a very low loading of a sulfonated ionomer (Nafion-like) from an orthogonal solvent, followed by brief humidity-free activation. The ionomer provides steric hindrance and localized ionic microenvironments to favor formation of small, defective Co“OHx/Co“O motifs at/near Co nodes (without bulk insulating coverage), creating a redox-active mediator network.
4. Crosslink/lock the scaffold: Activate the multifunctional linkers (thermal/UV depending on chemistry) to crosslink the MOF/ionomer composite, preventing morphological collapse during HTL deposition and operation.
5. Deposit the transport layer: Apply HTL (spiro-OMeTAD/PTAA) or NiOx atop the Schwarz P Co-MOF interlayer; complete devices and include controls: (i) no interlayer, (ii) flat Co-MOF (no Schwarz P), (iii) Schwarz P polymer only, (iv) Schwarz P Co-MOF without ionomer, (v) ionomer only.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
1. Quantify “low overpotential” in PSC-relevant terms: Use intensity-dependent J“V, Suns-Voc, and electroluminescence quantum efficiency (EQEEL) to extract non-radiative voltage loss; use impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and transient photovoltage/photocurrent (TPV/TPC) to quantify charge-transfer resistance and interfacial recombination.
2. Mechanistic proof of curvature/function: Use GISAXS/ellipsometry/SEM-TEM tomography to confirm bicontinuous Schwarz P-like morphology; measure accessible Co-site density via chemisorption probes and XPS/EXAFS for Co coordination changes with/without ionomer.
3. Interface defect passivation: Track trap density and surface recombination velocity via thermal admittance spectroscopy, time-resolved PL (TRPL), and absolute PLQY on perovskite films with the interlayer.
4. Ion migration and chemical stability: Perform bias-stress and light-soaking tests (MPP tracking at 1 sun, 65“85 °C optional) while monitoring hysteresis, Voc drift, and EIS signatures; use ToF-SIMS depth profiles for I−/Br−/Co/S distributions before/after aging to test halide immobilization and metal diffusion.
5. Performance and scaling checks: Report stabilized PCE, Voc/FF gains, and device-to-device variance; demonstrate compatibility with larger-area substrates (e.g., 1“10 cm2) by slot-die/spin hybrid deposition of the template and vapor-assisted MOF growth.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Curvature-engineered Schwarz P architectures have been empirically shown to increase electrocatalytic turnover by maximizing accessible coordination sites and lowering reaction barriers via electronic/adsorption optimization. Separately, carboxylic acid-based Co-MOFs can be transformed/activated to Co“OHx-like active motifs and achieve low overpotential in OER when modified with Nafion due to steric hindrance yielding smaller, more defective hydroxide domains with more active sites.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): In PSCs, the dominant losses and instability often originate at interfaces (trap-assisted recombination, energetic barriers, ion migration, chemical reactions with transport layers). The proposed Schwarz P Co-MOF interlayer is not used as a bulk conductor; it is a nanometric interfacial mediator/passivator: carboxylates coordinate Pb2+ to reduce traps (boost Voc), while the bicontinuous, ionomer-tuned Co-node chemistry provides a fast interfacial redox/charge-transfer pathway (lower interfacial overpotential/charge-transfer resistance) and ionic gating (reduced halide back-diffusion under bias).
3. Comparative Advantage: Versus a flat MOF or conventional SAMs, the Schwarz P scaffold provides (i) far higher interfacial site utilization at equal thickness, (ii) continuous percolation pathways for charge transfer without requiring thick layers that impede transport, and (iii) morphological locking that resists interlayer rupture during HTL deposition and thermal cycling. Versus adding catalytic dopants directly into perovskite, the interlayer localizes Co chemistry away from the bulk absorber, minimizing deep-level defect formation while still enabling interfacial kinetic acceleration and improved operational stability.

Hypothesis: A MXene-confined, mechanochemically pre-assembled 2D reticular ‘nanoreactor’ (COF/MOF-to-2D-polymer hybrid) that encapsulates atomically precise Ag44 clusters will create a chemically buffered and electronically percolating interfacial interlayer in perovskite solar cells, simultaneously (i) suppressing small-molecule oxidation in the hole-transport region by lowering interfacial oxygen/water activity and scavenging reactive oxygen species, and (ii) reducing non-radiative recombination by passivating under-coordinated Pb/I defects and homogenizing the interfacial electric field. The methodological adaptation is to replace conventional solution-phase additive blending (which degrades APNCs and yields uncontrolled phase segregation) with a two-stage confined synthesis: mechanochemical encapsulation of Ag44 into a redox-inert COF/MOF scaffold followed by MXene-gap confined 2D reticular growth/polymer-locking to form an ultrathin, continuous, solvent-resistant nanocomposite interlayer that can be laminated onto the perovskite without exposing Ag44 to halide-rich polar solvents. Mechanistically, the COF/MOF pore microenvironment stabilizes Ag44 against aggregation/oxidation; MXene provides a high-conductivity 2D electron reservoir enabling fast interfacial charge extraction and screening of ionic defect fields; and the 2D polymer ‘locking’ converts the reticular framework into a mechanically robust diffusion barrier that blocks O2/H2O ingress and suppresses dopant/small-molecule oxidation pathways that otherwise accelerate HTL/perovskite interfacial degradation.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select PSC stack to target oxidation-driven interfacial loss: glass/ITO/SAM (MeO-2PACz)/FA0.9Cs0.1Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3/perovskite-interface interlayer/undoped or lightly doped HTL (e.g., PTAA with minimized LiTFSI)/Au.
1.2 Prepare baseline controls: (A) no interlayer, (B) MXene-only ultrathin layer, (C) COF/MOF-only layer, (D) solution-blended Ag44 additive (expected to be unstable), (E) proposed nanocomposite interlayer.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Mechanochemical encapsulation (adapted from APNC@reticular frameworks):
- Synthesize/obtain Ag44(SR)30 (choose thiolate ligands with moderate polarity and perovskite-compatible binding, e.g., aromatic thiolates).
- Select a redox-inert COF (e.g., imine/β-ketoenamine-linked) or 2D MOF with pore aperture slightly larger than Ag44 core+ligand shell, prioritizing chemically neutral internal surfaces.
- Perform solvent-minimized ball-milling (or mortar grinding) of Ag44 + COF/MOF precursor/host under inert atmosphere to form Ag44@COF (or Ag44@MOF) without exposing clusters to polar halide solvents; confirm preserved Ag44 integrity (UV“vis fingerprints, XPS Ag 3d, MALDI/ESI where feasible).
2.2 MXene-gap confined 2D reticular growth (confined synthesis adaptation):
- Prepare Ti3C2Tx MXene flakes with controlled surface terminations (Tx tuned via mild post-treatments to enrich “O/“OH while limiting “F).
- Assemble a laminar MXene film (few nm effective thickness) on a sacrificial substrate or directly on the perovskite via dry transfer/lamination to avoid solvent attack.
- Introduce Ag44@COF (or Ag44@MOF) as a “seeded reticular paste” and confine it within MXene interlayer galleries by hot-press lamination at low temperature (<80“100 °C) under inert gas.
2.3 2D polymer ‘locking’ to prevent dissolution and set thickness:
- In the confined MXene galleries, trigger a mild, diffusion-limited polymerization/crosslinking that converts residual monomer/linker functionality into a 2D polymer network (e.g., interfacial Schiff-base reformation, photoinitiated crosslinking, or click-type reactions compatible with perovskite). The goal is a continuous 5“20 nm interlayer with (i) MXene percolation for conductivity, (ii) reticular porosity for gas buffering, and (iii) polymer locking for solvent/thermal robustness.
2.4 Device integration:
- Form perovskite films with standardized antisolvent protocol.
- Apply the pre-formed nanocomposite interlayer by dry transfer/lamination (or extremely nonpolar orthogonal solvent if unavoidable).
- Deposit HTL and top electrode.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural/chemical integrity:
- Verify Ag44 survival after integration: UV“vis (cluster signature), XPS (Ag oxidation state), TOF-SIMS depth profiling (Ag spatial localization), GIWAXS (reticular order), TEM on extracted cross-sections.
- Confirm interlayer continuity and thickness: cross-sectional SEM/TEM, AFM.
3.2 Mechanistic optoelectronic tests (link to recombination and field homogenization):
- Absolute PLQY and TRPL of perovskite with/without interlayer; target reduced non-radiative rate and increased quasi-Fermi level splitting.
- Impedance spectroscopy and transient photovoltage/photocurrent to quantify recombination resistance and carrier extraction.
- KPFM/UPS to map work function shifts and interfacial dipole formation; correlate with Voc changes.
3.3 Oxidation and stability quantification (small-molecule oxidation suppression):
- Track HTL dopant oxidation signatures (if doped controls are included) via UV“vis/EPR; monitor O2 uptake and ROS formation using operando probes where possible.
- Damp-heat and light-soaking: ISOS-L-2 or equivalent (1 sun, 65“85 °C, controlled RH) with maximum power point tracking; compare T80.
- Bias-stress ionic migration: measure hysteresis index, time-dependent Voc decay, and ToF-SIMS for halide/metal migration.
3.4 Benchmarking and statistics:
- >20 devices per condition; report mean±SD of PCE, Voc, FF.
- Failure-mode analysis post-aging (XRD for PbI2, XPS for iodine loss, contact degradation).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 demonstrates mechanochemical encapsulation preserves atomically precise nanoclusters (including Ag44) in COFs/MOFs, preventing degradation typical in liquid processing; Asset 2 shows layered materials (including MXenes) act as nanoreactors enabling confined synthesis of 2D MOFs/COFs/2D polymers and improved small-molecule oxidation catalysis—here inverted to oxidation suppression by controlling interfacial chemistry and transport. In PSCs, ultrathin interlayers that passivate defects and block O2/H2O are known to increase Voc and operational stability.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC performance is often limited by interfacial non-radiative recombination and oxidation-driven degradation in/near HTLs. The proposed adaptation explicitly targets these bottlenecks by (i) creating a dry-processable interlayer (compatible with fragile perovskites), (ii) confining reticular growth to guarantee nm-scale thickness control and coverage, and (iii) stabilizing Ag44 so its redox/field-modulating functionality persists under illumination and bias.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with solution-blended nanocomposites, the confined + mechanochemical route prevents Ag44 decomposition and phase segregation, yielding reproducible interfacial energetics and uniform coverage. Compared with MXene-only interlayers, the reticular/polymer matrix mitigates MXene-induced shunting and provides a diffusion/chemical buffer. Compared with COF/MOF-only layers, MXene percolation improves interfacial conductivity and reduces series resistance, while Ag44 introduces tunable interfacial dipoles and ROS buffering, collectively enabling higher Voc, improved FF, and markedly extended T80 under light/heat stress.

Hypothesis: Embedding a negative-Gaussian-curvature (Schwarz P“like) bicontinuous interlayer that hosts high-density FeN4 single-atom coordination (Fe“N“C SAC) at the perovskite/ETL interface will increase the utilization ratio of interfacial active sites for redox-mediated defect neutralization and oxygen/water radical quenching, thereby suppressing interfacial non-radiative recombination and chemically stabilizing the junction under bias/illumination. Mechanistically, the saddle-shaped (K<0) curvature increases accessible site fraction and reactant/product transport (O2/H2O, superoxide, iodide/iodine species) while simultaneously altering local electronic structure/adsorption energetics at FeN4 to lower barriers for undesired ROS consumption and halide-oxidation side reactions; this raises electrocatalytic activity specifically toward benign scavenging pathways and reduces catalytic pathways that accelerate perovskite degradation. The methodological adaptation is to repurpose the electrocatalyst architecture concept (bicontinuous negative-curvature SAC maximizing FeN4 utilization ratio) into a nanometer-thick, electronically selective, optically benign interfacial scaffold that functions as (i) a curvature-enabled ‘active-site amplifier’ and (ii) a catalytic chemical buffer layer for perovskite interfaces.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a high-Voc, stable 3D absorber (e.g., FA/Cs mixed-cation iodide-bromide tuned to ~1.55 eV) and a baseline device architecture where interfacial chemistry dominates stability losses (n“i“p: glass/ITO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/Au; and p“i“n: ITO/NiOx/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag for cross-validation).
1.2 Prepare a Fe“N“C precursor polymer/cubosome formulation capable of forming a Schwarz P“like bicontinuous mesophase at sub-50 nm thickness. Build a control library: (A) flat Fe“N“C layer (no bicontinuity), (B) bicontinuous carbon without Fe, (C) bicontinuous Fe present but not atomically dispersed (nanoclusters), (D) no interlayer.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Curvature templating at thin-film scale (adaptation of cubosome-templated SAC synthesis): deposit a cubosome-forming block-copolymer/phenolic-resin film (or similar carbonizable network) on the relevant transport layer (SnO2 or C60). Induce an ordered bicontinuous cubic mesophase (Schwarz P topology) via solvent-vapor annealing to lock in negative Gaussian curvature.
2.2 Introduce Fe and N coordination under confinement: infiltrate Fe and N precursors (e.g., Fe-porphyrin-like motif precursors or Fe salts + N-rich ligands) into the mesophase; then perform low-damage conversion to FeN4 sites using mild thermal treatment compatible with underlying layers (target ≤200“250 °C for ITO/SnO2, lower if on organic layers; if higher temperature needed, synthesize on a sacrificial substrate and transfer as a free-standing ultrathin network).
2.3 Densify/functionalize for PSC compatibility: apply an ultrathin wide-bandgap, ion-blocking skin (e.g., a few cycles of ALD Al2O3 or molecular crosslinking) that preserves bicontinuous porosity but prevents direct Fe contact with perovskite to avoid unwanted metal diffusion; tune work function via controlled N-speciation to maintain selective extraction (electron-selective near SnO2/C60, hole-selective near NiOx).
2.4 Interface integration: deposit perovskite atop the interlayer with crystallization control (antisolvent or gas-quench) ensuring conformal wetting into the bicontinuous topography without pinholes. Complete devices with standard HTL/ETL stacks.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural/chemical proof of adaptation: GISAXS/TEM tomography to confirm Schwarz P“like bicontinuity and curvature; BET/ellipsometric porosimetry for accessible surface area at thin-film scale; XAS (XANES/EXAFS) + Mössbauer to quantify FeN4 single-atom coordination vs clusters; XPS/NEXAFS to map N species and Fe oxidation state.
3.2 Quantify utilization ratio of FeN4 active sites in-operando: combine electrochemical redox titration (thin-film electrode in non-aqueous electrolyte) with operando spectroscopies (in-situ EPR/UV“Vis) to determine fraction of Fe sites participating in ROS scavenging and halide-redox buffering under light and bias proxies.
3.3 PSC performance and recombination diagnostics: JV (hysteresis), stabilized MPP, Suns-Voc, TRPL and absolute PLQY at 1 sun to extract quasi-Fermi level splitting; impedance spectroscopy to deconvolute interfacial charge-transfer vs recombination resistances; transient photovoltage/photocurrent to assess carrier lifetimes and extraction.
3.4 Mechanistic validation of catalytic buffering: illuminate devices in controlled O2/H2O atmospheres while tracking superoxide/iodine intermediates (EPR spin trapping; operando GIWAXS/ToF-SIMS for iodide migration and interfacial composition). Compare degradation kinetics (T80 under ISOS-L-2 / MPP tracking at 65“85 °C) across controls to attribute improvements specifically to (i) curvature (accessibility/transport) and (ii) FeN4 site chemistry (selective scavenging).
3.5 Failure analysis and guardrails: monitor Fe diffusion (ToF-SIMS depth profiles after aging), trap-density (SCLC), and band alignment (UPS/KPFM). Iterate skin-layer thickness and Fe loading to eliminate Voc penalties or shunts.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Negative Gaussian curvature bicontinuous architectures are empirically shown to increase surface area and active-site utilization ratio for FeN4 SACs, enhancing electrocatalytic activity through improved accessibility and modified adsorption energetics. In PSCs, the dominant losses often arise at interfaces via ROS-driven chemistry, halide redox, and defect-mediated non-radiative recombination—processes that can be mitigated by interfacial chemical buffering and passivation.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal does not import electrocatalysis generically; it adapts the curvature-enabled SAC concept into an ultrathin interfacial scaffold tailored to PSC constraints: low optical loss, band alignment control, ion/metal diffusion suppression, and compatibility with low-temperature processing. The FeN4 sites are positioned to act as chemically active ‘interfacial sinks’ for ROS and halide-redox intermediates while the bicontinuous topology maximizes the fraction of sites actually participating (high utilization ratio) in the confined PSC interface.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with flat passivation layers (2D perovskites, SAMs) that are chemically passive, the bicontinuous FeN4 interlayer adds an active catalytic buffering function without requiring thick layers. Compared with adding nanoparticles or redox additives, single-atom FeN4 reduces parasitic absorption/scattering and enables atom-efficient activity. The negative-curvature topology provides a unique lever—site accessibility/transport and curvature-tuned energetics—that directly targets the utilization ratio bottleneck, enabling stability gains under O2/H2O/light where conventional passivants often fail.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a chemically well-defined, Fe“N4-anchored Dion“Jacobson (DJ) type 2D perovskite surface phase can be deliberately constructed at 3D perovskite grain boundaries to function as an embedded oxygen redox buffer, rather than a passive passivation layer. Mechanistically, we posit that Fe“N4 motifs derived from a pre-leached, Mn-free HIB-based coordination fragment can be covalently anchored to undercoordinated Pb2+ sites via Pb“N coordination and halide (I−/Br−) bridging during crystallization, yielding a [(A′)PbX4]n DJ phase where A′ is a rigid, multidentate diammonium spacer derived from protonated hexaiminobenzene. This anchoring preserves a square-planar Fe“N4 ligand field with constrained, concave electronic density (analogous to the negative-curvature environment in bmFeSAC), but now embedded within the perovskite lattice. Under illumination and oxygen exposure, these Fe centers act as preferential electron acceptors for O2, shifting the O2/O2•− redox energetics away from Pb“I antibonding states, thereby suppressing superoxide-mediated lattice degradation while maintaining quasi-Fermi level splitting and vertical charge transport.
Plan: Step 1: Chemically realistic precursor and phase design.
Synthesize a Mn/Fe-HIB-MOF analog and subject it to solution-phase pre-leaching using ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) or diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid (DTPA) to quantitatively remove Mn (>99%, verified by ICP-MS), yielding Fe“N4“HIB fragments. Protonate HIB to form a rigid diammonium spacer (HIBH2^2+), targeting a DJ-type surface phase with nominal stoichiometry (HIBH2)PbX4. Prepare FA/Cs“Pb(I0.8Br0.2)3 precursor with 2“5 mol% excess HIBH2^2+ relative to Pb to confine the DJ phase to grain boundaries.

Step 2: Controlled incorporation during crystallization.
Disperse ≤0.3 wt% Fe“N4“HIB fragments into the perovskite precursor. During spin-coating and annealing (90“100 °C), Fe“N4 units coordinate to undercoordinated Pb2+ via Pb“N bonds, while halides bridge Fe-adjacent Pb octahedra, forming a coherent DJ/3D heterophase. No Mn is present at this stage. Formation is monitored in situ by GIWAXS to detect DJ (00l) reflections and suppressed bulk RP signatures.

Step 3: Structural and chemical validation.
Confirm Fe“N“Pb anchoring via XPS (Fe 2p/N 1s/Pb 4f chemical shifts), Fe K-edge XANES/EXAFS (coordination number ~4 N, no Fe“Fe scattering), and ToF-SIMS depth profiling to localize Fe at grain boundaries. STEM-EELS mapping will visualize Fe“N-rich regions confined to intergranular planes.

Step 4: Defining and measuring redox energetics.
Fabricate solid-state microelectrochemical devices using patterned Au microelectrodes contacting the perovskite film, a LiTFSI-doped PMMA gel electrolyte, and an Ag/AgCl quasi-reference. Use ferrocene/ferrocenium as an internal redox marker to calibrate potential. Measure oxygen reduction onset at Fe“N sites under dark and illuminated conditions. In parallel, perform bias-dependent XPS and operando spectroelectrochemistry under controlled O2 to extract O2 adsorption and reduction energetics. Complement with DFT calculations comparing O2/O2•− energetics at Fe“N4“DJ sites versus pristine Pb“I terminations.

Step 5: Functional impact and controls.
Quantify superoxide formation using EPR spin trapping and correlate with operando PL decay, TRPL, and quasi-Fermi level splitting. Measure trap density (SCLC), TPV/TPC, and mobility to assess recombination penalties. Include decisive controls: (i) Fe-free HIB spacer DJ phase, (ii) N-ligand-only fragments, (iii) Fe“N sites blocked by axial ligand coordination, and (iv) inert 2D passivation benchmarks. Evaluate device stability under ISOS-L-3 and compare Voc retention and cycle life.
Feasibility: 1. Chemical realism: By explicitly targeting a DJ-type 2D perovskite with a rigid diammonium HIB-derived spacer, the proposal aligns with known 2D/3D perovskite crystallization pathways and avoids unsupported assumptions about spontaneous phase formation. Pb“N coordination and halide bridging are chemically plausible and experimentally verifiable.
2. Mn management: Pre-leaching removes Mn prior to perovskite processing, eliminating uncontrolled diffusion or trap formation; residual Mn is quantified and correlated with electronic metrics, directly addressing reviewer concerns.
3. Redox rigor: The half-wave-potential concept is translated into a testable solid-state redox measurement with defined electrodes, reference calibration, and complementary spectroscopic and DFT-derived energetics, avoiding metaphorical use of aqueous ORR terminology.
4. Selectivity vs recombination: By confining Fe“N4 sites to grain-boundary DJ phases and benchmarking against multiple controls, the proposal quantitatively tests whether oxygen buffering occurs without increasing trap density or reducing QFLS. The approach preserves the original concept chain—bmFeSAC-inspired negative-curvature Fe“N4 chemistry repurposed as an embedded redox buffer—while grounding it in perovskite-specific chemistry and measurement frameworks.

Hypothesis: A Zr-based, defect-engineered MOF interfacial layer—implemented as a thymol-confined UiO-66/MIL-53 heterostructure (total thickness 10“20 nm) between FA/Cs/MA Pb(I/Br)3 and SnO2—will primarily enhance perovskite solar-cell Isc and stability through chemically robust defect passivation and ion-migration suppression, while a secondary, explicitly bounded tribo/piezo-electret polarization component can transiently modulate carrier extraction under mechanical excitation. Mechanistically, (i) missing-linker defects in UiO-66 and MIL-53 generate coordinatively unsaturated Zr“OH/Zr“O sites that form strong Zr“O“Pb linkages to under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide-vacancy-adjacent sites, reducing interfacial SRH recombination and increasing collection efficiency (Jsc/Isc) without sacrificing Voc; (ii) thymol confined in MOF pores acts as a dipolar, hydrogen-bonding ‘guest electret’ that (a) raises the activation barrier for mobile halides/A-site cations near the interface by disrupting perovskite surface solvation pathways and (b) locally screens defect-induced band-tail states, thereby suppressing ion-migration-driven hysteresis and light/bias-induced degradation; and (iii) any triboelectric contribution is treated as a time-dependent interfacial polarization (Δσ(t)) that produces a local field perturbation (ΔE) superimposed on the built-in field, with a priori success requiring ΔE/E_bi ≥ 1“5% in the perovskite interfacial depletion/extraction region over vibration frequencies relevant to wearable/ambient stimuli (10“500 Hz) and under encapsulation. The proposal directly addresses the reviewer concern by (a) defining a quantitative field-based criterion for triboelectric relevance relative to E_bi, (b) separating transient extraction modulation from true steady-state Isc enhancement (AM1.5G, no vibration), and (c) explicitly testing thymol retention, dipole orientation stability under bias/illumination, and absence of electronic trap formation.
Plan: Step 1 — MOF synthesis with calibrated defect densities and heterostructure architecture
1.1 UiO-66 defect series (Zr6O4(OH)4(BDC)6−x): modulated solvothermal synthesis using acetic acid or formic acid as modulators to target missing-linker defect densities of x ≈ 0 (nearly defect-free), 0.3, 0.6, and 1.0 per node equivalent (calibrated by TGA/1H NMR of digested MOF + SSNMR signatures of modulator binding as in defect-dynamics literature). Maintain crystallite size <50 nm to enable smooth ultrathin films.
1.2 MIL-53(Zr) (or MIL-53(Al) if Zr-MIL-53 proves unstable in the chosen solvent/binding conditions): introduce controlled defectivity via modulator/water-content tuning; verify breathing state and defect concentration by PXRD + gas sorption; select a ‘rigidified’ MIL-53 condition to minimize moisture-driven mechanical variability.
1.3 Heterostructure design: fabricate a bilayer UiO-66 (perovskite-facing, defect-rich for bonding) / MIL-53 (SnO2-facing, mechanically compliant and ion-blocking) with individual thicknesses 5“10 nm each (total 10“20 nm). Rationale: maximize Zr“O“Pb anchoring at the perovskite side while using MIL-53 as a porous reservoir for thymol electret/dipole stabilization and mechanical polarization coupling.

Step 2 — Thymol confinement and electronic-neutrality verification
2.1 Thymol loading by vapor-assisted infiltration (VAI) at controlled partial pressure and temperature (e.g., 40“70 °C) to target pore filling fractions of 10%, 30%, 60% (quantified by QCM mass uptake on MOF-coated quartz and confirmed by TGA/DSC + GC-MS of desorbed thymol).
2.2 Confinement stability protocol (mandatory):
  - Thermal retention: isothermal bake at 85 °C for 500 h in N2 and in dry air; measure remaining thymol by TGA/GC-MS.
  - Operational retention: continuous 1-sun illumination + maximum power point (MPP) bias for 200 h in encapsulated mini-modules; post-test quantify thymol by ToF-SIMS depth profiling and compare to pre-test.
2.3 Electronic neutrality screening: UPS/Kelvin probe to determine work-function shifts; SCLC trap-density measurements on electron-only and hole-only stacks to ensure thymol does not introduce deep traps (ΔN_t must not increase vs. thymol-free MOF).

Step 3 — Interfacial film formation on perovskite with defined chemistry
3.1 Deposit perovskite FA/Cs/MA Pb(I/Br)3 with a controlled surface halide deficiency series (mild and more defective surfaces) to test passivation robustness.
3.2 Form MOF interlayer by solution-compatible deposition (e.g., nanocrystal dispersion spin-coating or layer-by-layer growth) to achieve 10“20 nm continuous coverage. Enforce roughness <3 nm RMS (AFM) and pinhole-free coverage (conductive AFM mapping).
3.3 Chemical bonding confirmation (mandatory):
  - XPS: track Pb 4f shifts and appearance of Zr“O“Pb-related signatures; quantify reduction in metallic Pb0 after aging.
  - SSNMR (Zr“OH environment / modulator dynamics) to verify defect-site availability pre-bonding and its consumption/coordination change post-bonding.
  - GIWAXS: ensure perovskite lattice integrity; detect any undesired 2D phase formation.

Step 4 — Quantitative triboelectric-field framework and simulation-to-experiment closure
4.1 Analytical field estimate (defined deliverable): treat the MOF/perovskite interface as a polarized sheet charge density Δσ(t) generated by tribo/electret polarization under periodic strain ε(t). Use ΔE(t) ≈ Δσ(t)/ε0ε_eff within the interfacial region (ε_eff extracted from impedance and literature values). Benchmark against built-in field E_bi ≈ V_bi/L_depl (from C“V/Mott“Schottky and drift-diffusion fits). Predefine relevance threshold: time-averaged |ΔE| in the extraction zone must exceed 1“5% of E_bi under 0.1“1 g acceleration and 10“500 Hz.
4.2 Multiphysics simulation (COMSOL + drift-diffusion coupling):
  - Mechanical module: apply realistic encapsulated-device boundary conditions; input MOF elastic modulus (nanoindentation) and piezo/tribo effective polarization coefficients (fitted from independent MOF-film nanogenerator tests).
  - Electrostatics: map ΔV(x,t) across MOF/perovskite/ETL.
  - Device module: drift“diffusion with recombination (SRH + radiative) to compute ΔJ(t) and any change in steady-state Jsc when averaged over vibration cycles.
Deliverable: predicted ΔJsc(vibration) vs frequency/amplitude and explicit demonstration whether any enhancement is purely transient (AC modulation) or yields measurable DC shift under load.
4.3 Experimental decoupling of transient vs steady-state effects (mandatory design):
  - Measure J“V and stabilized Jsc at AM1.5G with no vibration (baseline steady-state benefit must come from passivation/ion blocking).
  - Apply controlled vibration/acoustic excitation while recording (i) DC Jsc shift (time-averaged) and (ii) AC photocurrent component via lock-in detection at the excitation frequency. Define success metrics:
    * Steady-state success: ≥3“8% increase in stabilized Jsc at 1 sun without vibration vs control.
    * Tribo-success (if present): a reproducible lock-in AC photocurrent signal and/or ≥0.5“1% DC Jsc shift under defined vibration conditions, consistent with COMSOL-predicted ΔE/E_bi.
  - Control stacks: (a) defect-poor MOF, (b) MOF without thymol, (c) thymol-free inert porous layer of similar thickness, (d) MOF layer placed away from interface (e.g., atop ETL) to test necessity of buried interfacial polarization.

Step 5 — Ion migration, recombination, and stability validation aligned to the hypothesis
5.1 Recombination/passivation: TRPL (lifetime increase), transient photovoltage/photocurrent (extraction time constants), and absolute PLQY at relevant carrier densities to verify reduced non-radiative recombination.
5.2 Ion migration: temperature-dependent impedance spectroscopy and bias-stress hysteresis quantification; extract activation energies for ionic processes. Success: increased ionic activation barrier and reduced low-frequency capacitance/hysteresis.
5.3 Operational stability: ISOS protocols (ISOS-L-2, ISOS-O-2 as available) at MPP with encapsulation; compare time-to-80% performance (T80) across control and proposed interlayers. Post-mortem ToF-SIMS for halide redistribution and XPS for interfacial chemical evolution.

Step 6 — Optional DFT/MLP-guided design loop (risk-reduction)
6.1 DFT: calculate binding energies and charge redistribution for Zr“O“Pb motifs at representative perovskite surface terminations and halide vacancies; screen how missing-linker density alters density of interfacial states.
6.2 Use machine-learned potentials (MTP/active learning as demonstrated for UiO-66/MIL-53) to sample defect-site distributions and guest (thymol) orientations at finite temperature, then feed dipole distributions into electrostatic modeling (input polarization density and relaxation times).
Feasibility: 1) Quantitative credibility of the triboelectric component (addressing the core critique):
- The proposal no longer assumes triboelectricity automatically increases Isc. It defines ΔE/E_bi and ΔJ metrics and forces simulation-to-experiment closure: Δσ(t) → ΔE(t) → drift“diffusion-predicted ΔJ(t) → lock-in measured AC photocurrent and possible DC shift. This directly tests whether the effect is transient modulation (AC component only) or yields a measurable time-averaged extraction benefit under realistic encapsulated vibrations.
- UiO-66 functionalization has empirically increased Isc in triboelectric nanogenerators (Asset 2), supporting that MOF chemistry can tune charge-transfer/polarization magnitude; here, we translate that into a bounded, field-based criterion relative to PSC built-in fields.

2) Robustness and primacy of the steady-state photovoltaic gain:
- Even if the triboelectric contribution proves marginal, the interlayer is still designed to deliver steady-state Jsc/stability gains via Zr“O“Pb bonding and defect passivation. Defect-rich Zr-MOF nodes provide reactive Zr“OH/Zr“O sites (Assets 4“5), which are chemically plausible anchoring points for under-coordinated perovskite surface Pb and vacancy-adjacent sites. This makes the project resilient: the highest-value outcome (lower interfacial recombination + suppressed ion migration) does not depend on vibration.

3) Thymol confinement and electronic neutrality (addressing reviewer doubts explicitly):
- Thymol is treated as a confined guest whose retention is experimentally validated (TGA/GC-MS/QCM, ToF-SIMS depth profiling after MPP stress), rather than assumed. The proposal also explicitly checks that thymol does not create electronic traps (SCLC, UPS/work-function shifts). The ‘repurposing’ logic is grounded in thymol’s demonstrated functional role when confined in MOF systems (Asset 1), but adapted here with PSC-relevant retention and trap-formation tests under bias/illumination.

4) Clear success metrics and discriminating controls:
- The revised plan separates (i) baseline steady-state Jsc improvement at 1-sun/no vibration (must be present) from (ii) any vibration-induced modulation quantified by lock-in detection. A structured control matrix (defect-poor MOF, no thymol, non-interfacial placement) ensures causal attribution to Zr“O“Pb bonding, thymol dipoles, and/or polarization effects.

5) Practicality of fabrication and characterization:
- Sub-20 nm MOF interlayers are realistic via nanocrystal dispersions or layer-by-layer growth, and the characterization suite (XPS, GIWAXS, SSNMR, impedance, TRPL, ToF-SIMS) directly maps onto the hypothesized mechanisms and known MOF defect/dynamics toolkits (Assets 3“5).

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a mechanically gated, ROS-scavenging “breathing electrode” built from a Zn-Car_MOF“carbon composite as the perovskite solar cell (PSC) top contact will simultaneously (i) reduce photo-oxidative degradation driven by singlet oxygen (^{1}O_{2}) by adsorption/physical removal of O2/H2O and catalytic quenching of ROS at the device surface, and (ii) preserve high power conversion efficiency by providing a low-barrier, conductive carbon current-collecting network. The methodological adaptation is to replace the conventional metal/Au (or carbon-only) top electrode with a laminated, microstructured tribo“piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator (TPHG) electrode stack that periodically modulates the local oxygen chemical potential and interfacial charge distribution through contact“separation microcycles. Mechanistically, cyclic piezo/tribo polarization in the electrode induces reversible “gating” of O2 uptake/release within Zn-Car_MOF pores while the carnosine“Zn coordination sites chemically quench ROS (including ^{1}O_{2}) and the carbon component provides fast lateral transport; together this converts an otherwise open-air PSC surface into a self-regulating, adsorption-dominated oxygen sink that suppresses ^{1}O_{2}-initiated halide/perovskite oxidation and interfacial non-radiative recombination.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and material preparation.
1.1 Synthesize Zn-Car_MOF microcrystals (100“500 nm) with controlled porosity and surface histidine/imidazole exposure (via modulated synthesis using carnosine:Zn ratio and pH) to maximize ROS interaction sites while maintaining chemical compatibility with iodide-rich perovskites.
1.2 Prepare a conductive carbon component as a hierarchical network: (i) few-layer graphene or CNTs for percolation, plus (ii) mesoporous carbon black for contact conformity. Form a Zn-Car_MOF/carbon composite ink where MOF is the oxygen/ROS-active phase and carbon is the continuous conductor.
1.3 Fabricate a flexible TPHG laminate that is not electrically wired into the PSC circuit: a patterned PDMS tribolayer + piezoelectric PVDF (or BaTiO3“PVDF) layer, designed for repeated contact“separation under ambient vibrations. The TPHG is used as a mechanically active cap/laminate that produces local polarization fields at the electrode surface rather than injecting current into the device.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Device architecture: inverted (p“i“n) PSC to enable low-temperature processing and stable top electrodes: glass/ITO/NiOx (or MeO-2PACz)/3D perovskite (FA/Cs mixed-cation)/C60 (or PCBM)/BCP.
2.2 Methodological adaptation—“breathing electrode” formation:
• Deposit (doctor-blade or screen-print) a 5“20 µm Zn-Car_MOF/carbon composite as the top electrode directly on BCP, optimized to be porous (gas-accessible) yet conductive.
• Laminate the TPHG film on top of this electrode with a microstructured spacer array (10“50 µm pillars) so that ambient mechanical stimuli generate periodic micro-contact without crushing the PSC.
2.3 Functional mechanism engineering:
• Engineer the MOF fraction and pore accessibility to maximize adsorption removal efficiency for oxygen/water: quantify O2 uptake isotherms and tune composite hydrophobicity (e.g., partial fluorinated binder in carbon ink) so the electrode preferentially sequesters O2 while limiting liquid water accumulation.
• Use the TPHG-induced periodic polarization to modulate adsorption/desorption kinetics: in the contact state, enhanced local fields and pressure promote O2 uptake into MOF pores and improve interfacial sealing; in the separation state, partial release prevents saturation and maintains long-term scavenging capacity.
• Ensure charge selectivity is preserved by maintaining a thin electron-selective layer (BCP) beneath the composite and by keeping the MOF electronically decoupled from the perovskite (MOF embedded within carbon matrix, minimizing direct MOF/perovskite charge extraction pathways that could introduce recombination).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 ROS and ^{1}O_{2} quantification under operational illumination:
• Operando EPR with TEMP/TEMPO for ^{1}O_{2} and DMPO for •OH/•O2−, comparing (a) standard metal electrode, (b) carbon-only electrode, (c) Zn-Car_MOF/carbon breathing electrode without TPHG laminate, (d) full breathing electrode + TPHG laminate under mechanical actuation.
• Complement with singlet oxygen sensor green (SOSG) in a sealed optical microcell placed against the electrode surface to map ^{1}O_{2} flux.
3.2 Adsorption removal efficiency and oxygen chemical potential control:
• Measure O2/H2O uptake of the composite (gravimetric sorption, QCM) and correlate to ^{1}O_{2} suppression rate constants.
• Use operando mass spectrometry (or sealed-chamber O2 sensor) to track O2 depletion near the device surface during illumination with/without mechanical cycling.
3.3 Photovoltaic performance and recombination analysis:
• J“V (forward/reverse), stabilized MPP tracking, Suns-Voc, and impedance spectroscopy to confirm unchanged charge-selective behavior.
• TRPL and transient photovoltage/photocurrent to quantify non-radiative recombination reduction attributed to lower oxidative defect formation.
3.4 Stability testing with mechanistic attribution:
• ISOS-L-2 (light soaking) and ISOS-O-2 (oxygen-containing atmosphere) with controlled vibration spectra to activate the laminate; track Voc, FF, and PCE decay.
• Post-mortem XPS/ToF-SIMS for iodate/lead oxide formation, and GIWAXS for phase changes, linking suppressed oxidation signatures to measured ^{1}O_{2} reductions.
3.5 Controls to isolate mechanisms:
• Replace Zn-Car_MOF with an isostructural non-antioxidant MOF (same porosity, no carnosine) to decouple adsorption from chemical quenching.
• Replace carbon percolation network with low-conductivity carbon to show conductivity“stability trade-offs.
• Use a non-piezo/tribo inert laminate (same mechanical barrier) to isolate the mechanically gated adsorption effect from simple encapsulation.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zn-Car_MOFs (carnosine“Zn bio-MOFs) provide chemically active coordination sites capable of interacting with ROS, while carbon composites are established as conductive, porous electrodes in PSCs. Literature demonstrates MOF-derived carbon systems can generate/mediate ROS and that carbon components enhance adsorption removal efficiency in oxidative environments; here we invert that logic to suppress ROS by sequestration and quenching rather than promoting AOP chemistry.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The approach targets a dominant PSC failure pathway—oxygen/light-driven interfacial oxidation—without injecting external bias or adding unstable molecular antioxidants into the perovskite bulk. By relocating ROS management into a replaceable, printable top electrode compatible with inverted PSC processing, the method aligns with scalable manufacturing (screen printing/lamination) and maintains high PCE via a continuous carbon conduction network.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike the rejected electrically addressable interlayer concept, this is a structurally novel, circuit-independent architecture: the TPHG functions as a mechanically active laminate that modulates adsorption kinetics rather than powering/biased electrochemistry. The breathing electrode provides (i) regenerative oxygen scavenging (avoids one-time antioxidant consumption), (ii) direct suppression of ^{1}O_{2} at the device/air interface, and (iii) scalable, metal-free top contacts that can improve stability and reduce cost/toxicity relative to noble-metal electrodes.

Hypothesis: If curvature in flexible inverted perovskite solar cells produces a *quantifiable* bending-induced electrostatic potential swing (Δφbend) across the absorber—arising from strain-gradient piezo/ flexoelectric polarization in the perovskite + curvature-amplified contact asymmetry—then this Δφbend will modulate the ionic electrochemical potential (μion) and interfacial band bending at the HTL-side, increasing low-frequency ionic capacitance (Cion), recombination activation, and J“V hysteresis, thereby degrading Voc under cycling. Embedding a *buried, sparse, vertically oriented* ferroelectric nanolaminate layer (sub-percolation platelet network) at a designed depth (100“250 nm from the HTL) will act as an internal electrostatic clamp that reduces ∂φ/∂κ (electric potential sensitivity to curvature κ) by (i) providing a high effective dielectric susceptibility χeff and (ii) adding a switchable remanent polarization Pr that can be oriented to oppose the curvature-induced field at the HTL-side. The hypothesis is falsifiable via (A) predicted Δφbend(κ) from an electromechanical stack model; (B) a required χeff/Pr threshold for a targeted suppression factor S = Δφbend,control/Δφbend,laminate; and (C) polarity dependence: reversing the ferroelectric dipole should *invert* the sign or increase the magnitude of Δφbend and hysteresis if screening—not generic passivation—is responsible. The refined approach overcomes feasibility concerns by (1) using platelets and passivation designed to retain switching (minimized depolarization via controlled shell thickness and partial screening), (2) aligning platelets with a demonstrably out-of-plane field geometry/dielectrophoresis rather than in-plane AC fields, (3) separating ferroelectric switching from ionic motion through blocking-layer test structures and time/frequency/temperature discrimination, and (4) employing matched-chemistry nonpolar platelet controls to isolate electrostatics from trap passivation.
Plan: PHASE 0 — Quantitative model + go/no-go gates (mandatory before full device campaigns)
0.1 Stack mechanics: compute neutral axis (z0) and strain profile εxx(z)=κ(z−z0) for the full flexible stack (PI / TCO or Ag-mesh/IZO / HTL / perovskite / ETL / top electrode / encapsulation). Use measured layer thicknesses and elastic moduli (nanoindentation or literature) to locate z0; report uncertainty. Define curvature κ=1/R for R=3,5,10 mm.
0.2 Electromechanical-to-electrostatic mapping (order-of-magnitude + FEM):
  • Baseline source term: represent bending-induced polarization density as Pbend(z)=μβend·∂ε/∂z ≈ μeff·κ (flexoelectric-like term) plus a possible piezo-like term if texture/strain breaks centrosymmetry locally. Use μeff as an extracted parameter from dedicated bending-KPFM measurements on pristine films (Phase 1), not assumed.
  • Solve Poisson with mobile-ion screening limits: bracket two regimes—(i) fast electronic screening/slow ionic (short-time, ‘frozen ions’), (ii) partial ionic screening (long-time). Implement as an effective Debye length λD,ion fitted from EIS/impedance spectroscopy of pristine devices. Outcome: predicted Δφbend at HTL-side and its relaxation time.
  • Laminate effect: treat embedded platelet layer as an effective medium slab with thickness tL (set by second-layer deposition thickness, 50“150 nm) and permittivity εL,eff( f, field ) plus optional remanent polarization Pr,eff·cosθ (θ: platelet tilt). Use Maxwell“Garnett mixing for εL,eff(φ,εplatelet,εPVK) with volume fraction φ=0.1“0.5 vol% (global) but locally higher within the buried slab; include depolarization reduction factor Nd for thin platelets.
  • Define screening target: require S≥3 reduction in |Δφbend| at HTL-side at κ corresponding to R=5 mm under ‘frozen-ion’ conditions (the condition most relevant to scan-direction hysteresis). This translates to a required εL,eff and/or Pr,eff. Output: predicted design window {φ, tL, depth d, θ-distribution}.
0.3 Feasibility gate G0 (pass/fail): proceed to device campaign only if model predicts S≥3 with realizable θ (≤20° mean tilt), and if the required Pr,eff does not exceed what is measured in Phase 1 composites.

PHASE 1 — De-risk ferroelectric functionality inside perovskite (materials-only proof)
1.1 Nanoplatelets: prepare BaTiO3 and K0.5Na0.5NbO3 (KNN) nanoplatelets with thickness 10“30 nm (revised from 5“20 nm to reduce size-suppressed remanence risk) and lateral size 200“800 nm. Target aspect ratio >20. Confirm via AFM/TEM.
1.2 Passivation shell (engineered for partial screening + non-shunting):
  • Use a bifunctional phosphonate monolayer (e.g., alkyl/aryl phosphonic acid) with controlled thickness ~1“2 nm; verify by XPS and ellipsometry on model oxide surfaces.
  • Add a secondary wide-bandgap inorganic “spacer” only if needed (e.g., 0.5“1 nm ALD Al2O3 on platelets before ligand) to suppress interfacial traps while keeping capacitance high. Reject shells >3 nm total (would overly depolarize).
1.3 Composite ferroelectric characterization in perovskite-like dielectric:
  • Prepare perovskite/composite films on conductive substrates with a symmetric capacitor geometry using ionic-blocking electrodes (e.g., ITO/NiOx as bottom, and sputtered Au with an ultrathin blocking layer such as ALD-Al2O3 1“2 nm to suppress halide exchange) to minimize ionic current during polarization measurements.
  • Measure Pr and switching using:
    - Double-wave method (DWM) / PUND with pulse widths 1“100 µs (ferroelectric timescale) and 1“100 ms (to detect ionic contamination). Ferroelectric signature: switching charge saturates at short pulses and shows weak temperature activation; ionic: strong pulse-width/temperature dependence.
    - Charge integration under triangular wave at multiple frequencies (100 Hz“100 kHz) to separate hysteretic polarization from ionic drift.
    - Cross-sectional PFM (after focused-ion-beam cross-section prep with low-damage conditions) to map switchable domains; require reversible phase contrast localized to platelets.
  • Retention/imprint tests: track Pr, coercive field, and imprint after (i) 1 sun equivalent light soaking at 45“60 °C, (ii) thermal cycling 25↔60 °C, (iii) bias stress ±0.8 V for 5“30 min in dark. Define gate G1: ≥30% of initial Pr retained after 24 h at 60 °C + light, and DWM indicates switching charge dominated by fast component.

PHASE 2 — Alignment that is truly out-of-plane (replace in-plane AC alignment)
2.1 Revised alignment geometry (out-of-plane field / dielectrophoresis):
  • Use patterned bottom electrodes (already present TCO/Ag-mesh) plus a temporary transparent top gate during wet-film stage (e.g., a removable PEDOT:PSS-coated PET sheet or ITO-PET) separated by a calibrated spacer (10“50 µm) to apply an out-of-plane AC field across the wet precursor.
  • Apply AC 50“500 kHz at field amplitude 10^4“5×10^5 V/m. Use high frequency specifically to reduce electrode polarization and ionic screening in the wet ionic film.
  • Optionally superimpose dielectrophoretic gradient (non-uniform field via interdigitated edge features) to promote vertical standing and suppress lateral chaining.
  • Immediately lock orientation via gas-quench/antisolvent and rapid crystallization.
2.2 Alignment quantification (mandatory):
  • GIWAXS: quantify Herman’s orientation factor for platelet-related scattering (or use oxide signature peaks) and perovskite texture changes. Target: orientation factor consistent with mean tilt ≤20°.
  • Cross-sectional SEM/TEM: compile orientation statistics (N≥200 platelets/sample) at three positions across coating width (center + two edges) to verify uniformity; report distribution.
  • Gate G2: if vertical orientation fraction (>70% within ±20° of normal) is not met, iterate field amplitude/frequency and wet-film viscosity (solvent ratio, precursor concentration) before device fabrication.

PHASE 3 — Device architecture + buried laminate implementation (absorber-centric, not interfacial)
3.1 Baseline flexible inverted PSC (constant across all groups): PI / (ITO on PI or Ag-mesh/IZO) / HTL (NiOx or PTAA) / perovskite / ETL (C60/BCP or PCBM/BCP) / top electrode (evaporated Ag OR printed Ag-carbon via dry press deposition; choose one and hold constant).
3.2 Buried placement (depth-controlled):
  • Two-step perovskite deposition:
    - Layer A (seed): 100“150 nm perovskite without platelets.
    - Layer B (laminate slab): 50“150 nm perovskite containing platelets at a locally higher fraction to yield global φ=0.1“0.5 vol% but slab-local φslab ~0.5“2 vol% (derived from Phase 0 modeling). This places the electrostatic clamp 100“250 nm from the HTL, not at the interface.
3.3 Poling protocol (decoupled from ion migration):
  • Perform poling only after encapsulation and only on devices with verified ionic-blocking layers for the poling experiment subset (see Phase 4). Use short, bipolar pulses (µs“ms) at amplitudes determined from Phase 1 coercive fields, rather than a single DC ≤1 V assumption.
  • Primary poling condition: pulse train (e.g., 10“10^3 pulses, 10“100 µs width) with amplitude producing the same field across the laminate slab as used in PUND switching; estimate internal field distribution using series-capacitance model (HTL/perovskite/ETL) and validate by comparing switching charge to capacitor test structures.
  • Include reverse-poling and “sham” pulse sequences below coercive threshold.

PHASE 4 — Controls strengthened to isolate electrostatics vs passivation (expanded set)
4.1 Control matrix (all with identical ligand chemistry):
  • C1: pristine perovskite.
  • C2: ferroelectric platelets, random orientation, unpoled.
  • C3: ferroelectric platelets, vertically aligned, unpoled.
  • C4: ferroelectric platelets, vertically aligned, poled +.
  • C5: ferroelectric platelets, vertically aligned, poled −.
  • C6 (mandatory passivation-matched nonpolar): identically passivated nonpolar platelets with matched geometry and surface chemistry, e.g., SrTiO3 or CaTiO3 (high-κ but paraelectric at operating T) prepared with identical phosphonate shell; this isolates chemistry/defect effects from remanence.
  • C7 (optional): same oxide core but thermally depolarized/phase-modified (if feasible) to remove remanence without changing surface.
4.2 Trap density metrics: SCLC (electron-only and hole-only), thermal admittance spectroscopy, and PL/TRPL to quantify trap density changes across groups. Use these in regression against hysteresis to ensure improvements are not purely trap-passivation driven.

PHASE 5 — Coupled mechanical“electrical testing with model-linked endpoints
5.1 Bending protocol: radii 3, 5, 10 mm; tensile vs compressive; cycling 10^2, 10^3, 3×10^3, 10^4; hold-at-curvature dwell tests (0“60 min) for relaxation kinetics.
5.2 In-situ J“V and MPP tracking: forward/reverse at scan rates 10“1000 mV/s, fixed pre-bias; mandatory MPP tracking under curvature to avoid scan artifacts.
5.3 In-situ EIS (curved): 1 MHz“0.1 Hz at Voc and near MPP, under 1-sun, held at fixed curvature. Fit with a constrained model including Rtr, Rrec, Cgeo, Cchem, and Cion with finite-length diffusion when required. Primary readouts: curvature-induced ΔCion and ΔRrec.
5.4 Direct Δφbend measurement and relaxation: time-resolved KPFM/SKP on partial stacks (no top metal) while bending/unbending; extract Δφbend(κ,t) and compare to Phase 0 predicted ∂φ/∂κ. Expect: aligned+poled shows reduced Δφbend amplitude and faster relaxation.
5.5 Ion migration validation: bias-stress ±0.8 V (dark) + recovery; ToF-SIMS depth profiles post-cycling focusing on HTL-side accumulation; correlate ToF-SIMS gradients with Cion changes.

Success criteria (quantitative, tied to model)
• Mechanical durability benchmark: ≥90% PCE retention after 3000 cycles at R=5 mm.
• Voc retention: ΔVoc ≤20“30 mV after 3000 cycles at R=5 mm.
• Hysteresis suppression: ≥50% reduction in hysteresis index vs C1 under bending.
• Ionic response stabilization: ≤20% increase in extracted Cion under bending relative to flat state (vs much larger in C1).
• Model validation: measured Δφbend(κ) reduced by ≥3× in aligned+poled vs C1, and polarity dependence observed (C4 vs C5 diverge in sign/magnitude consistent with screening).
Feasibility: Addresses (i) ferroelectric viability at nanoscale: the platelet thickness is revised upward (10“30 nm) to reduce remanence suppression; passivation shell is constrained to ~1“2 nm (≤3 nm total) to avoid excessive depolarization while preventing shunting. Ferroelectric switching/Pr retention is not assumed; it is gated by composite-appropriate measurements (PUND/DWM across frequency and pulse-width, cross-sectional PFM) under light/temperature/bias stress relevant to PSC operation. This directly tests depolarization, imprint, and retention in situ.

Addresses (ii) alignment realism: the in-plane AC field is replaced with an out-of-plane field geometry using a temporary top gate (parallel-plate) and high-frequency AC (50“500 kHz) to mitigate ionic screening and electrode polarization in wet precursors. Alignment is not asserted; it is quantified by GIWAXS orientation factors and cross-sectional TEM/SEM orientation statistics across the coating width, with an explicit gate (≥70% within ±20° of normal).

Addresses (iii) poling sufficiency and confounding ion migration: poling is redesigned from a low-DC-bias concept to a pulse-based protocol matched to measured coercive fields in blocking-layer capacitors. Ferroelectric switching is discriminated from ionic redistribution by (a) frequency/pulse-width dependence (fast vs slow components), (b) ionic-blocking test structures, and (c) time-resolved KPFM relaxation after poling/bending. This provides causality: if a fast, polarity-dependent Δφbend suppression occurs without slow ion signatures, the mechanism is ferroelectric screening; if only slow relaxation is seen, it indicates ionic redistribution.

Addresses (iv) missing quantitative coupling: a required, falsifiable electromechanical model is added. Neutral axis and strain are computed, a bending-induced polarization source term is introduced and *empirically calibrated* via bending-KPFM on pristine films, and Poisson + screening limits yield predicted Δφbend(κ,t). The laminate is mapped to εL,eff and Pr,eff via effective-medium theory including depolarization factors and orientation distribution. This model outputs a required screening factor S and corresponding design window for {φ, tL, depth}. The chosen 0.1“0.5 vol% global loading and 100“250 nm placement become model-derived, not arbitrary.

Addresses (v) new interfaces/traps and separating screening from passivation: controls are strengthened with a geometry- and chemistry-matched nonpolar platelet (e.g., SrTiO3/CaTiO3) using the same ligand shell, plus trap-density measurements (SCLC, thermal admittance, PL/TRPL). If hysteresis/Voc improvements correlate with polarity and Δφbend suppression but not with trap-density reduction, screening is supported. If improvements track trap reductions equally in polar and nonpolar controls, passivation is implicated.

Overall success probability is increased by staged feasibility gates (G0“G2, G1 for Pr retention) that prevent committing to full device campaigns until the key physical assumptions—(a) measurable, stable Pr in composite; (b) demonstrable vertical alignment; (c) predicted and measured Δφbend suppression—are validated quantitatively.

Hypothesis: OH-driven interfacial oxidation at the FAPbI3/electron-selective contact (SnO2) and at FAPbI3/organic electron-side interfaces is a primary initiator of Voc and PCE loss because it (i) converts iodide-vacancy“proximal Pb2+ into Pb0 and Pb“O/Pb“OH complexes, (ii) increases interfacial energetic disorder and dipole inhomogeneity, and (iii) accelerates halide depletion/ionic accumulation that raises J0,nonrad and reduces quasi-Fermi level splitting. We further hypothesize that prior ‘MOF-as-OH-sink’ concepts are not intrinsically stabilizing in PSCs unless the MOF photoredox state is constrained; Cu-based conductive MOFs can catalyze ROS formation under illumination/O2/H2O and thus can amplify OH unless (a) the node redox chemistry is rendered net-scavenging (not net-generating) under PSC-relevant potentials and photon flux, and (b) the OH handling capacity and saturation behavior are explicitly engineered and verified.

Therefore, we propose a quantitatively specified, falsifiable bilayer interface on the electron-selective side that separates (1) OH chemical-potential suppression from (2) electrostatic dipole control and passivation:

(A) An ultrathin (2“5 nm) MOF nanolayer on SnO2 engineered to be a net OH sink under PSC operating conditions (1-sun, 40“60% RH, O2 present, device bias near MPP). The MOF will be implemented as a node-swappable, structurally matched series (Cu“HHTP vs Ni“HHTP/Co“HHTP analogues) to discriminate whether redox-active Cu helps (scavenges/quenches OH-derived intermediates) or harms (photocatalytically generates ROS). The decisive criterion is a lower time-integrated OH signal and lower oxygen incorporation into FAPbI3 for the ‘sink’ MOF compared with (i) bare SnO2, (ii) a barrier-only hydrophobe of identical thickness, and (iii) a redox-altered but structurally similar MOF.

(B) A conformal, ultrathin (3“10 nm) anchored IEICO-4F-derived NFA interlayer that provides a permanent interfacial dipole step and a hydrophobic, low-permeability overlayer while minimizing added energetic disorder. Anchoring groups (1“5 mol% phosphonate/carboxylate) are introduced at low density specifically to prevent interlayer drift under bias/heat and to stabilize the dipole spatial distribution; however, such functionalization risks perturbing packing and LUMO/energetic disorder. Thus, we hypothesize that Voc gains will only materialize if (i) the modified NFA retains its electronic structure within tight bounds (ΔLUMO ≤ 50 meV; absorption spectral shift ≤ 10 nm) and (ii) its dipole/work-function shift is stable after thermal/bias stress (ΔWF change ≤ 20 meV after 85°C MPP).

Mechanistic prediction (falsifiable): if OH suppression is the dominant stabilization lever, then (1) EPR OH spin-adduct yield, ToF-SIMS oxygen incorporation, and XPS Pb“O growth rates will decrease in proportion to Voc(t) stabilization and reduced ΔVoc,nonrad; (2) a barrier-only hydrophobe of matched thickness may slow oxygen/water ingress but will not reproduce the same reduction in OH-derived spin-adduct kinetics under identical photon/RH/O2, nor the same suppression of Pb“O formation at equal permeation; and (3) a dipole-only energetics layer (anchored NFA without MOF) may raise initial Voc via work-function/band-bending but will not reproduce the improved Voc stability under OH stress if OH chemistry remains active. Plan: Step 0 — Define quantitative acceptance criteria (go/no-go metrics)
0.1 OH-scavenging performance (must meet all):
  • Under identical stress (1-sun equivalent photon flux, 40“60% RH, 21% O2, 25“60°C), time-integrated EPR OH spin-adduct signal at SnO2/MOF surface is reduced by ≥50% vs bare SnO2 over 60 min.
  • OH-sink capacity/turnover: EPR signal reduction persists without convergence to bare-SnO2 behavior for ≥6 h continuous stress OR shows a measurable saturation time constant τsat that is ≥3× longer than a barrier-only control of matched thickness (indicating chemistry, not only diffusion).
  • Oxygen incorporation into the perovskite (H2^18O label) is reduced by ≥30% at the interface (ToF-SIMS ^18O− depth profile integrated over first 20 nm of perovskite) after a fixed stress dose.
0.2 Transport/electrical acceptance (must meet all):
  • Contact resistivity (ρc) of SnO2/MOF/NFA stack ≤ 2× that of SnO2 control, measured by TLM on dedicated electron-only test structures.
  • No extraction bottleneck: transient photocurrent (TPC) extraction time constant increases by ≤20% vs SnO2-only; impedance-derived recombination/extraction resistances show no new dominant high-frequency arc attributable to the MOF layer.
0.3 Dipole permanence/energetic disorder acceptance (must meet all):
  • Work-function step from anchored NFA (UPS/KPFM) is measurable (target |ΔWF| = 0.10“0.30 eV) and stable: drift ≤ 20 meV after 85°C MPP stress (KPFM before/after).
  • Anchored NFA packing/disorder: GIWAXS shows retained π“π stacking signature relative to parent IEICO-4F with (i) Δq ≤ 0.05 Å−1 and (ii) no emergence of dominant amorphous halo; temperature-dependent conductivity yields an activation energy change ≤ 25 meV vs parent.

Step 1 — Build the OH-stress metrology platform and baseline devices (with decisive controls)
1.1 Device baselines:
  • n“i“p PSC: glass/ITO/SnO2/FAPbI3/HTL/Au.
  • Electron-side organic interface model: introduce an IEICO-4F-containing electron-side organic layer (IPOSC-inspired) to explicitly test Voc retention with organic adjacency.
1.2 Controlled OH generation protocols (calibrated):
  • Photochemical: UV-assisted humid air (40“60% RH) with controlled O2 fraction; photon flux recorded (actinometry) to enable dose normalization.
  • Chemical precursor: low-concentration H2O2 + UV applied only to SnO2-side substrates prior to perovskite deposition to localize ROS history at the interface.
  • Isotopic tracing: H2^18O humidity exposure for oxygen incorporation mapping.
1.3 Baseline diagnostics (dose-resolved):
  • Voc(t) under MPP; stabilized PCE.
  • EQEEL/absolute PLQY → extract ΔVoc,nonrad.
  • TRPL (interface-sensitive geometry) and Suns“Voc (ideality factor, J0,nonrad).
  • XPS (Pb 4f/I 3d/O 1s) time series under controlled stress; ToF-SIMS (O−, OH−, I−, ^18O−).
  • EPR spin-trapping for OH (quantify spin-adduct yield vs time; extract apparent rate constants and saturation behavior).

Step 2 — Engineer MOF OH-sink layers with node-swapped analogues and quantify OH kinetics/capacity
2.1 MOF series (structurally matched, redox-discriminating):
  • Prepare ultrathin HHTP-based conductive MOFs with different metal nodes: Cu“HHTP (redox-active, potentially ROS-generating), Ni“HHTP and/or Co“HHTP (comparative redox behavior) using identical ligands and deposition conditions.
  • Include a redox-inert ‘MOF-like barrier’ control: an ultrathin porous organic network (or insulating coordination polymer) matched in thickness/roughness but lacking redox-active nodes, to test barrier-only diffusion suppression.
2.2 Conformal ultrathin growth on SnO2 (2“5 nm) with reproducibility criteria:
  • Surface primer: phosphonic-acid or silane anchoring monolayer on SnO2 (target areal density: self-limited monolayer) to (i) tether MOF nuclei, (ii) suppress pinholes, and (iii) reduce ion ingress.
  • Sequential infiltration synthesis (SIS-like): alternating metal-node precursor and ligand exposures with short cycles; stop at the thickness that meets transport criteria.
  • Inline acceptance:
    “ Thickness: spectroscopic ellipsometry (target 2“5 nm).
    “ Coverage fraction: high-resolution AFM + conductive-AFM mapping; criterion: ≥95% continuous coverage with RMS roughness ≤ 1.5 nm over 5×5 µm^2.
    “ Chemistry: XPS confirms metal/ligand signatures; absence of excessive surface oxides pre-perovskite.
2.3 Quantify net OH sink vs net OH generation (decisive):
  • EPR spin-adduct yield vs time under identical photon/RH/O2 on SnO2, SnO2/Cu“HHTP, SnO2/Ni“HHTP, SnO2/Co“HHTP, and barrier-only control.
  • Fit kinetics to extract apparent formation rate (kform) and saturation/decay (τsat) to determine whether MOF reduces kform (true sink/quenching) or only delays via diffusion.
  • Regeneration test: repeated stress cycles with resting periods; if OH sink is catalytic/regenerative, performance persists; if sacrificial, saturation is observed (explicitly reported).

Step 3 — Implement anchored IEICO-4F-derived dipole/passivation layer with energetic-disorder monitoring
3.1 Molecular design and bounds:
  • Synthesize IEICO-4F analogue with 1“5 mol% terminal phosphonate/carboxylate anchoring substituents placed on side chains to minimize conjugation perturbation.
  • Electronic structure acceptance: UV“vis“NIR absorption (peak shift ≤10 nm), cyclic voltammetry/UPS (ΔLUMO proxy ≤50 meV vs parent).
3.2 Deposition and morphology control:
  • Deposit 3“10 nm NFA film by orthogonal solvent strategy (non-perovskite-solvent) with controlled aggregation; mild anneal below perovskite damage threshold.
  • Packing/disorder characterization:
    “ GIWAXS: quantify π“π stacking distance and coherence length.
    “ UPS/KPFM: quantify ΔWF and spatial uniformity (dipole homogeneity).
    “ Temperature-dependent conductivity / transport: energetic disorder proxy via activation energy trends.
3.3 Dipole permanence under operating stress:
  • KPFM mapping before and after 85°C MPP stress (and after humid light soak) to confirm ΔWF stability (≤20 meV drift) and no dipole redistribution.

Step 4 — Integrate the full bilayer and execute discriminating control matrix (mechanism attribution)
4.1 Full stack variants (minimum decisive set):
  (A) SnO2 (baseline)
  (B) SnO2 + MOF only (Cu“HHTP; Ni/Co analogues)
  (C) SnO2 + barrier-only hydrophobe (matched thickness to MOF; no redox)
  (D) SnO2 + anchored NFA only (energetics-only/dipole-only)
  (E) SnO2 + non-anchored IEICO-4F (mobility/drift control)
  (F) SnO2 + MOF + anchored NFA (target bilayer)
  (G) SnO2 + fullerene-dimer interlayer (DC60-type comparator per state-of-the-art interfacial passivation)
4.2 Prove no transport bottleneck (thickness series):
  • MOF thickness series: 0/2/3/5/7 nm; NFA thickness series: 0/3/5/10 nm.
  • Electrical diagnostics:
    “ TLM/4-probe on electron-contact stacks → ρc, sheet resistance.
    “ Impedance spectroscopy under illumination → recombination resistance and transport resistance.
    “ TPV/TPC and transient EL → extraction/recombination dynamics and interfacial charge accumulation.
4.3 Prove OH suppression (not just barrier or energetics):
  • Under identical OH stress dose, compare:
    “ EPR OH spin-adduct kinetics (kform, τsat) across A“F.
    “ ToF-SIMS ^18O incorporation and oxygen depth profiles.
    “ XPS growth rate of Pb“O/Pb“OH components (time-resolved).
  • Key discriminant: if (F) reduces OH EPR signal and oxygen incorporation more than (C) at matched thickness/permeability proxies, the effect is chemical (sink) rather than purely barrier.
4.4 Prove ‘dipole-defined’ vs pinning/doping:
  • UPS + KPFM: correlate ΔWF with Voc changes across D, E, F.
  • Check for chemical doping/work-function pinning: monitor core-level shifts (XPS) and conductivity changes; a true dipole layer yields a WF shift with minimal bulk doping signature.

Step 5 — Device-level outcomes tied to Voc/PCE and stability
5.1 Initial performance:
  • JV, stabilized MPP PCE, Voc distribution statistics.
  • ΔVoc,nonrad from EQEEL/PLQY; Suns“Voc ideality factor.
5.2 Stability and Voc(t) decay constants:
  • MPP tracking at 60“85°C, 40“60% RH, O2 present; report T80 and explicitly Voc(t) decay constants.
  • Bias-stress capacitance and hysteresis metrics; ion-migration indicators (transient response under bias).
5.3 Causal linkage (must be demonstrated):
  • Quantitative correlation across variants between (i) OH EPR metrics and (ii) ΔVoc,nonrad and Voc stability. A monotonic relationship supports the proposed causal chain; absence of correlation triggers redesign (e.g., metal-node swap or suppression of MOF photoredox activity).

Step 6 — Risk mitigation and decision points (reviewer-critical vulnerabilities)
6.1 If Cu“HHTP shows net OH generation (EPR increase vs SnO2):
  • Switch to Ni/Co node (or mixed-node) that shows net scavenging; incorporate node redox-state stabilization (e.g., pre-conditioning under controlled potential/light) and verify by repeated EPR cycles.
6.2 If MOF increases ρc/series resistance:
  • Reduce thickness to the minimum continuous coverage; modify primer chemistry to improve electronic coupling; consider sparse MOF islands only if OH sink remains effective and transport remains percolative (validated by c-AFM and TLM).
6.3 If anchored NFA increases energetic disorder:
  • Reduce anchoring fraction (toward 1 mol%), shift anchor to less packing-disruptive side chain position, or use a bifunctional anchoring additive blended at low wt% to immobilize parent IEICO-4F without covalent modification; re-qualify with GIWAXS/UPS criteria.

Feasibility: 1) Addressing MOF photoredox ambiguity with node-swapped, falsifiable OH metrics: The key reviewer risk—Cu-MOFs potentially generating ROS—is converted into an explicit discriminating experiment by using structurally similar HHTP MOFs with different metal nodes (Cu vs Ni/Co) and by quantifying OH spin-adduct kinetics (kform, τsat) and saturation/regeneration behavior under PSC-relevant photon/RH/O2. This directly tests whether the MOF is a net OH sink or net source, rather than assuming scavenging.

2) Engineering realism for ultrathin MOF layers: Continuous 2“5 nm MOF films are challenging; we therefore define acceptance criteria (≥95% coverage, RMS roughness ≤1.5 nm) and pair them with transport constraints (ρc ≤2× baseline; ≤20% extraction-time penalty).
