Hypothesis: A dual-interface-loss“minimized perovskite photoelectrochemical (PEC) platform can be realized by (i) replacing the conventional nanocrystal mesoporous ETL with a manufacturable, low-thermal-budget “PSC-like” mesoporous oxide scaffold whose *connectivity and texture are quantitatively engineered* to produce near-single-crystal electron percolation paths, and (ii) implementing a *dose-limited, verifiably sub-tunneling-length* AgI interlayer at the hole contact that reduces barrier-limited hole extraction and interfacial non-radiative recombination without triggering Ag/Cu/halide-driven failure. Mechanistically, the PSC-like scaffold outperforms nanoparticle ETLs not by increasing surface area alone (which can increase interface traps), but by reducing the energetic/kinetic penalty of grain boundaries through (a) higher crystallographic coherence length and (b) lower tortuosity percolation, which together shorten electron transport time (τtr) and reduce electron residence time at the oxide/perovskite interface; the predicted outcome is a measurable drop in interfacial recombination velocity (S) because recombination becomes extraction-limited less often. In parallel, a tightly controlled AgI layer (≤2 nm, continuous) at the HTL/metal interface provides field-assisted tunneling and mitigates interfacial band-bending and defect-mediated recombination (reduced SRH via halide-vacancy passivation and reduced barrier height), increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting (Voc) and FF. The PEC mode is not treated as an add-on; instead, a pinhole-validated inorganic barrier and a kinetic model that separates interfacial charge-transfer resistance (Rct) from diffusion/ohmic limits enables mapping of PEC-derived interfacial kinetics (Rct, recombination resistance, τrec) onto PV-mode non-radiative losses (PLQY/EQEEL-derived ΔVoc,nr), thereby preserving the DSSC → PEC kinetics → PV loss-analysis chain with falsifiable, gated milestones.
Plan: WP0 (Platform definition and preregistration of gates)
- Device absorber: FA0.83Cs0.17Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3 (or iodide-rich variant if required for AgI formation), identical crystallization across all arms (same precursor molarity, antisolvent timing, anneal).
- Two stack polarities for decoupling contacts:
  (R) regular: Glass/ITO/ETL/Perovskite/HTL/Metal
  (I) inverted: Glass/ITO/HTL/Perovskite/ETL/Metal
- Pre-register quantitative success criteria for each WP (below) and lock two ETL controls + four AgI controls.

WP1 (Highest-risk item #1): Manufacturable PSC-like mesoporous ETL scaffold with measurable texture/connectivity
Goal: deliver a reproducible recipe that yields a mesoporous oxide scaffold with (a) controlled porosity without collapse, (b) high crystallographic coherence, (c) measurable preferential orientation/texture, and (d) superior electronic transport vs state-of-the-art ETL controls under identical perovskite infiltration.

WP1.1 Scaffold fabrication (two manufacturable routes; one must pass gates)
Route A: Block-copolymer templated sol“gel + photonic/flash crystallization (low substrate thermal budget)
- Precursor: TiO2 (titanium alkoxide sol“gel) or SnO2 (tin chloride/alkoxide sol“gel) with amphiphilic BCP template (e.g., Pluronic F127/PS-b-PEO class) tuned for 10“30 nm pores.
- Film thickness: 120, 180, 240 nm (spin or slot-die on test substrates).
- Template removal + crystallization:
  - UV-ozone/oxygen plasma partial removal (to prevent catastrophic shrinkage), then photonic curing (xenon flash) with energy density sweep (e.g., 1“10 J cm−2, 1“10 pulses) under controlled ambient (N2/O2 ratio) to crystallize without prolonged heating.
  - Collapse-avoidance control: in situ ellipsometry (thickness shrinkage limit ≤20%) and ex situ porosimetry (see metrics).
Route B: Seeded nanocrystal “necking” + mild solvothermal fusion (≤150 °C)
- Deposit a mesoporous layer from monodisperse TiO2 or SnO2 nanocrystals (pre-synthesized, ligand-stripped) with a removable porogen.
- Apply aqueous/alcoholic solvothermal treatment (120“150 °C, sealed, ≤2 h) to induce oriented attachment/necking (grain boundary reduction) while preserving mesoporosity.
- Rationale: avoids flash-induced heterogeneous sintering; provides a second manufacturable path.

WP1.2 Quantitative structural metrics (pass/fail gates)
For each scaffold condition, measure:
1) Texture/orientation: GIWAXS texture factor (Herman’s orientation parameter or equivalent) with target: ≥0.3 increase vs nanoparticle mesoporous control; report pole figures.
2) Crystallinity/coherence: cross-sectional TEM + FFT-derived coherence length distribution; target median coherence length ≥30 nm with narrow distribution (IQR ≤20 nm).
3) Porosity/tortuosity: ellipsometric porosimetry or GISAXS-derived pore size; target pore diameter 15“25 nm; porosity 30“50%; tortuosity factor τtort ≤2.0 (extracted from diffusion of small probe molecules or reconstructed tomography on a subset).
4) Electronic transport in scaffold (without perovskite): TRMC (preferred) or contacted conductivity; target ≥3× increase in effective electron mobility/conductivity vs nanoparticle mesoporous ETL at comparable thickness.
5) Interface trap propensity screen: XPS (surface hydroxylation), UPS (work function), and a standardized perovskite-on-ETL PL quenching/PL lifetime assay to flag trap-rich surfaces.
Gate WP1 “GO”: meet criteria (2 of 3 structural targets + transport target) without porosity collapse (shrinkage ≤20%, continuous film by SEM).

WP1.3 Benchmark against two ETL controls (mandatory)
Controls fabricated and infiltrated identically:
C1: Standard mesoporous nanoparticle TiO2 (or SnO2) + compact layer.
C2: Nanowire/compact bilayer ETL (e.g., hydrothermal nanowires on compact or aligned nanorods) OR a state-of-the-art planar SnO2 with passivation (e.g., KCl/alkali passivated) as the “fast-transport/low-area” comparator.
All three ETLs receive the same perovskite infiltration protocol (WP1.4).

WP1.4 Identical perovskite infiltration protocol (controls interfacial chemistry)
- Vacuum-assisted infiltration into mesopores (standardized vacuum dose/time), solvent system fixed.
- Cap layer: thin 3D perovskite overlayer (e.g., 200“400 nm total absorber) to form hybrid meso/planar.
- Void quantification: cross-sectional SEM/TEM + image analysis (void fraction target ≤5%).

WP1.5 Kinetic performance gates linking structure → PV/PEC metrics
Primary transport/recombination targets (pre-registered):
- IMPS-derived transport time constant τtr: ≥2× reduction vs C1 at matched Jsc.
- TRPL (interface-sensitive excitation) or PLQY-derived implied Voc: ≥50% reduction in interfacial recombination velocity proxy (e.g., increased PL lifetime at ETL interface; or ΔVoc,nr improvement ≥25 mV vs C1).
- Device-level: FF improvement ≥2 absolute percentage points vs C1 in PV mode without sacrificing Jsc.

WP2 (Highest-risk item #2): AgI tunneling interlayer with thickness-control strategy, falsifiable tunneling criteria, and degradation forensics
Goal: obtain an AgI interlayer that is (i) continuous, (ii) in the tunneling thickness regime, (iii) reduces contact barrier and non-radiative recombination, and (iv) does not accelerate ion-migration-driven degradation (filamenting, Ag penetration, Cu corrosion).

WP2.1 Architecture and controlled Ag reservoir
- Base anode: Cu (as stress-test + cost focus).
- Ag source options (evaluate both):
  A) Sub-nm to 2 nm evaporated Ag between HTL and Cu (Ag(0) reservoir).
  B) Ag-doped HTL (low loading) + Cu, no discrete Ag film (reduces filament risk).
- HTLs: at least two chemically distinct HTLs to test generality and rule out HTL-specific effects (e.g., Spiro-OMeTAD vs PTAA vs NiOx-based).

WP2.2 Iodide chemical potential control without destabilizing perovskite
- “I-source” introduced only at the immediate HTL interface using a confined iodide reservoir (e.g., trace iodide salt in HTL topcoat or self-assembled iodide-bearing molecule), with total iodide areal density pre-calibrated.
- Hard constraint: perovskite stoichiometry/phase unchanged (GIWAXS peak positions/phase fraction stable; no new PbI2 beyond baseline).

WP2.3 Conditioning dose as the quantitative control loop (thickness-limited formation)
- Define conditioning “dose” D = (light intensity × time) + (bias × time) at fixed temperature; run a matrix (e.g., 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2 “sun·hour equivalents” with/without forward bias).
- After each dose, measure AgI thickness/continuity (WP2.4) and contact resistivity/barrier (WP2.5). Stop conditioning when tunneling criteria met or when Rs rises.

WP2.4 Direct thickness/continuity measurements (mandatory)
- Cross-sectional TEM/EELS on representative devices after specific D to quantify AgI thickness; target: continuous layer 0.5“2.0 nm; reject if >3 nm or discontinuous islands.
- Angle-resolved XPS depth profiling to confirm Ag“I chemical state and spatial confinement.

WP2.5 Falsifiable tunneling/contact criteria
- Contact resistivity via TLM (or c-TLM): target ≥30% reduction vs Ag-free Cu contact without increasing series resistance in full device.
- Barrier height/work-function alignment: UPS and/or KPFM; target measurable reduction in hole-injection barrier (ΔΦ ≥0.1“0.2 eV vs control).
- Non-radiative recombination metrics: EQEEL or PLQY-derived ΔVoc,nr improvement ≥20 mV at matched current density.
Gate WP2 “GO”: meet thickness window + improved contact resistivity + improved ΔVoc,nr with no Rs penalty.

WP2.6 Hard controls (mandatory falsification set)
- Ag-free control: HTL/Cu.
- I-source-free control: Ag present but no iodide reservoir.
- Halide variant controls: AgCl, AgBr (tests whether “AgX tunneling” is generic or iodide-specific).
- HTL dependence: at least two HTLs.

WP2.7 Degradation forensics and filament suppression
- ToF-SIMS depth profiles pre/post stress (illumination + bias) to detect Ag migration into perovskite and Cu diffusion.
- Cross-sectional SEM/TEM to identify filamenting/short pathways.
- Electrical signature: monitor hysteresis, shunt formation, and noise spectroscopy if available.
- Fail criteria: detectable Ag penetration into perovskite bulk above threshold (pre-defined SIMS signal ratio), rapid shunt increase, or catastrophic Rs increase.

WP3 (Highest-risk item #3): PEC barrier integrity, edge sealing, and kinetic model separating Rct from transport limits
Goal: create a PEC-operable perovskite device whose electrolyte-facing barrier is demonstrably pinhole-free at the relevant timescale, with a kinetic model that allows extraction of true interfacial charge-transfer parameters.

WP3.1 Barrier layer + edge seal (manufacturable stack)
- Barrier: ALD nanolaminate (e.g., Al2O3/SnO2 or Al2O3/TiO2), total 10“20 nm on the electrolyte-facing side (choose configuration based on illumination geometry).
- Edge seal: UV-curable epoxy + glass cap or chemically resistant encapsulant; define overlap/edge distance.

WP3.2 Pinhole/leakage testing (mandatory pass/fail)
- Electrochemical leakage: measure dark current in electrolyte vs bias; define maximum leakage current density (e.g., ≤10−6“10−5 A cm−2 at relevant bias) and stable over time.
- Dye-penetration test (analogous to barrier pinhole visualization): expose to dye/redox marker; inspect optical/PL change mapping.
- “Ca-test analog” for ionic ingress: use an ion-sensitive layer or electrical proxy to detect ingress rate; set threshold.
Gate WP3 “GO”: pass leakage + dye penetration + stability of leakage over defined soak time.

WP3.3 PEC electrolyte selection and compatibility screen
- Use non-aqueous redox mediators first (iodide/triiodide; cobalt complex) with defined diffusion coefficients; exclude mediators that chemically attack HTL/ETL.
- Compatibility: soak tests on isolated transport layers + barrier to quantify chemical change (XPS/UPS) before full PEC runs.

WP3.4 Kinetic model and parameter extraction (Rct vs diffusion/ohmic)
- Use EIS under illumination with equivalent circuit that includes: series resistance (Rs), charge-transfer resistance (Rct), chemical capacitance, diffusion element (Warburg) for mediator transport.
- Vary mediator concentration and stirring/flow to separate diffusion limitation from interfacial kinetics (Rct should be invariant with transport once diffusion is alleviated).
- Define mass-transport limit current; operate below this regime for kinetic mapping.

WP3.5 Mapping PEC kinetics to PV non-radiative losses (closing the chain)
- On the same physical device architecture (or sister devices), measure PV-mode PLQY/EQEEL and Suns-Voc to quantify ΔVoc,nr.
- Correlate changes in PEC-extracted recombination resistance/τrec (and ETL/HTL-specific Rct) with ΔVoc,nr and FF losses across ETL/AgI conditions.
Success criterion: statistically significant correlation (predefined) demonstrating that the same interface modifications shift both PEC Rct/τrec and PV ΔVoc,nr/FF in the predicted direction.

WP4 Integrated demonstration and stability
- PV benchmarking: stabilized MPP tracking, J“V hysteresis index, temperature-dependent Voc/FF to identify barrier-limited extraction.
- Stability matrix:
  (i) PV: continuous illumination in N2 (500“1000 h), plus elevated temperature subset.
  (ii) PEC: bias + illumination in electrolyte with barrier; track photocurrent retention.
- Post-mortem: ToF-SIMS/XPS/TEM on both contacts + barrier for failure attribution (Ag/Cu migration vs barrier pinholes vs interfacial decomposition).
Feasibility: Risk 1 (PSC-like scaffold manufacturability and true advantage): The revised plan replaces qualitative claims (“oriented, fused single-crystal domains”) with two concrete low-temperature fabrication routes and explicit, measurable structure/connectivity targets (GIWAXS texture factor, TEM coherence length distribution, porosity/tortuosity, TRMC/contacted transport). The advantage over nanoparticle ETLs is tested under identical perovskite infiltration with void quantification and against two strong ETL controls (nanoparticle mesoporous and nanowire/planar fast-transport control). Go/no-go gates are pre-registered in kinetic terms directly tied to the DSSC→PEC→PV logic (≥2× τtr reduction by IMPS; ≥25 mV ΔVoc,nr improvement or ≥50% interface recombination proxy reduction).

Risk 2 (AgI interlayer underconstrained and potentially destabilizing): The AgI element is converted into a dose-controlled, thickness-verified interlayer with falsifiable tunneling criteria: direct thickness/continuity measurement after defined conditioning doses (TEM/EELS, angle-resolved XPS), and correlation to contact resistivity (TLM) and barrier height (UPS/KPFM). Hard controls (Ag-free, I-source-free, AgCl/AgBr, multiple HTLs) make the “self-optimizing” hypothesis testable rather than assumed. Degradation forensics (ToF-SIMS for Ag/Cu migration; filament detection by cross-sectional microscopy; electrical shunt/Rs monitoring) provide explicit fail conditions to prevent pursuing a marginal efficiency gain that compromises stability.

Risk 3 (PEC idealization, pinholes/edge ingress, and kinetic ambiguity): The PEC module now includes barrier pinhole testing with quantitative pass/fail thresholds, an explicit edge-sealing protocol, and a kinetic modeling strategy that separates interfacial Rct from diffusion/ohmic limitations by varying mediator concentration and hydrodynamic conditions. Only after operating below mass-transport limits and passing leakage/pinhole gates will PEC-derived kinetics be used to map onto PV-mode non-radiative recombination metrics. This ensures the mechanistic linkage is defensible and not confounded by electrolyte transport or barrier failure.

Overall feasibility: Each high-risk innovation is now a gated work package with measurable structural/electrical criteria, mandatory controls, and failure forensics. This preserves the original DSSC-inspired rationale (high-area charge-transfer interface) while addressing the perovskite-specific failure modes (interface traps, ion migration, contact barriers, electrolyte ingress) with quantitative control loops and benchmarked comparisons.

Hypothesis: Embedding an ultrathin (20“60 nm) triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) interlayer with controlled negative Gaussian curvature at the perovskite/charge-transport interface increases the *effective utilization ratio* of passivation and extraction sites by jointly optimizing geometry, electrostatics, and interfacial chemistry. Specifically, (i) a bicontinuous Schwarz P or gyroid architecture with 5“12 nm necks maximizes specific surface area per projected area while preserving continuous electronic percolation and low contact resistance; finite-element Poisson“drift“diffusion modeling predicts that such curvature redistributes interfacial electric fields from localized asperity-driven hot-spots into a more spatially homogeneous field landscape, reducing field-assisted non-radiative recombination and ion-migration nucleation. (ii) The same geometry enhances accessibility of tethered amine passivants and radical-scavenging motifs, ensuring that a larger fraction of chemically present sites are kinetically contacted by photo-generated radicals and under-coordinated defects. (iii) Photo-induced oxidative coupling of selectively designed aromatic amines into a sparse, conjugated imine network proceeds with kinetics and thermodynamics that outcompete perovskite, SnO2, or C60 oxidation under tightly bounded oxidant chemical potential, thereby converting otherwise destructive ROS/free-radical chemistry into a self-limiting crosslinking reaction. The resulting imine network immobilizes mobile ionic species, passivates emergent defects, and introduces a controlled interfacial dipole that improves band alignment without creating deep trap states. Collectively, curvature-enabled electrostatic homogenization plus chemically selective, operation-triggered radical consumption raises Voc and operational stability while preserving FF, providing a quantitatively testable structure“property“utilization relationship rather than an empirical passivation effect.
Plan: 1. TPMS interlayer fabrication with explicit process window and electrical validation.
1.1 Block-copolymer (BCP) cubosome templating: Use PS-b-PEO (Mn_PS ≈ 32 kg mol⁻¹, Mn_PEO ≈ 11 kg mol⁻¹, Ð < 1.1) dissolved at 1.2“1.5 wt% in toluene/THF (7:3 v/v). Add 8“12 vol% swelling agent (1,3,5-trimethylbenzene) to access Schwarz P/gyroid phases with target lattice parameter 25“40 nm. Spin-coat at 2000“3000 rpm in 40“45% RH, 22“25 °C. Thermally anneal at 80 °C for 10 min to equilibrate the mesophase. Expected neck size: 5“12 nm after infiltration and shrinkage.
1.2 Sol“gel infiltration and shrinkage control: Infiltrate with an anhydrous ethanol solution containing (i) methyltriethoxysilane (MTES) as the backbone, (ii) 3-aminophenyltriethoxysilane and 4-aminobenzyltriethoxysilane (molar ratio MTES:amine-silane = 7:3), and (iii) 2 mol% bis-silane crosslinker. Water content fixed at H2O:Si = 1.2; acid catalysis with 0.01 M acetic acid. Condense at 60 °C for 30 min. Expected linear shrinkage ≤18%, yielding final TPMS thickness 20“60 nm.
1.3 Template removal and interface compatibility: Remove BCP by selective extraction in ethanol/THF (9:1) at 40 °C for 15 min. Verify no SnO2 etching (XPS Sn 3d) and no perovskite exposure at this step (TPMS fabricated only on SnO2 or on completed perovskite using orthogonal solvents). RMS roughness tolerance: <5 nm over 5 µm AFM scan to avoid shunting.
1.4 Electrical continuity and contact resistance: Lightly infiltrate (≤10 vol% pore filling) with the adjacent transport material (SnO2 sol for n“i“p or C60 by thermal evaporation) to ensure electronic percolation across the TPMS without blocking pores. Measure contact resistance by TLM; target Rc < 0.5 Ω·cm².

2. Geometry-resolved modeling and validation (mandatory mechanistic closure).
2.1 3D geometry reconstruction: Acquire electron tomography of TPMS interlayers (voxel size ≤2 nm). Reconstruct realistic meshes for Schwarz P and flat controls.
2.2 Finite-element simulations: Solve Poisson + drift“diffusion equations on reconstructed geometries to map electric-field magnitude, recombination rate sensitivity, and carrier extraction vs curvature and SSA. Include experimentally measured dielectric constants and trap densities. Output quantitative metrics: field variance (σ_E), local recombination enhancement factor, and effective contact resistance.
2.3 Experimental validation: Correlate modeled Rc and σ_E with TLM, impedance spectroscopy under bias, and Mott“Schottky analysis.

3. Chemically selective oxidative coupling with hard stop-criteria.
3.1 Amine design and selectivity: Use predominantly aromatic amines (aniline/benzylamine) with oxidation potentials 0.3“0.5 V lower than iodide oxidation, plus 5 mol% sterically hindered diamine to limit over-crosslinking.
3.2 Oxidative protocol: Pre-form a sparse imine network using trace O2 (10“50 ppm) under 1-sun illumination for 5“10 min, or 10⁻⁵“10⁻⁴ M ammonium persulfate in an orthogonal solvent followed by vacuum drying. During operation, rely only on photo-generated ROS.
3.3 Selectivity controls: Measure rate constants for amine→imine vs perovskite/SnO2/C60 oxidation on model films using in-situ FTIR and XPS. Hard stop-criteria: no detectable Pb⁰/PbOₓ growth (<1% XPS sensitivity), no iodide depletion by ToF-SIMS depth profiling after treatment.
3.4 Electronic impact assessment: Track band offsets (UPS/KPFM) and trap formation (DLTS/TRPL). Abort condition: emergence of new deep traps (>10¹⁵ cm⁻³).

4. Redefined utilization ratio with spatial calibration.
4.1 Site tagging: Incorporate 15N-labeled amines (20%) or F-tagged analogues. Use angle-resolved XPS and ToF-SIMS to spatially locate total vs reacted sites.
4.2 Quantitative definition: Utilization ratio = (number of tagged sites participating in defect passivation or radical quenching, inferred from proportional reduction in interfacial recombination velocity and EPR radical decay constant) / (total tagged sites present at the interface).
4.3 Calibration experiments: Systematically cap 25%, 50%, 75% of amines with inert acyl groups and demonstrate linear scaling between active-site fraction and implied Voc / EPR decay.

5. Device integration, yield, and failure modes.
5.1 Thickness/penetration limits: Confirm perovskite penetration into TPMS <5 nm by cross-sectional ToF-SIMS.
5.2 Yield analysis: Fabricate ≥30 devices per condition over 1 cm²; track shunt incidence and FF spread.
5.3 Stability testing: ISOS-L-2, ISOS-O-2, and 85 °C thermal aging correlated with EPR and chemical signatures.

Feasibility: This revised plan directly addresses the reviewers’ feasibility and mechanistic concerns. (i) The TPMS fabrication route is now bounded by explicit BCP molecular weights, solvent systems, humidity, condensation chemistry, shrinkage limits, and roughness tolerances, with defined strategies (partial transport-layer infiltration and TLM validation) to ensure electrical continuity and low series resistance. (ii) Geometry-resolved electrostatic and drift“diffusion modeling on reconstructed TPMS meshes replaces qualitative curvature arguments, yielding testable predictions for field variance, recombination sensitivity, and contact resistance that are experimentally validated. (iii) The oxidative coupling strategy is de-risked by a selectivity-first design: aromatic amines with favorable oxidation potentials, ultralow oxidant chemical potential, and explicit stop-criteria based on Pb/iodide speciation ensure that amine-to-imine formation kinetically outcompetes deleterious oxidation pathways. (iv) The utilization ratio is redefined with isotopic/elemental tagging, spatial localization, and site-blocking calibration, preventing narrative flexibility and enabling stoichiometric closure. Collectively, these refinements transform the concept from an ambitious architectural idea into a quantitatively constrained, manufacturable interfacial strategy aligned with high-efficiency PSC process windows.

Hypothesis: Embedding a MOF-derived, Schwarz P surface (bicontinuous negative-Gaussian-curvature) single-atom catalytic interlayer between the perovskite absorber and electron-transport layer will simultaneously (i) suppress interfacial non-radiative recombination and ion-migration-driven degradation and (ii) enable controllable electrochemical redox buffering measurable via half-wave potential shifts, thereby increasing Voc, FF, and operational stability. The methodological adaptation is to repurpose the Schwarz P bicontinuous architecture—originally used to maximize utilization of FeN4 active sites and raise ORR half-wave potential—into an ultrathin, electronically percolating interphase that couples (a) curvature-enhanced charge extraction and field homogenization, (b) Lewis-acid/base defect passivation through coordinatively unsaturated metal nodes, and (c) redox-stable single-atom centers whose half-wave potential is tuned to sit outside the perovskite operating Fermi-level window, preventing parasitic interfacial redox while still buffering transient charge and halide radicals.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a benchmark high-performance perovskite stack (e.g., n“i“p: FTO/SnO2/perovskite/Spiro-OMeTAD/Au and p“i“n: ITO/NiOx/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag) using a mixed-cation perovskite (FA-Cs, I/Br) to ensure state-of-the-art baseline PCE.
1.2 Define the interlayer target: 5“20 nm thickness, continuous bicontinuous channels, and electronically connected to ETL (or HTL in inverted) without introducing deep traps.
1.3 Prepare methane/biogas-relevant test atmospheres (dry CH4, CO2/CH4 mixtures, and humid CO2/CH4) for stability stress tests to evaluate whether the interlayer mitigates gas- and moisture-accelerated interfacial degradation.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Schwarz P template-to-interlayer conversion (methodological adaptation):
- Synthesize polymer cubosome templates that encode a Schwarz P minimal surface; infiltrate with a MOF precursor solution to form a conformal MOF network along the bicontinuous template.
- Convert the MOF/template composite into a MOF-derived N-doped carbon/metal-node hybrid with isolated single-atom M“N4 sites (M = Fe or Co) while preserving bicontinuous Schwarz P morphology (controlled pyrolysis with curvature-preserving ramp + sacrificial template removal).
- Post-functionalize residual metal nodes/defects with perovskite-compatible Lewis base groups (e.g., pyridine/thiophene-like moieties) via vapor-phase infiltration to avoid solvent damage to perovskite.
2.2 Half-wave-potential-guided interlayer energetics design:
- Use rotating disk electrode (RDE) electrochemistry on interlayer films to measure half-wave potential (E1/2) for a chosen redox probe and/or ORR surrogate; tune M identity, coordination environment, and N-doping to shift E1/2 so that the interlayer is redox-inert across the perovskite device operating electrochemical potential range (minimizing interfacial redox degradation).
- Implement a compositional series (Fe“N4, Co“N4, and mixed Fe/Co“N4; plus metal-free N-doped Schwarz P carbon) to decouple curvature vs. redox contributions.
2.3 Device integration:
- Deposit the Schwarz P interlayer by gentle, orthogonal processing (e.g., dry transfer/lamination or low-polarity dispersions with rapid evaporation) onto the ETL (or perovskite surface depending on stack) and complete PSC fabrication.
- For comparison, fabricate controls: (i) no interlayer, (ii) non-bicontinuous flat carbon/M“N4 layer, (iii) MOF-derived hollow carbon spheres (MOF-templated but not Schwarz P), and (iv) conventional molecular passivators.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Optoelectronic validation (mechanism: recombination/passivation):
- Quantify Voc gains via quasi-Fermi level splitting (absolute PL and QFLS mapping) and time-resolved PL; correlate with reduced non-radiative recombination at the interface.
- Perform impedance spectroscopy and intensity-dependent JV to separate transport, recombination, and interfacial capacitance changes attributed to the bicontinuous interlayer.
3.2 Structural/chemical validation (mechanism: defect coordination + ion blocking):
- Use XPS/UPS to confirm band alignment and chemical coordination (Pb“N, Pb“O, halide“metal interactions) and to measure interfacial dipole changes.
- Track ion migration using TOF-SIMS depth profiling (I−/Br−/MA+/FA+/Cs+), thermal bias stressing, and Kelvin probe force microscopy under illumination to test whether the Schwarz P interlayer reduces field hotspots and ion accumulation.
3.3 Half-wave potential as a predictive stability descriptor (mechanism: redox buffering vs parasitic redox):
- Establish a correlation between interlayer E1/2 and operational stability (MPP tracking at 65“85 °C, 1 sun, controlled O2/H2O/CH4/CO2 atmospheres). Hypothesis test: interlayers with E1/2 tuned away from device operating potentials show lower interfacial redox signatures (EPR for radicals, in situ Raman for iodide/iodine species).
3.4 Methane/biogas-relevant robustness:
- Expose completed devices to CH4 and CO2/CH4 mixtures with controlled humidity and trace H2S (ppm-level, optional) to emulate biogas; quantify PCE retention, Voc drift, and interfacial chemistry evolution. Evaluate whether the MOF-derived interlayer acts as a gas/moisture diffusion modulator without sacrificing charge extraction.
3.5 Scale-up check:
- Demonstrate coating/transfer on ≥25 cm2 substrates; evaluate uniformity (photoluminescence imaging, sheet resistance) and module-relevant metrics (aperture-area PCE, interconnect losses).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Schwarz P bicontinuous architectures are empirically linked to higher electrocatalytic activity and elevated half-wave potential through enhanced active-site utilization and curvature-driven lowering of reaction barriers; MOF-templated hollow/carbonized structures are established routes to produce M“N“C catalysts with high E1/2. Translating these principles to PSC interfaces is feasible because PSC performance is strongly limited by interfacial recombination, ion migration, and interfacial redox/chemical instability.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adapted interlayer is not used as an ORR catalyst in the PSC; instead, E1/2 becomes a tunable descriptor for interfacial redox inertness/buffering. The Schwarz P morphology provides a continuous, thin, high-surface-area contact that improves electronic percolation and homogenizes local electric fields, while MOF-derived coordinatively unsaturated sites and N-rich motifs passivate under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide vacancies.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to flat passivation molecules or non-bicontinuous carbons, the Schwarz P interlayer offers (i) curvature-enabled bicontinuous charge pathways with minimal thickness penalty, (ii) a higher density of accessible passivation/coordination sites without blocking transport, and (iii) a quantifiable, electrochemically measurable tuning knob (half-wave potential) to engineer interfacial redox stability. Relative to conventional MOF additives dispersed in perovskite, an engineered interphase localizes functionality where degradation is most severe and can be implemented as a scalable coating/transfer step compatible with large-area fabrication.

Hypothesis: An ultrathin, percolative Cu3(HHTP)2 or Ni3(HHTP)2 conductive-MOF (c‑MOF) nanonetwork grown by surfactant-confined, low-temperature interfacial synthesis at the buried perovskite/transport-layer contact will improve Voc and operational stability primarily through coordination-driven defect passivation and selective charge extraction, and—under explicitly defined PV-relevant transient high-irradiance stress—secondarily through ultrafast third-order nonlinear optical (χ(3)) response that suppresses hot-carrier“driven interfacial damage.

Mechanistic rationale (tightly bounded to reviewer critique):
1) Interface chemistry (dominant under 1-sun CW): catecholate O donors in HHTP chelate undercoordinated Pb2+ and interact with halide-vacancy-rich motifs, reducing surface recombination velocity and non-radiative losses; concurrently, the π-conjugated 2D MOF plane and metal“catecholate nodes provide electronically percolative extraction pathways and a tunable interfacial dipole that improves contact selectivity without introducing an insulating barrier.
2) PV-relevant stress scenario where χ(3) can matter: PSCs in the field and in module operation experience short, high-irradiance excursions that can locally exceed steady-state 1-sun due to (i) specular “sun-glint” and reflective focusing from nearby glass/metal surfaces and module frames, (ii) arc/partial-discharge events in strings and connectors producing ms“µs optical bursts, and (iii) manufacturing/inspection exposures (class-1“3R alignment lasers; LiDAR/ToF sources; pulsed indoor LED drivers) that can deliver kW“MW·cm−2 peak intensities in µs“fs windows on localized areas. While rare, these events are disproportionate drivers of interfacial hot-carrier spikes, local heating (ΔT), and accelerated ion-migration-assisted degradation at already defect-rich buried contacts.
3) χ(3) pathway (activated only during transients): the c‑MOF’s large χ(3) (manifesting as nonlinear absorption β and Kerr coefficient n2) introduces intensity-dependent loss and phase response at the interface, effectively clamping transient carrier generation near the contact and accelerating carrier/phonon dephasing (reduced hot-carrier lifetime and peak carrier temperature). This reduces the amplitude of the transient quasi-Fermi-level/field overshoot that otherwise increases interfacial recombination, local Joule heating, and defect formation. The proposal explicitly tests whether measured β/n2 at PV-relevant wavelengths and pulse widths quantitatively reduces (a) peak interfacial carrier temperature (ΔTe), (b) peak ΔT in the first 10“50 nm near the contact, and (c) the rate constant for a chosen degradation proxy (Voc loss rate under combined bias/light stress with superimposed pulses).

Critical boundary conditions to avoid over-claiming: under pure 1-sun CW without transient spikes, χ(3) is not expected to measurably contribute; thus, success criteria for the χ(3) novelty are defined only under the specified transient-stress protocol and must be supported by ultrafast spectroscopy at the buried interface plus a degradation-rate correlation.
Plan: A. Device stacks, controls, and interlayer acceptance criteria (defined up-front)
A1. Baseline stacks (two architectures to generalize interface physics):
- n“i“p: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/HTL/Au.
- p“i“n: glass/ITO/PTAA/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/C60/BCP/Ag.
A2. Perovskite surface termination control: generate iodide-rich vs PbI2-rich terminations by (i) slight precursor stoichiometry offsets (±1“2% PbI2), (ii) antisolvent timing shifts, and (iii) brief post-anneal variations. Baseline mapping: XPS (Pb 4f, I 3d), UPS, KPFM, absolute PLQY, and TRPL.
A3. Hard acceptance criteria for the c‑MOF interlayer (go/no-go gates):
- Added contact resistivity (ρc) from TLM or J“V/Rs extraction: ≤ 0.5 Ω·cm2 (stretch goal ≤ 0.2 Ω·cm2).
- Work-function (WF) shift window by UPS/KPFM: |ΔWF| ≤ 0.30 eV unless accompanied by improved selectivity (verified by reduced leakage current and improved ideality factor).
- Optical parasitics: ΔJsc loss from transmission/reflection modeling + EQE ≤ 0.3 mA·cm−2.
- Physical thickness/percolation: effective thickness 1“5 nm, surface coverage 30“80% (percolative but not blocking), verified by cross-sectional HR-TEM/EDX, AFM step-height on masked samples, and GIWAXS for 2D ordering.
- If any criterion fails: branch to (i) reduced coverage, (ii) alternate metal node (redox-inert MOF), or (iii) organic conjugated reference (see C3).

B. Surfactant-confined interfacial synthesis (methodological specificity and residue control)
B1. Design principle: confine MOF nucleation to an ultrathin 2D network while preventing bulk crystallites and avoiding perovskite dissolution.
B2. Surfactant templating parameters (explicit):
- Non-ionic amphiphile: Brij-58 or Triton X-100.
- Concentration: 0.05“0.20× CMC (sub-CMC) to form patchy/lamellar adsorption without micellar solubilization of perovskite organics.
- Deposition: dynamic spin-coating (e.g., 2000“4000 rpm, 20“40 s) of surfactant solution in anhydrous IPA:EA (70:30 v/v) with water ≤0.1 vol%.
- Residue removal: two-step rinse (anhydrous IPA then EA), followed by 60“80 °C vacuum bake (10“20 min). Residue check: ATR-FTIR (C“O“C bands), XPS C 1s deconvolution; acceptance: surfactant signal ≤5% of initial adlayer.
B3. MOF growth chemistry (perovskite-compatible window):
- Metal precursor: Cu(OAc)2 or Ni(OAc)2 at 0.5“2 mM in IPA:EA with water ≤0.1 vol%.
- Ligand: HHTP (2,3,6,7,10,11-hexahydroxytriphenylene) at 0.2“1 mM in EA with minimal base.
- Volatile base: triethylamine (TEA) 0.5“2 mM equivalent in vapor-assisted or trace liquid dosing; objective pH-equivalent: sufficient to partially deprotonate catechols while avoiding perovskite etching.
- Confined growth: sequential dosing (metal then ligand) with a 10“60 s reaction window at room temperature; quench by immediate rinse.
- Ultrasound: optional, only for precursor stock pre-mixing (not directly on perovskite) to avoid mechanical damage; if used during deposition, limit to <1 W·cm−2 equivalent, <10 s.
- Mild anneal: ≤90 °C, 5“10 min in N2.
B4. Percolation tuning knobs:
- Control surface coverage via (i) surfactant concentration, (ii) total precursor dose (mM·s), (iii) sequential cycle number (1“3 cycles).
- Target: sheet-like domains with lateral size 20“200 nm, forming a connected network but leaving transport-layer wetting intact.

C. Active-site engineering with bounded risk (avoid midgap states)
C1. Replace the original “co-ligand dilution to create unsaturated nodes” with a bounded, spectroscopy-gated strategy:
- Primary mode: pristine HHTP-MOF (no intentional unsaturation) as the default.
- Secondary mode (only if needed for binding density): introduce 1“3 mol% of a redox-inert, sterically hindered catechol analog (e.g., alkyl-substituted catechol) to modulate nucleation and binding density rather than creating open metal sites.
C2. Spectroscopic gating (must pass before devices):
- Sub-gap absorption/photothermal deflection spectroscopy (PDS) and UPS: no new deep sub-gap features >10% increase vs control.
- Time-resolved PL and absolute PLQY: QFLS must increase or remain unchanged; if QFLS decreases, abandon co-ligand approach.
C3. Mandatory redox-inert and “electronically similar” references beyond Zn:
- Redox-inert conductive MOF alternative: a Mg/Al-based catecholate-like framework is likely non-conductive; therefore use a two-pronged reference set:
  (i) A redox-inert, fully conjugated organic interlayer with strong Pb“O binding and π-system (e.g., a catechol-terminated oligothiophene or triphenylamine-catechol SAM/polymer) matched to similar thickness and optical density.
  (ii) A c‑MOF with less redox-active node chemistry relative to Cu/Ni: e.g., a Ni-based vs Cu-based comparison plus a metal-free conjugated covalent network (2D COF) thin interlayer where feasible, to separate “conjugation/percolation” from “metal redox.”

D. Quantifying χ(3) under PV-relevant transient scenarios + order-of-magnitude modeling
D1. Define the PV-relevant transient illumination protocol (two tiers):
- Tier-1 (module/field-like microsecond“millisecond bursts): superimpose high-intensity LED/laser diode pulses (e.g., 405/532/808 nm) with pulse width 1“1000 µs, duty cycle ≤1%, peak irradiance 10“200 suns equivalent on a 0.1“1 mm spot to emulate hot-spot/glint/arc optical bursts; keep average power near 1 sun.
- Tier-2 (inspection/laser exposure femto“nano pulses): 1030 nm or 800 nm pulses, 100 fs“10 ps, spot 50“200 µm, fluence adjusted below ablation but high enough to probe nonlinearities (device-safe window determined empirically).
D2. Measure β, n2, χ(3) on complete perovskite/interlayer/transport stacks (not standalone films):
- Open/closed aperture Z-scan at 532, 808, 1030 nm on representative buried-interface stacks on glass.
- Pump“probe reflectance/transmittance under device-like layering to extract intensity-dependent absorption and refractive index changes.
D3. Minimal quantitative link (order-of-magnitude) from β to reduced transient heating:
- Use Beer“Lambert with nonlinear absorption: dI/dz = −αI − βI^2.
- For a transient spike with peak intensity I0 at the interface, the incremental absorbed energy density in the first δ (10“50 nm) is ΔU ≈ ∫0^δ (αI + βI^2) dz × τpulse.
- If β<0 (saturable absorption/bleaching) or if the effective nonlinear response clamps I in the perovskite near the interface (via interlayer absorption/dispersion), predict a reduced ΔU in the perovskite and lower ΔT = ΔU/(ρCp). The sign and magnitude will be determined experimentally; the proposal will not assume bleaching vs RSA a priori.
- Map ΔT(t) into an Arrhenius acceleration factor for an interfacial degradation proxy kdeg ∝ exp(−Ea/kBT) (Ea extracted from separate temperature-accelerated tests). The goal is to show that the measured nonlinear response changes peak T by even a few K during spikes, producing a measurable change in kdeg under repeated bursts.
D4. Define a degradation-rate metric tied to the transient protocol:
- Track ΔVoc/Δt and ΔPLQY/Δt under ISOS-L-2-like bias+light at 65 °C with superimposed Tier-1 pulses; compare slopes with/without c‑MOF at matched initial Voc.

E. Mandatory ultrafast evidence at the buried interface (causality)
E1. Ultrafast transient absorption (TA) with interface sensitivity:
- Use front/back excitation geometries and selective probing to emphasize the buried interface (e.g., excite through transport layer if transparent; compare with excitation through glass).
- Extract hot-carrier cooling time constants and band-edge bleach recovery; acceptance: c‑MOF must reduce hot-carrier lifetime or reduce peak hot-carrier signature amplitude under high-fluence excitation without degrading low-fluence carrier lifetime.
E2. Terahertz (TRTS) or time-resolved microwave conductivity (TRMC):
- Quantify sub-ps to ns photoconductivity and momentum scattering time (proxy for dephasing).
- Acceptance: faster early-time decay (dephasing) plus equal or improved long-time extraction (in device-relevant stacks).
E3. Correlate ultrafast metrics to degradation:
- Across a small matrix (no interlayer / organic conjugated reference / Ni-MOF / Cu-MOF), correlate (i) hot-carrier lifetime reduction and/or peak photoconductivity suppression under spikes with (ii) reduced ΔVoc/Δt under superimposed-pulse aging.

F. Standard interface passivation/extraction validation (anchored, not optional)
F1. Energetics and passivation:
- Absolute PLQY → QFLS; compare QFLS“Voc (non-radiative voltage loss).
- UPS/KPFM band alignment, dipole formation.
- XPS for Pb“O coordination signatures; ToF-SIMS depth profiles for Cu/Ni/HHTP distribution.
F2. Recombination/extraction kinetics:
- TPV/TPC, EIS (recombination resistance, chemical capacitance), Suns-Voc, ideality factor vs intensity.
- Series resistance/contact selectivity: dark J“V, S-shaped curve screening, TLM on dedicated test structures.

G. De-risk Cu/Ni electrochemistry and diffusion (mandatory operando/after-stress diagnostics)
G1. Operando or quasi-operando bias+illumination spectroscopy:
- Near-ambient-pressure XPS (NAP-XPS) or operando XAS (Cu/Ni K-edge) under applied bias and illumination to detect oxidation state shifts indicative of redox shuttling.
- If operando is unavailable: staged bias+light exposures with rapid transfer to XPS/XAS (glovebox-integrated transfer).
G2. Metal diffusion/catalysis checks:
- ICP-MS of dissolved layers after selective etch; ToF-SIMS depth profiling pre/post stress (ISOS-L-2 and pulsed protocol).
- Acceptance: no measurable Cu/Ni migration into perovskite beyond detection threshold or a predefined limit (e.g., <10^19 atoms·cm−3 equivalent in the perovskite bulk region, adjusted to instrument sensitivity).
G3. Chemical stability controls:
- Monitor iodide oxidation/catalysis signatures: XPS I oxidation states, UV“vis changes, and any emergence of iodine-related species after stress.
- If redox activity observed: pivot to Ni-only (if Cu problematic) or to conjugated organic reference as the primary “χ(3) + passivation” platform.

H. Statistics and deliverables
- Device batches: n≥20 per condition; report stabilized PCE (MPP tracking), hysteresis index, Voc distribution.
- Deliverable 1: passivation/extraction benefit under CW 1-sun (baseline claim).
- Deliverable 2 (novelty claim): under defined transient protocol, demonstrate reduced degradation rate with quantitative linkage: measured β/n2/χ(3) + ultrafast dephasing/hot-carrier suppression + reduced ΔVoc/Δt.

Decision tree (explicit go/no-go)
- If Rs/ρc exceeds threshold or S-kink appears → reduce coverage/thickness; if persists → abandon c‑MOF for organic conjugated reference.
- If Cu shows diffusion/redox signatures → switch to Ni-only and/or redox-inert conjugated reference; repeat stability.
- If χ(3) measurable but no ultrafast or aging correlation → restrict claims to passivation/extraction only; χ(3) becomes a characterization side-result, not a central novelty.
Feasibility: 1) Why the χ(3) angle is now PV-relevant (anchored scenario): The revised plan no longer assumes χ(3) matters under steady 1-sun. Instead, it targets quantified short-duration, high-irradiance excursions (glint/hot-spot optical bursts, arc events, inspection/laser exposures, pulsed indoor drivers) that can create localized carrier and temperature spikes at buried interfaces—precisely where defect density and ion migration sensitivity are highest. This is the only regime where intensity-dependent absorption/dispersion can plausibly produce a measurable benefit.

2) Quantitative causality is built in: β and n2 will be measured on device-relevant stacks and inserted into a minimal absorption/heating model (nonlinear Beer“Lambert + ΔT estimation). The proposal then tests whether the predicted reduction in peak ΔT/ΔTe correlates with a directly measured reduction in degradation rate (ΔVoc/Δt) under an ISOS-like baseline plus superimposed pulses. This addresses the reviewer’s demand that Z-scan outputs map onto a device-relevant kinetic consequence.

3) Direct ultrafast evidence at the buried interface is mandatory: TA + TRTS/TRMC on layered stacks will quantify hot-carrier cooling/dephasing and early-time photoconductivity changes specifically attributable to the c‑MOF. The novelty claim is accepted only if these ultrafast signatures correlate with slower degradation under the transient protocol.

4) Electrochemical and diffusion risks are explicitly de-risked: Cu/Ni redox activity and diffusion are treated as primary failure modes. Operando/quasi-operando XPS/XAS plus ToF-SIMS/ICP-MS post-stress are included with explicit acceptance limits. A broader redox-inert, electronically similar reference set (conjugated organic interlayer; alternative conjugated network) ensures that any observed benefit can be separated from unintended metal-catalyzed chemistry.

5) Interlayer engineering is bounded by device constraints: The proposal specifies thickness (1“5 nm), percolation/coverage targets, WF shift windows, maximum allowed contact resistance, and optical-loss limits, all verified by cross-sectional TEM/EDX, GIWAXS, UPS/KPFM, TLM, and EQE. A go/no-go decision tree prevents over-optimization loops and ensures the interlayer cannot “win” by adding series resistance or parasitic absorption.

6) Interface-chemistry plausibility remains strong: Independent of χ(3), Pb“O chelation and defect passivation by oxygen-rich catecholate ligands are well-aligned with known perovskite defect chemistry. The c‑MOF adds percolative conductivity and tunable interfacial dipoles—addressing a common weakness of insulating passivators—while the surfactant-confined growth strategy is explicitly designed to avoid bulk crystallites and to minimize chemical damage/residue on sensitive perovskite surfaces.

Hypothesis: A low-temperature (≤70 °C substrate) sublimation“vapor phase pseudomorphic transformation (SVPT) of an ultrathin NiFe“LDH seed on mixed-halide FA/Cs perovskite can yield a conformal, electronically benign interlayer whose *function is conditional on its verified material identity*. We hypothesize two mutually exclusive, pre-registered outcomes with distinct, falsifiable mechanisms:

(A) **Crystalline Ni/Fe“imidazolate framework (true MOF) outcome**: If GIWAXS indexing and TEM/SAED confirm an oriented Ni/Fe“imidazolate lattice (or a known/topologically assignable Ni“imidazolate with Fe substitution) at 1“5 nm thickness, then (i) under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide-vacancy-adjacent Pb will be passivated primarily by N-donor coordination (Pb“N) from imidazolate, producing measurable Pb 4f / N 1s chemical shifts and a correlated increase in quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) and Voc; (ii) ionic motion (I− and A-site cations) will be suppressed by a reduction in the *effective interfacial diffusion coefficient* (Deff) under bias due to a continuous, rigid, nanoporosity-controlled barrier plus strengthened surface binding that lowers vacancy-mediated exchange; (iii) any claimed piezotronic benefit will be treated as a **separate hypothesis test** and is only expected if the converted layer is demonstrably non-centrosymmetric (SHG-positive and polar-domain PFM with consistent phase), producing an interfacial field of order 10^5“10^6 V m−1 under realistic device strain (≤0.1%), sufficient to cause a strain-correlated, contact-resistance-independent modulation of nonradiative recombination.

(B) **Amorphous metal“imidazolate/oxyhydroxide hybrid outcome (pivot)**: If SVPT yields an amorphous or poorly indexed Ni/Fe“imidazolate hybrid (no definitive MOF peaks; diffuse GIWAXS; local M“N/M“O coordination by XAS/XPS), we explicitly pivot the claim: the layer functions as a *metal“imidazolate coordination glass* where (i) passivation is dominated by Pb“N adducts and residual M“OH anchoring that increases surface formation energy for halide vacancies; (ii) ionic suppression is expected mainly from increased activation energy for ion exchange at the top interface (measurable from temperature-dependent drift/diffusion), rather than strict “size-selective” sieving; and (iii) piezotronics is not expected unless SHG indicates polar order.

Across both outcomes, Ni/Fe redox chemistry is treated as a risk: the interlayer is only viable if it does not catalyze iodide oxidation, does not inject deep traps, and does not produce an extraction barrier. Therefore, we hypothesize that a *chemically buffered* Ni:Fe ratio and controlled partial conversion (retaining ≤30% interfacial “OH spectral signature) will keep the work-function shift within ±0.2 eV and suppress formation of I3−/I2 signatures under stress, while maintaining or improving interfacial recombination velocity.

Primary ranked mechanism: **chemical passivation (Pb“N) → reduced interfacial recombination → Voc/QFLS gain**. Secondary: **ionic suppression quantified by Deff reduction**. Tertiary: **piezotronics only if symmetry criteria are met**.
Plan: 0) Pre-registration: go/no-go material specification and decision tree (before device claims)
   - Target thickness: 1.0“3.0 nm equivalent (ellipsometry/XRR on witness, cross-section TEM on device).
   - Continuity: ≥95% areal coverage with no pinholes >20 nm (plan-view HAADF-STEM + automated defect counting; conductive-AFM leakage map).
   - Composition window: Ni:Fe = 3:1 and 1:1 (ICP-MS on witness; XPS quantification), N content confirming imidazolate uptake (N 1s present with imidazolate component).
   - Phase identity go/no-go:
     (A) “MOF confirmed” if GIWAXS shows indexable Bragg peaks to a known/assignable Ni“imidazolate(-like) framework with preferred orientation and corroborated by TEM/SAED; OR
     (B) “Hybrid confirmed” if no indexable peaks but XAS/XPS shows M“N coordination and stable amorphous network.
   - If neither (no M“N; only oxyhydroxide): STOP (no passivation claim) and revise ligand delivery/chemistry.

1) Baseline device and surface standardization
   1.1 Device stack (n“i“p): glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA0.83Cs0.17)Pb(I0.83Br0.17)3 (~600 nm)/interlayer/HTL/Au.
   1.2 Perovskite top-surface conditioning to reduce uncontrolled termination variability:
       - Mild vacuum anneal (≤60 °C, 30 min) to desorb residual solvent.
       - Optional very dilute alkylammonium halide rinse (orthogonal, e.g., isopropanol with <1 mM FAI) as a *standardized* halide-rich termination; must be applied to all arms equally if used.
   1.3 Baseline characterization (before interlayer): XPS (Pb 4f, I 3d, Br 3d, N 1s), UPS/KPFM (work function), PL/TRPL/QFLS.

2) NiFe“LDH seed deposition (ultrathin and perovskite-safe)
   2.1 Deposition route: cyclic chemisorption (ALD-like) at ≤60“80 °C in dry N2 glovebox load-lock:
       - Cycle: brief exposure to ethanolic Ni(NO3)2 + Fe(NO3)3 (total metal 1“5 mM), purge, then mild base vapor (NH3 or urea decomposition in separated zone) to form hydroxide; repeat 1“5 cycles.
       - Thickness calibration: AFM step-height on masked witness + XRR.
   2.2 Seed controls: Ni-only LDH, Fe-only LDH, and inert ultrathin Al2O3 (~1 nm) as a barrier-only reference.

3) SVPT-on-perovskite with 2-methylimidazole (2-MIM): de-risked conversion mapping
   3.1 Reactor: sealed mini-reactor compatible with glovebox; independent T control of source and substrate; pressure control 10“200 mbar.
   3.2 Conversion matrix (DoE):
       - Source T: 90, 110, 130 °C.
       - Substrate T: 45, 60, 70 °C.
       - Time: 5, 15, 30 min.
       - Pulsed flux variant: 2 min on / 2 min off to limit deep diffusion.
   3.3 Partial conversion target: retain interfacial “OH signature ≤30% of initial LDH OH peak area (O 1s deconvolution) while maximizing M“N (N 1s imidazolate component).
   3.4 Hydrophobicity add-on (only after identity established): brief second vapor step (2-MIM + 5“10 mol% fluorinated imidazole) at same substrate T for 2“5 min; objective: increase water contact angle without increasing thickness >0.5 nm.

4) Material identity verification (mandatory before interpreting device gains)
   4.1 GIWAXS/GIXRD: identify peaks; quantify orientation factor; compare to candidate Ni“imidazolate references and simulated patterns.
   4.2 TEM/SAED (cross-section + plan-view): confirm nanosheet/lamellar preservation vs amorphous layer; map thickness/continuity.
   4.3 XPS/ToF-SIMS: confirm imidazolate incorporation (N 1s), metal distribution, and absence of excessive metal diffusion into perovskite.
   4.4 XAS (Ni/Fe K-edge on witness films): oxidation state and coordination (M“N vs M“O); screen for redox changes after light/heat bias.

5) Passivation mechanism: quantitative binding prediction + correlation
   5.1 DFT (or high-level cluster calculations if periodic MOF uncertain): compute binding energies of 2-MIM/imidazolate to representative perovskite surface motifs (PbI2-terminated, FA/halide-terminated, iodide-vacancy-adjacent Pb). Predict core-level shifts (qualitative) and interfacial dipole direction.
   5.2 Experimental binding metrics:
       - XPS: Pb 4f shift and emergence of Pb“N component; N 1s coordination shift.
       - UPS/KPFM: work-function and valence-level shifts; define acceptable band shift window: |ΔWF| ≤ 0.2 eV; otherwise flag as transport-risk.
   5.3 Designed correlation series:
       - Vary N uptake systematically (controlled by SVPT dose) at fixed thickness.
       - Plot QFLS and Voc vs Pb“N fraction (XPS) to establish causality; require monotonic correlation to validate passivation claim.

6) Ion migration suppression: replace “size-selective pores” with measurable Deff under bias
   6.1 Primary metric: effective diffusion coefficient Deff for iodide (and optionally A-site) under bias/illumination.
   6.2 Experiments:
       - Bias-stress ToF-SIMS: apply defined bias (e.g., ±1 V, 60 °C, fixed time), then quantify iodide redistribution depth profile; fit to drift“diffusion model to extract Deff.
       - Temperature-dependent transient ion drift (TID) or EIS-based ionic capacitance: extract activation energy (Ea) for ion motion; success criterion: ΔEa ≥ 0.1 eV vs control or Deff reduction ≥10×.
       - Edge/bypass control: fabricate devices with and without intentional edge sealing; compare Deff and hysteresis to verify whether grain-boundary/edge pathways dominate.

7) Piezotronics: treated as a hypothesis test with symmetry and artifact controls
   7.1 Symmetry requirement (go/no-go for piezotronics claim):
       - Second harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy positive from the interlayer region OR polarized-GIWAXS consistent with non-centrosymmetric order.
       - PFM must show switchable phase contrast not attributable to electrostatics (use band-excitation PFM + on/off field protocol).
   7.2 Quantitative estimate and target effect size:
       - Measure effective d33 (PFM calibrated) on witness films; estimate interfacial polarization under ε ≤0.1% strain.
       - Predicted device-relevant signature: strain-modulated Voc and PL intensity changes that track polarization sign and persist when series resistance is held constant.
   7.3 Artifact exclusion controls:
       - Dummy non-piezo interlayer: amorphous Al2O3 (same thickness) and/or centrosymmetric ZIF-8-like Zn“2-MIM layer.
       - Strain-insensitive electrical fixture + in situ 4-probe/contact resistance monitoring to decouple contact changes.
       - If strain effects correlate only with Rs changes, piezotronics claim rejected.

8) Redox/chemical risk controls for Ni/Fe
   8.1 Operando/near-operando screening:
       - Light + bias aging (MPP, 65“85 °C) followed by XPS/ToF-SIMS depth profiles for Ni/Fe migration and iodide oxidation markers.
       - XAS before/after stress to detect Ni/Fe oxidation state shifts.
   8.2 Acceptance criteria:
       - No measurable increase in oxidized iodine species signals relative to control; no Ni/Fe penetration beyond interlayer within SIMS detection limits.
       - Device does not show new deep-trap signature: ideality factor and temperature-dependent Voc should not worsen.

9) Device completion and benchmarking
   9.1 HTL selection based on measured work function: PTAA (anisole) or alternative compatible HTL; only proceed if UPS indicates no extraction barrier.
   9.2 Benchmark controls (thickness-matched): PEAI 2D cap, MeO-2PACz SAM, ~1 nm Al2O3.
   9.3 Performance statistics: ≥30 devices per condition; report Voc distribution, QFLS“Voc offset, hysteresis index, stabilized MPP.

10) Stability qualification (causal readouts linked to mechanisms)
   - ISOS-L2: MPP tracking at 65“85 °C in N2; ISOS-O2 in ambient.
   - Damp heat 85/85 (encapsulated) and humidity cycling (unencapsulated).
   - Post-mortem: XRD (PbI2), SEM/TEM (delamination), XPS/ToF-SIMS (iodide/metal redistribution), and correlate failure mode with Deff and Pb“N metrics.

Go/no-go decision points:
   - D1 (Material): must meet continuity + M“N evidence; otherwise stop.
   - D2 (Passivation): require QFLS increase ≥20 meV and monotonic correlation with Pb“N fraction; otherwise de-emphasize passivation claim.
   - D3 (Ion): require Deff reduction ≥10× or Ea increase ≥0.1 eV; otherwise barrier claim limited.
   - D4 (Piezotronics): require SHG-positive + strain effect independent of Rs; otherwise drop piezotronics from narrative.
Feasibility: This revision directly de-risks the central uncertainties by (i) **pre-registering material identity outcomes** (crystalline MOF vs amorphous hybrid) and tying each to distinct, testable device physics; (ii) making the dominant benefit **passivation-first**, quantified by DFT-predicted Pb“N binding and experimentally by XPS chemical shifts with a required QFLS/Voc correlation; (iii) replacing ambiguous “size selectivity” with an experimentally extracted **effective diffusion coefficient (Deff)** and activation energy for ion motion under bias, including edge/bypass controls to address grain-boundary leakage; (iv) demoting piezotronics to a **symmetry-gated hypothesis test** requiring SHG (non-centrosymmetry) and resistance-artifact exclusion; and (v) explicitly managing Ni/Fe redox risk with operando/near-operando oxidation-state and diffusion checks plus band-alignment acceptance limits (|ΔWF| ≤ 0.2 eV).

The SVPT concept remains feasible because ligand delivery is solvent-free and temperature-bounded, while the NiFe“LDH seed provides a templated, reactive scaffold that can incorporate N-donor ligands at low substrate temperatures. Crucially, the proposal no longer depends on assuming a canonical NiFe“(2-MIM) ZIF analogue exists at 45“70 °C; instead it formalizes a pivot to a metal“imidazolate hybrid if crystallinity is not achieved, preserving the core concept chain (SVPT-derived interlayer → Pb“N passivation + quantified ionic suppression → stability/Voc gains) while preventing over-claiming.

Hypothesis: Embedding a monolayer-level single-atom catalyst (SAC) array (M“N4 centers; M = Fe/Co) within a chemically robust, ultrathin conductive MOF-derived interlayer at the perovskite/ETL interface will simultaneously (i) suppress oxygen-driven degradation by kinetically controlling interfacial oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) via tuning the adsorption free energy of OH* toward the top of the ORR volcano and (ii) reduce non-radiative recombination by passivating halide-vacancy/undercoordinated-Pb surface states. The methodological adaptation is to repurpose rotating-disk ORR descriptor engineering (OH* free-energy targeting used for SAC screening) into a perovskite-specific ‘oxygen sink + defect-passivating’ interfacial architecture: a 2“5 nm SAC@porous-carbon/MOF nanolayer with high specific surface area (SSA) that is electronically coupled to the ETL (SnO2) but ionically and chemically decoupled from the perovskite through a thin 2D-perovskite/ionic-bonding anchoring motif. Mechanistically, optimized OH* binding on isolated M sites promotes a controlled 4e− ORR pathway (or benign peroxide suppression) on the SAC layer rather than on the perovskite/ETL contact, reducing superoxide/peroxide residence time at the perovskite surface, while the interlayer’s Lewis-base nodes coordinate Pb2+ and fill halide-vacancy related trap states, increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting and thereby increasing power density under operation.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a benchmark high-efficiency perovskite stack (e.g., glass/ITO/SnO2/(interlayer)/FA-Cs mixed-halide perovskite/spiro-OMeTAD/Au) and a reference without interlayer.
1.2 Build a controlled oxygen/moisture exposure platform: (a) dry O2, (b) O2 + 30“50% RH, (c) N2 control, with continuous MPP tracking and simultaneous in-situ electrochemical detection.
1.3 Pre-screen candidate SAC motifs using DFT: compute ΔG(OH*) on M“N4 sites embedded in (i) phthalocyanine-like coordination, (ii) N-doped graphene fragments, and (iii) MOF-node-like coordination. Use ΔG(OH*) as the primary descriptor to target a narrow window near the volcano apex for low ORR overpotential, while constraining Fermi-level alignment to avoid electron extraction barriers from SnO2.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Synthesize a conductive MOF thin film (2“5 nm) directly on SnO2 by vapor-assisted conversion or layer-by-layer growth (e.g., Zr-based or Fe-based MOF seed modified to be electronically percolating after mild pyrolysis at ≤250“300 °C, compatible with PSC processing). This is the adaptation: MOF chemistry and thickness are tuned for high SSA while staying below the carrier tunneling length to avoid series resistance.
2.2 Introduce isolated M atoms (Fe/Co) as M“N4 SACs within the MOF-derived carbonaceous network using a ‘confined coordination’ route: impregnate with metal precursors + nitrogen ligands, followed by low-temperature fixation to prevent nanoparticle formation (verify single-atom dispersion via HAADF-STEM and XAS).
2.3 Add a perovskite-facing anchoring/passivation skin (≤1 nm) by depositing a sparse 2D Ruddlesden“Popper forming salt (e.g., PEA/BA derivative bearing a coordinating group) that (i) blocks direct contact between SAC and halide lattice to prevent metal diffusion and (ii) provides Lewis-base coordination to undercoordinated Pb while maintaining electronic coupling.
2.4 Integrate the interlayer into full devices and also into ‘half-cells’ for mechanistic studies: SnO2/interlayer/perovskite and perovskite/interlayer/SnO2 test structures.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Electrochemical detection of ORR activity at the interface: use a solid-state three-electrode microcell geometry on SnO2/interlayer films (with oxygen dosing) to measure onset potentials and kinetics proxies; correlate with ΔG(OH*)-ranked SAC candidates.
3.2 Quantify oxygen-induced electronic losses: in-situ PL/TPV/TPC under controlled O2 to track non-radiative recombination changes, and EIS to separate charge-transfer resistance vs recombination resistance.
3.3 Identify degradation pathway suppression: operando XPS/ToF-SIMS to detect iodide oxidation products, Pb0 formation, and metal migration; EPR to quantify superoxide signals with/without interlayer.
3.4 Device metrics: compare Voc, FF, and stabilized power output (power density at MPP) under 1-sun and elevated temperature (65“85 °C) in O2/RH stress. Use statistical batches (n≥20) and accelerated lifetime modeling (e.g., T80 at MPP).
3.5 Mechanism-to-descriptor test: demonstrate that stability gain and power density retention scale with (i) measured ORR suppression at perovskite interface (lower superoxide signature) and (ii) SAC ΔG(OH*) proximity to target window, establishing causality rather than correlation.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: SAC ORR activity follows a volcano trend with adsorption free energy (OH*) as a universal descriptor, enabling rational selection of M“N4 motifs; high-SSA MOF-derived carbons and MN4 site-rich macrocycle/MOF systems are proven to deliver high limiting currents and power density in oxygen electrochemistry, indicating that thin, site-dense layers can strongly modulate oxygen reduction kinetics. In PSCs, oxygen/superoxide is a known driver of surface and interface degradation and can also introduce interfacial recombination; therefore, relocating/controlling ORR away from the perovskite contact while passivating traps is mechanistically aligned with known failure modes.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation is not simply adding a catalyst; it re-engineers the perovskite/ETL interface into a dual-function layer: (i) an ‘oxygen-reactivity governor’ designed using ORR descriptor engineering (ΔG(OH*)) and (ii) a perovskite-compatible passivation/anchoring skin to preserve band alignment and prevent metal diffusion. The film is nanometer-thin to maintain electron extraction and can be processed at low temperature to remain compatible with perovskite fabrication.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to conventional organic passivators or inert 2D layers, this interlayer actively modulates oxygen electrochemistry instead of only blocking oxygen diffusion, providing robustness under realistic oxygen ingress. Compared to nanoparticle catalysts, SACs maximize active-site utilization at minimal loading, reduce optical/electrical parasitics, and allow tunable OH* binding; the high SSA architecture increases the probability of oxygen capture and rapid conversion on the interlayer rather than on the perovskite, improving operational chemical stability and stabilized power density.

Hypothesis: Embedding a bicontinuous mesoporous single-atom M“N“C interlayer (Schwarz P-type architecture) directly at the perovskite/transport-layer interface will simultaneously (i) suppress interfacial non-radiative recombination by coordinative passivation of under-coordinated Pb/I (via FeN4 or CoN4 sites acting as Lewis base/electron-density modulators) and (ii) reduce interfacial electrochemical overpotential for parasitic redox processes (I3−/I−, O2/O2•−) by accelerating charge-transfer kinetics away from the perovskite lattice. A methodological adaptation is proposed: translate bmFeSAC-style negative Gaussian curvature bicontinuous mesoporosity—originally optimized for ORR—into a conformal, sub-30-nm-thick ‘electrocatalytic buffer’ that is electrically percolative but ion-blocking, and that can be metal-switched (Fe→Co or Fe/Co dual-SAC) to tune interfacial reaction energetics. Mechanistically, negative-curvature channels increase accessible single-atom site utilization while minimizing local current constriction; this lowers kinetic barriers (effective overpotential) for interfacial redox shuttling and flattens interfacial band bending, thereby increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting (higher Voc) and stabilizing operation under bias/illumination by diverting interfacial radicals from attacking the perovskite.

2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC bottlenecks are interfacial recombination and bias/illumination-driven interfacial electrochemistry coupled to ion migration. Hypothesis: If the nanohertz stochastic gravitational-wave background contains a GR tensor-mode component sourced predominantly by an astrophysical SMBHB population, then a detection statistic that (a) operates in the timing-model“marginalized, noise-whitened residual space, (b) explicitly projects cross-covariances onto an orthogonalized set of *effective* spatial kernels (HD quadrupole, monopole clock, dipole ephemeris, and optional beyond-GR/anisotropy bases), and (c) uses a robustness-first spectral treatment (paired constrained SMBHB-informed model and a semi-parametric alternative with weak regularization) will increase *true* detection probability at a fixed false-alarm rate while preventing biased significance under spectral mismatch. Mechanistically, the approach overcomes the key PTA bottleneck—leakage between common red processes and quadrupolar correlations—by enforcing separation where it matters statistically: after design-matrix projection and whitening under per-pulsar noise. In this projected space, the GLRT decomposes the cross-power into orthogonal kernel subspaces, concentrating evidence for HD correlations only in the component that survives both (i) timing-model marginalization and (ii) null-calibrated whitening, while simultaneously quantifying identifiability limits in mapping band-limited hc(f) to ΩGW(f) when SMBHB environmental coupling/eccentricity and population uncertainties induce degeneracies. The proposal therefore replaces claims of unique ΩGW inference with a falsifiable identifiability analysis and includes a guardrail against model-mismatch loss by running constrained and semi-parametric spectra in parallel and comparing their calibrated detection performance and coverage.
Plan: Step 0 — Data products and notation (pre-registered):
0.1 Use a PTA dataset with TOAs, timing models, and standard noise components (e.g., NANOGrav-like). For pulsar a, define post-fit residuals r_a and timing-model design matrix M_a.
0.2 Pre-register: (i) kernel set, (ii) spectral families, (iii) prior families and widths, (iv) null-calibration protocol, (v) diagnostics and stopping rules.

Step 1 — Timing-model marginalization and whitening (the space where kernels must be orthogonalized):
1.1 For each pulsar a, construct the projection matrix that marginalizes timing-model parameters:
  G_a = I - M_a (M_a^T N_a^{-1} M_a)^{-1} M_a^T N_a^{-1}
where N_a is the white-noise TOA covariance (EFAC/EQUAD/ECORR as applicable). Work with projected residuals: r̃_a = G_a r_a.
1.2 Build a scalable Gaussian-process likelihood in a low-rank Fourier basis for red processes. For each pulsar a, represent intrinsic red noise via Fourier design F_a with n_f frequencies; the red-noise covariance is F_a Φ_a F_a^T (Φ_a diagonal in Fourier coefficients).
1.3 Define the full projected covariance across all pulsars in block form:
  C = G (N + F Φ F^T + S(θ, spectral)) G^T
where S encodes spatially correlated processes (HD/monopole/dipole/optional). Implement whitening via Cholesky or iterative solves: define W such that W^T C0 W = I under the null model C0 (no HD term, but including fitted per-pulsar noise and monopole/dipole if desired). Use W to map data to whitened projected residuals y = W^T r̃.

Step 2 — Define *effective* spatial kernels and orthogonalize them in the whitened, projected space:
2.1 Start from theoretical sky kernels K_k(θ_ab):
  k ∈ {HD tensor, monopole(clock), dipole(ephemeris), alt-pol templates, anisotropy basis (optional)}.
2.2 Convert sky kernels into operators on the whitened data. In Fourier-bin i, the correlated cross-covariance contribution has the form:
  S_i = Σ_k A_{k,i}  (B_{k,i})
where B_{k,i} is the block matrix with (a,b) block proportional to K_k(θ_ab) times the Fourier-basis mapping for that bin.
2.3 Compute the kernel inner product in the *actual* experiment:
  ⟨B_k, B_l⟩ = tr( B_k^T  P  B_l  P )
where P is the operator induced by (i) design-matrix projection G and (ii) whitening W (equivalently work directly with whitened-projected operators: B̂_k = W^T G^T B_k G W).
2.4 Orthogonalize kernels using Gram“Schmidt (or SVD) under ⟨·,·⟩ to obtain an orthonormal basis {Ũ_m}. This ensures that “orthogonality” accounts for cadence heterogeneity, timing-model fits, and noise weighting—not just sky geometry.

Step 3 — Constrained GLRT derived in the projected/whitened basis (and its semi-parametric guardrail):
3.1 Parameterize the correlated signal in Fourier space. For each frequency bin i, model coefficients β_{m,i} multiplying orthonormal kernels Ũ_m.
3.2 Define two spectral families for the HD component (m = HD):
  (A) Constrained SMBHB-informed family: hc(f) = A (f/f_yr)^α × C_env(f; κ_env) × C_ecc(f; κ_ecc), where α≈−2/3 but allowed to vary in a bounded range; C_env and C_ecc are low-dimensional curvature modifiers (e.g., broken power-law turnover frequency f_b and smoothness η).
  (B) Semi-parametric family: free-spectrum with weak smoothness hyperprior (e.g., log hc,i with Gaussian random-walk prior or cubic spline with penalty λ). This is the mismatch guardrail.
3.3 Monopole/dipole/common processes: include monopole and dipole spectra in parallel as either (i) independent free-spectra with weak priors, or (ii) shared low-dimensional spectra, and quantify posterior covariance with HD.
3.4 GLRT derivation: in the whitened-projected domain, define the log-likelihood ratio between H1 (includes HD term) and H0 (no HD term) while always including timing-model marginalization and per-pulsar noise:
  Λ = 2[ max_{θ_noise, θ_corr∈H1} log p(y | θ_noise, θ_corr) − max_{θ_noise, θ_corr∈H0} log p(y | θ_noise, θ_corr) ].
Compute Λ for both spectral families: Λ_constrained and Λ_semiparam.
3.5 Decision rule (robustness-first): declare “HD-correlated detection” only if
  (i) Λ_semiparam exceeds a pre-registered null threshold (controls false alarm without relying on strong spectral assumptions), and
  (ii) Λ_constrained is not in significant tension with Λ_semiparam under posterior predictive checks (guards against prior-driven inflation), and

  • Use EoS-derived I bounds only to set extremely weak, order-of-magnitude constraints on A_torque (demonstrate via prior-to-posterior KL divergence that it is either informative or effectively ignorable).

Step 6 — Scalable computation and complexity:
6.1 Use Fourier-sum GP methods (low-rank) so that per-pulsar red-noise covariance is handled via Woodbury identities:
  (N + F Φ F^T)^{-1} = N^{-1} − N^{-1} F (Φ^{-1} + F^T N^{-1} F)^{-1} F^T N^{-1}.
6.2 Exploit block structure across pulsars; avoid forming full dense cross-covariances in the time domain. Work primarily in Fourier coefficient space where correlated processes factor by frequency bin.
6.3 Complexity targets: with P pulsars, typical n_TOA per pulsar, and n_f Fourier modes, aim for O(P n_TOA n_f^2 + P n_f^3) per likelihood evaluation (dominated by small-matrix inversions per pulsar and per frequency bin) rather than O((Σ n_TOA)^3).
6.4 Sampling/inference:

Step 7 — Null calibration, robustness, and coverage (to prevent inflated significance):

7.2 Prior sensitivity: repeat calibrations under widened/narrowed priors for spectral smoothness and SMBHB curvature; report impact on Λ thresholds and Bayes factors.
7.3 Mismatch injections: inject (i) pure SMBHB HD, (ii) HD with environmental turnover, (iii) anisotropic backgrounds, (iv) nonstationary common red processes, (v) monopole/dipole contaminants, and mixtures. Compare detection power/false-alarm for Λ_constrained vs Λ_semiparam.

2) Microphysics engine specification (mandatory specificity + validation ladder)
2.1 Engine choice: adopt and extend an open, benchmarkable photoionization/reflection workflow with explicit atomic level populations:
- Baseline: XSTAR (or Cloudy) for ion fractions and level populations in photoionized slabs, using AtomDB/CHIANTI line data where applicable.
- Reflection slab + Comptonization + angle dependence: couple the ionization solution to a radiative transfer/reflection solver that includes (i) Compton scattering redistribution (Klein“Nishina; Kompaneets or Monte Carlo kernel depending on regime), (ii) line emissivity/opacity with escape probability or Feautrier/ALI (accelerated lambda iteration) for the Fe L complex to capture line trapping, and (iii) continuum processes (bound-free, free-free) self-consistently.
- Practical implementation: start from an established reflection code that already supports high density and Comptonization (e.g., xillver/relxill family for continuum/hump benchmarks) and add/replace the Fe L treatment using the collisional“radiative module above. The goal is not to rewrite a full reflection ecosystem but to create a “Fe-L-corrected” emissivity generator whose outputs are validated against both (a) xillver/relxill for Fe K/hump and (b) line-rich photoionization benchmarks for Fe L.
2.2 Physics controls (explicit): parameters include (n_e, xi, A_Fe, T_e, incident Γ, E_cut, reflection fraction, slab optical depth τ, viewing angle μ). Treat microturbulence as a bounded nuisance (e.g., v_turb ≤ 500 km/s) to avoid absorbing transfer broadening.
2.3 Validation ladder (quantitative, code-to-code, then data-to-code):
- L0: Unit tests—energy conservation to <1% between incident and emergent (reflected+transmitted+thermalized) energy in the slab; positivity of emissivities/opacities.
- L1: Continuum/hump benchmark—match xillver outputs (Fe K edge region and 10“50 keV hump) within ≤2“3% over a grid in (xi, n_e, Γ, E_cut) at fixed A_Fe.
