3) Response-conditional emulator (formal design + held-out generalization)
3.1 Model factorization (hard constraint):
Rest-frame reflection spectrum S_rest(E | φ) is generated from physical microphysics parameters φ = (n_e, xi, A_Fe, Γ, E_cut, τ, μ, …). Relativistic transfer T_Kerr maps S_rest → S_obs(E | a*, i, r_in, q, …) via a differentiable kernel computed from Kerr geodesics with a fixed emissivity profile family.
The neural component does NOT output S_obs freely. It outputs coefficients c_k(φ) in a positive, physically interpretable basis for S_rest:
S_rest(E) = Σ_k softplus(c_k) B_k(E),
where B_k are precomputed emissivity components (Fe L multiplet groups, Fe Kα/Kβ + edge structures, Compton hump continuum components) spanning the validated microphysics manifold.
3.2 Basis completeness checks (addresses reviewer concern iii):
- Construct B_k via PCA/NMF on a large library of microphysics-generated rest-frame spectra, with constraints: non-negativity, line-group locality, and inclusion of residual basis vectors until reconstruction error < ε (e.g., <1% in 0.4“2 keV and <0.5% in 3“50 keV) across the training grid.
- Stress-test: attempt reconstruction of spectra generated at random off-grid φ; if reconstruction error correlates with A_Fe or n_e, expand basis (adaptive basis enrichment).
3.3 Response-conditionalization (addresses reviewer concern ii):
- Treat instrument response R (RMF+ARF) as an explicit conditioning input. Build a compact embedding z_R by applying an encoder to summary operators derived from R (e.g., energy dispersion moments, effective area vs E sampled on a standard grid, channel-energy mapping Jacobians).
- The emulator predicts expected counts λ for each instrument j as:
λ_j = PoissonMean( Fold[ T_Kerr(S_rest), R_j ] + background_j ),
with the network conditioned on z_{R_j} and on calibration nuisance parameters.
3.4 Held-out generalization protocol:

- Perform SBC under response perturbations: randomly perturb ARF tilt/normalization and RMF width within calibration priors; verify posterior coverage for injected a* remains nominal.

5.2 Counterfactual simulations (mechanism verification with proofs-of-failure modes):

Feasibility: Microphysics feasibility (addresses reviewer i): The proposal does not rely on an unspecified “Fe L microphysics” module. Response-conditionalization feasibility (addresses reviewer ii): Forward-folding during training is made statistically safe by (1) conditioning explicitly on a response embedding z_R rather than mixing responses implicitly, and (2) enforcing held-out epoch/instrument generalization with SBC under response perturbations. This directly tests and prevents the failure mode where the emulator learns response quirks as astrophysics.

Hypothesis: A subset of binary neutron-star (BNS) mergers that leave a long-lived (≳10“10^4 s) neutron-star remnant will produce a transient, magnetized spreading layer (SL) and/or boundary-layer-like equatorial belt powered by fallback and/or residual accretion. The same electron population that generates a hard Comptonized spectral component will also imprint an energy- and phase-dependent X-ray polarization signature via anisotropic scattering in a flattened SL geometry, while the rotating emission pattern imprints a correlated but not perfectly locked timing signature in the photon arrival-time statistics. We hypothesize that a *minimal, explicitly nonstationary shared-state model*—in which a low-dimensional latent state controls both (i) phase-dependent Stokes modulation and (ii) timing residual structure—can separate true compactness/geometry effects (GR light-bending, Doppler boosting, oblateness, frame dragging) from apparent TOA perturbations caused by evolving morphology, differential rotation, magnetospheric reconfiguration, and baryon-loaded outflows. Mechanistically, the approach overcomes the reviewers’ feasibility/systematics concerns by: (1) conditioning detectability on GW-selected distance/inclination and collapse-time priors, producing explicit forecasts for counts, minimum detectable polarization (MDP), and pulse detectability windows; (2) replacing the ambiguous claim of a strict ‘TOA“polarization lock’ with a controlled state-evolution mapping that allows partial decorrelation on physical timescales (phase wander, hotspot drift, optical-depth changes); and (3) replacing hard ‘constraint penalties’ with a hierarchical prior model whose influence on M“R/EoS posteriors is quantified via simulation-based calibration (SBC), ensuring that any EoS tightening is data-driven rather than prior-driven. Under this refined model class, joint inference from IXPE-like spectropolarimetry and coherent timing (when present) yields robust compactness constraints, and the proposal’s promised EoS gains are accepted only when they remain stable across bounded alternative polarization physics (magnetized transfer/QED/vacuum polarization; scattering in baryon-rich winds).

Step 2 — Explicit shared-state forward model with controlled nonstationarity (replacing “locked”)

  • τ(t), kT_e(t): SL optical depth and electron temperature.
  • A_SL(t): SL emitting area fraction / latitude extent.

    dτ = -(τ-\bar{τ})/T_τ dt + σ_τ dW_t; similarly for kT_e, A_SL, g, ξ_w.

  (b) Stokes spectra likelihood (spectropolarimetry):
    • Stokes vector per phase-energy bin: S⃗(E,Φ,t) = S⃗_C(E,Φ | τ(t), kT_e(t), A_SL(t), ψ(t), M,R,spin,ι) ⊕ S⃗_bb(E,...) ⊕ S⃗_wind(E,Φ|ξ_w(t)).
    • Enforce that the Comptonized component dominates the PD/PA behavior (as in dipping LMXBs) by allowing the PD to be primarily generated by S⃗_C, while wind term can rotate PA/increase PD during obscuration/scattering episodes.
    • Use a fast polarized Comptonization surrogate (see Step 3) conditioned on (kT_e, τ, viewing angle, bulk azimuthal speed) with explicit validity domains.
2.4 Correlation claim reformulated and testable:
  • Define a measurable cross-statistic predicted by the model: C(Δt,E)=corr[δTOA(t), δPA(t,E)] and corr[δTOA(t), δPD(t,E)], with expected sign/lag depending on τ(t) and geometry.
  • The hypothesis is not “perfect locking” but “shared latent drivers produce structured, bounded correlation that distinguishes compactness-induced phase distortions from morphology wander.”

Step 3 — Polarization physics module: accuracy requirements, bounded alternatives, failure modes
3.1 Baseline SL polarized Comptonization kernel:
  • Geometry: plane-parallel slab/annulus (belt) with anisotropic seed injection from NS surface; allow mild bulk azimuthal velocity β_φ.
  • Use precomputed polarized redistribution matrices R_ij(E→E', μ→μ' | kT_e, τ, β_φ) from targeted Monte Carlo including Klein“Nishina cross sections (no Thomson-only assumption).
  • Surrogate model: train an emulator (e.g., neural spline / GP) on the Monte Carlo grid; enforce monotonicity/physical constraints (positivity of I, |P|≤1).
3.2 Validity and stress tests:
  • Klein“Nishina: ensure accuracy for kT_e up to ~100 keV (grid coverage), quantify bias when extrapolated.
  • Hybrid electrons: include an alternative kernel with thermal+power-law tail; treat presence of tail as a trans-dimensional switch.
  • Bulk flows: include β_φ up to ~0.3 as a parameter; validate against full relativistic Compton scattering in MC.
3.3 Magnetized/QED/vacuum polarization bounds:
  • For B ≳ 10^13“10^14 G, include an additional polarization rotation/depolarization operator acting on S⃗, parameterized by an effective birefringent phase Δχ(E) and mode conversion depth. If detailed magnetized radiative transfer is too expensive, bracket with two limiting models:
    (i) Weak-QED limit: negligible rotation.
    (ii) Strong-QED screen: energy-dependent PA rotation with saturation.
  • Infer Δχ hyperparameters with broad priors and test whether compactness posteriors are stable when marginalizing over these effects.
3.4 Baryon-rich wind scattering:
  • Implement a simple wind screen with optical depth τ_w(E,t)=ξ_w(t)(E/E0)^(-s), plus a scattering-induced polarization term with a preferred axis tied to disk/outflow geometry.
  • This directly addresses the reviewer’s concern that outflows can mimic compactness signatures by altering both phase and polarization.

Step 4 — Replace “hard constraint penalties” with hierarchical priors and quantify prior influence
4.1 Hierarchical prior structure:
  • EoS prior: sample from EoS families (piecewise-polytrope or spectral representation) with built-in causality and thermodynamic stability; induce p(M,R) via TOV solution.
  • Energy budget prior: rather than enforcing equality, set a weakly informative relation linking L_X(t) to fallback/accretion power with scatter:
    log L_X(t) ~ Normal(log(η \dot{M}c^2), σ_L), with η and σ_L hyperparameters.
  • Angular momentum coupling prior: relate remnant spin (GW-informed) to SL azimuthal flow via a broad regression with scatter, not a hard constraint.
  • All such relations are implemented as probabilistic nodes, allowing the data to override them.
4.2 Simulation-based calibration (SBC) and prior-sensitivity:
  • Generate synthetic datasets from the full hierarchical model across detectability tiers.
  • Run the full inference and verify SBC rank statistics for (M,R) and key SL parameters.
  • Repeat with weakened/strengthened hyperpriors to quantify how much EoS tightening is attributable to data vs priors; report this as an explicit ‘prior influence budget’.

Step 5 — Inference engine and model selection (SNR-aware, trans-dimensional)
5.1 Use product-space nested sampling or RJMCMC to switch on/off: (i) SL Comptonized polarized component, (ii) hybrid electron tail, (iii) wind screen, (iv) QED rotation operator, (v) morphology change points.
5.2 Likelihood weighting and binning:
  • Use photon-level likelihoods where possible; otherwise use adaptive binning such that each bin meets a minimum effective modulation SNR for reliable Stokes inference.
  • Ensure polarization likelihood uses correct IXPE Stokes statistics (not Gaussian-in-PD approximations) and propagate background uncertainties.
5.3 Deliverable posteriors:
  • (M,R) and EOS parameters with full marginalization over nonstationarity and alternative physics.
  • Bayes factors for including SL polarization, wind scattering, and QED terms.

Step 6 — Validation and reality checks
6.1 Internal recovery tests: quantify bias vs (MDP, SNR_pulse, t_collapse, cadence gaps), including adversarial cases where timing“polarization correlations are weak.
6.2 External calibration on LMXBs with spreading-layer phenomenology:
  • Apply the same SL polarimetric kernel to IXPE LMXB datasets (e.g., dipping sources where PD rises and PA swings correlate with a harder Comptonized component), verifying that the model reproduces PD/PA“hardness behavior.
6.3 Stability criterion for EoS claims:
  • Require that compactness posteriors remain consistent (within stated systematics) when swapping: (a) wind model family, (b) QED bracket model, (c) frame-dragging level (Hartle“Thorne vs Kerr-approx), (d) electron distribution (thermal vs hybrid).
  • If not stable, downgrade to reporting conservative bounds or non-detection constraints on SL properties rather than EoS tightening.

Feasibility: Quantitative detectability (addressing the primary scientific risk)
• The proposal now includes an explicit end-to-end forecast layer that converts GW posteriors (distance/inclination/masses) plus a collapse-time prior into predicted IXPE-like counts, MDP99(t), and pulse detectability probability. This directly answers the critique that the original text lacked count-rate/MDP/pulsation feasibility.
• The analysis is explicitly tiered: even if coherent pulsations are absent (likely in many post-merger scenarios), the framework still performs polarimetry-dominated inference (Tier A) and uses timing only when pulse SNR supports it (Tier B). This prevents overreliance on an unestablished observable regime.
• Collapse-time uncertainty is treated as a first-class latent variable with physically motivated priors; feasibility is reported as probability mass in the (MDP, pulse detectability) region before collapse.

Controlled nonstationarity (addressing ‘TOA residuals dominated by evolving morphology’)
• The refined hypothesis removes the overstrong “locked” claim and replaces it with a state-space model x(t) that permits partial decorrelation between TOA residuals and polarization through explicit timescales (OU processes) and optional change points. This makes the causal link testable and falsifiable: the model predicts bounded correlations/phase lags rather than perfect locking.
• Timing is treated generatively (photon likelihood / profile likelihood) with explicit phase-wander components, preventing compactness inference from being spuriously driven by nonstationary morphology.

Replacing ambiguous penalties with hierarchical priors + SBC (addressing prior-driven tightening)
• Energy and angular-momentum ‘constraints’ are implemented as probabilistic relations with hyperparameters and scatter, not hard penalties. This avoids artificially narrowing M“R/EoS posteriors.
• Simulation-based calibration is added as a mandatory validation deliverable: we will demonstrate (i) calibrated coverage for M“R under the full pipeline and (ii) a quantified ‘prior influence budget’ by rerunning with altered hyperpriors.

Systematics budget for polarization physics in the post-merger regime
• The polarized Comptonization module is upgraded to explicitly include Klein“Nishina effects, mild bulk flows, and a trans-dimensional hybrid electron option; each has a defined validity regime and stress tests.

  “ Magnetized/QED/vacuum polarization is bracketed with a parameterized birefringent operator and limiting models, and its impact on compactness is marginalized.
  “ Baryon-rich wind scattering is explicitly modeled as a screen that can rotate PA and increase PD, preventing misattribution of outflow-induced effects to GR compactness.
• Strong-field GR systematics are bounded by comparing two frame-dragging treatments (Hartle“Thorne vs Kerr-approx), and EoS claims are conditioned on stability under this swap.

Why EoS leverage remains plausible without overpromising
• The proposal’s EoS leverage is now conditional: it is claimed only for Tier B datasets where both polarimetric modulation and timing are informative and where compactness posteriors remain stable across the alternative forward models and priors. Otherwise, the outcome is correctly downgraded to constraints on spreading-layer/outflow physics and upper limits on polarization.
• This aligns the technical sophistication of the joint inference with a realistic detectability and systematics budget, directly meeting the reviewers’ mandatory directive.

Hypothesis: Superheavy nuclides (Z≥104) synthesized in a subset of neutron-star-merger ejecta produce a measurable, falsifiable distortion in late-time kilonova heating that arises from transport—not from the instantaneous-local-thermalization approximation—because spontaneous-fission fragments inject energy in a high-dE/dx, high-rigidity charged-particle channel whose deposition depth and time-delay depend differently on expansion, ionization state, and magnetic trapping than the beta/gamma channels that dominate actinide-only scenarios. The key claim is not that nuclear uncertainties are bypassed, but that (i) for any physically allowed superheavy source term consistent with broad priors on half-lives/branching and fission fragment spectra, the mapping from ‘injected decay power’ to ‘deposited heat’ is constrained by first-principles charged-particle slowing-down and pitch-angle scattering in expanding, partially ionized plasma, yielding a restricted family of deposition kernels; and (ii) this family produces a distinctive, testable pattern in multi-band light curves and nebular-phase spectra: a late-time color/bolometric evolution that requires simultaneously (a) enhanced charged-particle deposition relative to gamma deposition and (b) a temporally non-local heat release (delayed deposition tail) that cannot be matched, after marginalization, by actinide-only decay plus standard uncertainties (opacity evolution, gamma escape, ejecta stratification) or by smooth central-engine injection. We will demonstrate identifiability via Bayesian model comparison on synthetic and real datasets, explicitly propagating superheavy nuclear-input uncertainty through a kernel-operator formalism coupled to multi-D radiative transfer without double counting.
Plan: Step 1 — Ejecta ensemble (astrophysical state space, controlled):
1.1 Build a physically constrained ejecta ensemble using numerical-relativity-informed parameterizations: total dynamical+wind mass M_ej∈[10^-3,10^-1] M_sun, velocity field v(r,θ) with homologous expansion v∝r after t0≈10“100 s, and axisymmetric density ρ(r,θ,t)=ρ0(θ)(t/t0)^-3.
1.2 Enforce causality-respecting equations of state through priors on compactness and tidal deformability (consistent with GW170817-like constraints), but keep macroscopic ejecta parameters free in inference to avoid over-conditioning.
1.3 Generate thermodynamic trajectories (entropy s, electron fraction Ye, expansion timescale τ) using a low-dimensional surrogate that spans: (A) lanthanide-poor, (B) lanthanide-rich, and (C) low-entropy, very neutron-rich channels favorable to superheavy formation. Each trajectory set produces an abundance “source-term family” rather than a single yield.

Step 2 — Kernel formalism (operator definition + governing equations):
2.1 Define the decay injection field for channel c∈{α, β±e, γ, fission fragments}:
Q_c(x,t,E,Ω)=∑_i n_i(x,t) λ_i b_{i,c} S_{i,c}(E,Ω),
where n_i is number density of nuclide i, λ_i its decay constant, b_{i,c} branching ratio into channel c, and S_{i,c} the normalized emission spectrum.
2.2 Define the deposition operator K acting on Q to yield volumetric heat deposition:
\dot{q}_dep(x,t)=∑_c \int d^3x' \int dt' \int dE \int dΩ\; K_c(x,t; x',t',E,Ω)\, Q_c(x',t',E,Ω).
K_c is a Green’s-function kernel encoding transport, energy loss, and escape in an expanding medium.
2.3 Transport approximations by channel (chosen to be accurate at late times t≳0.5 d when non-locality matters):
• γ-rays: grey/energy-dependent Monte Carlo or deterministic ray tracing in homologous expansion with absorption+Compton effective opacity κ_γ(E) (including Klein“Nishina), yielding an escape probability P_esc,γ(t;E,θ). Deposit via Compton electrons locally where interactions occur.
• β-electrons/α: continuous slowing down with pitch-angle scattering; treat with a 1D-in-radius Fokker“Planck (or Monte Carlo) in momentum space including adiabatic losses in expansion.
• Fission fragments: treat as heavy ions with initial kinetic-energy distribution (two-hump TKE with prior), charge state Z_eff(v,ne,T), and stopping dominated by Coulomb collisions with free electrons + bound-electron corrections. Use a CSDA+straggling correction to compute stopping length ℓ_ff(E,t) in a plasma with evolving ionization.
2.4 Plasma state and ionization closure:
Compute electron density ne(x,t) from Saha or collisional-radiative steady-state using local temperature from radiative transfer iterations; where non-LTE is expected (nebular phase), adopt an ionization parameterization ne=χ_e ρ/(μ_e m_p) with χ_e(t,θ) inferred with priors informed by lanthanide recombination physics. Stopping powers use ne and Coulomb logarithm lnΛ(T,ne).
2.5 Magnetic-field trapping:
Include an effective pitch-angle scattering mean free path λ_mfp = η r_L, with r_L=p/(Z_eff e B). Parameterize comoving B(t)=B0 (t/t0)^-2 (flux freezing) with prior B0∈[10^3,10^6] G at t0=10 s (broad, covering weak to strong trapping). This modifies the charged-particle kernel by reducing radial streaming and increasing residence time; implement via diffusion coefficient D≈(1/3) v λ_mfp and solve a diffusion-loss equation in the comoving frame.
2.6 Numerical scheme and coupling without double counting:
Iterate radiative transfer and deposition in operator-splitting:
(a) Given T, ρ, composition → compute opacities and plasma ionization.
(b) Evaluate deposition kernel K_c and compute \dot{q}_dep(x,t).
(c) Feed \dot{q}_dep as the sole radioactive/decay heat source into multi-D radiative transfer (e.g., Monte Carlo packets or moment-based solver). Energy conservation enforced by tracking injected decay energy minus escaped energy (γ and, if allowed, charged-particle escape) equals integrated deposition + adiabatic losses; verify by global budget checks per timestep.

Step 3 — Superheavy nuclear-input uncertainty model (priors + propagation):
3.1 Abundance parameterization (explicitly not “bypassed”):
Represent superheavy contribution by a parametric mass fraction X_SH at reference time t_ref=7.5 h (motivated by Asset 2), with X_SH prior log-uniform over [10^-6, 3×10^-2]. Allow the rest of heavy species to follow an actinide-rich baseline abundance vector from a standard r-process network, but marginalize over actinide production via an “actinide boost” parameter A_act.
3.2 Decay-chain and fission priors:
For an effective superheavy ensemble, define hyperparameters:
• half-life scale τ_SH (log-uniform 10^3“10^7 s),
• spontaneous-fission branching b_sf (Beta prior favoring high b_sf but allowing low),
• mean total kinetic energy ⟨TKE⟩ (Normal prior 170±20 MeV),
• fragment charge/mass split parameter (symmetric vs asymmetric mixture weight),
• prompt γ fraction f_γ (uniform/weakly informative), and delayed β component amplitude.
These hyperparameters generate S_ff(E) and channel partitions feeding Q_c.
3.3 Fission recycling/yield degeneracy control:
Include a nuisance “recycling opacity/thermalization” parameter that captures secondary heating from fission daughters, but constrain it with nuclear-physics-informed bounds. This prevents falsely attributing generic extra heating to superheavy fragments.
3.4 Uncertainty propagation:
Draw joint samples of (X_SH, τ_SH, b_sf, ⟨TKE⟩, yield-shape params, B0, η, χ_e(t), ejecta structure) → compute K → generate light curves/spectra. Quantify which observables remain stable (low variance) across nuclear priors while differing between SH and actinide-only models.

Step 4 — Observables and identifiability (falsifiable tests):
4.1 Define the data vector:
• Multi-band photometry: L_b(t) in optical/NIR/MIR bands, with emphasis on t≳3“30 d where γ escape and charged-particle deposition diverge.
• Color evolution: e.g., (F200W“F444W) for JWST-like filters, plus optical“NIR colors where available.
• Bolometric reconstruction with uncertainty.
• If spectra exist: nebular-phase line blanketing/continuum slope constraints used as weak composition/temperature priors (not claiming unique line IDs for superheavies).
4.2 Synthetic-data retrieval experiment (mandatory):
Generate mock datasets from:
(A) actinide-only + standard thermalization,
(B) actinide-only + full transport kernel,
(C) superheavy+actinide with full kernel,
(D) actinide-only + alternative power source (magnetar-like smooth injection with L∝(1+t/t_sd)^-2) and dust/opacity evolution.
Adopt realistic cadence/SNR: nightly sampling days 0.5“10, then every 3“5 days to day 40; photometric precision 0.05“0.1 mag (ground+HST) and 0.02“0.05 mag (JWST).
4.3 Model comparison:
Use Bayesian evidence (nested sampling) to compute Bayes factors K=Z_SH/Z_noSH under full marginalization over ejecta parameters, opacity evolution (time-dependent lanthanide fraction proxy), γ opacity scaling, ionization, and magnetic trapping. Define detection criterion: ln K > 5 (strong evidence) and posterior mass on X_SH above a threshold.
4.4 Minimal detectable superheavy fraction:
From retrieval, report X_SH,min such that ≥90% of realizations achieve ln K>5 given the cadence/SNR above, as a function of (M_ej, v, κ(t), B0). This directly answers “minimum required mass fraction”.
4.5 Application to real events:
Validate on AT2017gfo and AT2023vfi/GRB230307A-like light curves (Asset 1 context): first show actinide-only models can fit early times; then test whether late-time data prefer transport-only corrections or require an SH component. Report posterior odds and whether X_SH is bounded or only upper-limited.

Step 5 — Robustness and degeneracy stress tests:
5.1 Opacity evolution: include κ(t,θ) parameterization tied to recombination and composition gradients; verify SH inference is not an artifact of κ(t) flexibility.
5.2 Freeze-out/non-LTE: include a nebular “inefficiency” parameter that reduces thermal coupling; test whether it mimics SH signatures.
5.3 Gamma escape: allow κ_γ scaling and non-grey effects; ensure SH preference is not simply reduced γ trapping.
5.4 Engine/dust: include alternative components (smooth central engine; dust extinction/emission) and compute Bayes factors with/without them.

Deliverables:
• A publicly documented kernel module implementing K_c with selectable MC/deterministic solvers and verified energy conservation.
• Posterior constraints (or upper limits) on X_SH and associated nuclear hyperparameters for benchmark kilonovae.
• A detectability map X_SH,min(M_ej,v,κ,B0,cadence/SNR) guiding future JWST/HST/ELT follow-up strategies.
Feasibility: 1) The proposal no longer claims to eliminate nuclear uncertainties; instead it separates (a) source-term uncertainty (yields, half-lives, branching, fragment spectra) from (b) transport physics that is comparatively well constrained. By casting deposition as an explicit operator K acting on an injection field Q, we can propagate nuclear priors transparently and identify which late-time observables are controlled mainly by transport (robust) versus by poorly known nuclear microphysics (non-robust).
2) The kernel is implementable with established methods: γ transport via standard Monte Carlo with effective interaction physics; charged-particle energy loss via CSDA/Fokker“Planck using stopping-power theory with explicit plasma/ionization inputs; magnetic trapping via a diffusion-loss formulation parameterized by B0 and η. These components are individually validated in adjacent contexts (cosmic-ray transport, SN γ deposition) and can be benchmarked against limiting analytic scalings (e.g., deposition fraction ∝ t^-2 for freely streaming γ in homologous expansion).
3) Identifiability is addressed head-on with falsifiable Bayesian model comparison under realistic degeneracies. The synthetic retrieval suite includes actinide-only transport, opacity evolution, γ escape, non-LTE inefficiencies, dust, and magnetar-like injection. The requirement is not a qualitative ‘mismatch’ but quantified evidence (Bayes factors) and a derived minimum detectable X_SH.
4) Empirical plausibility is anchored in the literature assets: (i) kilonovae with lanthanide-rich ejecta of order ~0.02 M_sun (Asset 1) provide the regime where late-time transport/escape effects are observable; (ii) nucleosynthesis studies indicate superheavy mass fractions can reach X_{Z≥104}~3×10^-2 at ~hours post-merger under favorable conditions (Asset 2), setting a physically motivated upper range for our priors; and (iii) reported late-time deviations from simple heating laws motivate testing transport-based deposition.
5) Even null results are publishable and decisive: if Bayes factors consistently disfavor SH contributions and yield only stringent upper limits on X_SH across events, this constrains r-process pathways and superheavy production in neutron-star mergers in a way that conventional instantaneous-thermalization light-curve fits cannot.

Hypothesis: A two-stage, energy-conserving kilonova inference framework that (i) treats the r-process “naked heating rate” q_naked(t) as a Ye“(s,τexp)-conditioned latent process with nuclear-data hyperparameters shared across events, and (ii) propagates that power through an explicitly parameterized, atomic-physics-anchored opacity model κ(Ye,T,ρ,λ) and a calibrated transport/discrepancy model, will yield falsifiable and unbiased constraints on lanthanide-poor ejecta (Mej, vej, Ye and X_Ln) despite geometry/viewing-angle uncertainty and radiative-transfer model mismatch. Mechanistically, identifiability comes from combining orthogonal observables that couple differently to the nuclear vs transport sectors: (a) late-time bolometric decline and band-to-band fading ratios constrain q_naked(t) and particle-dependent thermalization efficiencies f_i(t) once diffusion becomes sub-dominant; (b) contemporaneous color temperature and near-IR spectral line-blanketing/broad-feature indices constrain κ(λ) normalization and slope tied to lanthanide fraction and ionization state; and (c) photospheric radius evolution (from SED fits) constrains the diffusion time/geometry. The key advance over single-stage ‘effective heating’ fits is that κ(Ye,T,ρ,λ) is not allowed to flex arbitrarily: it is restricted to a minimal, physically interpretable basis with priors informed by atomic-structure calculations, while any residual mismatch between the semi-analytic diffusion module and Monte Carlo radiative transfer is captured by a separately calibrated discrepancy emulator. Degeneracy-breaking is therefore not asserted but pre-registered as a set of recovery benchmarks under controlled κ-flexibility, geometry/viewing-angle variation, and afterglow contamination. Finally, EOS-conditioning is included only insofar as it demonstrably increases expected information gain on (Mej, vej, geometry) and thus on thermalization/diffusion, quantified via Bayes factors and mutual-information increments relative to an EOS-agnostic baseline.
Plan: Step 0 — Define observables and identifiability targets (pre-registered).
0.1 Observables vector per event: multi-band photometry (optical→NIR), optional spectra, and SED-derived summary statistics with propagated errors: (i) pseudo-bolometric luminosity L_bol(t) (with bandpass-dependent missing-flux uncertainty); (ii) color indices (e.g., g−r, r−i, i−J, J−H, H−K) as functions of time; (iii) SED-inferred color temperature T_c(t) and photospheric radius R_ph(t) with covariance; (iv) spectral “lanthanide blanketing indices” B_Ln(t) defined as flux ratios across broad NIR troughs (e.g., F(1.05“1.15µm)/F(1.25“1.35µm), F(1.45“1.55µm)/F(1.60“1.70µm)) and a continuum slope index S_NIR.
0.2 Pre-registered identifiability benchmarks (reported as coverage and bias): recovery of injected (median posterior error / true) for Ye, X_Ln, Mej, vej in synthetic tests under: (A) κ-model “minimal” flexibility; (B) κ-model “expanded” flexibility; (C) variable geometry and viewing angle; (D) with/without afterglow contamination; (E) with RT discrepancy turned on/off. Passing criterion: posterior 68% credible intervals achieve ≥60% empirical coverage and <0.3σ mean bias for Ye and log10 X_Ln; and Bayes factor prefers two-stage model over single-stage by lnK>5 in controlled injections where q_naked differs (Asset-2 regime).

Step 1 — Data assembly and uncertainty model.
1.1 Curate multi-event dataset: AT2017gfo plus JWST-quality GRB-associated KNe (e.g., GRB 230307A/AT 2023vfi-like) with consistent photometric calibration. Store: fluxes, calibration covariance (zero-point + bandpass), cadence gaps, host extinction priors, distance posteriors, and afterglow-monitoring constraints.
1.2 Likelihood includes: correlated photometric calibration nuisance parameters per instrument, extinction with R_V prior, distance marginalization, and an additive afterglow component per band modeled as F_AG(ν,t)=A_AG(ν/ν0)^{-β} (t/t0)^{-α} with priors from contemporaneous X-ray/optical afterglow fits (when available) or weakly informative priors otherwise.

Step 2 — Minimal explicit κ(Ye,T,ρ,λ) parameterization (atomic-physics-anchored).
2.1 Adopt a two-component ejecta model (blue/lanthanide-poor; red/lanthanide-rich). For each component c∈{b,r}, opacity is expressed as a low-dimensional basis capturing (i) overall normalization, (ii) wavelength slope/line-blanketing strength, and (iii) ionization/temperature transition:
κ_c(λ,T,ρ) = κ0,c · [ (λ/λ0)^{p_c} ] · [1 + a_c · S( (T−T_ion,c)/ΔT_c ) ] · (ρ/ρ0)^{u_c}.
Here S(x)=1/(1+e^{−x}) is a smooth transition encoding recombination/ionization-driven opacity change; κ0,c is baseline grey level; p_c captures NIR vs optical tilt (proxy for line density); a_c sets amplitude of the opacity jump across ionization; u_c is a weak density exponent (kept tightly prior-constrained).
2.2 Tie opacity parameters to composition with explicit, minimal composition mapping:
log10 κ0,c = A0,c + A_Ln · log10(X_Ln,c/X_ref)  with A_Ln>0,
T_ion,c = T0 + T_Ln · log10(X_Ln,c/X_ref),
p_c = p0 + p_Ln · log10(X_Ln,c/X_ref).
Blue component has prior X_Ln,b centered at 10^{−6}“10^{−4}; red at 10^{−3}“10^{−1} (broad but separated).
2.3 Atomic-physics-informed priors: (A_Ln, p_Ln, T_Ln, κ0 ranges) are assigned priors from lanthanide/actinide line-expansion opacity calculations (e.g., existing Kurucz/Tanaka/Kasen-style tables). Practically: fit the above basis to a published grid of κ(λ,T,ρ) tables across representative compositions to derive prior means/covariances; use those as Gaussian priors with inflation factor (e.g., ×2) to remain conservative.
2.4 Forecast separability (mandatory): before fitting data, run Fisher / mutual-information forecasts on a representative cadence + filter set (optical + NIR + JWST bands) to quantify which epochs/bands constrain (κ0,p,T_ion) independently of q_naked hyperparameters. Deliverable: heatmaps of expected MI(κ-params; data|model) and MI(q_naked-params; data|model) vs time and wavelength; identify a minimal “anchor” set of bands/epochs needed (e.g., ≥1 optical band at t<0.7 d plus ≥2 NIR bands at t≈1“7 d, plus at least one spectrum or two NIR color indices around recombination).

Step 3 — Stage A: nuclear heating latent process q_naked(t).
3.1 Precompute r-process network library across (Ye,s,τexp) for both dynamical ejecta and disk winds; store channel-decomposed specific heating:
q_naked(t)= Σ_i q_i(t),  i∈{β,e−,ν̄ losses; α; fission; γ}.
Also store emitted particle energy distributions needed for thermalization.
3.2 Emulator: train a conditional normalizing flow or GP with monotonic/time-smoothness regularization to output {q_i(t)} on a log-time grid. Inputs: (Ye, s, τexp) plus nuclear hyperparameters θ_nuc (mass model index, β-strength scaling, fission yield family). Output uncertainty includes emulator error + nuclear-model ensemble variance.
3.3 Shared hyperparameters: θ_nuc are population-level parameters inferred jointly across events; event-level latents include Ye,c distributions (e.g., Beta distribution parameters per component) and mixing fraction between components.

Step 4 — Stage B: deposition + transport with explicit discrepancy calibrated to Monte Carlo RT.
4.1 Thermalization (energy deposition): for each particle channel i, use a physics-motivated efficiency function
f_i(t|Mej,vej,B_trap,χ_e)= [1 + (t/t0,i)^{n_i}]^{−1},
with t0,i ∝ (Mej/vej^2)^{1/2} scaled by composition-dependent electron density proxy χ_e (linked to Ye) and magnetic trapping parameter B_trap (log-uniform prior over a conservative range). Enforce 0≤f_i≤1 and correct asymptotics; allow small multiplicative nuisance per channel (≤20%) to account for microphysics uncertainty.
q_dep(t)= Σ_i f_i(t) q_i(t).
4.2 Baseline diffusion/SED model (explicit): use a two-component Arnett-style homologous-expansion diffusion model with time-dependent photosphere, but multi-band emission approximated by a diluted blackbody with wavelength-dependent attenuation via κ(λ,T,ρ):
L_c(t) computed from diffusion equation with t_d,c ∝ (κ̄_c Mej,c / vej,c c)^{1/2} and geometric factor g(Ω_c,θ_view).
Spectral flux: F_λ(t) = Σ_c [ (R_ph,c(t)^2 / D^2) · ζ_c(t) · B_λ(T_c(t)) · exp(−τ_eff,c(λ,t)) ],
where τ_eff uses κ_c(λ,T,ρ) and homologous density profile. ζ_c is a color-correction factor with tight priors from RT comparisons.
4.3 Transport/discrepancy emulator (mandatory): calibrate residuals against a grid of Monte Carlo RT simulations spanning (Mej,vej,X_Ln,geometry,θ_view) and representative heating inputs.
Define residual process in log-flux space per band:
Δ_m(t,band) = log F_RT − log F_diff,
modeled as a GP or low-rank basis with coefficients predicted by a trained emulator E_Δ(params). In inference, predicted flux is F_pred=F_diff·exp(Δ_m), with Δ_m marginalized using the calibrated uncertainty. This prevents attributing RT mismatch to q_naked or κ.
4.4 Geometry/viewing-angle: include a minimal anisotropy parameterization (two-zone solid angles Ω_b,Ω_r and viewing angle θ_view) with priors informed by NR/RT studies; geometry enters both diffusion time (via g) and effective column density in τ_eff. Crucially, discrepancy emulator is trained across the same geometry range.

Step 5 — EOS-conditioned priors and incremental value quantification.
5.1 EOS-conditioned prior construction: map EOS parameters (subject to causality + M_max constraints) to plausible ejecta priors using NR-calibrated surrogate relations (e.g., Mej_dyn(R1.4,q), vej_dyn(R1.4,q), disk mass) and to Ye support for disk winds. Include GW-inferred constraints when available; otherwise use broad EOS prior.
5.2 Mandatory incremental-value test: run paired analyses for each event and for the population: (i) EOS-agnostic priors; (ii) EOS-conditioned priors (with/without GW constraints). Report expected information gain ΔI on (Mej,vej,θ_view) and downstream ΔI on Ye and X_Ln; compute Bayes factors for models with EOS-conditioning vs without, ensuring complexity is justified.

Step 6 — Inference engine and diagnostics.
6.1 Perform joint Bayesian inference with hierarchical structure: event-level parameters {Mej,c, vej,c, Ye,c distribution, X_Ln,c, Ω_c, θ_view, afterglow nuisances}; population-level θ_nuc and κ-basis hyperparameters (with atomic priors). Sampling via NUTS with reparameterizations (non-centered for hierarchical parts) or SMC with amortized proposals.
6.2 Degeneracy quantification: compute posterior mutual information and correlation structure among {q_naked hyperparameters, κ parameters, Mej, Ye, X_Ln} and compare against a baseline single-stage effective-heating model. Pre-register that success means a statistically significant reduction in posterior dependence corr(q_naked,κ) and improved coverage in synthetic recovery.

Step 7 — Validation program (falsifiable, mismatch-resistant).
7.1 Synthetic injections: generate mock datasets from Monte Carlo RT (not from the diffusion model) across controlled scenarios matching the pre-registered benchmarks in Step 0. Recover parameters under (a) correct κ-basis; (b) expanded κ-basis; (c) misspecified κ-basis; and with/without discrepancy emulator. Report failure modes explicitly.
7.2 Real-event cross-validation: fit early-time-only data (e.g., t<1 d) and predict late-time (t>1 d and JWST epochs), focusing on the Asset-2 regime (Ye≳0.3, late times). Score predictive log-likelihood and calibration of credible intervals.
7.3 Nuclear stress tests: rerun with alternative nuclear mass models/fission yields; quantify which θ_nuc drive q_naked differences in the inferred Ye range; propagate to Ye and X_Ln posteriors.
7.4 Deliverables: (i) public emulator for q_naked and RT discrepancy; (ii) κ-basis fits and priors derived from atomic tables; (iii) posterior samples for each event; (iv) a “bias map” showing how common heating-rate mis-specifications bias Mej,vej,Ye when κ is constrained vs unconstrained.

Milestones (practical):
M1: κ-basis + atomic prior fit + MI/Fisher forecast deliverable.
M2: RT grid + discrepancy emulator with documented error envelopes.
M3: End-to-end hierarchical inference on synthetic RT injections meeting coverage criteria.
M4: Multi-event real-data analysis with EOS-value quantification (Bayes factors / ΔI).

Feasibility: Addressing the reviewer’s core concern—degeneracy-breaking being under-specified—the revised plan makes identifiability falsifiable and robust to mismatch in four concrete ways.

(1) Minimal explicit κ(Ye,T,ρ,λ) with atomic priors (degeneracy is not shifted into an unconstrained κ): κ is restricted to a low-dimensional, interpretable basis (normalization κ0, wavelength tilt p, and an ionization-transition term via T_ion and amplitude a) with composition-linked mappings to X_Ln. Priors are not hand-wavy; they are obtained by fitting this basis to published atomic-structure opacity tables and carried into inference as Gaussian priors (inflated conservatively). This directly answers the critique that a too-flexible κ would reintroduce the heating/opacity degeneracy.

(2) Orthogonal leverage is demonstrated before fitting (not asserted): Fisher/mutual-information forecasts on the actual cadence+filters quantify which epochs/bands/spectral indices constrain κ separately from q_naked. This operationalizes the claim that late-time slopes and NIR blanketing indices disentangle nuclear vs opacity/ionization effects, and it yields a concrete observing/inference requirement (minimum band/epoch set) rather than a qualitative argument.

(3) Transport approximation is specified and protected by a calibrated discrepancy model: the diffusion/SED module is explicitly defined (two-component Arnett-like diffusion plus wavelength-dependent attenuation). Crucially, any systematic mismatch relative to Monte Carlo RT is not absorbed by q_naked or κ because a residual emulator Δ_m(params,t,band) is trained on an RT grid and marginalized during inference. This prevents HMC/SMC from becoming overconfident and misattributing RT errors to nuclear-heating features—directly satisfying the mandatory directive.

(4) EOS-conditioning is justified quantitatively, not by appeal: the proposal commits to paired analyses (EOS-agnostic vs EOS-conditioned, with/without GW constraints) and reports Bayes factors and expected information gain on (Mej,vej,geometry) and downstream (Ye,X_Ln). If EOS-conditioning does not increase information in a measurable way, it will be removed or down-weighted; thus it cannot become a complexity add-on that drives results by prior.

Empirical and literature grounding (Assets 1“2): Asset 2 motivates explicit treatment of q_naked in the Ye≳0.3, t≳1 d regime where standard heating prescriptions bias inference; Asset 1 demonstrates that composition differences (lanthanide-poor vs rich) have observable consequences and that JWST-quality data are sufficiently constraining to meaningfully test these models, including heavy-element synthesis pathways. The revised framework translates these motivations into a constrained statistical architecture with pre-registered recovery benchmarks and an RT-calibrated discrepancy channel, making the central claim testable and resilient to model mismatch.

Hypothesis: Neutron stars retained in mass-segregated globular-cluster cores do not experience intrinsic, cluster-induced distortions of their X-ray pulsations; instead, the dense stellar environment introduces structured confusion and background mixing that bias periodicity detection and pulse-profile inference. We hypothesize that explicitly modeling this environment at the event level—via a PSF-based source“background“neighbor mixture model informed (but not dominated) by mass-segregation constraints—will reduce bias and variance in (i) periodicity detection statistics and (ii) neutron-star compactness (M/R) inference from pulse profiles. The mechanistic advance is that segregation-informed spatial priors improve identifiability only when they act to down-weight mis-localized or contaminating photons without overwhelming the likelihood; when this condition is met, degeneracies among hot-spot geometry, beaming, background fraction, and compactness are demonstrably reduced, whereas mis-specified segregation models are self-diagnosed through posterior predictive checks and Bayes-factor penalties.
Plan: Step 1: Event-level mixture model and calibrated detection statistic.
1.1 Construct an explicit photon-level likelihood for crowded cluster cores:
For each event i with arrival time t_i, detector position x_i, and energy E_i,
  L_i = sum_{k=1}^{N_src} π_k(r_k) P_PSF(x_i | k, E_i) P_spec(E_i | k) P_time(t_i | k, θ_k)
      + π_bg P_bg(x_i, E_i, t_i).
Here π_k are membership weights (summing to <1), P_PSF is an energy-dependent PSF mixing matrix (Chandra: sub-arcsec; NICER: large PSF), and P_time encodes periodic or null timing models.
1.2 Define a weighted periodicity statistic: a generalized weighted Z^2_n / H-test where weights w_i,k = π_k P_PSF(x_i|k,E_i) / (π_bg P_bg + sum_k π_k P_PSF). Derive the null distribution analytically under the mixture model and calibrate via Monte Carlo to control false-alarm probability under non-i.i.d. weights.
1.3 For NICER, marginalize over unresolved neighbors using Chandra-informed priors on source positions and fluxes; treat NICER photons as draws from the same mixture with collapsed spatial information.

Step 2: Segregation-informed but robust spatial priors.
2.1 Infer mass-to-light (M/L) gradients using a family of dynamical models (Jeans + distribution-function models) that explicitly marginalize over velocity anisotropy, binary heating, and retained black-hole fractions. Produce a hyper-posterior over remnant concentration rather than a single n_NS(r).
2.2 Translate this into weakly informative membership priors π_k(r,F) with variance inflation to prevent prior dominance; include a mis-specification parameter that broadens π_k if the data prefer less segregation.

Step 3: Pulse-profile inference with explicit identifiability tests.
3.1 Forward-model pulse profiles using GR ray tracing (Schwarzschild + Doppler; Hartle“Thorne for fast rotators) coupled to instrument response. Parameters: (M,R), spot colatitude/size, observer inclination, beaming law, background fraction.
3.2 EoS parameterization: spectral or piecewise-polytrope representation with hard constraints (TOV consistency, causality c_s<=c, thermodynamic stability, M_max>=2 M_sun). Use a precomputed TOV + ray-tracing emulator (Gaussian-process or neural surrogate) to ensure tractability.
3.3 Joint likelihood: L = Π_i L_i (mixture model) × L_pulse(M,R,geometry | weighted photons). Demonstrate identifiability by comparing Fisher matrices and posterior volumes with/without segregation-informed weights; require that likelihood curvature, not prior truncation, drives uncertainty reduction.

Step 4: Validation in the intended regime.
4.1 Synthetic crowded-field tests: inject known pulsations into real Chandra core images and NICER event lists with controlled blends; recover periods and (M,R) under correct and mis-specified segregation priors.
4.2 Robustness checks: vary anisotropy, BH retention, and binary fractions to quantify bias in recovered compactness.
4.3 External comparison: apply the same pipeline to field NICER pulsars artificially blended with cluster-like backgrounds to isolate the effect of confusion modeling.

Deliverables: (i) calibrated weighted periodicity catalog with controlled false-alarm rates, (ii) cluster-member pulse-profile constraints with demonstrated identifiability, (iii) open-source mixture-model timing framework.
Feasibility: The proposal directly addresses reviewer concerns by reframing the mechanism as bias/variance reduction under structured confusion rather than physical modulation of pulsations. Mass segregation enters only as a probabilistic prior that is marginalized over competing dynamical assumptions (anisotropy, BH retention, binaries), limiting model dependence. Identifiability is explicitly tested through simulation and curvature-based diagnostics, ensuring improvements arise from the likelihood, not prior volume restriction. Engineering details—PSF mixing matrices, weighted Z^2_n/H statistics with calibrated nulls, and a surrogate-assisted TOV+ray-tracing engine—render the hierarchical inference computationally tractable. Validation in synthetic crowded regimes directly exercises the new failure modes absent in field pulsar tests, making the approach both rigorous and realistic.

Hypothesis: In neutron-star X-ray binaries with a super-orbital period, the observed phase-locked evolution of X-ray flux, polarization degree (PD), and polarization angle (PA) is driven primarily by periodic changes in the line-of-sight“dependent Mueller-matrix transfer through a precessing/warped, partially covering Comptonizing medium (corona/wind/inner disk rim) that both (i) scatters photons from the boundary/spreading layer and disk and (ii) absorbs/occults them with energy-dependent partial covering. The key mechanistic claim is not that the transfer operator remains in a single idealized symmetry class, but that for the geometries relevant to super-orbital modulation the transfer can be parameterized by a low-dimensional set of time-varying geometric angles and optical depths, which in turn imposes testable structure on the harmonic content of the super-orbital Stokes vector.

Specifically, we posit a generative model in which the observed energy-dependent Stokes vector S(E,φ) = (I,Q,U) at super-orbital phase φ is the sum of (a) an intrinsic emission component from the neutron-star boundary/spreading layer plus disk with a bounded, physically parameterized intrinsic polarization field, and (b) a reprocessed component produced by single-to-moderate order Compton scattering in a tilted, precessing medium with optional azimuthal asymmetry. The periodic evolution of the medium’s orientation and covering fraction yields phase-dependent rotations and amplitude changes in Q and U through the Mueller matrix of scattering, while absorption/partial covering primarily modulates I and can indirectly enhance PD by preferentially suppressing the less-polarized component. We will test whether the measured super-orbital Fourier coefficients of I,Q,U are jointly consistent with this Mueller+covering generative model, and we will quantify (via identifiability analysis under IXPE response and count rates) which physical parameters are recoverable and whether harmonic truncation at n≤2 is justified for specific targets (or whether higher harmonics are demanded by asymmetry/multiple scattering).

This refined approach overcomes the reviewers’ concerns by replacing the prior ‘eigenmode’ narrative with a forward-folded, event-level inference pipeline: (1) a concrete Mueller-matrix transfer + partial covering model that predicts the phase-harmonic content of the full Stokes vector; (2) explicit modeling of intrinsic polarization from the boundary/spreading layer rather than assuming it is unpolarized; (3) joint spectral+polarimetric likelihood at the event level (or fully forward-folded) that avoids post-hoc subtraction of polarized components; and (4) a simulation-calibrated sensitivity/identifiability framework demonstrating which harmonics and parameters can be constrained given IXPE modulation factors, energy dispersion, and realistic backgrounds.

If retained, the EOS deliverable is explicitly scoped: geometry/covering/scattering constraints from super-orbital polarimetry will be used as informative priors on anisotropy/visibility parameters in existing pulse-profile likelihoods for a named target where such modeling is already mature (Her X-1), enabling a quantified forecast of compactness uncertainty reduction.
Plan: Step 0 — Target selection and observing configuration (deliverable: target-specific forecast table)
0.1 Select primary target Her X-1 (known super-orbital cycle with IXPE epochs spanning Main-on/Short-on; Asset 3). Secondary exploratory targets: GX 13+1 and Cir X-1 (demonstrated PA rotation/PD changes tied to spectral state/dips; Assets 1“2) if super-orbital ephemerides and phase coverage are adequate.
0.2 For each target, assemble ephemerides (super-orbital phase model with uncertainties) and define phase bins that balance harmonic recovery and S/N (initially 8“16 bins; revised after Fisher/mocks).
0.3 Acquire strictly contemporaneous broadband spectroscopy where available (NICER; NuSTAR if feasible) to constrain spectral components and absorption/partial covering that are degenerate with polarization in narrow IXPE band.

Step 1 — Explicit generative forward model (deliverable: written model equations + code module)
We model the observed Stokes vector at detector energy channel j and super-orbital phase φ as a forward-folded integral over true photon energy E:
1.1 Source model (true-energy domain):
S_src(E,φ) = S_dir(E,φ) + S_scat(E,φ).

1.2 Direct (intrinsic) component with parameterized intrinsic polarization:
S_dir(E,φ) = A_pc(E,φ) \times [I0(E,φ) \cdot (1, p0(E,φ)cos2ψ0(φ), p0(E,φ)sin2ψ0(φ))].
Here A_pc(E,φ) is a partial-covering/absorption operator acting on intensity (and, if needed, weakly on Q,U if dichroism is tested but default is scalar attenuation):
A_pc(E,φ) = (1 - f_cov(φ)) + f_cov(φ)\,exp[-N_H(φ)\,σ(E)]
with f_cov(φ)∈[0,1].
Intrinsic polarization is not forced to zero: p0(E,φ) is bounded by physically motivated priors (e.g., p0 ≤ 5% as a conservative envelope for electron-scattering atmospheres with GR light bending; tighter priors can be target-specific) and may include a low-order harmonic dependence:
p0(E,φ)=p0,0(E)+p0,1(E)cos(φ-δp) (optional, model-selected).
ψ0(φ)=ψ0,0 + ψ0,1cos(φ-δψ) (optional).

1.3 Scattered/reprocessed component via Mueller-matrix transfer through a precessing medium:
S_scat(E,φ)= \int dE'\; K(E,E'|kT_e,τ)\; M(\Theta(φ),\Phi(φ),g)\; S_seed(E',φ).
- K(E,E'|kT_e,τ) is an energy-redistribution kernel (single/multiple scattering approximation). For initial inference we use a controlled-order expansion: mixture of unscattered + once-scattered + twice-scattered terms with weights determined by τ (e.g., w0=exp(-τ), w1=τexp(-τ), w2=τ^2 exp(-τ)/2), and energy shifts parameterized by kT_e; this is calibrated/validated with Monte Carlo in Step 4.
- M is the linear-polarization Mueller matrix for Compton/Thomson scattering integrated over the medium’s angular distribution; it depends on the instantaneous scattering geometry described by a small set of angles:
\Theta(φ) = viewing-scatter angle distribution controlled by disk/corona tilt β, precession phase φ, and observer inclination i; \Phi(φ) encodes the rotation of the scattering plane on the sky.
- g is an asymmetry parameter controlling deviation from axisymmetry (g=0 axisymmetric; g>0 allows m=1 azimuthal brightness/optical-depth variation). This is the explicit mechanism for generating higher harmonics if required; g is tested via model comparison.
- S_seed(E',φ) is the seed Stokes vector from boundary/spreading layer + disk, sharing (p0,ψ0) parameterization but allowing a separate spectral shape.

1.4 Super-orbital geometry parameterization (precession/warp):
We do not assume perfect axisymmetry. We parameterize:
- β: tilt between medium symmetry axis and neutron-star spin (or binary angular momentum).
- i: inclination (prior from literature).
- φ0: super-orbital phase zero-point.
- g and χ_g: amplitude and phase of azimuthal asymmetry.
- τ(φ)=τ0+τ1cos(φ-δτ) (optional), and f_cov(φ)=f0+f1cos(φ-δf) (optional), enabling absorption/scattering modulation.

1.5 Prediction of harmonic content:
From the generative model we compute S(E,φ) and then Fourier coefficients up to n_max, but n_max is not fixed a priori; it is selected by evidence and by sensitivity forecasts. The ‘n≤2’ case is treated as a hypothesis to be tested (via Bayes factors) rather than a hard constraint.

Step 2 — Instrument-aware likelihood: event-level (preferred) or fully forward-folded (deliverable: validated inference pipeline)
2.1 Use IXPE event lists with per-event energy channel, time, and azimuthal scattering angle α. The standard polarimetric measurement equation is:
P(α|E,φ) ∝ 1 + μ(E) [ q(E,φ)cos2α + u(E,φ)sin2α ],
where μ(E) is the modulation factor and (q,u)=(Q/I,U/I) in the detector frame.
2.2 Build a joint likelihood over events that models simultaneously:
- spectral intensity through the IXPE ARF/RMF,
- background (with its own Stokes parameters, typically unpolarized but allowed a nuisance polarization with tight priors),
- phase dependence through the super-orbital ephemeris.
Concretely, maximize/posterior-sample:
ln L = Σ_events ln [ (R_src+R_bkg)^{-1} (R_src P_src(α|E,φ)+R_bkg P_bkg(α|E)) ],
with R_src predicted by forward-folding S(E,φ) through response matrices. This avoids post-hoc ‘subtract Comptonized Stokes’ operations and correctly handles energy-dependent μ(E) and dispersion.
2.3 Simultaneously fit NICER/NuSTAR spectra (where available) with a coupled spectral model sharing (kT_e, τ, N_H, f_cov, component normalizations), thereby breaking degeneracies between absorption, Comptonization, and polarization.
2.4 Sampling strategy: use nested sampling (for robust evidence/Bayes factors for harmonic/asymmetry order) or HMC where differentiable components permit; validate with posterior predictive checks in (α,E,φ) space.

Step 3 — Identifiability, sensitivity, and harmonic truncation justification (deliverable: recoverability maps + decision on n_max)
3.1 Fisher-matrix or simulation-based inference (SBI-lite) forecasts using realistic IXPE count rates per phase bin for each target, including μ(E), background, and planned exposure.
3.2 Evaluate parameter recoverability and degeneracy structure for θ = {β, τ0, τ1, δτ, kT_e, f0, f1, δf, p0,0(E) hyperparameters, ψ0,0, g, χ_g}.
Outputs:
- Which parameters are constrained (posterior width vs prior width).
- Which harmonic orders are detectable (expected S/N of Fourier coefficients of Q,U).
- Under what conditions higher harmonics (n≥3) become necessary (e.g., g>0, strong τ modulation, multiple scattering contributions).
3.3 Use Bayes-factor model comparison on mocks and then on data for:
- n_max ∈ {1,2,3,4},
- g=0 vs g free,
- τ(φ) constant vs modulated,
- intrinsic polarization constant vs modulated.
This directly answers the reviewer concern that n≤2 may be invalid in realistic media.

Step 4 — End-to-end validation with Monte Carlo and injection studies (deliverable: bias/coverage report)
4.1 Generate synthetic IXPE event lists using a Monte Carlo Compton scattering code (or validated public tool) for representative geometries:
- axisymmetric precessing slab/torus (baseline),
- warped/azimuthally asymmetric medium (g>0),
- varying covering fraction with energy-dependent absorption.
4.2 Forward-fold through IXPE response and reconstruct with the exact inference pipeline.
4.3 Quantify bias and frequentist coverage for key parameters (β, τ0, kT_e, f1, g) and for recovered Fourier amplitudes/phases of (Q,U).
4.4 Systematics stress tests:
- modulation factor calibration uncertainty (nuisance scaling),
- background mis-modeling,
- ephemeris/phase smearing.

Step 5 — Science products and cross-source synthesis (deliverable: physically interpretable harmonic atlas)
5.1 For each target, report posterior constraints on:
- geometry (β, i-consistency),
- scattering/absorption modulation (τ(φ), f_cov(φ), N_H(φ)),
- intrinsic polarization bounds (p0, ψ0) and whether data require intrinsic modulation.
5.2 Provide derived, directly observable predictions:
- phase offset between I(φ) minima (dips/occultation) and extrema in PD and PA,
- energy dependence of harmonic amplitudes (diagnostic of kT_e vs absorption).
5.3 Cross-source comparison in a common parameter space: e.g., (β, τ1/τ0, f1, g) versus observed PA rotation amplitude, connecting Assets 1“3 into a unified mechanism (dips/obscuration-enhanced PD; orbital vs super-orbital PA rotation; stable PA with PD increase in Short-on).

Step 6 — Optional downstream EOS linkage (explicit, scoped, forecasted) (deliverable: compactness-uncertainty forecast for Her X-1)
6.1 For Her X-1, connect inferred scattering/covering geometry to pulse-profile modeling by constraining nuisance parameters that encode anisotropy/visibility:
- prior on additional phase-dependent attenuation A_pc(φ) during Short-on,
- prior on scattering-induced polarization contribution and its phase relative to spin pulse.
6.2 Implement a joint/conditional analysis: use SOSFT posteriors as priors in an existing pulse-profile likelihood (public or in-collaboration), and forecast Δu/u (u=GM/Rc^2) improvement via Fisher propagation.
6.3 Success criterion: demonstrate (with mocks) a quantified reduction (e.g., ≥20% decrease) in compactness credible interval width under realistic IXPE+timing data, or else drop EOS deliverable and report only geometry/transfer constraints.

Feasibility: Empirical grounding from IXPE: existing IXPE results already show super-orbital/state-linked PD changes (Her X-1 Short-on vs Main-on; Asset 3) and large PA rotations correlated with hardness/dips (GX 13+1, Cir X-1; Assets 1“2). These behaviors are exactly the signatures expected when partial covering and scattering geometry change coherently with phase.

Why the revised method is technically credible:
- Fully specified forward model: We explicitly model S(E,φ) through a Mueller-matrix scattering operator combined with an absorption/partial-covering term, allowing non-axisymmetry via g and allowing τ and covering fraction to be phase-modulated. This removes the over-claimed ‘symmetry class’ argument and replaces it with testable, parameterized physics.
- Instrument-correct inference: We avoid biased “component subtraction” by fitting at the event level (α,E,φ) with μ(E) and full response folding, optionally coupled to NICER/NuSTAR spectra. This directly addresses the additivity/response concern for polarized mixtures.
- Identifiability is demonstrated, not assumed: Harmonic truncation (n≤2) is treated as a model-selection outcome supported by Fisher/SBI forecasts and Bayes factors under realistic IXPE count rates and backgrounds, rather than imposed as a symmetry rule that could be violated by multiple scattering/asymmetry.
- Intrinsic polarization is parameterized: Boundary/spreading-layer emission is allowed to carry nonzero polarization with physically bounded priors and optional low-order phase dependence, and we quantify how this uncertainty propagates into geometry/τ posteriors.
- End-to-end validation: Injection/recovery on fully forward-folded synthetic IXPE event lists provides bias/coverage guarantees and quantifies sensitivity to systematics (μ calibration, background, ephemeris smearing).

Practical feasibility:
- Data availability: Her X-1 has multiple IXPE epochs tied to super-orbital states; the same pipeline applies to dipping/hardness-modulated LMXBs when a stable super-orbital ephemeris and phase coverage exist.
- Computational tractability: The proposed kernel+Mueller parameterization is low-dimensional and can be evaluated rapidly, while Monte Carlo is reserved for calibration/validation rather than being required inside the sampler.
- Deliverables are scoped with go/no-go criteria: If identifiability forecasts show that certain parameters (e.g., g or τ1) are not recoverable for a given exposure, the model complexity will be reduced via evidence-based selection; similarly, the EOS linkage is retained only if a quantified compactness-information gain can be demonstrated for Her X-1.

Hypothesis: Neutron-star EOS stiffness determines the radial stratification ρ(r), pressure scale height H(r), and composition gradients that set the local Alfvén frequency spectrum ωA(r) and buoyancy coupling, which in turn control (a) the onset/saturation of Tayler-type non-axisymmetric instabilities and (b) the efficiency with which internal mixed poloidal“toroidal reconfiguration transmits (or fails to transmit) magnetic flux through the crust into the exterior. When the crust“magnetosphere matching is treated with an explicit, physics-based closure (elastic crust + resistive/Hall induction in the crust + resistive/force-free exterior), the resulting time-dependent external multipole content and effective dipole moment μeff(t) becomes a well-defined, gauge-invariant observable of the interior evolution rather than a tunable functional. We hypothesize that, at fixed accreted mass and spin, EOS-dependent stratification shifts the instability saturation into distinct regimes of μeff(t) amplitude and variability: (i) a “stable-channeling” regime with sufficiently persistent μeff(t) enabling coherent AMXP pulsations, (ii) a “variable-magnetosphere” regime with enhanced low-frequency μeff(t) fluctuations that elevate torque-noise/pulse-phase wander and modify disk truncation, and (iii) a “weak-external-field” endpoint after accretion/cooling that maps onto the RMSP dipole distribution. Because Hall drift and temperature-dependent resistivity introduce characteristic timescale/phase signatures that differ from pure EOS-driven changes (Hall: dispersive spectral transfer across ℓ; resistive: monotonic damping with known T scaling), jointly fitting μeff(t) statistics, truncation-radius variability, and radio/X-ray jet diagnostics can disentangle EOS stiffness from transport microphysics. The refined approach overcomes the reviewers’ identifiability concern by (1) replacing parameterized magnetosphere/jet closures with explicit crust-to-exterior matching that uniquely defines μeff(t), (2) including the leading non-ideal terms (Hall + η(T,Qi)) and crustal elasticity that control flux transmission during/after accretion, and (3) pre-registering sensitivity/degeneracy tests (Fisher/adjoint) that quantify which EOS density bands are constrained by which observables and under what sample size and systematic budgets.
Plan: Step 0 — Scope control and parameterization (pre-registered):
0.1 EOS parameterization (piecewise polytrope): Use a 3“4 segment piecewise-polytropic core joined to a fixed crust EOS. Inference parameters: {Γ1,Γ2,Γ3, ρ12,ρ23} (or equivalent pressure-at-fixed-density nodes), with hard priors enforcing thermodynamic stability and causality (0 < c_s^2 ≤ c^2) and Mmax ≥ 2 M⊙.
0.2 Transport/microphysics parameters (explicit, minimal but non-ideal):
  • Hall: include Hall term with electron number density ne(r) from the stratification; treat an uncertainty scale factor fHall multiplying ne (bounded prior) to represent composition/superconductivity uncertainty.
  • Resistivity: η(r,T)=η0(r;Qi) (T/T0)^α with α pre-set by dominant scattering regime; nuisance parameters: impurity parameter Qi (bounded) and normalization η0 scale factor fη.
  • Thermal evolution: a minimal, observable-informed T(t) model: outburst heating + exponential cooling with timescale τcool (nuisance, bounded by LMXB constraints), feeding η(T).
0.3 Crust elasticity (minimal coupling that matters for μeff): adopt a linear elastic crust with shear modulus μshear(ρ) and yielding threshold σbreak; implement as an elastic back-reaction on magnetic stresses at the crust (magneto-elastic induction), allowing plastic “slip” when σ>σbreak via a capped effective viscosity (one nuisance parameter controlling slip rate).
0.4 Observational nuisance set (explicit): distance d, inclination i, beaming factor bX (pulsations), radio radiative efficiency εR, and accretion-rate red-noise parameters (amplitude Aṁ, spectral slope β) for torque/pulse-phase noise.

Step 1 — Replace parameterized closures with an explicit, validated interior→exterior mapping:
1.1 Forward model domains (3-region coupling):
  (I) Interior + crust induction: evolve B with Hall+resistive induction on a fixed GR background (Cowling), using stratification from the EOS family.
  (II) Elastic crust: magneto-elastic coupling via stress balance at the crustal lattice; track shear strain energy and enforce yield criterion.
  (III) Exterior magnetosphere: solve axisymmetric+non-axisymmetric (low-m) resistive force-free electrodynamics (RFFE) or force-free with a thin resistive layer at the surface.
1.2 Boundary conditions at the stellar surface (explicit): enforce continuity of normal B and tangential E; allow surface currents consistent with the crustal electric field from Hall+η. This defines the exterior solution uniquely; μeff(t) is extracted from the asymptotic ℓ=1 component of the exterior field (spherical-harmonic decomposition) at r ≫ R.
1.3 Disk truncation and pulsation condition without free functionals:
  • Compute magnetospheric pressure balance using the exterior field solution at the equatorial plane: rm(t) from B_ext(r,θ=π/2,t) via standard balance with ṁ(t). No free “magnetization functional”; only nuisance accretion noise model.

Hypothesis: In Aql X-1 hard/intermediate states, variability in the Comptonization parameter y is not treated as a stand-alone “geometry marker” but as a measurable consequence of a coupled change in (i) coronal heating-to-cooling balance and (ii) coronal/disk geometry that is independently constrained by reflection and reverberation. Specifically: when the inner flow becomes more vertically extended (coronal height h increases) and/or the disk truncation radius Rin moves outward, the seed-photon energy density seen by the corona decreases, allowing higher kTe and/or lower τ to yield a higher y at fixed luminosity partition; simultaneously the reflection fraction Rrefl and reverberation lag spectrum shift in a predictable manner (via light-travel-time and solid-angle changes). We further hypothesize that any gamma-ray counterpart (0.1“300 GeV) arises only if non-thermal particle power is dissipated at a jet/outflow distance z sufficiently large that gamma“gamma opacity against the intense keV photon field is <1; thus, gamma-ray transparency is a deterministic function of (Lx, Rin, h, z, viewing angle) rather than a post-hoc veto. The refined approach overcomes reviewer-identified non-uniqueness by (a) explicitly parameterizing geometry (Rin, h, coronal size Rc, and jet dissipation distance z) and enforcing that the same geometry must jointly explain y, the high-energy cutoff and reflection spectrum, and reverberation/covariance timing; and (b) making gamma-ray emission and attenuation predictive through a physically parameterized emission zone and photon-field geometry. The falsifiable signature is a state-dependent mapping: increases in y must co-occur with (or precede, within a propagation lag model) measurable shifts in reflection fraction, iron-line broadening, and reverberation lags consistent with the inferred Rin/h; and any inferred gamma-ray flux must require z above a model-predicted minimum zmin(Lx,Rin,h) to satisfy tau_γγ(E,z)<1 while remaining consistent with X-ray cutoff constraints on kTe and the non-thermal electron fraction.

  - NuSTAR (3“79 keV): broadband continuum, high-energy cutoff constraints, and reflection (Fe line + Compton hump).
  - INTEGRAL (when available): extension above NuSTAR to strengthen cutoff/compactness constraints.
  - Fermi-LAT (0.1“300 GeV): unbinned likelihood light curves and epoch-stacked analyses; include upper limits as proper likelihood terms.

1.2 Products (per epoch and within-epoch segments matched to stationarity):
  - X-ray: (i) time-averaged spectrum, (ii) time-resolved spectra in segments, (iii) power spectral density, (iv) covariance spectra, (v) cross-spectral phase/time lags.
  - Reflection/reverberation constraints (mandatory):
    a) Reflection fraction Rrefl and iron line profile (broadening) from NuSTAR fits using a lamppost reflection model (e.g., relxilllp-like parameterization: Rin, h, i, AFe, ξion).

Step 2 (Coupled generative model; spectra + reflection + timing + LAT)
2.1 X-ray continuum module (physics-constrained):
  - Thermal component: disk + boundary layer (BL) parameterized such that Lth is tied to \dot{M} and geometry (with nuisance fcol, i, D).
  - Comptonization component: produces the hard tail with parameters (kTe, τ, fNT) and seed photon field from thermal component; define y(t)=4(kTe/mec^2)*max(τ,τ^2) as a derived quantity.
  - Compactness: ℓ = Lheat σT/(Rc mec^3); include pair balance prior/penalty by linking allowable (kTe, τ, ℓ) to avoid unphysical regimes smoothly (e.g., via an approximate pair-equilibrium manifold likelihood term rather than rejection).
2.2 Reflection module (geometry observable; breaks y“geometry degeneracy):
  - Use lamppost-style reflection with explicit h and Rin affecting emissivity and Rrefl; include iron-line broadening constraints and Compton hump.
  - Jointly fit NuSTAR spectrum with NICER where overlap exists; reflection parameters (h, Rin, i, AFe, ξion) are shared across instruments with Cinst.
2.3 Spectral-timing / state-space module (directionality):
  - Latent evolution: model \dot{M}(t) as a stochastic process (e.g., CARMA / OU mixture) driving thermal variability; allow a response transfer function to Comptonization and reflection.
  - Enforce causality through parameterized impulse responses rather than hard inequalities: transfer kernels have support only for t>0 and characteristic timescales tied to Rin and viscous/propagation times; reverberation lags tied to h/c.
  - Likelihood includes cross-spectra (complex) to fit covariance and phase lags, ensuring the “thermal leads power-law” behavior is not post-fitted but required.
2.4 Gamma-ray emission module with explicit z and target fields (addresses underconstrained pp/IC):

Maximum electron energy is constrained by requiring consistency with the X-ray cutoff/Comptonization tail (i.e., fNT cannot produce an X-ray excess inconsistent with NuSTAR).
    (ii) Hadronic pp: parameterize baryon loading via jet kinetic power fraction and a target column/interaction efficiency in a compact “dissipation zone” at distance z. Use a minimal, identifiable parameterization: fpp(z)=1-exp[-n(z) σpp lzone], where n(z) is tied to outflow mass rate (set by Ljet and assumed bulk Lorentz factor prior) and lzone is a fractional zone size (prior-limited). This avoids an unconstrained free n and size simultaneously.
  - Gamma-ray attenuation: compute τγγ(E,z) using the same disk+corona geometry (Rin,h,Lth) and apply exp(-τγγ) deterministically.
  - Prediction: LAT counts generated from convolving Fγ,esc(E) with LAT IRFs per epoch.

Hypothesis: Type II“like burst trains with QPOs can be explained by a small, explicitly enumerated class of relaxation oscillators in the inner accretion flow, but the driver is not assumed a priori to be an oscillating radiation-pressure shock. Instead, we hypothesize that (H1) shock-gated inner-flow oscillations, (H2) magnetospheric gating/propeller cycles, and (H3) disk thermal“viscous limit cycles occupy distinct, falsifiable regions in a joint observable space spanned by (i) νQPO“hardness and νQPO“energy-dependent rms relations, (ii) burst rise/decay scalings with dynamical vs viscous timescales, (iii) harmonic content and phase lags of the QPO through the burst phase, and (iv) recurrence“fluence“persistent-luminosity scaling. The central claim is that mechanistic identifiability becomes achievable when the inference model hard-codes each mechanism’s governing timescale, energy reservoir, and closure (including radiative source terms), and when the νQPO mapping is fixed to pre-registered, mechanistically derived relations rather than being left flexible. For the shock-gated hypothesis specifically, we adopt a GR-aware, radiatively cooled, vertically integrated inner-flow model with an effective (but validated) radiative-hydrodynamic jump condition; the burst sharp decay is predicted to track a post-shock advective drainage time tdec ~ tad(Rs), and νQPO is predicted to track the inverse of the same advective/infall time with a fixed scaling that implies a tight νQPO“tdec anticorrelation and a specific phase relation between flux and hardness. For neutron stars, we further hypothesize that a thermonuclear module is required (and statistically preferred) precisely in regimes where the peak-to-persistent luminosity ratio β controls cooling-tail detectability (as in IGR J17480-2446): the model will attribute non-cooling thermonuclear bursts to high persistent backgrounds and lower peak temperatures without misclassifying them as accretion-gated events. Peak luminosity is treated with mechanism-specific caps: a photospheric/local Eddington-limited cap with redshift and composition dependence for NS, versus a geometry/Comptonization-limited phenomenological cap for BH candidates. Finally, EOS inference is posed not as ‘tighter by default’ but as a hierarchical constraint that is only claimed when posterior predictive checks demonstrate that nuisance parameters (distance, anisotropy, color correction, composition) do not dominate the compactness posterior; otherwise the outcome is a principled null result that still yields robust burst-mechanism classification.

The decisive advance over phenomenological broken-power-law fitting is to replace the vague “energy“momentum conservation” claim with a minimal, closed set of coupled dynamical + radiative relations that map directly to the observed data products: (i) an X-ray spectral-energy-distribution model with time-dependent absorption (N_H) so that plateau/decline cannot be mimicked by hardness evolution; (ii) an afterglow closure relation tying X-ray flux, spectral slope, and temporal slope to blast-wave energy E_k, circumburst density profile (k=0 or 2), and microphysics (ε_e, ε_B, p); and (iii) a “radio inevitability” criterion for H_jTDE: for any parameter set that explains the X-rays, the model predicts a minimum late-time GHz radio flux (or a distribution over fluxes under informed priors) that must be consistent with detected radio emission or stringent upper limits. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that EP240408a and 2XMM J104608.7-594306 are not physically associated, and that any apparent spatial overlap arises from a combination of non-Gaussian, energy-dependent localization systematics and source confusion in crowded soft“X-ray fields. Crucially, we refine the original claim by explicitly delimiting *when* mechanistic emission priors can influence sky localization rather than only post-localization classification. The key mechanism is the coupling between photon energy and inferred centroid position induced by (i) EP/Swift energy-dependent PSF asymmetries, (ii) vignetting gradients across the field, and (iii) structured background. We posit that only in regimes where the expected centroid shift Δθ(E) is comparable to or larger than the statistical centroid uncertainty (σ_stat) can physically constrained spectral“temporal models materially alter p(sky|data). Under those conditions—quantified a priori—joint inference prevents overconfident associations that would otherwise require unphysical neutron-star (NS) parameters (e.g., violation of causal EOS compactness or magnetospheric power limits) or implausible jetted TDE energetics. The framework is explicitly symmetric: it can falsify non-association by confirming association if, and only if, the localization posterior overlap and astrophysical parameters jointly satisfy pre-registered physical and statistical thresholds.
Plan: Step 1: Quantify localization“spectrum coupling and define applicability regime.
1.1 Using EP and Swift/XRT calibration products, derive Δθ(E) = |∂θ_centroid/∂E| by forward-modeling the PSF and vignetting across the detector for representative off-axis angles of EP240408a. Compute the expected centroid shift for realistic spectral families (soft thermal, cutoff power law) and compare to σ_stat from photon counting.
1.2 Define a pre-registered applicability criterion: mechanistic priors are allowed to feed back into p(sky|data) only if max_E Δθ(E) ≥ 0.3 σ_stat or if background gradients induce comparable shifts, quantified via blank-sky fields.

Step 2: Instrument-aware hierarchical localization (localization improvement only).
2.1 Implement an event-level generative model p(data|sky, spectrum, bkg, attitude, calib) using EP/Swift event lists, GTIs, exposure maps, and attitude histories. Localization parameters are inferred jointly with spectral parameters, but without astrophysical priors beyond minimal spectral smoothness.
