Step 2 (Expanded latent-state model including non-ideal physics and geometry)
2.1 Latent state vector and dynamics (addresses reviewer points i“iii):
  - z(t) = {Δφ(t), Ab(t), Erec(t) impulses, σeff(t) (or κ(t)), α, noise hyperparameters}.
  - Dynamics: continuous relaxation + impulsive jumps:
    • dΔφ/dt = −Δφ/τtw + Σj Aj δ(t−tj)
    • dσeff/dt (or dκ/dt) = −(σeff−σ0)/τσ + Σj Bj δ(t−tj)
    • Impulse times tj are the burst times (radio) plus a latent set that can generate X-ray-only events; inference allows for radio-censored impulses.
  - α treated as a marginalized nuisance parameter with informative priors (e.g., isotropic prior in cos α, optionally tightened by pulse-profile constraints); not fixed.
2.2 Observation models (radio + torque + X-ray) with explicit degeneracy handling:
  (A) Radio burst point process and morphology
  - Conditional intensity: λ(t) = λ0 + g1(Erec, Δφ, Ab) × g2(σeff/κ) × g3(geometry), where g2 encodes plasma-loading suppression/enhancement of coherent emission.
  - Burst fluence distribution: p(F | Erec, κ, geometry) as a heavy-tailed distribution (e.g., truncated power law or log-normal mixture) with parameters linked to Erec.
  - Include propagation nuisance: scattering timescale τsc, spectral index, and detection completeness Fmin via an explicit selection function S(F, W, DMerr).

  (B) Spin-down/torque likelihood with non-ideal control
  - Replace “torque = FFE(Δφ,Ab,Bdip,α)” with a resistive/loaded magnetosphere torque surrogate:
    • N(t) = N0(Bdip, α) × [1 + aΔ T(Δφ, Ab) + aσ H(σeff/κ) + a× cross-terms]
    where T encodes twist-driven current changes and H encodes conductivity/pair-loading effects that alter open-field current and effective spindown.
  - Timing model: phase φ(t) integrated from ν(t), with red timing noise modeled as a power-law Gaussian process (or state-space CARMA) added to torque, plus discrete micro-glitch terms allowed but penalized by priors.
  - Crucially: the model allows torque perturbations without requiring unique mapping from closed twist to open current; identifiability comes from joint constraints with radio and X-ray and from injection studies.

  (C) X-ray spectral and pulse-profile likelihood
  - Use an RCS-informed emulator to map {Δφ, Ab, τRCS, kT, Γ} → energy-resolved pulse shapes and spectra.
  - Explicitly allow partial decoupling: Δφ inferred from X-ray profile/spectral hardening may not perfectly track torque if σeff/κ changes dominate open-field behavior—this is the core robustness feature.

    • resistivity/conductivity proxy (σeff) or pair-loading proxy (κ)
    • obliquity α (at least a coarse grid)
  - Use force-free as a baseline but include resistive prescriptions (FFE→RFFE interpolation) to emulate dissipative, pair-producing conditions; calibrate surrogate outputs against published resistive magnetosphere results where available.
  - Enforce physical constraints: ∇·B=0, energy conservation budget (Poynting flux + dissipation), and monotonicity/causality constraints on how σeff affects torque.

Step 3 (Mandatory identifiability + feasibility package: end-to-end injections, forecasts, and Bayes factors)

3.4 Bayes-factor forecast for burst“torque association (reviewer-mandated)
  - Define model comparison:
    • M1: bursts associated with torque steps with lag distribution p(Δt)
    • M0: bursts independent of torque perturbations (torque variations from red noise + σeff/κ drift)

Hypothesis: Z-source low-mass X-ray binaries traverse discrete, branch-dependent thermodynamic regimes in the neutron-star boundary layer (BL) and immediately adjacent inner disk, and these regime changes deterministically control (i) the centroid frequencies and (ii) the quality factors (Q) of the dominant timing components through a small set of physically coupled quantities: BL scale height H, effective sound speed c_s, radiative diffusion time t_diff, and shear/viscous damping time t_visc. We hypothesize that across the Z track (HB→NB→FB) the BL transitions between (A) a radiation-pressure-supported, optically thick spreading layer with short t_diff and strong radiative damping (low Q) and (B) a thinner, higher-c_s, less radiatively damped layer (higher Q), and that each observed QPO family corresponds to a pre-registered eigenfamily of this BL+transition-layer system. 

To address reviewer concerns about degeneracy/mode misidentification, we refine the forward model to a ‘two-zone’ BL framework with explicit eigenfamilies and a strict mode-identification protocol: (1) a compressible BL/slab supports acoustic p-modes and a buoyancy-modified branch (g/p mixed) whose eigenfrequencies scale with c_s/H and whose Q is set by radiative diffusion (t_diff) plus turbulent viscosity (alpha_BL); (2) a narrow transition layer (TL) connecting BL to the inner disk supports a low-frequency corrugation/tilt mode whose restoring torque depends on radiation pressure and effective gravity g_eff. The key mechanistic claim is that X-ray colors constrain (tau_es, T_e, y, and the BL luminosity fraction f_BL), which in turn uniquely determine H, c_s, and t_diff (via radiative equilibrium and hydrostatic balance), thereby fixing both frequency and damping for each eigenfamily. 

Radio: rather than an asserted ‘charge-starvation’ criterion, we posit a minimal, testable magnetospheric circuit + opacity gate. The same BL regimes modulate the pair injection rate into the closed magnetosphere (through gamma-gamma pair production in the BL Comptonizing field) and the baryon/wind loading near the light cylinder (through radiation-driven outflow). Coherent GHz bursts can escape only when (i) the magnetospheric potential drop exceeds a pair-screening threshold (insufficient pair supply) AND (ii) the surrounding plasma satisfies explicit propagation constraints (free“free absorption, induced Compton scattering, and Raman/strong scattering limits). This yields a quantitative, falsifiable prediction: a narrow region(s) in color-color space where (a) pair screening is weak enough for a reconnection/maser-like event and simultaneously (b) the surrounding optical depths at ~0.4“1.6 GHz are <1, producing a state-conditioned fluence distribution observable by CHIME; otherwise, the proposal defaults to an upper-limit/opacity-limited constraint on any intrinsic burst rate.

Finally, we downgrade equation-of-state (EoS) claims to a forecastable, conditional deliverable: the program aims to measure compactness-dependent redshift/Keplerian scalings only insofar as identifiability simulations show a non-negligible Fisher information on (M,R) after marginalizing over BL systematics, distance, inclination, and instrument calibration. The refined approach overcomes the reviewers’ concerns by (i) pre-registering eigenfamilies and branch-wise mode-ID rules, (ii) adding explicit damping physics and nuisance/systematic parameters to avoid overconfident posteriors, (iii) performing end-to-end simulation-based calibration (SBC) to demonstrate identifiability and realistic uncertainty, and (iv) conducting formal model comparison against leading competing timing models (relativistic precession / diskoseismic / TL models) to prevent confirmation-by-regularization.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration, competing models, and data products (before any fitting)
0.1 Pre-register QPO component definitions and mode-ID rules (per source):
  - Components: kHz QPO pair (nu_u, nu_l) where detected; HBO (15“60 Hz), NBO (~4“8 Hz), FB noise/peaked noise (if present), and broadband break(s).
  - Operational extraction: multi-Lorentzian decomposition with priors on centroid ordering and width hierarchy; energy-dependent rms trends recorded.
  - Mode-ID mapping (fixed before inference):
    * nu_u: BL acoustic p1 mode (radial order n=1) or its GR-redshifted equivalent.
    * nu_l: BL acoustic p2 or mixed g/p branch depending on Q and energy dependence; selection rule uses Q ratio and phase-lag sign when available.
    * HBO: TL corrugation/tilt mode frequency set by g_eff and radiation torque (branch-dependent).
    * NBO: BL thermal“radiative relaxation oscillation (limit-cycle linearization) with frequency ~ (2π t_th)^-1, where t_th is a radiative/viscous thermal time.
  - If any component violates pre-registered discriminants (below), it is flagged ‘unmodeled’ and excluded from BL-only claims (used only in model comparison).
0.2 Competing timing models for formal comparison (per source):
  - Model B (disk/relativistic precession): RPM-style mapping of nu_u, nu_l, HBO to orbital, periastron-precession, and nodal-precession frequencies with phenomenological damping.
  - Model C (diskoseismic): inner disk g- and c-modes tied to spectral state proxies.
  - Model D (transition-layer model): TL oscillations with Compton cloud parameters.
  - All models share the same observation model (bandpass, PDS fitting) and the same systematics terms.

Step 1 — Target selection and synchronized multi-mission state definition
1.1 Targets: Sco X-1, GX 17+2, GX 5-1, Cyg X-2 (Z sources). Controls: high-dynamic-range atolls (e.g., 4U 1608“52, Aql X-1 when coverage allows) to test whether inferred BL regimes and mode mapping are Z-specific.
1.2 State coordinates: define a standardized color-color plane using response-folded spectral families, but additionally define a scalar arc-length coordinate s along the Z track with branch labels (HB/NB/FB) via a mixture-of-curves segmentation algorithm with uncertainty (posterior over branch assignment). This reduces sensitivity to instrument bandpass differences.
1.3 Timing extraction: for each segment (16“128 s, multiple energy bands), compute PDS; fit with multi-Lorentzian model returning posterior samples for (nu_i, Q_i, rms_i) and covariance.
1.4 Cross-instrument calibration: explicit nuisance parameters for effective area tilt and energy-scale offset per mission; carry into inference so M,R are not driven by calibration artifacts.

Step 2 — Refined BL+TL forward model with explicit identifiability controls
2.1 Two-zone thermodynamic structure:
  - Zone 1 (BL/spreading layer): hydrostatic balance with radiation pressure fraction beta_rad = P_rad/(P_rad+P_gas); scale height H determined by local flux F and g_eff; radiative diffusion time t_diff ~ (tau_es H)/c; electron temperature T_e and tau_es constrained by Compton y = (4kT_e/m_ec^2) max(tau_es, tau_es^2).
  - Zone 2 (TL): thickness H_TL and effective density set by continuity with disk inner boundary; includes a parametric radiation torque term.
  - Shared parameters per state (s): (tau_es(s), T_e(s), f_BL(s), beta_rad(s), alpha_BL(s), H_TL(s)) plus global (M,R) and distance/inclination nuisance (D, i).
2.2 Eigenfamily solver and damping (explicit):
  - Solve for BL acoustic eigenmodes using a stratified slab with radiative diffusion: ω_n ≈ nπ c_s/H × (1+GR corrections) and damping rate γ_n = γ_rad + γ_visc where:
    * γ_rad derived from diffusion approximation: γ_rad ∝ (t_diff)^-1 × Φ_n(beta_rad) (mode-structure factor computed numerically);
    * γ_visc ∝ alpha_BL Ω_K (with Ω_K evaluated at an effective radius near R, including redshift).
  - TL corrugation/tilt mode: ω_TL set by (g_eff/H_TL)^{1/2} times a radiation-torque modifier Ψ(beta_rad, f_BL).
  - Thermal“radiative relaxation mode (NBO): ω_th ≈ (t_th)^-1 with t_th computed from local thermal content / radiative cooling using the same F, tau_es, and T_e.
  - Output: predicted (nu_u, Q_u), (nu_l, Q_l), (nu_HBO, Q_HBO), (nu_NBO, Q_NBO) as functions of state parameters and (M,R).
2.3 Observation model linking spectra→colors (emulator with physical closure):
  - Build a differentiable emulator trained on radiative transfer grids (Comptonization + reflection + disk) that maps (tau_es, T_e, f_BL, beta_rad, i) to instrument-folded colors.
  - Enforce energy conservation: L_tot(s)=η(M,R) \dot{M}(s) c^2 and L_BL(s)=f_BL(s) L_tot(s); priors on η from GR binding energy.
  - Include spectral degeneracy breakers: use multi-band colors (soft, hard, very-hard) and, where available, spectral fits (e.g., NICER soft band) to constrain tau_es“T_e.

Step 3 — Identifiability/forecasting (MANDATORY) with end-to-end simulations
3.1 Simulation design (per source):
  - Generate synthetic Z tracks with realistic scatter in colors and timing based on the forward model, spanning HB/NB/FB with branch-dependent parameter trajectories.
  - Inject competing ‘contaminant’ timing components (disk/magnetospheric) at controlled amplitudes to test robustness of mode-ID rules.
  - Apply instrument response folding (RXTE, NICER) and timing measurement noise (segment length, deadtime approximation), producing mock PDS and mock colors.
3.2 Identifiability metrics:
  - Parameter recovery: posterior contraction and bias for (tau_es(s), T_e(s), beta_rad(s), alpha_BL(s), H_TL(s)) and global (M,R). Require <0.3σ mean bias across SBC trials.
  - Mode-ID fidelity: confusion matrix between true and inferred component↔mode assignment using pre-registered discriminants (e.g., predicted energy-dependence of rms, Q-vs-frequency scaling with t_diff).
  - Degeneracy audits: compute local Fisher information and posterior correlation structure; demonstrate that centroids+Q together break tau_es“alpha_BL degeneracy (since Q depends on γ_rad+γ_visc while ν depends mainly on c_s/H).
3.3 Forecast for (M,R) improvement (MANDATORY):
  - Compare three scenarios: (i) timing-only, (ii) colors+timing with full systematics, (iii) colors+timing plus external priors (distance, inclination, known constraints).
  - Quantify expected reduction in area of the (M,R) credible region relative to baseline literature priors; pre-specify a success threshold (e.g., ≥25% area reduction for at least one source or for a hierarchical combination).
  - If threshold not met in simulations with realistic systematics, re-scope deliverable to constraints on BL physics (alpha_BL, beta_rad trajectories) rather than EoS.

Step 4 — Inference architecture (simplified to address redundancy critique)
4.1 Replace the operator-learning layer with a strictly auxiliary diagnostic, not a driver:
  - Primary inference uses the forward BL+TL model directly.
  - A local response operator K_s is computed post hoc from the posterior predictive Jacobian (d timing / d s) to summarize branch-resolved sensitivities; it is not learned as an additional flexible model. This removes the risk of Jacobian regularization baking in incorrect derivatives.
4.2 Hierarchical Bayesian fit:
  - Per-source state functions: represent tau_es(s), T_e(s), beta_rad(s), alpha_BL(s), f_BL(s) with branch-wise Gaussian processes constrained to be smooth within branches and allowed sharp changes at vertices (HB/NB/FB junctions) via change-point priors.
  - Global parameters: (M,R) with EoS-family prior only if forecasts show information gain; otherwise use broad physical priors.
  - Likelihood: joint over colors, timing (nu,Q,rms with covariances), with calibration nuisance parameters.
4.3 Model comparison:
  - Compute WAIC/LOO and Bayes factors (where stable) among Model A (BL+TL) and Models B“D.
  - Pre-register decision rule: BL-only claim supported only if Model A decisively outperforms others across branches and if residual structure shows no systematic branch-dependent misfit.

Step 5 — Radio: minimal magnetospheric circuit + opacity gate; otherwise upper limits
5.1 Magnetospheric pair-screening submodel (minimal, testable):
  - Pair injection rate \dot{N}_±(s) estimated from BL photon field using a parametric gamma-gamma efficiency tied to y and T_e (calibrated to plausible magnetar/NS magnetosphere scalings; treated with wide priors).
  - Magnetospheric potential drop ΔV(s) computed from a rotating dipole with accretion-modified open flux fraction; reconnection/burst ‘attempt rate’ λ_int(s) increases with ΔV and decreases with \dot{N}_± (pair screening).
  - This produces an intrinsic burst energy distribution: dN/dE ∝ E^{-α} exp(-E/E_max(s)), with E_max(s) tied to available magnetic energy in the reconnecting volume and ΔV.
5.2 Propagation/escape (critical, reviewer-requested):
  - Compute free“free optical depth τ_ff(ν,s) through a radiation-driven wind/BL atmosphere parameterized by mass-loss \dot{M}_w(s) ∝ L(s) and density profile n_e(r) ∝ \dot{M}_w/(r^2 v_w).
  - Compute induced Compton scattering constraint τ_ind(ν,s) using brightness temperature inferred from E and emission size; require τ_ind<1 for escape.
  - Compute multipath/scattering broadening and absorption consistent with dense environments; define an overall escape probability P_esc(ν,s)=exp[-(τ_ff+τ_ind+τ_scatt)].
  - Observable burst rate: λ_obs(s)=λ_int(s)×P_esc(ν,s).
5.3 CHIME detection model:
  - Fold λ_obs(s) through CHIME exposure, beam response, and fluence threshold distribution to predict detection counts and a fluence CDF per state.
  - If the escape model predicts P_esc≪1 for all plausible parameters, pivot deliverable to: stringent state-resolved upper limits on λ_int(s) given non-detections (propagation-limited inference).
5.4 Validation strategy:
  - State-conditioned search windows: use contemporaneous X-ray state estimates (NICER where possible) to test whether detections (or upper limits) correlate with predicted high P_esc×λ_int regions.

Step 6 — Deliverables and go/no-go criteria
6.1 Go/no-go (post-forecast):
  - Proceed with (M,R)/EoS inference only if SBC+forecast shows meaningful information gain under systematics.
  - Proceed with intrinsic radio-burst claims only if escape model admits non-negligible P_esc in some Z-track region; otherwise publish state-resolved upper limits and propagation constraints.
6.2 Primary outputs:
  - Branch-resolved maps over the standardized color plane: inferred (tau_es, T_e, beta_rad, alpha_BL, f_BL), predicted (nu_i, Q_i), and residuals.
  - Model-comparison results vs competing timing models.
  - Radio: predicted (or constrained) λ_obs(s) and fluence distributions with explicit absorption/induced-scattering bounds.
Feasibility: Boundary-layer model realism/identifiability: The revised plan removes the single-layer ambiguity by adopting a two-zone BL+TL structure with explicit eigenfamilies and damping channels. Crucially, we commit to end-to-end simulation-based calibration (SBC) and Fisher/posterior correlation audits demonstrating that the chosen parameterization can recover both centroids and Q factors across branches, or else it will transparently fail and trigger scope reduction. Mode misidentification risk is mitigated by pre-registered component definitions and discriminants (Q“ν scaling with t_diff, branch-dependent continuity, and energy-dependent rms/lag behavior when available), plus explicit ‘unmodeled component’ handling.

Radio speculation control: The qualitative trigger is replaced by a minimal circuit-plus-opacity gate that produces quantitative, testable predictions: an intrinsic attempt rate (pair-screening controlled) multiplied by an escape probability derived from free“free and induced Compton constraints in a radiation-driven wind/BL environment. This directly addresses the reviewer’s point that non-detections may be non-informative: under this framework, non-detections constrain either λ_int(s) (if P_esc is non-negligible) or they constrain the environmental opacity (if P_esc is forced small), both of which are scientifically interpretable. The model outputs an explicit fluence distribution folded through CHIME sensitivity and exposure, enabling likelihood-based inference rather than post hoc association.

Operator-learning redundancy: The response-operator concept is retained only as a posterior diagnostic derived from the physics model’s Jacobian, eliminating an extra flexible layer that could introduce overconfidence or bake-in incorrect derivatives.

EoS/MR claims moderated and forecasted: The revised proposal includes a mandatory forecast quantifying how much (M,R) can improve after marginalizing over calibration, distance/inclination, and BL/disk systematics, with a pre-specified success threshold and a contingency plan that re-scopes to robust BL-physics constraints if compactness information is too weak. This directly addresses the critique that Z-source systematics often dominate and prevents overstated nuclear-physics deliverables.

Empirical grounding: Asset 2 supports the existence of branch-structured, tightly linked color“timing behavior in Z sources and high-dynamic-range atolls, motivating a branch-resolved physical mapping rather than purely empirical correlations. Asset 1 motivates targeted CHIME analyses for compact binaries but, in this revision, CHIME is used within an explicitly propagation-limited framework to ensure that both detections and non-detections yield informative constraints.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the precursor emission and the observed quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in GRB 211211A are produced by discrete, tidal-stress“driven yielding episodes in the crust of a magnetar component during the last ~10^2“10^3 s of inspiral, and that the QPO frequencies trace excitation of a specific magneto-elastic mode family (torsional crustal modes hybridized with core Alfvén continua) whose eigenfrequencies and damping are controlled by the internal magnetic field and equation of state (EoS). The proposal resolves the reviewers’ identified bottlenecks by replacing the ill-posed notion of “nonlinear Love-number modification” with a rigorously closed forward-modeling stack: (i) an explicitly stated inspiral/trajectory framework (PN/EOB orbital driver) matched to (ii) a GR perturbation calculation on a TOV background to compute the time-dependent tidal stress field inside an elastic, dissipative crust up to a physically defined yield criterion, which then seeds (iii) a reduced magneto-elastic excitation and magnetosphere-coupling model that predicts both the timing/energetics of precursor energy release and the QPO frequency evolution. This architecture produces falsifiable, phase-resolved predictions linking orbital phase → crustal failure cadence → released energy → mode frequencies, and yields discriminants against non-tidal alternatives (e.g., accretion-powered precursors or jet-instability QPOs) through the predicted chirp-like evolution and orbital-phase locking of the QPOs and failure episodes.
Plan: 1) Choose a single, internally consistent spacetime/trajectory framework and matching conditions.
   1.1 Inspiral driver: use an EOB (effective-one-body) or 3.5PN TaylorT4 orbital phase evolution including standard adiabatic tides (linear) and spin-orbit terms up to a stated order (baseline: 3.5PN point-mass + leading-order tidal phase corrections). This provides r(t), Ωorb(t), and the companion’s tidal field multipoles as functions of time.
   1.2 Stellar background: construct a non-rotating (or slow-rotation Hartle“Thorne at O(χ)) TOV magnetar model for each candidate EoS. Fix M, R, and crust thickness from the EoS; treat the internal magnetic field as a parameterized axisymmetric configuration that enters the magneto-elastic step (below) rather than the background metric.
   1.3 Matching: compute the external quadrupolar tidal field from the PN/EOB trajectory and match it to the GR even-parity l=2 metric perturbation boundary condition at the stellar surface (standard tidal perturbation matching). Deliverable: a verified r(t), Ω(t) pipeline consistent with the GR perturbation boundary conditions.

2) Compute a time-dependent tidal stress/strain field in the crust (abandon “Love-number modification”).
   2.1 Linear GR tidal response (pre-yield): solve the static/low-frequency GR perturbation equations for the l=2 tidal deformation on a TOV background to obtain the strain/stress tensor distribution in the crust as a function of instantaneous tidal field amplitude Eij(t). Use the “instantaneous equilibrium” approximation while explicitly validating it against the orbital timescale (Ωorb) and crustal shear-wave crossing time; state the regime of validity (late inspiral but before strong dynamical tide resonance).
   2.2 Elastic constitutive law: implement an isotropic Coulomb solid crust with shear modulus μ(ρ, T, Z, impurity) using standard microphysical fits; include temperature dependence through a prescribed thermal profile and include a Maxwell visco-elastic element (Kelvin“Voigt or standard linear solid) to model dissipation and stress relaxation on a timescale τvisc.
   2.3 Yield criterion and dissipation: adopt a von Mises yield criterion with breaking strain εbreak(T, impurity) (baseline range 0.01“0.1) and implement plastic flow/heating when σVM exceeds σyield. Parameterize plastic dissipation via an effective plastic viscosity ηpl and compute local heating ΔT from dissipated work, updating μ(T) self-consistently (magneto-thermal feedback at reduced order).
   2.4 Output: a time series of yielding events defined by when/where σVM crosses threshold, yielding episode duration, dissipated energy Eheat, and a “failure patch” size and location on the crust. Deliverable: orbital-phase“tagged failure catalog and energy budget.

3) Specify the magnetic coupling pathway with a concrete reduced magneto-elastic model and QPO identification.
   3.1 Mode family selection (operational QPO mapping): identify the QPOs with torsional (axial) magneto-elastic oscillations: crustal torsional shear modes coupled to core Alfvén continua in the presence of an internal B-field (Bint). This is the only mode family carried forward in the baseline model.
   3.2 Eigenmode computation (reduced model): compute torsional magneto-elastic eigenfrequencies and damping using a 1D/2D axisymmetric model: (i) elastic crust with μ(ρ,T), (ii) magnetized fluid core with Alfvén speed vA(B,ρ), and (iii) coupling at the crust-core boundary. Use established magneto-elastic wave equations in the Cowling approximation (δgμν=0) as the baseline; justify this approximation for frequency predictions (QPOs) versus GW phase modeling.
   3.3 Excitation by failure: map each failure patch to an impulse/forcing term that injects energy into the torsional displacement field (initial condition Δξφ localized to the patch, amplitude set by released elastic + magnetic stress energy). Compute resulting mode amplitudes and the expected QPO spectrum and its time evolution as Ωorb increases and the failure patch distribution changes.
   3.4 Magnetosphere and radiation channel: couple surface torsional motion to a force-free magnetosphere using a boundary driving prescription (twist angle Δψ(t) proportional to surface shear). Parameterize the conversion from injected magnetospheric energy to observable gamma-ray precursor fluence with an efficiency εrad and beaming factor fb; treat these as nuisance parameters in inference.
   3.5 Output: predicted QPO frequencies (and their drift), quality factors (damping), and precursor light-curve morphology (timing/fluence) tied to orbital phase and failure episodes.

4) Forward model: explicit mapping from orbital phase → failures → emission/QPOs, plus discriminant predictions.
   4.1 Scaling relations (deliverable-ready): derive and numerically validate scalings:
       • Failure cadence: Δt between failures decreases with increasing tidal field ∝ r(t)^{-3}; predict a monotonic acceleration of event rate approaching merger.
       • Failure timing/phase locking: events cluster near specific orbital phases if the stress pattern is dominated by l=2 geometry; predict correlation with orbital phase (modulo precession if included).
       • QPO frequency set: fQPO ≈ f_torsional(Bint,EoS,crust thickness) with weak dependence on orbital frequency, but with possible stepwise changes when heating/plasticity changes μ(T).
       • Energy per event: Eevent ≈ ∫(σ:Δε)dV over failure patch plus magnetic untwisting energy; predict a bounded distribution with a high-end cutoff controlled by εbreak and patch size.
   4.2 Discriminants vs competing scenarios:
       (D1) Orbital-phase locking: tidal model predicts precursor sub-structure/QPO onset times tied to Ωorb(t); accretion/jet-instability models generally do not predict phase-locked repetition tied to a calculable inspiral chirp.
       (D2) Frequency clustering: torsional magneto-elastic QPOs should appear in discrete bands tied to EoS/Bint, rather than broadband or drifting purely with jet dynamics.
       (D3) Precursor-to-merger timing relation: predicted window of activity begins when σVM first reaches yield at a calculable separation; this provides a falsifiable relation between precursor lead time and binary parameters.

5) Inference framework with explicit likelihood, nuisance parameters, and identifiability tests.
   5.1 Data model: use observed precursor light curve (event times, durations, fluences) and QPO measurements (frequencies, uncertainties, quality factors, time stamps). Optionally incorporate constraints on distance and host environment as priors.
   5.2 Likelihood:
       • Timing: Poisson (or clustered point-process) likelihood for failure events with rate λ(t|θ) predicted by the stress/yield model.
       • Fluence: lognormal likelihood for event fluences given Eevent with nuisance parameters εrad and fb; marginalize over (εrad, fb).
       • QPOs: Gaussian likelihood in measured fQPO(t) with model frequencies from eigenmode solver; include a mixture model for multiple mode identifications if needed.
   5.3 Priors: EoS prior from maximum mass and causality; Bint prior broad log-uniform (10^14“10^16 G internal), εbreak prior informed by crust simulations; distance/beaming priors from GRB population constraints.
   5.4 Synthetic recovery / identifiability: generate mock datasets from the forward model across a grid of (EoS, Bint, εbreak, τvisc) and perform Bayesian recovery to demonstrate which parameters are identifiable and which are degenerate with εrad/fb. Deliverable: identifiability report and required data quality thresholds.

6) Validation and robustness checks.
   6.1 Consistency checks: verify stress field against Newtonian elastic limits in weak-field regime; verify energy conservation between tidal work, dissipated heat, and injected mode energy.
   6.2 Sensitivity tests: vary thermal profile, impurity parameter, and viscosity model; quantify impact on predicted failure cadence and QPO damping.
   6.3 Extension path (optional, not baseline): incorporate dynamical tide resonances if the orbital frequency approaches relevant mode frequencies; include slow rotation and precession only after baseline closure.

Deliverables (explicit): (A) a phase-resolved failure catalog as a function of EoS/Bint; (B) a QPO frequency atlas tied to magneto-elastic mode family with damping predictions; (C) a precursor forward model generating light curves conditioned on inspiral parameters; (D) a full Bayesian inference code with synthetic recovery demonstrating identifiability; (E) at least one falsifiable discriminant (orbital-phase locking + frequency banding) benchmarked against non-tidal alternatives.
Feasibility: 1) Closed, approximation-driven modeling stack (addresses internal inconsistency).
   The proposal now commits to a single coherent architecture: PN/EOB provides the inspiral trajectory and tidal field; GR perturbations on a TOV background provide the interior tidal stress field; nonlinearity enters only through a physically defined yield/plasticity law, not through redefined Love numbers. Magnetic/radiative complexity is confined to a reduced magneto-elastic + force-free coupling model whose assumptions are stated (Cowling approximation for mode frequencies; parameterized radiative efficiency), avoiding gauge inconsistencies from mixing “fully relativistic” claims with under-defined PN dynamics.

2) Love-number issue resolved (addresses critique ii).
   Love numbers remain in their proper role (linear response descriptor) and are not modified to represent nonlinear failure. Instead, the key computed quantity is σVM(t,r,θ) in the crust and its crossing of a specified yield surface, including dissipation and heating—an executable route to failure predictions.

3) Magnetic coupling made operational (addresses critique iii).
   Crust failure is mapped to a concrete excitation mechanism for a specified QPO-producing mode family: torsional magneto-elastic oscillations (crustal torsional modes hybridized with core Alfvén continua). The proposal explicitly computes eigenfrequencies/damping and uses a boundary-driving prescription to connect surface shear to magnetospheric twist and radiative output, with εrad and beaming treated as nuisance parameters rather than assumed constants.

4) Observables operationalized with falsifiable predictions (addresses critique iv).
   The forward model provides explicit outputs: (i) event timing distributions and their orbital-phase dependence; (ii) precursor fluence distributions with a calculable high-end cutoff; (iii) QPO frequency bands and stepwise evolution tied to μ(T) changes from dissipation. Discriminants are stated: orbital-phase locking and discrete frequency banding are expected in the tidal-failure model but not generically in accretion-powered or jet-instability scenarios.

5) Inference defined and testable (addresses critique v).
   A likelihood is specified for timing, fluence, and QPO frequencies with clear nuisance parameters (distance, beaming, radiative efficiency) explicitly marginalized. Identifiability is not assumed; it is demonstrated via synthetic recovery tests to show which combinations of (EoS, Bint, εbreak, viscosity) can be constrained by the available observables.

6) Empirical and literature anchoring.
   The physical pathway is directly grounded in the established tidal-force“induced crust breaking framework for magnetars in compact binaries (Asset 2) and the broader motivation to connect compact-object interaction dynamics to periodic or quasi-periodic high-energy/radio phenomenology (Asset 1 provides contextual support that compact binaries can imprint periodic activity). The proposed deliverables are therefore not speculative extensions but controlled refinements that convert the concept chain into a quantitative, falsifiable, and computationally tractable program.

Hypothesis: In atoll-source neutron-star LMXBs, the observable IXPE polarization degree and angle variability across accretion states and dipping intervals can be robustly decomposed into three physically distinct contributions—(i) polarized electron scattering in a hydrostatic boundary/spreading layer (BL/SL) anchored to the neutron-star surface, (ii) weakly polarized or depolarized emission from the disk and corona, and (iii) state- and phase-dependent attenuation and scattering in a *dynamical*, photoionized dip/wind absorber. We hypothesize that enforcing this regime separation, while coupling a minimal but self-consistent polarized radiative transfer solver for the BL/SL to a photoionization model for the atmosphere and an independent dynamical slab model for the dip material, resolves the key identifiability bottlenecks highlighted by reviewers. Specifically, N VII (supported by O VIII/Ne IX) acts not as a unique depth ruler but as a *consistency tracer* of the ionization parameter and column in the atmosphere and wind; when combined with energy-resolved PD/PA that are dominantly sensitive to the BL/SL scattering optical depth, latitude extent, inclination, and GR light bending, this framework enables a data-driven isolation of the compactness-sensitive polarization signatures. By integrating spin-induced oblateness, Doppler boosting, and polarization parallel transport as first-class parameters, and by explicitly marginalizing over disk/corona polarization contributions, the refined approach yields M/R constraints that are likelihood-driven rather than prior-dominated, while remaining computationally feasible and empirically testable with current IXPE and grating data.
Plan: Step 1: Regime-separated source and data selection.
1. Select one benchmark atoll source with existing or proposed deep IXPE exposure (>500 ks) and confirmed dipping behavior (e.g., GX 13+1“like systems), coordinated with XMM-Newton RGS or Chandra HETGS and NICER.
2. Segment data into three regimes: (a) non-dip banana state, (b) non-dip island state, and (c) dip intervals. Only regime (a,b) are assumed to have a hydrostatic NS atmosphere/BL; regime (c) explicitly relaxes hydrostatic balance for the absorber.
3. Extract IXPE energy-resolved Stokes (I,Q,U) spectra (2“8 keV) per regime; extract grating spectra focusing on N VII Lyα/edge and corroborating O VIII/Ne IX lines; derive hardness“intensity and timing diagnostics to label state.

Step 2: Explicit emission decomposition with state-dependent priors.
1. Implement a three-component emission model:
   (i) Boundary/spreading layer (BL/SL): thermal“Comptonized emission tied to the NS surface; primary source of polarization via electron scattering.
   (ii) Accretion disk: multi-temperature disk emission with low intrinsic polarization (<1“2%), angle fixed to disk plane.

  • plateau duration window (e.g., 60“100 d consistent with ECSN models),
  • late-time magnitude limits/detections translated into bolometric bounds with nuisance parameters for extinction and bandpass corrections.
1.2 Crab energetics likelihood: L_Crab(θ) from filament proper motions + spectroscopy:
  • priors/likelihood for M_ej and E_k,
  • constraints on homologous expansion age consistency.
1.3 Non-radioactive power separation: include a pulsar spin-down luminosity model L_psr(t; φ_psr) with priors from Crab pulsar present-day P, \dot P and braking index, propagating uncertainty into late-time luminosity bounds rather than assuming negligible/known contribution.
1.4 Inner-heating constraints: incorporate 44Ti non-detection/upper limits and nebular ionization constraints into L_heat(θ) to bound late-time internal energy injection that could masquerade as gamma deposition.
1.5 Geometry/asymmetry constraints: include low-order morphological constraints (e.g., dominant asymmetry axis from line-of-sight velocity maps) as weak priors on the dipole direction n_k, without overinterpreting small-scale structure.

Step 2 — Forward model architecture (transport + minimal composition/mixing)
2.1 Homologous ejecta model:
  • Spherically averaged density profile ρ0(v) chosen from a compact family (e.g., broken power-law with fixed outer slope, free break velocity tied to E_k and M_ej).
  • Radioactivity distribution: an IGE-rich component with radial support controlled by v_mix. Implement as X_Ni(v) ∝ exp[−(v/v_mix)^α] truncated at v_max, normalized to M_Ni.
  • Optional Ni dipole: X_Ni(v,Ω)=X_Ni(v)[1 + a1_Ni Y10(Ω·n_Ni)], with |a1_Ni| constrained to keep X_Ni≥0.
2.2 Gamma-ray deposition model:
  • Monte-Carlo gamma transport for 56Ni→56Co→56Fe including Compton scattering + photoabsorption in expanding ejecta.
  • Output deposition fraction f_dep(t; θ) and emergent gamma luminosity. Bolometric model: L_bol(t)=f_dep L_decay(M_Ni)+L_psr(t; φ_psr) with nuisance thermalization efficiency for pulsar power.
2.3 Nuclear-physics feasibility (soft, not dominating): apply broad, simulation-informed priors on M_Ni and v_mix consistent with ECSN freeze-out (low-entropy, neutron-rich) but explicitly quantify prior sensitivity; do not impose high-dimensional NSE constraints that can dominate sparse data.

Step 3 — Explicit recoil model decoupled from Ni (addresses key critique)
3.1 Total momentum anisotropy parameterization:
  • Define the ejecta momentum dipole P1 = p1 (2E_k M_ej)^{1/2} in direction n_k.
  • Enforce recoil via momentum conservation: V_k = −P1 / M_rem, optionally plus a bounded neutrino-anisotropy term V_ν with a conservative prior range informed by CCSN theory.
3.2 Joint inference: infer (R,P,global,φ_psr) simultaneously from the combined likelihood L = L_hist × L_Crab × L_heat × L_geom.
3.3 Simulation calibration of Ni“momentum correlation:
  • Assemble a calibration dataset from published multi-D ECSN simulations (and, if needed, a small number of iron-core low-energy models) extracting: (a) 56Ni dipole moment a1_Ni, (b) total momentum dipole p1, (c) ejecta energy and mass.
  • Fit a hierarchical relation p1 ~ Normal(β0 + β1 a1_Ni + β2 v_mix + …, σ_corr) with wide priors, allowing weak/no correlation.
  • Use this only to *interpret* inferred a1_Ni relative to p1, not to force p1 from Ni.

Step 4 — Formal identifiability demonstration using the *actual* SN 1054/Crab likelihood
4.1 Fisher-information / local identifiability:
  • Compute the Fisher matrix (or expected information) for θ at the posterior mode using numerical derivatives of summary observables (late-time luminosity bounds, deposition fraction at key epochs, energetics constraints).
  • Report which parameter combinations are constrained (eigenvalue spectrum), demonstrating that only {M_Ni, v_mix, p1 (and possibly a1_Ni)} are identifiable.
4.2 SBI-based identifiability stress test with real-data summaries:
  • Use simulation-based inference (e.g., neural posterior estimation) over θ but with the *same* censored/interval likelihood structure as SN 1054 historical constraints.
  • Perform posterior shrinkage tests: show posterior contraction relative to priors for identifiable parameters; demonstrate non-contraction for non-identifiable ones and remove them from the model.
4.3 Prior-dominance quantification:
  • Re-run inference under at least two materially different priors for v_mix and p1 (broad vs simulation-informed) and report sensitivity; require qualitative conclusions (e.g., long-delay enhancement in NS binaries) to be robust.

Step 5 — Population synthesis target change: ECSN → NS“NS / NS“BH delay-time prediction (mandatory directive option i)
5.1 Post-SN binary mapping:
  • Use impulsive mass loss + vector kick V_k with isotropic n_k (or weakly informed by Crab axis) to compute survival probability and post-SN (a,e).
  • Compute GW inspiral delay times via Peters equations.
5.2 Mixture model of supernova channels:
  • Build a two-channel kernel: ECSN-conditioned kick distribution from this work + an iron-core CCSN kick baseline from literature.
  • Convolve with cosmic star-formation and metallicity evolution to obtain merger-rate vs redshift for NS“NS and NS“BH.
5.3 Controlled ablation study for falsifiability:
  • Vary common-envelope efficiency, natal spin assumptions, and metallicity-dependent winds across standard ranges.
  • Demonstrate which observables remain discriminating: (i) fraction of long-delay mergers, (ii) local merger rate normalization given calibration, (iii) eccentricity at formation (where relevant), and (iv) mass distribution shifts from ECSN-formed NS masses.
5.4 Comparison to GW constraints:
  • Use LVK population posteriors for NS“NS/NS“BH (rates, masses, spins where available) to compute hierarchical likelihoods for mixture fractions and validate whether an ECSN component is supported or constrained.

Step 6 — Validation deliverables and falsification
6.1 Crab/SN1054 self-consistency checks:
  • Ensure inferred M_Ni and v_mix predict late-time heating consistent with 44Ti limits and nebular ionization.
  • Ensure (M_ej, E_k) match filament kinematics.
6.2 External cross-checks on modern ECSN candidates:
  • Apply the reduced-parameter inversion (M_Ni, v_mix) to a small set of ECSN-like or low-luminosity II-P events with late-time photometry to validate the transport model and inferred mixing depths.
6.3 Simulation agreement:
  • Verify inferred p1 implies kick magnitudes consistent with the low-kick expectation for ECSNe (if supported) while allowing the data to reject that (via broad priors) if required.

The inverse problem is reduced to a small parameter set whose imprint on observables is direct: M(56Ni) sets the decay power scale; v_mix controls the gamma-ray optical depth evolution (via column density seen by decay sites); and p1 sets the recoil via momentum conservation. We will formally demonstrate which parameters are constrained using (i) Fisher-information eigen-analysis and (ii) SBI posterior contraction under the actual censored historical-light-curve likelihood, addressing the underdetermination critique.

2) The kick inference is no longer logically tied to 56Ni as a proxy. The model fits an explicit, low-order *total* mass“velocity anisotropy parameter (p1, direction), and only then evaluates whether 56Ni anisotropy correlates with momentum anisotropy using multi-D ECSN simulations. This removes the unjustified assumption that Ni-bearing plumes dominate linear momentum while still allowing the hypothesis to be tested quantitatively.

3) The multi-messenger extension is made physically coherent by targeting NS“NS/NS“BH populations, where ECSN outcomes (NS formation, low explosion energy, potentially low kicks) directly control binary survival and delay times. This avoids the weak transfer argument to BH“BH. Falsifiability is protected via a controlled ablation study over binary-evolution uncertainties, isolating which GW observables (especially the long-delay fraction) remain diagnostic after marginalization.

4) Empirical anchoring is strengthened by leveraging Asset 2’s first-principles ECSN light-curve expectations (shock breakout/plateau/tail behavior and low 56Ni yields) and by aligning the SN1054 interpretation with Crab energetics and pulsar spin-down constraints. The forward model uses explicit gamma-ray transport (not an unconstrained emulator), but only to propagate the reduced set of physically meaningful parameters into observable bounds.

5) Deliverables are reproducible and discriminating. The proposal outputs (a) a minimal posterior over {M_Ni, v_mix, p1} for SN 1054, (b) a calibrated (or explicitly weak) Ni“momentum correlation from multi-D ECSN simulations, and (c) an ECSN-conditioned kick kernel for NS“NS/NS“BH delay-time predictions with uncertainty and ablation quantified—each component falsifiable against Crab constraints, modern ECSN-like events, and GW population statistics.

Hypothesis: The apparent universal broken power-law in repeating-FRB burst energy functions (break near ~10^38 erg in FAST catalogs for FRB 20201124A and FRB 20220912A) is not primarily a radiative-selection artifact but the statistical signature of a strain-limited, self-organized critical (SOC) failure process in a magnetar crust whose maximum avalanche size is set by nuclear-physics-controlled yielding and crust thickness (EoS dependent). The observed frequency-magnitude relationship emerges from SOC avalanche dynamics, while the break energy corresponds to the largest connected failure patch permitted by the crust’s elastic correlation length under strong magnetic stresses. We will test this with a structurally novel methodological adaptation: replace broken-power-law fitting and hierarchical selection modeling with a physics-closed, event-sequence inversion that (i) learns a latent, time-dependent stress field (a hidden-state variable) governed by a constrained stochastic differential equation (stress loading + threshold-triggered avalanches) and (ii) maps stress drops to radio energies through a magnetospheric conversion functional constrained by energy conservation and Alfvén crossing-time causality. This ‘SOC-state-space inversion’ uses burst times + energies jointly (not energies alone) to identify whether a true maximum avalanche scale exists, and directly translates the inferred maximum correlated failure area into neutron-star crust and EoS constraints. Plasma turbulence is treated as an independent, measurable propagation layer that perturbs polarization/RM statistics but cannot by construction generate a hard maximum avalanche size in the latent stress dynamics; thus, the method mechanistically discriminates intrinsic SOC break physics from propagation effects.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Build a SOC state-space generative model for crustal stress.
- Latent state: a global or multi-zone stress variable x(t) representing magnetically loaded shear stress in the crust.
- Loading: dx/dt = \dot{x}_load + \sigma_x dW_t (slow drive), with \dot{x}_load constrained by magnetar spin-down/magnetic evolution timescales.
- Failure rule: when x(t) exceeds a yield threshold x_c (distributed across zones), an avalanche occurs, producing a stress drop \Delta x drawn from an SOC kernel with finite-size cutoff determined by the maximum correlated rupture area A_max.
- Crucial adaptation: A_max is not a free statistical break; it is parameterized as A_max = f(R, \Delta R_crust, \mu, \sigma_break, B) with explicit dependence on crust thickness \Delta R_crust and shear modulus \mu from candidate EoS, and breaking strain \sigma_break from nuclear pasta/microphysics priors.

2.2 Map stress drops to radio burst energies with physical closure.
- Radiated energy model: E_radio = \eta \; E_elastic(\Delta x, A, \Delta R_crust), where E_elastic is computed from elastic theory (shear energy density integrated over rupture volume), and \eta is a bounded conversion efficiency constrained by magnetospheric energetics.
- Causality constraint: impose a hard prior that burst duration/energy release is limited by Alfvén crossing time t_A \sim L/v_A and magnetospheric impedance, ruling out unphysical combinations of (A, \Delta x, E_radio) for given B and density profile.
- This creates a mechanistic guarantee: an apparent energy break can only arise from a finite A_max (intrinsic) or from a change in \eta(E) that is itself bounded by magnetospheric physics, not from arbitrary piecewise power-law fitting.

2.3 Observation model that is propagation-aware but non-degenerate with the intrinsic cutoff.
- Use a detection model based on measured widths and telescope sensitivity: P(detect|E_radio, W, \nu) from radiometer equation and pipeline thresholds.
- Incorporate plasma-turbulence effects only through independently constrained nuisance parameters that modify observed width/polarization (e.g., scattering broadening, depolarization), with priors anchored by RM structure-function/turbulence proxies (Steps 1.3“1.4).
- Structural novelty: propagation enters only the measurement channel; the latent SOC dynamics are inferred primarily from joint timing+energy statistics (including waiting-time distributions and energy“waiting-time correlations), which turbulence cannot reproduce.

2.4 Inference engine: constrained sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) with physics-projectors.
- Implement particle filtering / particle MCMC for the thresholded jump-SDE with avalanches, using “physics-projectors” that reject particles violating (i) energy conservation bounds between E_elastic and E_radio, (ii) causality via t_A, and (iii) EoS-causality (sound speed < c) and maximum-mass constraints for the adopted EoS family.
- Fit both sources jointly with shared microphysical hyperparameters (e.g., \sigma_break distribution, \eta prior family) and source-specific B-field/environment parameters.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Synthetic recovery with controlled ground truth.
- Generate mock catalogs from the SOC state-space model across a grid of (\Delta R_crust, \sigma_break, B, A_max) and add turbulence-like measurement distortions consistent with RM SF statistics. Verify unbiased recovery of A_max and EoS-linked parameters.
- Show that broken-power-law fits (baseline) spuriously recover a “universal break” even when A_max differs, whereas the SOC inversion recovers the correct source-to-source variation (or true universality).

3.2 Mechanistic discrimination tests.
- Compare models: (M1) intrinsic SOC with finite-size cutoff A_max; (M2) SOC without finite-size cutoff but with stronger propagation/detection truncation; (M3) purely phenomenological broken power law.
- Use Bayes factors / marginal likelihood via SMC, plus posterior predictive checks on: waiting-time distribution, clustering, energy“waiting-time coupling, and high-energy tail behavior.

3.3 Nuclear-physics/EoS translation.
- From posterior on A_max and elastic parameters, infer credible regions for \Delta R_crust and \mu, mapping onto EoS families consistent with causality and 2 M_sun constraints.
- Quantify how strongly the inferred maximum avalanche size constrains breaking strain \sigma_break and the presence/extent of nuclear pasta layers.

3.4 Cross-observable validation with FRB 20201124A turbulence diagnostics.
- Verify that inferred propagation nuisance parameters reproduce observed RM SF stochastic amplitude and depolarization/scattering trends, without shifting the inferred intrinsic A_max.
- Use the binary geometric RM component as an external consistency check: ensure orbital-phase-dependent RM changes do not correlate with inferred intrinsic stress state (a falsifiable non-correlation prediction if the break is intrinsic).

3.5 Robustness and reproducibility.
- Ablation: fit timing-only, energy-only, and joint timing+energy; demonstrate that only the joint SOC inversion stably identifies a finite-size cutoff.
- Release an open, unit-tested inference code and simulated catalogs covering expected FAST selection functions.

Hypothesis: Nearly spherical accretion onto a rapidly spinning, moderately magnetized neutron star (A0538-66“like; B ~ 10^10“10^12 G at the footprint depending on multipolarity) generically admits a *magnetically anisotropic, 2D-stable* microphysical bifurcation in the near-surface settling/impact region: as the local mass flux per unit area \(\dot m(\theta,t)\) rises, the Coulomb stopping column \(y_s\) of infalling ions (computed with B-modified Coulomb drag and pitch-angle diffusion) crosses the *direction-dependent* radiative diffusion column \(y_{\rm diff,\parallel/\perp}\) of the heated electrons/radiation field. When \(y_s \approx y_{\rm diff}\), feedback among (i) ion energy deposition profile, (ii) Compton heating/cooling, and (iii) pair-assisted opacity produces a *sharp* transition from a dense, efficiently cooled, charge-rich boundary layer to an optically thinner, Compton-heated, pair-regulated layer in which the emergent low-entropy charge supply to open field lines drops rapidly.

The refined mechanism overcomes the reviewer-identified risks by explicitly demonstrating (1) that the threshold remains sharp once (a) field-guided inflow and lateral radiative leakage are included in axisymmetry, and (b) B-dependent scattering/transport and ion stopping are treated self-consistently; and (2) that the radio burst energetics and observability are closed by a quantitative mapping from gap power and pair multiplicity to escaping radio energy and spectrum under induced-scattering and free-free constraints in the inner wind.

In this picture, FRB-like bursts are produced by *charge-starvation episodes* in the polar-cap/current-closure circuit. When the surface column enters the hot/pair-regulated state, the number flux of charges with sufficiently low enthalpy to supply \(J_{\rm req}\) collapses on a microphysical timescale comparable to (or shorter than) the magnetospheric gap growth time. The magnetosphere responds by developing \(E_\parallel\), initiating a pair cascade. A calculable fraction \(\epsilon_{\rm rad}\) of the gap power is converted into coherent radio emission via curvature-driven bunching/maser (mode-dependent) in a pair-loaded plasma, with emission frequency set by the local plasma/curvature scales and the spectrum/escape set by induced Compton/Raman and wind free-free absorption. The per-system burst efficiency is anchored directly to A0538-66 observables via a pre-registered compactness/luminosity threshold and a predicted spectral pivot/hardness behavior. Convolving this per-system burst rate with the redshift-dependent formation rate of A0538-66 analog Be/XRBs yields an FRB source formation rate vs redshift; the proposal also explicitly contrasts why an analogous mechanism is suppressed or altered in black-hole accretors (no surface stopping layer; no anchored current-closure gap at a conducting surface), making the NS surface an essential ingredient.

Feasibility: 1) Addressing the geometry/B-field risk directly: the revised core deliverable is not a 1D bifurcation claim but a *measured sharpness* result from an axisymmetric, anisotropic-transport, B-modified microphysics solver. By explicitly including (i) field-guided inflow, (ii) lateral radiative leakage, (iii) spreading-layer advection, and (iv) magnetized cross sections for scattering and kinetic ion stopping, the proposal either demonstrates robustness of the \(y_s\sim y_{\rm diff}\) transition or falsifies it. The sharpness metric \(S\) and its dependence on \(B\) and lateral leakage provide a reviewer-requested proof, not an assertion.

Hypothesis: GX 13+1’s Fe XXV/XXVI wind is launched from a narrow annulus at r_launch ≈ (1“3) r_in where magnetospheric truncation and radiation pressure jointly set the effective potential and mass-loading: (i) when r_in expands (larger r_m from lower \dot{M} or larger μ), the open magnetic flux and lever arm increase, driving a faster, lower-column, more highly ionized magneto-centrifugal/radiative-MHD wind; simultaneously the reflector solid angle and relativistic broadening decrease because the optically thick disk is truncated farther out and wind scattering increases; (ii) when r_in contracts, radiation/thermal driving dominates with lower terminal speeds, larger columns, and stronger relativistic reflection from smaller radii. The refined approach overcomes standard degeneracies by making r_in the single shared latent state that simultaneously constrains (a) the dynamical velocity scale v(r) via a pre-specified wind topology calibrated to radiative-MHD simulations (limiting model flexibility), (b) the ionization structure through self-consistent density and illumination tied to \dot{M} and geometry, and (c) timing observables through pre-registered competing QPO→r_in mappings that are adjudicated using falsifiable discriminants (energy-dependent lags, harmonic content, Q/coherence).
