Plan: A. Data set construction (state coverage + strict simultaneity)
1) Primary target (GX 13+1): assemble strictly simultaneous or bracketed (≤12 hr) observations with: Chandra/HETG (Fe K absorption line centroids/widths; Fe XXV/XXVI), XMM-Newton/RGS (soft-band absorption/emission for density/ionization constraints where usable), NuSTAR (reflection hump + Fe emission profile; high-energy continuum), NICER (broadband continuum + high-S/N timing; energy-resolved lags).
2) State labeling: reproduce a consistent hardness“intensity and color“color classification using RXTE legacy definitions (Asset 1) mapped onto NICER/NuSTAR bands via response-folded synthetic colors; define 6“10 “analysis epochs” chosen to span: strong wind detections, weak/non-detections, and jet-coexistence regimes.
3) Timing products (per epoch): compute PSDs and cross-spectra in multiple energy bands; extract candidate QPOs (centroid ν, Q, rms), harmonic structure, coherence, and phase/time lags vs energy; compute covariance spectra to isolate variable components.
4) Spectral products (per epoch): build jointly fit spectra with instrument cross-normalizations and time-filtering matched to timing intervals; retain unbinned counts for Poisson likelihood where feasible.

B. Wind forward model: fixed topology + calibrated emulator + propagated model error
B1) Adopt a concrete wind class (pre-registered): a Blandford“Payne“like magneto-centrifugal streamline family with radiative acceleration and Compton heating/cooling (“BP+rad” hybrid), implemented as follows.
  • Streamline geometry: self-similar poloidal streamlines anchored at r0 with opening angle set by a single parameter θ0; launch annulus r0 ∈ [r_launch,min, r_launch,max] with r_launch = k r_in and k ∈ [1,3].
  • Enforced invariants along each streamline (hard constraints in the generator):
    - Mass loading κ = ρ v_p / B_p (constant on a streamline)
    - Field-line angular velocity Ω_F (constant)
    - Total specific angular momentum L = r v_φ − (r B_φ)/(4π κ) (constant)
    - Bernoulli integral including radiative work term W_rad (parameterized from local flux and force multiplier)
  • Acceleration components:
    - Magneto-centrifugal: determined by Ω_F and Alfvén radius r_A = λ^{1/2} r0 (λ is magnetic lever arm)
    - Radiative: line+electron scattering as an additive acceleration a_rad = (κ_es F/c) (1+M(t,ξ)), where M is a force multiplier dependent on ionization ξ and optical depth parameter t.
  • What is inferred vs fixed:
    - Inferred (global): r_in per epoch, k, θ0, λ (or equivalently r_A/r0), κ (or base density normalization), covering factor Ω/4π, microturbulence v_turb, metallicity Z_Fe (with informative prior), and a wind clumping factor f_cl (lognormal prior).
    - Fixed/parametrically limited: streamline functional form, invariant set, and allowed parameter ranges anchored to simulation calibration (below).

B2) Emulator calibration and validation (mandatory to prevent “physics-washing”)
1) Calibration grid: build/curate a published radiative-MHD simulation grid (or a community dataset) spanning NS-LMXB-relevant regimes: L/L_Edd ∈ [0.2,1.2], μ (or B) spanning 10^8“10^10 G-equivalent truncation, and inclinations i ∈ [40°,80°]. If full NS radiative-MHD grids are sparse, use: (i) radiative-MHD disk wind grids (BH/AGN-scaled) for ionization/acceleration behavior + (ii) separate magnetospheric truncation scalings for r_in; then treat mismatch as emulator error.
2) Outputs emulated: for each epoch’s continuum, emulate mappings from (r0, λ, κ, θ0, L/L_Edd, spectral shape) → profiles of v(r), n(r), and column N_H(ξ) along sightline.
3) Emulator architecture: Gaussian-process or normalizing-flow emulator with explicit uncertainty σ_emul(x); validate with held-out simulations; require ≤10“20% predictive error in v_inf and log ξ at the relevant columns for Fe XXV/XXVI (report as a validation table).
4) Likelihood propagation: include emulator error as additive covariance in the predicted optical depth τ(E): τ_pred(E) ~ N(τ_model(E), σ_emul(E)^2), ensuring posteriors broaden when the surrogate is uncertain.

B3) Photoionization and line formation (physics-anchored)
1) Compute ion fractions using XSTAR/Cloudy tables conditioned on the fitted SED; but do not fit “free” multi-zones. Instead, ionization structure follows n(r) and F(r) from the wind generator: ξ(r)=L_ion/(n r^2).
2) Line optical depths: integrate along line of sight through the streamline bundle; include velocity shear and v_turb for line broadening; predict centroids/blueshifts, equivalent widths, and line ratios Fe XXV/Fe XXVI.
3) Include electron scattering in the wind as an energy-dependent attenuation and as a contributor to reflection dilution, with τ_es tied to wind column.

C. Inner disk / magnetosphere module (latent r_in with physical bounds)
1) Parameterization: r_in,epoch = max(R_NS, η r_m), with r_m = C (μ^4/(2GM \dot{M}^2))^{1/7}. Infer μ and C×η jointly with informative priors from NS-LMXB population ranges; allow epoch-to-epoch variation via \dot{M} (from continuum) and a stochastic term δr capturing short-timescale truncation jitter.
2) Accretion viability constraints: enforce r_in < r_co (corotation) for stable accretion; if spin is unknown, treat ν_spin as a nuisance parameter with broad prior and propagate to r_co; reject propeller solutions unless data demand (model comparison).

D. Reflection + continuum with conservative systematics (EoS demoted)
1) Reflection model: use a high-density relativistic reflection suite allowing ionization gradients (radial stratification) and variable disk density; treat emissivity profile as flexible but regularized (e.g., broken power law with priors) and include wind scattering screen (from B3).
2) Systematic model components (explicit nuisance terms):
  • Density/ionization stratification hyperparameters with wide priors
  • Calibration offsets between instruments
  • A “reflection bias” term capturing unmodeled coronal geometry (broad prior on height/compactness proxies)
3) Output policy: report r_in posteriors robust to these nuisance terms; only translate to (M,R_NS) under explicitly labeled scenarios (e.g., “optimistic systematics” vs “conservative systematics”) and never as the primary success metric.

E. Timing link: pre-registered competing mappings + discriminants
E1) Pre-register 3 QPO→r_in hypotheses (no post-hoc invention)
Model T1 (Keplerian): ν_QPO = ν_K(r_in) = (1/2π) (GM/r_in^3)^{1/2}.
Model T2 (Lense“Thirring precession): ν_QPO = ν_LT(r_in, a_*) with a_* as nuisance; requires specific lag-energy signatures and coherence trends.
Model T3 (Beat-frequency family): ν_QPO = ν_K(r_in) − ν_spin (ν_spin nuisance).

E2) Discriminants beyond frequency (mandatory)
For each detected QPO, require fits to:
  • Energy dependence of fractional rms (e.g., increasing with energy vs peaking)
  • Phase/time lags vs energy at ν_QPO (hard vs soft lags; magnitude)
  • Harmonic content (presence/absence; relative phase)
  • Coherence/Q vs spectral hardness
Define a model selection criterion using Bayes factors with an Occam penalty and require that at least two discriminants favor the selected timing model; otherwise downweight timing by inflating σ_ν (treat as weakly informative).

F. Joint inference and identifiability controls
1) Bayesian engine: HMC/NUTS on the joint likelihood: L = L_spectra(counts|model) × L_timing(PSD/cross-spectra|model) × priors.
2) Identifiability checks:
  • Simulation-based calibration: generate synthetic datasets from the forward model across the parameter prior and verify recovery of r_in and wind parameters.
  • Posterior predictive checks targeting the key mechanistic coupling: correlation between absorption blueshift and reflection broadening mediated by r_in.
3) Benchmarking: compare against (i) standard multi-zone XSTAR absorption + phenomenological reflection and (ii) reflection-only fits; quantify uncertainty shrinkage in r_launch and r_in and check for prior-dominance via sensitivity to prior widening.

G. Transfer-source calibration (local magnetic diagnostics prioritized)
1) GRO J1744-28 (Asset 2): apply the same wind+reflection framework; test whether the model naturally supports large inferred r_in ~ O(10^2 GM/c^2) and high outflow velocities without unphysical energetics; use this as a calibration point for μ“r_in scaling.
2) SAX J1808.4-3658 (Asset 3): use pulse-profile/visibility constraints to inform r_in geometry in a system with known magnetic channeling; treat these as an external validation of the r_in inference machinery (not by importing its priors into GX 13+1).

H. Deliverables (re-scoped)
Primary: posterior of r_in(t), r_launch, wind \dot{M}_wind, v_inf, Ω/4π, and ion fractions; validated discrimination among timing mappings; quantified emulator error budget.
Secondary (conditional): constraints on μ/B and (M,R_NS) only under conservative systematic scenarios; explicit statement of what assumptions are required for EoS relevance.
Feasibility: 1) Addressing QPO non-uniqueness (Critique 1): the proposal no longer treats “QPO frequency → r_in” as a single deterministic link. It pre-registers three physically standard mappings (Keplerian, Lense“Thirring, beat-frequency) and requires additional, falsifiable timing observables (energy-dependent lags, harmonics, coherence/Q trends) as discriminants. If discriminants are inconclusive, the timing term is automatically weakened (inflated uncertainty), preventing model-dependent bias from dominating r_in.

2) Making the wind surrogate constrained and testable (Critique 2): the wind is not an open-ended “multi-zone” absorber. It is a fixed-topology BP+rad streamline family with explicit invariants (κ, Ω_F, L, Bernoulli+W_rad) and a small, declared set of inferred parameters (k, θ0, λ, κ, Ω/4π, v_turb, f_cl). Flexibility is further controlled by calibrating an emulator to a published radiative-MHD simulation grid and propagating emulator error into the likelihood; this prevents overconfident or overly flexible fits from reintroducing degeneracies.

3) Demoting/removing Galactic RM-based magnetic-sign priors (Critique 3; Mandatory Directive): the Galactic counterclockwise-field prior is removed from the inference pipeline because its information content for the magnetospheric/disk-wind field at ~10“10^3 km is negligible relative to local field geometry uncertainties. Magnetic inference instead comes from local/transfer diagnostics: consistency of μ with truncation-driven r_in evolution, energetics constraints, and cross-source validation against systems with magnetic channeling (SAX J1808.4-3658) and large r_in with wind signatures (GRO J1744-28).

4) Preventing overreach on EoS/TOV (Critique 4; Mandatory Directive): EoS constraints are explicitly re-scoped as secondary and conditional. Reflection modeling includes conservative systematics (ionization/density stratification, emissivity uncertainty, wind scattering) with wide priors, and results will be reported in tiered scenarios (conservative vs optimistic) with stress tests. The primary success criterion is mechanistic closure on r_in“wind coupling and robust posteriors on r_in and wind properties, not tight (M,R_NS).

5) Why identifiability is plausible in practice: GX 13+1 provides simultaneous wind + jet regimes at high luminosity (Asset 1), offering the required dynamic range where truncation and radiation both plausibly matter. The model’s key breaking of degeneracy is observationally anchored: r_in affects (a) reflection broadening and continuum geometry, while the same r_in sets the dynamical velocity scale and column distribution in the wind; observing correlated changes in Fe absorption blueshift/strength and reflection shape across epochs provides a cross-constraint that is unavailable in spectral-only fits. Transfer-source tests (Assets 2“3) provide external validation that the same r_in machinery reproduces known large-truncation and pulse-profile behaviors, reducing the risk that GX 13+1 results are an artifact of model flexibility.

Hypothesis: NS“NS mergers occurring in (or projected against) globular clusters can—under a restricted, testable region of fallback + jet/cocoon parameter space—produce an early-time (hours“days) Chandra-band (0.5“8 keV) component whose variability is governed by Comptonization in a compact, mildly relativistic, optically-thin-to-marginal corona (transition-layer / cocoon-shock interface) operating near an Eddington-regulated radiation-pressure equilibrium. Mechanism: (i) fallback power injected into a baryon-loaded, magnetized coronal volume heats electrons to kTe ~ 10“80 keV; (ii) intense soft-photon compactness drives rapid Compton cooling and e± pair balance that self-regulates the Thomson depth to tauT ~ 0.3“3 (with Klein“Nishina suppression limiting high-energy scattering), producing a narrow relation between L/L_Edd, kTe, and tauT; (iii) the same scattering random-walk plus light-travel time across size R ~ (1“30)×10^6 cm imprints an energy-dependent Fourier phase lag that increases with photon energy (hard lag) and scales approximately as tlag(E,f) ~ tesc(E)/(1 + (2π f tesc)^2) with tesc ~ (R/c)×max(1, tauT, tauT^2), yielding millisecond“second lags for plausible remnant-scale radii. Identifiability claim (explicit): this coronal model predicts (a) a correlated triplet {L/L_Edd, spectral cutoff Ec ~ 2“3 kTe, lag“energy slope d tlag/d lnE} constrained by electron+photon energy equations + pair balance, whereas an off-axis synchrotron afterglow predicts no intrinsic Compton hard lags at ms“s scales and instead yields either near-zero interband lag or frequency-independent geometric/curvature delays at much longer (≫R/c) timescales; dust scattering predicts soft, delayed halos with strong angular dependence and a distinct energy scaling of delay ∝ E^{-2}. Thus, by enforcing the closure and jointly fitting spectra + cross-spectra (and polarization when available), we can (1) robustly decide whether any Comptonizing corona is required at all, and (2) if required, infer only the realistically accessible remnant property: whether a long-lived NS/engine exists that can sustain compactness/high compactness pair-regulated heating for ≳hours“days versus prompt BH cases where early emission is dominated by afterglow and/or rapidly fading fallback with no stable Eddington-regulated corona signature. Any EOS statement is explicitly conditioned: we target classification (long-lived NS vs prompt BH) and exclude claims of precise mass“radius inference unless beaming/opacity are independently constrained.
Plan: Step 0 (Scope control & decision points)
0.1 Primary deliverable: a quantitative identifiability/feasibility package and a model-comparison pipeline that outputs Bayes factors between (A) afterglow-only and (B) afterglow+Eddington-regulated Compton corona, plus confounders (dust halo, LMXB/UCXB).
0.2 Pre-registered detection criterion: declare corona “required” only if ln BF(B vs A) > 5 and posterior predictive checks pass for lag“energy and cutoff“lag coupling.

Step 1 (Physical model specification: fallback + cocoon → corona source terms)
1.1 Fallback power: adopt a minimal, explicit fallback prescription
   Ṁfb(t) = Ṁ0 (t/t0)^{-5/3}, with t0 = 0.1“1 s and Ṁ0 set by fallback mass Mfb = 10^{-6}“10^{-2} Msun.
   Lheat(t) = ηh Ṁfb c^2 with ηh = 10^{-4}“10^{-2} (engine-to-corona heating efficiency). This defines the heating compactness.
1.2 Geometry: assume a quasi-spherical or toroidal compact corona of characteristic radius R(t)=R0 (t/tref)^αR with R0 = (1“30)×10^6 cm, αR in [0, 0.5]. Seed photons come from a thermalized cocoon/photosphere or NS surface layer with temperature Ts(t) and luminosity Ls(t) constrained by energy conservation (below).
1.3 Baryon loading: specify entrainment from cocoon/ejecta as
   dMb/dt = ξb Ṁfb + ξe (Mej/t) exp(-t/tej), with Mej from GW-informed priors and ξb, ξe ∈ [0,1]. Electron density sets τT via τT(t)=σT ne(t) R(t) with ne determined by Mb plus pairs.
1.4 Magnetized heating: adopt a testable magnetic dissipation law
   Q+ = ϵB (B^2/8π) (V/R) with B parameterized via plasma beta β = Pgas/PB and constrained by requiring sub-equipartition (β≥0.1). This fixes electron heating fraction δe.

Step 2 (Replace Eddington “cap” with an explicit closure: coupled energy + pair balance + KN opacity)
2.1 Electron energy equation (volume-averaged):
   d(Ue)/dt = Q+_e(t) − QComp(t) − Qsyn(t) − Qad(t) − QCoul(t)
   where QComp uses full KN-corrected Compton kernel (or an accurate fitting formula) and includes seed photon energy density Uph.
2.2 Photon energy equation (for the Comptonized component):
   d(Uph)/dt = Qseed(t) + QComp(t) − (Uph/tesc)
   with escape time tesc = (R/c)×(1+τeff), τeff = τT + τ±, and photon diffusion corrected for τ>1 (tesc ~ (R/c)×(1+τ+τ^2)).
2.3 Pair balance (steady or stiff ODE):
   d n±/dt = ṅγγ(T_e,Uph) − n+ n− ⟨σann v⟩ − n±/tadv
   with γγ computed from the high-energy tail of the Comptonized spectrum; this self-regulates τ± and thus τeff.
2.4 Composition-dependent opacity: include κ = κes(Y_e, X, Z) with corrections for partially ionized heavy r-process ejecta if relevant; propagate as a systematic prior. KN suppression enters the effective scattering opacity at high energies.
2.5 Radiation-pressure / momentum consistency (testable constraint, not a cap):
   Require Liso(t) and inferred outflow rate satisfy
   Ṁw v∞ ≥ (Ω/4π) Liso/c
   where Ω encodes beaming; v∞ constrained by ejecta/cocoon priors. This rejects unphysical solutions.
2.6 Output predictive relations: from (2.1“2.4) derive a narrow manifold in parameter space linking
   (i) L/L_Edd, (ii) Ec ≈ 2“3 kTe, (iii) τT, and (iv) lag“energy slope.
   This manifold is what makes the corona identifiable beyond a flexible lag fit.

Step 3 (Predict lag amplitude & frequency scaling; detectability with Chandra)
3.1 Cross-spectrum model: compute complex transfer function H(E,f) from the time-dependent Compton Green’s function (Kompaneets/Monte Carlo hybrid). Then
   C12(f)=X1(f)X2*(f), phase φ12(f)=arg⟨C12⟩, lag tlag=φ12/(2πf), coherence γ^2(f)=|⟨C12⟩|^2/(⟨|X1|^2⟩⟨|X2|^2⟩).
3.2 Scaling expectation for feasibility: for kTe~20“50 keV and τ~0.5“2, typical scattering order to go from ~1 keV to ~5 keV is Nsc ~ ln(E2/E1)/ln(1+4θ+16θ^2) with θ=kTe/mec^2; tlag(E) ~ Nsc×(R/c)×max(1,τ). This yields:
   R=10^7 cm → R/c≈0.33 ms; Nsc~5“20 → lags ~ 2“20 ms (τ~1)
   R=10^9 cm → R/c≈33 ms; lags ~0.2“2 s.
   The proposal therefore explicitly targets ms“s lags and tests whether R must be too large/small to be physical.
3.3 Chandra detectability budget (explicit, to be implemented with PIMMS/ChaRT+MARX):
   Inputs: expected 0.5“8 keV flux Fx(t), spectral shape from the closure (Γ, Ec), NH, off-axis angle, frame time.
   For each planned exposure Texp, compute expected counts in bands B1=0.5“2, B2=2“4, B3=4“8.
   Lag S/N requirement: use standard cross-spectral variance approximations; for M averaged segments, the phase-lag uncertainty
   σφ ≈ sqrt((1−γ^2)/(2γ^2 M)). Translate to σt = σφ/(2π f).
   Design goal: achieve σt < 0.3 tlag at f in [0.01, 10] Hz (set by event duration/segment length and count rate).
3.4 Observing strategy derived from budget:
   If expected count rate <~0.05 ct/s, classical Fourier lag detection is infeasible; switch to time-domain Bayesian hierarchical “shot/noise” models to constrain transfer-function moments only (upper limits on lag). If >~0.2 ct/s, attempt full cross-spectrum.

Step 4 (Data program: events, globular-cluster fields, and contamination controls)
4.1 Merger anchors: GW170817 reanalysis (as a control where afterglow is favored) + all GW triggers with credible sky localization and Chandra follow-up (including non-detections to inform priors).
4.2 Globular cluster program (quantified targeting):
   (i) Milky Way GCs: systematic archival mining for fast transients and short-lived point sources temporally coincident with GW alerts (post-O4/O5), plus baseline variability characterization.
   (ii) Local Group GCs (M31): deep Chandra fields to build an empirical interloper prior (UCXB/LMXB luminosity function and variability).
4.3 Astrometric association: compute chance alignment probability using local source density and cluster half-light radius; include proper motion corrections for MW clusters.

Step 5 (Confounder-discrimination module: explicit competing generative models)
5.1 Off-axis afterglow variability/curvature: include a structured-jet synchrotron model with microphysical priors; allow density fluctuations; predict interband lags from synchrotron cooling (typically soft lags) and compare sign/frequency dependence.
5.2 Dust scattering: forward-model halo surface brightness vs time and energy (delay ∝ E^{-2}, angular broadening); use Chandra imaging to separate point source vs halo contribution; include as a mixture component in the likelihood.
5.3 Instrument/systematics: simulate deadtime/background, dithering, PSF energy dependence; require coherence behavior consistent with astrophysical transfer functions; apply null tests using background regions.
5.4 UCXB/LMXB in GCs: incorporate a dedicated interloper library informed by globular cluster UCXB theory and observed near-/super-Eddington behavior:
   - Prior on L distribution flattening near L_Edd (from UCXB luminosity-function arguments)
   - Spectral states with Comptonization, but with characteristic sizes/timescales and (when available) polarization constraints.
   Classification uses: transient timescale (merger afterglow monotonic rise/decay vs LMXB state transitions), recurrence, and spatial probability.

Step 6 (Inference architecture)
6.1 Forward model: time-dependent corona closure (Step 2) → spectrum + light curve + transfer function H(E,f) → predicted cross-spectra and (optional) polarization.
6.2 Hierarchical Bayesian fit:
   Likelihood terms: Poisson spectral counts; Gaussian/log-normal light-curve errors; complex cross-spectrum likelihood; polarization likelihood (PF, PA).
   Priors: GW distance/inclination; ejecta mass/velocity; cluster priors; instrument priors.
6.3 Model comparison: compute Bayes factors among {afterglow, afterglow+dust, afterglow+corona, UCXB/LMXB}.

Step 7 (Injection“recovery benchmarks; EOS claim conditioned)
7.1 Synthetic injections: generate populations spanning prompt-BH vs long-lived NS engine; vary R, τ, Te, beaming, and afterglow parameters; inject into realistic Chandra response and cadence.
7.2 Recovery metrics:
   - Correct model selection fraction vs counts
   - Bias/variance on (R, τ, kTe) and on the binary classification long-lived NS vs prompt BH.
7.3 EOS linkage downgraded and quantified: report only the achievable posterior odds on long-lived NS vs prompt BH under beaming/opacity marginalization. Any mapping to maximum NS mass is presented as conditional (requires external beaming constraints), and only if injection studies show robustness.
Feasibility: 1) Quantitative plausibility of corona parameters and lags (addressing identifiability)
The revised proposal no longer asserts that GW170817 requires a corona; instead it treats GW170817 as a control case and asks whether any merger exhibits the predicted closure-coupled lag/cutoff signature. Using the explicit closure (coupled electron+photon energy equations + pair balance + KN corrections), the model naturally self-regulates to τT~O(1) and kTe~tens of keV when the compactness is high; this is exactly the regime where Comptonization produces hard lags. The predicted lag scale is set by tesc~(R/c)×max(1,τ,τ^2) times a scattering-order factor Nsc(E), yielding ms“s lags for remnant-scale radii (10^7“10^9 cm). This is a falsifiable prediction: if inferred lags require R≫10^10“10^11 cm, the corona interpretation is rejected.

2) Detectability with Chandra is explicitly budgeted (addressing S/N critique)
The plan includes a mandatory PIMMS/ChaRT+MARX count-rate and band-count computation per candidate, and uses standard cross-spectral uncertainty relations to determine whether Fourier-lag inference is feasible in a given observation. If count rates are too low (as is common for distant mergers), the pipeline downgrades to upper limits on transfer-function moments rather than overfitting an unconstrained lag model. Observing cadence and exposure times are therefore derived from measurable requirements: target σt < 0.3 tlag at frequencies allowed by the segment length and count rate, and require coherence constraints to avoid spurious lags.

3) Eddington “closure” is replaced with a testable microphysical closure (addressing underspecification)
The previous luminosity cap is replaced by explicit, coupled evolution equations with KN Compton cooling, pair production/annihilation, composition-dependent opacity, and a momentum-consistency constraint for any implied outflow/beaming. This yields a narrow manifold linking L/L_Edd, Ec~2“3kTe, τeff, and lag“energy slope—turning Eddington regulation from a hand-waving cap into a predictive, falsifiable relation. Solutions that violate pair balance, energy conservation, or momentum balance are rejected.

4) Rigorous discrimination against confounders (addressing degeneracy critique)
Competing generative models are implemented explicitly: structured-jet afterglow (including curvature and density fluctuations), dust scattering halos with their distinctive E^{-2} delay scaling and spatial broadening, and GC UCXB/LMXB populations with empirical priors on luminosity functions and variability. The inference requires not just a lag detection but also the closure-coupled spectral cutoff/lag relation and consistency of coherence behavior. Instrumental systematics are controlled through end-to-end response simulations and background/region null tests.

5) Globular cluster rationale is quantified and de-risked (addressing rate/contamination critique)

1. Target outputs: y_pm = (f_peak, \dot f_peak, τ_damp, E_GW,pm, M_ej, v_ej, collapse_flag).
2. Inputs: binary parameters (M_chirp,q,χ_eff), cold EOS summary features plus transition parameters (e.g., R_1.6, Λ_1.4, ρ_t, Δε, min(c_s^2) in window), and thermal parameters (Γ_th or Γ_1,Γ_2).
3. Surrogate form: heteroscedastic Bayesian neural network or Gaussian Process with structured mean:
   y_pm = m(x) + ξ,  ξ ~ N(0, Σ_surr(x))
   where m(x) includes known scalings (e.g., f_peak ∝ √(M_tot/R_rem^3)) as inductive bias, and Σ_surr(x) is learned.
4. Training set (NR atlas):
   - Baseline hadronic EOS: ~15 EOS × (q ∈ {1.0,0.85,0.7}) × (M_tot ∈ {2.6,2.7,2.8,2.9} M_⊙) → ~180 runs.
   - Hybrid EOS (transition sweep): ~20 EOS constructed by varying (ρ_t,Δε,w,min c_s^2) × same mass-ratio/mass grid → ~240 runs.
   - Thermal sector sweep: for a subset (~40 runs), vary Γ_th (or Γ_1,Γ_2) to decorrelate thermal vs latent-heat effects.
   Total new/curated runs: ~420 (allowing a mix of existing public catalogs + targeted new simulations).
5. Accuracy requirements (quantitative):
   - f_peak RMS error ≤ 50“80 Hz; τ_damp fractional error ≤ 20“30% (realistic given current NR variability).
   - Calibration verified via 5-fold EOS-holdout (withheld EOS families) and posterior predictive checks.
6. Uncertainty propagation in inference:
   - Likelihood uses p(d_pm | y_pm) convolved with surrogate predictive distribution N(m(x), Σ_surr(x)).
   - For upper limits, integrate predicted spectra distribution over nuisance amplitude and Σ_surr.

Step 5 — “Energy-budget coupling” reformulated as soft, testable constraints (avoid dominance/bias)
1. Do not hard-enforce unobservable channels (neutrinos/shocks). Instead introduce an explicit latent partition vector ϕ with broad priors:
   E_bind → (E_GW,pm, E_ν, E_sh, E_ej, E_rad)
2. Constrain only robust inequalities and bookkeeping identities:
   - E_ej + E_rad ≤ α (E_orb + E_rot) with α∈(0,1) inferred (broad prior).
   - E_rad constrained by kilonova L_bol(t) through standard r-process heating model with nuisance opacity/thermalization.
3. Validate that Bayes factors for latent heat are stable under widening/narrowing priors on ϕ; report sensitivity.

Step 6 — Hierarchical inference and identifiability quantification
1. Hierarchical Bayesian model over events and pulsars:
   - Global parameters: EOS fields (a,b,ρ_t,w), thermal parameters (Γ_th/Γ_1,Γ_2), surrogate hyperparameters fixed from training.
   - Event-specific: (m1,m2,χ_eff, distance, inclination, calibration, EM opacities).
2. Sampler: gradient-based MCMC (NUTS) using implicit gradients of Π (smooth mode) or subgradient-enabled HMC / Metropolis-within-Gibbs (Maxwell mode).
3. Identifiability mapping:
   - Compute functional Fisher information / sensitivity kernels of u(ρ) and k(ρ) under inspiral-only vs +NICER vs +post-merger vs +EM.
   - Perform controlled injections: (a) pure thermal change with no latent heat, (b) latent heat with fixed thermal, (c) both—quantify posterior cross-correlation Corr(Δε,Γ_th) and failure rates.
4. Model comparison:
   - Compare models M0: k(ρ)≡0 (no latent heat) vs M1: k(ρ) allowed, using marginal likelihood estimators (bridge sampling / nested sampling on reduced parameter set) and report robustness to surrogate error inflation.

Step 7 — Validation milestones and failure-mode handling
1. Closure: verify (by construction) causality/thermodynamics; additionally check numerical tolerances and report any projection solver failures.
2. EOS-holdout NR validation: ensure surrogate generalizes to unseen EOS families (critical for avoiding “atlas bias”).
3. Stress tests:
   - Inflate Σ_surr by factors {1,2,3} and recompute Bayes factors.
   - Remove EM or post-merger contributions to verify that the transition signal is not an artifact of a single messenger.

Deliverables
- A publicly documented Π operator (objective, constraints, solver settings), including differentiability mode (smooth vs Maxwell) and diagnostics.
- A probabilistic post-merger surrogate with published training coverage, errors, and EOS-holdout tests.
- Posterior constraints on (ρ_t,Δε,w,min c_s^2) with quantified degeneracies vs Γ_th and with sensitivity to post-merger non-detections.
Feasibility: 1) Projection operator Π feasibility and differentiability
- The revised proposal replaces conceptual “projection” with an explicit proximal constrained optimization on a discretized density grid, solvable via augmented Lagrangian / interior-point methods. Smooth ε-regularized transitions enable implicit differentiation through KKT systems (standard in differentiable optimization). The exact Maxwell limit is handled with semismooth Newton + subgradients, with explicit failure-mode handling (hard reject + diagnostics), satisfying the reviewer requirement for a testable specification.

2) Post-merger sector: preventing unverifiable energy assumptions from dominating
- The energy-budget link is re-scoped from hard enforcement of poorly observed channels (neutrinos/shocks) to (i) bookkeeping identities and (ii) robust inequality constraints with broad priors over partition fractions. This makes the coupling falsifiable (posterior checks) and reduces risk of biased Bayes factors. Post-merger information enters primarily through a probabilistic surrogate whose uncertainty is explicitly marginalized, so inference remains conservative when post-merger data are weak or absent (Assets 3“4 motivate measurability; non-detections are supported).

3) NR atlas and computational budget (quantified)
- The atlas is bounded to ~420 runs with structured coverage over (EOS family, q, M_tot) and targeted sweeps over transition and thermal parameters. This size is aligned with current community-scale NR campaigns and is compatible with constructing a heteroscedastic surrogate. Critically, the design includes EOS-holdout validation to avoid overfitting to a narrow EOS subset.

4) Separating cold latent-heat effects from finite-T effects (addressing identifiability)
- A minimal thermal sector (Γ_th or two-segment Γ_th(ρ)) is introduced as an explicit inference component, preventing the latent-heat kernel from acting as a catch-all for thermal pressure support. Controlled injections explicitly quantify Corr(Δε,Γ_th) and the extent to which post-merger frequency shifts can be mimicked by thermal modeling (Assets 2“4).

5) Expected information gain under realistic post-merger outcomes
- The plan explicitly supports upper limits/stacked constraints in the 1“4 kHz band and marginalizes surrogate uncertainties; thus, even in the likely near-term scenario of non-detections, the framework remains informative through inspiral + NICER + high-mass pulsars (Assets 1“3). For next-generation detectors, the proposal sets quantitative surrogate accuracy targets (≤50“80 Hz on f_peak) consistent with resolving EOS-driven shifts discussed in the literature (Assets 3“4), enabling a realistic pathway to improved constraints.

6) Scientific coherence with established empirical constraints
- Inspiral Λ constraints (GW170817-like) and NICER M“R posteriors already restrict stiffness (Asset 1) and hybrid-star transition parameter space via tidal deformability (Asset 2). Post-merger morphology sensitivity to finite-T microphysics (Asset 4) is leveraged, but now with a thermal parameterization that explicitly models this sensitivity rather than conflating it with latent heat. Multimessenger synthesis follows the established logic of combining inspiral and EM constraints to bound EOS behavior (Asset 3).

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the prompt-collapse probability of binary neutron star (BNS) mergers can be meaningfully constrained—without overclaiming sensitivity—by a detector-realistic, physically constrained *joint* inference that couples (i) gravitational-wave (GW) posteriors on chirp mass and mass ratio, (ii) NR-calibrated prompt-collapse threshold relations with explicit uncertainty hyperparameters, and (iii) a forward model for MeV neutrino detection that correctly reflects the dominant channels in each detector (IBD-dominated in water Cherenkov; collective rate excess in IceCube). The mechanism is not that extragalactic neutrino non-detections are generically informative, but that for a subset of events (nearby, high-mass, well-localized, or stacked in a population analysis) neutrino data provide *directional evidence* that breaks a specific degeneracy: high total mass can imply prompt collapse, yet some EOS permit a short-lived hypermassive NS (HMNS) with substantial neutrino emission. By embedding NR-calibrated M_th(M_TOV, R_1.6, q, \chi_eff) relations and a neutrino-luminosity“lifetime emulator (with transport systematics) into the likelihood, neutrino non-detections (or weak burst-like excesses) become probabilistic constraints on remnant lifetime that propagate to the prompt-collapse probability. Core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) enter the causal chain only as a quantitatively modeled competing hypothesis/background in the hierarchical coincidence model (time-windowed CCSN neutrino bursts and non-CBC GW transients), enabling correct false-coincidence accounting and preventing spuriously strong constraints from chance neutrino activity.
Plan: Step 0 — Define event classes, observables, and detectors (architecture-level specification):
0.1 Event set: LVK BNS candidates with posterior samples over (\mathcal{M}_c, q, \chi_eff, D_L, \iota, sky) and (where available) EM counterpart constraints on ejecta/opacity (kilonova) or upper limits.
0.2 Neutrino instruments: Super-K/Hyper-K (event-level MeV analysis), IceCube (burst analysis via DOM rate residuals). We will not treat IceCube as ES event reconstruction at MeV.
0.3 Time windows: prompt (−10 s, +10 s) and extended cooling (−10 s, +100 s, and +1 hr) for HMNS/SMNS scenarios, with detector-dependent deadtime and background handled explicitly.

Step 1 — Replace the hard TOV boundary with NR-calibrated prompt-collapse threshold modeling:
1.1 Adopt an NR-calibrated threshold mass model of the form
M_th = k(\mathcal{C}_{1.6})\, M_TOV \times f_q(q) \times f_\chi(\chi_eff) + \epsilon_th,
where \mathcal{C}_{1.6} = GM_{1.6}/(R_{1.6}c^2), k(\mathcal{C}_{1.6}) is a calibrated function (e.g., linear/quadratic in compactness), and f_q, f_\chi encode mass-ratio and spin corrections motivated by NR ensembles. \epsilon_th is a stochastic calibration residual.
1.2 Hyperparameters: place priors on the calibration coefficients and residual scatter (\sigma_th) informed by published NR fit uncertainties; treat them as hierarchical parameters to propagate modeling uncertainty.
1.3 Prompt-collapse probability for each event is then
P_PC = P(M_tot > M_th | GW, EOS, hyperparams),
computed by Monte Carlo over GW posterior samples and EOS/hyperparameter draws.

Step 2 — EOS and remnant model with explicit degeneracies (identifiability-aware):
2.1 EOS parameterization: use a spectral or piecewise-polytrope representation constrained by causality and maximum mass; map to (M_TOV, R_{1.6}, tidal deformabilities \Lambda_1,\Lambda_2).
2.2 Remnant lifetime/emission model: build a fast emulator (Gaussian process or neural surrogate trained on NR + neutrino-transport simulation suites) for:
(a) L_\nu(t; M_tot, q, EOS, remnant_state),
(b) mean energies \langle E_{\bar\nu_e}\rangle, \langle E_{\nu_e}\rangle,
(c) HMNS/SMNS lifetime distribution \tau_rem with parameters dependent on proximity to threshold \Delta = M_th − M_tot and angular momentum.
2.3 Transport systematics: include a discrete nuisance index for neutrino-transport prescription class (e.g., leakage vs M1 vs Boltzmann-informed), or continuous scaling parameters (A_L for luminosity normalization, A_E for mean-energy) with priors calibrated from cross-code comparisons.
2.4 EM coupling (optional per event): use kilonova-informed priors on ejecta mass/velocity as a soft constraint on remnant fate (e.g., prompt collapse suppresses disk winds/blue component). Implement as a likelihood term or informative prior on disk mass and lifetime.

Step 3 — Detector-realistic neutrino forward model (IBD+ES in water Cherenkov; IceCube burst formalism):
3.1 Super-K/Hyper-K:
(a) Compute expected differential event rate for inverse beta decay (dominant): \bar\nu_e + p → e^+ + n, including detection efficiency, energy threshold, and fiducial mass.
(b) Include sub-dominant elastic scattering (ES) \nu + e^- → \nu + e^- to retain directional information when applicable; treat ES as an auxiliary channel, not the primary one.
(c) Include backgrounds (solar, atmospheric, spallation) with data-driven rates; likelihood is Poisson in reconstructed energy/time bins, marginalizing over background-rate nuisance parameters.
3.2 IceCube:
(a) Use the standard MeV burst method: model the expected collective DOM count-rate excess \Delta r(t) from a neutrino flux, including detector noise, correlated systematics, and seasonal baseline variations.
(b) Likelihood: Gaussian (or appropriate count-based approximation) over time-binned rate residuals with covariance estimated from off-source data.
3.3 Joint neutrino likelihood: multiply SK/HK and IceCube likelihoods when both are available; include detector calibration nuisance parameters.

Step 4 — Competing-hypothesis mixture model including CCSN (coherence with concept chain):
4.1 Introduce a hierarchical mixture for neutrino activity in the coincidence window:
H0: background-only;
H_BNS: neutrinos from the BNS remnant model;
H_CCSN: neutrino burst from a Galactic/nearby CCSN (with its own time profile and spectrum) potentially coincident in time by chance.
4.2 Use CCSN priors/rates (Galactic CCSN rate, detection horizon for SK/IceCube) to set mixture weights; this prevents attributing any neutrino-rate anomaly to BNS by default.
4.3 If desired, include a non-CBC GW transient hypothesis for CCSN-like GW signals to avoid mis-association in low-significance triggers.

Step 5 — Forecasting information gain vs distance (mandatory quantitative rigor):
5.1 Fisher/Bayes-factor forecasts: for representative BNS classes (GW170817-like; GW190425-like high chirp mass), compute expected neutrino log Bayes factor \ln B_{BNS,H0} and expected reduction in entropy/variance of P_PC as a function of D_L (e.g., 10“300 Mpc) for SK, HK, IceCube.
5.2 Identify regimes:
(a) Nearby (\lesssim 10“20 Mpc): single-event constraints can be non-prior-dominated.
(b) Typical LVK distances: single-event neutrino constraints weak; rely on population stacking and on ruling out extreme luminosity“lifetime combinations.
(c) 3G detectors: early-warning localization (per Asset 5) enables optimal neutrino/EM windowing and background suppression, improving odds of informative events.

Step 6 — Validation, identifiability, and calibration (simulation-based):
6.1 Build synthetic populations over (EOS, M_tot, q, \chi_eff, D_L) using astrophysical priors; inject neutrino and GW data with detector responses.
6.2 Simulation-based calibration (SBC): verify coverage of P_PC and remnant-lifetime posteriors under the full hierarchical model; diagnose prior-dominance by comparing posterior-to-prior KL divergence across distance bins.
6.3 Posterior predictive checks: verify time/energy distributions in SK/HK and rate residuals in IceCube.
6.4 Model comparison: compute Bayes factors for models with/without neutrino information, and with different transport systematics; report where neutrino data change P_PC materially.

Step 7 — Deliverables:
7.1 Publicly documented pipeline integrating LVK posterior samples + neutrino forward models.
7.2 A set of forecasting curves (information gain vs distance) and a decision rule for when neutrino data should be included in low-latency prompt-collapse inference.
7.3 A hierarchical population constraint on prompt-collapse fraction as a function of chirp mass, with EOS/threshold-model uncertainties propagated.
Feasibility: 1) Addressing limited extragalactic MeV neutrino sensitivity (reviewer concern): The proposal explicitly predicts when constraints are informative via Fisher/Bayes-factor forecasts versus distance, and it is designed to (a) extract real information for rare nearby events, and (b) still yield population-level constraints by stacking many non-detections without claiming per-event detectability at typical LVK distances. This reframes neutrino non-detections as weak evidence that trims extreme neutrino-luminosity“lifetime regions rather than as standalone detections.

2) Detector realism and correct channel usage: For water Cherenkov we model IBD as the dominant channel and ES as auxiliary; for IceCube we use the burst rate-excess formalism rather than event-by-event ES. Backgrounds and efficiencies enter as nuisance parameters with off-source calibration, preventing artificially tight posteriors.

3) GR stability and prompt-collapse modeling beyond static TOV: Prompt collapse is not encoded as a hard TOV boundary. Instead we use NR-calibrated threshold relations M_th(M_TOV, R_1.6, q, \chi_eff) with explicit hyperparameters and residual scatter, which is the standard way the community captures thermal/rotational support and mass-ratio dependence. This directly responds to the oversimplification critique and propagates modeling uncertainty into P_PC.

4) Degeneracies and identifiability: EOS parameters, remnant lifetime, and neutrino emission are explicitly coupled through an emulator with transport-systematic nuisance parameters. Identifiability is demonstrated through simulation-based calibration and KL-divergence diagnostics that quantify when posteriors are prior-dominated, ensuring the analysis does not over-interpret null results.

5) Coherent role of CCSN in the concept chain: CCSN is incorporated only as a competing-hypothesis/background component in the hierarchical mixture model for neutrino (and optionally GW) coincidences, with quantitative rate priors. This makes CCSN scientifically necessary (false-coincidence control), not an appended topic.

6) Empirical anchoring to provided assets: The neutrino non-detection logic and fluence-limit treatment is consistent with the SK-style coincidence analyses (Asset 1). The GW-driven remnant/engine inference and the need for physically grounded energetics echoes the calorimetric philosophy (Asset 2) while remaining focused on BNS. Chirp mass as a stable GW observable (Asset 3) and the high prompt-collapse probability regime for high-mass BNS like GW190425 (Asset 4) define the target parameter space where this method is most likely to add value. Early-warning localization capabilities (Asset 5) motivate low-latency windowing and improved background control for future detectors.

Hypothesis: GRB 170817A“like events can exhibit (i) a physically distinct, low-fluence precursor and (ii) a hard short pulse with a ~seconds-scale waiting time when the jet is launched into a baryon-rich, angle-dependent post-merger wind whose optical depth and breakout conditions evolve on the same timescale as r-process heating changes the ejecta temperature/composition and hence opacity. Mechanistically, the precursor arises from shock breakout / photospheric emission of a mildly relativistic cocoon or jet head when the wind optical depth first drops below unity along the observer’s line of sight, while the hard short pulse is produced only after a cleaner, higher-Γ channel forms (or the jet core emerges) and internal dissipation becomes visible. A single physics-constrained, differentiable multi-messenger inverse model (GW tidal deformability + jet“ejecta hydrodynamics + radiative transfer + kilonova microphysics) overcomes the key limitation of sequential fits by forcing the same small set of ejecta/engine parameters to simultaneously satisfy: (1) GW-inferred tidal parameters and distance/inclination, (2) the GRB fluence and two-component temporal structure (precursor + hard pulse, plus soft-tail/afterglow upper limits), and (3) the optical kilonova luminosity/color evolution set by r-process heating and Ye-dependent opacity. This shared-parameter closure removes otherwise unconstrained degeneracies (viewing angle vs. baryon loading vs. jet structure vs. opacity evolution) that can fit any one dataset in isolation but not all three at once.

The previously proposed intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) environmental perturbation is restricted to a narrowly defined, testable configuration space: an IMBH with M_L ∈ [10^2,10^4] M⊙ acting as a gravitational lens with small impact parameter (b comparable to the Einstein radius) along the GW/γ-ray line of sight, which can produce a detectable, frequency-dependent amplification and phase/time-delay perturbation in the GW signal (wave-optics regime) and/or a measurable relative arrival-time perturbation between GW and γ-rays only if the lensing geometry is near-aligned. We pre-register a null hypothesis (no detectable IMBH lensing; report upper limits on lensing strength and translate to constraints on M_L and b) because generic tidal/tertiary effects from such masses at astrophysically plausible separations are expected to be below LIGO/Virgo systematic floors. The IMBH channel is therefore treated as a targeted, falsifiable lensing test—not as a free ‘complexity absorber’—and is only activated in inference if (a) Bayes factors exceed a pre-specified threshold against a no-lens model and (b) injection“recovery tests show controlled false-positive rates under waveform/calibration systematics.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration (guards against unfalsifiable complexity)
0.1 Define two model classes and decision rules before analysis:
  • M0 (baseline multi-messenger model): no IMBH lensing.
  • M1 (IMBH lensing): includes only line-of-sight lensing parameters (M_L, y=b/R_E, lens redshift ≈ host, no arbitrary waveform ‘patch’ terms).
0.2 Pre-specify detection/claim criteria:
  • Require log Bayes factor ln B10 > 5 AND posterior on y confined to the near-aligned regime (e.g., y<1.5) AND successful simulation-based calibration (SBC) false-positive rate <1% under M0.
0.3 If criteria not met: report upper limits on lensing strength; do not interpret residuals as IMBH evidence.

Step 1 — Quantitative order-of-magnitude detectability calculations (mandatory)
1.1 IMBH lensing time-delay scale (geometric optics upper bound):
  • For a point-mass lens, the characteristic lensing time scale is t0 = 4GM_L/c^3 ≈ 19.7 μs (M_L/M⊙).
  • Thus t0 ≈ 2 ms (10^2 M⊙), 20 ms (10^3 M⊙), 0.2 s (10^4 M⊙).
  • A relative GW“γ arrival-time perturbation due to lensing requires near alignment; otherwise the effective delay is far smaller than t0.
  • Compare to GW170817 γ delay (~2 s): an IMBH lens cannot explain the bulk delay unless M_L ≳ 10^5 M⊙ or extreme alignment; hence we do NOT model the 2 s delay as lensing.
1.2 Wave-optics regime relevant for LIGO band:
  • Dimensionless frequency parameter w = 8πGM_L f / c^3.
  • At f=100 Hz: w ≈ 0.12 (100 M⊙), 1.2 (10^3 M⊙), 12 (10^4 M⊙).
  • Therefore M_L ~ 10^3“10^4 M⊙ can produce frequency-dependent interference (amplitude/phase modulations) across 30“500 Hz, but only for small y.
1.3 Systematics floor comparison:
  • We will benchmark detectability against (i) published LIGO amplitude/phase calibration uncertainty envelopes for O2 and (ii) waveform-model systematics assessed by comparing at least two independent BNS waveform families.
  • If injected lensing signatures at (M_L,y) are not recoverable above these floors in SBC, that region is removed from the claimed testable space.

Step 2 — Data assembly (anchored to the provided assets)
2.1 GW: public LIGO/Virgo strain for GW170817; include calibration uncertainty marginalization.
2.2 γ-rays: Fermi-GBM + INTEGRAL time-tagged events / binned light curves and spectra; enforce instrument response (DRM) in-likelihood. Use INTEGRAL fluence constraint (75“2000 keV) and upper limits on soft γ afterglow explicitly as censored-data likelihood terms.
2.3 Optical: kilonova photometry/spectra time series for AT2017gfo; incorporate bandpasses and extinction.
2.4 Control sample for precursor regularization: Fermi/GBM short GRBs with statistically significant precursors (from systematic searches) with response matrices retained; use only to learn population-informed priors (not to “train away” GW170817 specifics).

Step 3 — Forward model architecture (differentiable, physics-constrained, with calibrated uncertainty)
3.1 Global parameter vector θ (core):
  • BNS: chirp mass, mass ratio, spins (restricted), tidal deformabilities (Λ1,Λ2) via an EoS parameterization.
  • Remnant/engine: prompt BH vs. hypermassive NS lifetime τ_rem (parametrized), jet power L_j(t), launch delay, baryon pollution parameter.
  • Ejecta: dynamical + wind components with M_ej, v_ej, angular structure, Ye distribution parameters.
  • Radiative: microphysical opacity κ(T,Ye), thermalization efficiency, r-process heating normalization.
  • Viewing geometry: inclination/θ_v consistent with GW constraints.
3.2 Module A (GW + EoS):
  • EoS parameterization: piecewise-polytrope or spectral EoS with explicit constraints: causality (c_s≤c), thermodynamic stability, and M_max ≥ 2.0 M⊙.
  • Waveforms: evaluate at least two BNS waveform models; marginalize waveform-systematic uncertainty by model averaging.
  • Output: GW likelihood with gradients for HMC/NUTS.
3.3 Module B (Jet“ejecta interaction + radiation surrogate):
  • High-fidelity simulator set: special relativistic (or GR-informed) hydrodynamics (RHD) of jet propagation through anisotropic wind + Monte Carlo radiative transfer (RT) for emergent γ spectra.
  • Surrogate type: Bayesian neural operator or emulator ensemble (e.g., deep ensemble + heteroscedastic head) that outputs both mean and predictive variance for time-resolved spectra and light curves.
  • Hard constraints via penalties and parameterizations:
    “ Energy-momentum conservation enforced as integral constraints on the surrogate outputs (e.g., penalty on ∂_μ T^{μν} residuals aggregated over the domain).
    “ Optical depth positivity and causal propagation (no superluminal breakout front).
    “ Baryon-loading/Γ consistency: enforce Γ(θ,t) bounded by available energy per baryon.
  • Outputs: precursor timing/fluence/spectrum (thermal vs non-thermal likelihood mixture), hard pulse properties, and predicted soft γ afterglow flux for comparison to upper limits.
3.4 Module C (Nuclear microphysics closure for kilonova):
  • Heating rate: calibrated analytic r-process heating law with uncertainty hyperparameters; opacity κ(T,Ye) from tabulated fits; two-component (blue/red) ejecta parameterization with Ye-linked opacities.
  • Radiative transfer (optical/IR) either via (i) a fast validated semi-analytic transport solver with uncertainty term, or (ii) an emulator trained on kilonova RT grids.
  • Output: multi-band light curves and color evolution tied to the same (M_ej,v_ej,Ye,geometry) used in Module B.

Step 4 — Emulator training design (mandatory specificity)
4.1 Simulation campaign design (RHD+γ RT):
  • Parameter ranges (initial):
    “ Jet luminosity L_j: 10^49“10^52 erg/s; duration 0.05“2 s.
    “ Jet opening/core angle: 2°“15°; structured wings slope range.
    “ Wind/ejecta mass: 10^-4“10^-1 M⊙; velocity 0.05“0.3c; angular stratification parameters.
    “ Opacity control via Ye: Ye ∈ [0.05,0.4] mapped to κ(T,Ye) priors.
    “ Viewing angle θ_v: 0°“40°.
  • Sampling strategy:
    “ Stage I: Latin hypercube / Sobol space-filling (≈300 RHD runs) to cover global behavior.
    “ Stage II: adaptive refinement (≈200 additional runs) targeting regions of high posterior mass and high emulator error (active learning based on expected information gain).
  • RT post-processing: for each RHD run, compute emergent spectra/light curves in GBM/INTEGRAL bands with at least two microphysics settings to span opacity/heating uncertainty.
4.2 Emulator uncertainty model:
  • Use a Bayesian/ensemble emulator returning predictive variance σ_em^2(t,E) and propagate it into the likelihood as an additive model discrepancy term: C_total = C_obs + C_em(θ) + C_cal.
  • Calibrate C_em using out-of-sample validation (≥20% held-out runs) and coverage diagnostics (e.g., 90% predictive intervals contain truth ~90% of the time).

Step 5 — Identifiability and simulation-based calibration (mandatory)
5.1 Identifiability metrics:
  • Compute local sensitivities (Fisher-information proxies) of (precursor delay, hard-pulse fluence, optical colors) to (θ_v, M_ej, L_j, Ye, τ_rem).
  • Require that posterior contraction is not driven solely by priors: enforce a “data informativity” threshold (e.g., KL divergence from prior) for key parameters.
5.2 SBC protocol:
  • Generate ≥500 synthetic multi-messenger datasets drawn from the prior, with realistic noise: GW noise consistent with O2 PSD + calibration uncertainty; GBM/INTEGRAL Poisson counts with DRM; optical photometric errors and cadence.
  • Fit with the full pipeline; verify rank statistics uniformity for θ_v, baryon loading proxy, breakout time, and τ_rem.
  • Model-mismatch tests: inject from (a) semi-analytic cocoon model and (b) alternative jet structure not in training set; quantify bias and inflate C_em if needed.

Step 6 — Baseline model comparison (mandatory)
6.1 Implement simpler physical baselines:
  • Baseline B1: semi-analytic cocoon shock breakout + structured jet prompt emission with parametric spectra.
  • Baseline B2: structured jet prompt + independent kilonova fit (sequential) representing standard practice.
6.2 Compare M0 to B1/B2 using Bayes factors with identical priors on shared parameters; require measurable evidence (pre-registered) that M0 improves joint predictive performance without overfitting (e.g., ln B(M0/B1) > 5).

Step 7 — IMBH lensing test (restricted, falsifiable)
7.1 IMBH model (M1) includes only:
  • Point-mass lens parameters: M_L ∈ [10^2,10^4] M⊙; y ∈ [0,3]; lens redshift fixed near host; no arbitrary phase polynomials.
  • Wave-optics amplification factor applied to GW frequency-domain waveform; compute induced amplitude/phase modulations.
7.2 Detectability map:
  • Injection“recovery across (M_L,y) grid; compute detection probability at fixed false-positive rate under M0.
  • Publicly report the “testable region” where recovery is robust above systematics floors; outside this region, the proposal commits to upper limits only.
7.3 Coupling to EM is limited to geometry consistency checks (not free anisotropy knobs):
  • We do NOT add an IMBH-driven ejecta anisotropy parameter unless it is independently required by data; any claimed coherence must come from the inferred θ_v/distance and lensing-consistent magnification constraints.

Step 8 — Deliverables
8.1 Posterior predictive reconstructions: INTEGRAL fluence; γ hard-pulse timing; soft γ afterglow upper limits; optical light curves/colors.
8.2 Published, calibrated emulator with documented coverage; SBC report; and (if applicable) IMBH lensing upper limits/detection statement under pre-registered criteria.
Feasibility: 1) Why the joint differentiable model is feasible and improves identifiability: GW170817 has high-SNR GW data plus uniquely rich EM constraints (γ fluence and stringent afterglow limits; well-sampled kilonova). - Perform variational inference over latent trajectories and EOS parameters.

Hypothesis: A stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) consistent with general relativity can be statistically identified in the NANOGrav 15-year dataset only through explicit generative model comparison, in which a transverse“traceless (TT) spin-2 metric-perturbation field is inferred jointly with — not in isolation from — physically parameterized non-GW correlated processes. The hypothesis is that identifiability of a genuine SGWB arises not because TT structure alone forbids contaminants, but because (i) the TT spin-2 field induces a uniquely constrained redshift response operator with fixed E/B and multipole couplings across pulsars and frequencies, while (ii) competing processes (solar-system ephemeris errors, clock errors, chromatic ISM/solar-wind processes, and flexible non-TT low-l correlated fields) imprint measurably different covariance structure once modeled with correct forward physics. By embedding the TT field within a complete likelihood that also includes these alternative generative processes, and by restricting binary-environment noise modeling to a calibrated hierarchical prior for a small, astrophysically justified subset of black widow/redback systems, the analysis can demonstrate—via Bayes factors and Fisher forecasts—that only a TT-consistent field simultaneously explains the observed quadrupolar correlations, their spectral slope, and their E/B content without violating pulsar-specific timing constraints. The SGWB inference is therefore elevated from a kernel-detection problem to a falsifiable field-level model selection problem.
Plan: Step 1: Data and baseline likelihood construction.
1.1 Ingest the full NANOGrav 15-year timing-residual dataset, timing-model design matrices, backend/receiver metadata, and published white/red noise characterizations. Retain low-frequency timing-model parameters (spin-down, astrometry) in the likelihood rather than pre-fitting.
1.2 Construct the Fourier-domain residual likelihood with explicit separation into Earth-term and pulsar-term contributions, marginalizing pulsar terms analytically under distance priors (Gaussian in parallax or DM-based distance) and assuming random pulsar-term phases.

Step 2: Explicit generative model components (mandatory competing hypotheses).
2.1 TT SGWB field model:
- Define a stationary Gaussian spin-2 metric perturbation field h_ab(f, n) expanded in spin-2 spherical harmonics:
  h(f, n) = Σ_{l=2..l_max,m} [a^E_{lm}(f) _2Y_{lm}(n) + a^B_{lm}(f) _2Y_{lm}(n)].
- Impose isotropy or controlled anisotropy via priors: ⟨a^X_{lm}(f)a^{X'}_{l'm'}(f')⟩ = δ(f−f')δ_{ll'}δ_{mm'}δ_{XX'} C_l^X(f), with C_l^X(f) ≥ 0 enforced by log-amplitude or Cholesky parameterization.
- Map coefficients to per-pulsar Fourier residuals using the exact linear response operator:
  r_p(f) = Σ_{lm,X} R^X_{p,lm}(f; \hat{n}_p) a^X_{lm}(f),
  where R includes antenna pattern factors, Earth-term projection, and analytic marginalization over pulsar-term phases.

2.2 Competing correlated processes (included simultaneously):
- Solar-system ephemeris (SSE): Parameterize barycentric position errors via principal-component modes (as in BAYESEPHEM) with physically motivated priors.
- Clock error: Include a monopolar red process common to all pulsars with independent spectrum from the SGWB.
- Chromatic common process: Model frequency-dependent red noise with ν^{-2} or ν^{-4} scaling, representing solar wind / ISM contributions.
- Flexible non-TT low-l field: Introduce a scalar correlated sky field expanded in ordinary spherical harmonics (l ≤ 4) to capture generic low-l correlations not constrained to TT structure.

Step 3: Restricted binary-environment noise module (refined WD component).
3.1 Scope limitation: Apply only to a predefined subset of black widow and redback systems with observed eclipses, wind signatures, or measured \dot{P}_b.
3.2 Hierarchical prior (not hard constraints):
- Introduce latent orbital-variability processes with PSD amplitudes drawn from hyperpriors calibrated on observed \dot{P}_b, eclipse fraction, and historical timing-noise measurements.
- Allow correlations between orbital-variability noise and spin noise, but with population-level variance parameters inferred from the data.
3.3 Injection tests: Quantify how inclusion/exclusion of this module shifts SGWB Bayes factors and quadrupolar power recovery.

Step 4: Inference and computational strategy.
4.1 Likelihood factorization: Block parameters into (i) TT field coefficients per frequency, (ii) competing correlated-process amplitudes, (iii) per-pulsar noise terms, (iv) binary-environment hyperparameters.
4.2 Sampling: Use blocked Gibbs or HMC-within-Gibbs, exploiting linear-Gaussian structure of the field coefficients; validate scaling with l_max ≤ 6 and O(30“50) frequency bins.

Step 5: Validation and identifiability demonstrations.
5.1 Fisher-matrix and Bayes-factor forecasts using NANOGrav15 cadence/sky distribution to show separability of TT SGWB from non-TT low-l fields and chromatic processes.
5.2 Injection campaigns with pure TT SGWB, pure SSE/clock/chromatic processes, and mixtures.
5.3 E/B and multipole diagnostics computed directly on the reconstructed PTA redshift field (gradient/curl decomposition), without invoking astrometric VSH unless used purely as an external comparison.

Step 6: Optional astrometric consistency check (clearly defined or omitted).
6.1 If included, define the transfer function from TT metric perturbations to both PTA redshift and Gaia astrometric deflection fields in the overlapping nHz band, and compare only integrated quadrupolar power with published Gaia limits; otherwise, restrict consistency tests to PTA-internal E/B diagnostics.
Feasibility: The revised proposal directly addresses reviewer concerns by abandoning the claim that TT-by-construction inference alone excludes contaminants. Instead, feasibility rests on explicit generative model comparison, a standard and scalable PTA methodology. All competing processes included (SSE, clock, chromatic noise, scalar correlated fields) already exist in validated PTA pipelines; the novelty lies in embedding them alongside a spin-2 harmonic field representation with controlled anisotropy priors. The linear operator from spin-2 coefficients to timing residuals is well defined and computationally tractable, enabling analytic marginalization over pulsar terms. Restricting the binary-environment module to a small, relevant subset avoids overreach and replaces unphysical hard energy bounds with empirically calibrated hierarchical priors. Computational cost is bounded by low l_max and modest frequency resolution, and blocked sampling exploits the Gaussian structure of the latent field. The outcome is a falsifiable, quantitatively testable framework that can demonstrate—via Bayes factors and injections—whether the NANOGrav common red process is uniquely consistent with a TT SGWB.
