Hypothesis: A physically constrained, multi-messenger correlation inference that jointly fits pulsar timing residual cross-correlations (Hellings-Downs) and astrometric quasar proper-motion correlations can separate true stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) power from pulsar-specific white-noise contamination and clock/ephemeris systematics, yielding tighter and less biased posteriors on characteristic strain h_c(f) and hence on gravitational-wave energy density Omega_GW(f). Mechanism: the SGWB induces a unique quadrupolar spatial correlation kernel fixed by General Relativity (HD curve) that coherently couples all pulsar pairs and, independently, produces an astrometric quadrupole in quasar proper motions; in contrast, (i) pulsar white noise is uncorrelated between pulsars and lacks the HD angular dependence, and (ii) terrestrial time-standard errors act as a monopolar common process. Methodological adaptation: modify standard PTA Bayesian cross-correlation pipelines by replacing the usual free-form common-red process with a 'kernel-factorized' likelihood in which the cross-covariance is constrained to be a sum of physically admissible spatial kernels (HD quadrupole, monopole clock, dipole ephemeris) and whose SGWB spectrum is parameterized via an equation-of-state (EOS)-aware source prior that maps neutron-star structure (via TOV + causality bounds) to an allowed merger/phase-transition SGWB spectral family; the same SGWB spectral parameters are simultaneously required to explain/limit the Gaia astrometric HD curve, enforcing cross-domain consistency and reducing degeneracy with white-noise parameters.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Acquire PTA timing data products (e.g., NANOGrav-style time-of-arrival residuals, design matrices, observing-system metadata) and construct per-pulsar noise baselines including EFAC/EQUAD/ECORR-like white-noise parameters plus intrinsic red noise.
1.2 Acquire Gaia quasar proper-motion catalog and associated covariance systematics model; build quasar-pair angular-separation binned correlation estimates and/or vector spherical harmonics (VSH) summary coefficients.
1.3 Define a unified reference frequency grid (nHz band) and consistent conventions linking characteristic strain h_c(f), timing-residual power, and Omega_GW(f), including cosmological factors (H0) and ensuring units/normalizations are identical across PTA and astrometry.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Kernel-factorized multi-kernel covariance: implement a joint Gaussian-process likelihood with cross-covariance C_ij(f) = S_GW(f) * Gamma_HD(theta_ij) + S_clk(f) * Gamma_monopole + S_eph(f) * Gamma_dipole(theta_ij, n_hat) where Gamma_HD is the Hellings-Downs curve, Gamma_monopole is constant across pairs, and Gamma_dipole encodes ephemeris directionality; enforce positive-semidefinite constraints by parameterizing each spectral density S_x(f) with nonnegative basis weights.
2.2 White-noise adaptation: instead of fitting each pulsar’s white-noise parameters independently (which can absorb weak correlated power), introduce a hierarchical white-noise model with observing-system group-level hyperpriors and explicit constraints that forbid white-noise components from generating inter-pulsar correlations. Concretely, white-noise enters only the auto-covariances with block-diagonal structure, and hyperpriors shrink EFAC/EQUAD/ECORR to instrument-calibrated ranges to reduce leakage into the correlated kernel.
2.3 EOS-aware SGWB spectral prior (nuclear physics integration): augment the SGWB spectral model beyond a generic power law by a mixture family whose components are derived from physically simulated source populations sensitive to neutron-star EOS (e.g., post-merger oscillations, possible first-order phase transitions, r-mode instability contributions) while enforcing causality (sound speed <= c), thermodynamic stability, and TOV consistency. Precompute a surrogate mapping from EOS parameter sets -> allowed SGWB spectral shapes S_GW(f) in the PTA band; use this as an informative prior on S_GW(f) rather than an unconstrained spline.
2.4 Astrometric coupling: add a second likelihood term for Gaia in which the predicted correlated proper-motion field has quadrupolar VSH coefficients determined by the same S_GW(f) (frequency-integrated response appropriate to Gaia time baseline). The adaptation is to treat the Gaia 'astrometric HD curve' as an external correlated-kernel measurement sharing the SGWB parameters, rather than as an independent upper limit.
2.5 Inference engine: perform joint sampling (e.g., Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with constrained parameterizations for PSD positivity) and compute Bayes factors comparing (A) SGWB+clock+ephemeris vs (B) clock+ephemeris only vs (C) uncorrelated red-noise only, ensuring model selection is driven by spatial correlation structure.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Injection-recovery: inject synthetic SGWB signals with known h_c(f) and known HD correlations into real PTA noise realizations, including realistic white-noise miscalibration; quantify bias/variance on recovered Omega_GW(f) with and without the hierarchical white-noise adaptation and EOS-aware priors.
3.2 Null tests for systematics: rotate pulsar sky positions (breaking true HD geometry) and verify SGWB evidence collapses; perform time-scrambles to confirm correlations are not from shared observing cadence.
3.3 Cross-messenger consistency: verify the posterior predictive distribution for the Gaia astrometric HD curve is consistent with observed quasar correlations; if inconsistent, identify whether the mismatch is due to Gaia systematics, incorrect SGWB spectral assumptions, or non-GR polarizations.
3.4 Nuclear-physics deliverables: translate recovered Omega_GW(f) constraints into exclusions on EOS families and on phase-transition parameters (latent heat, transition density) using the surrogate mapping, reporting constraints consistent with causality and maximum-mass observations.
3.5 Robustness: repeat with different pulsar subsets and different white-noise hyperprior strengths; demonstrate that HD correlation detection significance and inferred h_c are stable to these choices.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: General Relativity fixes the HD quadrupolar angular correlation for an isotropic tensor SGWB, while clock (monopole) and ephemeris (dipole) kernels provide a complete low-order correlated-systematics basis routinely used in PTA analyses. Astrometric quasar proper motions admit an analogous quadrupolar response, and existing work has already constructed an astrometric HD curve and translated it to h_c and Omega_GW upper limits, demonstrating empirical viability.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): High-energy astrophysics and nuclear physics enter through physically constrained priors on SGWB spectral shapes linked to neutron-star microphysics (EOS, phase structure) and through enforcing relativistic kernel structure rather than black-box correlation fits. The joint PTA+Gaia approach leverages independent observables of the same spacetime strain field, turning what are typically separate analyses into a single physically coupled inference.
3. Comparative Advantage: (i) Reduced degeneracy: hierarchical white-noise modeling plus strict block-diagonal enforcement prevents white-noise parameters from absorbing correlated power, improving separation of true HD correlations from misestimated measurement noise. (ii) Stronger identifiability: requiring one SGWB spectrum to explain both timing and astrometric correlations suppresses false positives driven by PTA-specific systematics and tightens h_c/Omega_GW posteriors. (iii) Physics-grounded constraints: EOS-aware, causality-respecting spectral priors enable direct nuclear-physics inference (and avoid unphysical spectral fits), improving interpretability and robustness compared to unconstrained power-law-only pipelines.

Hypothesis: Kilonova-associated compact-binary mergers that exhibit a fading/plateau-like X-ray counterpart are powered by (at least) one of two physically distinct channels—(A) an external-shock afterglow from an angularly structured outflow (jet+cocoon energy stratification) viewed off-axis and/or (B) a long-lived central engine whose luminosity is only partially coupled to the forward shock (magnetar spin-down and/or fallback)—and these channels imprint *probabilistic* (not hard) cross-band relations between (i) X-ray temporal behavior, (ii) late-time radio rise/peak, and (iii) kilonova ejecta energetics. The key methodological claim is that unbiased discrimination and parameter inference require explicitly marginalizing over synchrotron spectral regimes and model inadequacy, rather than enforcing approximate closure relations or ad hoc temporal-ordering inequalities.

We hypothesize that a regime-marginalized, physics-constrained multi-messenger state-space model (PC‑MMSSI‑RM) will outperform standard band-by-band fitting and unconstrained joint regression because it (1) propagates dynamical constraints through time (energy/momentum evolution with optional injection) while (2) *integrating over uncertainty in emission regime membership* (ordering of νa, νm, νc relative to each observing band) and (3) *explicitly modeling approximation error* (microphysics evolution, scintillation, trans-relativistic transition, absorption), thereby preventing overconfident posteriors when the canonical closure assumptions fail. In this framework, the apparent ‘temporal ordering’ between an X-ray fade and a radio rise is not imposed; it emerges as a posterior-predictive consequence of the inferred regime trajectories and dynamics. Finally, coupling GW posteriors to central-engine viability is informative only if the remnant-lifetime mapping is treated as model-uncertain; we therefore predict that comparing at least two remnant evolution prescriptions with hyperpriors (prompt-collapse threshold vs differential-rotation-supported magnetar) will yield robust remnant-lifetime constraints without allowing an overly informative EoS prior to dominate EM inference.
Plan: Step 1 — Data assembly, homogenization, and selection modeling
1.1 Sample definition:
- Primary sample: BNS/NSBH candidates with public GW posterior samples (LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA), identified kilonova candidates (UV/optical/NIR photometry and, when available, spectra), X-ray light curves with either detections or meaningful upper limits spanning ≥ hours to days (Swift/XRT, NICER, Chandra/XMM), and radio follow-up (VLA/MeerKAT/ATCA/GMRT) including deep non-detections.
- Include at least one ‘template’ event with well-studied multi-wavelength behavior (GW170817-like) as an internal validation anchor; include at least one high-energy transient with a fading X-ray counterpart and weak/absent optical/radio constraints (EP-like) as a stress-test for regime ambiguity and censored likelihood handling.

1.2 Time/flux standardization:
- Convert all times to rest-frame using redshift posteriors (spectroscopic when available; otherwise host photometric-redshift prior).
- Calibrate fluxes to common conventions with instrument response where needed; include per-instrument calibration nuisance parameters (multiplicative flux scale with Gaussian prior) and additive background terms for low-S/N regimes.

1.3 Observing-coverage and selection effects:
- Construct band-dependent coverage masks: cadence, limiting flux (or sensitivity curve), and scheduling windows.
- Likelihood conditions on “observed given scheduled” rather than assuming uniform sampling; incorporate detection efficiency for each band (especially radio) as part of the generative model.


Step 2 — Generative model: regime-marginalized broadband synchrotron + optional engine + kilonova, in a state-space framework
2.1 Latent state vector and dynamics (dimension reduction included):
- Latent physical state at time t:
  x(t) = {log E(t), log n, θobs, jet-structure params, microphysics params, regime indicators, engine params, kilonova ejecta params, nuisance/systematics}.
- Dimension reduction choices (to control particle degeneracy):
  (i) Use a parsimonious structured-jet parameterization (e.g., Gaussian or power-law angular structure) with 3“4 parameters total: {Ecore, θc, aE, Γcore} (or equivalent), rather than free-form angular bins.
  (ii) External density assumed constant ISM initially; allow wind-like profile as a discrete alternative model (k∈{0,2}) and marginalize.
  (iii) Microphysics: start with constant {εe, εB, p} with weakly informative priors; include an optional slow evolution model εB(t)=εB,0 (t/t0)^αB with αB ~ Normal(0,σ) as a discrepancy-capturing extension, not default.

2.2 Synchrotron emission with explicit spectral-regime marginalization (Mandatory Directive #1):
- For each epoch and band b with observing frequency νb, define the break frequencies νa(t), νm(t), νc(t) and peak flux Fmax(t) from the dynamical state.
- Introduce a discrete regime variable rb(t) encoding the ordering of {νa,νm,νc} relative to νb. Example regime set R includes the commonly relevant slow/fast cooling cases and self-absorption placements; e.g.:
  R = { (νa<νm<νc), (νm<νa<νc), (νm<νc<νa), (νa<νc<νm), … } × {slow, fast}, pruned to physically allowed subsets for the inferred parameters.
- Likelihood is regime-marginalized:
  p(Fb(t)|x(t)) = Σ_{r∈R} p(Fb(t)|x(t),r) p(r|x(t))
  where p(r|x(t)) is induced by the implied ordering probabilities (softened with tolerance to avoid discontinuous regime switching).
- Model discrepancy hyperparameters:
  Add multiplicative scatter terms per band and per spectral segment:
  log Fb,obs(t) ~ Normal(log Fb,model(t), σstat^2 + σsys,b^2 + σseg(r)^2)
  where σseg(r) captures closure-relation inadequacy (e.g., evolving breaks, weak microphysics evolution, trans-relativistic deviations).
- Scintillation and radio systematics:
  In radio, add an extra variance term σscint(t,ν) informed by standard scintillation prescriptions, with a hyperparameter scaling factor to absorb model mismatch.

2.3 Engine + energy injection as a probabilistic coupling, not a hard constraint:
- External-shock energy evolution:
  dE/dt = ξ(t) Lengine(t) − Lrad,FS(t)
  with coupling efficiency ξ(t) ∈ [0,1]. Parameterize ξ(t)=sigmoid(ξ0 + ξ1 log(t/t0)) to allow early/late coupling differences.
- Engine channels:
  (i) Magnetar spin-down: Lsd(t)=L0 (1+t/tsd)^{-2} with (B, P0) mapped to (L0, tsd).
  (ii) Fallback accretion: Lfb(t)=L1 (t/t1)^{-5/3} with cutoff time and radiative efficiency.
- X-ray emission model allows mixture:
  FX(t)=ηX,FS FFS,X(t) + ηX,eng Feng,X(t)
  where ηX terms are efficiencies; Feng,X may be a fraction of Lengine with absorption and spectral index. This prevents forcing X-rays to be afterglow-only when an internal/engine component is present.

2.4 Kilonova module with surrogate and discrepancy:
- Multi-component ejecta: {Mej,i, vej,i, Xlan,i} for i∈{blue, purple, red} (or a 2-component minimal model if data are sparse).
- Heating constraints: impose r-process heating rate priors (e.g., power-law with uncertain normalization) as soft priors; include a thermalization efficiency model with uncertainty hyperparameters.
- Radiative transfer surrogate: train/employ an emulator (e.g., GP/NN) validated to ≤0.1 mag RMS in bands used for inference; include emulator error σemu(λ,t) in the likelihood.


Step 3 — Remnant-lifetime mapping with model uncertainty (Mandatory Directive #2)
3.1 EoS-constrained priors (not dominating):
- Use GW posterior samples for (Mchirp, q, \tilde{Λ}) to infer component masses and tidal deformabilities.
- Adopt a parametric EoS family (piecewise polytrope or spectral) with causality (cs≤c) and stability enforced.

3.2 Two remnant evolution prescriptions (compared and/or averaged):
Model A: Prompt-collapse threshold (PC) prescription
- Use an empirical threshold relation Mth = k(Cmax, R1.6, …) Mmax,TOV with uncertainty; collapse is prompt if Mtot > Mth.
- Survival time τ is then effectively ~ dynamical (≪1 s), with a soft transition width ΔM modeling uncertainty.

Model B: Differential-rotation-supported magnetar (DR) prescription
- If not prompt-collapse, remnant survival time τ = min(τDR, τsd, τν) where:
  τDR: differential rotation removal timescale with log-uniform prior spanning 10“10^4 s (magnetic braking/viscosity uncertainty)
  τsd: spin-down time from magnetar parameters
  τν: neutrino cooling / thermal support decay timescale with broad prior.
- Implement τ as a latent variable with hyperpriors; connect τ to allowed engine luminosity duration and total injected energy.

3.3 Bayesian model comparison / stacking:
- Either (i) perform explicit model selection between A and B via Bayes factors, or (ii) use Bayesian stacking/model averaging to propagate remnant-model uncertainty into downstream EM parameters.
- Posterior check: verify that inferred τ and engine luminosity do not overpredict observed gamma-ray limits when applicable.


Step 4 — Inference engine, computational plan, and diagnostics (Mandatory Directive #3)
4.1 Inference strategy (hybrid SMC + PMCMC with tempering):
- Use SMC with likelihood tempering to mitigate particle impoverishment in high dimension.
- Conditional SMC / particle Gibbs for blocks with strong temporal dependence (E(t), regime trajectories).
- Blocked sampling:
  Block 1: GW/EoS/remnant hyperparameters
  Block 2: Kilonova parameters
  Block 3: Afterglow/jet/microphysics
  Block 4: Engine + coupling ξ(t)
  Block 5: Systematics/discrepancy terms

4.2 Particle count scaling and complexity targets:
- Start with Np ~ 2,000 particles for single-event fits; scale to 5,000“20,000 for multi-event hierarchical inference depending on ESS.
- Target effective sample size ESS/Np ≥ 0.2 after each tempering step; adapt tempering increments to maintain ESS.
- Wall-time budget: ensure each forward evaluation (afterglow+engine+regime marginalization+KN surrogate) ≤ 5“20 ms; this sets feasibility for ~10^7 evaluations on an HPC allocation.

4.3 Surrogate accuracy targets and validation:
- Kilonova surrogate: ≤0.1 mag RMS; include σemu in likelihood.
- Afterglow fast evaluator: precompute/fit a reduced-order surrogate for dynamical evolution if needed; validate against a high-fidelity code on a Latin hypercube design.

4.4 Diagnostics for particle degeneracy and identifiability:
- Monitor ESS, resampling frequency, ancestor diversity, and parameter R-hat / rank plots (simulation-based calibration).
- If degeneracy occurs:
  (i) tighten dimension reduction (fix k=0 unless data demand otherwise; restrict microphysics evolution),
  (ii) increase tempering steps,
  (iii) use rejuvenation moves with gradient-informed proposals on continuous blocks,
  (iv) switch to variational initialization + PMCMC refinement.


Step 5 — Derived X-ray“radio timing relations (emergent, then checked)
5.1 Derivation within the model:
- For each posterior draw, compute the implied light curves and extract summary times: tX,break (end of plateau / start of decline), tR,peak (radio peak), and slopes αX, αR.
- The ‘temporal ordering’ becomes a posterior distribution over Δt = tR,peak − tX,break conditioned on the inferred regime path and dynamics, rather than a pre-imposed inequality.

5.2 Assumption checks:
- Posterior probability that X-ray band lies above/below νc at relevant epochs; probability of fast vs slow cooling; probability that X-rays are engine-dominated (ηX,eng fraction).
- Only when posterior mass concentrates in a regime subset do we report simplified analytic relations; otherwise we report regime-averaged predictive intervals.


Step 6 — Validation, ablations, and deliverables
6.1 Synthetic injection campaigns:
- Generate simulated datasets spanning: prompt-collapse, long-lived magnetar with partial coupling, structured jet off-axis, cocoon-dominated, and mixed engine+afterglow X-rays.
- Include evolving break frequencies, modest microphysics drift, scintillation in radio, and realistic cadence/upper limits.

6.2 Ablation study (Mandatory Directive #4):
Quantify sensitivity and bias when removing or simplifying:
- (A) regime marginalization (force a single regime)
- (B) discrepancy hyperparameters (σseg→0)
- (C) remnant model uncertainty (use only Model A or only Model B)
- (D) radio censoring likelihood (treat as detections at limit or omit)
- (E) surrogate error terms (σemu→0)
Report changes in posterior coverage (SBC), Bayes factors, and key parameters (n, θobs, E, Mej, τ).

6.3 Posterior predictive checks:
- Jointly reproduce detections and non-detections, spectral indices, and cross-band covariance.
- Explicitly test whether the model overpredicts radio given X-ray fits, and whether regime probabilities are consistent with observed spectral slopes.

6.4 Deliverables:
- Public pipeline implementing PC‑MMSSI‑RM with documented likelihood components, discrepancy terms, and model-averaging over remnant prescriptions.
- A catalog of physically consistent multi-messenger posteriors for the curated sample.
- A follow-up decision product: given early X-ray evolution and GW posterior, output a predictive distribution for radio detectability vs time/frequency to optimize scheduling.
Feasibility: Scientific feasibility (addresses over-constraint and bias risk):
- Closure relations are treated as *regime-conditioned approximations* rather than hard constraints. By marginalizing over spectral regimes and including discrepancy hyperparameters (per segment and per band), the model remains valid when breaks traverse bands, microphysics drift modestly, or when trans-relativistic/scintillation effects perturb canonical slopes. This directly prevents the failure mode identified by reviewers: excluding the true model via infinite barriers.
- The X-ray“radio ‘ordering’ is not imposed. Timing relations are derived from posterior predictive light curves under explicitly stated assumptions (regime membership and dominance of FS vs engine), and we include posterior checks to verify whether those assumptions hold. This converts an ad hoc discriminator into an auditable inference product.

Remnant/EoS coupling feasibility (prevents an overly informative prior):
- The remnant-lifetime mapping is explicitly model-uncertain: we implement and compare two prescriptions (prompt-collapse threshold vs differential-rotation-supported magnetar) with broad hyperpriors on poorly known timescales (magnetic braking, neutrino cooling). This ensures GW-to-τ coupling is informative only when supported by EM data, reducing the chance of an artificially narrow, prior-driven remnant lifetime.

Computational feasibility (addresses engineering risk):
- We reduce state dimension via a low-parameter structured-jet model, discrete model indices for density profile and remnant prescription, and optional (not default) microphysics evolution.
- We set explicit surrogate accuracy targets (≤0.1 mag for kilonova) and carry surrogate error into the likelihood to avoid overconfident inference.
- We specify particle scaling, ESS-based tempering, blocked inference, and fallback remedies for particle impoverishment (dimension tightening, increased tempering, rejuvenation moves, variational initialization). This operationalizes the computational plan rather than gesturing at “SMC + surrogates.”

Empirical grounding:
- Multi-wavelength joint constraints have been demonstrated in GW170817-like systems where structured jets and kilonova components are simultaneously constrained, and radio data critically restrict density/microphysics. The proposed extension is the statistically disciplined handling of regime ambiguity and model discrepancy, which is essential for events with fading X-ray counterparts and sparse/upper-limit radio data (including EP-like cases).

Hypothesis: In BH“NS mergers that enter a transient black-hole-pulsar state, fast magnetosonic compressive pulses launched by magnetospheric deformation steepen into a monster shock only if the outgoing wave packet encounters a radially localized breakdown of force-free conditions (finite inertia/baryon loading) that creates a super-fast magnetosonic transition layer. We hypothesize that the location and strength of this transition layer—and thus the shock energetics that power the hot outflow and prompt EM counterparts—depend measurably on the neutron-star EOS through its control of (i) magnetospheric density supply and (ii) collapse/ringdown-driven boundary motion. Methodological adaptation: develop a physically constrained, multi-regime GRMHD“FFE hybrid solver that replaces standard ad-hoc FFE-to-MHD “density floors” with a conservative, characteristic-matched interface plus EOS-conditioned pair/baryon injection closure, ensuring causality and Rankine“Hugoniot consistency across the fast magnetosonic surface and enabling reliable prediction of shock formation and outflow observables.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Construct a suite of BH“NS merger initial data spanning NS EOS families (soft/medium/stiff; constrained to causal sound speed cs<=c and maximum mass constraints) and NS magnetic dipole inclinations.
1.2 For each EOS, precompute consistent NS structure (mass-radius, compactness, tidal deformability) and magnetospheric footpoint motion profiles through inspiral-to-plunge using GR (ensuring consistent metric evolution and BH spin).
1.3 Define a minimal microphysical injection model: EOS-conditioned surface baryon ablation + curvature-radiation pair supply, parameterized by compactness and surface gravity, producing an inertia map that is negligible in most of the magnetosphere but can become finite in current sheets and in the outgoing compressive wave.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Implement a hybrid GR solver with domain decomposition: inner region evolved with conservative GRMHD (shock-capturing, constrained transport), outer region evolved with GR force-free electrodynamics (FFE). Couple them with a new characteristic-matched interface at a moving radius r_int(t) chosen to track where magnetization sigma=B^2/(4pi rho h c^2) crosses a target threshold.
2.2 Methodological adaptation (core): replace common “density/pressure floors” and diffusive handoff with a Riemann-characteristic projection across the interface. Specifically, decompose the state into incoming/outgoing characteristic fields for the fast magnetosonic and Alfven modes; enforce continuity of the tangential E and B fields, enforce conservative flux matching for energy-momentum, and impose Rankine“Hugoniot jump conditions for compressive/fast-mode steepening when gradients exceed a shock sensor threshold.
2.3 Embed physics constraints directly: (i) enforce E·B=0 and E^2<B^2 in the FFE region via constrained transport plus a Lagrange-multiplier correction that minimally adjusts E to satisfy the invariant; (ii) enforce causal EOS in the GRMHD region using tabulated EOS with slope limiting to keep cs<=c; (iii) enforce global energy-angular momentum accounting by tracking Poynting, matter, and gravitational fluxes through world-tube surfaces.
2.4 Add an EOS-conditioned injection closure at the interface and in current sheets: inject minimal inertia consistent with the microphysical supply model (pair multiplicity + baryon ablation) rather than numerical floors; injection rate is constrained to keep sigma above a controlled bound except where the computed wave pressure forces sigma downward, enabling a physically motivated super-fast transition layer.
2.5 Diagnostics: compute (a) fast magnetosonic Mach number and the formation of a super-fast region; (b) shock formation radius and compression ratio; (c) hot-outflow enthalpy, baryon loading, and magnetization; (d) time-domain modulation from BH quasi-normal mode forcing (ringdown) imprinted on the compressive wave train.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Code verification: recover analytic/benchmark solutions—force-free wave propagation, relativistic MHD shocks, and magnetosonic mode speeds in curved spacetime; demonstrate interface stability and convergence with refinement.
3.2 Cross-regime validation: reproduce key qualitative features from prior literature assets: outgoing compressive waves/fast magnetosonic pulses (Asset 1), monster shock launching a hot outflow (Asset 2), and BH“NS-induced fast-mode waves steepening into monster shocks with a transient black-hole-pulsar configuration (Asset 3).
3.3 EOS inference test: generate synthetic multimessenger observables (prompt gamma/X transient energetics, FRB-like coherent precursor proxy based on Poynting spikes, and timing modulation linked to ringdown); quantify how inferred shock radius/strength correlates with tidal deformability and compactness. Use Bayesian model comparison to show that the adapted interface/injection model yields tighter EOS posteriors than standard floor-based hybrids.
3.4 Robustness: vary magnetic inclination, BH spin, and injection uncertainties; demonstrate that shock/no-shock bifurcation and hot-outflow baryon loading are controlled by physically interpretable dimensionless numbers (sigma profile slope, fast-mode steepening parameter, compactness-controlled injection), not by numerical artifacts.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Existing GRMHD/FFE studies already show fast magnetosonic compressive pulses that can steepen into shocks and launch hot outflows during collapse/merger; however, shock formation and baryon loading are notoriously sensitive to how inertia is introduced in nominally force-free regions. The proposed characteristic-matched interface and EOS-conditioned injection directly target this known failure mode while preserving conservation laws and invariants.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): High-energy astrophysical outflows straddle regimes from magnetically dominated (FFE-like) to inertia-dominated (MHD-like). A characteristic-based coupling respects the hyperbolic structure of both systems (fast/Alfven modes) and enforces physically correct transmission/reflection of compressive/fast magnetosonic waves, which is essential for predicting monster-shock onset. EOS constraints enter via compactness/tidal effects and causality-limited thermodynamics, connecting nuclear physics to shock energetics and hot-outflow baryon content.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with standard hybrid schemes that rely on numerical floors and diffusive handoffs, the adapted method (i) reduces spurious shock triggering/suppression by enforcing Rankine“Hugoniot-consistent steepening, (ii) yields physically interpretable control over baryon loading through an injection closure linked to EOS-dependent surface conditions, and (iii) improves multimessenger predictivity (shock radius, outflow magnetization, ringdown modulation) necessary for EOS inference from prompt EM counterparts to GW events.

Hypothesis: Impulsive magnetospheric energy release events in the Galactic Center (either intrinsic to Sagittarius A*’s magnetized funnel or driven by nearby compact objects such as SGR J1745-2900) generate a force-free electrodynamic (FFE) fast-mode pulse that steepens into a magnetosonic shock and deposits a predictable fraction of its Poynting flux into surrounding molecular clouds, producing a coupled UV-flash + delayed Chandra X-ray fluorescence/light-echo signature. Methodological adaptation: we will modify standard time-dependent FFE solvers by embedding a physically constrained, reduced microphysics closure (FFE→radiation+cloud transfer) that converts the shock’s electromagnetic dissipation into UV emissivity and K-shell fluorescence, while enforcing invariants (E·B=0, B^2−E^2>0, charge conservation) via constrained transport and variational projection; this guarantees that inferred injection histories and the resulting electromagnetic counterpart templates remain consistent with force-free dynamics and with radiative transfer through clumpy molecular clouds. Mechanism: in FFE, an impulsive twist/reconnection event launches a fast magnetosonic disturbance with dominantly transverse fields; geometric focusing near the central engine and non-linear steepening create current sheets where dissipation occurs. The dissipated Poynting flux accelerates electrons that (i) produce prompt UV via synchrotron/curvature components and (ii) irradiate nearby molecular material; in dense clouds, photoionization yields UV reprocessing and Fe Kα fluorescence, producing an X-ray echo observable with Chandra. Because FFE fixes the field topology and energy flux transport, the UV-to-X-ray (echo) energy partition and timing are not free parameters but are constrained by field invariants, cloud column density, and light-travel geometry—enabling a physically grounded electromagnetic counterpart model for Galactic-center transients.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Compile Chandra archival event lists and imaging for Sgr A* region covering known flare epochs and molecular-cloud Fe Kα echo monitoring; extract time-resolved spectra/light curves for candidate reflection nebulae (e.g., Sgr B2-like substructures) and for the central point source region with careful pileup and background treatment.
1.2 Assemble molecular cloud 3D/kinematic priors from existing CO/CS line surveys (positions, velocity components, approximate distances) to build a probabilistic light-travel-time kernel for each cloud clump.
1.3 Define a small set of physically motivated injection scenarios: (A) Sgr A* funnel twist/reconnection; (B) magnetar-driven pulse; (C) hybrid. For each, specify initial magnetic topology and characteristic scales consistent with measured Galactic-center field constraints.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Implement a time-dependent, general-relativistic-appropriate FFE module in a simplified Kerr background (or pseudo-Newtonian approximation for targeted radii), using constrained-transport evolution for B and a variational projection step each timestep to enforce E·B=0 and B^2−E^2>0; include a positivity-preserving limiter that prevents superluminal drift in under-resolved current sheets.
2.2 Methodological adaptation (key): couple the FFE solver to a reduced dissipation+emission closure at current sheets: introduce an invariant-based dissipation functional Q = α * max(0, J·E) constrained so that global energy conservation holds (Poynting flux loss equals radiated+particle energy gain), and map Q into a two-channel emissivity model—prompt UV (synchrotron/curvature-like with parameters tied to local B and dissipation scale) plus an ionizing/X-ray photon field.

1. Generative pulse-transfer model (core adaptation): model the observed photon time series in each energy band E as
   x_E(t) = [s(t; \nu, \dot{\nu}, orbit) * h_E(t; \Theta(t))] + b_E(t),
   where s(t) is the intrinsic spin-locked pulse train (including harmonics), and h_E is an energy-dependent impulse response function (IRF) representing scattering/propagation in the accretion shock/column/boundary layer; \Theta(t) are physical state parameters tied to accretion rate.
2. Physics-constrained IRF family:
   - Use a minimum-parameter IRF whose moments are physically interpretable and bounded: mean delay \langle\tau_E\rangle, variance \sigma^2_{\tau,E}, and a causal tail index. Enforce strict causality: h_E(\tau<0)=0, \int h_E d\tau = 1.
   - Link \langle\tau_E\rangle and \sigma_{\tau,E} to Comptonization and size constraints: optical depth \tau_T(t), electron temperature kT_e(t), and characteristic size \ell(t) with \ell \le f\,R (f<~a few), so \langle\tau\rangle \sim (N_{sc}/c)\lambda and N_{sc} consistent with Kompaneets y-parameter (y \approx 4kT_e/m_ec^2\,\max(\tau_T,\tau_T^2)). This ties timing lags directly to spectral hardness and flux.
   - Enforce energy and angular-momentum budgets: luminosity sets maximum heating power available to the scattering region; require that inferred Compton y and coronal heating fraction do not exceed L_X.
3. Frequency-domain deconvolution timing estimator:
   - Work in Fourier domain for each segment. The complex Fourier coefficient at harmonic n and energy E satisfies X_{n,E} = S_n \cdot H_{n,E}(\Theta) + noise. Here H_{n,E} is the Fourier transform of h_E.
   - Jointly fit across energies and harmonics to infer (i) the intrinsic rotational phase evolution (\nu, \dot{\nu}), and (ii) the IRF parameters \Theta(t) that vary with flux.
   - Key identifiability lever: intrinsic spin shifts produce energy-independent phase drifts at fixed harmonic, while propagation IRF produces an energy-dependent phase \arg H_{n,E} and amplitude attenuation |H_{n,E}|; constrain both using the measured cross-spectral lags and pulsed fractions.

Hypothesis: Neutron star“black hole (NSBH) coalescences produce detectable electromagnetic (EM) counterparts primarily when the neutron star is tidally disrupted outside the black hole ISCO, and that same disruption changes (i) the remnant/ejecta properties that power kilonova/afterglow emission and (ii) the terminal gravitational-wave (GW) signal morphology at high frequencies. The key methodological claim is not that a >700 Hz “cutoff” is always measurable, but that a rigorously specified, bias-controlled generative model—explicitly separating a latent disruption state D and ejecta properties E—enables two complementary inference pathways: (A) a conservative GW-only pathway where disruption affects inference only through EoS-consistent priors and (when identifiable) a statistically validated high-frequency disruption component, and (B) a GW+EM pathway where EM data constrain E (and thus D) without double-counting NR fits. This architecture overcomes reviewer-noted risks by (1) enforcing conditional-independence structure so NR-calibrated mappings are used once via shared latent variables rather than twice as pseudo-independent evidence, (2) activating the waveform-level disruption imprint only in a quantified identifiability regime (network/SNR/bandwidth threshold) that is robust to calibration and known waveform systematics (precession, higher modes, PSD uncertainty), and (3) improving follow-up efficiency primarily via physically consistent reweighting of distance“inclination and q“spin“EoS degeneracies into an explicit sky-dependent detectability map, rather than claiming unconditional localization area reductions. The measurable outcome is a ranked, telescope-specific EM detectability sky map and a set of preregistered ablation results that state exactly when (and why) EoS constraints, disruption-imprint waveform terms, and EM coupling improve 3D localization and reduce false-positive follow-up burden for HLV/HKLV/HIKLV networks.
Plan: Step 0 — Define a bias-controlled generative model (graphical model + factorized likelihood).
0.1 Latent variables and observed data.
- Intrinsic binary parameters: θ_int = {m_NS, m_BH, χ_BH (magnitude), tilt β, spin azimuth, (optionally) χ_NS}, extrinsic parameters: θ_ext = {α, δ, d_L, ι, ψ, t_c, φ_c}.
- Neutron-star EoS hyperparameters: ϕ_EoS via spectral parameterization; derived NS structure: {R(m_NS), C(m_NS), Λ(m_NS)}.
- Latent disruption state: D ∈ {0,1} (non-disruptive / disruptive).
- Latent ejecta and remnant properties: E = {M_ej, v_ej, X_lan (or Y_e), disk mass M_disk, polar/equatorial partition}, and jet/afterglow parameters J (optional): {E_jet, θ_j, n_ISM, ε_e, ε_B}.
- Observables: GW strain data d_GW from detector network; EM photometry/spectra/upper limits d_EM with cadence/censoring.

0.2 NR-informed maps as conditional distributions (used once).
- Disruption probability model: p(D=1 | θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR) where κ_NR indexes an NR-fit family; built from R_tid/R_ISCO with a calibrated transition width. This is not a delta-function threshold; it is a probabilistic classifier with uncertainty.
- Ejecta model: p(E | D, θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR) (NR-calibrated fits + intrinsic scatter).
- EM radiative-transfer surrogate: p(d_EM | E, θ_ext, κ_RT) with κ_RT an RT/surrogate family index; includes detection/non-detection likelihood with survey depth and cadence.

0.3 GW likelihood with optional disruption-imprint component under identifiability gating.
- Baseline: p(d_GW | θ_int, θ_ext, ϕ_EoS, κ_wf, κ_cal, κ_PSD) using waveform family κ_wf (including precession/higher modes variants) and calibration/PSD nuisance parameters.
- Disruption-imprint augmentation: introduce a physically motivated spectral modification S(f; θ_int, ϕ_EoS, D, κ_NR) applied only if the data support it (see Step 2). Importantly, the imprint’s amplitude is not freely fit without penalty: it is tied to θ_int and ϕ_EoS through D with explicit uncertainty.

0.4 Full joint posterior with selection effects.
Write the hierarchical posterior (schematically):

p(θ_int, θ_ext, ϕ_EoS, D, E, κ_NR, κ_RT, κ_wf, κ_cal, κ_PSD | d_GW, d_EM, S_GW, S_EM)
∝ p(d_GW | θ_int, θ_ext, ϕ_EoS, D, κ_NR, κ_wf, κ_cal, κ_PSD)
  × p(d_EM | E, θ_ext, κ_RT)
  × p(E | D, θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR)
  × p(D | θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR)
  × p(θ_int, θ_ext) p(ϕ_EoS) p(κ_NR) p(κ_RT) p(κ_wf) p(κ_cal) p(κ_PSD)
  × [α_sel(θ_int, θ_ext, E)]^{-1}.

Selection factor α_sel accounts for:
- GW selection: P(det_GW | θ_int, θ_ext, κ_PSD, network) via injection-based efficiency or semi-analytic SNR thresholding.
- EM selection (if conditioning on EM-triggered follow-up or detection): P(followed-up/identified | sky position, depth, cadence, host extinction) and censoring via upper limits.

This factorization prevents double-counting: NR information enters only through p(D|…) and p(E|D, …) (shared latent variables), while GW and EM data contribute through separate likelihoods p(d_GW|…) and p(d_EM|…).

Step 1 — Data/model assembly with explicit domain coverage and OOD safeguards.
1.1 Simulation suite.
- Generate NSBH populations over q = m_BH/m_NS, BH spin magnitude |χ_BH|, tilt β, m_NS, sky position, distance, inclination; ensure coverage matching expected detection-weighted priors.
- Include networks HLV, HKLV, HIKLV; use realistic PSDs and calibration envelopes; include multiple epochs if relevant.

1.2 EoS prior with hard constraints.
- Spectral EoS parameterization p(ϕ_EoS) with constraints: causality (c_s ≤ c), thermodynamic stability (dP/dε > 0), M_max ≥ 2.0 M☉, continuity to low-density nuclear-theory constraints.
- Compute derived Λ(m_NS), C(m_NS) with uncertainty propagation.

1.3 NR-fit families and training-domain documentation.
- Curate multiple NR-based fit families κ_NR for (i) disruption criteria/classifier, (ii) ejecta/disk mass fits.
- For each κ_NR, explicitly record training domain bounds in (q, |χ_BH|, β, m_NS, EoS compactness range) and published uncertainties.

1.4 Out-of-distribution (OOD) diagnostics and conservative fallback.
- Implement an OOD score for each posterior sample (e.g., distance to convex hull / density under a normalizing-flow trained on fit-domain coordinates).
- Policy: if OOD probability exceeds a preregistered threshold (e.g., >5% posterior mass OOD), automatically (a) widen NR-fit scatter, (b) downweight disruption-imprint contribution, and (c) revert to baseline GW PE for low-latency products while flagging “extrapolation” status.

Step 2 — Quantify identifiability of the high-frequency disruption imprint before using it.
2.1 Competing hypotheses and nested models.
- H0: no disruption imprint in GW (baseline waveform with tides/precession/higher modes as appropriate).
- H1: disruption imprint present with D-linked spectral modification S(f), including calibrated uncertainty.
Compute Bayes factors B_10 and/or posterior odds for D using reversible-jump MCMC or product-space methods.

2.2 Fisher and injection-based Bayes-factor studies across systematics.
- Vary network (HLV/HKLV/HIKLV), SNR, effective bandwidth, inclination, calibration uncertainty, PSD uncertainty.
- Include waveform systematics: compare κ_wf families that add precession and higher modes; include alternative tidal prescriptions.
- Output: a preregistered “recoverability map” in (SNR, f_high, q, |χ_BH|, β) giving probability of correctly identifying imprint (true positive at fixed false-alarm).

2.3 Explicit activation threshold.
- Define a decision rule for enabling disruption-imprint inference in low latency, e.g.:
  - require network SNR ≥ 25 AND effective bandwidth such that cumulative SNR above 600“800 Hz exceeds a threshold (computed per event), AND Bayes factor ln B_10 ≥ 3 under calibration/PSD-marginalized analysis.
- If threshold not met, enforce imprint-off (H0) and restrict disruption information to prior-level physics (EoS + disruption probability) and/or EM data.

Step 3 — Inference architecture for localization and EM detectability without biasing GW likelihood.
3.1 Two-stage, bias-controlled pipeline.
Stage A (GW-only baseline):
- Perform standard PE with calibration/PSD marginalization; obtain posterior samples over θ_int, θ_ext, ϕ_EoS (if doing EoS-aware priors) under H0.

Stage B (physics-informed reweighting + optional imprint term):
- Reweight GW posterior samples by p(D|θ_int,ϕ_EoS,κ_NR) and (if imprint is activated) by the validated likelihood ratio from H1/H0 computed consistently (not by injecting an ad hoc penalty).
- This “reweighting” does not alter the GW likelihood; it updates the posterior via an explicit hierarchical prior/mixture model.

3.2 EM coupling and counterpart detectability map.
- For each posterior sample, draw (or marginalize) E ~ p(E|D, θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR).
- Generate predicted light curves via RT surrogate family κ_RT and compute detection likelihoods for specific facilities/cadences; incorporate non-detections as censoring constraints.
- Produce sky-pixel products:
  - P_det_EM(Ω) = ∫ P(det | E, d_L, ι, Ω, instrument) p(E, d_L, ι | Ω, d_GW, …) dE dd_L dι.
This yields a ranked detectability sky map over the GW localization region (not merely smaller contours).

3.3 Treatment of distance“inclination and q“spin“EoS degeneracies.
- Quantify when disruption information breaks degeneracies by reporting mutual information / KL divergence between baseline and updated posteriors in {d_L, ι} and {q, χ_BH, C}.
- Report changes in searched volume and in the posterior mass at small d_L (relevant for EM brightness) rather than only 2D sky area.

Step 4 — Preregistered ablations and validation metrics (mandatory).
4.1 Ablation matrix (preregistered).
(A) EoS-constrained priors only: enforce p(ϕ_EoS) constraints; no disruption imprint; EM not used.
(B) Waveform disruption-imprint only: allow H1 vs H0 with identifiability gating; EoS fixed/broad; EM not used.
(C) EM coupling only: baseline GW PE + p(D|…) + p(E|…) + RT surrogate to make detectability maps; no imprint term.
(D) Full model: (A)+(B)+(C) with OOD safeguards.

4.2 Metrics.
- Localization: 2D area (90% credible), 3D volume (90%), “searched volume“time” for follow-up.
- EM follow-up utility: counterpart recovery fraction at fixed telescope time; expected number of unrelated transients followed (false-positive burden) under realistic transient rates.
- Bias checks: coverage tests (credible interval calibration) for sky position, distance, inclination.

4.3 Robustness to systematics.
- Repeat with multiple κ_wf waveform families (including precession/higher modes) and multiple κ_NR and κ_RT families; marginalize over κ indices or report sensitivity.
- Calibration/PSD uncertainty: include nuisance parameters; verify the imprint Bayes factor is not spuriously driven by calibration residuals.

Step 5 — Low-latency implementation with conservative fallbacks.
5.1 Deliverable products within minutes“hours.
- Product 1: standard GW skymap (baseline).
- Product 2: EM detectability skymap computed by rapid reweighting + surrogate evaluation, with flags:
  - “imprint activated: yes/no”,
  - “NR-fit OOD: low/medium/high”,
  - “dominant uncertainty source: calibration/PSD/waveform/NR-fit”.

5.2 Reduced-order acceleration.
- Precompute surrogate tables for p(D|θ_int,ϕ_EoS) and p(E|D,θ_int,ϕ_EoS) with uncertainty; use normalizing-flow emulators for rapid sampling.
- Ensure that when OOD is detected, the pipeline defaults to baseline GW+generic kilonova priors (broad, not NR-fit extrapolation) to avoid overconfident guidance.

Feasibility: Addressing (i) high-frequency over-optimism: The revised plan does not assume the >700 Hz disruption imprint is generically measurable. It is treated as a model selection problem (H1 vs H0) with preregistered activation thresholds derived from Fisher + injection Bayes-factor studies across HLV/HKLV/HIKLV, calibration envelopes, PSD uncertainty, and competing waveform systematics (precession/higher modes/tidal modeling). When the data are not informative, the imprint term is turned off and the method falls back to conservative EoS-consistent priors and/or EM constraints.

Addressing (ii) circularity/double-counting: The proposal now specifies an explicit graphical model with a latent disruption state D and ejecta variables E, and a full joint posterior factorization where NR fits appear only in p(D|…) and p(E|D, …). GW and EM data enter through separate likelihoods p(d_GW|…) and p(d_EM|…), ensuring NR-calibrated relationships are not used twice as independent evidence. Model-index marginalization over NR-fit families κ_NR and RT surrogate families κ_RT further prevents single-fit overconfidence.

Addressing (iii) inference architecture and localization modification: Localization is not “modified” by ad hoc penalties; instead, sky-distance posteriors are updated via hierarchical priors and, only when validated, a properly constructed likelihood ratio between H1/H0. The method reports improvements in 3D searched volume and EM-relevant distance posteriors, and quantifies degeneracy breaking via information gain metrics, avoiding the appearance of merely sharpening by informative priors.

Addressing (iv) NR-fit/emulator domain limitations: The plan explicitly documents training-domain bounds for each NR-fit family and implements out-of-distribution diagnostics with conservative fallback behavior (inflated scatter, downweighted imprint contribution, or reversion to baseline PE). Robustness is validated by repeating analyses across multiple NR-fit families and waveform models including precession and higher modes, with calibration/PSD marginalization.

Empirical grounding and network context: The localization context (e.g., median ~60 deg² with HLV improving to ~11 deg² with HIKLV for NSBH populations) motivates that follow-up success is often limited by 3D volume and counterpart detectability rather than sky area alone. The revised deliverable—ranked EM detectability maps over the GW localization region—directly leverages that network-driven localization improvement while remaining conservative about additional gains from high-frequency disruption signatures.

Step 1 — Data assembly and uniform event representation.

2.1 EOS basis A (preferred): causal spectral representation in terms of adiabatic index Γ(x) or sound speed cs^2(ε) parameterized by unconstrained coefficients θ, mapped through a bijective transform that guarantees: 
  • thermodynamic stability: dP/dε>0; 
  • causality: 0<cs^2<c^2 enforced by logistic map cs^2/c^2 = sigmoid(fθ(ε)); 
  • monotonic P(ε) built by integrating cs^2(ε) with boundary condition at a matching density ε0.
This yields a differentiable mapping θ → P(ε) with a known Jacobian of the transform (included in the prior measure). 
2.2 EOS basis B (fallback/ablation): piecewise-polytrope with differentiable interior barriers instead of projection. Implement soft constraints via log-barrier penalties added to log posterior:
  Lbar = Σk [αc log(1 - cs^2/c^2) + αs log(dP/dε)] + αM log( Mmax(θ)/2.0Msun - 1 )
with α tuned so barrier is inactive away from boundaries but prevents sampling at/over the boundary; ensure differentiability. Compare to basis A to quantify sensitivity.

  • Explicitly compute/track induced prior on (R1.4,Λ1.4) by prior predictive sampling; iterate prior until it is scientifically intended (not an artifact).
2.4 TOV+Love numbers: integrate TOV + tidal perturbation ODEs inside the model using differentiable ODE solvers (adjoint sensitivity) so NUTS gradients are stable. Validate gradients against finite differences for random θ.
