The regularization strength is fixed by requiring that the reconstructed δE(t) does not violate the compactness and optical-depth constraints for radio transparency.
- Nuclear-physics constraint layer: impose hard bounds on the total injected energy (≲ few × 10^52 erg) and injection timescale (≲ 10“100 s source-frame) derived from neutron-to-strange quark matter conversion calculations, while allowing neutron-star engines only continuous, monotonic spin-down“like δE(t). This constitutes a structural modification of afterglow analysis: the data are mapped into an energy-injection impulse response space constrained by EOS physics.
- Population-level comparison: classify events based on whether their reconstructed δE(t) requires an impulsive, super-Eddington component inconsistent with neutron-star spin-down but consistent with strange-star conversion energetics.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
- Consistency checks: forward-model the reconstructed δE(t) through full hydrodynamic simulations to ensure that the inferred impulse reproduces both X-ray and radio behavior, including self-absorption and cooling-break evolution.
- Synthetic tests: inject artificial strange-star“like impulses and neutron-star“like continuous injections into simulated afterglows across redshift and density distributions; quantify the false-positive rate of the inversion method.
- Cross-domain validation: compare the inferred impulse energies and timescales with independent nuclear-physics predictions for quark deconfinement and with observed super-Eddington luminosities in compact objects.
- Statistical assessment: evaluate the fraction of events requiring impulsive injections and test correlations with host environment and redshift to rule out selection or viewing-angle effects.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Relativistic blast-wave theory admits a well-defined causal response to energy perturbations, and strange-star formation is predicted to release a finite latent energy on short timescales. Empirically, several short-GRB afterglows show deviations from simple power-law decay that are not uniquely explained by geometry.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The Green’s-function inversion respects causality, conservation laws, and synchrotron radiation physics, while the nuclear-physics constraint layer directly incorporates EOS-driven limits on energy release—a natural bridge between high-energy astrophysics and dense-matter physics.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike parametric or hierarchical fitting, this approach does not assume an engine model a priori. It isolates a physically interpretable impulse signature that cannot be mimicked by smooth magnetar spin-down or viewing-angle effects, providing a sharper, mechanism-level discriminator between neutron-star and strange-star remnants.

Hypothesis: Phase-resolved optical spectroscopy plus multiband time-series photometry of millisecond-pulsar binaries in NGC 6752 can deliver likelihood-dominated (not prior-dominated) constraints on orbital inclination i, companion filling factor f_RL, companion mass M2 (including discrimination between HeWD and massive CO/ONe WD companions), and neutron-star mass MNS, by jointly fitting (1) a radial-velocity (RV) curve and phase-dependent line profiles that constrain K2, vrot sin i, Teff(phase), and log g, and (2) multiband light curves whose ellipsoidal harmonics and Doppler boosting encode i and f_RL once distance/reddening and atmosphere physics are controlled. The mechanism for breaking the dominant optical degeneracy (i“f_RL“Teff/albedo“distance/reddening“asymmetric heating) is explicit: (a) the RV mass function + rotational broadening ties i and f_RL through vrot sin i ≈ (2πR2/Pb) sin i (with R2 set by Roche geometry and f_RL), thereby converting the usual photometric i“f_RL degeneracy into a constrained geometric problem; (b) WD/MS atmosphere models (composition-dependent) connect the observed SED and line blanketing to Teff and log g, which—combined with cluster distance and reddening hyperparameters—yields a radius R2 estimate and thus a second, independent constraint on f_RL; (c) physically motivated irradiation with controlled asymmetry (wind/shock offset + heat redistribution) explains phase shifts and unequal maxima without resorting to an unconstrained temperature map that would reabsorb inclination information. The neutron-star EoS/TOV coupling is not used to claim direct optical sensitivity to (M,R); instead, EoS inference is restricted to what is supported by likelihood pathways: MNS from timing mass function + optical K2 (+ i from the joint model) and, where available, WD mass from (log g, R2) combined with finite-temperature WD mass“radius relations. A TOV/EoS prior is applied only at the final stage as a consistency filter (causality/max-mass) on the resulting MNS posteriors, unless simulations demonstrate measurable sensitivity to relativistic photometric terms at the achieved precision.
Plan: Step 0 — Target and data audit (NGC 6752-specific).
0.1 Target list: start with PSR J1911−5958A (COM J1911−5958A) as the anchor system (known optical counterpart; inclination already constrained >70° in prior work). Add any additional MSP binaries with published timing solutions and candidate counterparts from HST/VLT deep imaging catalogs; include IMBP candidates (optically brighter, potentially massive WDs) if present.
0.2 Membership and contamination screening: require (i) counterpart proper motion consistent with NGC 6752 (Gaia/HST PM where available), (ii) CMD position consistent with WD/MS companion locus at cluster distance, (iii) systemic velocity consistency with cluster radial velocity within uncertainties. Flag ambiguous cases and model non-membership as a mixture component in the likelihood.

Step 1 — Observing program with quantified requirements (spectroscopy + photometry).
1.1 Spectroscopy requirements (K2, log g, vrot sin i):
- Telescope/instrument class: 8“10 m (e.g., VLT/FORS2 or X-shooter; Gemini/GMOS; Magellan/IMACS for imaging + MagE for spectroscopy), chosen based on counterpart magnitude and crowding.
- Spectral resolving power: baseline R ≈ 6000“10000 (Δv ≈ 30“50 km/s) to recover K2 at ≤5“10 km/s and measure vrot sin i ≳ 30 km/s (or place informative upper limits). For bright IMBP WD counterparts (if V≲22“23), target R ≈ 10000; for faint (V≈23“25), accept R≈6000 with more epochs.
- Phase sampling: ≥12 spectra uniformly spaced in orbital phase for Pb≈8.8 h (PSR J1911−5958A-like), with exposure times capped to limit phase smearing to <0.03 cycles per exposure (Δt < 0.03 Pb ≈ 950 s for Pb=8.8 h). Prefer 18“24 epochs to diagnose asymmetric heating (line strength/Teff variation).
- Per-epoch SNR: design for SNR≈10“15 per resolution element in the continuum (or in key lines) to enable cross-correlation RVs and atmosphere fitting; if only SNR≈5“8 is feasible, prioritize K2 via template cross-correlation and treat log g constraints as weaker with explicit inflation.
- Wavelength coverage: include Balmer lines for DA WDs (Hβ“Hδ region) and He lines for DB/HeWD candidates; include blue-optical (≈380“520 nm) where line diagnostics are strongest, plus red-optical for SED anchoring if possible.

1.2 Photometry requirements (ellipsoidal + color curves under crowding):
- Instrumentation: HST (WFC3/UVIS) preferred for crowding-limited fields; if ground-based, use AO-assisted imagers when possible; otherwise difference-image analysis (DIA) on seeing-limited data.
- Bands: at minimum 3 bands spanning blue-to-red (e.g., U/B, V, I) to constrain Teff and reddening degeneracy; ideally 5 bands (U,B,V,R,I) but not required if spectroscopy provides Teff/log g.
- Cadence: ≥100 phase points per band over ≥2 orbits to average stochastic variability and mitigate systematics. For Pb≈8.8 h, cadence ≈2“5 min (exposure+overhead) is sufficient.
- Photometric precision target: ≤0.01“0.02 mag per point for detecting ellipsoidal harmonics and Doppler boosting at the few percent level; if only 0.03“0.05 mag is achievable, rely more heavily on RV + vrot sin i constraints and report reduced identifiability.
- Cross-epoch calibration: if simultaneous multiband is not feasible, interleave bands with strict barycentric time-stamping and apply nightly zeropoint tying using cluster standards; propagate calibration uncertainty explicitly.

1.3 Crowding/blending mitigation plan:
- Use PSF-fitting photometry (DAOPHOT/DOLPHOT or equivalent) and forced photometry at the timing position.
- Inject-and-recover artificial stars near each target to quantify blending bias and photometric error under local crowding.
- Include a “third-light” (blend flux) parameter per band in the forward model with priors anchored by high-resolution imaging; this prevents inclination bias from unmodeled contamination.

Step 2 — Forward model architecture (explicitly constrained; controlled complexity).
2.1 Orbital and Roche geometry:
- Use exact binary relations for the mass function and Keplerian geometry.
- Companion surface: Roche equipotential with filling factor f_RL ∈ (0.7, 1.0] (or broader if justified by CMD radius constraints).
- Surface brightness includes gravity darkening and limb darkening using atmosphere-specific coefficients (not generic). For convective envelopes (MS-like), allow β≈0.08; for radiative, β≈0.25; for WD companions, treat as radiative.

2.2 Spectroscopic component (likelihood-driving constraints):
- RV model: K2, γ (systemic), phase zero-point tied to radio timing ephemeris with allowed small offset (Gaussian prior from timing uncertainty).
- Rotational broadening: compute vrot sin i from R2 and synchronous rotation assumption; include a parameter for asynchronism (Ω/Ωsync) with tight prior centered on 1 (width set by tidal timescale expectations), to avoid bias if not perfectly locked.
- Atmosphere inference: fit Teff and log g using grids:
  * HeWD grids (He atmosphere; appropriate line diagnostics), DA/DB WD grids, and (if non-degenerate companion is plausible) low-mass MS atmosphere grids.
  * Include composition class as a discrete model with evidences compared (Bayes factors) rather than forcing a single choice.
- Emulator policy: use an interpolator/emulator only as a speed layer; enforce validation by (i) k-fold cross-validation on the grid, (ii) maximum interpolation error budget (e.g., ΔTeff < 1“2%, Δlog g < 0.05“0.1 dex where SNR permits), (iii) explicit nuisance inflation if the target sits near grid edges.

2.3 Photometric component:
- Ellipsoidal modulation computed from Roche geometry + atmosphere limb/gravity darkening; fit per band simultaneously.
- Doppler boosting included with bandpass-dependent beaming factor derived from the fitted SED slope (not assumed constant).
- Extinction: hierarchical E(B−V) model with (i) cluster mean prior, (ii) per-target differential reddening offset, and (iii) residual scatter term constrained by nearby stars.
- Distance: hierarchical distance modulus prior from cluster measurements; allow small depth dispersion for NGC 6752 and propagate to R2.
- Third light: per-band additive flux with informative priors from image decomposition.

2.4 Irradiation and asymmetry model (physically motivated; limited degrees of freedom):
- Base heating: incident flux Finc(θ,φ) ∝ Lirr / (4πa^2) × cosψ, truncated at zero for the nightside.
- Reprocessing efficiency: parameter ε (combining albedo and thermalization) with physically bounded prior ε∈[0,1].
- Heat redistribution: single parameter η controlling day-to-night diffusion (e.g., η=0 no redistribution; η→1 strong smoothing). Implement via a low-order solution of a diffusion/relaxation operator rather than free spherical harmonics, to prevent the map from absorbing inclination.
- Asymmetry from intrabinary shock / wind anisotropy: include one hotspot-offset term: shift the sub-pulsar heating pattern by an angle Δφshock (prior centered near 0 with width informed by typical black-widow/redback offsets), plus an amplitude modifier Ashock. This captures phase shifts and unequal maxima with only 2 extra parameters.
- Optional complexity control: only introduce higher-order asymmetry if posterior predictive checks demand it (Bayesian model comparison).

Step 3 — Identifiability, requirements, and simulation-based error budget (mandatory directive).
3.1 Synthetic data generation (NGC 6752-quality):
- Build end-to-end mock datasets with crowding noise, third-light contamination, differential reddening residuals, and realistic cadence.
- Simulate multiple regimes: (A) HeWD-like companion (Teff~10“20 kK), (B) massive WD companion (CO/ONe; higher log g), (C) MS-like companion (if applicable), across inclinations i=50“85°, filling factors f_RL=0.8“1.0, and plausible ε,η,Δφshock.
- Include instrument-specific throughput and resolution to match the planned setups.

3.2 Parameter identifiability matrix (what the likelihood constrains):
- Run inference on mocks under incremental model stacks:
  S0: photometry-only, phenomenological heating;
  S1: + multiband + extinction/distance hierarchical;
  S2: + RV curve (K2);
  S3: + vrot sin i constraint from line profiles;
  S4: + atmosphere grid constraints on Teff/log g;
  S5: + physically bounded irradiation with η and Δφshock;
  (Optional) S6: + relativistic beaming refinement.
- For each stack, report expected posterior widths (e.g., σi, σMNS, σM2, σf_RL) and mutual information / Bayes factors relative to simpler stacks.
- Define success criteria before observing: e.g., σi ≤ 2“3° and σMNS ≤ 0.1“0.2 Msun for the anchor system under achievable SNR; relaxed goals for fainter targets.

3.3 K2/log g recoverability validation:
- Inject known K2 and vrot sin i into synthetic spectra and test recovery under R and SNR conditions; quantify bias vs. phase smearing and template mismatch.
- For log g, quantify the minimum SNR/R required to distinguish HeWD-like (log g~6“7) from massive WD (log g~8“9) at >3σ, or state explicitly when log g becomes non-identifiable and classification must rely on CMD radius + WD cooling tracks.

3.4 Decision on TOV/EoS coupling:
- Baseline: do not use TOV priors to tighten i or heating parameters.
- Only if simulations show detectable optical sensitivity to relativistic photometric terms at achieved precision (e.g., Doppler boosting detected at >5σ and consistent across bands), consider adding compactness-dependent terms; otherwise restrict EoS inference to mapping the measured MNS distribution to EoS hyperposteriors with causality/max-mass constraints.

Step 4 — Inference and deliverables.
4.1 Bayesian inference engine: HMC/NUTS for continuous parameters; reversible-jump or marginalization for discrete atmosphere class (DA/DB/HeWD/MS). Parameterization uses cos i, log f_RL, and bounded transforms for ε,η.
4.2 Outputs per system:
- i, K2, q, MNS, M2 with full covariance;
- Companion classification probability (HeWD vs massive WD vs other);
- Evidence for irradiation asymmetry (Δφshock) and redistribution (η);
- Blend flux posteriors and quality-of-fit diagnostics.
4.3 Population/cluster-level analysis:
- Hierarchical modeling of distance modulus, reddening field residuals, and a contamination fraction.
- Correlate inferred companion type and system parameters with projected cluster-centric radius to test exchange-encounter predictions.

Step 5 — External benchmarking.
5.1 Validate the pipeline on field eclipsing/high-inclination systems where i is independently known (e.g., eclipsing AMXP-like geometry constraints) by degrading data to NGC 6752 SNR/cadence and confirming unbiased recovery of i and masses.
5.2 Reproduce published results for PSR J1911−5958A-like systems as a sanity check, then demonstrate posterior tightening attributable specifically to adding vrot sin i + atmosphere + controlled-asymmetry irradiation.
Feasibility: Empirical basis and pathway to constraints: Prior optical work on an NGC 6752 MSP companion already demonstrates inclination constraints >70° from RV+photometry; optical detection of IMBP companions shows massive WDs are observable with large telescopes. The revised plan makes the primary information channels explicitly likelihood-driven: K2 provides q through the mass function; vrot sin i + Roche geometry constrains R2 sin i and thus i and f_RL; atmosphere-based Teff/log g + cluster distance/reddening yields R2 and an independent handle on f_RL and WD type; multiband ellipsoidal harmonics and Doppler boosting add inclination leverage once third light and reddening are controlled.

Addressing reviewer doubts about EoS coupling: The proposal no longer claims that neutron-star compactness measurably imprints on the companion’s optical light curve in typical MSP+WD systems. TOV/EoS enters only after obtaining MNS posteriors from timing + optical constraints, as a physically consistent mapping to EoS families (causality/max-mass), unless simulations demonstrate an actual measurable optical pathway at the achieved precision.

Quantified requirements and crowding realism: The observing plan specifies telescope class, resolving power, SNR targets, phase sampling, and phase-smearing limits appropriate to Pb~hours binaries, and it incorporates cluster-specific systematics (crowding/blending, differential reddening, depth) as explicit nuisance parameters with priors informed by artificial-star tests and high-resolution imaging. This prevents under-modeled blending from masquerading as inclination or heating asymmetry.

Controlled irradiation complexity: Instead of an unconstrained spherical-harmonic temperature map, the heating model uses a bounded efficiency ε, a single redistribution parameter η, and a minimal physically motivated asymmetry term (Δφshock, Ashock). Complexity is only increased if demanded by posterior predictive checks, limiting the risk that flexible maps absorb inclination information.

Mandatory identifiability analysis: The plan includes an end-to-end simulation program that will report posterior shrinkage and identifiability under incremental model stacks, demonstrating which parameters are actually constrained for NGC 6752-quality data and defining success/failure criteria before full execution.

Hypothesis: Coherent radio bursts (including nanoshots associated with pulsar Type II emission) are produced when plasmoid mergers in the magnetospheric current sheet just beyond the light cylinder trigger fast-magnetosonic wave packets whose phase coherence is preserved by a reconnection-driven, charge-starved parallel electric field (E||) that also initiates hadron-loading and subsequent secondary-particle cascades. We hypothesize that the joint occurrence and timing of (i) plasmoid-merger electromagnetic precursors and (ii) nuclear/secondary-particle signatures are controlled by a single dimensionless control parameter, \(\Pi \equiv \sigma_{LC}\,\tau_{rec}\,\Omega\) (magnetization at the LC times reconnection timescale times spin), which sets the plasmoid hierarchy and the radiative coherence bandwidth. Methodological adaptation: extend standard PIC reconnection simulations to a physically constrained, multi-species radiation-kinetic PIC framework by (a) embedding a relativistic resistive-force-free (RFF) global magnetosphere solution as a dynamically consistent boundary/driver for local PIC patches across the LC current sheet, and (b) adding a baryon/meson production + decay module implemented as a conservative Monte-Carlo collision operator that enforces exact energy-momentum and charge conservation at each event, enabling self-consistent coupling between reconnection microphysics, coherent radio emission, and Type II-like secondary particle production.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Build a global rotating magnetosphere solution (RFF / GRFFE) for a set of pulsar/magnetar-like parameters spanning \(B_{LC}\), \(\Omega\), and inclination; extract time-dependent boundary fields, currents, and plasma injection prescriptions at and beyond the light cylinder.
1.2 Select observational targets with known coherent bursts (e.g., Crab-like nanoshots; intermittent coherent bursts from radio-quiet/X-ray-bright neutron stars) and compile contemporaneous constraints (spin, \(\dot\nu\), distance, X-ray luminosity). Define prediction metrics: burst energy distribution, nanoshot duration, polarization swings, and phase alignment with high-energy emission.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Patch-based coupled simulation: deploy multiple local PIC domains tiled along the equatorial current sheet beyond the LC, each driven by the global RFF boundary conditions (fields + Poynting flux + injected pair density). Implement a two-way coupling by feeding back coarse-grained effective conductivity/particle loading from PIC to the global model on timescales \(\gtrsim\Omega^{-1}\) while preserving causality (no superluminal information transfer; explicit time-lagged updates).
2.2 Conservative radiation-kinetic extension: augment PIC with (i) curvature/synchrotron radiation reaction for leptons and (ii) a nuclear/secondary module: baryon injection tied to reconnection heating (parameterized initially by an ion fraction \(f_i\) but evolved by local charge-starvation criteria), followed by inelastic p-\(\gamma\) and p-p channels producing mesons; implement meson decay into secondary leptons/photons as a Monte-Carlo operator that exactly conserves 4-momentum and charge per interaction and respects threshold kinematics.
2.3 Coherent emission extraction without black-box assumptions: compute far-field radio emission from the simulated current density \(\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x},t)\) using retarded potentials; isolate fast-magnetosonic wave packets launched by plasmoid mergers and quantify phase coherence via cross-spectral density across the emitting region. Enforce numerical constraints: divergence cleaning for \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0\), charge conservation via current deposition schemes, and resolution studies to ensure plasmoid hierarchy convergence.
2.4 Mechanism tests: deliberately control \(\Pi\) by varying \(\sigma_{LC}\), reconnection rate (via guide field and effective resistivity), and \(\Omega\); quantify how the plasmoid merger rate, secondary-sheet formation, and wave-packet coherence scale with \(\Pi\). Run counterfactual suites: lepton-only vs lepton+ion; suppressed E|| vs self-consistent E||; to isolate the causal role of charge starvation and hadron-loading.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Validation against known Type II emission phenomenology: compare simulated nanoshot duration distributions and GHz-band brightness temperatures to Crab-like constraints; test predicted phase relation between radio nanoshots and high-energy pulses (from simulated curvature/synchrotron emissivity maps folded by rotation).
3.2 Multi-messenger/nuclear physics linkage: compute predicted neutrino spectra and secondary gamma-ray components from meson decay; derive joint constraints on ion fraction \(f_i\) and magnetospheric potential drops consistent with nuclear thresholds. Use these to place bounds on magnetospheric baryon loading that feed back to neutron-star surface composition/EOS inferences (via allowed outflow mass loading and pair multiplicity requirements).
3.3 Uncertainty quantification: perform Bayesian calibration over \(f_i\), injection multiplicity, and reconnection parameters using physically constrained priors (causality, energy budget from spin-down, and charge/current closure). Report posterior predictive distributions for burst rates and energetics, and identify falsifiable signatures: (i) a tight scaling of coherence bandwidth with \(\Pi\); (ii) correlated enhancement of secondary signatures when E||-driven charge starvation is strongest; (iii) polarization angle swings tied to secondary current-sheet formation during plasmoid mergers.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 2 provides first-principles evidence that plasmoid mergers in the current sheet beyond the light cylinder generate coherent radio emission (nanoshots) via fast-magnetosonic waves; Asset 1 establishes that coherent bursts can arise even from historically radio-quiet neutron stars, motivating a mechanism that can switch on intermittently. Reconnection, plasmoid instability, and retarded-potential radiation extraction are mature techniques; radiation-reaction PIC is established; conservative Monte-Carlo collision operators with exact 4-momentum conservation are standard in high-energy transport.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The key limitation of existing PIC studies is incomplete closure between global magnetospheric electrodynamics and local kinetic reconnection, and the omission of nuclear/secondary channels that can become relevant when charge starvation produces large E|| and hadron loading. The proposed RFF-to-PIC patch coupling preserves Maxwell constraints and causal information flow while allowing microphysics to modify effective conductivity and particle loading. The nuclear module is implemented as a conservation-law-preserving operator consistent with threshold kinematics, maintaining strict adherence to physical laws.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with stand-alone local PIC or purely global force-free models, the adapted multi-scale, multi-species framework can (i) predict absolute burst energetics from the spin-down-fed Poynting flux, (ii) generate directly comparable observables (radio waveforms, spectra, polarization) from first principles, and (iii) produce falsifiable multi-messenger correlations (secondary gamma/neutrino components) that constrain magnetospheric baryon loading and, indirectly, neutron-star surface composition/EOS. This turns coherent radio bursts from phenomenological signatures into quantitative probes of magnetospheric current closure and high-energy/nuclear processes near the light cylinder.

Hypothesis: Collapsars are constrained to be a sub-dominant Galactic r-process site (integrated contribution ≤~20% at 90% credibility) because the same engine variables that control (i) neutrino-irradiation and hence the wind electron-fraction Ye(t) distribution (setting lanthanide/actinide production) also control (ii) the accretion power available for disk mass loss and (iii) the jet-driven 56Ni production plus fallback (setting the effective Fe mass retained by the ISM). When these couplings are enforced by lepton-number/energy conservation and causal neutrino-timescale constraints, collapsars occupy a testably tight joint correlation manifold in (Mr, MFe, r-pattern-shape/actinide class) with limited intrinsic scatter set primarily by geometry and fallback. This manifold implies: (a) actinide-capable Ye tails (low-Ye mass fraction) require wind conditions that are dynamically decoupled from the Fe-producing jet/shocked mantle, generating extreme event-level [r/Fe] excursions; (b) the frequency of actinide-boost patterns and the ESS radionuclide ratios (129I/244Pu/247Cm) jointly cap the allowed rate of such events relative to Fe production and ISM mixing. The refined approach overcomes prior degeneracies by (1) pre-registering quantitative emulator accuracy targets on physically measurable engine outputs (not arbitrary yields), (2) demonstrating with a pilot simulation/scaling suite that collapsars cannot span the broad free-yield family without violating neutrino-transport/energetics constraints, and (3) embedding mixing/retention and ESS local-sampling as hierarchical nuisance layers with synthetic-data identifiability tests, preventing these systematics from absorbing the same [Eu/Fe] scatter attributed to Fe“r decoupling.
Plan: Pre-registered identifiability + validation program (mandatory and gating):
0.1 Pre-register (OSF-style) the exact model classes, emulator targets/metrics, synthetic-data tests, and stopping/falsification criteria below; analysis code will lock likelihood and priors before ingesting the full stellar+ESS dataset.
0.2 Gating decision points: (G1) emulator meets predictive targets on held-out simulations; (G2) intrinsic scatter of the collapsar Mr“MFe“pattern manifold is demonstrably narrow enough to be discriminating; (G3) collapsar fraction is identifiable in synthetic recovery under mixing/ESS nuisance mis-specification comparable to UMP/VMP uncertainties. Failure at any gate triggers scope reduction to reporting non-identifiability bounds rather than a decisive upper limit.

Step 1: Data assembly with explicit summaries used in the likelihood
1.1 Stellar sample (UMP/VMP; [Fe/H] ≤ -2.5, plus extension to -1.5 for continuity): homogenize abundances and uncertainties for Eu, Ba, La, Dy, plus Th and U where available; record selection function metadata (survey, S/N, detection limits).
1.2 Construct pattern-shape summary vector y_pat per star using robust, noise-aware ratios (examples; final set pre-registered):
  - R_L2 = log10[(La+Ce+Nd)/(Eu)] (lanthanide vs 2nd-peak proxy)
  - R_A = log10[(Th or U)/Eu] when available; otherwise an actinide-boost class label C_A ∈ {boost, normal, unknown} with probabilistic classification.
  - R_1 = log10[(Sr+Y+Zr)/Eu] where available to test light-r vs main-r coupling.
1.3 ESS radionuclides: compile 129I, 244Pu, 247Cm (and stable anchors where needed) with a likelihood that includes (i) measurement uncertainty, (ii) isolation-time prior family, and (iii) local sampling variance (defined in Step 4).

Step 2: Engine-to-yield emulator with concrete training/validation and target accuracies
2.1 Define the minimal emulator outputs (must be predicted, not treated as free): for each collapsar engine parameter vector θ, emulator returns a joint distribution over ejecta components:
  - Disk-wind: Mwind, plus time-resolved Ye(t) distribution summarized as (i) low-Ye mass fraction f_<0.23, (ii) mean Ye and variance, (iii) entropy s and expansion timescale τ distributions (or their principal components).
  - Jet/shock: 56Ni mass M_Ni (mapped to effective Fe yield MFe after decay), and fallback fraction f_fb (effective retained Fe = (1-f_fb)M_Ni).
  - Correlation structure: Cov(Mwind, f_<0.23, MFe, f_fb) (at minimum a rank-correlation + scatter model).
2.2 Engine parameterization (kept low-dimensional to prevent emulator-as-free-table): θ = {\dot{M}_0, t_acc, a_BH, Φ_B, Z_prog, α_visc, f_out} where:
  - \dot{M}_0 and t_acc parameterize an accretion-rate history \dot{M}(t)=\dot{M}_0 exp(-t/t_acc) (or a two-segment broken exponential; pre-registered choice).
  - a_BH (spin), Φ_B (magnetic flux proxy controlling jet power), Z_prog (metallicity proxy affecting angular momentum loss), α_visc (disk viscosity proxy), f_out (wind mass-loading efficiency).
2.3 Training data generation: hybrid simulation suite with explicit neutrino-treatment calibration.
  (A) Primary suite: axisymmetric GRMHD collapsar-disk simulations with approximate neutrino transport (e.g., leakage/M1) spanning a Latin hypercube in (θ) with N_train ≈ 50“100 runs (feasible scale), each producing time series of neutrino luminosities/mean energies and outflow properties.
  (B) Calibration set: small number (N_cal ≈ 5“10) of higher-fidelity neutrino-transport calculations (where available in-house or from collaborators/literature) used to calibrate a correction map from approximate transport → effective Ye(t) statistics (posterior over calibration parameters).
  (C) Literature-anchored scalings: incorporate published relations linking \dot{M}, a_BH, Φ_B to jet power and Ni synthesis/fallback as priors with uncertainty, not as hard-coded truths.
2.4 Dimensionality reduction: represent Ye(t), s(t), τ(t) distributions by principal components (PCs) of binned histograms over time; emulator predicts PC coefficients plus Mwind, MFe, f_fb. This prevents unconstrained flexibility while retaining physically relevant variation.
2.5 Emulator architecture and uncertainty: multi-output Gaussian Process (or Bayesian neural network with monotonic/positivity constraints) that returns predictive mean + covariance; enforce:
  - Positivity: Mwind, MFe ≥ 0; 0≤Ye≤1.
  - Energy/baryon bookkeeping: Mwind ≤ f_out * M_disk, and integrated wind kinetic+binding energy bounded by accretion power ≈ η \dot{M} c^2 with η(a_BH) prior.
  - Causality prior: Ye evolution timescale cannot be shorter than local dynamical time/light-crossing proxy set by inner disk radius.
2.6 Quantitative predictive targets (pre-registered; emulator must meet on held-out runs):
  - Mwind and MFe: ≤ 0.2 dex RMSE; calibrated predictive intervals with 80% coverage.
  - f_<0.23 (actinide-capable low-Ye tail mass fraction): absolute error ≤ 0.05 and/or ≤ 25% relative, whichever larger; 80% interval coverage.
  - PC reconstruction error for Ye-histograms: ≤ 10% in L1 distance on held-out simulations.
If these targets are not met, collapsar contribution inference is declared non-decisive and reported as sensitivity-limited.

Step 3: Demonstrate and quantify the tight Mr“MFe“pattern manifold (pilot + uncertainty)
3.1 From the emulator outputs, compute r-process ejecta mass Mr via a nuclear-network surrogate mapping (Ye,s,τ)→ yields (Step 5). Track both total Mr and actinide mass proxy M_A (e.g., A≥232 mass).
3.2 Explicit manifold model: fit a probabilistic relation
  log Mr = α0 + αFe log MFe + αY logit(f_<0.23) + ε,
with intrinsic scatter σ_int (hyperparameter) and test whether σ_int is “narrow” enough to be discriminating.
3.3 Pre-registered discriminating criterion: if σ_int(log Mr | MFe, pattern) > 0.6 dex, then collapsars are effectively free-yield at the level relevant for [Eu/Fe] scatter, and the proposal will pivot to reporting that collapsar fraction is not identifiable from abundance scatter alone.
3.4 Geometry/mixing/fallback sensitivity: explicitly propagate uncertainties from jet opening angle, breakout success probability, and fallback distribution by introducing nuisance parameters with priors informed by Ic-BL/hypernova constraints; quantify their contribution to σ_int.

Step 4: GCE + mixing/retention kernel as hierarchical nuisance layers with identifiability tests
4.1 Stochastic event-level GCE: each enrichment event draws (MFe, Mr, pattern summary) from either NSM or collapsar population models; events are injected into gas parcels with a mixing mass M_mix drawn from a kernel.
4.2 Kernel family (hierarchical nuisance): allow multiple plausible kernels for UMP/VMP:
  - K1: lognormal mixing mass with metallicity dependence: log M_mix ∼ N(μ0+μ1[Fe/H], σ_mix)
  - K2: turbulent-diffusion motivated kernel with heavy tails (Student-t in log M_mix)
  - Retention/outflow: a mass-loading factor η_out([Fe/H]) controlling what fraction of ejecta is retained.
4.3 Identifiability safeguard: impose cross-channel constraints that kernels cannot arbitrarily absorb: (i) kernel acts similarly on Fe and r for a given event except for a physically motivated velocity/escape modifier that differs between NSM and collapsar; (ii) kernel hyperparameters are partially anchored by independent constraints on early ISM mixing scales (priors wide but proper).
4.4 Synthetic-data recovery program (mandatory): generate mock catalogs under known truth with:
  - True kernels K1/K2 and mis-specified kernels in inference.
  - Varying collapsar fractions (0%, 10%, 20%, 50%).
  - Survey-like censoring (non-detections of Th/U; Eu detection thresholds).
Success criterion: posterior on collapsar fraction must recover truth within ±0.1 (absolute) for true fractions ≤0.2 under kernel mis-specification; otherwise claims are weakened to upper limits conditional on kernel class.

Step 5: Likelihood mapping from (Ye,s,τ) to pattern summaries with nuclear-physics hyperparameters
5.1 Nuclear-network surrogate: train an emulator of full reaction-network outputs on a grid in (Ye, s, τ) relevant to disk winds, returning elemental yields for Sr“U. Use a physically structured surrogate (e.g., sparse grid + GP residuals) rather than a flexible black box.
5.2 Pattern summary likelihood: for each event draw, compute predicted y_pat and compare to observed stellar y_pat with measurement covariance; incorporate an intrinsic “main-r pattern” scatter term constrained by data (not free per model).
5.3 Actinide-boost classification likelihood: define P(C_A=boost | y_pat, nuclear hyperparameters) using thresholds on Th/Eu (or U/Eu) with probabilistic treatment of non-detections.
5.4 Nuclear uncertainty propagation: introduce hyperparameters for key nuclear inputs (e.g., fission fragment distribution family, β-decay rate scalings in relevant mass region) with priors from nuclear theory ranges; marginalize them jointly with astrophysical parameters. Require that discriminants persist across nuclear-hyperparameter posterior support; otherwise report nuclear-limited degeneracy.

Step 6: ESS radionuclides with explicit local-sampling likelihood
6.1 Model ESS as a local draw from the Galactic event field: the Solar birth cloud samples a finite spatiotemporal neighborhood with volume V_loc and timescale Δt_loc (nuisance with priors).
6.2 For each posterior draw of Galactic event rates/yields, compute the distribution of ESS ratios by Monte Carlo sampling of local events (Poisson counts for NSM/collapsar within V_loc,Δt_loc) plus isolation time t_iso. This yields P(R_ESS | model) rather than a deterministic mapping.
6.3 Isolation-time prior family: test at least two pre-registered prior families (e.g., loguniform vs truncated Gaussian informed by disk formation timescales). Compare Bayes factors marginalized over these priors to avoid overclaiming from a single isolation model.

Step 7: Model comparison, falsification, and deliverables
7.1 Competing models: (A) NSM-only; (B) NSM+collapsar with physical coupling manifold; (C) NSM+collapsar free-yield (diagnostic control only, not for astrophysical interpretation).
7.2 Falsification targets (pre-registered):
  - If the coupled collapsar model predicts an actinide-boost frequency inconsistent with data at >90% posterior predictive discrepancy, collapsar contribution is driven to negligible.
  - If ESS ratios cannot be matched without invoking collapsar fraction >0.2 under all allowed isolation/local-sampling priors, then either (i) model is missing a site, or (ii) nuclear systematics dominate; report explicitly.
7.3 Outputs: posterior upper bound on collapsar r-process fraction with robustness table across kernel families, ESS priors, and nuclear hyperparameters; posterior predictive distribution for Mr“MFe correlation and expected [r/Fe] tail frequency in UMP/VMP stars.
Feasibility: 1) Emulator will not become a flexible yield table because it is constrained and audited against simulation-derived engine outputs with pre-registered quantitative error bars (Mwind, MFe, f_<0.23, Ye-PCs) and physical bookkeeping (energy/lepton-number/casuality). The calibration layer explicitly accounts for approximate neutrino transport bias using a small high-fidelity set, producing a traceable uncertainty budget rather than unconstrained freedom.
2) The proposal directly answers the reviewer concern about whether the Mr“MFe“pattern manifold is genuinely tight by (i) explicitly fitting and reporting intrinsic scatter σ_int and (ii) imposing a pre-registered discriminating threshold (σ_int ≤ 0.6 dex required for decisiveness). This converts the key claim (narrow manifold) into a falsifiable intermediate deliverable before full GCE inference.
3) Mixing/retention and ESS local sampling are treated as hierarchical nuisance layers, and identifiability is demonstrated (or refuted) via synthetic-data recovery under deliberate kernel mis-specification and realistic censoring. This prevents the kernel from silently absorbing [Eu/Fe] scatter and ensures that any inferred collapsar fraction is not an artifact of a chosen mixing model.
4) The mapping from (Ye,s,τ) to pattern-shape and actinide-boost classification is made explicit through a nuclear-network surrogate with nuclear-physics hyperparameters marginalized in the inference. This ensures discrimination is not dominated by an arbitrary surrogate choice and quantifies when nuclear uncertainties weaken the collapsar constraint.
5) The combined constraints are empirically well-matched to the three literature anchors: radionuclide limits on collapsar contribution (Asset 1), age/abundance-pattern evidence for multiple r-process sites and spatial/temporal structure (Asset 2), and Fe-mass vs required r-mass tension for collapsars (Asset 3). The proposal operationalizes these into a single hierarchical framework with explicit validation gates, making the decisive-discrimination claim contingent on measurable intermediate success criteria rather than assumed tight correlations.

Hypothesis: AT 2023vfi“class kilonovae exhibit a late-time (>5“20 d rest-frame) near-infrared (NIR) heating floor set by actinide-chain alpha decays plus spontaneous fission of neutron-rich trans-lead nuclei, producing a dimensionless NIR curvature/decline signature that is quantitatively distinct from any lanthanide-only radioactive heating model once realistic thermalization physics is enforced. This uniqueness arises because (i) alpha- and fission-powered heating have a slower temporal decay index and harder particle energy spectrum than beta-dominated lanthanide decay, leading to measurably different wavelength-dependent thermalization efficiencies and temperature evolution, and (ii) these effects persist under variations in ejecta mass, velocity, geometry, and ionization when nuclear reaction-flow constraints, detailed balance limits, and causality-limited EOS priors restrict the space of physically realizable ejecta conditions. By embedding an explicitly network-anchored nuclear microphysics surrogate—trained on thousands of full r-process trajectories spanning Ye“entropy“expansion histories allowed by numerical relativity—inside a reduced-order, differentiable radiative-transfer forward model, the inference eliminates unphysical degeneracies (e.g., between opacity and heating) that allow lanthanide-only models to masquerade as actinide-rich solutions in unconstrained lightcurve fitting.
Plan: Step 1: Microphysics training set specification and coverage.
1. Nuclear network backbone: Use SkyNet and PRISM r-process network codes as ground truth, cross-validated against WinNet for a subset. Include three nuclear mass models (FRDM2012, Duflo“Zuker, HFB-24) and two fission yield prescriptions (GEF 2016, FREYA-based phenomenology). Spontaneous and beta-delayed fission channels are included explicitly.
2. Trajectory library: Generate ~6,000 thermodynamic trajectories covering Ye ∈ [0.01, 0.35], entropy s ∈ [5, 80] k_B/baryon, and expansion timescale tau ∈ [1, 100] ms, with density“temperature histories drawn from NR-informed ejecta models (dynamical + disk wind) across a causality-limited EOS family (cs ≤ c, Mmax ≥ 2 Msun). Sampling is Latin-hypercube with adaptive refinement in low-Ye regions where actinide production occurs.
3. Outputs stored per trajectory: full isotopic yields (A up to ~280), time-dependent heating separated into beta, alpha, spontaneous fission, neutrino losses, and particle-energy spectra used to compute thermalization efficiencies. Late-time (1“50 d) heating kernels are archived as validated summary statistics.
4. Surrogate architecture: Physics-informed operator network that maps (Ye distribution moments, s, tau, EOS label) → (heating kernels, opacity moments, actinide mass fractions). Hard constraints enforced via stoichiometric null-space parameterization for baryon/charge conservation; soft constraints enforce (n,γ)-(γ,n) equilibrium limits during high-T phases. Uncertain nuclear inputs enter as low-dimensional correction coefficients tied to the mass model and fission yields.
5. Coverage metric: Define a posterior-support coverage score as the Mahalanobis distance between inferred ejecta conditions and the convex hull of training trajectories; inference is restricted to regions with ≥99% surrogate fidelity as validated against withheld network runs.

Step 2: Radiative-transfer forward model and computational tractability.
1. Reduced-order RT: Construct a basis-expansion (POD) reduced-order axisymmetric RT model calibrated against a full Monte Carlo RT code (e.g., POSSIS) over ~1,000 training simulations spanning ejecta masses, velocities, angular structures, and compositions. The ROM reproduces broadband and low-resolution spectral fluxes to <5% error over optical“NIR bands.
2. Differentiability: Implement the ROM in JAX with analytic gradients, enabling HMC/NUTS. Residual model discrepancy is included as a Gaussian process in wavelength“time space, calibrated on RT validation runs.
3. Opacity and heating coupling: Wavelength-dependent opacity moments are computed on-the-fly from surrogate-predicted lanthanide and actinide fractions; multi-channel heating (beta/alpha/fission) is propagated with species-dependent thermalization efficiencies.

Step 3: Identifiability diagnostics and injection“recovery.
1. Define a quantitative diagnostic: the dimensionless NIR curvature statistic C_NIR = [ (d^2 ln L_λ / d(ln t)^2 ) averaged over 1.5“3 μm and t = 7“20 d ], which is insensitive to absolute luminosity scaling and distance errors.
2. Synthetic tests: Perform injection“recovery on mock datasets with realistic photometric noise, host subtraction uncertainty, viewing-angle variation, dust formation parametrizations, and non-LTE ionization perturbations. Compare lanthanide-only vs actinide+fission injections.
3. Model comparison: Pre-register Bayes-factor thresholds (e.g., ln B > 5) for claiming preference of actinide-inclusive models, and perform prior-sensitivity analysis on ejecta mass and opacity priors.

Step 4: Application to data and cross-event validation.
1. Apply the pipeline to AT 2023vfi with GW170817/AT2017gfo used for calibration of RT discrepancy terms.
2. Cross-event transfer: Nuclear correction factors learned from GW170817-class events are held fixed when fitting AT 2023vfi to test universality.
3. Deliverables: Posterior constraints on actinide mass fraction, EOS-linked Ye distributions, and predictions for JWST/ELT late-time NIR spectra.
Feasibility: The proposal addresses reviewer concerns by anchoring the microphysics surrogate to explicit, large-scale r-process network calculations with clearly specified mass models, fission prescriptions, and thousands of Ye“s“tau trajectories covering the physically allowed EOS-conditioned ejecta space. A quantitative coverage metric ensures that inference never extrapolates beyond validated surrogate domains. Identifiability is no longer asserted qualitatively: a dimensionless NIR curvature diagnostic is pre-defined and stress-tested via injection“recovery under realistic radiative-transfer, ionization, dust, geometry, and photometric systematics, directly demonstrating when lanthanide-only models fail. Computational feasibility is ensured by a verified reduced-order, differentiable RT model with calibrated discrepancy, making gradient-based HMC tractable while preserving physical accuracy. Finally, pre-registered Bayesian model-comparison criteria and prior-sensitivity analyses prevent over-claiming uniqueness, yielding a conservative yet powerful framework for determining whether AT 2023vfi-class events synthesize measurable actinide and superheavy nuclei.

Hypothesis: A single microphysical control parameter—time-dependent effective rigidity set by crustal yield plus core phase-transition-driven moment-of-inertia anomalies—simultaneously shapes (i) the waiting-time distribution of impulsive magnetar energy releases and (ii) the degree of one-sided (asymmetric) relativistic ejecta that produces the observed expansion/deceleration in the SGR 1806-20 radio afterglow; the same parameter predicts a population-level spin-evolution “waiting-time pile-up” in accreting Z sources when they traverse a deconfinement critical line. Methodological adaptation: we will modify standard Bayesian hierarchical inference of transient outflows by replacing ad hoc priors/likelihoods with a physics-constrained, piecewise-deterministic state-space model whose latent state evolves under torque balance (for Z sources) and magnetic stress accumulation (for magnetars), but whose jump (burst/flare) hazard and ejecta anisotropy are jointly generated by an EOS- and phase-transition-aware constitutive law that enforces causality, energy-momentum conservation, and TOV-consistent compactness. Mechanism: (1) near a deconfinement transition, dI/dΩ changes sign/steepness, producing a spindown “stall” (enhanced waiting time) in Z sources; (2) the same stiff/soft response of dense matter controls how quickly magnetic/elastic stresses reach yield, setting a non-Poisson (approximately lognormal) waiting-time distribution; (3) once yield occurs, asymmetric slip localized to one hemisphere launches a momentum-imbalanced outflow whose centroid proper motion and anisotropic expansion follow directly from the conserved impulse imparted to the external shock, explaining SGR 1806-20’s 0.26c centroid motion and contemporaneous expansion deceleration.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Compile Z-source timing/spectral tracks for a representative sample (including known Z sources with long-term spin/torque proxies where available), extracting segment-wise torque indicators and constructing empirical “residence time” (waiting time) along the Z track (HB/NB/FB) with uncertainty.
1.2 Compile SGR 1806-20 burst catalog waiting times (including the active 2003“2004 phase) and the 2004 giant flare radio afterglow observables: time series of angular size (major/minor axes), centroid proper motion, flux evolution, polarization fraction/angle.
1.3 Define a family of dense-matter EOS parameterizations that explicitly include/omit a first-order deconfinement transition (e.g., spectral or piecewise-polytrope for hadronic sector + constant-sound-speed quark sector), enforcing: (i) dp/dε <= c^2 (causality), (ii) thermodynamic stability, (iii) TOV maximum mass >= 2 Msun, and (iv) continuity conditions at the transition.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Adaptation A (physics-constrained hazard model): Build a piecewise-deterministic Markov process (PDMP) latent state x(t) = {Ω(t), B(t), σ(t), I(Ω;EOS), Q(t)} where σ is crustal stress proxy and Q indicates proximity to a phase boundary. Between events, evolve deterministically:
- Accreting Z sources: dΩ/dt = [N_acc(Ṁ,Z-state) - N_mag(Ω,B)]/I(Ω;EOS) with I computed from TOV+Hartle-Thorne slow-rotation or calibrated GR fits; include deconfinement-induced I(Ω) nonlinearity.
- Magnetar: dσ/dt = F(B,Ω,thermal state) representing stress accumulation from magnetic field evolution and spin-down.
Events occur with hazard λ(t) = λ0 * exp[g(σ/σ_y(EOS), dI/dΩ, thermal proxy)], where σ_y is EOS-dependent yield threshold (effective rigidity), producing non-Poisson waiting times.
2.2 Adaptation B (impulse-conserving asymmetric outflow module): Replace standard isotropic afterglow fits with an anisotropic thin-shell shock model where the ejecta momentum distribution is expanded in low-order spherical harmonics and truncated to a dipole+quadrupole consistent with observed 2:1 axis ratio. Enforce global energy-momentum conservation: total impulse P_ej and energy E_ej satisfy E_ej >= P_ej^2/(2M_ej) and shock evolution obeys d(M_sw v)/dt = -dP_rad/dt with radiative losses bounded. Couple the dipole amplitude to the same yield variable that sets λ(t): A1 ∝ (localized slip fraction) = h(σ/σ_y).
2.3 Joint hierarchical inference: Fit Z-source residence-time data + magnetar waiting-time series + SGR 1806-20 radio morphology/centroid/polarization using a single hyperparameter set controlling EOS (including transition strength), σ_y(EOS), and mapping coefficients. Use Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with constrained parameter transforms to guarantee causality/TOV constraints; compute I(Ω) and compactness self-consistently per EOS draw.
2.4 Posterior predictive checks targeted to the chain: predict (i) enhanced waiting times/pile-up region for Z sources near the critical line, (ii) lognormal-like waiting-time statistics for SGR bursts with parameter drift during active phase, (iii) synchronized centroid motion + expansion deceleration for the giant flare afterglow when dipole impulse dominates, and (iv) polarization evolution consistent with an elongated, one-sided shock.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Model comparison: Bayes factors / information criteria between (i) no phase transition vs transition EOS families, and (ii) isotropic vs impulse-conserving anisotropic outflow, and (iii) memoryless Poisson hazard vs PDMP hazard.
3.2 Identifiability and robustness: synthetic-data injection studies varying distance, ambient density gradients, and observational cadence to confirm recovery of transition-induced dI/dΩ features and outflow dipole amplitude.
3.3 Physical consistency audits: verify energy budget against observed GF energetics; ensure inferred ejecta mass/energy do not violate magnetar magnetic free energy; ensure inferred Z-source torque histories remain consistent with accretion luminosity bounds.
3.4 Falsifiable predictions: (i) Z sources should cluster in residence time at luminosities/track positions corresponding to Ω where dI/dΩ anomalies occur; (ii) magnetars with stronger inferred anisotropy in radio afterglows should exhibit broader/heavier-tailed waiting-time distributions during active phases; (iii) if future magnetar GFs show smaller centroid motion, the model predicts correspondingly reduced dipole impulse and a measurable shift toward more Poisson-like waiting times.
Feasibility: 1. This directly encodes domain constraints (TOV structure, causality, conservation laws) into the inference architecture, rather than learning black-box correlations.
3. This multi-dataset constraint should sharply reduce degeneracies (e.g., ambient density vs energy vs anisotropy) that limit current inferences.

Hypothesis: Post-flare spectral softening in SGR 1806-20 is produced by a magnetospheric pair-cascade collapse triggered by transient proton injection into closed field lines, which increases the resonant cyclotron scattering (RCS) opacity while simultaneously changing the electrodynamic boundary condition that sets the spin-down torque. We hypothesize that a causality- and EOS-consistent inference of this mechanism becomes possible only if one replaces phenomenological spectral fits and polynomial timing solutions with a single latent-state model in which (i) the RCS transfer operator is computed from charge-separated e± plus ion (proton) distributions constrained by Maxwell + radiation-drag balance, and (ii) the timing model is replaced by a torque-closure relation derived from the same magnetospheric conductivity and open-flux fraction. Methodological adaptation: we will adapt state-space Bayesian filtering (Kalman/particle filtering) used in precision timing into a physically constrained, differentiable magnetar “spectral“torque filter” whose transition model is the discretized, energy-conserving evolution of twist angle and charge density, and whose observation models are Swift XRT count spectra and pulse phase/TOAs. The mechanistic guarantee is that proton mass loading modifies the ion fraction, suppresses pair multiplicity via increased charge screening and enhanced photon down-scattering, yielding a softer X-ray spectrum; the same conductivity change reduces the effective current closure to the open zone, producing a predictable, signed change in ẋν correlated with the softening trajectory.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and data preparation.
1.1 Acquire SGR 1806-20 time-tagged event (TTE) and spectrum products from Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory (XRT) spanning pre-activity, flare aftermath windows, and subsequent decay; incorporate high time-resolution windows when available. Supplement with Chandra/XMM-Newton epochs for cross-calibration of absorption (NH) and baseline spectral components.
1.2 Produce jointly phase-connected TOAs and pulse profiles using a minimal timing solution per contiguous interval (to avoid absorbing torque into high-order polynomials). Quantify red timing noise with a stationary power-law process estimated from off-event segments.
1.3 Construct phase-resolved spectra (coarse phase bins) and phase-averaged spectra with consistent response matrices; explicitly propagate instrument response uncertainties and background.

Step 2: Implement the adapted methodology (physically constrained spectral“torque state-space filter).
2.1 Define latent physical state vector x(t) = { Δφ(t) twist angle, ne±(r,t) pair density proxy, ni(r,t) ion/proton density proxy, Te(t) effective scattering electron temperature, uB(t) magnetospheric energy reservoir, Ω(t) spin frequency } with a low-dimensional radial parametrization (e.g., 2“3 basis functions along closed field lines) so inference is identifiable with Swift data quality.
2.2 Transition model (structural adaptation): discretize a constrained evolution law rather than using generic random walks.
- Enforce energy conservation: duB/dt = -Lx(t) - Pout(t), where Lx is radiative power from RCS + surface thermal emission and Pout accounts for particle escape; both are computed from the same charge distributions.
- Enforce charge/current closure: relate current density J|| to Δφ and conductivity σ(ne±,ni,Te) with a radiation-drag-limited Ohm’s law, ensuring ∇·J=0 on closed lines.
- Proton injection term: ni(t) receives an impulse/decay component representing flare-driven ion loading; its amplitude is bounded by independent mass/energy partition priors informed by radio-nebula energetics (order-of-magnitude constraints only), without assuming the rejected draft’s direct mass-to-opacity mapping.
- Causality/EOS constraint linkage: incorporate a compactness prior (M/R) consistent with causal neutron-star EOS families; compactness enters the light-bending kernel and surface-to-magnetosphere seed photon spectrum, preventing unphysical spectral softening explanations via arbitrary emitting area/temperature.
2.3 Observation model for X-ray spectra: replace a power-law index with a precomputed/differentiable RCS transfer operator.
- Compute the emergent spectrum as a convolution of a surface seed (blackbody + possible hotspot) with an RCS kernel K(E|ne±,ni,Te,B,Δφ), where resonant scattering optical depth and energy redistribution are derived from the charge-separated plasma composition; include proton contribution via ion cyclotron resonance tails and via its effect on pair screening (primary lever is on ne± and the scattering depth).
- Forward-fold through Swift responses to predict counts per channel and per phase bin.
2.4 Observation model for timing: replace polynomial ν,ẋν fits with torque closure.
- Use N(t) = Nff(Ω,B) * g(Δφ, σ), where Nff is the force-free spin-down scaling and g is computed from the inferred conductivity/open-flux fraction; propagate Ω(t) deterministically with this torque plus a red-noise term whose hyperparameters are inferred from quiescence.
- Predict TOAs/pulse phases from Ω(t) with a minimal set of timing parameters (position, binary none) and compare to measured TOAs.
2.5 Inference engine (key adaptation): perform sequential Bayesian inference (Rao-Blackwellized particle filter or unscented Kalman filter with constrained projection) on p(x1:T | spectra, TOAs).
- Constrained projection step enforces: uB ≥ 0, σ ≥ 0, causality/EOS compactness bounds, and global energy budget consistency.
- Output is a time series posterior for latent states and derived quantities: predicted softening rate, torque change, pair multiplicity trajectory, and proton fraction.

Step 3: Validation and analysis.
3.1 Simulation-based calibration: generate synthetic Swift-like spectra/TOAs from known latent trajectories (including proton-injection vs no-proton scenarios) to verify identifiability and unbiased recovery under instrument response and red noise.
3.2 Model comparison: compute Bayes factors / LOO-CV between (A) full spectral“torque filter, (B) filter without proton/ion degree of freedom, (C) filter with free phenomenological spectral index but physical torque, and (D) standard independent analyses. Require that improvements arise from predictive performance on held-out epochs (not merely better in-sample likelihood).
3.3 Mechanism tests: verify predicted sign and lag structure: proton-injection → reduced pair multiplicity → increased RCS depth/energy down-scattering → spectral softening; simultaneously σ change → modified g(Δφ,σ) → measurable change in ẋν. Quantify whether the observed softening and torque change are consistent with a single latent trajectory.
3.4 Nuclear-physics deliverable: translate compactness-constrained posterior on emitting geometry + seed spectrum to limits on M/R within causal EOS families; report which EOS families are excluded when requiring consistency with both spectral evolution and timing-derived torque closure.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Magnetar post-flare softening and pulsed-fraction changes are empirically established for SGR 1806-20 (post-2004 giant flare). Magnetospheric RCS is the standard physical mechanism for shaping magnetar X-ray spectra, and force-free/finite-conductivity prescriptions exist for linking magnetospheric state to spin-down torque. Independent evidence for substantial baryonic ejecta in the 2004 event motivates an ion-injection degree of freedom, but the proposal tests it quantitatively rather than assuming it.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): State-space filtering is mature in pulsar timing, but here it is structurally adapted so the latent evolution is not a generic stochastic process: it is a discretized, constraint-projected magnetospheric energy/charge evolution that obeys conservation laws, positivity, and causal EOS compactness bounds. The same latent state generates both Swift X-ray spectra (forward-folded counts) and TOAs (via torque closure), ensuring physical consistency without a black-box correlator.
3. Comparative Advantage: Standard approaches either (i) fit spectra phenomenologically and interpret after the fact, or (ii) absorb torque variability into high-order timing noise, preventing mechanistic attribution. The proposed constrained spectral“torque filter yields (a) time-resolved posteriors for twist, pair multiplicity, and proton fraction with quantified uncertainties, (b) falsifiable lag/phase predictions connecting softening and ẋν, and (c) EOS-relevant compactness constraints anchored jointly by radiative transfer and timing electrodynamics, improving robustness against degeneracies in spectral fitting alone.
